This game goes to show that a tiny, one-man dev studio can create a more interesting, engaging, addictive, and deep game than companies with budgets in the tens of millions.
The graphics are really pleasant to look at -- kind of a memory of a simpler time in computer gaming, but with a really modern feel. The gameplay is EXTREMELY accessible -- it's a sort of buffet where you can attempt to manage as many elements as you feel comfortable with. The game doesn't force anything on you.
I felt comfortable as a new player learning the basics, doing contracts and attempting my first few (failed) software projects.
I still feel the exact same way now that I'm trying some of the deeper or more complex features of the game -- project management, strategically picking outsourcing jobs to affect competitors and stock prices, renting out my hosting infrastructure, and building large office towers.
I can't recommend this game enough. It's the perfect sweet spot between realism, sandbox simulation, and super-fun management gameplay, without ever getting formulaic, boring, or repetitive. There's no "right answer" -- just a fun sandbox simulation about building a tech company.

Having played most dev games around, I have to say this game is really worth the purchase. It is probably not revolutionary in the genre, but it adds a few elements and it offers a very enjoyable gameplay. The "build" mode is great fun and definitely a big plus, Software Inc. also introduces a nice automation system (Project Management) that none of its competitors has. I think tycoon games always need good automation systems if you don't want to go insane with micro-management in late game! It is not an easy game and has a relatively steep learning curve, which is a plus for me, but others might not feel the same way. Even in pre-release, it is very playable and you can even forget it is an incomplete game (very rare thing for a pre-release!). I hope the developer keeps on building on the huge potential this game has, but I warmly recommend it even as it is to anyone who loves complex simulation games with a bit of challange in it!

Now I have to admit when I first started playing this game I had quite low expectations of it. I absolutely love rhythm games but I couldnt see how they could successfully combine this into a RPG style. Although I was proved wrong as this game is AMAZING!!
The mechanics of the game are very unique and there is nothing quite like it. You use the rhythm of the music to fight a battle. To this you use the arrow keys and click them as soon as the arrow reaches the bottom of the screen. And this is when it gets unique. You have 3 fields to control via this rhythm ability. Mana, Attack and Defense. Mana is collected and can be used to cast spells in the attack field. You can switch through these fields at your free will. You need to make sure that you use each field correctly and at the right time to survive and win the battle.
The story of this game is what most suprised me. It had me hooked throughout the entire thing. There are many twists in the story that keep you guessing throughout the game. The voice is acting is very well done and the characters are very likable. You really do get to know the characters. In a rhythm game a gripping story is the last thing I would have expected. I am not going to go into detail about the story but just experience it for yourself and you will see how great it is.
The whole look of the game is completely incredible. The art style gives a real great look to the game that compliments the awesome gameplay.
Throughout the floors you get different items. You have collect these items through playing the levels. I felt the items abilitys were very well balanced and contributed well to the gameplay. These items are obtained through a random drop rate on levels. Some items have a very low drop rate on levels later on the game. Unfortunetely this is where my only bad point comes from this game. To get these items it can become very grindy with you having to repeat these levels multiple times in a row just to get it. This can get very boring after a while.
I'll end this review with the best part of the game, the soundtrack. It is made of music by Ronald Jenkees and Michael Wade Hamilton. I always feel that a game has a great soundtrack when I like it so much that I even listen to it outside of the game itself, and with this one I did. It is incredible and goes great with a rhythm game.
Overall this game is a true masterpiece and a bit of a hidden gem. This game is possibly one of the best I have ever played and I really highly recommend it.

Dying light is Techland’s 2015 spiritual successor to their previously-developed series Dead Island. Although the game shares many similarities with Dead Island such as levelled loot, level-ups, skill trees, co-op, and character progression, it’s still worth purchasing this game for its many new features and the innovative, but sometimes clunky, parkour mechanics. In 2016 Techland released one expansion titled “The Following” as well as the free DLC “Parkour Fever” and another paid DLC titled “The Bozak Horde” beforehand.The game, as of the time of this review, is still getting new content made by Techland themselves. So let’s see how this game holds up 2 years after release and if the mixed reception at launch is still true
In Dying Light, you play as Kyle Crane, a man hired by the fictional GRE to track down sensitive files stolen by one of their own operatives in the city of Harran, based off of modern-day Istanbul, Turkey. Without spoiling much, let’s just say that things quickly turn sour and you end up as an errand boy at one of the remaining strongholds in the area to gain their trust and track down the aforementioned rogue operative.
The setting of Harran itself is a great contrast from most modern zombie games which take place wealthy countries with plenty of firearms to go around and sturdy housing to holdout in. Instead, much of Dying Light’s first act takes place in the slums with poorly-paved roads, poorly-built housing with wooden awnings that you could potentially fall through with one wrong jump, and plenty of clustered buildings to jump between. The game’s second act, one that I won’t spoil much of, is a city with more modern-looking buildings with cables linking from one building to the next and ziplines hanging from towers and other tall buildings which contrasts nicely with the first act’s shanties and cramped alleyways.
Dying Light’s gameplay is very similar to the previous Dead Island titles but with more polish and the addition of parkour and a true open world as well as a day and night cycle that affects gameplay dramatically. During the night, zombies become stronger and a new zombie, the Volatile is added to mix but you are given an incentive to play during the night by the doubled XP gains.. The Volatiles provide a great early game threat as inexperienced players will rush to safe areas dotted about the two areas in the game during the evening hours to avoid unnecessary confrontation with these enemies whilst more experienced ones will use this time to level up faster. In addition to the standard zombie and Volatile, Dying Light also has 5 other zombie types which I’ll keep a secret as to not spoil the experience.
Let’s now address the feature that was advertised the most in Dying Light aside from the nighttime mechanics - the parkour. While the game’s parkour feels spotty at times with the player character sometimes launching himself off of walls with one wrong button press, the system does work most of the time and ends up being one of the most satisfying movement systems I’ve personally experienced in gaming, even more than other games with parkour mechanics such as Mirror’s Edge and, to an extent, Assassin’s Creed. As the player progresses through the game and levels up, he can unlock more parkour moves such as a slide, the ability to roll before hitting the ground to negate fall damage, and a brief wall-climbing ability as well as much more.
The combat system, on the other hand, has only seen polish and new features since Dead Island. Dying Light’s combat system allows you to break a zombie’s bones, cut them into pieces with bladed weapons, blow them up with homemade grenades, set them on fire with molotovs, swing your two-handed weapons around in a circle around you to kill off the horde surrounding you, and, like I said before, much more.
Dead Island’s weapon modification system returns with even more ways to modify the game’s arsenal of baseball bats, katanas, Egyptian swords, cricket bats, wrenches, machetes, pickaxes, etcetera, with electricity, fire, nails, and even toxins if you so desire. Though, sadly, gun modifications like those found in Dead Island do not return.
Dying Light’s Chrome Engine 6 provides stunning displays of graphical fidelity and beauty despite the supposed downgrades given to the game as well as the orange filter and film grain added over everything. Weapons will get bloody and broken with use, zombies’ bodies will become damaged as you fight them, and occasionally heads will explode when a bullet passes through them making the game’s gore and weapon durability system responsive and detailed.
In summary, Dying Light is an experience you should pay the 60 USD or whatever your country’s equivalent may be. Who will love this game? Fans of Dead Island,Horror, and zombies in general. Who will hate this game? Those who are easily motion sick, tired of zombies, or those who strongly disliked Dead Island.

Nevermind the length of this game because it is absolutely one of the most beautiful games you will ever play. Memorable, atmospheric, and hauntingly immersive at every turn of the game. Many will call this a straight-forward "walking simulator" and for the most part it is just that. Throughout the game you play as a detective named Paul Prospero who investigates into the disappearance of a young boy named Ethan Carter. Without spoiling a single thing, you pick up pieces of what may have happened to him by solving murders throughout the valley of Red Creek. In order to solve these murders you must figure out in which order the individual murders took place by identifying clues and placing them in the correct order. It may sound simplistic but you must use logic and careful inspection of the area in order to successfully figure out what happened for each murder. Other than the murders to investigate, the game boasts one of the most photo-realistic graphics I have ever seen. Just strolling through the area is breath-taking and convinces you that you are in a real place. The draw of the game in general is the story and its ending, which not only sums up the game neatly but also makes your head spin. This game sets a very high standard for any so called "walking simulator" because it is able to completely immerse you throughout its length. In conclusion, I highly recommend you buy this game, if not only just to screenshot a part of the game’s landscape!

Many have called The Vanishing of Ethan Carter a walking simulator and I can't really argue with that. I am, however, entirely OK with it. It's an impactful, atmospheric experience to hike through this painterly landscape with events going on around you that regularly blur the line between the supernatural and the mundane. The violence in this game is, in fact, more affecting since you as the player never swing a sword or fire a gun.
Puzzles await you at numerous locations in the valley. They use simple mechanics, mostly to good effect. This game isn't trying to be a full on puzzle game, there aren't enough puzzles for that, but what's there generally does a good job of keeping you thinking and feeling involved. A few of them did frustrate me though. Keeping things vague, there was an instance where the missing piece that I needed was a smallish object on the ground that I didn't realize I could pick up until it was highlighted as I stumbled over it. Another case left me unsure where to go when a small drop in water level opened up a new path that wasn't sufficiently obvious.
Clocking in at five hours for a thorough, 100% completion playthrough, this game's biggest weakness is that the journey ends too soon. I switched from the Redux version to the original for a second time through and this time finished everything in 110 minutes. I noticed little difference between the two versions. No change in the story or puzzles and the visuals were about the same. The save system in Redux is superior and the default camera movement controls were also preferable in Redux. Unfortunately, with the mysteries of the story unraveled, my second go-round lost much of the magic. There isn't much replay value here unless you just want to look at the scenery, which may very well be worthwhile in VR, but I can't comment on that from personal experience.

King Arthur's Gold is a brilliant take on a 2-D side scrolling Multiplayer Action game. With four different game modes and plenty of maps, this game is a good purchase. The game is very simplistic while staying complex at the same time.  There are three classes to choose from which can be changed at any time. First we have the builder who is the ideal class for CTF. A builder's objective is to collect resources and use them to build structures. These can range from simple towers, to elaborate spike/boulder traps. Builders also create workshops which benefit their team and are almost needed for a team to be successful. Next we have knights, truly a storm the gates kind of class. They have the most health and have a shield which can be used to slow fall and skid across the ground. Shields are ideal for blocking archer's attacks and even close courter encounters. The knights can charge their standard ability to do a devastating double attack flinging them forward. Knights can purchase bombs and other explosive devices from a workshop with gold earned from kills. Buying the most expensive raid device, the keg, is the best for clearing a large enemy structure. Though carrying a keg eliminates the use of the sword. The final class is the mobile yet strong archer. Archers can use their secondary to grapple and fling around allowing for great mobility. They’re standard arrow attack can be charged to fire three consecutive arrows. Multiple kinds of arrows can be purchased from the archer workshop as well. These can be used in different scenarios. Overall the classes are a core part of the game and make the game play well. I would rate this game a 9/10 and would highly recommend playing it with friends.

I always had a certain fondness for tower defense. In StarCraft, I'd spend more time stacking cannons than playing the ladder, and Team Fortress 2's MvM mode reveals a certain primal fun of killing tons of heartless, unfeeling dudes. To that end, Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten presents a well-rounded, core dude-killing experience, but the cracks in the polish are evident.
You're given six classes to play, all fairly standard for the genre: heavy damage, light damage, healer, ranged, status effects, and tank. Upgrade trees for each class are fleshed out for the game's length, and most powers are distinct from the moment you first receive them. Leveling up your characters before and during battle using "Psi" adds a certain urgency to the fight, and doesn't feel forced.
But between battles there exists some friction between the player and the imperfect interface. Between the fast-forward of battle and the clunky number-comparison engine to power up your party, you'll be wishing for a patch to streamline or automate the process. You could do worse but you could do better; not even trendy not-loading-but-loading-messages like 'reticulating splines' or 'powering up the thermal core' are to be seen. You might hope to find some solace in the story, but it's just as hacked-on as the interface and I couldn't be bothered to follow it.
My first playthrough entailed of spamming rangers (long-range) with the range upgrade and blew through the game without breaking a sweat, but in Hero Mode, where you limit yourself to one of each class, is where the game's difficulty felt most appropriate. Oftentimes you'll have three or four spawn points to deal with, and you'll need to consider the most optimal placement to cover all your bases, evoking the puzzle modes of yore.
All in all I'm giving this a weak recommendation. The game itself is pretty solid - gameplay is mostly balanced, and it can be as hard as you want it to be. The lore isn't engaging and you won't miss much from skipping it; on the other hand, if you're the type for a story maybe tower defense wasn't going to be your cup of tea anyway. If it goes on sale again for 90% off you'll get a fun one-off to pick up and play, not unlike something you'd find on a phone or tablet. Otherwise, you may feel you aren't getting enough bang for your buck.

This game has a lot of potential and is quite playable right now. At present, however, it requires a lot of micromanagement which can be really tedious if you’re running a larger company.
I fully recommend it and the dev is quite active so it’s good to support him, but I hope that they will add some really necessary quality of life features such as an automation of smaller projects or better teamwork inside your teams without the need to assign dozens of rooms to small teams. I will elaborate futher in this review.
1. The way you’re designing programs - it allows a very deep level of customization as the mods clearly show.
2. Mods - even now there are quite a few great mods that add a nice variety of features - new programs, new scenarios, and new furniture (you can even build a full bathroom thanks to them, not just the vanilla “poop machine”).
3. The team chemistry and different characteristics of your employees show promise and already allow you to have many different types of people in your company, some of which are easier to deal with, and some can really be a pain in the neck.
4. The game simulates the market up until the moment you start your own business, meaning that there are many different programs and established corporations for you to compete with. It is a bit rudimentary as the whole world is treated as a one, huge market, but it’s ok. Although I really hope that in the future they will realistically simulate how market kept changing and globalizing - largely local in the 80s but global in the 90s and 00s,
5. The 80s - my favorite era of software development, full of pioneers and experiments. Not that many games include it and that’s a shame,
6, Outsourcing - you don’t have to design everything yourself. You can make some good money working for someone else.
7. Marketing, press releases, release dates, announcements, ads - it’s all done pretty well but it’s weird that you can only buy ads AFTER the release (not counting press builds and announcements).
1. Individual skills - your employees must be the best in everything or the quality will suffer. You can’t have an algorithm expert who would be average with system stuff - he would lower the quality significantly. I think that the game should not let someone with poor skills in a certain area to do what he’s not good at. If he can, great, but you should be able to set a minimal level for each employee to contribute to each field - an algorithm expert who can’t do much else should do just that, and not endanger the whole project.
2. Less micromanagement, Teams are a very good addition but you really need to create a lot of them. Artists are the worst - you usually require less art units than code ones and so artists finish the job sooner. If they’re in the same team as the programmers, you can’t just order them to stop and do something else. Not really a problem yet, but as teams shouldn’t share a room, you require a lot of smaller rooms which can get tedious - if a project requires 2 artists and you have 4 in your team, it will be finished slowly, the same when you have a 4 artists team and 2 projects that require 2 each. It's much better to create 2 separate teams but then you also need 2 rooms. Also, this screws up your leaders - instead of having one lead to help a larger group of maybe 10 employees, you need one to nanny 2 artists while the other handles 8 programmers and designers. Also, when you’re taking on several small project that someone outsources, you have to keep checking the progress - it won’t end automatically, and won’t even move to beta once all the required units of code are done.
3. Ability to rent offices in a larger building and move to a new building. Or repurpose an old warehouse.
4. I would really love a dev support for somewhat realistic scenarios - like making sure that company A will produce X consoles in 1990 no matter what, while Microsoft will outclass non-human opponents like in real-life, which could then lead to great real-world mods,
5. Recommended employees - this one needs some overhaul. I understand that with coding you can’t really hire 50 programmers when you really need 5 and expect they’ll do it 10 times faster, and this could even lead to chaos, meaning that it would take even longer. That’s fine, although hiring 6 when 5 are recommended could speed things up, while in the game it only slowers it. Seemingly even if the programmer is currently training and not physically in the company, bothering no one. Artists, however, don’t work this way - they have certain bits to do, and do them, the smaller they are the faster they tend to do them. Hiring 3 artists when 1 is recommended should speed things up. Maybe not 3 times faster, but perhaps twice as fast.
6. Reputation - it seems like it’s as hard to build a reputation in the 80s as it is in the 2010s. It requires a lot of great releases to become noticed. I think that this should be somewhat overhauled, along with the market percentages I mentioned before. Currently there are only several workflow programs on the market and they already dominate it in the 1980, while there should be many less common ones instead and so if a company develops a truly outstanding product when the market is not yet saturated, that company should become a lot more famous than a company that develops a great CAD program today when there are a lot of those already, some for quite a long time. The same with new programs - it was easier to create a Spotify when there were no companies as large as Spotify today, than it would have been now. In 1980 most program types were new and there were no truly dominant companies yet and the game should reflect that.
7. The building designing part is qute cool but not perfect. It suffers from some poor design choices - you can’t for example build a room inside a room - consequently you can’t build a big rectangle and then add the rooms and if you do so, you’re kinda screwed.
Anyway, those are issues I can understand since it’s only Early Access. The game seems to be moving in a good direction and those shouldn’t leave an impression that this game is bad - it is definitely not.

This game is excellent. Normally, RPGs and music games both face issues, but I can't readily see them in this title. It took the gameplay of Rockband: Unplugged for the PSP and made it actually functional, and into an intuitive battle system. The RPG elements, with the ability to gain and lose levels as you spend time bettering your character, made character building interesting and every upgrade felt impactful. The voice acting was well done too, though similarly with There Came an Echo the character development was not endearing, focused too much on antagonistic dialouge rather than meaningful trait building. Still, however, you can skip these scenes so you can get away from that as much as possible.
The game itself, I'll warn, has little replay value. There's no software to add custom tracks like in Audiosurf, the music gets used on multiple levels and, given you are grinding, you get to hear the songs over and over again. If the music was bad, this would have been worse of an issue but I can't honestly say that the songs were terrible and didn't go so far as to play abrasive music from Dubstep, etc. Other things I'd change would be additions of things like local PvP, clearer labeling on the spell circle to tell which spell was which and what numbers corresponded to which slice of the circle, and more than seven levels/three battle senarios per level.
All in all it is a fun game. For 5$, it has about as much content as you'd expect and with as polished as it looks, sounds, and feels I can't recommend it enough.

Games like Sequence are the reason Kickstarter and the Indie Game movement exist. It's not a perfect game, not everyone is going to enjoy it and it will never receive a lot of fame and recognition. However, for the niche audience that can appreciate it, Sequence is a game like no other.
The closest thing I can relate Sequence to is Puzzle Quest. The game doesn't play like Puzzle Quest but what that game did for Match-3 games, Sequence does for the rhythm genre. The base game has you traveling up a tower by fighting enemies, collecting their dropped items, and synthesising items such as keys, weapons and armor. Battles give you experience which will level up your stats while armor and weapons are equipable and can also improve your abilities.
Where Sequence differs from the average dungeon crawler is that combat is played out by putting you in a rhythm system similar to StepMania, if you're using a keyboard, but with three separate boards. One board is defensive, one board is for building mana and one is for casting spells. On the first board, any notes that you miss will count as damage against you so catching them defends your HP. The second board will have a constant stream of notes. Missing them doesn't hurt you but catching them restores your mana which you need to cast spells. The last board stays dormant until you cast spells, the only way to damage your opponents. When you cast a spell, it takes mana and makes you complete a short rhythm sequence. Failing it causes the spell to fail but completing it will cast that spell. While it can be a lot to juggle at once, the game does a great job of teaching you and ramping up the difficulty slowly in order to build your skills both in game and out.
The gameplay by itself is fun for a while but as the entire game is built around grinding items and EXP, it would get boring very quickly if it weren't for the well written story pushing players forward. The tone reminded me of The World Ends With You in the best possible way, but felt wholy unique. Your main character finds himself waking up in a tower with no idea how he got there. The voice of a girl named Naia tells you that you are stuck in this tower/game and you will need to make your way up 7 floors to escape so off you go. While there are some predictable moments, the story as a whole never becomes too transparent and despite a few moments when I swore I was done after one more battle, curiosity kept me pushing ever forward. The characters are all voiced as well and while none are particularly mind-blowing, it's a nice touch and the quality stayed consistent throughout. If you do find your bar set particularly high in regards to VO quality, they do have an option to turn it off as well although I doubt this will be necessary for most people.
That's not to say the game isn't without it's rough spots. For a music-based game, Sequence has a surprisingly limited soundtrack of only about 10 songs that show up in battle. This means several monsters will have you playing the same songs repeatedly. Thankfully, they aren't bad and some of them I didn't mind repeating but considering each monster all but requires multiple playthroughs anyway, don't be surprised if you wind up hearing the same song 10+ times. As that suggests too, the gameplay is simply too grindy and while item drops are pretty common, it can be irritating when you need one specific item and have to fight the same monster over and over just to move forward. Finally, the song balance is a bit odd as by the end of the game, the length of the song decided more battles for me than my HP did. It felt like very artificial difficulty (you lose if the song ends before killing the enemy) and it would have been nicer to have some of the songs be just a bit longer, especially in Floor 7. Depending on your strategy, you may not have a problem with this but it showed up several times in my game.
Overall, if you're looking for something different and enjoy music gameplay, Sequence is worth a shot.

Been playing CIV since CIV I.  I like each new version for different reasons.  This is the most radically different with the hex based map and single unit per hex.  It took a while to get the hang of it, but I now prefer it to Civ IV which I had the most hours on.

Bring your civilization, turn by turn, from the Dawn of Time to the Space Age. In a standard game, on a map composed of hexagons that hold different terrains, like impassable mountains, hills, jungles, plains and rivers, you start with a settler and a warrior unit. You select a good spot to found your first city and explore the map, fight off Barbarians, make friends with City States, and found new cities to get access to strategic resources.
Climbing the extensive tech tree allows you get better units, buildings, the ability to build improvements on the map like roads, mines, plantations etc. You might want to invest a large number of turns on the construction of a unique World Wonder, which provides you with permanent benefits or built up your army and take your neighbors world wonder containing city. The pacing of the game is such that new units and abilities, wonders and building are not overwhelming.
Sooner or later you will make contact with other civilizations, engage in diplomacy and warfare. All the while keeping an eye on the happiness of your population and your gold income per turn.
There are a number of paths to victory. For the peaceful citybuilder a diplomatic or cultural victory seems the way to go, for the more bellicose taking over all other civilizations capital will result in a conquest victory, for the studious a space victory when completing construction of a spaceship.
TL:DR
One of my all time favorite games! With excellent workshop mods and community patches this game provides a lot of replayability.

Metro 2033 takes place almost entirely in the Russian subway system (the Metro) post nuclear apocalypse. Designed as a massive, labyrinthian fallout shelter, the survivors of a war long past have built a ramshackle society in the tunnels, each station developing it's own personality, laws, and politics. Life is tough in the dark and filthy catacombs; crumbling infrastructure, limited or no electricity, scarce resources, disease runs rampant, radiation hot spots, clashing ideologies have lead to eternal war between certain stations, and to top things off there are mutant, ratlike creatures roaming the tracks, attacking travelers and trying to breach the outposts. Then a new threat emerges: the dark ones. Lanky, humanoid beings that attack a victim's mind, driving them mad may spell the end of the Metro and civilization altogether. You play Artyom, a young man tasked with executing a plan to stop the dark ones and save what's left of humanity.
 
   Based on the novel by Dmitry Glukhovsky, Metro 2033 is the gold standard of linear storytelling in video games. Granted, the subway setting makes it easy to usher the player down the tracks on rails (literally), but 4A Games manages to tell a dense, multi-layered story full of moral ambiguity, political intrigue, and excitement while offering enough variety and player control that it seems perfectly paced. There's downtime when there needs to be downtime, the combat can get oppressively tense, there's so much ambient dialogue that it oftentimes runs together, letting you pick up on so many small details after multiple playthroughs. If this were a movie, it would be the template for how to properly edit a film. It's also a template for how to properly adapt a three hundred page novel into a video game.
 
  You never step out of Artyom's shoes, to the point the game is almost an Artyom simulator. You can pull up a notebook and a compass to guide you in a general direction, a lighter to see in the dark and burn away the many cobwebs that will slow your movement, an electric light that drains over time, requiring you to manually crank the portable generator (which leaves you vulnerable to attacks). There are air powered weapons like a BB gun that need to be pumped up for maximum velocity, the pressure leaking over time. When you venture out of the Metro or in certain toxic sections underground, you need to equip a gas mask to breathe, and the air filters need to be swapped out periodically. Take damage while wearing a mask and it will start to crack, obscuring your vision before it breaks completely and you have to scavenge a fresh one. Blood, grime, and various other liquids can also be wiped from the mask with a push of a button. This fiddly survival plate spinning could be obnoxious if handled poorly, but in Metro 2033 they are core mechanics that make the game.
 
  Like the rest of the game, combat is up close, deadly, and dirty. Mutants viciously attack in numbers, climbing the walls and using vents in the ceiling and holes in the ground to flank you. Your weapons are cobbled together pieces of junk, firing either homemade ammunition of questionable effectiveness or prewar bullets... that also act as your currency. So you have to make the decision to either spray and pray and hope for the best, or literally shoot your money away. Human enemies can either be easier to deal with or an overwhelming force depending on how patient you are. Sneaking through a Nazi or Commie stronghold undetected is ideal, taking advantage of the shadows and snuffing out lanterns to remain hidden. Inevitably♥♥♥♥♥♥will hit the fan, though, and the soldiers can be downright brutal, hiding behind cover and blinding you with headlamps while you pick apart their armor piece by piece.
 
  The lighting in particular is gorgeous in Metro 2033. In a game that's not afraid to throw the player in the dark, the different lighting effects cast by so many variations of light sources and fires and glowing mushrooms is astonishing. The game looks great overall, too, with only the human faces looking a little waxy and unintentionally disturbing. Granted, the “Redux” version is a remaster, but nothing else quite looks like a Metro game. Probably because 4A Games made their own engine specifically for them, they stand on their own, and they are beautifully grim.
 
  Metro may look like just another post apocalyptic shooter, but there is so much more here. The fiction, the survival mechanics, and the deadly serious but somber and science fiction tone are all wholly unique. This is how you tell a story.

With rich and luxurious graphics and a believable and densely built city this game is simply gorgeous to run about in. The story is good enough to be followed and aside from a few (apparently) timed missions you are mostly left to your own devices in terms of what and when you choose to do.
Getting around the map is all about parkour. Running, jumping and climbing across the rooftops, sprinting across roads and around zombies in order to climb another wall, to get to another roof…
Its brilliant. The entire climbing thing is dealt with very well, and is fairly forgiving if you can keep the jump button pumped. Your character will make some great leaps and scramble up walls in order to stay on the roofs and as you progress your climbing and jumping ability increases until you are capable of some spectacular acrobatics at high speed across the whole city, avoiding most of the zombies in the process.
The zombies are, well, zombies. Mostly shambling things, but with a few that will suddenly surprise you with quick movements. There are also much faster and more aggressive zombies that tend to appear in response to loud noises - still quite killable but they tend to bring along lots more zombies with their own screaming and raving, so care has to be taken to make sure you don’t get backed into a corner..
For the most part the ambience of the city is excellent, with a constant background barrage of zombies groaning and shrieking, and it is extremely good fun to rampage through it all, hacking zombies to bits in the process. There are tense moments when you misjudge a jump and land on top of a group of zombies, but for the most part it is possible to hack your way out and to (relative) safety.
And then comes the night…
If the ambience during the day is excellent, the ambience of the night is stupendous. From the moment the sun begins to set, while you get radio warnings of the approach of darkness, you can hear the difference all around you and the city begins to howl. The darkness and shadows in this game are very well done and night can be a terrifying experience …
Which leads to the real zombies.
During the day you have to be a bit careful to make sure you don’t get mobbed - not too hard because you are faster than most zombies and you can climb like a monkey. There are a few faster zombies who climb almost as well as you, although they don’t seem to get the hang of jumping too well. These guys can be a real pain but can still be taken down with modest weapons or even a well timed kick as they clamber onto a roof.
However, at night a different kind of zombie appears. These are seriously bad♥♥♥♥♥and the best way to deal with them is to run away as fast as you can go, preferably to a safe zone (some of which you get to set up). They are fast. They can climb and jump. They are really, really hard to kill and coupled with the excellent atmosphere and lighting they make night missions really tense.
Overall an excellent game all around that allows for some great zombie destruction and/or some careful stealth movements. Worth buying just for the climbing but with the added bonus of zombies! Win - Win!

What an amazing co-op experience. One of the best I feel on PC. The only thing better than one person s******* themselves is two. Combine a solid combat experience, engaging story, scary immersive sounds and environment, zombie hordes, and an amusing crafting system in an apocalyptic open world and you have found a winner.
I am always on the lookout for coop features and I have played my fair share of zombie games. Its taken a while for me to get around to this one but its been worth the wait. If your into your zombie games/walking dead etc and especially coop I would highly recommend you give this a shot. It has an immersive fairly large open world/city that has experienced a disaster and without spoiling anything you are sent in. The story starts from there.
Now I have seen criticism of the story. All I can say is for myself and gf we found the story so far engaging. We initially ignored a lot of the side missions which was a mistake, they themselves can be quite interesting with some obvious thought gone into them and you need the experience and the more cash and items you find the better honestly.
Gameplay consists of free world roaming using parkour and other methods scavenging and looting for cash/weapons and crafting parts. All the while avoiding or fighting the excellent zombie hordes. There are two aspects to the game, day and night which affect the zombies, exp earned, difficulty and the level of bowel tightening (scary sounds).
As with most sandboxes the freedom to approach and solve the missions how you choose is refreshing. The combat is solid and expansive with all kinds of dropkicks, elbow smashes and different weapon attacks to take the fight to the zombie hordes. The upgrade system is quite amusing attaching a range of mods (toxic, fire, shock etc) to weapons creating hybrid weapons of destruction which are all shown visually on the weapons themselves. (think meat cleaver with a battery and wires attacked for shocking combined with a small arc welder for burning at the end)
Overall a highly recommended coop experience even if your not into the zombie thing.

Worms World Party Remastered is a re-release of the 2001 smash hit, Worms World Party. This game was released in July 2015.  The remastered edition has proven to not be as popular as the predecessors with only 6000 people picking this game up from Steam.
The gameplay of Worms World Party Remastered is essentially the same as the original game. Absolutely everything is the same. The huge selection of weapons in your worm’s arsenal makes a return; the classics are still here such as bazookas and grenades, along with some of the newer weapons such as exploding sheep, homing pigeons and napalm strikes. The game has a single player mode, online multiplayer, and local multiplayer. I only played a couple of matches in the single player mode against the AI, but this proved to be a difficult matter, simply because the AI in this game totally knows how to control their weapons more than me, and can take the wind and other elements into consideration, meaning you'll probably get beaten.
That being said, the multiplayer is where you'll get the most fun out of Worms as you should well know if you played the other games in the series. The online play is broken though, I tried playing and it is a convoluted mess. You have to put in IP addresses of servers, ports, everything that shouldn't be needed to be done in a remastered version of the game - when I finally managed to get it all set up, there was two people playing...two people in the multiplayer side of this game. There was no point me trying to get into the game as they were just sat in their own two separate lobbies themselves.  Where I had the most enjoyment and gameplay was in the local multiplayer playing with my partner.
Before you start a match, you get to create your own team of worms, giving your team a name, then naming all of your individual worms - next you can give your team a style of voice, with a large selection of accents to just from, customize your worms grave stones, and your teams flag. Finally you also get to choose your teams "victory" music which plays when you win a match.  The hot potatoes style gameplay of passing the controller between each other works just fine, as we were both laughing at each other's failings on their turns. One matched slowly turned into eight or nine matches, it became very competitive at times too.
The graphics in Worms World Party Remastered didn't really get a massive revamp over the previous games; the resolution did get upped to 1080p though, which is a nice plus to see. The UI is clean and easy to navigate around. The audio in Worms’s games is always fascinating to me. The cute little worm voices which act as a sort of commentator to your turns all have a comical value attached to their lines. All of the weapons have an over the top sound effect with them too. The holy hand grenade is just beautiful
Worms is always a pick and play sort of game, I had played the previous game so I knew what to do, but my partner who had never played a worms game before was easily able to pick up the controls after a turn or two of playing, don't tell her I said this, but she actually got quite good and managed to beat me more times than I am happy to admit! If you feel that you want a little extra challenge in the game though, you can give one team more worms than the other one, giving you a handicap situation.
Every single match in worms has a randomly generated world. You'll never fight on the same map more than once. The worlds which the game creates can sometimes give one team an unfair advantage, such as hiding a couple of worms in a remote location with no hope of them either doing anything remotely for a few turns, but this also means they can't get hurt for a few turns.  Along with the randomly generated terrain, there are also a number of weapon crate drops which happen at random points too; these crates hold the more rarer and powerful weapons such as nuclear tests and air strikes for example. On top of these weapon crates, you'll also find utility crates which hold more useful tools such as blowtorches, parachutes, teleports and many more of the more random items in the arsenal.
Worms World Party Remastered does not have an end to the amount of content you can get out of it. You could literally play this game for hours on end and not get bored of it. We have only been playing the game for three hours now and see no reason for us wanting to stop anytime soon. This is definitely a game to keep installed for when you want to have a couple of games with your friends on the local multiplayer mode.
Even though Worms World Party Remastered is supposedly the better version of the World Party game, it still had technical problems. Firstly, the game will refuse to run if your screens resolution is anything higher than 1080p. I had to lower my settings to this from 4k in Windows before I could even get past the main menu screen. The technical jargon that you need to do for any sort of online multiplayer should not be present in a remastered game. The game is on Steam so it should just run off the Steams network multiplayer options. Be warned, when playing online too; your external IP address is clearly shown for everyone to see... The only other small issue is that the menus also don't show in 1080, they are in 640 by 480. Whilst this isn’t a massive problem, the game shouldn’t really be advertising itself for being completely 1080. The game also works very well with the Steam controller as well as the regular Xbox pad.
Worms World Party Remastered is definitely a game I will recommend, purely because it works on newer operating systems without you having to download patches and mods. I will say that you should only be looking at picking this game up if you plan on playing it locally with friends. The single player is not worth it, and the online multiplayer is non-existent now once you manage to get past the strange setup. Playing this game with friends will bring plenty of exciting times and tons of fun for a very little price of £10, 99.

It's a good little one. Looks a bit like Terraria and plays like a buildwar focused platformer. I'm going into detail so this is the TL:DR section.
Gamemodes:
Capture the Flag(s)
Take the Halls (King of the Hill)
Classes :
Archer - Bow and Grappling hook to swing around.
Knight - Sword and shield for blocking damage.
Builder - Pickaxe and the ability to build/mine.
Essentially the game begins and you have some time (Sometimes around 5mins) to construct a fortress that will protect your flag or hall. There is a no rush zone so you can't progress into the middle of the map and the "no-mans-land". Sometimes the halls are located here and can only be captured when the game starts.
In CTF you get gold for playing your role. Killing or building basically. Then you can buy special ammo like fire arrows, grenades or the tower-levelling "Keg" which is pretty much what the Uruk-Hai carries into the wall at Helmsdeep in Lord of the Rings.
In Take the Halls your build squad constructs factories that produce ammo, bombs, catapults and so forth which you go and collect and then die before you get to use (lol). Enemies can capture pretty much everything so don't die carrying a Keg!
The combat is pretty solid. A knight can block all damage from an archer using his shield but this leaves him open to being stabbed or shot from behind. A knight has charge attack that stuns but if you use it too slowly you yourself are stunned. Fire arrows burn wooden structures, bomb arrows work like artillery. There are warships and lots of other stuff.
Constant repair of a fortress against assault is the greatest challenge late-game. If one team is reduced to their last flag or Hall they will reinforce it until it's nearly impenetrable but they need a constant supply of stone to keep it in shape. Eventually defensive lines always break in my experience as the attacking team can afford to simply spam explosives and bring down whatever defence is in place.
Anyway that's my reccomendation and is crazy lengthy. o/

RE-REVIEW:
Some people out there may be thinking that Mafia II is another open-world crime game akin to GTA and Sleeping Dogs, and for the most part they would be correct. However, Mafia II is easily distinguished from other titles by it's 1940s-50s theme and the games insistance of dropping the F bomb after every three words of dialog. The game is like any other open world crime game out there: steal cars, kick down doors and murder anything that dares to breath in your visual range. While I enjoyed Mafia II for the most part, I later found the game to devolve into a bland repetition of missions, eventually all the murdering sprees begin to feel alike and are easily forgettable, characters are just as forgettable and even outright dislikeable. An example comes from that kid who was a friend of Joe (Joe and Vito being the only members of the game's cast who actually stick in the players memory) who has an atrocious high-pitched voice and try-hard wannabe attitude that left me wanting to shoot him my damn self. The game also lacks replayability in the missions as they are linear and lack any measurable variation, plagued also with the bane of my gaming existance: Checkpoint saves, how I loathe them.
So basically, Mafia II is okay to mediocre, one really would not miss much by giving it a miss, but if you feel like immersing yourself in a bygone era and be granted the freedom to mow down innocent bystanders with your vintage convertable, give Mafia II a go.

This game is amazing. If a game that combines rhythm game and RPG appeals to you then this game would be something to look at even if that combination of genre wasn't so rare.
First off to all the people who aren't scared off from thinking of potential problems or weirdness already, it's not just "let's smash these genres together". It's very functional as a rhythm game and they made that part of gameplay the "battle" portion of the RPG. You switch between "fields" to either defend against attacks, cast spells or regain mana. The balance of strength of attacks and difficulty pulling them off feels nice and natural and the game overall feels just wonderfully made. Like any RPG you might need to grind a little but just remember to pay attention to getting good equipment and good spell usage and it shouldn't get too bad. I think the only negative I can really think about gameplay is there isn't any "turn based" alternative for anyone that isn't physically capable of playing a timing based game, but for the rest of it it's good to go.
Music and visual aesthetics might depend a bit on individual taste to say for sure but I personally loved both in this game.  The story is awesome too, unlike a lot of other RPG's it doesn't give you a ton of story which works since plenty of the interest comes in the mystery and uncertainty. You get just a few cutscenes every floor, long enough to enjoy the strange characters but not so long you forget you're playing a video game. Trust me there's not really any throw away characters.
Saddly as much as I'd like to go on I don't know how much deeper I can dig without risking any spoilers or rambling on too much, but trust me when I say this is a unique gem of a game worth playing through to the end.

- The writing and voice acting is annoying. If you go to negative reviews you will see this overwhelmingly stated... you can just skip the dialogue... or just not get SO bothered by it... it's not like there is a ton of dialogue in the game. There is a decent amount, but all save the tutorial is skippable.
But, as a positive, the general premise of the game is fun and it has some great ideas. It's a fun game if you don't mind "grinding" some DDR to get loot to craft items, etc.
If you can look past the negatives above and are even remotely interested in rhythm games and RPGs I suggest this game. If you are only an RPG fan and not much for rhythm games... even then I suggest it (just play at the easiest difficulty). At 5$ you cannot go wrong with this game.

Rating: 8.5/10
What is it?
First Person RPG in a vampire setting.
The Good:
+ Character creation is excellent. You start off by choosing your vampire clan. Each clan has its own set of abilities. Two clans in particular really change the game up: The Malkavians and the nosferatu really play differently from the other clans offering some nice replay value.
+ Lots of stats to further build your character. Play as a melee, stealth, guns, hacking etc.  Build a character that fits your play style
+ The plot and characters are interesting, they really flesh out the story and dialogue.
+ Great main and side missions
+ Multiple ways of completing your missions depending on your character build. Go in guns blazing, or sneak in through the back, etc.
+ A lengthy game that never feels boring or drawn out simply because the developers did a good job of keeping things interesting all the way through.
The Bad:
- Technical and texture glitches. The game was officially patched however there were still plenty of bugs left over. You must play with some of the unofficial patches. I was playing with a widescreen mod which may have contributed to all the texture anomalies.
-The combat feels less polished then the rest of the game. Melee combat goes into third person view which could be off putting to some. Using guns can be very frustrating and probably won't be worth it until you invest some heavy experience points into the firearm skill. Guns probably won't be effective until half way through the game.
- Some really annoying parts of the game.  Luckily it was far and few between to really hurt the overall experience.
Conclusion
A great game, and if you love RPG's this is a great game that you can't go wrong with. Possibly one of the best vampire games out there.

Metro 2033 takes place almost entirely in the Russian subway system (the Metro) post nuclear apocalypse. Designed as a massive, labyrinthian fallout shelter, the survivors of a war long past have built a ramshackle society in the tunnels, each station developing it's own personality, laws, and politics. Life is tough in the dark and filthy catacombs; crumbling infrastructure, limited or no electricity, scarce resources, disease runs rampant, radiation hot spots, clashing ideologies have lead to eternal war between certain stations, and to top things off there are mutant, ratlike creatures roaming the tracks, attacking travelers and trying to breach the outposts. Then a new threat emerges: the dark ones. Lanky, humanoid beings that attack a victim's mind, driving them mad may spell the end of the Metro and civilization altogether. You play Artyom, a young man tasked with executing a plan to stop the dark ones and save what's left of humanity.
 
   Based on the novel by Dmitry Glukhovsky, Metro 2033 is the gold standard of linear storytelling in video games. Granted, the subway setting makes it easy to usher the player down the tracks on rails (literally), but 4A Games manages to tell a dense, multi-layered story full of moral ambiguity, political intrigue, and excitement while offering enough variety and player control that it seems perfectly paced. There's downtime when there needs to be downtime, the combat can get oppressively tense, there's so much ambient dialogue that it oftentimes runs together, letting you pick up on so many small details after multiple playthroughs. If this were a movie, it would be the template for how to properly edit a film. It's also a template for how to properly adapt a three hundred page novel into a video game.
 
  You never step out of Artyom's shoes, to the point the game is almost an Artyom simulator. You can pull up a notebook and a compass to guide you in a general direction, a lighter to see in the dark and burn away the many cobwebs that will slow your movement, an electric light that drains over time, requiring you to manually crank the portable generator (which leaves you vulnerable to attacks). There are air powered weapons like a BB gun that need to be pumped up for maximum velocity, the pressure leaking over time. When you venture out of the Metro or in certain toxic sections underground, you need to equip a gas mask to breathe, and the air filters need to be swapped out periodically. Take damage while wearing a mask and it will start to crack, obscuring your vision before it breaks completely and you have to scavenge a fresh one. Blood, grime, and various other liquids can also be wiped from the mask with a push of a button. This fiddly survival plate spinning could be obnoxious if handled poorly, but in Metro 2033 they are core mechanics that make the game.
 
  Like the rest of the game, combat is up close, deadly, and dirty. Mutants viciously attack in numbers, climbing the walls and using vents in the ceiling and holes in the ground to flank you. Your weapons are cobbled together pieces of junk, firing either homemade ammunition of questionable effectiveness or prewar bullets... that also act as your currency. So you have to make the decision to either spray and pray and hope for the best, or literally shoot your money away. Human enemies can either be easier to deal with or an overwhelming force depending on how patient you are. Sneaking through a Nazi or Commie stronghold undetected is ideal, taking advantage of the shadows and snuffing out lanterns to remain hidden. Inevitably♥♥♥♥♥♥will hit the fan, though, and the soldiers can be downright brutal, hiding behind cover and blinding you with headlamps while you pick apart their armor piece by piece.
 
  The lighting in particular is gorgeous in Metro 2033. In a game that's not afraid to throw the player in the dark, the different lighting effects cast by so many variations of light sources and fires and glowing mushrooms is astonishing. The game looks great overall, too, with only the human faces looking a little waxy and unintentionally disturbing. Granted, the “Redux” version is a remaster, but nothing else quite looks like a Metro game. Probably because 4A Games made their own engine specifically for them, they stand on their own, and they are beautifully grim.
 
  Metro may look like just another post apocalyptic shooter, but there is so much more here. The fiction, the survival mechanics, and the deadly serious but somber and science fiction tone are all wholly unique. This is how you tell a story.

First of all, the most important thing about this game: It's a WALKING SIMULATOR.
It's something you should definitely know about before you decide to purchase it. What do I mean with this term? The game has very little interaction ond the gameplay is limited to walking around, touching an occasional item or reading some notes. But most of the time, you're just walking, looking at absolutely gorgeous landscapes. .
I have nothing against games, where you don't fight or which simply aren't very dynamic - one of my absolutely favourite games is Amnesia: The Dark Descent, and truth be told, I expected something at least remotely similar with Vanishing of Ethan Carter. Maybe not so dark, but with a similar level of interaction, story unraveling slowly by notes, letters or diaries, and the element of threat, which you can't fight directly. Found neither of these of course - there is little you can do in the world of the game, and the puzzles are either nonexistent, or very, very easy and linear. There were parts of the game which I completed without even trying to think about them - just touched the only interactive object around or followed something. So, is the game challenging? No, definitely not.
The story is something, that should be the strongest point of such game. When you can't do much with the world and objects, there is no threat of any kind and no people to interact with (the game doesn't have a single npc, apart from watching the cutscenes from the past), it is the story's role to keep the player invested. And unfortunately, the game failed for me even here. The story, while it has its strong points and seems quite intriguing, definitely inspired by H.P. Lovecraft, isn't really mindblowing. Storytelling is rather clumsy, closed in few cutscenes <SPOILERS AHEAD> where the character witnesses the murders of various people or listens to short dialogues between Ethan and his family. The characters are the weakest point of the story in my opinion - they appear to be very, very flat. A mean older brother, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ uncle, timid father... they are all just black and white trophies, with rather questionable relationships. It's obvious that player should sympathize with Ethan, who is nice and likes to write stories, while his unkind, ignorant or cruel relatives are supposed to be the antagonists. It's a very naive sort of a story, even with a nice twist at the end, I wouldn't call it well-written or interesting. <END OF SPOILERS>
What about positives? Well, the game is absolutely breathtaking. Beautiful locations, great atmosphere, a load of details showing the effort that was put into building the world... a lot of elements just makes the game visually gorgeous. There were many places where I just stood and looked at around, completely enchanted by how amazingly it all looks like. Music is almost a spiritual experience, it fits the locations and scenes perfectly, not to mention how beautiful it is on its own. Atmosphere, created by both visuals and music is the strongest point of the game for my opinion. Walking around the forest near the town or exploring the vale with the lake is a great experience, I was absolutely amazed by these locations and the tracks chosen for them.
Overally, the game was an interesting, though rather disappointing experience, especially with so many positive reviews. I personally didn't enjoy it too much, felt rather frustrated by the specific storytelling and lack of challenge, but I liked the atmosphere, music and visuals. Exploring the valley is a great experience on its own, but I think it feels more like an interactive demo for Unreal engine, than actual game. There's little to no interaction for the player, you are there to witness, not to participate, which makes the gameplay very passive. You have no influence over anything, and the fact that you arrive after the events, being able only to see what happened, gives a feeling that you actually missed the story. It would be far more interesting if unraveling the past was combined with participating in some current events.
Also, this game definitely isn't a horror. Is it even actualy scary? No. Disturbing? Not really. Intense? Definitely not. Quite eerie, but if you're looking for a scary game, look somewhere else. There is literally one jumpscare, but it's rather weak, resembling a bit the screamer videos. Also, walking right into it has no concequences and it can be easily avoided.
If you like games like Dear Esther or Gone Home, you'll be delighted. If you're looking for something more interactive... think twice. Another thing to point out is how short the game is - it took me only three hours to complete it, and I'm the kind of player who tries to explore, find and see everyting.

"Seduce Me" is a game that I've played before it was released on Steam. I've decided to revisit it, not out of sentiment this time, but purely out of curiosity. I remember not liking it very much and nothing did change in that aspect. That being said, I'm not surprise by "very positive" rating, even though, as you can see, this is a negative review. It's not as easy to "not recommend" this game, mainly because it's free - and don't get me wrong, I'm not saying that there isn't anyone who likes this game for what it is. The thing is, "Seduce Me" offers the amount of content that many 10-20$ visual novels don't - but that is more of those games issue than something that should give "Seduce Me" free pass from critic. Still, it has decent voice acting, a lot of characters, various romance options, many endings and it tries to be more serious (and fails at that, but the effort is still worth mentioning). Of course there are few things to be said about both the quantity and quality of said content, but I get to that a little bit later.
The best thing about this game is that it brings up the subject of sexual abuse and consent and it does it well. Also, I've seen there is an achievement for not agreeing for sex and, as it's stated, "it's okay to say no". Some of you may think that it's not something worth mentioning, but with the amount of otome games (for example, most titles from Dogenzaka Lab) that force MC into situations where she is sexually harassed and sometimes even♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(because, you know, according to game logic, she is saying no, but actually, she will change her mind at some point or another, so it's totally fine!) and in XXI century are trying to present it as something natural and even "romantic", it's good to see that there are games with different message.
Now for the fair amount of bad stuff:
This is what this game creates. When you actually replay it and decide to use "skip" option for seen dialogue, you will notice that there are very small differences between routes, especially if we consider the main cast (the incubi brothers). There are more variety on female routes, but still, it's not nearly enough to be impressed. Quality over quantity - five well-crafted, very different romances would be more satisfying than nine that felt rushed and repeatable.
More than it should be, actually, because on technical level it's fine. Story is waaaay of in terms of pace, there isn't any feel of real danger, characters acts silly, Malix seem more like a plot device and a pretext than a fleshed out character, not to mention villain, and the dialogues wanders too often into "let's throw some exposition now" area. It's easy to notice even during first time we, as players, experience MC talking to her friends. That's very nice that you think I have right to be a lesbian, Suzu and it's also nice, that you ask me if I'm even interested in having a relationship, but if we are really friends, you should already know the answer. Especially, since Naomi is presented as someone who loves to bring up this type of subjects.
Okay, I will present you know with hypothetical scenario. You are entering the house, your house, that you assume is empty. You find there five men lying on the floor, cover in blood. Then one of them stands up and kiss you without your consent. And then they introduce themselves as incubi. I'm not even sure if I would be there long enough to hear it, because at the first sight of this crime-looking scene, I would be out of that house and calling the police. And if the kiss happens, I'm running away from there, also calling for the police. And if the "incubi" stuff happens, I'm double out of there, running as fast as I can, because at that point I'm pretty sure these guys are not just dangerous, but also insane. But okay. Let's say you did stay, for whatever reason, and then they prove to you that they are, indeed, incubi. Then you faint. Then you wake up. And then you... have dinner? Nice little conversation, after which one of guys tells you, that he will always be there for you, if you want? You get a creepy mascot and a bit of flirty stuff floating around. Yes. That is what happens in the game, there's no: "f**k, I'm around some demons, am I safe? Should I call an exorcist? I watch so many horror movies, what if they only pretend to be nice and they intend to make me their love slave"? Nothing of that sort. And then, MC, out of her good heart, offers incubi to stay. D'a
No. That wouldn't happen in real circumstances. The idea of incubi may be unrealistic. That doesn't mean that characters are free to act in irrational manner.
Pick whichever you want. If you are somehow not even slightly impressed by incubi visiting you, I'm pretty sure you still would be terrified at the sight of devil that is threatening you with a gun. Or kidnaping you. But if you want, you can go ahead and fight him or scream at him and act like you are some sort of mad woman instead of, you know, actual human girl, that would be way to scared for that.
You have demons at your house. And most of the times, they make you some food or clean around. Why aren't you with them, questioning them about everything from the very first moment? That seems like a natural reaction, but instead, let's prepare for party or go out with friends, right?
. I'm sorry, but pretty much every scene, no matter if it was a kiss or something more, feels like it was torn away from fan fiction and not a good one.
. Seriously, how? When? What makes MC so interesting to incubi? Her lack of realism? Is that it? She doesn't have nearly enough scenes with her "chosen one", so you won't get the feeling that the relationship is progressing in a meaningful and natural way. You are in love and just deal with it! And if you think to yourself: "Wait... Those are incubi. Are my feeling real, or are they manipulating me?" - MC doesn't have those sort of doubts for long, if she does at all.
Wow, that was longer than I expected. If you somehow lasted till the end, you know my reasoning already. If you here just to hear final verdict, it's pretty obvious - the game is free, so if you want to play it, go for it, no regrets. Is it worth your time though? Not really.

This game is fairly well-known around Steam, at least by the types that play the visual novels. It features sex demons, weird foot massage scenes, and romantic interests that are meant to really bring the story into light. The cast was fairly impressive, which was what quite a few of us checked this out for to begin with, and the game is free.

Now, this all seems well and good, but you can't have a game without a few flaws added into the mix. Or more than a few, as I view it, but those are to be covered later. Until then, we shall focus on the aspects of the game that added to the experience, and hope that this is enough to earn it a positive rating. But, as you should already know, I wasn't all that impressed.
The game does a fairly okay job of giving meaning to the universe that is presented to you. It contains all the aforementioned sex demons and the various conflicts scattered about, but it also tries to flesh out the human world as well. Each ending is based on the choices you've made, whether you've favored the demons or those of your own kind, and it can be changed quite a bit based on what you eat for lunch (actually, that was pointless).
Thinking back, I think that was one of the only things that really stuck out to me. Of course, this is an important thing to consider when making judgements, but that alone cannot make a great game. There were things missing, that is a definite, and this contributed quite a bit to the final judgement.
While I said that the story was diverse, I meant it in a very narrow way. The ways to get to the ending were just about all that was made to be different than the others. The structure is nearly identical whichever path you choose. There's the meeting, the bonding, the action, and the ending. Not only is that apparent, but events always occur in the same way. Well, mostly. The bonding is the only thing that's off on this, as far as I can remember, as this is one of the key things that lead to you understanding that character. However, outside of this, little of the other things that have been done in the game affect the major events all that greatly.
Now, the art. I honestly don't know what to make of this. Is it good? Is it bad? Sometimes the art can look rather impressive, but at other times it looks like the work of a beginner.  Perhaps the shading has gone a bit wonky, or something isn't quite proportionate. Perhaps it might be Diana's dress which irks me to no end. In any case, the art can be lackluster more often than not. Certainly isn't the best work I've seen.
And, here is a problem that's bound to come up whenever one attempts to let the player seduce nearly every character in the game, solve various other conflicts, and still have past events to consider: underdeveloped relationships and storylines. Suzu's story, I believe, had something to do with her family and the pressure she'd been going through because of their reputation. Is this expanded upon? No. Just too busy trying to resist the endless charm of the boys and their somewhat fully-developed story that is ultimately superior to Suzu's.
Let's hope that the sequel can make amends to these various holes in the storyline, yes? I tried to be vague when covering the events of the story, but they are covered nonetheless, so be wary. My overall feelings on this game are rather in the gray area, and I'm not one to reccomend a game that doesn't meet all of my standards.

As a long-time rhythm game (in this case Stepmania) player, I was really excited for Sequence. The game looked to be just the right mix between rhythm and RPG elements, with a fun soundtrack to back it up. Unfortunately the game gets a little too grindy for my taste - you can beat pretty much any encounter in the game provided that you're a high enough level.
Leveling up is a chore though, and the bonus for beating an enemy skillfully isn't enough to outweigh the immense grind. A lot of the depth of the game involved simple grinding to get better levels, as later bosses had too much health and an item or a couple of levels was enough to make it easy. The grinding is really boring though as the regular creatures usually don't pose much threat.
If you're a fan of rhythm games I'd recommend picking it up, but if you're new maybe give it a pass or play it on a lower difficulty. I played it on Hard because it said "for the not musically challenged," but most of the difficulty came from luck not going in my favor.

And for the first time I want to get further and deeper through the game… and it’s a rhythm game! The hardcore rhythm gamers will probably enjoy this, and the casual ones will like this, and the non rhythm gamers will still enjoy it for feeling more like a puzzle game.
Give this game a chance!

When I first started to play this game I didn't really expect much out of it, truth be told. It had earned a rather nasty reputation over the years but it was on sale and I decided to try it out. It was a decision I would not regret.
Graphics 5/10 - The graphics in this game have not aged well to say the least but don't let that discourage you. If you can look past the dated appearance of the game you will find plenty to enjoy.
Sound 9/10 - The sound design in this game is fantastic. Although the sound effects can lack impact at times, the soundtrack really sets the mood for the world of darkness. More then once I found my heart racing in anticipation over what would be around the next corner. Play the haunted house level in this game and you will know what I mean (very atmospheric!).
Level Design 7/10 - With the exception of the games main huds, the levels in this game are all pretty linear. It would have been nice if the game gave more alternate routes to your destinations, Deus Ex style. It does indeed do that at times if you keep an eye open for them (or your investigate skill is high enough) but such events are few and far between. Despite this though, I never felt bored on my first playthrough.
Story 9/10 - The story in the game is masterfully woven. I found myself constantly thinking about who I should trust and distrust. In one case you can discover a potential allies true motivations before the end of the game and tell them to go to hell but with the others you have to take a leap of faith and hope your instincts are on the ball. This adds a level of uncertainty to your actions as you feel more and more like a diposable pawn with no will of your own, surrounded by master manipulators who wish to use your skills for their own gain and then toss you aside like yesterdays news.
Quests 10/10 - The quests in this game really shine. Investigate and evil cult, track down a supernatural serial killer or take down a group of famous vampire hunters. This game really keeps your interest by giving you well written quests that are not only entertaining, but also give you the feeling that you are making this dark world a better place with each step you take.
Bugs Presence 2/10 - When this game was released it had a ton of bugs since Activision rushed it to market. However, there is an unofficial patch for this game - which is still being updated - that removes nearly all of these issues and then some. It also adds plenty of new content into the game so I would HIGHLY recommend it. In fact, I've heard it's pretty much essential since this game can't run really well on modern operating systems without it, which makes perfect sense given the games age. There are still some minor bugs present, sometimes I would have difficulty climbing a certain set of stairs or would partially clipp through a wall but these instances are minor and quite rare so they were never an impediment for me.
All in all, this game is worth a purchase. I've played through it several times with different clans and enjoyed it every single time. At only 20 bucks you certainly can't go wrong. Hopefully, someday we will get a sequel to this game, with all the potential on display I can only hope for a sequel. The MMO was a bust but I will remain hopeful for the future of this franchise now that Paradox holds the reigns to the kingdom.

Software Inc is a management game of creating a small software house and culturing it until it festers into a corporate blight upon the digital kingdom. You start by building a small room or two, staffed by a handful of programmers (or even just your company’s founder) and working on other people’s contracts. If you have the money or the courage, you can develop your own software.
There’s a decent amount of freedom in terms of how you achieve digital dominance. You can make editing tools for creators, business tools for offices, videogames for consoles and (given the time and expertise) even a whole operating system of your own. Selling these and moving onto the next big thing (command-line to GUI, 2D graphics to 3D graphics) will see you expand and grow, and all the while time advances, prompting panicked renovations as you install new computers to each of your employees’ desks in an effort to keep up with the competition.
Sadly, the products don’t appear as anything tangible – there’s no cardboard box to be proud of, or shots of how it looks on-screen. Instead your software appears as entries in the charts, or as reviews in the ‘Software Times’. Sometimes you’ll get a place in a Top 5 listicle and that’s always a good feeling. Then, next year, you’ll see your program’s position slip from 2nd place to 5th and you’ll be fuming. “What the hell is Lion X anyway?” you’ll scream.
