Kyle Crane is to zombies as Turtles are to foot clan.
Likely the best zombie action survival parkour game ever. Dead Island already introduced the combat system, and much like that, Dying Light truly breathes through its visceral and physical melee combat. The zombies are a joy to beat down, kick around, dropkick, grab and tackle. There's often times so many of them, it's better to just avoid the overwhelming odds and run away. The fluid movement co-stars alongside the combat and almost every place becomes accessible, the detailed world giving an opportunity to escape any bad situation in almost any direction. Night time makes the player more vulnerable and the fast parkour sprints with enemies right behind do have a feeling of their own entirely.
Graphics and weather look mostly very good (the background ocean being oddly out of place), some indoor environments impressive even, and the lighting particularly succeeds in making the world bathe in warm sunlight. The night is mostly pitch black without a flashlight, which is wonderfully realistic as darkness obscures your path. Getting cornered by zombies in some dark narrow place also evokes a primal fight or flight reaction, even if most of the game you're in control. Heights are also used effectively, I could feel my hands sweat climbing that bridge!
Grappling hook, while handy, defies laws of physics, the materials collected are mostly the same few items supporting a pretty thin crafting system and the skills are there not to develop a character but just to unlock new abilities. The RPG elements are unremarkable, but Dying Light would hardly need any of it. That weapon deals that much damage, let's rock. Messing around with zombies has never been so much fun.

This is Worms World Party, just the way I remember it. It's the best Worms game ever made, and, after years of terrible Worms games and 3D, it has aged remarkably well. Running without issues on Windows 10.
It's getting alot of justified criticism due to the word 'Remastered'--it shouldn't be called a remaster, rather a 'Steam edition'. It is false advertising. This is because the game has  is still in the original resolution outside the gameplay, and not much has actually been 'remastered', apart from the gameplay, which is in 1080p and a solid 60fps. It's the same game with more resolution options tacked on and Steamworks support.
However, why would this matter? Of all the games, a 2D Worms game is the last one that needs to be in 1080p and 60fps. There are also new audio and sound effects, which, as a fan of the original release in 2001, I really appreciate.
This is the same game that shipped in 2001, with 1080p gameplay and new audio. However, despite the false advertising, I'm still inclined to give this a positive review. This is because this is a working version of Worms World Party for modern operating systems--the old 2001 'Sold Out' version, which I still own a physical copy of, no longer works with Windows 7, nevermind Windows 10 which I recently upgraded to. I have been longing to play Worms World Party again for many years, so I am thrilled to be able to do that again.
So in short, if you don't care about the false advertising and, like me, just want to play LAN or Local games of Worms World Party for nostalgic value or fun, pick it up. It was my first Worms game, and has always been my favourite, due to the amount of fond memories I have of it :)

To start off, I just wanted to state that I am NOT a fan of tower defense type games. I find them repetitive, grindy, bland, and not innovative.
BUT, Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten is a true gem in the tower defense genre. It combines the elements of a tower defense game along with rpg elements, which gives the game a surprisingly fun twist. Instead of just placing troops that do not have meaning around, I was able to level up my characters and as I progressed I learned their stories.
Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten is not only a tower defense game, it has a story, unlike many games of the same genre. The story was nothing special, but there was a story nonetheless.
If you're an achievement hunter (♥♥♥♥♥) like I am, then you'll be disappointed because a few of the achievements are a bit grindy. On the other hand, the developers were nice enough to allow you to go into the Options and increase exp and gold gain by 300%. I cannot stress enough how this option is amazing and that I think more devs should implement it, because of how grindy some achievements are. This also makes the game a little bit more on the easier side. I hardly ever lost a round. I can count on both hands how many times I've lost.
The game is very simple, I was able to beat the base game without generic recruits. I did recruit the generic characters in order to obtain all the gold stars/side quests. The UI is also very simple. Skill trees are simple. Everything about this game is very simple, easy to learn, and relaxing.
If you're looking for a casual game, then I'd definitely recommend this game. A lot of times, I find myself on this game when I am watching tv or a movie.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten. It's a true gem of it's genre and should not be dismissed so easily, just because it's a casual tower defense game.

It's been a long time since I tried any shooters, and Metro 2033 Redux made it a pleasant reintroduction to the genre for me. I wouldn't really give it, as some do, the tag 'horror' though. Sure, its focus is on mutants and dark surroundings, but it isn't all that scary. Some opportunities for a good scare were left untouched (for example in the library, where the Librarians get introduced: you're walking around, expecting a huge monster around any corner, but instead you just finish the level and in the next level it is there - the Librarian, but already in plain sight).
The story is somewhat clunky and leaves many questions unanswered. Personally, I was constantly mixing up people or wondering who was who. The ending felt a little unsatisfying. No big boss to slay or anything alike. Just a decision you have to make. And I actually had to replay that part, because I couldn't jump over the Dark One to get to the missile guidance system. If it is supposed to make you want to read the book, it is succesful.
Gameplay is smooth and original. The game isn't easy, which I like a lot. When I thought I was going to have an easy time up in the light outside - opposed to the darkness of the Metro - I guess I couldn't be more wrong. Loved the whole gas mask idea, which gives you this feeling of urgency at all times. The graphics are very nice, and so are all effects: flies that land on your gas mask when you get close to corpses, snow, fog, wind - all very well done.
Something that annoyed me, however, was the saving system in this game. I like automatic saves, because I can keep playing without having to pause to save the game. But the moment at which those saves are made is crucial, and even more so if there is no ability to load older saves (without restarting the whole mission). If you run out of gas mask filters because you had lost your way, and the game is saved right when you found where you had to go, you're in for some pain.
At first I didn't think the soundtrack was anything special, but as the game progressed I had to take it back. It really adds to the great atmosphere. And after a long mission (mostly on my own, partly with an annoying kid on my back) in the darkness of the Metro, that guitar music in the safety of a station really helps to get your adrenaline down.
One last thing about the mutants and weapons. Most of them are confined to very specific areas, which means you encounter them only once in the game. I think this is quite a shame; I would have liked to see more differentation in this, so the game would be less predictable. Their movement can look quite ugly as well, when they jump and land with their feet inside a wall for example. My first complaint also counts for the weapons - the flamethrower is introduced when the game is almost finished already.
Pros:
- Very good gameplay and graphics
- Fitting soundtrack
- Great difficulty
Cons:

When I first started to play this game I didn't really expect much out of it, truth be told. It had earned a rather nasty reputation over the years but it was on sale and I decided to try it out. It was a decision I would not regret.
Graphics 5/10 - The graphics in this game have not aged well to say the least but don't let that discourage you. If you can look past the dated appearance of the game you will find plenty to enjoy.
Sound 9/10 - The sound design in this game is fantastic. Although the sound effects can lack impact at times, the soundtrack really sets the mood for the world of darkness. More then once I found my heart racing in anticipation over what would be around the next corner. Play the haunted house level in this game and you will know what I mean (very atmospheric!).
Level Design 7/10 - With the exception of the games main huds, the levels in this game are all pretty linear. It would have been nice if the game gave more alternate routes to your destinations, Deus Ex style. It does indeed do that at times if you keep an eye open for them (or your investigate skill is high enough) but such events are few and far between. Despite this though, I never felt bored on my first playthrough.
Story 9/10 - The story in the game is masterfully woven. I found myself constantly thinking about who I should trust and distrust. In one case you can discover a potential allies true motivations before the end of the game and tell them to go to hell but with the others you have to take a leap of faith and hope your instincts are on the ball. This adds a level of uncertainty to your actions as you feel more and more like a diposable pawn with no will of your own, surrounded by master manipulators who wish to use your skills for their own gain and then toss you aside like yesterdays news.
Quests 10/10 - The quests in this game really shine. Investigate and evil cult, track down a supernatural serial killer or take down a group of famous vampire hunters. This game really keeps your interest by giving you well written quests that are not only entertaining, but also give you the feeling that you are making this dark world a better place with each step you take.
Bugs Presence 2/10 - When this game was released it had a ton of bugs since Activision rushed it to market. However, there is an unofficial patch for this game - which is still being updated - that removes nearly all of these issues and then some. It also adds plenty of new content into the game so I would HIGHLY recommend it. In fact, I've heard it's pretty much essential since this game can't run really well on modern operating systems without it, which makes perfect sense given the games age. There are still some minor bugs present, sometimes I would have difficulty climbing a certain set of stairs or would partially clipp through a wall but these instances are minor and quite rare so they were never an impediment for me.
All in all, this game is worth a purchase. I've played through it several times with different clans and enjoyed it every single time. At only 20 bucks you certainly can't go wrong. Hopefully, someday we will get a sequel to this game, with all the potential on display I can only hope for a sequel. The MMO was a bust but I will remain hopeful for the future of this franchise now that Paradox holds the reigns to the kingdom.

Is this a good game? Yes.
Should you buy this game? No.
Worms World Party is at it's core, the great 2D Worms game that we have all come to love over the years. It is Worms at it's greatest.
However, this game is being sold under false pretenses. Instead of having the title 'Worms World Party Remastered', it should actually be called 'Worms World Party Steam Edition'. Team 17 have taken Worms World Party and done as little work as possible in order to get it working with modern computers and modern monitors.
The standout improvements to the game are 1080p support, and controller support. The problem is that these are about the only major improvements to this nearly 15 year old game and even those improvements come with caveats. For instance, the 1080p support is only when in game. The main menus have not been improved from the 15 year old game and are extremely low resolution. Controller support feels a bit tacked on as things like scrolling and positioning don't work as well as they should.
It is quite obvious that this is just a port of the original game as many of the limitations of the original are still present. Probably the most egregious of these issues is the way multiplayer is handled. More specifically hosting of multiplayer games. You can't install the game then go straight into hosting multiplayer games. In order to host a game you first need to go into your router and set up port forwarding. You then need to edit the registry and finally you need to enter your WAN IP address into the game. This is unacceptable.
The hosting issue alone has nearly killed the community for this game dead. I have seen the ridiculous situation where there were 10 people in a lobby all wanting to play a multiplayer game but none of them could host a game so no one could play. I ended up writing a Steam guide to try and help people get around this problem.
It is this hosting problem which I think has led to the multiplayer being pretty much dead. The game has only been out for a week and the average player count is 9.5 players per hour
. This number is also made up of people playing single player as well. Good luck trying to find a multiplayer game.
Then there is the menus. They look like they are presented in 640x480 resolution and they look dated design wise as well. When in game the resolution is 1080p but the weapon select screen is not scaled properly so is very small and makes it difficult to see what the icons are.
Those are the major issues but there are quite a few other little niggles.
This game is not a remaster. It is a quick cash grab. The original game has had a minimal amount of work done to it to make it compatible with modern computers and that is about it.
We have been complaining to Team 17 on the forums and the Team 17 rep told us he would have a plan of action to present to us in order to improve the game by the end of the week. The end of the week has come and gone with no word from the rep.
I believe it is pretty unlikely that the game will ever be improved as there is no financial incentive for Team 17 to do so. The game is dead on arrival.
Basically I would say to any potential buyers, don't do it. Don't support Team 17 who have taken the good will of their fans for granted for too long. This is a quick cash grab and the game has no future. Don't waste your money or time on this.

The only "remastering" they've done is improve the screen resolution in-game (frontend menus are still 640x480), replace the in-game sound effects with sounds from later Worms games (which can thankfully be turned off) and touched up some of the frontend graphics.
Other than that, it's almost identical to WWP at launch, which means it lacks many of the features, enhancements and improvements that come with the similarly-priced Worms Armageddon. The game also struggles to run on modern systems - I get, at best, 35 FPS, compared with the 60 FPS I get in Worms Armageddon.
If you really want the featureset of WWP, wait for a major patch. If you just want a good Worms game, get Worms Armageddon instead. It's the same price, uses a near-identical game engine, and runs a Hell of a lot nicer.

There is a phenomenon that when something is done too well, it fails to impress.
I vacillated about whether to recommend this game, but I ultimately decided that my experience of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, unfortunately, is subject to that phenomenon. The Astronauts did a wonderful job with this game from a technical perspective, which is something everyone should support. The graphics are fantastic, the music hauntingly beautiful, and the voice-acting emotionally wrenching. That being said, the story is lacking and even the beautiful world doesn't give the game enough depth to make up for the weakness of the plot, particularly the ending. There was something about the world that just didn't draw me in--perhaps they walked the line between real and surreal so well that I was never convinced it was either. The ending is both twist and ambiguous, and I wasn't surprised by the twist and I hadn't been drawn in enough to care about the ambiguity. It just didn't leave a mark, positive or negative.
After giving it some more reflection, (I’ve updated this review) I can say that my problem with the plot of Ethan Carter is less a problem with this game itself (though I have given my complaints) and more likely a problem with the genre. To me exploration felt more like looking at a painting than actually stepping into a real world, and following the story felt more like checking off a list than solving a mystery.
That I don't recommend The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is my statement that if I had the opportunity to do it over, I would have done something different--entered a different story in a different world if you will. But most importantly, I would have done something in a different format—like reading a book—a clear indication of my dislike for the genre. I will be watching the future developments from The Astronauts and I do hope for another opportunity to play another game made with the same rare technical skill as this one.
Bottom line: if you like walking simulators (and this is a bit more than just a walking simulator), get this one. If you are unsure of the genre, Ethan Carter is unlikely to change your mind.

Let me start by saying one thing: I don’t like TDs. Too many of them revolve around mechanics I consider boring, such as interest, and generally, they don’t offer much beyond the core, basic gameplay expected from the genre. With that out of the way, I’ll try to explain how Defender’s Quest won me over.
It’s impossible not to mention the fantastic writing present in the game: The story is overall serious, but the script makes no commitment to sounding mature or gritty. To the contrary: while some may argue the cast is composed of very standard archetypes, it’s still highly varied, and the humorous exchanges between the characters are a joy to see. Ironically, it’s their likability that makes the story much easier to care about, not presentation or “visceral” experiences. Take notes, games industry.
While I’m at it, the soundtrack is also a very strong point, and is included in the game’s folder for free. Plot and music are hardly all the game has to offer, though. As I said, I don’t like TDs and what impresses me the most about Defender’s Quest is how it carefully avoids annoying mechanics I’ve come to associate with the genre.
In this game, you don’t have to worry about insane resource management (interest) or fast finger movement (since you can pause mid-wave). It’s only about character loadout and positioning. That doesn’t mean it’s easy, but that it’s the right kind of hard. That it offers depth.
Going through the game should take you about five hours, but that can increase tenfold if you try to finish all level variations and challenges. For me, it clocked at just over sixty hours, and was definitely worth its price. I can recommend it to anyone looking for a twist on the traditional TD formula.

This game is quite addictive and I've been impressed with the details that provide a lot of replay value. As with any tower defense game, your goal is to prevent enemy units from reaching your tower. In this case, your tower is a librarian who has obtained magical powers to battle in the realm between life and death. To defend herself, she can cast some magic spells and she can pull her allies (berserkers, archers, healers, knights, ice mages, and dragons) into her realm and position them for defense. Besides the librarian, all units act on their own once placed. The defenders' skills and the librarian's spells can all be leveled up by earning experience. The skill trees, along with armor and weapons, provide the ability to customize each defender's strengths.
What makes the game addictive is the variation. Each battle provides a different set of enemies and a different map with sometimes challenging unit placement options. As the game progresses, the type, number, and skill of available defenders increases which provides for different strategies to be employed. Each battle can also be completed at one of four difficulty levels, with higher levels producing different, more powerful, more numerous enemies. Completing battles perfectly (with no tower damage) unlocks bonus levels for additional variation. Once the main story is completed (10 - 20 hours depending on replays, bonus levels, etc.), a "Play+" option allows the story to be run again, this time with additional side quests, newly-enhanced enemies, upgraded weapons/armor, etc. The librarian's journal is also unlocked, adding some more humor to the game (which was already very light hearted in tone).

What sets this game apart from Bloons? What makes it more entertaining than most TD's I've played? I'd say it's the story and different kinds of gameplay styles that seamlessly make its way into the regular gameplay. It has so much content, finishing the final level only means that you have the New game+ and new side quests to explore. The comedic dialogue, though not the greatest, does provide an interesting read. The 'towers' or more specifically, classes, vary in type and techniques. There's not a whole lot of grinding, which plagues most RPG's. It's a simple game to learn and is easy to pick up. There's little to no penalty to losing a wave (though you can actually change that if you'd like in the options) and the game should run fairly well on most computers. Here we have a very unique RPG game known as Sequence. This game is a RPG game with Dancing Stage elements added. The way it is used is very cool, and I do think that more people should try it out.
The story is quite good, the characters are memorable, and the music is great. I will easily give this a dice throw score of 5.

Personally used a DS4 gamepad for Sequence. Having played through it using only the gamepad, I have no idea how it handles with a keyboard, but I can say that the gamepad felt completely natural to use. Switching through the fields using the triggers was outright cathartic.
Sequence is a gameplay-focused game, and the gameplay is as fantastic as it is interesting. The field-based rhythm combat isn't just a novelty, it has handfuls of legitimate merit. I'd even go so far as to call it innovative. The inherent multi-tasking and battle system means that the game is less execution-heavy than you might like, but playing on Hard did mean that Piano Jam left my fingers aching nonetheless.
Battle system itself revolves around the use of skills and micromanaging several fields. Things start to fall apart here - the usefulness of skills is determined by your stats (automatically allocated after each level-up) entirely and utterly. Pulling off a skill doesn't nearly matter as much as the stats behind it, and at several points in the game I had to go to a previous area to grind up a few levels because I was simply unable to deal enough damage to defeat an enemy in the time allocated (you only have until the song ends). Taking into account that the insurmountable enemies in question were rather easy otherwise, it was a total chore.
Stats don't belong in this game - instead of skillfully outmaneuvering the enemy through sick beats, you're either painfully chipping away at their health pool or utterly annihilating them, and all in the space of about 2-3 levels.
The reason this game has so many stats is because it also bills itself as an RPG, and stats are a required part of that I guess. It fails as one. There's no sense of playing a role whatsoever, and the worldbuilding is so thin it completely collapses under itself at several points. All the item descriptions are all completely irrelevant puns (funny ones, but quick wit doesn't flesh out a world), and the entire premise is waved off by the characters as intentionally arbitrary, which tries as hard to engage as a prince betrothed to a simian. This game is about as much an RPG as your average dating sim.
You progress through the game through the game's shallow crafting system. Choose an enemy to fight, and they have a chance to drop an item. Use these items to craft an item that will allow you to progress to the next area. How quickly you are able to craft this item depends on whether or not an enemy decides to drop the item. While it should be noted that there are some late-game items that increase item drop rate, the progression remains steadfastly a nightmare. Farming for items isn't fun. Whoever thought it was fun is a monster.
Combine this with that crafting recipes requires EXP. On it's own, this is a fantastic idea. However, combined with the stat-dependent gameplay and already tedious farm-based progression, it does nothing but serve to remind yourself how much of a chore it should have been to get through the game, had it not had the lucky break of being legitimately enjoyable to play. I don't see myself replaying it anytime soon, though.
The character banter is alright, though the story is so horrendous that I was left shocked by the sheer contrived garage leaking out of that final 10 minute exposition dump that sold itself as an ending. Shocked at a point I'd long since become apathetic. It's almost impressive how bad the plot is. The weak sense of intrigue initially spiked is just dragged out and finally shot like a dying dog. The super secret Sequel hook is hilariously nothing as well.
Art direction, I found, was fine, outside of rather cheap-looking UI. There's not enough of it though - there's a total of about 8 area images, and a single sprite per character or monster. No CGs for major events, and even those scarce few images are reused to hell and back. There's budget, and then there's ridiculous.
In spite of these problems, I completely and totally recommend that you play Sequence. The choice of music is stellar, the mechanics responsive, and as a whole the game is plain fun. The gameplay doesn't just carry it, it vaults it to the finish line. I'd love to see a sequel.
Regardless of its other issues (they're important to know, and I've spent the majority of the review ragging on them as a result), they're superficial to the very meaty game itself. And that's the bottom line.

I've played about 26 hours of this game as of the time I'm writing this review, and I believe that's enough time to write some credible thoughts on this game.
If I had to rate this game on a scale of one to one-hundred, I would rate my singleplayer experience eighty-two. The graphics are rather complex (for their time), but still hold up nicely today and are well optimized for play on modern PCs. The controls feel natural and smooth.
First, let's look at user interface. The main menu is a little rough looking, and the selection interface is quite confusing, But once you get used to it it's fine. You have four game mode options, being Campaign, Multiplayer, Instant Action, and Galactic Conquest.
I'll get multiplyer out of the way first. The multiplayer used to work on a program called Game Spy, which Lucasarts took down a while back, so multiplayer is largely unavailable. You CAN still play multiplayer through the means of an outside program, but I haven't gotten around to using, so I can't give my thoughts on multiplayer, though from what I've seen it looks pretty good.
Next is Campaign mode, which is the largest singleplayer component of the game. The story is that you're a member of the 501st legion of clone troopers. You experience the events of episode III Revenge of the Sith through the eyes of a clone trooper, and later the rise of the empire, all the way to the events on Hoth. It's a fun time, but even on normal difficulty you'll have a little trouble with a couple of the stages.
Now, about Instant Action. Oh man is this fun. You can set up your own staged missions by selecting different maps for a mini-campaign, as well as just select small maps for a little bit of quick fun. This is where you'll be sinking most of your time into. As a lifelong Star Wars fan, I can safely say that this really captures the magic of the original trilogy.
the prequel movies as well.
You have two kinds of battles, which are land battles and space battles (duh). In land battles you just have a battle between either the Rebellion and The Empire, or the Republic and the CIS. You have a choice from several classes which boil down down to the Soldier, the Heavy Soldier, the sharpshooter the Engineer, the Leader, and the wild card. For the the wild card is a Droideka (as freaking awesome as it sounds), for the Empire it's a Dark Trooper (pretty awesome), for the Rebels it's a Wookiee Warrior (pretty cool), and the best one, In the Blue corner, for the Republic, the flying fighter, the rocketeering rioter, we have the Jet Trooper. It's a dude with a rocket launcher and a jetpack. Yeah. You have four gamemodes, which are Hunt, one flag CTF, two flag CTF, and conquest. Hunt is where you ... Um ... Y'know, I'm not quite sure, I can't figure it out for the life of me. One and two flag CTF is about as simple as it sounds. Conquest is good ol' capture points, which is is just about any multiplayer first/third person shooter game I can think of.
The other game type are space battles, which are cinematic and awesome as the movies. Not quite, but still awesome. You have to get in a spaceship and A: infiltrate and cripple a capitol ship from the inside out, and then bomb the poor, massive, helpless ship into oblivion or B: Just hop into a fighter and go have some extremely starwarsy fun.
The next gamemode is Galactic Conquest. You have a large map of the Star Wars galaxy where you can control your fleet of Star Destroyers/Mon Cali ships/Venator-class Assult Cruisers/CIS Capitol Ships. It's like a whole new campaign for the star wars galaxy, and it's pretty cool.
Overall I had a great time playing the game so far, and highly reccomend the game to anyone, especially star wars fans. Hope this review was helpful to you.

I don't consider myself an avid game-critic. In fact, so far as I can remember this is the first time I've actually posted a review about a game on Steam, or ever, for that matter.
Let me start by saying this: Helldivers is a truly amazing game. Really. I love the concept, the mechanics, the story. The moment I saw it I knew I had to have it. It really knows how to set you in the right mood: The Starship-Troopers-Esc cinematic in the beginning already lets you know you're in for a great time. The story is both simple to grasp and yet somehow pseudo-subtle in its criticism. The gameplay - everything you could hope for: varied, team-oriented, with emphasis on strategic planning before and tactical thinking during missions. The world dynamically changes, so there is a lot of replay value, and you really feel invested in everything you do.
So then why, despite all the aforementioned praise, am I not recommending the game? Well because in my honest opinion the game fails to deliver on one thing. It's one teeny-tiny little nibble of a problem, and yet one that for me managed to soil all the great things I think of this game: The camera.
Now this may be a very insignificant peeve to rant about in an overly convoluted review, but it really astounded me how such a small detail, that has so much impact in ANY proper videogame, was somehow overlooked. To be clear to those who haven't played this game yet: The camera in the game is always centered to the middle of the group of players in the team. It doesn't sound that bad, but the problem is once people start spreading out, even marginally, the camera doesn't follow them around, and so they become blind to whatever is outside the edge of the screen. This is especially a problem, given that a core mechanic of gameplay is to eliminate patrols before they spot you (which you can't properly do, when you can't see them coming). It also virtually eliminates any effectiveness of setting up a perimeter and guarding several enemy approaches, since you end up just limiting everyone's field of view, and getting taken out by enemies you can't even see (and enemies DO show up from multiple directions). The simple solution seems to be to just stick very very close together, which I gathered was indeed the developer's intention, only friendly-fire is also a core mechanic of gameplay, and with people running around trying to stay out of harms way, and with mech-suits that can squash you if you get in their way, this also becomes counter-productive and tiresome.
Now, I know this has been an ongoing debate on the PC-port's community, and I know many advocates of this "feature" argue that it was intended to encourage teamwork and prevent people from splintering off and going solo. I understand and completely agree this game was intended to be played in a team, and that it should be encouraged and enforced in the mechanics, but surely there are better ways to do so without handicapping a group of people who are trying to play tactically: If the goal is to prevent people from wandering off then by all means tether players together - prevent a group of people from straying too far away from each other physically. That's only my opinion, and one idea of how what I consider to be a major problem could be solved, but there are countless other options.
To the developers: All I'm saying is that it warrants at least some consideration. In Magicka, which I own and adore, the fixed camera works because it focuses on a scene, rather than the players, and its zoomed out enough to allow for flexability. On Playstation the higher screen resolution and couch-play works and probably complements the standard mechanic better. Please consider the fact that, given the core game mechanics, the camera behavior is a jarring juxtaposition that more often than not works against the common player.
Thank you for your time.

FIrst of all, let's make one thing clear: All of the negative reviews, including this one, are not towards the actual gameplay,
was a fantastic game all those years ago, and is just as much fun to play today, same as
and of course,
. The reason for the masses of bad reviews is because Team 17's idea of "Remastered" is far from the truth of what a remastered version of a game should be. As a seasoned fan of the Worms series ever since the Amiga days, it really pains me to click "Not Recommended" on this review...
, it's essentially exactly the same as the original, but with 1080p In-game Graphics (this does not include the in-game menus unfortunately) and 60 FPS gameplay, both of which have been a part of
for a long time now, so ultimately it's nothing new, and seeming as how they're almost exactly the same game, it feels very much like we have been cheated paying £10.00 for something that isn't new and far from actually being remastered.
itself does offer a handful of features and content that were never included in
, the Wormpot options for example make for a ton of unique options to give the gameplay a litlte more variety, it also has more missions and a co-op online mode, but aside from that,
is easily still the superior game due-to the fact that it has recieved constant updates for many, many years after it's release.
What I expected to get from
was the second coming of a
so to speak, the entire game being completely remastered, updated and with a new layer of polish to compensate for todays standards, but most of the updated and awesome features included in
were not included in
, what we were left with was nothing more than an option to use some remastered sound effects as opposed to the classic ones. I am thankful that the new sounds are fully optional instead of being forced down your throat though as it just doesn't feel the same without the classics.
Right now, this needs a lot of work to justify it's price tag and the title of "Remastered", online play doesn't even work properly as of the moment without some pain-staking workarounds (see the 'Guides' section on the Community Hub), the frame rate can sometimes be incredibly choppy and the fact that Team 17 didn't think to include the updates that Worms Armageddon received just baffles me...
Just before this was released, they delayed it's release a little longer after discovering a bug that they wanted to fix first, which shows Team 17 care about their products, they always have done and I salute them for that, but re-releasing a game that hit shelves over a decade ago when
is already available and vastly superior is just something that I can't support.
I am hoping that this game gets the patches that it deserves and truly needs to live up to what we all hoped it would be, but until that happens, I'm sorry, but I just can't recommend this to anybody else, I even told my brothers to steer well clear of this game and stick with
instead, and I give the same advice to all of you. Don't pay for an inferior product when there is a better and very similar option available instead.

About these soundeffects: I'm very gratefull that Team17 gives you the option whether to use these new effects, or stick with the classic set. While I respect the effort they put into the new  effects, they just sound too overdone for my taste.
If you have Worms Armageddon, there's a few different consideration. WWPR, just like the original WWP, added the Wormpot feature: 3 slots where you can set additional rules/features. such as red blood graphics or earthquakes between each turn. Be advised, however, that hosting from behind a router is less easily setup compared to W:A. WWP doesn't have the Hostbuddy system. So if you want to host, you'll have to portforward (there's a guide on here already which worked for me)
Performance: NO, WWPR does not yet perform at the promised 60fps for me (I get 40 to 50 with R9-270x). For me, even if this doesn't end up being fixed, the gameplay is smooth enough and there's no need to worry about it. So if this is your only fear about buying this game, I would suggest you just try it. Either it works and you'll have one hell of a blast, or you can easily get a refund from steam.

I've played about 26 hours of this game as of the time I'm writing this review, and I believe that's enough time to write some credible thoughts on this game.
If I had to rate this game on a scale of one to one-hundred, I would rate my singleplayer experience eighty-two. The graphics are rather complex (for their time), but still hold up nicely today and are well optimized for play on modern PCs. The controls feel natural and smooth.
First, let's look at user interface. The main menu is a little rough looking, and the selection interface is quite confusing, But once you get used to it it's fine. You have four game mode options, being Campaign, Multiplayer, Instant Action, and Galactic Conquest.
I'll get multiplyer out of the way first. The multiplayer used to work on a program called Game Spy, which Lucasarts took down a while back, so multiplayer is largely unavailable. You CAN still play multiplayer through the means of an outside program, but I haven't gotten around to using, so I can't give my thoughts on multiplayer, though from what I've seen it looks pretty good.
Next is Campaign mode, which is the largest singleplayer component of the game. The story is that you're a member of the 501st legion of clone troopers. You experience the events of episode III Revenge of the Sith through the eyes of a clone trooper, and later the rise of the empire, all the way to the events on Hoth. It's a fun time, but even on normal difficulty you'll have a little trouble with a couple of the stages.
Now, about Instant Action. Oh man is this fun. You can set up your own staged missions by selecting different maps for a mini-campaign, as well as just select small maps for a little bit of quick fun. This is where you'll be sinking most of your time into. As a lifelong Star Wars fan, I can safely say that this really captures the magic of the original trilogy.
the prequel movies as well.
You have two kinds of battles, which are land battles and space battles (duh). In land battles you just have a battle between either the Rebellion and The Empire, or the Republic and the CIS. You have a choice from several classes which boil down down to the Soldier, the Heavy Soldier, the sharpshooter the Engineer, the Leader, and the wild card. For the the wild card is a Droideka (as freaking awesome as it sounds), for the Empire it's a Dark Trooper (pretty awesome), for the Rebels it's a Wookiee Warrior (pretty cool), and the best one, In the Blue corner, for the Republic, the flying fighter, the rocketeering rioter, we have the Jet Trooper. It's a dude with a rocket launcher and a jetpack. Yeah. You have four gamemodes, which are Hunt, one flag CTF, two flag CTF, and conquest. Hunt is where you ... Um ... Y'know, I'm not quite sure, I can't figure it out for the life of me. One and two flag CTF is about as simple as it sounds. Conquest is good ol' capture points, which is is just about any multiplayer first/third person shooter game I can think of.
The other game type are space battles, which are cinematic and awesome as the movies. Not quite, but still awesome. You have to get in a spaceship and A: infiltrate and cripple a capitol ship from the inside out, and then bomb the poor, massive, helpless ship into oblivion or B: Just hop into a fighter and go have some extremely starwarsy fun.
The next gamemode is Galactic Conquest. You have a large map of the Star Wars galaxy where you can control your fleet of Star Destroyers/Mon Cali ships/Venator-class Assult Cruisers/CIS Capitol Ships. It's like a whole new campaign for the star wars galaxy, and it's pretty cool.
Overall I had a great time playing the game so far, and highly reccomend the game to anyone, especially star wars fans. Hope this review was helpful to you.

Very unique spin on an otherwise commonly used rhythm game mechanic.
Anyone who has played rhythm games is all too familiar with the standard mechanic of having 4 columns of arrows falling in tune with the music. Sequence manages to make a very strong tactical/multi-tasking game out of it by having 3 seperate grids. One grid is the mana grid, which you use to get mana to cast spells - it's very common to miss lots of beats here in preference to landing beats on the other 2 grids. This is also where the beats primarily follow the song. Another grid is the defensive grid - beats that fall here and you don't hit will reduce your HP until you hit 0 and lose. The other grid is the spell grid. At any time you have the mana for it, you can choose to cast a spell - the effects vary from dealing damage to the enemy, healing, lifestealing, hitting the enemy with damage over time, giving yourself a mana boost, boosting the strength of the next spell you cast. Each individual spell has its own beat combination that doesn't change with the exception of inverting a few presses, left instead of right, etc, and also significant changes between difficulties. All these different spells are balanced by difficulty of input, how much blank space is there in between beats (to allow for swapping to other grids), as well as cooldown before you can cast that same spell again. Anything less than 100% on a spell input results in it failing, going on cooldown, and using up mana.
All those different factors result in a very frantic level of multi-tasking that I have never seen in this genre, and continuously leaves me mentally engaged, instead of just sitting back and hitting buttons corresponding to a beatmap all day. Incredibly satisfied with Sequence for gameplay originality and engagement.
Music: I'm not that big of an electronica fan, however, Ronald Jenkees has made a good effort to change my mind on that. The music for the beatmaps are all catchy. DJplaeskool did a good job with the rest of the soundtrack.
Writing/dialogue: There is a large community wide disagreement between enjoyment and annoyance of the dialogue between the 2 main characters, so your mileage will vary heavily in that regard. What I can say from an objective point of view is that it is very mechanically solid, all the characters in the game have lots of personality, and the voice acting also performs just as well as the writing.
Story: The story is neat and fairly original, and with an excellent great reveal at the end.
RPG Elements: Probably my least favorite aspect of the game, but they work solidly enough. In order to progress to a higher level in the tower, you need to do the same 3 beatmaps on the existing level enough times to collect enough drops to craft a key to be able to start the boss fight to go to the next level. This part is just fine, since it encourages a not-excessive amount of replaying the same content to a good amount of replayability. By collecting those drops, you can also craft items that make it so your spells are stronger, you have more survivability, and/or a larger mana pool. There's also experience that gets used to improve those stats via level ups, and gets used in crafting. The big reason why I'm iffy on this, is that especially on the higher difficulties, I put myself in a dilemma of whether I just need to get less bad at the game, or if I just need to grind out some better stats to give me a better fighting chance.
Overall: All the parts come to work together without any major flaws to spoil the image, and where the game truly excels is its innovative take with the 3-grid system.

Bit of a mixed bag, Sequence is a rhythm game about using three different playing to fight monsters.  There's the defense field in which you defend against incoming attacks by aggressors by blocking their attacks pressing the corresponding keys.  The spell field in which you cast spells with different effects such as DoT, healing, or fast recharge low damage spells.  And the mana field in which you replenish mana, which is used to cast spells, you can only have one of these fields open at a time and there is a time limit for defeating the monster, which is an interesting concept.  The monsters have a chance of dropping various items, the lower the more rare and they all give a different amount of experience. You use your experience to craft items, spell scrolls, or keys which you use to use to progress, herein lies some of the problems of the game.  It feels like a grind, just a huge grind.  You end up wasting so much time either killing the same monster over and over again to find that ONE item you need to make better gear or spells, and you can end up wasting all of that precious expereince you earned making you down on experience, although you do lose out on some items.  It just gets very very repetitive around floor four you notice none of the spells bring anything new to the table.  It doesn't help the writing isn't super compelling.  Not to mention the music is reused and the only time you feel like you're actually playing a rhythm game is when you're in the mana field, which is when the keys actually feel like they correspond to the music.  It's got cute ideas but it's riddled with flaws, it's worth checking out if you feel confident sinking money into just to get a feel for it, hey if you're into the grind and slamming on keys for 10 seconds at a time (roughly how long it takes to get your mana replensihed) then be my guest.

My point is, you're gonna have to make a lot of difficult decisions in the heat of battle in this game, and don't mess up, cause getting everyone on your side killed is amazingly easy! (For example, accidentally open all the doors and leak out the oxygen. Whoops! Then again, you could use the same trick when enemies board your ship. Makes them really re-think the whole boarding thing. Strategy!) Lots of variety in how you handle difficult situations both in and out of combat, loads of different ways to build and upgrade your ship, and  lots of ships (plus different ship layouts!) to unlock. One of the best rogue-like games out there, and well worth the money.
In short, FTL: Faster Than Light is a damn awesome and fun game.

Imagine you're the captain of the starship Enterprise.
Only in this case this is not the starship Enterprise. And you're not one of the good guys. And your ship is slow, and weak, and its armament is crap, and you're running for your life away from an incoming army trying to dethrone the corrupt government you serve.
So you run, and run, and do as best as you can to improve your ship and crew as you go on.
And then a missile strikes your ship, and the air starts escaping into the void. You struggle, you fight back, you fail. And you die.
And then you try it all again like in some sick, twisted recurrent nightmare. Running and running down a seemingly infinite space corridor as a monster lurches behind you.
And you die again, and it's awesome.

There is a reason the term NES-Hard exists... because old games from the c64 nes and first pc's were so @#*&ing hard they were virtually unplayable. "You Have to Win the Game" by Pirate Hearts is a throwback to the days of vga graphics and floppy disks. The only problem I have with this game is that, although it expresses the fun and simple enjoyment of old games  it also includes some of the problems and darker sides of what should have stayed in the past. You will die more than you @#*&ing move in this game, it will make you rue the day you downloaded it. From the start, players can be killed from any number of "beginners traps" the world is non-linear, meaning that the player can progress through the world in any way the want. Provided of course the have the correct items. The Game will trick novice players into taking an impossible path that forces you to exit and restart. The learning curve is steep, and it can be hard to figure out which way you need to go to progress (plus finding all of the items is tedious). On the bright side you will have quite a game to finish, as the open world is pretty big for such a small game (less than 120 MBs). The replay value is emensive due to the hard difficulty, different modes, and DLC, which I might add lets you play as a cat. What more could you ask for? In conclusion I would only recommend this game to someone looking for a challenge in this qwirky unique game.

I have been playing this game since the closed Beta, and by now I gues the game actualy has become what it was meant to become, in other words: it has reached its final destination. In the game's developement process there were ups and downs, sometimes i would stop playing the game for about 3 months, but it doesn't metter, since i am judging the game by its current state. In my opinion the game has improved drasticaly and is right now a very intresting, challanging and actualy  atleast attepmted to be a fair experience. The game is not perfect ofcourse, it disappoints greatly at some points.
The game will be intresting for you, if you either love RTS or love the World War 2 theme. In terms of beeing an RTS game it is unique, just like CoH 1 or DoW 2. It also offers a great variety: 5 factions and alot of different commanders for each faction, who indeed influence your tactics, gameplay and overall approach on the faction. So there is alot of room to play around, and i think this makes the game intresting in the first place.
The negative part of CoH 2 would probobly be performance and balance. While I have to say that by balance, i don't actualy mean that the game is unbalanced, at least in its current state. What I want to say is, that it is harder to play some factions then the other, so if you can deal with the challange, this is the game for you.
The real downside is the performance.  I dont want to go into details, i'll just say that you would need a good CPU and atleast 8 GB of Ram. Yes graphic card is actualy not AS important as CPU for this, you can check the benchmarks on the web yourself.
Many people complain about alot of DLCs for this game and DLC factions and bla bla. The game has enough content without DLC, if you want something new and exciting you can go ahead and buy a commander or a faction. Btw you can actualy buy a faction seperately without buying  the base game and play. So from my point of view, since the basic game was actualy a full price experience, DLCs for this game are for sure the positive, rather then negative. There is also no pay2win as you might suspect.
Other then that it is a No. 2 RTS on my list right behind Dawn of War 2.

There is a suprising amount of depth involved in deciding where to place your unused talent points. Each character is Namable and has cosmetic customizable options. Naming a Character after yourself makes you want to use that character which is alot of fun to role play. If your into that sort of thing.The town's have places to recruit new allies and buy new weapon and armor.
The map plays out alot like Mario World or the equivalent and you can go back and beat older levels on harder diff's to get better gear and level. There is also a storyline written by some type of Wrinting/English major and the writing isn't too terrible. Some if it will give you a laugh and some will just make you scratch your head. But all in all this game is a lot of fun and is definitely worth the little money asked.

Oh dear God I love this game. This is a really addictive and difficult (On hard difficulty at least) rhythm RPG. You have to switch between three panels, each of which you can see in the background even if you're not using them. The defence panel is to stop attacks that enemies throw at you, any missed will cause you to take damage. The spell panel comes up with the rhythm of any spell you cast, and missing even one will cause the spell to fail. Finally, the mana panel has rhythm which fits the song and replenishes the ability to use spells. Very difficult to keep track of the three, yet whenever you mess up you KNOW it's your fault. It also lasts a fair amount of time, however the necessary random drops can be quite frustrating. ALWAYS make all items you can on a floor, they will be needed.

I have to admit, this game surprised me. I got this game from a bundle and decided to install it to try it out. I end up really liking it and played it until the very end. It's a rhythm based game, you have to change between 3 panels with Q and E, you use the arrows to hit the notes.
When I saw the tutorial I thought the game would be insanely confusing and hard to play, but it's quite nicely done, as you see all 3 panels at once at any time, so you see what is coming.
The art is really cool, the music is awesome and the story is even more awesome! I wanted to play until the end to know what happens... It's full of surprises, it's hiralious and you get hooked right into the story.
The spells aren't limited to only damage, you have shielding, direct damage, DOT, healing, boosts... Alot of different spells to use. You have to kill the monsters and ascend floors until you reach the top. All monsters have specific drops which you have a certain percentage of getting everytime you kill them (with music of course). You also have to craft/find your gear and you can learn new spells by using scrolls and completing the songs with high accuracy or note combos.
Theres not many bad things to say about the game... My only real issue with the game is the hitboxes... Sometimes it looks like you miss but it actually works and sometimes you think you succesfully hit the note but you didin't. Luckily this rarely happens so it didin't affect me too much. Maybe i'm just bad at the game though, I don't know!
This game is definately worth looking into, especially since it is only 4.99$. I'd say anybody that likes good stories or rhythm/music-based games should really try it out!

Maybe not the deepest game, maybe not the prettiest, and not the smartest. But it doesn't need to be, because it's just a ton of fun.

The multiplayer is very convenient and simple, and requires about 30 seconds to understand. That's how multiplayer should be, if you ask me. You can see all your friends conveniently, and hop into their games at an instant. Setting your game to "public" will allow anyone to hop into your game impromptu, but you can turn this off. You can also set up a beacon for higher priority if you really need/want more players helping you. It's really easy to hop into someone's game and help them out instantly, too, and can be a good way to meet friends or something.

The gameplay is simple on the surface, with lots to unlock, and some slightly more complex mechanics deeper in. You can have virtually whatever playstyle you want. Go simple, more complex, solo, squad based. This game has it all. There's even a large world map, where all the players in the game contribute to a similar cause. Gives a sense of community.
Don't wanna buy two copies to play with a friend? Local multiplayer has you covered (note that when playing locally, you won't progress as individuals - but you'll progress together. Not major, but it's something to note).
For 20 bucks (or cheaper if it was on sale, like in my case), this game has pretty good value. Replayability isn't a focus, but there's a lot to do in the meantime, and playing with friends can be a whole new experience. Highly recommended.

Just turn off the lights, crank your volume up and immerse yourself into the world of metro. This is easily one of the best story-driven games I have ever played. Also I would highly recommend playing on survival hardcore ranger difficulty for best experience.

Metro 2033 is an incredibly atmospheric and fun game that will immerse you and with Exodus coming I just had to make this review!
The gameplay in this game is fantastic, with the gas mask and flashlight mechanics, this game will totally immerse you in the atmosphere of the Metro universe. The transition between levels makes sense and the progression of Artyom's gear is also well done. Listening in on citizens of the Metro conversing with one another is very fun, and sad at times too!
The combat in this game is intense, especially on Hardcore and Ranger mode, trading shots while wiping your mask make the combat in this game a treat and feel great, the enemies and weapons in the game are varied as well, from the lowly bandit to the heavily armored soldier. The stealth sections are great and allow replayability for the game as there are different endings depending on your actions through out the game!
The only thing I don't really like is that Artyom is a silent protagonist, if he can talk in the loading screen why can't he talk in the actual game, as alot of characters who talk to him seem like they're talking to themselves, that and the AI can be a bit silly at times, nothing too bad though.
The story in this game is very interesting and will hold your attention as you follow the same person from the novel Artyom Alekseyevich Chyornyj, the game offers many memorible characters, you'll recognize them when you see them! The voice acting is very well done as well as the story telling in the game, through Artyom's journals.
The sounds design in this game is amazing, from mutant screams to the blast of a quad-barreled shotgun, the guns in this game feel real in their sounds and the sound track is great and fits the game very well. The small sound of water droplets and wind, further the immersion of this game.
The attention to detail in the game was very good, definately a step up from the original. The lighting in the game, that with the overall art design make the game look beautiful, the game was for sure ahead of most games at the time! Though there were a few "flickering" terrain bugs, there is also a lack of options to customize your graphics settings..
Small problems aside, Metro 2033 REDUX is a great game, and is definitly worth it's asking price. All in all this game gets an
A great game with a few tiny problems, that won't interfere with your experience!

Ah, Metro. S.T.A.L.K.E.R's brother in arms in the Russian-Oriented Nuclear wasteland theme. Metro 2033 is a rather short, but fleshed out game that has one of the best atmospheres I've ever seen, or experienced in a video game. Instead of giving you repetetive quests, and giving you a 30 hour game with 4 hours of fun(Looking at you, fallout.), Metro gives you these fleshed out, densely packed levels that make you use your brain. The game also incorporates moral points, which in turn, determine your ending. I saw the metro exodus trailer, and the sale, and decided to buy both Last light and 2033. I can tell you, that if you're into a survival-horror game, buy this. The soundtrack is also amazing. The only thing I don't like about the game, is the indecisive mutant AI. I liked the human PvE levels way more than the mutant ones.
All in all, I'll give Metro 2033 a 9.5/10. Solid game, and I hope exodus is the same to come.

This game is a pure perfection. First time I ever played it was back at 2004 on my old computer. I was glad it worked for me, it was lagging badly and I couldn't play it but I finished it with 30 minutes long loading screens LOL. Because my computer was so slow but this game was so amazing I didn't care.
I bought the game again from steam recently because those CDs I bought are scratched and I wanted to play it again so hard.
POSITIVE:
This game my friends, this game is THIS game, if you know what I mean. It's an RPG thriller, action, horror game (FPS or 3. person by your choice) with a dose of free roaming. But don't think of GTA or something. The city you are exploring is devided on 4 sections with special sections for some of the main missions. And you can travell between them by taxi. Another strong potential of this game are the interiors. There is a lot of buildings, haunted or not. And a lot of side quest all original and not repeating. So you have a lot of opportunities to upgrade your skills and your arsenal.
The most beautiful thing about this game is the atmosphere and the scene in where the story is situated. You play as a child of night. As a vampire. At the start of the game, you will choose your clan, and devide your skill points. Every clan has its own special powers, clothing and the way of speaking. And your goal is to learn and to survive. In the big city of LA you can act as the one with a golden tongue and persuade everyone to leave you alone, or if you are not one of the golden-mouthed, you can always choose the way of shooting through or fighting. You can also choose to sneak, and open your way by hacking or lockpicking skills... there is a lot of options how to finish your quest and so on.
As a vampire, you must feed. But you must be carefull that noone sees you feeding, or you are going to break the masquerade laws of the vampire world, and that means, showing to the simple mortals that vampires exists, and that must not happen, or the vampire hunters will come and try to destroy you. Also never kill your innocent victim, or you will lose your humanity points and that will starts to slowly awaken the beast inside of you and that will result in loosing control of your character. So if you want to be a big powerfull vampire, you must know how to behave.
Another amazing thing about the game is the story line. You can also finish the main story in many ways. By choosing sides, or acting neutral and also by decisions.
NEGATIVE:
The game is a little old, so the graphics are none of the best. And you may encounter small bugs, but there are a lot of patches out so it's not a big deal. The game is working well also without them. So do not worry.
You may encounter problems when running on new systems and computers. You may need to fix resolution with a patch to run in on widescreen HD monitors. But that is really not a problem. There is a lot of instructions on the internet.
OVERALL:
You can play this game again and again. Trying other clans, other skills, other ways of finishing the side and main quests, and trying other decisions to complete the story differently. It really is worth buying and playing. I strongly recommend it to everyone.

To start, let me be frank: If you like (a) class based, hack-N-Slash, Terraria/TF2/Stronghold type game(s), then you will definitely enjoy King Arthur's Gold (a.k.a. KAG).
Now, let me explain exactly why you'll enjoy this game: It's just plain dumb fun and perfect for close-knit gaming between a group of friends. Don't get me wrong though, hopping in a random server and just playing to your heart's content is just as fun too!
There are several different game modes, all of which are very rewarding and fun to take part in. I can't necessarily choose a favorite. There is CTF, "Take The Halls" ( similar to capture-points), Team Deathmatch and a few others. For the most part, people mainly seem to play the two prior game-types, but that's okay. Those are, I would easily say, the most fun.
There are three classes to choose from in KAG: Builder, Knight and Archer.
The Knight is your mainstay, hack'N'slash, kill-them-all-before-they-can-regroup type player. With his shield, not only can he infinitely dodge arrows and sword strikes (as long as you're facing the right way.. be warned.. lol) but he can also use it as a convenient kite to gently glide down treaterous falls from high cliffs and walls. Moreso, he can also do the invert by using his shield as a sort of surf board to skip across large bodies of water (.... or, land ...... yes... land.. it's awesome), even if/when launched out of a catapault (.. !!! ..)
The Archer is just what you'd expect, and more. The Archer is the only [certified badass] class which has available to him a grappling hook. He can scale walls, climb trees or just swing under an over-hang of a cliff and lob arrows into unsuspecting faces. He's very weak though, considering he has no means to defend himself, and you have to charge his arrows to fire. Did I mention, if you charge it long enough, you can get an attackk boost and fire three arrows in rapid succession? You can do a similar thing with the Knight (doing two large swings in succession, rather than simple stabs at the enemy)
The Builder is the back-bone of every team, being the ONLY class that is able to fortify and defend points by constructing wood or stone walls. They are also the ONLY class that can build player huts: specific types of huts pertaining to the different classes (and sometimes all of them; the bakery is a wonderful place to replenish much needed HP from a fresh, juicy burger or three!!). The Builder can also distribute tools and with their siege huts, other players can order equipment such as catapults, ships and other various equipment to help them utterly decimate any and all opposition!!
If you like Terraria, if you like playing as an engineer in TF2, if you like the castle building aspects of Stronghold, if you enjoy playing a tank in your favorite hack'n'slash or if you just enjoy dumbass, fun indie games: pick this game up, now.
The one downside to this game: if you are NOT familiar with any of the previously mentioned games or game genres, then the learning curve is slightly above average. The only reason being is that the controls are only as adaptive as Terraria. In particular, the builder class is the only trully, somwhat difficult class to play. The one reason is that it can be a little finicky to select items on the map and pick things up, but it isn't impossible to do so by any means.
On the other hand, the tutorials are a great place to start figuring things out and are very helpful and informative. If you play with a friend or people who you know who have already played or own it, then you would have no problem at all learning the easy way how to do all the things KAG has to offer. When in doubt, ask a friend!
So, If your'e still greatly interested, but perhaps slightly hesitant to buy this game by the end of reading this recommendation, let me just finish with this: If you even relatively like or enjoy any of those similar aspects from other games and genres- for $10, KAG is definitely a game you'll get your money's worth.

I played the Redux version of this game.  Steam insisted I play the original version for at least 5 minutes to post a review (there appears to be no reviews section or store page for Redux), so that's why I'm  only showing those 5 minutes here.
This game is stunningly beautiful.  The view of across the water when you first reach the shore is breathtaking and the whole environment seems very realistic and immersive.  The music complements the visuals well, and helps set the mood.  I found the game eerie at many points, but never scary.
I also found the storytelling excellent, but it's difficult to explain exactly why I liked it without spoiling the story.  The puzzles are relatively simple, and while the game insists it does not hold your hand, you should be able to figure out what's going on pretty quickly.  It's fair to say that they may be a little too easy, but that didn't detract from my enjoyment of the game.
The game is short and can easily be completed in about 3 hours, probably less if you don't feel compelled to wander off to every corner of the map looking for secrets and enjoying the scenery.  I enjoyed completing every step of the game, including stopping to read the handwritten stories and newspaper clippings you find along the way.
Most of the achievements are simply for progressing through the main storyline.  The remaining few are side quests you encounter while progressing.  The game helps you find most of them if you miss them, but there is one it doesn't seem to lead you to, for the achievement "Unfinished story."
My only real complaint is that in some places where narration is triggered, if you wander away too quickly, you might cut off the narration by mistake.  After a couple times making this error, I learned to just stop and listen until the narration seemed to be finished.
I don't see much replay value to this game, but I definitely recommend playing it one time through if you get a chance.  $20 may be a bit steep for a 3-hour game, but it shows up on sale from time to time if you prefer to pick it up cheaper.

I have been playing this game since the closed Beta, and by now I gues the game actualy has become what it was meant to become, in other words: it has reached its final destination. In the game's developement process there were ups and downs, sometimes i would stop playing the game for about 3 months, but it doesn't metter, since i am judging the game by its current state. In my opinion the game has improved drasticaly and is right now a very intresting, challanging and actualy  atleast attepmted to be a fair experience. The game is not perfect ofcourse, it disappoints greatly at some points.
The game will be intresting for you, if you either love RTS or love the World War 2 theme. In terms of beeing an RTS game it is unique, just like CoH 1 or DoW 2. It also offers a great variety: 5 factions and alot of different commanders for each faction, who indeed influence your tactics, gameplay and overall approach on the faction. So there is alot of room to play around, and i think this makes the game intresting in the first place.
The negative part of CoH 2 would probobly be performance and balance. While I have to say that by balance, i don't actualy mean that the game is unbalanced, at least in its current state. What I want to say is, that it is harder to play some factions then the other, so if you can deal with the challange, this is the game for you.
The real downside is the performance.  I dont want to go into details, i'll just say that you would need a good CPU and atleast 8 GB of Ram. Yes graphic card is actualy not AS important as CPU for this, you can check the benchmarks on the web yourself.
Many people complain about alot of DLCs for this game and DLC factions and bla bla. The game has enough content without DLC, if you want something new and exciting you can go ahead and buy a commander or a faction. Btw you can actualy buy a faction seperately without buying  the base game and play. So from my point of view, since the basic game was actualy a full price experience, DLCs for this game are for sure the positive, rather then negative. There is also no pay2win as you might suspect.
Other then that it is a No. 2 RTS on my list right behind Dawn of War 2.

Alpha 9 is finally public! I never played the previous Alpha 8 version, only this one while on the testing branch, so I thought it only right that I wait before posting my own thoughts.
Considering that just one guy is making this, all on his lonesome, it's freaking amazing. IMO the dedication and attention to detail puts even some AAA games to shame... for an Early Access game this is remarkably stable, smooth-running and virtually bug-free, and updates are regular and hit the nail every time. Frankly, I consider this the best value-for-money I've ever spent on a game, any game, and I'm a long way from done just yet!
Even though very much pursuing his own vision, the dev has shown himself to be open to feedback and actually listens to what players have to say, which is a growing rarity in this day & age. Obviously he has to pick & choose from the multitude of suggestions and half-baked ideas, but I've even seen stuff just mentioned in a casual discussion between players actually appear in the game just days later... now THAT's a dev aiming to make the best game he can.
Is it perfect? No, it's still Early Access for a reason, but it's definitely heading in the right direction and the core gameplay is absolutely superb,
. There's the rub: it plays as a pretty unique cross between The Sims, a building game, and a very detailed economic / business & logistics simulation. If you actually enjoy all of these aspects in your gaming then the chances are you will absolutely love this, but just about everyone else should at least get more than their money's worth and have some real fun doing so!
If you like micro managed sims buy it.

HELLDIVERS is a game that shines in many ways. For once, the great sense of humor, the great gameplay, interesting setting, top-notch co-op action as well as the challenging missions. All together resonate in a great feeling of satisfaction with every move, every shot, every kill, every objective, every successful mission and war.
You play a fairly good-looking member of an elite unit of space warriors to defend your culture and spread democracy upon alien races with your guns and stylish capes. If you haven't pressed the buy button by now, something is either utterly wrong with you or you're just not a fan of capes.
Every mission starts off with a selection of weapons, perks and stratagems, which are essentially supply drops in various ways as for example an airstrike, ammo, defense drones, mechs, tanks or other vehicles, turrets and many, many, many more. Your arsenal is almost as vast and endless as the waves of enemies you may or may not slaughter with while stylishly swinging your cape around after having been shot out of your ship in a landing capsule.
As for the missions, they come in different difficulties, although you won't find yourself going over medium ones too often. They are composed of a variety of different objectives that need to be completed in order to be allowed to extract from the mission, stylishly swinging your cape around while you wait for the ship. You can choose where to land in your mission and in which order to complete your objectives. After you've completed your mission, you get a reward and community influence depending on your success and difficulty.
The influence is used in the galactic map. After enough influence has been collected by the players, you take over a sector from the aliens and are able to attack the next one until you've taken or lost them all. Paired with the unlockable weapons and stratagems, upgrades, encyclopedia entries and capes, this makes a great possibility to keep up motivation and fun over longer terms. You'll find yourself coming back to the game again and again, even if it's just to swing your cape around.
Another reason to come back is the great co-op action. Never have I enjoyed friendly fire in a game this much. Whenever I have friends over, I'll show them HELLDIVERS to play together. With up to 4 people, things may get stressful, especially if one of them is a jerk who gets a kick off killing his teammates, another one is a pyromaniac who enjoys napalm strikes and volcanoes a bit too much and the last one may enjoy his cape a little too much. But even if it doesn't work out in the end, and it rarely does in these cases, you'll still have had a great time laughing together. Often enough, even with online players.
And if co-op isn't for you, there's still a ton of things to enjoy besides the capes. HELLDIVERS has awesome mechanics, just randomly running around and firing into armadas of enemies can be fun, achievement a creative and unlocking them requires you to be creative, too. Approaching missions in different ways, collecting upgrades, unlocking weapons, doing boss runs, there's a lot of potential for everyone here. It's well worth it's price, even with the DLCs.
A definite recommendation for everyone who enjoys either games or capes in any way.

Simply put, this is the best game I've ever played, and I've played tons of them over the span of 20+ years of gaming.
I'm a huge RPG fan. Easily my favorite genre. I've heard a lot about Bloodlines and people saying how great it was but I didn't get a chance to play it until recently. I'm so glad I finally played it because it is superb.
It's got an incredible, believable atmosphere of dread that draws you in completely and hooks you from the first minute of the game. You get a great first-person view and the game takes place in modern day locations, such as downtown Los Angeles, or a mansion in the hills overlooking the city. You'll visit 4 distinct sections of LA by night. It's got a great story with plenty of intrigue, interesting characters, some dark humor and excellent RPG systems under the hood that all come together to provide a fantastic gaming experience. The RPG systems are based on the pen-and-paper game and are old-school. Note - The gunplay is based on stats, not modern first-person shooters, so expect to have to work your stats up in order to do big damage in this game.
The biggest thing to mention about this game, for me, is the incredible amount of branching and interconnected dialogue where your choices actually matter and different things will happen based on how you play the game. There are several different vampire clans that actually have their own stories and goals to accomplish, so you can play the game several times just based on that. Beyond that, you get to make choices of how to handle people and situations all the time. Unexpected outcomes can happen if you make the "wrong" decision, and the game always keeps you on your toes. It's some of the finest role-playing you will ever find in an RPG, literally ever. It's up there with Planescape: Torment, Arcanum and CRPGs like that in that area.
It's also got it's share of creepiness. You'll explore some levels that will scare you, and it also explores some dark and disturbing themes at times.
As I said at the beginning, it's the best game I've ever played. Classic CRPG that will probably never be topped.
