, a book from 1725 published by the end of the 3rd Polo-Indonesian War by an unknown author. This has been roughly translated from Polish, and may be biased.
"The Polish were greatly humiliated by the loss of yet another war with the Indonesians. In a statement from General Hernan Cortes, 'Indonesia is a stinking country full of fat, rice-eating people. Poland is glad to be fighting them, despite the loss on each of the three wars. The moment of glory that every loyal Pole is looking forward to is when the Polish army finally cuts off the head of Gajah Mada.' This demonstrates the nationalistic fervor that every Pole should have, and once Poland finally triumphs over the Indonesians is the moment Indonesia falls."
This next excerpt is from:
, a book from 1737, published a decade after the end of the 3rd Polo-Indonesian war. Authored by Gajah Mada.
"The noise of battle was overwhelming. Blood covered my body as I cleaved the head of another man by my sabre, splitting his skull in two. By the time the Knights of Jakarta charged the Winged Hussars, our losses were great. We lost two thousand men in that one skirmish alone, and over ten thousand others in the rest of the battle. While I had fought in the two other wars with Casimir, even engaging in personal combat with the man himself, I had never seen this much dead men. Deep inside me, I pledged to myself, never again. So, when Casimir offered me 25 000 Indogold every 6 years for peace, I took it immediately."
This last excerpt is from:
, a book from 1939, by a Polish Noble of Indonesian ancestry.
"The First Polo-Indonesian war was a war for Cahokia, the Polish allied city-state neighboring Siribaya, an Indonesian city, which Indonesia had invaded unsuccessfully. However, while the Polish army was humongous for its time, it was easily destroyed by Indonesian Kris Swordsmen. The shame of having to give up (Old) Lodz, what we now call Ayutthaya, kicked off the rivalry between Poland and Indonesia, which would last for centuries.
This rivalry culminated in the Second Polo-Indonesian war, or the Retaking of Old Lodz. This time, the Polish brought ten thousand men, the largest standing army at the time. The main goal was to take Ayutthaya, or Old Lodz. Yet again, the invasion was foiled by Kris Swordsmen and catapults, the Polish army having to live in shame until their army recovered.
This resulted in the 3rd Polo-Indonesian war, where the Polish Winged Hussars and Kievan Impis invaded the border to Siribaya. This was met with some success, making Indonesia the weakest nation in terms of military, but was met with failure yet again due to new Indonesian technology, such as cannons, entering the battlefield. This war was much longer than the previous two, lasting 40 years.
The shame of the Poles was great after losing three consecutive wars at full strength, and this shame culminated in the 4th Polo-Indonesian war. Like before, the Polish were the aggressor, but this is the last time they ever did.
The 5th Polo-Indonesian war was a war for Ethiopia. It started with the conference of 1887 between Gajah Mada and Haile Sellasie, both discussing and agreeing to make a possible invasion of Poland.
This invasion was set to happen in 1897, a decade after. However, two years before that, Poland invaded Ethiopia. Two years later, Indonesia invaded Poland by 1897, coming close to Warsaw once again. In the peace treaty, (New) Lodz, a colony close to the South Pole, had to be ceded to Indonesia, which soon became New Ayutthaya.
However, even if the war had ended, Ethiopia was still at war with Poland, with the recent  peace allowing Poland to focus on one front. Soon after, Ethiopia was invaded by Arabia to the north. This caused Poland to push even harder. Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, was soon taken by Poland. Harar, Ethiopia's second most populous city was taken by Arabia.
In immediate retaliation against Poland for capturing Addis Ababa, Indonesia declared war, starting the 6th war, known to both Poles and Indonesians as 'The Great War', which started in 1913 and ended 25 years later in 1938.
The Great War is arguably the deadliest of them all, killing 300 million people over the course of a quarter century. Numerous offensives killed millions, and it was the first to incorporate deadly trench warfare in the first 10 years. Winged Hussars were still in service at the time, which drove the Indonesians to make a trench square, a modern twist on the classic square formation.
By 1937, Warsaw was captured by Indonesians.
By 1938, after a few offensives into the province of Poznan, the treaty of Wroclaw was signed, with Poland ceding Warsaw to Indonesia and Addis Ababa back to Ethiopia.
This war was the greatest shame of Poland, and effectively broke the nation in spirit and in economy. Millions of Poles and Indonesians dead, and even a few thousand Ethiopians from the Polish and Indonesian Foreign Legions, all for vengeance."
This game, when you interweave stories upon stories on the wars and alliances between civilizations, is one of the best there is. Unfortunately, this game falls under that category of "games that can't decide what they want to be."
As a lot of people have already said, this game has great atmosphere and visually stunning. I grew up in a small town with crumbling buildings like Red Creek Valley, so I had a heavy dose of nostalgia going for me the entire time I was playing.
The way you investigating "crime scenes" was also what appealed to me about this game. It's about as close to experiencing Sherlock Holmes's "mind palace" as I've gotten in a game.
This is where I'm going to get into spoilers.
"The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" came out in the aftermath of "Amnesia: The Dark Descent," and it very much feels like it's trying to be a lighter version of that game. There's that same Lovecraftian feel, as well as the feeling of hopelessness because--unlike so many first-person games--both Amnesia and Ethan Carter don't give you a weapon. But unlike Amnesia, there's barely any real threat to you in Ethan Carter. It's basically like reading an interactive book--the reader might be scared by it, and it may even be powerful enough to effect how he lives his life, but ultimately it can't harm him.
All of this being said, there are a lot of good gameplay elements in this game that could provide the building blocks for an amazing game in the future, if put into the right hands. As said above, the way you investigate crime scenes in this game was very interesting and the only other game I can think of where I've seen something like it is the "Batman: Arkham" series. The replay value, however, is very poor, if it exists at all. In the two years since I've played this game, I've never had a moment where I've thought "You know, I should reinstall The Vanishing of Ethan Carter so I can play it again."
If you're still not convinced that you're better off spending your money on something else, then at least wait until the game goes on sale. For one, the game isn't that long--you can probably beat it in a day if you have nothing else to do. That alone makes the $20 price tag seem ridiculous. If you must have Ethan Carter, wait for it to go on sale. If you pay anything more than $5.99 for it, you're getting ripped off.

The atmosphere is great and the visual design is amongst the best I've seen, although this is not enough to carry this otherwise underwhelming game. You're thrown in the woods and left to figure stuff out by yourself. In principle this is great, except that the game still has you on a leash. An invisible leash, which translates into you to randomly go to places in the hope of triggering some progression. The little snippets of story you uncover are nice, and the first section of the game is consequently strong, yet falls quickly into a lull when you arrive to the main storyline which pretends to be deeper and more complex than it actually is, using the unreliable narrator scope and flashbacks to convey a very superficial story. Furthermore it makes no sense internally, how the first half of the game ties in with the latter. Wrapped up with underwhelming and repetitive gameplay, the game is an overall lackluster. As mentioned, you are to walk around the map looking for items and then place them in the correct spot. There are some guessing games in which you reconstruct the chronology of an event, and there is a horribly designed maze game. Story games can be amazing, and I'm amongst the ones who enjoyed the likes of Dear Esther and Gone Home. This game fails horribly in even being close to a decent narrative game.
That being said, the visual design is top notch and the atmosphere is great. The map is well designed, interesting, and the landscape is pleasing. The music contributes greatly to the game, and gives it a somewhat eerie feel. Unfortunately the poor storyline drags the atmosphere down around the second part of the game. Altogether, I'm left feeling very unimpressed by this game.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a masterpiece of visual arts and liquid soundscapes, and it begs to be played with a good headset.
It's adventure's design is so classically not hand-holded, yet so modernly presented and effective, that alone makes the game succeed.
Add to the equation the most magical, life-like visual experience to ever grace a videogame and the masterfully composed soundtrack; then stir all up with a noir engrossing plot, beautiful fable-like writing and suggestive voice acting.
What you get is such a truely unique recipe: a compelling sensory experience of exploration and discovery that it's difficult to explain with words.
Every player should witness it with his own eyes and ears, to really understand what the Vanishing of Ethan Carter is all about.

I've put more time than I should have into this game, and now I feel compelled to give it an actual review. But before that, some background. I don't play visual novels, and under most circumstances, the idea of spending so much time reading a dumb, interactive picture book would make me dry-heave. However, for some odd reason, I was feeling uncharacteristically drawn to this for some reason. Whether or not it was because of my current situation at life at the time is something that I neither remember nor care about, but it is the only explanation as to why I would try this out. So, with that out of the way, let's get into it.
This is not good.
The voice acting is fine, the music is tolerable, and the character art is alright. I don't want to dwell on the art, considering I can't draw and everyone has their own style, but I took 100 level art perspectives course, so I feel obligated to criticize. When any of the characters face the screen, it looks awkward. There's a reason the sideways profiles are preferred. Some of the CGs look weird, but I'll chalk that up to the personal touches of the artist.
The writing is dry, and a lot of the characters lack substance. For the sake of my own time, I won't go into the depth of the characters. Just know that you're only going to find archetypes with hints of character sprinkled on them. Of course, if I said that I didn't find myself even remotely drawn in by the characters, I'd be lying. The writer was not incompetent by any means, which is more than I can say for some professionals.
That being said, of course, I don't think there's a lot of good here. It mostly reads like mediocre fanfiction, but you should take my opinions with a grain of salt. The closest I've come to liking VNs is Doki Doki Literature Club and the social parts of Persona games, so I'm not the person to really recommend a visual novel. Of course, the game isn't that long, so if you're even slightly interested, play it. However, for the reviews sake, I'll tell anyone with tastes similar to mine to not waste their time.

Seriously? It's like they took everything they learned from making Dead Island and improved on and polished it til you get this little gem right here. Well I mean the story is still your typical cliche nonsense but the gameplay is so so much better. For one, there are LOADS of active skills you can unlock and use like the ability to throw zombies around, drop kick them, stomp on their faces, slide into them, etc. And due to the way the game works, you can max out all your skill trees with nothing more than a little time and patience.
Unlike in Dead Island, the guns are actually useful and the gunplay is much better. Heck, it's good enough that you could just go around guns blazing and not even bother using melee weapons. The downside to that is noise makes fast zombies spawn and swarm your @ss like a bunch of killer bees after disturbing their nest. Also bullets.
Same applies to any kind of explosives. Grenades, explosive barrels found in the environment naturally and the like will all attract attention, so there's a certain risk/reward balance to using guns and other loud means of killing zombies. Do you go around shooting everything and causing big explosions that'll cause nigh endless waves of fast zombies trying to have your♥♥♥♥♥for dinner, or do you go about your business quietly and use melee weapons, unarmed techniques, the environmental traps that aren't super loud and the bow and crossbow?
One thing I like about this game is that during missions involving human enemies and room clearing, you can actually stealth them so long as you don't get caught, cause if you do, everyone magically becomes aware of your presence and remain on red alert until you get rid of them all. But yeah, being able to stealth stuff like that in a game like this which really isn't meant for that feels very satisfying.
One other thing I kinda disliked, but only applies to The Following dlc, is how the zombies can outrun your car when you only have level 1 parts equipped. You do seem to get way faster when you get offroad suspension, but seriously, a zombie on foot can outrun a flipping car? Seriously come the f*ck on :|
It's utter nonsense I tell ya
Semi related to that, I hate the way every volatile and viral goes nuts whenever you attack one of them, even if you manage to do so silently. If I one shot a zombo with my crossbow, you'd think that wouldn't set them off. So yeah, that's one of the few things I actually dislike about this game.
Another thing I liked about this game is being able to completely stealth any mission involving clearing a building of hostile humans. The game's really not meant for that, but it's still possible nonetheless, so long as you don't get spotted, cause if you do, everyone magically knows you're there and they remain on red alert til you hunt down and finish off every last one of them, cause mgs or sc this ain't. That being said, it's super satisfying to stealth an entire mission in this way in a game that really wasn't meant to be played this way. Course it really helps to have a bow (preferably bozak or ranger, cause the regular bow you get in game is a smelly piece of rancid dogsh*t) or a crossbow and some of the stealhier skills like the takedown from behind. You could just rely on using some like an axe or machete, but that's not quite as reliable as the ol vertebral realignment.
One of the best changes I feel was getting rid of the workbenches. You do all your crafting in the field and you never have to interrupt the natural flow of gameplay to go find a stupid bench so you can make a million molotovs to throw at zombies. You just put the stuff together on the spot and bam, you got things to use.
There is one last thing I feel is kinda really pointless a bit annoying: repair slots. This really doesn't add much to the game. It just forces you to continually replace your weapons as they wear down. But the thing is, you can also find socketable gems just like in diablo. Thing is, you can't remove them. So if your weapon breaks down permanently, say goodbye to all those upgrade gems. There is one, ONE way to get around this, and that is to do blue shield escort missions. Problem is, they only show up roughly 28% through the game, and even then, it's kind of a crapshoot getting them to appear, and sometimes the guy just flat out f*cking dies while you're trying to make him not die. Then you have to wait literally forever for it to respawn again.
That being said, once you have some really great weapons, you won't have to repair it all that much, and there are TONS of ways to kill the zombies without weapons. Like drop kick or sliding into them and pushing them into a spike trap or onto a car fire. Tossing them off of cliffs and the like. Using the slide kick to lame them all then stomp all their faces into mush. Or using the stun reversal followed up with the stun kill move to instakill them. Or using the vault stun followed up by a stun kill or a takedown from behind. There are @ssloads of ways to kill the zombies without ever necessitating use of any kind of weapon at all.

I've been buying a lot of bundles recently, I picked up ~20 in July, and Sequence has been one of my favorite pulls thus far.
*NOTE: This review will be fairly biased, as I enjoy dj-ing/mixing electronic dance music.
If you like rhythm games like Tap Tap Revolution, music - in particular the electronic dance music genre, grinding, and crafting, then you will really enjoy this game.
does a lot of the music for the game, and if you like his style then you will love the music found here.
The aesthetics of the game are nice - the artstyle for the characters and backgrounds are well-detailed. The music is very, very good, however, if you do not like the electronic genre, then you may get tired of hearing the music, and this is critical because it is the core of the gameplay and (so far) the variety is not too expansive. You will also grind quite a bit, so you will be hearing the same tracks repeatedly.
The story is decent, nothing too fancy. The voice acting is not bad, and the comedic banter between the main characters is funny at times. There is also some teasing of common RPG elements, which I always find very nice when not overdone.
The controls are easy to familiarize yourself with - you use the WASD keyes and/or the arrow keys in combination with the numbers (spell hotkeys) and Q and E. The tutorial is skip-able but extremely important for understanding the mechanics of the game. The learning curve is moderate to difficult - especially if you are not used to playing rhythm games. I am pretty good at beatmatching by ear, so I tried the 2nd hardest difficulty and had to tone it down a level - my finger dexterity on the keys are still rusty; however, I plan to do a playthrough on the hardest difficulty once I beat the game.
Gameplay is very, very fun if you are interested in the rhythm genre. You have three windows, Defence, Spells, and Mana. Arrow kills will fall in the Defence and Mana windows, and you can swap your active window with the Q and E skills (left and right respectively). If you fail to press an arrow key in the Defence window, you lose health depending on the type of arrow (basic white color = -1 HP, and so forth). If you fail to press an arrow key in the Mana window, there is no effect.
Arrows will only fall in the Spells window when you activate one of your spells with the number hotkeys, however, you must also have enough mana to cast the spell. Failing to press even a single arrow key in the Spells window will cause you to fail in casting it and you will not be refunded your mana. Spells are the way you damage your opponent, and you can also heal yourself. I believe you can only have 4 active spells at a time (you start with 2 slots and unlock more as you progress through the tower).
Between battles, you can craft and equip different items. There are 7 floors in the tower you wake up in, and you are given new crafting recipes as you reach new floors. One item will always give a permanent bonus (ex: +1 to offence), and others can be new spells, armor, or weapons. You can also scrap your items for experience points. When you craft, you have to pay exp. to increase the chance of success (you can even pay lose levels if you want to pay that much exp); if you fail, you are not refunded the exp.
Levelling up is done automatically, you do not have to allocate skill points.
As you progress through the game, monsters will have a unique "guardian ability" for each floor - for example, on the 2nd floor enemies (once per battle) can activate an ability that makes the falling arrow keys fade to invisibility as they reach the lower quarter of your window. Listening to the beat of the music really, really helps because the keystrokes tend to match the beat very well. With enough practice, you can even swap windows freely and continue pressing arrow keys to the beat. There is a craftable item for each floor that allows you to ignore guardian effects (except when you fight the bosses).
Boss battles are fun and the character's are pretty funny. Each boss will use their guardian effect more frequently, and you cannot negate it with the inhibition item.
If you are interested in rhythm games, definitely pick up this fantastic game.
Highly recommend!

A lot of love was put into this title, and I feel like it deserves due notice. My experience was on medium difficulty of someone who is not musically inclined, though I am a fan of rhythm games.
The RPG aspect of the title is somewhat limited. There's three equipment slots, but overall there's a clear progression of "this item is pretty much completely better than this other one," blandly increasing stats, though they -- like all the other items in the game -- may have punny item descriptions or names. The accessories slot, the third item slot, is interesting though -- if you ever find yourself needing certain items to progress, two later-game items let you increase your item drop rate at the cost of decreasing your stats, essentially. Or you can have a more unique attribute like doubling critical hit chance or decreasing spell cooldown. Leveling up is an across-the-board boost to your stats, but one interesting mechanic is in crafting -- you have to trade exp for chance to craft, exp is a currency. The level cap is 34, but you can beat the game in your mid-20s. I beat it at level 28 with relative ease compared to the grinding (more on that later).
Spells are acquired to directly combat enemies. They are all balanced differently (mana cost, damage, length of time to cast the spell, spell cooldown, difficulty of the arrow sequence) so there's plenty of choices in gameplay style. You can have a maximum of 6 spell slots to unload direct damage, damage over time, healing, and life-draining spells. There are also two buffing spells that boost the damage of the next spell, and a barrier spell to decrease the number of arrows thrown your way on the defence field. You can ALSO play the game significantly more aggresively by using the Convert spells to trade a bit of health for a load of mana, allowing you to ignore the defence and mana fields if you want to try your skill at hammering out life drain and heal spells in between Converts.
The rhythm aspect is definitely its strenth. The higher BPM, the more chaotic. Managing all three fields is ideal for defeating enemies within the time limit of the song and for the most fun in general, as you bounce seemlessly between defending, attacking, and recharging. On medium difficulty, it seems like the game is SIGNIFICANTLY more merciful: players do NOT have to have perfect coordination -- just have an arrow in the space of the outlines and you'll hit it. There's not "perfect" or "ok" score like in DDR to tell you how precise you were(n't). Perhaps this is changed in the higher difficulties, especially since the game mentions that players who are more musically inclined should play them.
One of the weaknesses of the game is definitely fatigue and pacing. For a rhythm game, there are NOT a lot of songs -- about 25 in total, including background music that isn't used in combat, when there are 7 floors of 3-4 enemies each with a boss on each floor. Before getting items to increase drop rate, you may spend 5+ fights on each enemy to acquire their drops. Even with decreasing the number of encounters, you will hear the same songs over and over again on different floors, though spaced out decently well so it's not completely repetitive. If you don't like the two artists who contribute 99% of the music or the combat system itself, then you will not enjoy this game for very long (I highly recommend checking out bits of the soundtrack; not every song is like Piano Jam or On Cue, they tend to be more like Super Fun or Derty).
The story starts off fairly cliche and parodying, but it develops over the course of the game. Voice acting is good regardless of content; as an indie game, it's interesting that the programmer/writer also voices the main character fairly well. I highly recommend sticking to it (assuming, of course, a seemingly weak story is the main sticking point to enjoying the game). The final boss throws a curveball into the setting if you didn't pick up the foreshadowing before, and there is a hidden ending. And, of course, perhaps you will enjoy the story throughout because of its humor; others have praised it, but I was ambivalent.
Overall, there's at least ten hours of gameplay, likely more for a 100% completion. It has a nice amount of replayability since the game allows you to change difficulty up to the third floor (wherein you should be able to decide the right difficulty for you), an incredibly low price, decent RPG mechanics, fairly unique rhythm mechanics, and servicable art (it's a rhythm game with THREE FIELDS, you have neither room nor need to show much more). A niche title as a rhythm game alone, but one of the best for those who want a rhythm game with progression. Buy it, especially if it's on sale for $2 like it was the Christmas I bought it!

This is a no-brainer purchase/must-play for anyone who is familiar with White Wolf's World of Darkness franchise, anyone who has played the first of the legacy Vampire the Masquerade games, anyone who plays LARP or tabletop versions of VtM, or really anyone who is even vaguely interested in an introduction to the rich lore offered by an immersive and addictive tabletop game series. Unlike with Vampire the Masquerade: Redemption, where you are forced to play out the storyline set before you from the perspective of a "true" Brujah, this game gives you the choice of what clan you are to be embraced under, and it gives you a taste of the what the game world is really about, allowing your choices to affect the events that play out around you. Ofcourse, there are still linear aspects of the game, and a few glitches here and there, but thankfully there is an entire decade of reliable user-made updates that improve upon those, along with increases in graphics and presentation. All around, this is an excellent game that I would recommend to so many of my friends that are interested in dark fantasy role playing games.

‘The vanishing of Ethan Carter’ is an example as to why video games are art.
‘The Vanishing of Ethan Carter’ has one of the most vibrant, beautiful and mysterious worlds that I have seen in recent games. It gives you little to no advice on what to do, leaving the new player to wander aimlessly in an open world. So take your time to explore. This game doesn’t play around when it tells you it won’t be holding your hand.
This game combines the ‘walking simulator’ experience with engaging and challenging gameplay. It also combines different types of challenges, surprising the player. though I must say the difficulty seemed to decrease nearing its climax, allowing more of a ‘flow’ in the storyline but at times it was simply a bit too easy compared to the rest of the game. It definitely focuses more on the story than gameplay.
The music in this game is absolutely stunning and a huge contribution to the atmosphere. It’s a present element but not overpowering, inviting the player to enjoy the equally enchanting scenery.
The redux version saves more frequently and eliminates a few aspectes of the game that were considered ‘immersion breaking’ (trying to be spoiler free).
Video review:

This is a game with a captivating story that is fun to play when you have a guide. The reason I say with a guide is that this game literally does not provide any help whatsoever on what to do in this world. There is no map (
), no tutorial, no help/hint system,  no indicator arrows, etc. The map is truly open and you can go in any direction you want. The voiceover is used only for the story and provides no help on what to do next.
The scenery and music is beautiful. I enjoyed walking around this world and unraveling the story. It really does have a nice atmosphere to it. I considered only one part of the game scary. The rest of it I considered light and mysterious (although it tries to be dark, but how can you be scared/dark in such beautiful surroundings! :) ).
I actually spent 6.4 hours (6.2 redux and 0.2 original) on this game in total, but it is not reflected in my stats because I played the redux version for the majority of the time. I found it better than the original in its graphics and save system. Also, this 6.4 hours was me running around the world enjoying the scenery and not knowing exactly what to do (I tried not to use the guide as much as possible). The actual game time is around 4 hours including getting all the achievements.

It is a disappointing game with fantastic presentation and a subpar story.
I would give this game a "neutral" review, but unless Steam won't allow me to do that, this game gets a sad pass. In games of this genre I'm most interested in getting a interesting story, enough game mechanics to not make me snore and a stellar locations to give those art-loving eyes some enjoyment. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter only provides the latter.
Graphics and music are jaw-dropping. Attention to detail, pretty foliage, carefully crafted assets, textures and lighting... This game really pushes Unreal Engine 3 up to V-Max. If you are coming into this game for visual feast alone, I could recommend this game for you. Still, I personally cannot give such an easy pass to story and gameplay.
I was expecting a great, thrilling, paranormal murder and investigation story and basically I got one, but I'm not really satisfied. Plot starts of really interesting, but it plays out most of it's cards too quickly, to the point where it all starts to feel really cliche. The straw that broke the camels back however, is the ending which both explains and justifies many of my complains but in the extremely clumsy and unsatisfying way. Voice-overs are rare, pacing is solid, but not great and environmental storytelling is bare-bones. Overall, story department is the place where this game seriously drops the ball.
Gameplay is only a bit better. Thank heavens that this "walking simulator" gives you some proper  puzzles. This is very refreshing - they tried to give you some agency in the game and for the most part they succeed. You don't really feel that you are on the interactionless excursion. Unfortunately, the novelty and variety of problems and puzzles seriously drops down in later parts of the game. Mechanics are samey, there aren't any "gameplay twists" or new ideas. That results in gameplay that tried, but didn't hold my attention through whole journey...
4 hour journey... This game isn't really worth a asking price. I got it for equivalent of 6 bucks and I'm not really feeling that I will return to this game anymore for story or gameplay. Sure, there is a Redux version with new Unreal Engine 4 and I will check it out for visuals alone, but If you are not into watching and exploring a beautiful virtual landscapes, there isn't anything other noteworthy about this game. Take my caution and if you want to try this game anyways, try to snatch it on strong discount.

Kind of a
thing. Atmosphere, horror, a few jump scares. Very beautiful world (Unreal Engine 4) with nothing to do in it.
Very short too. Background story is a crude horror/mystery tale about a family possessed by a ghost and killing each other, largely told through a narrator and letters strewn across the game world (lame excuse for lacking real content and interactivity).
Your job is to reconstruct who killed who, and this is how it goes:
You run around and come across typical adventure items (a lamp, an axe, a dead body, etc.), but you cannot interact or do anything with them. All you have to do is
all items in a certain area, which automatically prompts a flashback scene with 5 story elements and you have to guess the sequence of events, like this: (1) he picked up the axe, (2) he talked to his brother, (3) he went over to the chapel, (4) he killed his uncle, (5) he talked to his mother. That's it. Then you head to the next area, find all its items, flashback pops up..... You do this guess-the-sequence thing for the fate of each family member. That's all there is, basically.
What game? At best, this is a 3D tech demo for UE, not a game. Shame on the Polish developers for charging money for a demo.

Is it good? Well it's half four in the morning and I've just finished playing the game end to end, despite only getting around 13fps (original, not even the redux). Engaging and beautiful, the story drags you along and one of the puzzles in particular (portals puzzle) was brilliant.

I don't know what I expected going into this game, but I had cold chills by the time I finished it.  The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is incredibly short, but a worthwhile experience that is hard to say too much about without ruining the journey in the game.  Yes, it's beautiful and atmospheric, but the real beauty is in the journey that the playable character goes from the first moment until the very last.  Yes, it will get weird at times, but stick with it and it will be a memorable experience for sure.

When I first read reports about Defender's Quest and watched the initial trailer, I was expecting a pretty standard RPG plot and characters. Much to my delight, I was half-wrong. The plot might be your tried and true "unlikely hero saves the world because, well, destiny" fare, but the characters and the writing are frequently reminiscent of the humor that characterized the Penny Arcade: OTRSPOD games.
One notable feature of the game is that it does engage in some of the good, old-fashioned grinding that some RPGs are famous for, but this game lets you control just how "grindy" it is, giving you control of how much XP and scrap (money) that you receive at the end of each battle. This allows players to either keep the default settings and go through the basic plot, or to turn up the rewards to max so that they don't have to spend days grinding the same level over and over for XP so that they can run the special challenges.
Each level has four settings ranging from Casual, where enemies have lessened HP and damage potential, to Extreme, where you better be ready because foes will WRECK an underpowered group. Playing extreme challenges unlock rewards for your party, giving you unique equipment and larger XP and scrap rewards, so there is a reason to tackle these challenges.
A new game+ feature is a welcome sight, and the fact that this mode allows you to unlock upgrades for your unique gear gives you an incentive to play again.
Overall, I found the game to be fun and engaging, well worth the price of admission.

When I bought the game I thought "well, there's just another TD game". But, it turns out that it's not your average build and kill game. For the first 4 hours I've been trying to finish up the story of the game. The story took me in and I just wanted to know how it all ends. If you are thinking about buying this game read on to see why you probably should.
After playing 12 hours of the game I have finished the main story and went on to do some harder difficulties and other challenges. This game is fun in it's own unique way. Not only do you get an interesting story to follow, but also get stuck in character menu thinking how you should level up the skills for each fighter.
The only hotkey you will probably need to remember is "space bar" for pause. That is the only thing you will constantly hit to allow yourself some time to think before everything goes to hell. The game can be challenging even on the normal level.
. After your done with Normal, you can move on to a New Game+, which is way harder and more challenging.
And yes, this is an RPG game. You will probably spend more time looking at the level up menu for characters rather than fighting monsters. It's not bad at all, but be prepared to think and compare different builds for the same class of fighter. There are 7 types of characters – Berserker, Ranger, Healer, Ice mage, Knight, Dragon and Librarian ( who is the thing that you actually need to protect).
The simple graphics was also done in a pretty good way. All characters are different and you can easily tell the difference. Everything looks the way it should in this kind of game. The only thing I noticed is that when the Ice mage casts his spells it can be quite hard to see the enemy and how much health they still have. On a positive note, the graphics look smooth overall and you won't feel like your playing the game from the 80's at the same time. To add to this I can also point out that the soundtrack is very good. It fits the theme of the game very nice and allows you to feel emotions from the battle field and from dialogues.
I am yet not sure how many hours you can play until you finish everything, but I would guess it's quite a bit. I think this game will keep you from sleeping for at least a few hours after you should have gone to bed.
I honestly think that this game is a must have product for not just RPG and TD lovers but also for average gamers. If you have missed the sale don't worry, you won't regret buying a game for a full price.

I've been binging Otome recently, and personally I feel like there are better free otome to be played than Seduce Me. It is enjoyable in it's own right, but if you're looking for more than an enjoyable time waster steer clear. The bloopers were the best part of the game to me
so...
POSITIVES
-A ton of routes! A ton!!! Like, so many routes! You can date like, everyone but your family! It's great! Okay more specifically you can date the five incubi, of course, both of your human friends, a human who works at your grandfather's company AND the bad guy! ...I have mixed feelings on some of these routes though.
-When I say you can date everyone I do mean everyone. Girl and boy options! If that's what you like then it's here.
-For the most the models are quite pretty and well done, not stunner like some others but pretty good.
-Full voice acting!!! In english! It's not super pro standout, but it is pretty good.
-It's free. Nothing to lose but your dignity.
-Pretty unique concept, I don't think I've ever heard of anything incubi based for otome... actually, in general really.
-Some good comedic moments.
-I almost forgot but the game has music. It's there. It's not bad. As you can tell it's not really memorable (or maybe I didn't play long enough) but it's not ear-grating or intrusive.
-Characters are likeable and all have their own individual stories, I enjoyed piecing together things about the story by completing the different routes.
-You can choose your own name, for those who like that in an otome.
-The bloopers are included and hilarious.
NEGATIVES
-Some of the character models look a liiiiiittle bit off. Suzu, I'm looking at you.
-Characters are kind of... archetypical. We have our sensible megane, our hot blooded tsundere, our childish ball-of-sunshine, our princely flirt and our quiet bookworm. The same goes for the rest of the characters. If you want something groundbreaking keep looking.
-Demon routes are very repetitive. Like, 'ahhhhhhhhhhh this again' five times. I never finished all their routes.
-
-Cheesy as all hell.
-Little variety in the endings, aside from the bad ends. Those are varried.
-Can be too short, I feel like it was cut short and that there should have been more to it. I suppose there is a sequel but...
-The sequel costs money. .-.
-I DON'T KNOW HOW I FEEL ABOUT THE SITUATION IN GENERAL IT ALL FEELS VERY WEIRD
-It feels like Mika is stuck going along with other's whims, despite how hard the writers tried to make her strong. Sometimes she's hotheaded and sometimes she's content to stand meekly behind. It's all very confusing if I'm honest.
-Doesn't really leave much to think about.
-Only play because it's free, otherwise not worth it. Seriously.
TIPS (spoilers???)
-The skip button is your best friend for the incubi's routes. Make use of it.
-The hearts that show up when you make choices at the start tell you who's favor you're winning. The human's have compass looking things. Black is Damien, Blue is Matthew, Red is Eric, Green is Sam and Yellow is James.
-Make a save when they ask you whether you want to stay and prep for the party or go out with your friends.
-Don't think about things too hard or the entire game becomes really dumb. Don't be too aware of troupes or it becomes dumb. Don't question why Mika puts up with some of this stuff and forgives so easily or it becomes dumb. The game is really dumb.
-Triggers! Everywhere! Even the game says so.
The "auto" button doesn't work and the game has an actual trigger warning at the beginning.

I've spent countless hours playing the original version of Worms World Party on the Sega Dreamcast. When I saw the announcement that this was coming in a "remastered" version to PC I could not have been more excited.
Unfortunately, this game did not deliver like I thought it would on Day 1. As many others have noted, the menu screen is at a very low resolution. With Team17 touting 1080p and 60FPS, one would think that they would deliver this "standard" throughout every aspect of the game.
All I can say is this... If you are interested in this game, just give it some more time for Team17 to fix some of the Day 1 issues. However, with the "trend" in gaming of companies delivering broken products on Day 1, I am not happy that Team17 fell into this trap as well.
A bit of a PSA to game companies: Please delay your game if you know it is not ready for release yet. You have a greater chance of losing fans if you release broken product than if you were to delay the game and have a proper release.

- Even you find enough people to play. You need to struggle like 15 to 90 minutes open ports, change your net settings etc to host a decent game. Even at Worms Armageddon you can easily host a game with hostingbuddy but not at wwpr.
- Some voices are wrong, missing.
If you have Worms Armageddon or Worms World Party do not buy that game. If you dont have well I think Worms Armageddon is still better. At least you can able to play online... Waited like 2 weeks for WWPR (released with 1 week delay) and I am just heartbroken.

When there's a game, and that game say, Company of Heroes 2 has a few nations that you play in a multiplayer based strategy, game then there's going to be diiferent ways of learning to play those nations.
But today we're not here to talk about COH2 we are here to talk about a little kid named Jimmy.  Now Jimmy is a little kid that just bought company of heroes 2 with his mom's credit card, and little Jimmy decides to go ahead and play his first multiplayer game as let's say, the Axis (Germany in this case).
Now Jimmy plays this and he picks up on the quick and fast paced aggressiveness of the Germans fairly quickly.  But next Jimmy decides to go play as on of the Allied powers (USSR this time).  But what Jimmy didn't realize is that maybe all nations weren't created for the same aggressive purpose as Germany was, so little Jimmy lost his second game of Company of Heroes 2, and decided to leave a bad review about the Allies being underpowered and the Germans being overpowered.  But in reality little butthurt Jimmy didn't give himself (and the Allies) the time they needed for him to create a strategy for him to roll over the Germans with guerilla hit and run tactics, but instead jumped to conclusions and wrote an 'inconclusive' review.
I'll tell you why it's inconclusive. It's inconclusive because Jimmy's little (now butthurt) brain is only used to being aggressive and rushing his enemies with overwhelming force.  But Jimmy's brain doesn't think about how the little guy reacts to these attacks, (maybe not always in the 'right way') and Jimmy continues his attacks.
But.  When the little guy does develop a plan-and on Jimmy's 43rd game of playing Germany, when Jimmy finally thinks hes got it.  He sees it.  Penals with flamethrowers in an M3 half-track.  Jimmy thinks to himself "oh that's interesting", and hits it with a panzerfaust, and Jimmy's infantry is pinned by a nearby maxim.  Oh what's that? Here come the penals.  Jimmy finally loses.  On his 43rd straight game.  A 43 win streak and he is beaten.  Jimmy then writes another review that the Germans are now underpowered, and explains more about his double butthurtness (In both ends).
This process goes on for almost 3 years, with back and forth reviews about who is over/underpowered.  Relic desperately tries to find a medium and can't.  But that's the thing.  Shouldn't we as the players use an RTS as an RTS? Shouldn't we devise a plan or a strategy/strategies throughout the game? The answer is yes.  It is people like Jimmy who have wrecked this beautiful game.
I fully recommend this game and all of its glory 10/10-Pixo, 8.4/10-IGN, 8/10-PC Gamer, 4/5-Metacritic.
If you made it thus far in the review don't forget to leave your opinion of what you thought of my review with a thumbs up or down.

Metro 2033 Redux is a beautiful but somber reimagining of the original Metro 2033. WIth graphical and gameplay updates, this is the definitive version of a game that wasn't recognized as much as its succesor.
Graphics: Beautiful and Atmospheric. The amzing colour pallet really sets the tone for the game, and makes you feel like you live in this world. The first time I went above ground, I was absolutely blown away by how beautiful it looked. 10/10
Gameplay: Very good. Some issues with stealth but overall the shooting is satisfying and enemies go down with a reasonable amount of bullets. Save your ammo and filters, though. You'll need them. 9/10
Story: This game has the best story out of any game I have ever played. The writing is amazing and the acting is above average. A wonderful story that kept me guessing and playing. 10/10
Music/Sound: Absolutely wonderful. The sounds and music do all they can to keep you 100 percent immersed in the game. 10/10
Replayibility: I know I will be playing this game again to get the good ending. Also, its amazingly fun and scary. 10/10
Overall: 49/50. A video game masterpiece. This is a must have in any steam library. You will love this game.

is an interesting and highly atmospheric game that boasts a mixture of exploration and detective game elements. The detective scenes are well done and never become overly confusing, but they make up less than half of the gameplay. A majority of the gameplay involves walking around, (and probably getting lost), searching for the next scene. This isn’t a bad thing, though, as the ambiance and graphics are absolutely stellar; and the gameworld is a joy to explore. That said, if you aren’t really a fan of slow-paced games without action, colloquially dubbed: “walking-simulators,” then you may find this boring. But if you can appreciate its beauty and take solace in the fact it isn’t a pure walking-simulator and has a number of puzzle-solving scenes, you will probably enjoy
.
Without a doubt, the best feature of this game is the gorgeous gameworld and atmosphere. But it is more than just beautiful graphics that create this exceptional experience. The soundscape and overall ambiance are also leading contributors. Shortly after first beginning to play this game I found myself crossing a long railway bridge over a lake and I was immediately sucked in by the aesthetics. But I quickly realized that I was captivated by more than the visual view, and that the creaking and groaning effects of the bridge were reinforcing the immersive experience at an exceptional level. This aesthetic and atmospheric experience is established early and maintains its integrity throughout the game.
The actual narrative is interesting and mysterious. The onus is on the player to piece together the narrative and make sense of it. Depending on how much you bother to read and listen, the story becomes more clear or convoluted. I enjoyed the experience; however I do feel like some of the elements of the storyline could have been more fleshed out and explained more clearly.
The gameplay is comprised of mostly exploration, but also has a strong aspect of puzzle-solving elements. As you wander the gameworld you will come across several mysteries, in the form of both murder scenes and supernatural enigmas, which need to be solved through detective work. The mechanics of the puzzle-solving involve discovering the necessary clues in the gameworld and performing the necessary deductions.
There isn’t any action whatsoever throughout the whole game, save for one small area where you may get a jump-scare and sent back to a checkpoint. But even that area is extremely easy to navigate and never really amounts to much action. This is a good thing, as forcing combat or action into the game would have probably only ruined the atmosphere.
One gripe with the game that I have, and also many others have, is that there is no manual saving. I have said it a number of times in my reviews before and I will continue to say it: there is no reason for a PC game in the current generation and beyond to not allow manual saving. I don’t care what kind of game it is, I personally believe people should be able to choose if they want to use manual saves or not. And besides, in
there is no combat and there are no decision trees, so “save-scumming” (as it is so eloquently called) isn’t even a factor here. Compounding the issue, the checkpoint system isn’t very well-crafted and the distance between checkpoints can be ridiculously far. You need to solve a puzzle or discover the next area in order to prompt the game to save, so if you are stuck and want to stop playing, you will either have to check a guide to finish your current objective or accept the fact you will have to start over when you return. And of course, there is also a possibility of a power outage or system crash. Fortunately, this issue was somewhat alleviated in the
version of the game by significantly increasing the frequency of checkpoints. Yet I still find the lack of manual saving to be a serious fault.
As for the
version, if your computer can handle it, you should probably play that version. You get both versions together with the purchase of the game. Besides having higher quality graphics from UE4, there are also some subtle changes and improvements (like the aforementioned increase in checkpoints). I personally opted to play the original version, because I’m weird like that, but I will probably come back and play the
version in a few years when the story has faded from my memory.

and
. If you like relaxing and investigative games, or are curious about them,

This is not a happy game. But I found it is a good game. The major piece missing is a proper save mechanism. You have to finish a puzzle to reach an autosave. I had to solve the same parts of a puzzle a few times because I didn't have time to finish the puzzle in one sitting.
The mood is of a cool, wet autumn with no warm place to rest. The puzzles are not impossibly hard, once you finish them, but it did take time to realize what you were supposed to do from time to time such as when the words were spinning over an object; noticing that they sometimes got closer together or further apart. Then there was the Sea Thing puzzle where you wonder: Now what do I do? Then, suddenly, you see that all you have to do is...oh, better not give that one away.
Most puzzles were similar and it does take time to realize the importance of "Sense" and how it lets you know you are not quite done with this puzzle. Getting all the STEAM achievements is the hardest part. You must assume every item has a purpose even if you cannot see what it is and so you must spend a great deal of time just going from place to place trying to make sense of say: a handgrenade. That said, search everywhere, leave no path untested and the achievements will be yours. Of course, I forgot the sniper rifle...I saw no reason beyond the achievement for that!
Final Verdict: A somber, sad and sometimes scary game (won't tell you where I jumped but I did) that is well worth the time if you like solving mysteries. 4 of 5 Stars.

There is a lot to like about this game - it is entirely Free To Play (no hidden fees to unlock any part of the game), it is fully-voiced by a well-chosen cast, and includes a likeable set of characters. The romance-options are varied and actually include more than the five incubi that the title and summary imply, and also allow for same-sex relationships (or no relationship at all, if the player is so inclined).The story itself, while necessarily making use of the most basic story-elements of the otome-genre, actually veers off the beaten track and delves into the realm of demons, devils and magic and shows some creative ideas as far as world-building is concerned. As for non-story-related features,
includes both a CG gallery, and a good range of Steam-Achievements to unlock.
is not perfect, of course. The art style could perhaps have done with more detail, and every now and then the differences in recording quality of the different voice actors becomes apparent. Additionally, while offering a number of directions to take the story in, passages can become repetitive and are sometimes copied word-for-word in various routes. (This becomes most obvious, if one only plays through the male LI's routes.)
Overall, however, the quality of this game far exceeded my expectations. (Although I tend to have lower expectations for FTP titles.) The title may be a bit corny, but it does hit the mark.  Otome is still a niche genre, both among Visual Novels, and in the West in general, so it's good to see original content. And despite some small kinks, the whole thing comes together well - the effort and love poured into this project is quite apparent.
There are also some DLCs available (and apparently more to come - though sadly not on Steam yet) with flexible pricing options, as well as a sequel, which is already out on Steam (not FTP).

When there's a game, and that game say, Company of Heroes 2 has a few nations that you play in a multiplayer based strategy, game then there's going to be diiferent ways of learning to play those nations.
But today we're not here to talk about COH2 we are here to talk about a little kid named Jimmy.  Now Jimmy is a little kid that just bought company of heroes 2 with his mom's credit card, and little Jimmy decides to go ahead and play his first multiplayer game as let's say, the Axis (Germany in this case).
Now Jimmy plays this and he picks up on the quick and fast paced aggressiveness of the Germans fairly quickly.  But next Jimmy decides to go play as on of the Allied powers (USSR this time).  But what Jimmy didn't realize is that maybe all nations weren't created for the same aggressive purpose as Germany was, so little Jimmy lost his second game of Company of Heroes 2, and decided to leave a bad review about the Allies being underpowered and the Germans being overpowered.  But in reality little butthurt Jimmy didn't give himself (and the Allies) the time they needed for him to create a strategy for him to roll over the Germans with guerilla hit and run tactics, but instead jumped to conclusions and wrote an 'inconclusive' review.
I'll tell you why it's inconclusive. It's inconclusive because Jimmy's little (now butthurt) brain is only used to being aggressive and rushing his enemies with overwhelming force.  But Jimmy's brain doesn't think about how the little guy reacts to these attacks, (maybe not always in the 'right way') and Jimmy continues his attacks.
But.  When the little guy does develop a plan-and on Jimmy's 43rd game of playing Germany, when Jimmy finally thinks hes got it.  He sees it.  Penals with flamethrowers in an M3 half-track.  Jimmy thinks to himself "oh that's interesting", and hits it with a panzerfaust, and Jimmy's infantry is pinned by a nearby maxim.  Oh what's that? Here come the penals.  Jimmy finally loses.  On his 43rd straight game.  A 43 win streak and he is beaten.  Jimmy then writes another review that the Germans are now underpowered, and explains more about his double butthurtness (In both ends).
This process goes on for almost 3 years, with back and forth reviews about who is over/underpowered.  Relic desperately tries to find a medium and can't.  But that's the thing.  Shouldn't we as the players use an RTS as an RTS? Shouldn't we devise a plan or a strategy/strategies throughout the game? The answer is yes.  It is people like Jimmy who have wrecked this beautiful game.
I fully recommend this game and all of its glory 10/10-Pixo, 8.4/10-IGN, 8/10-PC Gamer, 4/5-Metacritic.

Software Inc is a superbly detailed simulator of excellent quality, depth, replayability and entetainment value. It's instantly clear that the developer poured his heart into this game. This game flawlessly blends the builder, software and sims genres. Software Inc leaps beyond the compeition. There's no arbitrary sliders or component micromanagement as seen in other games in the software/game development genre, but there's still plenty for the player to do. From designing, decorating and upgrading facilities, to choosing contracts to fulfill, parameters for developmet of software, pricing of that software, hiring the employees with the right personality traits and skills, building and managing teams, hiring staff to maintain your facilities, managing utility expenses, advertising, research, patenting, buying out competitors, ensuring your software and pricing is competitive, choosing distributors, becoming a distributor yourself, and much more. The other games of this genre are so basic as to seem as though they belong in arcades by comparison. You've been playing phone aps. This is a simultator build for a computer.

A Story About My Uncle combines two of my favorite aesthetics into one game: abstract runic designs and floating islands. I fell in love with the thumbnail art in the store was so hopeful that it would be good. Fortunately, those two things are great. You'll find one of the most awesome twilight skies in gaming with waterfalls dressing floating islands and runic symbols illuminating decorating the landscape. Some of the foliage looks out of place, like two different art styles came together in the same painting, and the character models and animation are poor. With that, much of the voice acting could be better and the audio could be cleaner so that voices sound like they are coming from characters and not being read into a mic, complete with faint mic hiss. These gripes are present but not enough to dramatically affect my enjoyment of the game.
The gameplay simply involves getting from point A to point B using a grappling hook, power jumps, and a pair of rocket boots. The grappling hook pulls you towards your target rather than swinging, so you have to release early and use your air control to go around the rock you are flying towards to keep your momentum up. There is no demand to move quickly, like a time limit or grading system, so you can take the game as fast or slow as you want, but I found trying to go as fast and far as possible to be the most fun. Howver, there is a distinct feeling of loss of momentum when connecting with a new grapple, which is immensely dissatisfying and can be frustrating, especially when doing time trials. Furthermore, what feels like inconsistent physics and even grappling distance can make determined time trial runs immensely frustrating. Taken at one's own pace, ASAMY is brilliant, but when going for a fast time, little details can become massive pains.
This game inspired a feeling in me no other game has really elicited: trust. Trust that when I throw myself into a void, that there will be something for me to grab hold of. I quickly, confidently, yet desperately search for a floating rock, still falling, still knowing that it must be there. When I see it, I know that I can reach it and, even though I have no idea where it is taking me or where my next grapple point or recharge point will be, I trust that it will be there and fly through the air with determination. It is a remarkable sensation. I finished my first playthrough in about 2 hours, but I will go back through for the personal satisfaction of flying farther and doing better.

This game is basically a dungeon crawler in space. You have one ship to start out with and a crew of brave adventurers and your goal is to get some sensitive military data on the enemy mothership to your base. All the while you are being dogged by constant pursuit of the bad guys.
You have sectors and in each sector you have nodes. Each node you jump to has either a store, an encounter, or an event. These are boiled down to battles, escort missions, or choices. Game is pretty much risk-reward based on the choice encounters because you either risk a teammate for gain or you have the special action necessary to get it with no risk. Example would be coming across an alien ship and they are requesting assistance. If you have a member of that species crew on board or a unique tool on board your ship you can use it to get a successful encounter and some scrap or items. If not you figuratively roll the dice and the outcome is usually dog♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Throughout these adventures you are mean to make forward progress, so planning is key, because if you fall behind and get too greedy the rebel pursuit catches up and you are forced into rather tough confrontations early on which usually leads to failure. So your goal for every sector is make the most out of your limited turns and stock up on items, upgrades and crew.
As you get further along the enemies you encounter obviously become better equipped so you get a sense of struggle as you go along. I will say that your game will largely be determined a success or failure by about the second or third sector. If you are still struggling and taking lots of damage by the time the third sector comes along you may as well restart and I'll get to the reason why below.
At the end of all the sectors, provided you made it there, you will now be in the final sector where there is no rebel pursuit because you are literally at the mothership. It will travel in a linear course directly to your base to wipe it out. Your job is to intercept it. Problem. I will say that the game, up until this point, is actually childs play. The mothership is a three tiered boss fight that has, in my opinion, one of the most drastic swings in difficulty I've seen in a game. It will punish you if you are not 100% set up in a role. The weaponry and defensive capabilities of this ship are nuts. Multiple rooms quite spread out, isolated weapon systems, and the ability to cloak itself as well as fire immense damage in a volley make this thing a pure nightmare. In all honesty the subsequent battles with the other two stages almost aren't as bad as the first stage. So if you barely beat the first part, don't panick because most likely the rest of the fights will only be easier. But that first stage is just god awful.
Once you beat the game you start to unlock new ship layouts which offer different play styles, crew, and room patterns. New ships altogether can be unlocked when certain criteria are met, which lends to the games immense amount of replayability.
In short, it's well worth the money.

A unique approach to roguelikes, heavily based upon micromanaging your crew, there will always be a challenging run ahead of you that can go from a perfect run to instant destruction.
So here is some wisdom that will most likely help you survive :)
-Upgrade shields early. Seriously, its essential to survive (although mostly useless unless in pairs)
-Fire+open doors to space=no fire (or O2, upgrade at least once)
-Upgraded doors+venting O2=screw most boarding parties
-Weapons have different travel and refire rates, Ion goes slower - time your bursts
-Weapons can be reorganized, this changes what ions or damage knocks out. Vulcan first slot if you have it.
-If turtling the enemy crew to death instead of the ship is an option, it means more loot!
-A diverse crew gets you more blue options
-Zoltans provide power and can keep essential systems operating inside a nebula
-Engine gives dodge. So does cloak. You can dodge missiles
-Drones can be shot down randomly if they get in the way, this can be somewhat timed with practice
-Drones that fire upon incoming lasers and attack drones have a short cooldown. Burst is key, sacrificial drone optional.
The hacking drone can also be abused with this.
-Hack the hack is a valid tactic to keep you alive against the enemy flagship
For the rest, experience pays off, enjoy a surprisingly diverse gem.

First: YOU NEED TO PATCH THIS GAME IN ORDER TO PLAY IT. [This is 100% true for those of you using Windows 7, especially if you only have the Home Premium Edition.] If you are going to patch it, I recommend getting the True Patch Gold Edition. It includes all the previous patches that make a difference in playability, as well as improving the look  and of the game. You can easily find where to get this patch and how to install it with Google.
Second: If you are going to mod your game, do so after playing it through the first time so you can experience the game in its original form, as well as become familiar with the game controls. Why is this? Most mods make the game MUCH more challenging, in addition to lengthening the game itself with alternative disciplines, bloodlines/clans, and missions. The mod that I recommend is the Camarilla Edition. It includes previous patches and makes the game more "realistic" in terms of what a Vampire's bloodlust would be. You also get a whole slew of new costumes for your character, and more missions.
Third: This game, even though it is not lackluster in terms of graphics and general gameplay when compared to others, it had the makings of something great. Fans are what has made this game so great, since the developers were not actually able to finish the game entirely. So, now, since World of Darkness Online has been cancelled until further notice, this will be the only game with the Masquerade that fans will be able to enjoy.
So, don't purchase this game if you are looking for something graphically beautiful. Don't purchase it if you're looking for smooth gameplay....
Purchase this game if you like Vampires. Purchase it if you like adventure. And most importantly: purchase it if you like quirky characters.  Experience something that fans have made great.

An original and entertaining FPS though not without its minor flaws.  Sets up a bleak and frightening world that really draws you in through the setting, sound, and narrative.  Game is short, but felt it was long enough.  Story won't blow you away, but still felt unique amongst the overpopulated post-apocalyptic game settings out there.  Also a story of too grand of a scale probably would not mesh well with the atmosphere of hopelessless.
FPS mechanics are not the smoothest, but once you get the hang of them, they work well enough.

The Redux of
by Quicksilver is just what - in my opinion - the original needed.  Graphical upgrades, some redone voice work, and significant optimization fixes from the beefy 4A engine make the entire experience incredibly immersive as you partake in protagonist Artyom's journey to save his home in a post-apocalyptic Russian wasteland.
has a lot going for it.  The most apparent however, is the atmosphere.  It's on point 100% through the game.  This comes from a mix of great elements - graphically it's very impressive, the sound design is great, and well-done character voice acting (following TB's advice, played in Russian with English subtitles) makes it feel as though one is genuinely a part of the metro.  There's a dynamic shift in tone between the surface and the subway environments themselves, as one offers a usually bright but lifeless Moscow whereas the tunnels can be very eerie.  All locations however, felt tense above all else.  On the surface, one is pressured by the use of a gas mask of which filters determine how long one can stay above the surface - by expending filters or having it broken through combat.  Subway tunnels themselves contain all forms of life; irradiated spiders, Nazis, electrical anomalies and more.  All of which have a desire to kill you.  Tension is relieved at some subway stations, which allows the player to stock up on supplies and rest a little between particularly active story segments.
Furthermore, it should be said that the combat is
.  I'd say the shotguns in this game feel better than in any other game I've played.  There's a lot of weapon and enemy variety; you'll often have to change your playstyle as supplies dwindle or new foes arrive.  For example, most of the wildlife will want to rend you limb from limb - so a shotgun is good for that.  However dealing with Nazis is probably best with a silenced pistol.  There's more than one way to play through each level, which has provided me with some replayability to some aspect.
I think the last thing I'll add is an attention to detail.  This is a game that will often reward exploration by leaving filters in an overturned car, or hiding a key for a safe out of sight somewhere in a level.  The sound effect of collecting those materials feels
good, especially if you play on one of the higher difficulties where supplies are more limited.  One of which is ranger mode which I absolutely recommend you play through with once you're familiar with the controls and quicktime element events.  Ranger mode makes use of the great cues to put more responsibility on the player, heightening the immersion you'll experience.  There's a lot of them; Artyom's breathing will get raspy as he exhausts a filter, flashlights dim until recharged, blood must be wiped off your gas mask, weapon magazines need to be estimated before discarding, etc.
Now, that's not to say that
is without flaw.  The most common that I've seen others complaining about is how linear the game tends to play.  Now, I don't have any problems with linearity per sé, I think many narrative-driven games would fall flat on their face without a designated path for the player to take.
may prove that wrong.  However I think the problem here is that the story in and of itself is rather limited.  You're on more of a journey than going through a story, most of which is fleshed out further in
.  Without strong story or character developments, some players are definitely going to be put off by how the game proceeds.
I would say though, that I've got a gripe with some of the level design.  Being set underground for the most part, you're often playing through the game with a limited flashlight and a lighter.  Though there's a designated start and end to each segment, I often found myself getting lost on some of the more expansive areas.  One particular location on the surface has Artyom maneuvering through a building in the dark, where getting from said building back to the street is hidden under some stairs.  Sometimes it isn't easy to navigate around the levels, and the player may burn through some filters if they don't know where to go.
Otherwise I don't have much to complain about.  The game seems locked at a <90 FOV, which hurt my eyes after long periods, and I couldn't see results from after editing the .cfg file.  Artyom can feel bulky at times, and some platforming doesn't handle as well as it could.  Some controls (such as what to press during a QTE or a non-fatal takedown) are not listed under the options menu, so ranger mode really requires that the player knows what they're doing. Stealth is completely dependent on standing in the dark and not making too much noise, both of which can be very ambiguous at times.
I think
is absolutely worth your time if you like anything from the adventure, FPS, or post-apocalyptic genres.  It has a lot to offer if you're interested in a new adventure, just killin' Nazis, or simply want to bench-test your PC.  It runs well, feels good and at the end of the day can provide an 8-hr experience at a third of the price of most new titles.

The mouse cursor still tracks like it is on a 4:3 screen so moving up and down is normal but left and right movements of the cursor are just too fast.
I have 3 screens and WWP was playing in the centre screen.
Now the game menu runs in psudeo full screen which caused some issues.
When you move the mouse to the left or right of the game window you actually scroll on to the other screens that arent used in the game. You try to move the cursor back to the game screen and it sometimes blocks the cursor leaving it on the unused screen.
I had to move the cursor back and forth a few times and it eventually went back to the game screen. N.B. because the left and right scroll is accelerated due to the 4:3 stretch you can get the cursor to the middle screen but I actually had the cursor go from my left screen, past the WWP screen in the middle, and to my right screen because the cursor was so fast in the game screen.
Starting a game is just like it used to be on the original WWP but the stretched menus just don't look nice.
Once in a game it played just like it used to.
The updated sounds were nice but just didn't match the graphics.
The graphics are the same as the original WWP and the old soundbanks just fit better.
Moving the cursor off the screen isn't a problem during a game since moving the mouse will just move the camera or weapon selection cursor.
The game defaulted to my 2560x1440 graphics but the game didn't run like it was 60FPS.
It was a bit choppy and just seemed dated.
I quit the match changed the graphics to 1680x1050.
I loaded a match and it was smooth but still looked the same as WWP back in the day.
I quit WWP completely and saw that because I changed the game resolution to a lower resolution than my 2560x1440 desktop it had shifted all of my cursors that were on the lower part of the desktop up higher!
Luckily I have DesktopOK running so I can just restore the icons to their original positions easily but this is just rediculous.
This game was a rushed port, which is odd since they had delays, and I recommend only die hard Worms fans purchase it.
I didn't try online play and only had a quick few test solo games and it plays ok in lower resolutions but the implimentation of the game seems like it's still designed for Windows 95/98 or XP.
One other issue that I encountered was loading the game.
If you load the game and in the part with the developer Team 17 and Tick Tock names appear you click on a different screen the game screen will minimize but you can't restore it.
Alt-Tab doesn't show the game is running and I had to kill W2.exe with task manager to quit and then I reloaded the game.
There's just too many issues with the game and I think it should have been redesigned for Windows 7/8/10 not just ported like this.
Team 17 please release some major patches to fix everything that is broken so we can enjoy this game on our new computers without these issues.

RPG game design is blended incredibly well with rhythm gameplay to make a game unlike any other on the market. Would definitely recommend to anyone interested in RPGs who wants something a little different.

A different sort of rhythm game, Sequence manages to incorporate some RPG elements into the gameplay. Sequence is a pretty fun game with solid soundtracks. The player has to battle enemies to get drops to build more equipment that provides bonuses, build new spells, or build a key to the next level. When battling enemies, there are three columns that the player must pay attention to; defense, attack, and mana. You take damage every time you let a stroke through defense, you attack by using a spell and hitting everything in the sequence in the attack column, and you get mana to cast more spells by hitting strokes in the mana column. A combination of solid music, unique gameplay, and a fun experience at a low price makes this game a recommend.

I first bought Dying Light on my PS4 through a fake, secondary account, because I saw a bit of it and decided that it probably was worth my money. PS4 games in my country are always expensive, hence the fake account, but I really wanted to play this game. I already knew the devs because of Dead Island, one of my favorite games back then. So, I bought the game, played, loved it since the beginning. And about a week later my fake account was terminated. I was angry, of course, but damn I wanted to keep playing what I thought was the best game I could've bought for my console. So I surrendered to Sony and bought the original game disk. Finished it, did every secondary mission, challenges, quarantine zones, got a set of legendary weapons including a 3k dmg legendary Katana.
And later I heard about The Following DLC. I had built my own PC meanwhile, so I bought the game again on steam, and this time I went through the whole thing alongside a friend. And then I wondered why I hadn't done this back on the PS4. This game is the perfect zombie game so far, and the Techland guys are aware of this, still updating the game almost 3 years after initial release. Graphics are good, even for today's games, but they are quite recycled, although you can always expect this from RPGs like this one. Gameplay is awesome, you can go freerunning through Harran and behead thousands of zombies along the way without problems. The Story is a bit cliché, but it's enjoyable nonetheless, both main storyline and the Following. But what I find the most satisfying is grinding for weapons and mutilating any zombies that come across your path.
So, all in all, this game is fun from playing the story alone to murdering the entire zombie population of Harran with your friends.
Yes, I only did this review for the achievement. I don't care.
Dying Light's free running mechanics allow for the perfect open world experience with the right amount of freedom allowing the player to traverse the city of Haran as they please.

The game is from the creators of Magicka but on a higher budget, I believe. So it's the same style of above-camera view but the gameplay is some kind of starship troopers parody where you and your homies will do your best to bring MANAGED DEMOCRACY to every region on the galaxy. There are 3 different races of enemys which play unique and a ♥♥♥♥ton of diversified weapons, veichles, airstrikes, gadgets and stuff to poke around with.
