Personally I feel this game should be in every single persons library. It is honestly my favourite game on Steam. FTL is a top down 2D 'Better haul butt because the nasty Rebel scum are chasing me across the galaxy' game. I'll try get straight to the point about why you should acquire this masterpiece of a game.
Pros:
-Toaster friendly. Literally I have yet to find anyone who has said they cannot run it.
-PLENTY of ships to try unlock in the Vanilla version. Even when you have unlocked them you can still replay them and you could have a completely different experience.
-The ability to rename your crew members is vital for determining who you secretly want to die so you can replace them.
-Multiple species even in Vanilla.
Mantis are basically intergalactic raptors from Jurassic Park who'll mess up you/your enemies day.
Rockmen are your trusty tank.
Engi's are the kid you'd sit next to in school to get the answers from.
Zoltans always brighten up your day (Play it to get the pun)
Humans die quick...good.
Slugmen. Imagine Professor X from the X Men but in a 5/6 foot tall Slug body. Known to end sentences with 'ssssss'.
Lanius..my favourite. Metal-lusting monsters who take your breath away..literally.
-In game achievements.
-The game is actually funny, the dialogue can be intriguing, stressful or just so crudely fun all at the same time. I've been playing this game for over a year and i'm still finding new jokes and texts that I hadn't seen before.
-My Rockman is bigger than yours.
-Micromanagement. Weapons, Crew positions, Hacking, Teleporting, Mind Control, Drone Control, Cloaking and diverting power..all (in theory) can be done in a fraction of a second meaning you can stomp your enemies with tactics and basically the ability to adapt to any situation.
Bonus Pro:
-Mods. Sick of getting caught by the Rebels? There's a completely free mod that will disable them from chasing you so you can explore every jump in a solar system. There are also extra campaign mods, overhauls, new ships..the list is endless.
Just to be fair, here are what I'd consider its only flaws.
Cons:
-No saves. Doesn't personally bother me but be warned, if you die. You die. Then it's all the way back to the start.
-Some will find it boring, clearly those are Rebels in disguise.
-No steam achievements. Again, doesn't bother me but for those who are achievement hunting this isn't the game for you.
-Singleplayer only. I get why it is, the micro-management would only work for one person but a part of me does long for a multiplayer.
-Don't trust the Slugs.
-STAY. AWAY. FROM. SPACE. SPIDERS.
Not to be one of those people, but this game is a 10/10 and no, it has nothing to do with the giant Mantis that's standing behind me...send help.

If you're sick and tired of the cliche shooters we get recycled every year with nothing innovative, new or challenging, this game is for you.
Metro 2033 Redux offers a singleplayer story experience, that doesn't let gameplay gets in it's way.
Playing on any non-ranger difficulty will destroy the whole ''Metro'' experience and will be less fun and challenging than playing on a Ranger difficulty.
It's one of the first games (to my knowledge) that does difficulty well, the ranger difficulty not only makes the enemies deal significant more damage, but you do aswell!
Giving you a more realistic feeling to how much damage you can take. To me it gave me the feeling like i was playing on insurgency, arma difficulty even though you can take more hits than in those games.
And the HUD is not cluttered with UI (infact there's almost no UI).
When you progress through the game you will encounter new enemies, weapons and environments that are really wel designed.
You're not just given two weapons that you'll have to old and only being able to pick up enemy weapons. But at so often You can customize your weapons at a shop or trade them in or sell them. Since ammo can be scarce you are often forced to pick up a new weapon, just because you weren't too carefull enough about your ammo count.
Factory ammunition is used as currency but can also be used as actual ammo, incase you don't have any ammo left.
You will go from peacefull environments, directly into hostile environments encountering beast and man alike. Fighting humans has a more stealthy aproach, while fighting beasts or mutants can/will result into waves of enemies coming to you.
Tips:
To get the full ''Metro'' experience as stated before I highly recommend any ranger difficulty. But also to play with the russian language and subs enabled, you may have to get used to it. But I find it no problem in reading subs and playing the game at once.
Also if you're encountering performance problems, try lowering SSAO.

This is an excerpt from:
, a book from 1725 published by the end of the 3rd Polo-Indonesian War by an unknown author. This has been roughly translated from Polish, and may be biased.
"The Polish were greatly humiliated by the loss of yet another war with the Indonesians. In a statement from General Hernan Cortes, 'Indonesia is a stinking country full of fat, rice-eating people. Poland is glad to be fighting them, despite the loss on each of the three wars. The moment of glory that every loyal Pole is looking forward to is when the Polish army finally cuts off the head of Gajah Mada.' This demonstrates the nationalistic fervor that every Pole should have, and once Poland finally triumphs over the Indonesians is the moment Indonesia falls."
This next excerpt is from:
, a book from 1737, published a decade after the end of the 3rd Polo-Indonesian war. Authored by Gajah Mada.
"The noise of battle was overwhelming. Blood covered my body as I cleaved the head of another man by my sabre, splitting his skull in two. By the time the Knights of Jakarta charged the Winged Hussars, our losses were great. We lost two thousand men in that one skirmish alone, and over ten thousand others in the rest of the battle. While I had fought in the two other wars with Casimir, even engaging in personal combat with the man himself, I had never seen this much dead men. Deep inside me, I pledged to myself, never again. So, when Casimir offered me 25 000 Indogold every 6 years for peace, I took it immediately."
This last excerpt is from:
, a book from 1939, by a Polish Noble of Indonesian ancestry.
"The First Polo-Indonesian war was a war for Cahokia, the Polish allied city-state neighboring Siribaya, an Indonesian city, which Indonesia had invaded unsuccessfully. However, while the Polish army was humongous for its time, it was easily destroyed by Indonesian Kris Swordsmen. The shame of having to give up (Old) Lodz, what we now call Ayutthaya, kicked off the rivalry between Poland and Indonesia, which would last for centuries.
This rivalry culminated in the Second Polo-Indonesian war, or the Retaking of Old Lodz. This time, the Polish brought ten thousand men, the largest standing army at the time. The main goal was to take Ayutthaya, or Old Lodz. Yet again, the invasion was foiled by Kris Swordsmen and catapults, the Polish army having to live in shame until their army recovered.
This resulted in the 3rd Polo-Indonesian war, where the Polish Winged Hussars and Kievan Impis invaded the border to Siribaya. This was met with some success, making Indonesia the weakest nation in terms of military, but was met with failure yet again due to new Indonesian technology, such as cannons, entering the battlefield. This war was much longer than the previous two, lasting 40 years.
The shame of the Poles was great after losing three consecutive wars at full strength, and this shame culminated in the 4th Polo-Indonesian war. Like before, the Polish were the aggressor, but this is the last time they ever did.
The 5th Polo-Indonesian war was a war for Ethiopia. It started with the conference of 1887 between Gajah Mada and Haile Sellasie, both discussing and agreeing to make a possible invasion of Poland.
This invasion was set to happen in 1897, a decade after. However, two years before that, Poland invaded Ethiopia. Two years later, Indonesia invaded Poland by 1897, coming close to Warsaw once again. In the peace treaty, (New) Lodz, a colony close to the South Pole, had to be ceded to Indonesia, which soon became New Ayutthaya.
However, even if the war had ended, Ethiopia was still at war with Poland, with the recent  peace allowing Poland to focus on one front. Soon after, Ethiopia was invaded by Arabia to the north. This caused Poland to push even harder. Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, was soon taken by Poland. Harar, Ethiopia's second most populous city was taken by Arabia.
In immediate retaliation against Poland for capturing Addis Ababa, Indonesia declared war, starting the 6th war, known to both Poles and Indonesians as 'The Great War', which started in 1913 and ended 25 years later in 1938.
The Great War is arguably the deadliest of them all, killing 300 million people over the course of a quarter century. Numerous offensives killed millions, and it was the first to incorporate deadly trench warfare in the first 10 years. Winged Hussars were still in service at the time, which drove the Indonesians to make a trench square, a modern twist on the classic square formation.
By 1937, Warsaw was captured by Indonesians.
By 1938, after a few offensives into the province of Poznan, the treaty of Wroclaw was signed, with Poland ceding Warsaw to Indonesia and Addis Ababa back to Ethiopia.
This war was the greatest shame of Poland, and effectively broke the nation in spirit and in economy. Millions of Poles and Indonesians dead, and even a few thousand Ethiopians from the Polish and Indonesian Foreign Legions, all for vengeance."

The short version:  buy it if it's on sale.  It's a well-conceived game, but some things feel like they were missing on delivery.
The long version:
This game is something of a first-person puzzle/mystery game.  You play the part of a private/paranormal investigator that has been called to a remote, sleepy town by the titular character, Ethan Carter.  You take control of this character as he has arrived on foot by following the abandoned railway tracks.  As you draw nearer to Ethan's location, you have to solve various puzzles and mysteries that help to describe the events surrounding the remote location and its run-down condition.
The game looks beautiful, and the world is impressive to look at.  As you walk about you'll be treated to many screenshot-worthy views.  They made the world relatively easy to traverse and understand, although there are a few nooks and dead-ends that seem like they could have contained some sort of content, but didn't.  There are also several rooms that are plunged into pitch darkness, and it feels like you're being shoed out of a room that had to be put into the floorplan, but didn't have any significance to the game's plot.  There are also at least one building that you can enter, but has disappointingly little content.
The puzzles are interesting, but not challenging.  The player character has the ability to sense things through the spirit world.  When you touch a location of apparent interest, words will play across the screen, representing the detective's musings about what happened.  If you must find a puzzle piece, the word for the object will float on the screen and allow you to visualize where it is, and what direction it is from where you are standing.  On the one hand, without such a feature, key items would be quite difficult to find in the world.  On the other hand, it feels like a better tool could have been given to the player to reward some sort of deductive thinking.
The game also ends rather quickly.  For a player like myself that enjoys exploration, I found that I had already naturally unlocked the "extra" content simply by scouring each area as I proceeded.  The content is named "unfinished story," which seems to prove the notion that this game isn't quite complete.
The ending is interesting, but the twist felt somewhat unsatisfying, and even discredits most of the discoveries earlier in the game.  We're robbed of the truths we have been uncovering and given a more dull, realistic one.
This game is worth an afternoon of playtime, but cannot offer much more.  With that in mind, if you enjoy first-person mystery games, there will be enjoyable moments in store.  Hopefully that will help you make your decision about this game.

This is a fine example of interactive art and storytelling!
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter (reviewed as the Redux version) is not a traditional game but closer to the interactive storytelling and exploration found in Adventure games.  There is one glaring difference from traditional Adventure games and Ethan Carter: the visuals.  The visuals are breathtaking and so photorealistic you will continually be in awe regardless if you are looking at light shafts, grains of sand, or cowebs.
One might say, why are such visuals required for a game like this?  Immersion.  There are two goals of this game: a great  immersive developing story (or story of stories.)
For my rating scheme, I definitely rank this amoung the highest of interactive stories.  Take one part Penumbra, one part Far Cry (with no action), and layer in a fancy detective like Sherlock Holmes or L.A. Noire and you roughly define this game.  For some, that may not be a good mix.  For others, who like exploring and discovering things on their own, it is a perfect blend.  There is no way for me to compare it to others as there are so few games like this.
Albiet the game is short, which took me about 4 hours, you could definitely complete it in less with less exploration.  I also ran into zero bugs.  The story, "puzzles", visuals, and voice acting are definitely great.  I can't wait to see more from this very small developer (the Astronauts) as they know how to execute this genre well.

Do I recommend this game? Depends on what you're purchasing it for. I'll keep my post plain and simple.
If you're looking for online competitive play, I do NOT recommend it. as countless others have said, this is an incredibly huge cash grab. It's been turned in to a pay to win game, in the most literal sense. I challenged a friend who hadn't played COH in any capacity, but is familiar with RTS games (not the greatest player, not the worst, middle of the road). Without mods of any sort (using both OKW/US and British expansions), we sparred. He had access to buyable commanders, I had what was unlocked via playing (level 90, no prestige). He slaughtered me simply by having more potent commanders.
Now, if you're interested in this game looking to modify it and play with friends against A.I., then it has the potential to become a fun game.  The community had to take this game down to it's basics, rebalance everything, and basically modify the game very close to not resembling the original game to make it playable.
The "single player" side of this game seems like an afterthought. It's nothing special, and leaves no lasting impact, or knowledge that can transfer over in to multiplayer like the original game did.
TL;DR: Don't buy for a competitive online experience, play against A.I. on a heavily modified version of the game. Don't purchase this game for singleplayer content.

Personally I feel this game should be in every single persons library. It is honestly my favourite game on Steam. FTL is a top down 2D 'Better haul butt because the nasty Rebel scum are chasing me across the galaxy' game. I'll try get straight to the point about why you should acquire this masterpiece of a game.
Pros:
-Toaster friendly. Literally I have yet to find anyone who has said they cannot run it.
-PLENTY of ships to try unlock in the Vanilla version. Even when you have unlocked them you can still replay them and you could have a completely different experience.
-The ability to rename your crew members is vital for determining who you secretly want to die so you can replace them.
-Multiple species even in Vanilla.
Mantis are basically intergalactic raptors from Jurassic Park who'll mess up you/your enemies day.
Rockmen are your trusty tank.
Engi's are the kid you'd sit next to in school to get the answers from.
Zoltans always brighten up your day (Play it to get the pun)
Humans die quick...good.
Slugmen. Imagine Professor X from the X Men but in a 5/6 foot tall Slug body. Known to end sentences with 'ssssss'.
Lanius..my favourite. Metal-lusting monsters who take your breath away..literally.
-In game achievements.
-The game is actually funny, the dialogue can be intriguing, stressful or just so crudely fun all at the same time. I've been playing this game for over a year and i'm still finding new jokes and texts that I hadn't seen before.
-My Rockman is bigger than yours.
-Micromanagement. Weapons, Crew positions, Hacking, Teleporting, Mind Control, Drone Control, Cloaking and diverting power..all (in theory) can be done in a fraction of a second meaning you can stomp your enemies with tactics and basically the ability to adapt to any situation.
Bonus Pro:
-Mods. Sick of getting caught by the Rebels? There's a completely free mod that will disable them from chasing you so you can explore every jump in a solar system. There are also extra campaign mods, overhauls, new ships..the list is endless.
Just to be fair, here are what I'd consider its only flaws.
Cons:
-No saves. Doesn't personally bother me but be warned, if you die. You die. Then it's all the way back to the start.
-Some will find it boring, clearly those are Rebels in disguise.
-No steam achievements. Again, doesn't bother me but for those who are achievement hunting this isn't the game for you.

Metro 2033 is an atmospheric first person shooter with survival and stealth elements. It's based on popular Russian book with the same name. You play as Artyom, a young man who needs to fight his way through the ruined metro tunnels and streets of post-apocalyptic Moscow. This Redux edition is a remastered version of the original Metro 2033 ported to a newer engine.
The custom engine used in the Metro games is quite impressive visually and this redux version looks great for the most part. Unfortunately the lighting model is quite simple and the shadows often look dated. Some of the facial animations are pretty low quality too.
The game also defaults to an extremely narrow FOV. The FOV can only be adjusted through a config file and using a non-default FOV will lead to some visual glitches.
The sound effects are pretty decent for the most part. Some weapons sound quite weak, however (the flamethrower in particular is just terrible). The sound track is rather forgettable as well and the English voice acting is truly dreadful. The Russian voices are much better and fit the setting much better. Too bad a lot of the NPC chatter doesn't have subtitles at all.
The survival elements in Metro 2033 are well done. You need to scrounge for ammo and supplies and both are often in short supply. Too bad this was pretty much the only aspect of Metro 2033 gameplay I actually liked.
The game features some of my most hated elements in an FPS game, including extremely linear levels, quick time events, lack of manual saves and terrible enemy AI. It's therefore not very surprising I didn't enjoy the game that much.
The levels themselves are awfully linear and full of invisible walls. This is understandable enough when you are in the actual metro tunnels, but rather annoying when you are exploring the ruined streets and buildings. The game even has some terrible rail shooter sections.
Neither normal combat nor stealth is particularly enjoyable either. Stealth gameplay is extremely simple and not particularly enjoyable. Combat isn't much better due to poor controls and abyssmal AI. The human enemies are especially bad as they will happily get stuck in obstacles and doorways. Mutant enemies fare a little better, mainly because you normally fight them in fixed areas.
The lack of manual saves is also a major annoyance, particularly since many of the checkpoints are poorly placed. And finally, the game does include a few QTEs just to make things extra annoying.
The game does provide a decent level of challenge on Survival/Normal difficulty. Rather interestingly the game does allow you to pick between two different playstyles, Survival and Spartan. The Survival is closer to the original Metro 2033 experience whereas Spartan provides more action-oriented gameplay with less focus on survival elements and stealth.
The controls are pretty bad with a mouse and keyboard. The mouse sensitivity is implemented poorly and the rather annoying mouse acceleration can only be adjusted through a config file. The game also lacks many important hotkeys and having to pick secondary weapons through the weapon wheel is a major pain. Overall I found the whole minimalistic and "immersive" UI rather tedious and annoying.
The setting itself is great, as should be expected from a game based on a popular book. Too bad the actual writing isn't very good. I'm guessing the poor English translation is to blame here.
The game is quite buggy. Enemies will walk through doors and even walls and on several occasions story scripts didn't fire properly. There are also some odd issues with the audio mixing.
Metro 2033 has nice visuals, great atmosphere and an interesting setting. Too bad the gameplay is pretty terrible and the game in general is quite unpolished. I know the game has its fans, but personally I wouldn't recommend it.

King Arthur's Gold is a medieval combat game made by the same game company responsible for the 2D shooter, Soldat. It's a polished game, both single and multiplayer, which really shines in large battles, where the action is fast and fluid. Movement in this game is quick, responsive, and tactile. This allows you to vary your attacks greatly between jumping off a roof and landing on an offenders head as an archer... All the way to doing a slash after running up the wall as a knight, generating momentum and height to help your swing. The building in this game is intuitive, but also has a range of depth, if you are smart enough and have the resources you might even find yourself building upside-down spike traps, trampolines lining the bottom, and springing expectant enemies into an overhead trap block section, to be impaled. All in all, if you enjoy games in which you can build and destroy the entire battlefield to change the course of a game, and not just (for instance) one specific building per levelution, KAG might be for you. A solid 8/10.

Probably the best top down twin stick shooter co op action out there. I'm surprised it's not more popular than it already is.
GOOD
+ Great diverse gameplay - 3 alien races to fight, 4 player slots that can be filled by local or online friends (or online matchmaking), 12 mission levels of difficulty, multiple objective types, dozens of weapons and abilities to unlock (through mission progression) and upgrade (by picking up research samples)
+ Good balance of choice in strategies and loadouts - while some weapons and abilities (or stratagems) are better than others, none of them are OP and most of them are quite useful in certain situations
+ Emphasis on teamwork - mid to high level missions become way too tough for solo play, and 4 players using the same screen with friendly fire on means that everyone either learns to properly cooperate or dies repeatedly
+ Quite hilarious - think of Magicka in a Starship Troopers setting
+ Endless replay value - missions are procedurally generated, enemies are endless and all individual players contribute their efforts to a global war effort (that can be won or lost, depending on player performance) - this is a game you can play long term in quick short sessions
+ Nice DLCs - all of them add nice weapons and stratagem packs that expand the already diverse base game
BAD
- While you are encouraged to cooperate with online players as best you can, the in-game reputation system doesn't really add up to anything - all the positive and/or negative feedback you get expires after a week, so why bother?
- There's also unfortunately a drop-off point where all samples become pointless (after completing all upgrades) and they'll just keep up adding in your inventory (especially due to group play) for nothing
In short, a must buy for 4 player gaming sessions.

This is an excerpt from:
, a book from 1725 published by the end of the 3rd Polo-Indonesian War by an unknown author. This has been roughly translated from Polish, and may be biased.
"The Polish were greatly humiliated by the loss of yet another war with the Indonesians. In a statement from General Hernan Cortes, 'Indonesia is a stinking country full of fat, rice-eating people. Poland is glad to be fighting them, despite the loss on each of the three wars. The moment of glory that every loyal Pole is looking forward to is when the Polish army finally cuts off the head of Gajah Mada.' This demonstrates the nationalistic fervor that every Pole should have, and once Poland finally triumphs over the Indonesians is the moment Indonesia falls."
This next excerpt is from:
, a book from 1737, published a decade after the end of the 3rd Polo-Indonesian war. Authored by Gajah Mada.
"The noise of battle was overwhelming. Blood covered my body as I cleaved the head of another man by my sabre, splitting his skull in two. By the time the Knights of Jakarta charged the Winged Hussars, our losses were great. We lost two thousand men in that one skirmish alone, and over ten thousand others in the rest of the battle. While I had fought in the two other wars with Casimir, even engaging in personal combat with the man himself, I had never seen this much dead men. Deep inside me, I pledged to myself, never again. So, when Casimir offered me 25 000 Indogold every 6 years for peace, I took it immediately."
This last excerpt is from:
, a book from 1939, by a Polish Noble of Indonesian ancestry.
"The First Polo-Indonesian war was a war for Cahokia, the Polish allied city-state neighboring Siribaya, an Indonesian city, which Indonesia had invaded unsuccessfully. However, while the Polish army was humongous for its time, it was easily destroyed by Indonesian Kris Swordsmen. The shame of having to give up (Old) Lodz, what we now call Ayutthaya, kicked off the rivalry between Poland and Indonesia, which would last for centuries.
This rivalry culminated in the Second Polo-Indonesian war, or the Retaking of Old Lodz. This time, the Polish brought ten thousand men, the largest standing army at the time. The main goal was to take Ayutthaya, or Old Lodz. Yet again, the invasion was foiled by Kris Swordsmen and catapults, the Polish army having to live in shame until their army recovered.
This resulted in the 3rd Polo-Indonesian war, where the Polish Winged Hussars and Kievan Impis invaded the border to Siribaya. This was met with some success, making Indonesia the weakest nation in terms of military, but was met with failure yet again due to new Indonesian technology, such as cannons, entering the battlefield. This war was much longer than the previous two, lasting 40 years.
The shame of the Poles was great after losing three consecutive wars at full strength, and this shame culminated in the 4th Polo-Indonesian war. Like before, the Polish were the aggressor, but this is the last time they ever did.
The 5th Polo-Indonesian war was a war for Ethiopia. It started with the conference of 1887 between Gajah Mada and Haile Sellasie, both discussing and agreeing to make a possible invasion of Poland.
This invasion was set to happen in 1897, a decade after. However, two years before that, Poland invaded Ethiopia. Two years later, Indonesia invaded Poland by 1897, coming close to Warsaw once again. In the peace treaty, (New) Lodz, a colony close to the South Pole, had to be ceded to Indonesia, which soon became New Ayutthaya.
However, even if the war had ended, Ethiopia was still at war with Poland, with the recent  peace allowing Poland to focus on one front. Soon after, Ethiopia was invaded by Arabia to the north. This caused Poland to push even harder. Addis Ababa, the Ethiopian capital, was soon taken by Poland. Harar, Ethiopia's second most populous city was taken by Arabia.
In immediate retaliation against Poland for capturing Addis Ababa, Indonesia declared war, starting the 6th war, known to both Poles and Indonesians as 'The Great War', which started in 1913 and ended 25 years later in 1938.
The Great War is arguably the deadliest of them all, killing 300 million people over the course of a quarter century. Numerous offensives killed millions, and it was the first to incorporate deadly trench warfare in the first 10 years. Winged Hussars were still in service at the time, which drove the Indonesians to make a trench square, a modern twist on the classic square formation.
By 1937, Warsaw was captured by Indonesians.
By 1938, after a few offensives into the province of Poznan, the treaty of Wroclaw was signed, with Poland ceding Warsaw to Indonesia and Addis Ababa back to Ethiopia.
This war was the greatest shame of Poland, and effectively broke the nation in spirit and in economy. Millions of Poles and Indonesians dead, and even a few thousand Ethiopians from the Polish and Indonesian Foreign Legions, all for vengeance."

Now having an idea of what I was supposed to be doing, I could focus on what the game had to offer, and it was beautiful.
The game is full of picturesque landscapes and stunning scenes to look at. You won't even need to try to keep an eye out for these scenic views, they just naturally pop out as you're wandering around following the story, so you won't miss out on anything if you're not specifically looking for the best viewing positions. The screenshots shown on the store page really don't do it justice. Complimenting the gorgous visuals is an excellent soundtrack. It seemed to fit perfectly with what I was seeing, seamlessly transitioning from no music, to a calm serenade, to a haunting background track without you really noticing.
The story was engaging, and I loved being a part of piecing the scenes together and then watching it unfold. It was a fantastic experience overall, my only gripe was the lack of instruction, but in hindsight I imagine adding any kind of tutorial or instruction to the start of the game would only ruin the immersion so it's probably better without.
Highly recommended as a way to keep yourself entertained for a few hours on a lazy weekend.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter revolves about finding the boy (Ethan) who wants to be a writer - so he creates many interesting supernatural short stories. Who are you, you might ask - let's say that doesn't matter. You are there to investigate what happened with Ethan and his family that got possessed by evil.
What distinguish this game from other walking simulators, is definitely the graphics, sounds and music. It's made so delicately that you'll enjoy every second walking in the Red Creek Valley. And if you are more impatient or just want to quickly return somewhere, don't worry, developers allowed you to sprint (this is not Dear Esther). The nature around you feels like modded Skyrim that even on newest desktop builds run on low FPS, but Unreal Engine 4 makes a difference and this game, since the Redux edition that you get for free, runs great!
The gameplay itself is casual, most of the time you'll be exploring the valley, with interludes of dark memories of Carter family, and interludes where Ethan's short stories become real. Those stories are really nice and there's the one that stands out from the others - I won't spoil much, I'll just say that the Lovecraftian horror fans will get excited.
What's worse is the length of the game, the game offers about 3 hours of entertainment with getting all achievements, and not much replayability. That fact is compensated with the beautiful environment and precious soundtrack. In the end it's all about your priorities, if you prefer the environment and story, or the length.
I understand if you don't want to pay 19 euros for a short walking simulator but trust me - if you will see it on sale, buy it. It's a great experience.

Performance:
* no SLI support
* ran at 1440p60fps (vsync on) on a (single) gtx 980, with about 50-60% utilization with everything maxed.
Pros:
* actually looks really damn nice considering it's an indie game and the cheap price
* the grapple/swing mechanics are a lot of fun
* the large expansive world (sometimes got too large and overwhelming)
* no loading screens
* a fair bit of hidden secrets and story that you have to zoom in to see and understand (in the first room, if you look around, you can see the plot synopsis of what's going to happen in the next 5 mins, written on a few papers scattered around)
* the voice acting for the most part was great.
* has an FOV slider! (goes from 60-120, I played it at 100 just fine.)
Neutral:
* completed it in about 4 to 4.5 hours. Probably could have gotten through it in 3 if I wasn't screwing around so much.
* seemed that there were multiple ways to get through several of the levels.
* no map or minimap, easy to get lost and not know where to go, but more realistic I guess.
* need a mouse and keyboard to play. it's a precision first person shooter/action platformer, you need to be able to make fast and accurate shots to the next grapple area while freefalling down.
* mouse acceleration on by default, but easy to turn off in the options.
* the game gets dark and hard to see sometimes, but makes for a great appeal when you fall down to the dark abyss after you miss a grapple. Adjustable gamma in options, but that's not enough.
* graphics options are just acceptable imo. (
)
Cons:
* not too much replayability (aside from trying to complete the levels faster/with fewer hooks)
* there were several times I got confused and had no idea where I was going or where the next objective was. Several times I just jumped off the cliff without knowing where the next grapple spot was.
* one time during the story, your "double jump" gets arbitrarily broken and unusable, only to get fixed in the next zone.
* there is no obvious way to make a followup. The way the game ends makes it obvious that it's a standalone game, which is a shame, I want to explore more of the wonderful world that they built and fly around in the air more.
It's a great little piece that more people should play. Perhaps not at the full ($13-ish), but if you pick it up for $4 or less, then absolutely get it. It's gone down to $2 a few times on other sites (check isthereanydeal) and for that price you can't afford to not get this game.

A fun tower defense game where the towers are replaced by heroes that you level up. The story scenes aren't the best, but the gameplay is good. For $1.50 on sale, anyone that enjoys tower defense should get it.

Seeing how the game was flash based and not too heavy on visual details, I was skeptical about this game. I usually compare tower defense and flash to something on Kongregate, but I was pleasantly surprised by the quality. Its a Tower-Defense RPG hybrid where your 'towers' level up as you progress through the maps. Each stage has extra difficulties to come back to for additional challenge and rewards through unique armor or weapons that you can give to your teammates. You can change the AI for targeting, which comes in handy during challenge stages and boss fights. When you're done with the game, you can also replay the game with New Game+ and unlock your previous team (while facing minions with new abilities, and unlocking unique item powers). The story isn't anything new, but the characters are engaging enough to let that slide. The music isn't anything to write home about, but it strays from being too annoying like most flash looped music (the title screen being the exception).
If you like Tower Defense games, Defender's Quest is polished in the right places and worth the weight, especially on sale.

Let me premise by saying that I'm a fan of Tower Defense game and purchased this game at 90% off for a grand total of $1.49, as such, this game was an absolute steal!
The game feels well paced, making sure you have the ability to beat the next level with adequate skill, but rewards you for taking the time to perfect a level. If you're looking for a deeper challenge, you can replay earlier levels at a higher difficulty, or if you're feeling stuck or underpowered you have the option to go back a few levels until you're prepared to advance.
The actual game itself revolves around a band of characters replete with customizable appearances, skills, invetory, and a set base class that allows for a wide variety of playstyles and setups. The actual mechanics of the game are designed to allow you to either place your towers (units) down and work from there, or micromanage them for greater effect. As you progress you'll be unlocking spells to engage you further and allow for more in depth strategy.
That all being said, I find myself falling most in love with the games charming and quirky characters that really sell the rather contrived story. Through the course of the game you'll meet a wide variety of personalites that play off of each other with a dry sense of humor and extremely comedic results. They each feel consistant and defined, and it's always a pleasure to see how they interact when they're not dealing with the plot. Even the main character has witty dialogue and interplay with the party, making you feel legitimately connected to people who are essentially stationary sources of damage in the actual game.
The only point that could be held against it is the fact that the graphics and art style feel 'cheap'. The world map and actual gameplay is set in the old sprite style that we've all seen for the past few decades, and it makes the game feel dated. When you're watching the games cutscenes, you're stuck looking at a few stationary characters that look like the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ combination of paper cutouts and Protector characters. It's nice that they took the time to set up full cutscenes and dialogue, but the graphics just aren't there.
As it stands, I'd say that this game is a real gem. On sale for 90% I'd say 'buy it' every time no matter who you are. If you find it on sale for anything over 25%, at least give it a good look, hopefully you'll like what you see. For the full price of $15, it's still a great game for fans of the genre.

If your aren't already convinced by the wealth of positive reviews then this won't do much more, but I want to jump on the positive review train to give this game some extra love, because it definitely deserves it!
What makes this game stand out is the detail.  You get a significant level control over your company, from high level strategy and approach down to which month a particular employee gets to go on holiday.  The level of control can seem daunting at first, but there are helpful tutorials in game and out, and once you have the basics down the mechanics provide a lot of freedom for the direction in which you would like to go.  The graphics are simple, but the style is effective, and with this comes a low load on performance requirements meaning accessibility for older or lower powered systems is almost a guarantee!
With a one man development team it does mean that stable updated can be slow going, but the developer regular releases his testing branch work via Steam betas, and is always keen to listen and learn from players.  Communication is good, and players are rarely left in the dark about any near or planned developments, as the developer is always excited to share new ideas and clearly passionate about the project.
What this means is a great project, at a more than good price tag, great fun to play now, and a lot of exciting developments coming in the near future!!
TL;DR -
Fulfilling and enjoyable experience, with an excellent dev, absolutely worthy of support!

DDR/Frequency/Amplitude with an RPG twist.
If you have ever been a fan of rhythm games, particularly those by Harmonix, you (hopefully) have come across the Frequency/Amplitude series. With its rapid track-switching gameplay, it was a unique and underappreciated entry in gaming history. Now, Sequence takes the track switching mechanic, applies simple DDR-style controls, and turns it into a monster-fighting RPG. It might sound crazy, but this is probably one of the best genre hybrids since Puzzle Fighter or Bust-a Move.

I reallly enjoy rhythm games and this is an interesting take on the classic genre. I find the rpg elements flesh it out to make it an enjoyable experinece for a variety of gamers. I find the the controls are weird on keyboard, but that can be fixed if you use a controller. This means the game is more optimized for XBOX 360 controllers, so buyers beware if you only use keyboard.
Yeah, it's cool.
This is an amazing and addicting game. The graphics are wonderful.

If I had to describe Sequence in one word it would be this: Fun. But I'm not going describing it in one word. I'm going to describe it in as many words as I can--and--hopefully in the clearest way possible. As the trailers will tell you Sequence is a lot like a DDR game. It has a great mix of rhythm and rpg elements laced within 4.99 (and as I write this review, 1.99) dollars of pure fun. The games mechanics sound difficult at first but once you get a grasp of them it really is just like a dance stepping game (dance stepping...yeah). You have three different fields, Magic, Defense, and Mana that you must use to defend yourself against a selection of creative monsters and even more creative (or perhaps creative-er...if that were a word) bosses in order to solve four things: Where are you? Who took you to said where? Who is this chick talking to you over an intercom system? Why the heck is there an intercom system in what looks to be a tower straight from a fantasy game?
The games plot: You are a young man named Ky, a university student who was brought to some unknown world where each wrong move could essentially be your last. But not to worry though! A very slick talking female voice is there to help you through your adventure through conveluted tower. With her aid you'll hopefully beat all fo the bosses and get to the 7th floor of the tower and...well...that's all the game tells you.
One thing I will tell you though is if you are looking for closure this isn't the game for that. The ending to this game isn't bad--no I found it highly satisfying. But it felt very cliff hanger...y for a game that as of right now is just a one shot. I assume this is so it can have some kind of sequel. Something I personally have my fingers crossed for. The music is wonderful, I'd never heard of Ronald Jenkins before this game and let me tell you I'm glad I did. Go ahead and look up his music to get a taste of what you'll hear in-game.
As with any grinding rpg you may find yourself feeling a bit bored from the repetitive fights, forging of materials through recipies and other little minute chores you have to do in the game. But I personally believe the music is what helps bring it together. Nothing ever really FEELS like a chore in this game. The monsters are relatively balanced, after you defeat and gather what you need for a boss you will feel like top dog for a few brief moments before getting brought back down a peg or two from the next monster one floor up. The only complaint I have is that the particle effect is too much for my computer and has a tendency to lag and affect your rhythm. This could just be my computer though. The dialogue is very well versed and thought out. Smooth gameplay mechanics and you rarely feel any mistakes made is anything but your own.
And the item descriptions. Oh the item descriptions.
Needless to say, I have a bit of a bias for this game and I want anyone reading this to take that in terms with this review. This is a very niche kind of game. If you love DDR games you'll love this to death I'm sure. But I do recommend checking it out for its low price alone.
Update: This game still holds up. Though its 2010 culture references can seem a bit forced at times.

Sequence is an amazing music driven game with phenomenal dialogue lines and voice acting, the storyline is also very compelling. Totally worth the full price, I strongly recommend this game for everyone!

Sequence is a Hybrid of a Rhythm game and an RPG.
Every combat is done in the way of a rhythm game like, say, Guitar Hero. With each battle you gain experience, materials and equipment, which you can all use to become more powerful, and face harder enemies, progressing through the story.
That may or may not seem like it works for you, but trust me, they've done a damn fine job with it!
You're Ky, and you wake up in a Tower, with amnesia. Everything inside feels like a weird game in which you're but a pawn. You life is in danger, or so you're told, and so you fight for survival, learning about the place and its purposes on the way.
While the story did feel a bit cheesy for the most part, it did have a few cool ideas, and a few twists to keep it interesting. It's not the main focus on the game, but I think it added quite a lot of character to it.
There's not much in way of graphic style in this one.
The graphics consist mainly of hand drawn backgrounds and characters, with a bit of animation when they talk. It's not bad, by any means, just not something that you'll play this game for.
Even during the battles, each spell you cast (more on that later) only produces a few sparkles as visual effects, but it's just enough not to feel empty. All in all, it's very simple, and let's you focus on the gameplay, while maintaining an appealing look.
The only criticism I have of it is that certain spells will overload the screen with particles, obstructing necessary information.
Another thing, regarding the interface. Outside of battle it's nothing special, but it's certainly easy to navigate. But when in-battle, it gives you every bit of information necessary without having to look for it too hard. And this is a great since, since this game WILL challenge your multi-tasking abilities (in a good way!).
Good job on that! Keeping it simple, yet complete.
I would now talk about the music, but music and gameplay are directly tied in Sequence. So I'll try to summarize gameplay and then talk about its strengths and weaknesses.
As I said before, you're in a Tower. You're guided by Naia, who gives you recipes as you go along.
You go from floor to floor, with a Boss Fight in the end of each.
When you enter a floor, you'll be given recipes for Equipment, Spells, and a Key and Inhibitor for that floor. There are 3 enemies in each, which drop 3 different materials, for you to craft later. When you craft the key, you're able to unlock the door to the next floor, and fight the Guardian.
Your characters has Mana (to cast spells), Health, Defense (to lower the damage you take), and Offense (to increase the damage you deal through spells).
You can improve these either by leveling up, or by wearing different pieces of equipment. Equipment is mainly linear in its progression, without many sidegrades.
Trinkets, on the other hand, are a bit different. These can improve your spells' cost, their cooldown, make battles harder to improve item drops, etc. These are actually more tailored for different types of gameplay, and some have pretty cool effects.
Some you get by crafting, others you can get by enemy drops.
The Inhibitor is used to lower the Guardians' effects (more on that later).
Then, there are spells. You can craft them, and then have to learn them. How do you learn them? You play a certain track on the game, with an added challenge (which can be a note streak, or a given accuracy). These are carefuly designed, as they would be in Guitar Hero, with different button presses following the notes' pattern (to an extent, of course).
They weren't too hard, mostly. But the final one was way more challenging, but also very fun to play, so I won't complain.
This pretty much it for when you're outside the battles.
How are the battles, then?
Well, there will be arrows falling, to the beat, and you'll have to press them. Pretty simple. But that's not all, of course.
(There are single notes, or doubles. For these, you have 2 sets of "arrows" on the controller/keyboard, to make it easier, specially on a controller. It works really well, and you'll find yourself a master of it by the end, and it feels great! The game does a very good way to constantly challenge you, making you better, without being frustrating.)
In every battle, you have 3 screens you need to pay attention to.
One, is your Defense screen. Each arrow you miss here will damage you, so you need to keep an eye on it.
Another one is your Mana screen. This one has the same spell learning pattern, making it the closest to the song, with a lot more notes. Each failed note doesn't penalize you, but you gain one Mana for each note you strike, which is needed to cast spells.
Finally, you have your Spell screen. You have a spell wheel, with your different spells (you have a limited number that you choose outside the battles). Each has a different effect and costs more/less mana, with a bigger/lesser cooldown.
Each time you activate a spell, its notes will start dropping. The spell is cast if you strike them all. If you fail a single on, bye bye mana.
That's it, mostly. Your objective is to lower your opponent's life before he does yours. Every piece of information (damage dealt, received, mana, etc.) is easily visible to you, which is great.
You will be constantly switching between these 3 screens during the battles, which sometimes gets a bit chaotic at later stages, but never too bad. The whole game is a constant balance between when you can afford to take damage, when you need mana, and so on, rarely feeling stale!
With each enemy is a song associated, so you'll repeat some on them quite a lot for their items/experience, but it's not too grindy.
One more important aspect is the Guardians! Each one has a special ability, that'll mess you up, during their fight, and the fights in their floor.
These can go from obstructing your different screens (so that you need to be there to see what's happening) to accelerating the tempo of the songs, or the last one, that switches the arrows. This one was diabolical. Everything you had learned goes to hell, and you need to play everything in reverse. But it doesn't last long, so it's all good.
It's these differences that keep some of the battles very interesting, and you never know when it might throw you off of your comfort zone!
The music was done by DJPlaeskool and Ronald Jenkees. It's a mix of electronic/synth music, with a bit of rock. It's wasn't something I was into at the start of the game, but it started growing on me. I ended up enjoying the music quite a bit, although I won't listen to most of it outside the game.
Although, the last song, and so freaking epic... Man, I wasn't expecting that. That song had changes in tempo that worked great musically and from a gameplay standpoint! (It's called Piano Jam, search it on youtube). That one I'll be listening to for a while. Great job!
So, I enjoyed the music, but I do believe it lacks a bit in replayability comparatively with other rhythm games. But it's also a very unique and very well designed game. I ended up enjoying it way more than I expected, and it had many brilliant design choices.
There isn't much negative to say about it, really, aside from having to grind a bit, and perhaps looking a bit too simple. But even that didn't really lower the experience much for me.
I really enjoyed Sequence, and I think it does a great job of mixing the rhythmic combat and RPG elements.
One thing though, is that during the battles, while the notes do fall on the beat, there isn't as big of a connection to the notes and there is on the Mana screen (or the spell learning). Each spell has a pattern (with some random elements) that is independent of the song, and the enemies as well. So, it might not feel like like you're playing the music.

This is one of the deepest and most rewarding tycoon games that I have ever played. Unlike some other tycoon games that where fun such as planet coaster, this made you think about the business side of your company. I will admit that it took me a while to pick up on most of the finer details of the game (I would say about 20 hours or me figuring it out to really get good at it), but what kept me going and playing this game even though I was struggling and at the start not having much fun, was the fact that I saw the depth and potential of this title; I am very glad I stuck with it.  There are still several things that need to be polished or flushed-out, but even in its current state if you want a deeper tycoon game, then pick up this title.
Some tips: Just because your character is good at development (let's say 2D), he is not good at developing anything that is not his specialty (like audio). I assumed (wrongly) that if your character was strong in development he got a boost in the one you chose and a slight penalty in the others, not so. Albeit I think if you can design 3D in real life, that most of your skills would carry over to 2D, this game treats one like learning math, and one like learning English (just because you improve in one does not affect the other). Also managing team size is very important as 10 people working on a project might be less productive than a 2-man team.
Things the game needs to improve: wall placement tool is sometimes wonky and annoying. The stock market portion does not feel fleshed out. I also want set number of companies, it seems that if there are <21 companies the game just generates a new one. I want to buy up all the companies, or have some kind of end game.  For contract/deals I want to be able to issue them. For example, if I make an OS, I was to be able to go to another company and say hey for $x I will pay you to port your program to my OS, or make it exclusive to my OS, things that you do in real life. I also think the distribution system is still too wonky as the workload is high and you make no money, it is a loss leader from my experience. Also like most tycoon games, once you hit your rhythm it start to just snow ball, you struggle to make a million, then you explode to 5 million, then all of the sudden you are 50 million, and in the blink of an eye you are 200+ million.

Absolutely superb game. Dense atmosphere, a well realized world, and exellent writing make this game an underrated gem.
Its not perfect, but its pretty close. It fumbles a bit with combat, and has some frustrating levels here and there; but is an otherwise fantastic experience. It has good length, too; although it does end a bit abruptly.(The money started running out for the developers, sadly) One of the few versions of vampire lore in recent years that really does the source material justice. In short, if you like vampires or RPGs, this is THE definitive game.
UPDATE: I return to this review several years after my original playthrough, after replaying countless times and sampling a few of the lovely mods to elaborate on my original stances. This game is just short of being a masterpiece, and I'll tell you why.
Its potent atmosphere and twisted spirit brought to life by the exellent visual design, voice acting, and writing make it a thoroughly compelling experience. The characters and world are stunningly well realized and highly memorable, making perfect use of White Wolf's venerable tabletop-rpg property. It grips the player in a way few games can boast.
The replay value is extremely impressive, even to this day. The various clans play almost like different games. Whether you skulk the sewers as a grotesque Nosferatu, blend with society as a Toreador, or scream at stop signs as a Malkavian, every playthrough adapts to your choices and identity within the world. Just like any good RPG does.
But despite this, the key to the games appeal is slightly harder to quantify. To put simply and in irritating cliche;
The game bleeds passion. Every little detail, every little peculiar nuace reeks of a developer that genuinely loved their product. The game is filled with minute "Hey, wouldnt it be neat if we did this?" moments, like the aforementioned incident where the "crazy" vampire clan has an entire conversation with a stop sign. A completely optional and missable passing moment that speaks volumes about the attitude with which the game was developed.
I'll be brief with my criticisms, since I dont believe any of them are true deal-breakers. Its three things:
1. Combat. The combat has aged poorly and, while fun in short bursts, quickly grows tiresome.
2. Bugs. The game requires a community patch to be playable, and even then I have encountered odd bugs, glitches, and crashes.
3. The warrens.
Remember how I said that the combat is best enjoyed in quick bursts? Whoever designed the warrens level of the game clearly missed that memo. A labyrinthine combat mission that drags out far past its welcome.
BONUS ROUND: If you've played through the game a multitude of times and thirst for more, the Clan Quest mod is an exellent way of sparking new life into a playthrough.

I like this game, but I wouldn't recommend it over the original Company of Heroes.
As with nearly all major games today, this game suffers from its focus on DLC. The original Company of Heroes never felt incomplete in any area. Its Opposing Fronts expansion was a complete additional game with two new armies each with their own campaign with the same level of quality as the base game.
After purchasing Company of Heroes 2, it is obviously full of huge DLC holes. Even the DLC itself feels incomplete. The OWK, American, and British armies don't include their own campaigns. Except sort of for the Americans in the form of the additional DLC Ardennes Assault.
The core game is much less polished than the original. As an example, in the original Company of Heroes every unit had its own unique voice and dialog, including complete separate sets of dialog for if the unit was in or out of combat, if it was day or night, lightly or heavily damaged, and even for different types of weather (the expansion had some missions in the rain). In Company of Heroes 2 many units use only generic dialog, such as the Panther tank which doesn't seem to know it's a Panther and the Raketenwerfer which sometimes calls itself an MG-34 (it re-uses most of the MG-34 dialog for some reason). Kubelwagens ended up with no dialog for capturing territory (they just are silent as if they are not responding), which happened after a huge balance patch that completely changed the role of this unit from a suppression unit to a fast territory capture unit.
This leads to the next issue, where patches have had to completely rearrange parts of the gameplay rather than just fine-tune the balance. It's obvious that not enough time was spent planning and balancing the different armies. A recent patch even turned off the snowstorm weather effects in all multiplayer maps, even though this was one of the original hyped effects shown in the earliest trailers for the game.
Overall, Company of Heroes 2 feels like the original game with better graphics and worse armies. There are definitely some improvements, like the ability to have infantry jump over fences and the ability to tell vehicles to drive in reverse, but this still feels like something that could have been patched into the original.

Finally an early access game I don't regret
Other than some titles that feel like playable tech demos without actual game behind it, this one I enjoyed. I would really like for the devs to not add more features but to flesh out things that are already there. And I cannot stress enough that I did not experience a single crash or other hiccup during 50 hours of play (!!), but I also think the gameplay is unbalanced and ultimately not challenging at all.
Features
+ The core (building, forming teams, defining products, watch their progress) is fun!
+ You really feel like a software developer
- Hosting and defining different server farms is cool, but as of now not interesting. There are no impactul events like outages or spikes, total failures that ruin your work if you didnt plan for it. Have enough and forget about it.
- Distribution channels, insurance, company takeovers are clearly unfinished. Either the devs find a fun and meaningful way to include them or they should scrap them and focus on other things.
UI
+ Cloning tool work great, so building a multi-storey office is quite easy
+ Wall clock shows actual ingame time ;-)
+ I like the programming "animation". Looks legit
0 Graphic quality is okay for this type of game
- The game often does not provide the information I want
* Are Development taks assigned to SCM
* How well does an employee fit into teams (without assigning them first)
* How much does a team member contribute to the progress?
* How big an impact does the furniture/his skills/ actually have?
* Why does a product not sell?
- Or is cumbersome to use
* Porting multiple products to other OS
* Scrolling in lists to pick the correct team
Gameplay / Balancing - This might need the most work! (Played on hard btw)
- Outstanding quality products with every single feature in the book sell only a few copies, while the good game with only two features rakes in millions. It seems to only depend on your overall standing in that market segment
- 3D-Editors eventually sell to millions of customers grossing half a billion $ easily and while OS usually don't attract much customers, if they do that sort of ends the game. You can overtake all competitors within DAYS
- Competitors spamming the market with OS, yet its unclear what attracts customers to a specific OS. It's not a unique buquet of top notch software not available on other OS. Tried it.
- Full blown marketing offensive on all channels costs 6k + salaries ....
- Competitors pay you by the month to develop their stuff, so you are incentivies to keep finished work around till the last mont
- Customer decisions overall totally unclear. There are not multiple products with different features - Every product has every feature and of them has all the customers.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines was rushed and pushed out the door by Activision. As a result, the game is rather buggy, featuring shoddy AI, missing content, broken stealth mechanics, and other annoyances.
In spite of that, this is perhaps one of my favorite games I've ever played. This is an absolutely charming and underrated game.
It's a closed sandbox RPG: think Deus Ex (a masterpiece) but set in the modern world... and with vampires and other creatures of the night.
There are seven different vampire clans you can choose to be part of. Can't decide which one? Then take the quiz the game offers, I got the Tremere: the spellcasting mages that use blood as their mana. Allowing you to steal an opponent's blood from a distance or internally "boil" their blood until they explode into a visceral masterpiece. It's rather adorable, honestly.
The gameplay is similar to Deus Ex, an RPG first person action game with multiple choices affecting the story, thus each playthrough is different from the other.
There are multiple weapons to use: firearms, melee weapons, and your own clan skills are all fun to use. There is also a skill tree allowing you to customize and enchance your proficiency in certain categories, although many of the skills are rather useless save for a few circumstances.
The graphics aren't too shabby to be honest. This is the first game to use the Source engine (even before Half Life 2) and while dated by today's standards, is still a fairly nice game to look at. The facial animations in particular look great.
The atmosphere though is simply wonderful: the characters all feel real, the voice acting is well done, and this game's world just feels alive in its own undead way. The writing is top notch too, this is one of the funniest games I've ever played, and I still haven't started my second playthrough as a Malkavian!
The bugs I mentioned before? There are fanmade fixes for them (I recommend the unofficial patch), in fact there are a lot of mods available for this game. Proof of its quality.
Overall, despite its flaws, this is an awesome game that I recommend for anyone who enjoyed Deus Ex, or you really like vampires.

Not wanting to give away too much, the game has some vey mature and dark themes, which is something I really enjoyed about the game. Given the seedy setting of LA, there is a deep connection of the social issues the games presents that can be paralelles with those seen within our own modern society. There are several plot missions that relfect on such issues as  aids, discrimination, and violence. Showing that despite the dark humor this game has, there is also a variety of intellectual ideas woven into games tone.
Overall, despite the obivious graphical and technical short comings stated by other reviwers, this game is filled with charm and dark humor. While my opinion is rivaled greatly, I do not recommend Faster Than Light to the average gamer.
I like rogue-like games and I've played quite a few of them, but this one in perticular feels less like a game that is meant to be played and beaten and more like an RNG Luck based game. Now luck is obviously the main basis of all Rogue-like games (Binding of Issac, Downwell, Diehard Dungeon, etc.) But those games are played in short trails that can end fast but be replayed easily. FTL plays like a game about micromanaging and building yourself up, but when it's so easy to lose all the hard work it becomes frustrating to play.
In a good rogue-like, such as Binding of Issac, it's not hard to upgrade yourself and unlock content that makes the game easier and more replayable, but in FTL unlocking new ships or layouts of ships feels almost impossible. I feel like as though FTL should have more to it to make the game actually beatable after a few play-throughs instead of this grind and buy system. When the game can turn against your favor so easily, grinding makes it more difficult.
Now it's easy to tell people "Well it's supposed to be difficult, you're supposed to get good at it." which makes since in most games that have extreme difficulty curves, but those curves aren't all about how lucky you have to be. There's no real skill in such a heavily randomized game. I've seen debates on the game's "Easy" mode and how it is in fact not easy at all. People argued that easy is relative and how the game's settings of easy aren't that the game is easier to play and beat but instead easier to play and survive for longer. Now while this is true and it would be fine in other games, as I stated before, the game is somewhat designed to punish you for attempting to grind and explore.
In conclusion, I feel as though Faster Than Light is not a good rogue-like, yet it is a good game. I, however, do not recommend it due to it's heavily luck based and "grind to succeed, yet be punished at random" gameplay. If Faster Than Light is still being worked on, which I doubt, I would like to see the game become more than what it is now to me.

Embarrassed. That would be one word I could use if someone asked me how I felt right now. But hey, it's okay. I was bored and the game was free so technically I didn't lose more than my dignity. The game wasn't completely horrible and it was able to give me many good laughs... even though they were mostly on the game's expense.
However, I can still smile and give the maker of this game a big piece of that 'At least you tried' cake.
Over all, Seduce Me the Otome is a wonderful mix of all those possible reverse harem anime cliches you can think of with a nice spice of demons and cheesy, cringe worthy lines that make you feel sorry for the voice actors.
We have the classic bunch of male characters: Mr. Shy guy, Mr. Flirty guy, Mr. Wise guy, Mr. Tough guy and Mr. Childish guy. The two female friends of the heroine are Ms. Caring but humorless and Ms. Tough girl.
- The voice acting was pretty decent, occasionally really good.
- The music, when there was some, was really nice.
- Some of the characters were good.
- There was some suprising endings and more romances that I knew (I haven't played most of them).
- Like many others who've reviewed this game, the lack of "real" choices annoyed me too.
If you want you can click trough the whole story in mere minutes. You just need remember where the important choices are (or you can just save before choosing anything). Oh, just a tip: remember to choose carefully your house cleaning pal.
- The art... oh god, the art. I'm so sorry, but when you make a visual novel or a dating sim it is VERY IMPORTANT that the players feel attracted to the characters. I don't know if this is supposed to be a message of some sort, but when you have to say "he/she has a very nice personality!" in some character's defence in a cheesy, romantic visual novel... you know there's something amiss there.
- Lack of music. It's not all that bad, but it could've made the game a bit livelier. At one point I actually forgot that I had the game running on the background and noticed it when I was shutting down my computer.
- The writing. Like I already mentioned, some of the lines were bad, and when I say bad, I mean really really bad.
The plot was also slightly childish and worthy of more than a few face palms. Many things were left without explanation or those explanations were so poorly done that they just made me sigh. I also hated how the father of the heroine was written. He was a "bad guy" just for the sake of it and was probably supposed to make us feel sorry for the daughter, and speaking about bad "explanations" the reason her father was such an asshat was explained very poorly.
- The endings. Some of them were so disappointing and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that they just left me staring at the screen. Couldn't even believe the game was over when I returned to the main menu.
So, that's what I thought about this game. You'll have more fun if you take a drink every time something here makes you roll your eyes or facepalm, although you'll probably be completely wasted after ten minutes into the game...
But hey... at least its free. :)

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is the emotional and macabre story of a detective with paranormal powers trying to find a lost boy who led a troubled life. The overall visual atmosphere of the game is outstanding and the story itself keeps you hooked the entire game, dying to know what eldritch terror lurks around the next corner of Ethan's disappearance. The controls are very simple and the game is mostly straightforward without holding you by the hand and walking you along. Other than the interactable objects which make themselves known to you when you come close enough to them, the game gives you no direction at all as to what to do. It is up to you to follow the story and look out for the clues in dialogue/writing/etc. This really allows you to immerse yourself into the story and really separates this game from the typical "box ticker" storyline game we are so used to seeing these days.
I personally found the ending to be kind of a let-down (not necessarily in the emotional sense but moreso in the writing aspect) but I would not say that it detracts from the overall experience of the game. I'm sure that most people were fine with it but I just expected much more... given the impressiveness of the rest of the game.
That being said, I would give the game a solid 4/5 stars where the only thing keeping it from 5 would be my aforementioned issue with the ending and how short the game actually is. Other than those two issues, this game was absolutely worth my money and time.

So I've always been the kind of guy who will buy a game and play it for a while before shelving it and probably never coming back to it again. However when I bought Helldivers a year ago when it (finally) got ported over to the PC, I can't help but find myself come back to it constantly and falling in love with it again and again.
Helldivers is a twin-stick shooter that puts you in the shoes of one of Super Earth's most valiant defenders of freedom and democracy named, funnily enough, the Helldivers. Dropped right into enemy territory and using a wide variety of weaponry and artillery, you must traverse a randomly generated map (which can take place on a variety of different terrain like on desert, volcanic or even in huge planetwide urban centres) completing all the objectives before calling for extraction and standing your ground till your ride arrives.
Each planet you liberate not only nets you some new gear or xp but also contributes to a meta-campaign that the whole community contributes to where humanity is fighting a war on 3 fronts against the Cyborgs, Bugs and Illuminate. Were it is possible to knock each race out of the war by a successful invasion of their home planet but were it is also possible for Super-Earth to fall should any of them push that far.
Before you prepare to drop in you get to pick the loadout you drop in with which comprises of your primary weapon, a perk and 4 stratagems slots. Stratagems are various bits and bobs you can call in at any time during the mission which could be anything from a simple ammo drop to a mech to an orbital laser strike and so much more. The brilliant thing about this system is that there are no restrictions to what you can put in these slots and you can even put multiples of the same stratagem in different slots which allows for a large diversity in the number of builds you can create. Combine this with the different races you are fighting that have their own strengths and weaknesses and you will find yourself changing out gear quite a bit to best fit what you are trying to accomplish.
The community in-game while not large is certainly quite friendly and helpful. Heck I've befriend so many people I even had to tag everyone I've met in-game as a Helldiver since they've taken a significant portion of my friends list! The reason why the community is in a good state is due in part to the cooperative nature of the game but also as the game features a commendation system. This allows you to commend people if they were fun to play with or report them if they are particularly malicious. If you get too many reports then you only get to play with others who've also been misbehaving.
However despite the fact that I feel like I have to gush over this game every time I think about it, I will concede that there are a few things that people might not be so stoked over. Things like the shared screen that every player has do deal with can feel a little awkward at first, the war system can prevent you from unlocking some vanilla gear and fighting against your favourite race and the boss fights can be done using some cheap tactics and give way too much influence over regular helldive missions in my opinion.
However, with all that said and done though I still have a blast when I pick the game up and dive right in. Whether its just doing some regular dives with randoms or grabbing some buds together and running a theme that restricts the equipment we can take. This game has never failed to entertain me and make me shout FREEEEEEEEEEEEEDOM in the text chat.
I would totally recommend if you do decide to buy the game to get the Deluxe Edition, as getting all the DLC's will really expand on the number of tools you have at your disposal and for the most part are actually quite useful, even if at first they seem quite crap (you also get all the cosmetic stuff that came with each individual pack which to own in my opinion is more important ;)

Software Inc. is a mix of a Sims-like construction planner and a very UI-based economy simulation. I personally enjoyed every minute of my roughly 45 hours of playthrough, but I now reached the point where my company has achieved everything that could be considered a challenge. From this experience I can very much recommend the game to very patient simulation players with a liking for strategic details.
Many negative reviews say that the UI is badly designed ond convoluted. Despite the learning curve being pretty steep I had no problems at all with the UI - most things are pretty much self-explanatory, you just have to take the time to explore it a bit and read the tooltips. The tutorial was helpful to me, I just did not like that it made me read tutorials for very advanced features I would not need anyway until mid or end game. But I never used a third party guide or even tips from the forums and still "won" the game with my first company.
On the other hand, some of the mechanics just don't work at the moment or are pretty hard to control (e.g. connecting server farms, especially large ones, assigning workplaces to specific workers and some of the building tools).
What I liked about the game is the interplay of building and team logistic. There are several ways to make your software firm efficient (e.g. choosing between the "one-team-per-franchise" or the "one-team-per-role" organization or the decision between large cubicle-office vs. small room offices). All strategies require different building styles and development chains.
But all of this interesting stuff is mid to late game content. In the beginning of the game, the excitement of whether your company will make the release in time to pay the bills might keep you entertained, but at the same time the endless cycle of production -> dumb minigames -> marketing -> reinvestment (until you finally manage to satisfy the market demands) feels dull after a while. Once you find your software niche, it starts to get interesting with respect to team and building management, but if you succeed, there is really nothing you could do wrong anymore. Your first real hit software will most of the time give you an enormous financial boost. All of a sudden, you won't ever look at a price tag again. Only the best is good enough and of course you will never release a piece of software too early so that your work will always result in "outstanding" software. But where's the fun if everything you do is always "outstanding"?
The game starts in the year 1980. At around 2003 I had a perfect market recognition and millions of fans for every single type of product. There were no more new features to unlock that I could add into new releases and there was no more research to be conducted to stay ahead of the competitors. Instead, I turned so insanely rich that I would just buy every IP from my competitors that could even remotely threaten my monopoly. That was the point were I considered the game finished (with the only feature left to explore being a holo computer in the year 2020 for my workers that would slightly increase programming speed and with the only thing left to do being to earn more money until I could buy every single firm)
The graphics of the game seemed odd at first, but you really grow to like the simplistic models. It might not be state of the art, but the design is definitely cute and the exaggerated animations are worth a chuckle. Unfortunately there was no music yet.
