Let me say first that FTL is a somewhat ok game and I do still play it from time to time.  My negative review is due to it's continued utter randomness, basic gameplay, and complete lack of balance.  These things should have been corrected by now, considering the age of the product.  I'll get more into that in a minute, but first...
FTL, or Faster Than Light, is a basic top-down ship management game.  By management I mean you actually don’t “fly” the ship, in the normal sense of the word.  You view the ship as a top-down map and can move crew around from various rooms and systems, open and close doors, adjust power levels, buy upgrades, perform repairs, and use a star chart to jump from location to location.  Combat is done by somewhat of a “split screen” mode, whereas your ship’s top-down view appears on the left and the enemy’s is on the right.  You don’t truly see the ships facing off any more than a rocket/laser shoots off your side of the screen and appears on their side either missing or hitting the area you targeted.  In all honesty, it’s quite basic.
Excitement in FTL comes from the progression through the systems.  Everything is pretty much random so you never actually know what’s at the next jump location.  That said, there are ship upgrades that will let you scan the immediate area around you or you can get lucky and pick up a star chart in your travels, both of which help give you a bit of a heads up.
The biggest drawbacks to FTL are the absolute randomness, unbalanced encounters, and the two primary objectives being exact opposites of each other.  As stated earlier, I thought these issues would have been dealt with by now but they haven't.  Let me explain further.  Your first objective in FTL is to upgrade your ship as much as possible.  This is done by either performing deeds, having luck with exploration, buying/selling items at a station, or through victorious combat.  You’ll need these upgrades to deal with encounters, as well as an end-boss battle you’ll face later.  The fact that all your encounters are random makes your success/failure in upgrading your ship practically a stroke of luck.  Your second objective in FTL is to stay ahead of a rebel fleet that is hot on your tail.  This, unfortunately, leads you to having to rush through systems so you don’t get the time to perform deeds, have luck with exploration, or buy/sell items at every station.  You can see where I’m going here…
Thankfully one of these two dilemmas can be dealt with.  That’s right; with a little modification to the game (wait, didn't I say I was leaving mods out?) you can turn off the rebel fleet so you can fully explore each system.  You would think that would give you an advantage right?  Here’s the kicker.  It doesn’t.  Surprise!  With everything being so random even having the ability to explore every system can leave you at a disadvantage.   It all comes down to luck, seriously.  It can be argued, and some do profoundly, but skill has very little to do with success in this game.  But wait, it doesn’t end there…
If you’re foolish enough to leave the Advanced Edition content enabled you’ll face a slew of ever ridiculously overpowered enemies that can make the final boss look like a walk in the park.  You’ll face everything from mind manipulation, to system hacking, to ridiculously overpowered weaponry, and pulsars that seem to always disable your shields/weapons while only effecting the enemy's less critical systems.  Sometimes you can even face all these things at the same time!
Just as an example…  I had been playing for about an hour, exploring every system as much as I could.  Sadly I was getting all garbage loot, nothing higher than level 2.  I was just a few systems away from the final boss’ system, in friendly (green) territory, when I happened upon a pirate ship.  No problem.  I had fully upgraded shields, heavily upgraded engines (evade), 4 varying weapons (1 missile, 1 beam, 1 rocket, 1 bomb) that would ensure damage was done, and both combat and repair drones ready for action.  I was prepared, right?  Ohhhh no.  I was so outgunned it wasn’t funny.
The first thing the enemy ship did was fire a hacker that latched itself onto my shield room.  There go my shields, one by one.  The second weapon that fired was a missile that punched a hole right into my oxygen room, taking it out.  Got my repair drone on that, so I wasn't too worried.  Then they unleashed their mind control device that made my weapon officer disable my weapons.  It took me a little bit of crew adjusting, but I was holding my own.  Just when I thought I was getting everything back under control the fourth weapon started firing.  Seriously? A vulcan chaingun!  Less than 30 seconds later I had fires in almost every room, every system was destroyed (red), and quickly following that my ship exploded…  By that time I hadn’t even breached their pitiful level 2 shields.  You wanna talk about a lack of balance?  That fight was absolute B.S.
Now, I’m not someone who writes a negative review just on one bad experience.  In all my time playing I've had it both ways.  I’ve had it so easy that I, quite literally, walked through every system and then just decimated the final boss.  There is absolutely no balance to the game!  It’s all based on luck.  That’s probably why it’s so successful.  It’s like a lottery ticket.  Sometimes you lose but occasionally you get that winner.  People love to gamble, and that’s what you do every time you click to start a new game.
Still, it doesn’t make it a good game.  Maybe a distraction from time to time.  As a game I’d call it mediocre at best.  That said, I won’t recommend it since there are much better titles out there that fit this same genre.
Seriously?  All the trouble I went through to write a really good review and you want to skip it?  Fine...  It's unbalanced and very luck-based.   You happy now?  Hardly explains anything...  Stop being lazy and go read the rest!  ;)

I just finished this crazy game using Wesp's Unofficial 9.0 Basic patch.
The Pros:
- Hollywood, "movie quality" dialogue and voice acting.
- Gripping, well written story arc.
- The most advanced facial animations that I have ever experienced in a RPG.
- Interesting quests with great level design ( the haunted house was so scary that I felt queasy ).
- Characters that will make you fall in love, hate or laugh.
- Adult themes that include: sex; drugs; addiction; child abuse; slavery; trafficking.
- The developers had a crazy, dirty, wild sense of humour.
- Addictive. I ended up pulling all-nighters, playing until 6am, many times.
The Cons:
- The game obviously needed a few months of work before being released. I got stuck on textures and trapped between a closing door and the door hinge ( annoying ). NPCs can see through a door, if the door is open ( wallhacking ).
- Stealth is random and broken to the point of being laughable.
- Firearms did not seem particularly useable ( it takes to long for sights to become useable ).
- Your choices don't matter ; the RPG is on rails.
- Melee and swordplay seem so-so in the beginning of the game but grew on me, over time. The end game was a bit tedious though.
- The pacing seems off. The game deceptively starts off as a run off the mill RPG and scales into Spielberg / George Lucas.
- You only gain 1 xp for completing a quest and you need 3 XP points, just to raise a stat, so levelling is very slow.
- There is too much obvious busywork in the game ( running from place to place and running home, to read emails on a laptop ).
Conclusion: I would play Vampire: The Masquerade after playing classic, universally accepted, top quality RPGs such as: Might and Magic 6: Mandate of Heaven; Knights of the Old Republic 1; Deux Ex 1; Deus Ex - Human Revolution.

The first tower defense game I played was Desktop Tower Defense, a simple game that is on a grid and sends wave after wave of enemy at you.  This was a fun game mechanic and it would pop up with different themes in different games through the years. But, it was not until Defender’s Quest: Valley of the Forgotten that I found a game that used that mechanics to great effect in an Role Playing Game fashion.
The opening of the game shows you as the main character being dragged out of her house and thrown into the Pit. She has the plague but also realizes she has special powers.  From here it opens the ability to play the game.  She can bring warriors into the Half-Way Realm and allow them to kill the revenants, monsters people turn into after they die of the plague. The story starts taking twists from there as you follow what has really been happening to two kingdoms and what the ultimate goal is.
There are a host of characters that arrive in the game and each comes with their own personality.  The first people you find are barbarians, who wear no armor and are humorously suicidal in their combat tactics. Then you meet the rangers, who are far more practical about their need for survival. Each of the units you meet have a person who is going to be seen in cut scenes and helps give you a feel of the personality of that unit.
Each of the units levels up, gains new skills, and can even be upgraded with new equipment.  Most of this is done in towns.  When in a town you can recruit units you have access to, but need to keep a close eye on the cost as the more units you have, the higher the price for the next one.  Gear comes in two main forms armor and weapons. There are also things that your main character can equip, but those mainly augment her abilities and are not purchasable.  When a character gains experience they level up just like you would expect in a normal RPG. Each unit has a skill tree with two branches. This means one barbarian might do a lot more damage and another might recover from wounds faster, it is up to you how you want them to work.
This game was not  anywhere on my radar and that is sad because it is a great game.  The units seem well thought out so as to be different and fit a certain use at a certain time. The story told through still frames is well done with attention to facial expressions and a great sense of humor. This game is a great one, and the team at Level Up Labs is already working on another.

Sequence: 8.5/10
The first thing I’d like to touch upon is the engaging gameplay. Think Guitar Hero, but more complex; directional arrows will fall from the screen and you must match them at the bottom, to the beat of the song. But where it becomes more complicated is that there’s “three screens” – one for offense (casting spells, which lowers your opponents health, heals you, etc.), one for mana (which is the resources for spells), and defense (in which you counter your opponent’s attacks; if you match the arrows, you don’t take damage, but if you don’t, you take damage equal to what the arrow is worth). This leads to a very fun experience, because you must decide on the fly if you want to cast X spell at that time, while managing mana and seeing if you want to finish that spell, or negate the damage incoming to you, etc. The spell must be finished completely, without mistake, to be cast; if you mess up one note, it doesn’t do anything, so the more rewarding the spell, the more difficult to pull off. I am not ashamed to admit that I had to shelf my “best” healing spell for a moderate heal because I could never pull it off. The game is at its best when you’re on equal terms with your opponent, having to juggle mana, spells, and defense. Unfortunately, the difficulty isn’t always there, and I’ve been able to literally completely ignore defense and just go for mana and spells. This is okay when the enemy is essentially a “gear check”, so to speak, but it happened more than I’d like. The game has seven floors (perhaps more, I’m currently on floor six of a stated seven), and each floor has a “special power” (that is designed to hinder you) for each fight: for the sixth floor, for example, you can’t see the screens you’re not currently selecting. Another power is that you’re unable to switch screens until the timer is expired, so you better make sure you’re on the defensive screen, or you’re going to be taking a lot of damage.
I would like to note that I was very surprised at how well the (controller, never tested the keyboard) controls worked; I was swapping screens and hitting notes effortlessly, and I can count the amount of times I was disoriented / confused on my hand.
Being a rhythm game, the music is important, and Sequence delivers. I’d like to note that I enjoy it so much I’ll be throwing the tracks on my iPod for repeated listening. Said tracks are varied so it’s not just the same type of music, although I do wish there was more variety when you’re grinding; hearing the same song all the time on the same enemy did kind of get on my nerves. But, still, they’re good songs, so I don’t mind much. For each song, the tempo dictates how the notes are going to hit you: if it’s a slow song, there’ll be fewer notes, but they’ll count for more, while the opposite is true for frantic music.
While the story does exist, it’s not very engaging. I am – as I’m sure a lot of others are – tired of the main character waking up and not knowing what’s going on / amnesia / what-have-you. The dialog between the main character and your ally is often amusing (they’ve had discussions which includes ♥♥♥♥♥, “…like a Disney without hidden sexual innuendo, they were missing something”, etc.) that I’ve forgiven the absence of the story. And, without spoilers, the dialog made me care for the plot development about two-thirds of the way through the game, so the plot is a lot better than most games in this genre.
My largest complaint is the grinding required to advance in the story. I am at heart an RPG-enthusiast, so I really don’t mind grinding – usually I enjoy it. Sequence, however, doesn’t pull grinding off very well, though. The game employs a crafting element to the game, which is required to use to advance. You can craft items such as permanent health increases, items that disable the hindering “special powers” that each floor uses against you, and, most importantly, key items that allow you to challenge the boss for that specific floor. To get these specific items, you must defeat certain enemies, and upon defeating them, you have a percentage chance to get one of three items that they carry. This wouldn’t be so bad, except you must often get a 25% drop from multiple enemies, and this quickly becomes annoying when they pose no threat to you. Without said grinding, however, the game would be at least half as long, so I don’t mind it too much…but enough to complain about it. ;)
Another small complaint is the difficulty curve. In the beginning, it was about perfect for me and my difficulty setting (I chose the default “normal” difficulty), since I wasn’t fully aware of how to time the notes and how the game worked, etc. Then floors two through five didn’t give me many problems…and then the sixth floor is kicking my♥♥♥♥♥ I feel like they’re trying to prolong the game with unnecessarily high “gear checks” at this point. This would be more forgivable if said difficulty curve was more spread out and not super noticeable after having a very easy time previously.
Overall, I am very impressed with this gem of a game that I paid $1 for (among two other solid games). In fact, I like it so much that I played five straight hours of it one day, and am planning on putting all of the songs on my iPod to listen to later.
While there are some small flaws in my eyes, the positives far outweigh the negatives.
TL:DR = 8.5/10;
Pro = Gameplay is very fun, music is great, fun dialog.
Con = Unnecessarily long, RNG-reliant grinding, spiked difficulty curve.

I love tycoon and management games, and Software Inc is the best I've played for quite awhile!
It is very satisfying going from a startup company with just yourself in basically a hovel, to a small success with a few employees and luxuries (like a toilet, heater, and coffee machine) to a monstorous multinational with hundreds of employees, gobbling up your competition and dominating the market.
I strongly suggest watching a few let's plays while you play, to get the hang of things. Because the tutorials and info on the game is a little lacking at the moment.
Things get a bit too easy too quickly after your first "big" success, you don't really have to worry about money anymore after that, but it's still fun to build and expand.
The game also runs great and has very few bugs or glitches.
I can definitely see myself sinking a lot of time into this game in a borderline OCD kind of way, which is basically what you want from a tycoon game.
For those who want a tower defense game with rpg elements this game will not disappoint.

If you are looking for the best RTS game this is it. It might sound very subjective, but it is a completely objective opinion.
If you like WW2 in any manner this is the game for you. When you are done playing this game every time you see anything that is sort of WW2 you will  probably get the urge to play COH2.
By far the best strategy game when it comes to graphics. The visual effects when Stalin's Hammer (really big gun) blows up a Kubelwagen (a really small vehicle) is definitely one of the best things you will ever see in a RTS. When a 88mm pak shoots at a IS2 heavy tank it  will make you feel like Hitler when he found out he hates Jews.
I know there is a lot of debate that graphics does not matter in games, but when you see COH2 you will simply just change your mind.
If you want to play the single player campaign I will recommend it, but the real fun is in multiplayer: the thing about COH2 is that a big army (tanks and infantry) can easily be defeated by a small force of infantry, support weapons and ONE WELL PLACED MINE. Most strategy games that I have played with my friends will usually end up in just two big armies battling one another, bUt with COH2 it is a whole other story. Like I said, ONE MINE CAN CHANGE HOW A WHOLE MATCH GOES. You can make your own opinion if that is a good or bad thing for this game, but in multiplayer it is certainly a good thing.
The thing about this game is that I don't want to write a book about it. I WANT TO PLAY IT. So I can tell you guys/girls what I think about this game for the next year and this review can be published by Hitlers far off family, but you will still not feel the satisfaction of COH2. I 100% recommend this game. It will make you mad, but believe me, it is a helluva feeling when you know your making someone rage behind their screen because you just killed their tiger with one anti-tank gun and ONE WELL PLACED MINE.

Wow. Sequence, we've got a lot to talk about.
Sequence is basically a DDR/ITG + RPG mashup, which may sound odd, but it works pretty fluently. Even as someone who's been an avid fan of the four-arrow dance games for over a decade, it took me a while to get fully accommodated with Sequence's unique gameplay.
However, one thing I certainly did not expect from a game like this was a compelling plot with brilliantly well-written and fully voiced characters. Sequence's story gives the game a
of depth and was probably the driving factor for me. Definitely a huge highlight of this game.
I could nit pick for quite a while, though. The music isn't anything extraordinary, it can be a bit grindy at times (as both item crafting and item drops are chance based), and the battle interface could use a little bit of work to make it easier to see what spells are ready, what the mana cost is, how much you have at the time, etc. Since I played with the keyboard, having all the tutorials and controls based around a 360 controller was also a tad confusing.
Sequence is pretty fun and I would recommend it to rhythm game/RPG fans or people who enjoy a really good story.

Some may compare this title to “Dear Esther”, but this comparison is a bit off.
The “Vanishing of Ethan Carter” is First person exploration game, which takes part in a beautiful and interesting world of Red Creek Valley. The visuals are done quite well, the views are truly breath taking and technically the game is well made with no bugs, glitches, FPS drops what so ever.
Like I wrote, game looks beautiful, great lighting and texture quality. In my play-trough I used to stop and watch the views a lot. Also the art direction, in game music and world design helps the game to be a more immersive experience. Game is stable and technically almost perfect, also there are no loading times which is quite impressive for such a big world.  However I played the redux version, so take that for notice.
You are detective Paul Prospero, who is looking for missing boy called Ethan Carter. On the story you will encounter some challenging and not so challenging puzzles, will see some paranormal activities and visit some beautifully crafted places. In the opening scenes game writes that it will not hold your hand and it doesn't. Game never really explains it self, so I found myself in second third of the game realizing, that I didn’t finish a lot of puzzles which reveal the story, however developers predicted such situations, so the world is made in such way that you can easily back track a lot of stuff, without reloading or taking long walks to the places you’ve missed.  World isn’t linear, you can visit places and do objectives in order you discover them. Narrative also brings up some great quotes which leaves you thinking.
My only complain with this wonderful interactive adventure is, that it could be a bit longer, maybe for 2-3 hours, because I wanted to explore and see more of Red Creek Valley. The game took me about 4 hours to complete and it’s definitely worth its price.
I gave it 9.0

The story is equally interesting, and keeps you engaged and moving forward.  The puzzles are simple, but necessarily so since there's no controls to worry about.  I wouldn't want the puzzles to get in the way of progress of the story.  The ending is pretty surreal, and instead of "a twist" cheapening the whole experience, it strengthens it very nicely. You know why? It's free, but worth so much more than that. New items and abilities are earned, allowing access to hithero-impossible paths, with enough tangential extras to tempt players into revisiting this charming game time and time again. Did you find the secret word? How about that 100% completion? What is the deal with the cats?
The icing on this delicious cake is in the form of the beautiful CGA/EGA style graphics and cute minimalist sound. This entire package is more than the sum of its parts, and really a rewarding experience. Gratis.

A beautiful story about a genius inventor and his nephew. A Story About My Uncle, is one of these modern art installation games, but features actually challenging gameplay in the form of 1st person platforming. The game has a bunch of really well made movement mechanics, which I won't explain in detail because they are very fun to discover along the story.
I said beautiful before, and I meant the graphics too. Really nice art style, atmospheric environments, every chapter has its own distinct look and they are very enjoyable to look at. The beauty is also in the narration, the spoken lines of the narrator are good stuff, and they help you along this adventure. There are also many subtle things going on in the game world, relating to the story, for example: you can encounter lines of text written in a weird language, which you can learn to translate yourself. I recommend figuring things out, it really is worth it. Going into detail would once again spoil the experience.
I'm one of those people who enjoy experiencing visual stories, even without actual gameplay mechanics, but I know some people really don't like such experiences (e.g. Dear Esther). I strongly recommend this game to anyone who didn't like Dear Esther because of the lack of gameplay mechanics, I think this is a game that has what you were looking for.
Go on an adventure, play A Story About My Uncle, figure things out and overcome the platforming challenges, in the end you might be surprised by how beautiful this story is.

Okay so this is NOT A BAD GAME BY ANY MEANS, some parts are outstanding by any standards, while other parts fall flat. I think the think that distinguishes this from a game I would wholly recommend is that there are parts that are so frustrating it ceases to be fun, and also because the game did not meet my (admittedly high) expectations. What I mean to say is it is good, but could be a lot better.
Let me start out with the good things:
-The scenery! I love it. The game's landscape is eye candy.
-You get to meet some cute frog aliens.
-There is a cool "boss" level.
-The framing device of a man telling his daughter a bedtime story works well. I got some good Narnia vibes. Prepare yourself for a wonderful adventure!
-There is something exhilerating about the gameplay, the jumping and swinging around like Spiderman or something. It's lovely.
-Gets challenging.
-Some cute easter eggs, example: a gameboy with "A Story About My Uncle" title screen.
Now, the bad:
-Pretty short.
-A lot of bugs, getting caught in the terrain in some places, or the grapple being juuuust too close to the edge of a platform, causing you to get caught and sort of wiggle endlessly in front of the platform instead of landing on the top of it (giving you no choice but to let go and fall to your death).
-While I appreciate that there isn't some kind of "locking" system in place with the grapple, because the gameplay really is exciting and challenging the way it is, the game punishes you a lot if your aim is even just a liiittle off, which is a shame, because it eventually gets frustrating.
-You are going to fall a lot.
-There are areas where there are not enough checkpoints.
-Voice acting is not bad, but definitely not stellar.
-Small nitpick, but outside of what you need to do to progress there is very very little you can do to interact with the environment.
-They go overboard with the easter eggs at some points and it kind of broke immersion for me. It's been a while since I played but I believe there was a My Little Pony reference, a Game of Thrones Reference, and a Breaking Bad reference. None of them adding anything to the experience.
Conclusion: Definitely buy it if it goes on sale! But don't get your expectations too high (like I did) because you'll probably be disappointed.

Defender's Quest is a Tower-Defense/RPG Hybrid (Think Final Fantasy Tactics meets Tower Defense).
Defender's Quest tightly focuses on three things: tactical depth, customization, and story. That means no random encounters, no spikey-haired emo kids, no forced time sinks, and no tedious, repetitive battles.
The battle system builds off of tower defense, with individual characters taking the place of towers. Each character levels-up, learns skills, and equips gear individually, allowing the player to customize their battle experience and strategy. The overall game structure is similar to "tactical" RPG's, but with a real-time battle system. Game speed is adjustable, and commands can even be issued while the game is paused.
It also features an engaging, character-driven story written by an actual English major! The story strives to be fast-paced, snappy, and always relevant to gameplay. Events and dialogue explain things as they become relevant to the player, minimizing exposition.
Finally, it's got options and accessibility settings out the wazoo, so that you can have the best possible experience!

Perhaps this games best feature is the ability to blend some modern day realism with a dose a fantasy terror. The "dungeon" areas are really not boring and offer up a challenge for several playthroughs. The environments are fairly detailed and the overall map desing usually makes sense. The older graphics also do little to diminish the gore factor in this game. Some scenes should not be redone in HD. The game is plagued with several tech issues if you are running a newer operating system. The game works fine normally if you run in compatbility mode as an admin. Also be sure not to auto-update as this can cause crashing. I also recommend downloading the unofficial patches as they really do add more depth and refinement to the overall gameplay. So wether you are a fan of "Blade" or "Twilight", then this game has something for you.

I really wanted this game back when it came out. Since I was on an extended gaming break at the time and had an old computer I missed out on it. But it always lurked in the back of my mind. Now I finally have and can emphatically state that the decades wait was worth it... With one caveat.
First of all, you must get the unofficial patch, which is easily found and installed. Once that is in place you can start enjoying this absolute gem of a game.
It's not the best at any one gameplay element. Melee combat is a bit clunky, ranged combat somewhat underpowered. Stealth is too easy and infiltration a bit simple. But that's exactly the thing - the sheer amount of choice and ways to achieve goals is incredible and puts many far more advanced games to shame. There is very rarely just one way to reach a destination but many. The choice of which clan you belong to (equivalent to choosing a race in standard rpgs) truly matters and makes the game have lasting value. On a new game you can either choose your clan or answer a series of questions to determine the clan. If you decide to buy this game I highly recommend that you answer the questions on your first playthrough.
Add to this that the story is pretty good, the plot and progression of the story is great, every choice matters and there are tons of sidequests and you've got a real winner. Highly recommended.

With the exception of "CUPID", "Long Live the Queen" and the SNES version of "Angelique", I can't say that I've ever been compelled to play visual novels - and that was even when Suikoden jumped into the field with their own a few years ago (with an astounding, vivid soundtrack at that). So I suppose you could say that I'm attempting a review that's a little less rose-tinted.
Recommended by a friend of mine, SMtO is for the most part, fairly straightforward. I can see why some would like it whilst others would be frustrated with it. I can only imagine the challenges that the writer had to face when trying to create up to 22 various endings for you to play with. I confess for the most part, I did gasp and chuckle at some of the consequences and choices that you had to make (something-something-Sarlacc-pit).
There are perhaps some questionable behaviours and actions that happen in the story (if the sight of several men appearing at your house wasn't bizarre in itself), but given what comes out later in the story, it's made clear that this is the tip of the iceberg.
You are [NameGoesHere] Anderson, an 18-year-old about to graduate when you find out that your grandfather has passed away. The opening was very well-paced and it was a delight to gradually learn about who you were, your relationship with others and how you end up in a mansion that's bequeathed to you in your grandfather's will. Your father hastily whisks you into the mansion and your adventure begins.
One of the fundamental problems I had with the story was how fast you had to get to know your suitors. With so many romance options available (demon and non-demon alike), it's difficult to appreciate these dynamic characters such as Erik and Suzu when we spend just a few short scenes with them.
There were these brief, subtle glimpses into each person's inner-struggles, but as a reader who enjoys character-driven plotlines over just a straightforward story, I did find this a pity. It ran the risk of me putting them into generalised anime stereotypes, but this may be down to my own lack of experience with these types of games.
You could also argue that the story also drew me in enough to care about these characters - to demand a little more knowledge about them before diving into the romantic pool of incu-hugs.
It's a pity that the experience is a short one. I finished it within two hours, but this was without romancing anyone - I honestly didn't think that you had to make a choice so soon; that said, it encourages you to play it again and again to find out more and stretch out past your initial impressions of it.
In terms of the voices, you could tell that they were doing their best. I did feel at times that they were a little excessive, but this is far from a problem. It did bring the characters to life. Occasionally they were unintentionally amusing and somewhat silly, but some of them were especially good, such as the voice for Diana.
And whoever played the voice of Malix needs a high five. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥
In summary, SMtO is an entertaining game. At times it can be silly and occasionally hard to take seriously, but impossible to dismiss. I never felt like I was wasting my time, even when I didn't romance a single person. With an arsenal of content, story and people to explore and learn about, it's worth keeping on your radar.

Disclaimer: The review hours played are from "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter" not "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter Redux" version I played (it took me about 9hs). But Steam only let users to review on the original game.
- An interesting story to discover while you reconstruct events that happened on different places of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter world. You must like, detective stories with a few twists and of course exploring and observe details.
- For a "walking sim" the difficulty of the puzzles are decent. Many walking sims these days are a bit stray forward. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter does this well with clever design of the map, of course with classic design hints but it feels different than any other games of the genre.
- Voice acting and music are decent. Maybe the music shines a bit more. The best incidental song is at the last part of the game:
- You can miss a few reconstruction of events and easter eggs but at the end you can backtrack so enjoy explore more if you liked the overall game.
- Graphics are great. One of the best looking Unreal Engine 4 games out there. Textures are pretty cleverer scattered through the map without much memory consumption. The Redux version was for free for those who own the original game and it looks a lot better. New shaders for some buildings and reflective objects, interiors are soften with a bit of fake GI and post process effects. Vegetation clipping is more "organic" (agh! that hipster word!). Water looks better with screen space reflections and a new normal bump pattern and daylight scenes have better color grading in some areas
You can see more here:
but I will say something VERY VERY important.
On video you'll miss A LOT of detail. You should play this game, even as a benchmark.
- Game lenght depends on your pace and if you try to find those few hidden achievements (there are four I guess). Of course I recommend a guide for two of them but the two others "home" and "the tunnel" are hard to miss.
- The ending was better than expected :')
- Joystick scheme during recontruction of events could have been better. Zoom with the LT don't have pressure sensitivity (I hate that!)
- Characters models, and rigging are a bit clunky (but this doesn't affect the story much).

Sequence is an entirely unique game which combines rhythm gaming with RPG mechanics. Three boards drop arrows simultaneously in a DDR fashion - one for attack, one for defense, and one for regeneration of mana with which to attack further. The player rotates between the boards while pressing the arrows in time with music in order to win the battle, gain experience and items, craft weapons, and learn new spells.
It's quite fun, if a bit short. The voice acting is quite solid for a budget title, the music is fairly good, and the graphics are perfectly serviceable if quite static - however, for the type of game it is, that doesn't get in the way.
The story gets a little odd (if predictably so) towards the end, but all in all, I had a lot of fun throughout. It's more for rhythm game fans than RPG fans, as those mechanics are the dominant ones, but it's definitely worth a look if you want to try something different.

I get it, it sucks to pay for licensing, but when the majority of your game requires that you listen to music while pecking at a keyboard, you might want to make sure you get a few more songs. I found myself taking breaks because I was literally sick of the same songs over and over again. I wish this game had more songs, because it was pretty fun to play. I recieved this game as a gift from a nice individual who surprised with it after seeing I had it on my wishlist (which I added it there before all the reviews came in as it looked cool). I was very excited to play it as it reminded me of old games I had seen before (and I love puzzle games like room puzzles and such). The puzzles are simpler than most puzzles I encounter in other games when I set them to easy. Even simplier than the starter Professor Layton puzzles (which is saying something). Puzzle number 7, which you will see many people complain about, is the only one that doesn't follow this. It uses a reference only the game dev understands as there are no hints outside of the fact that the number needed is on the back of another game's box. That is all you are told. While I actually really enjoy puzzles that require you to do some researching or scavenger hunting to solve, this one was far too obscure. There was no hints to which game box we needed in game or even an idea of where to start looking. Without the devs leaving a picture of the game box in the forums after people asked, you would probably never find out unless you had the right game in your house and had the time for all the trial and error. A better clue would have probably saved this game some of the negativity.
Overall, the game is immensly short. The asking price does seem a bit steep considering there are mobile games with more to them that are cheaper.
I don't reccommend the game at any more than $1 if you find it on sale, and even then you probably won't feel like you missed anything after playing.

Taiku Mansion tells the story of Ethan, who decided to visit the mansion of an old friend after receiving a voicemail from them. When he arrived, he was locked in and must escape before dawn: all told by a hooded figure. Let me make this clear – through the entire game, we do not know who this hooded person is.
The entire plot itself has a lot of holes, and left me with questions. But it seems, (without stating any spoilers) that there could be a sequel.
The gameplay fits that of your typical Escape game, where your only method of interaction is with your mouse. There’s 9 puzzles which you must complete, all scattered around the map – I’d also add that it’s a fairly small area to be considered a mansion. It’s only 2 floors, and with a puzzle in each room counts up to only 9. Nothing more to add here.
The graphics is where things go icky. Everything you see of the mansion and puzzles are presented as small photos. These pictures doesn’t fill even half of the screen, and are of low quality. It’s similar to what would happen if you attempted to stretch the size of a 400x300 image (or less) into a 1036x768. All you get is a blurry, pixelated mess. That’s coming from my own experience with re-sizing images, and that fits the situation for the photos in this game. That, which is also slapped onto a black storyboard with nothing but directions underneath it. The options are actions and where you can go, such as Hallway, Open Door and Western/Eastern. You also have the option to see the full map of the (tiny) mansion.
I feel that a huge part of the design and gameplay was ruined because the developers decided to establish it as a storyboard, instead of a first-person or third-person point of view. I find myself with a better feel and connection to the atmosphere when placed into the said environment as the character them self.
Sadly this is not the case, and with the unsatisfactory plot line, it gets a thumbs down from me. Thankfully I received the game for free, as I would not recommend buying.

Are you a masochist? Do you hate yourself? Do you like the pain and agony of shaky design? If so, stop reading and buy this game. Otherwise keep reading. A Story About My Uncle suffers from something I'm going to start calling "violent design". In other words, its poor design that makes the player suffer. Is it an adventure game? Exploration? Puzzle? Platformer? The designers obviously couldn’t decide and the player suffers for it. The story is so-so and far to slow to feel story "driven". The platforming is violent towards players in that it is inconsistent, requires the player to be shrewd, yet tricks the player into thinking the design fosters creativity. For example, why is the player limited to three grapples? If its story-adventure, unlimited grapples would have helped the player ignore design shortcomings. If its puzzle-platformer, three grapples should be enough as long as the player is accurate and creative. Unfortunately, the design in this game forces the player to play exactly how they want you to. If you innovate you die. If you can't keep up with the inconsistent grapple distances and objects, you die. Each "puzzle" must be taken on its own terms, the grapple effectiveness changes with each; this forces the player to proceed slowly and with much frustration. Given that the overall theme seems to be story and exploration based, where taking in the environment is most important, the restrictive design seems counterintuitive. At one point the game dares the player not to use the grapple; here its most obvious design flaws are made clear. Platformers should be smooth and momentum based, puzzle games ought to be clever; this section asks you to play a puzzle game using platforms that is both clunky and not clever. It’s just memorization through trial and error masquerading as a free-running, open experience. It mocks the player by suggesting they should be able to travel freely and quickly but punishes them for trying to rely on any kind of design by changing the rules. I'm hoping, once my frustration cools down, to give it another try. However, I'm starting to get really annoyed at this kind of design. Most players may not be old enough to appreciate how bad this design philosophy is but that doesn't justify calling it good.

I know there are a ton of tower defense games out there... and even a few that propose to add RPG-like elements.  Defender's quest is different, and different good.  The game strikes that perfect balance by replacing the "towers" with NPCs.  The difficulty ramp-up is near perfect for a game and gives you as much challenge as you want without subjecting you to any levels where you fall off a difficulty cliff.  If something's just a little too hard, or you're trying to get a better result?  Level up your guys or buy them beter equipment.
Yes, the game runs at a fixed resolution and no, the cutscenes (which tell an engrossing tale) are done with limited animation, but that's really OK.   The limitations don't detract from the game and you can tell all of the love and time and effort went into perfecting gameplay and giving you plenty of it.
If you're lukewarm on tower defense because you don't like the repetition, this game's for you.  If you're a die-hard TD fanatic, this game's for you.  Accessible, perfect ramp-up, plenty of content, and a story.  Definitely this game is one to get.

Not a character played by Keith David, actually Keith David, the actor. That's before you even reach the actual open world part of the game, where superpowers, giant alien robots, guns that shoot dubstep and 'Rowdy' Roddy Piper await you. To put just how intensely absurd this game is, the Steam award I just nominated it for is 'The “Best Use of a Giant, Sentient Can of Energy Drink With Eye Lasers” Award'.
SR4 began life as a stand-alone expansion pack to 3, so it uses the same map, but the gameplay is so radically different you'll barely notice: rather than driving around Steelport, you'll be free-running up the sides of buildings and gliding around, Prototype-style. Likewise, comparing 4 to GTA is now pointless; although I have heard it described as 'a better Crackdown than Crackdown,' and there's a strong hint of Mass Effect 2 in there too with the 'romance' feature ("Hey Kinzie, wanna f*ck?"). The game as a whole tends to be easier than SR3, although/because the other superpowers add an extra dimension to combat, so now you can fling ice-blasts around or send out shock-waves by stomping and such-like as well as shooting plain-old guns at enemies, who also have a lot more variation now that robots and aliens have been added to the mix. There's a few new faces, but the focus is mainly on revisiting backstories and characters from past games, brought (back) to life with some truly excellent voice-acting and animation.
Also, now that online is working once more and we've got a newly-opened Steam workshop, I for one welcome our new
Deep Silver overlords. Although I'll be truly fascinated to see how Saints Row 5 is going to get bigger.

Ah, Half-Life: the only game universe that nobody ever seems to have a bad word for. And it's no surprise, with better voice acting, a better plot, better graphics and game engine, and better gameplay than any other first-person shooter in the history of the world. So to say that the new outing is more of the same is less of a damning statement than it might be. But it's still a damning statement.
Because Episode One is a funny fish all round. It isn't really a mission pack and certainly not an entirely new game. It isn't even an episode one in the Star Wars prequel sense you might expect. The best way to describe it is simply as an extension pack. It places you back in the action from the precise moment at which Half-Life 2 left off, and you continue from there on. The reason for the Episode One label is that this is the first of several extension episodes to be released that continue the story. Valve itself describes the game as "a four- to six-hour adventure of greater density and detail than non-episodic releases". Which is to say that a lot happens quite fast and then suddenly it's over.

There are a couple of very good reasons to play Sequence. Firstly, the gameplay is spot on. Like most rhythm games you are simply required to hit buttons in time to the music, but Sequence has some interesting mechanics. You have three lanes of incoming notes that you can switch between at any time. One of them is defensive; any notes you miss here deplete your health. In another lane you must time your button presses to increase your mana, which is used for spellcasting. The third lane is for the spells themselves. Once you cast a spell you need to hit a short sequence of notes in this lane for the spell to actually take effect.
This leads to quite a frenetic experience where you're constantly shifting between offense and defense. It can be frustrating and it takes some getting used to, but once you get the hang of it, it's pure gaming bliss that rivals the old classic Amplitude, not to mention Guitar Hero.
The other, and possibly more significant, reason to play this game is the music. Much of the music is provided by Ronald Jenkees, a man of prodigious melodic talent. I've played Sequence for a good few hours, but I've spent much, much more time listening to the music of Jenkees. It's truly phenomenal, and even if you have no interest in this game I'd recommend checking it out.
Sequence is not perfect. There are RPG elements, and while they work well enough I can't help thinking that so, so much more could have been done with them. I'm put in mind of Puzzle Quest, another game which combined RPG elements with a totally different style of game, but did it in a much more dynamic way. Perhaps the makers of Sequence didn't have the time or resources to go that far, but I do believe they could have come up with something a little more compelling that repetitive grind they've got in this game. Maybe for the sequel?

A Story About My Uncle follows a young boy who goes off searching for his uncle in a fantastical world inhabited by frog people. To do so he uses a device which lets him grapple to most types of walls in the world. And that is the basis of the game's gameplay. It's a first person platformer where the sole objective is getting from A to B. There are no diversions here, there are no enemies or sidequests or an open world to explore. You can find some collectibles along the way, but that's about it. Thankfully the game is very short so the platforming aspect doesn't manage to get boring.
And to that point it's a shame that the developers didn't really fully explore the complexities of the platforming they created with this game. There are checkpoints on almost every platform and the time you spend in the air is very short, so if you fail you probably lost around 5 secs of progress, which makes the game very easy (but also not frustrating, which is nice). Only at the very end you can start stringing together longer grappling jumps as a new option to refill your grapple device in the air opens up. Everything else is pretty straightforward.
The world that they set up also feels underdeveloped, there are only passing mentions of it in the narration, and not much is actually explained. Perhaps there isn't much time to do that as the game length is about 2 hours if you're going just straight from beginning to the end. You can do some time trails on all the levels, and you can go back and select the level you want to replay if you'd like to get some perfect run achievements. Other than that there isn't much replayability in this short game.
All in all it's a good first outing from the developer, the game simply feels underdeveloped in a lot of areas. Get it on a discount and you'll be fine with the purchase though.

Software Inc.: the land of a hundred thousand UI windows.
I very badly wanted to like this game. I dumped hours into Game Dev Tycoon and regularly play games like Cities: Skylines wishing I could start and manage my own company in game. Then I heard about Software Inc., and immediately plunged into it, expecting a fantastic and detailed sim. And to be clear, that's what Software Inc. is at its core - an extremely detailed sim.
However, it's far too impenetrable in its current state. The developer has succumbed to feature creep and the tutorials for the game are nowhere near as verbose and informative as they need to be relative to how many things you need to manage. Additionally, many of the core game mechanics are hidden behind menus and right-click panels ad infinitum. Some serious thought needs to be dedicated to the game's UI, because a simulation game with a bad UI is the absolute bane of the genre.
I'm certain that somewhere under the tens of windows the first tutorials instruct you to open, Software Inc. is a deep and well-made simulation. But until it becomes far more clear to play - you should NOT have to look up third-party guides to start your first playthrough, contrary to what many on the reviews for this game say - I simply cannot recommend this game to anybody other than the most dedicated and hardcore simulation players. Prison Architect is another game that suffered from this problem early in its development, but recovered from it spectacularly. I certainly hope the developer of this one takes a page or two from that playbook, and I look forward to seeing what comes in future updates.
I expect people to be upset to see a thumbs down on the reviews for this game, but I won't refund this game simply because I genuinely believe in this game's ability to succeed. I'll keep trying to figure it out until something clicks.

Haaaa, this is a tough one.
Vampires: The Masquerade is a semi-famous Pen&Paper rulebook which, duh, is about Vampires and their Masquerade to stay hidden from humanity. This game is one of the few (if not the only) PC adaption.
Clear pro's of VtMB: The story is quite solid, the characters are quite finely fleshed out. The atmosphere of the game is fitting and the background&setting (naturally, when derived from a RP rulebook) nice to explore.
Aaaaand, that's about it.
On the other hand, the list of downsides: The game is old. Obviously this means it has an outdated graphic engine, but that really isn't a big deal (at least not to me). HOWEVER, the gameplay is as well OLD. It puts you back into the days of awful backtracking. It doesn't have all those nifty features you would be used from modern RPGs. The fights feel sluggish and uninspiring, the animations/hitboxes don't seem to match whatsoever.
There are quite a few bugs in the game, too. Actually, you can't even start the game on a 64bit system unless you download yourself an unofficial patch to fix the problem. (And another to fix up the game's limited resolution options.)
In total, VtMB was, no doubt, at it's release a REALLY formidable RPG with an immensely powerful and detailed background. By today's measure, however, it's barely a better interactive story teller with fundamental RPG elements.
Rating: 5/10, sorry, I like the Franchise and the P&P, but the game just isn't playable past it's 'classic' value
As such, I can only recommend this game to nostalgiast who WANT to play old games or hardcore VtM fans and only below a price of 5€.

Beautiful realistic graphics, an amazing soundtrack, breathtaking locations, a captivating atmosphere and an intriguing story all help to make this game an unforgettable experience. The game doesn't hold your hand - from the start you are on your own, and it is up to you to figure out how to proceed.
You play as Paul Prospero, a supernatural detective, who has come to the stunning, but quiet, Red Creek Valley to look for a boy named Ethan Carter. As you travel around the different locations you will discover more about what happened, as well as learn about Ethan and his family.
Some people call this game a walking simulator, but I think those people were expecting something like Amnesia or the like. The game is a narrative experience, so focus is on the story. The plot is excellent and has quite a few twists and surprises, some of it clearly inspired by the works of the early 20th century horror author H.P. Lovecraft.
If you do not like story-heavy games, where you have to piece together different parts and make up the missing links yourself, then this game is not for you. The game isn't really scary, but while walking around, you can't help but get a feeling of dread, especially if you get really caught up in the story. However there is one part that may include jumpscares - it is necessary to truly complete the game, but it can be skipped if it is a problem.
I spent about 8 hours on this game, but it can easily be completed in a much shorter time, like 2-3 hours. I spent a long time simply admiring the environments and walking around feeling the atmosphere, sometimes even stopping to just think about the story. If I have to think of any improvements, the game could have been slightly longer, and it will probably be a while before you truly understand the story.
Get it if you want to get an intriguing experience, dive deep into a complex story or simply just try something a little different.

Let's get this out of the way: this is a narrative-and-exploration-driven game. This is a downside for some people. Personally, I enjoy these games. This is, in my opinion, the ultimate of these games  out there. At least, the popular ones. I am sure someone who is more into these games than I am could rattle off a list of games that do this concept better.
For me, Vanishing Ethan's Carter is a combination of an intriguing story, great visuals, great audio, interesting gameplay and novel mechanics. The biggest strength is clearly the game's visuals. The environements are incredible, high-res, and realistic. I cannot think of a time when I could even see tiling or repeating textures. Along with them, the sound design is great. The ambient noise and music lends a great atmospheric nature to the game.
Another strength for me is the mechanics. The "put the scene in order" game is fun and novel, although sometimes difficult to understand why a part of a scene is represented by an object or in a location when, sometimes, that object or location is never seen in the final cinematic.
The weakness in Carter's Vanishing Ethan is really more of a weak strength: the story. Don't get me wrong, it has several good twists. The problem I have is that it's confusing, particularly near the end. It feels like we needed a final "put all the cinematics in order" game to make sure I had the timeline right. Then there's the final twist which seems almost like a cop-out to me, but it has a lot of symbolism so it kind of gets away with it.
Overall, this game is well-worth the money you put into it. If you enjoy exploration games, you will probably enjoy this. If you don't, consider getting it during a sale!

TL;DR: If you ever even remotely enjoyed a tower defense type of game, you seriously need to play this one. If you haven't but like rpgs, this is your best bet to find out what a great TD can be like, with the RPG elements to help carry you along. Really, if the (very generous) demo to this game doesn't get you hooked, then tower defense may simply not be your genre, and at least now you know. ;)
*** ***
Defender's Quest is one of those games that without too much fanfare and fancy graphics simply get gameplay right. The rpg elements are well embedded, the story is not just an excuse for progression, the dialogues are well written and funny, the music is good and sets the mood nicely - but it's really all just about the balanced, fun, just-one-more-level gameplay.
It takes place in a plague colony, where the afflicted are turned into horrors controlled by a necromancer master villain. Your hero realizes she's capable of bringing herself and her allies into a halfway world, where the horrors and ultimately the villain can be fought with. While this is a simple enough premise, the way it brilliantly ties the story to the game's mechanics is one of the stellar design aspects of the game. (More on that
, if you're interested in game design).
Due to the fact that you customize the appearance of your pawns, equip them with weapons and armour, and train them towards permanent experience that you can put towards an interesting skill tree, you end up becoming more attached to them then if you just had "towers" to play with. Especially your set crew of 6 archetypical towers/heroes is a fun bunch with entertaining banter in the (skippable) cut scenes, and by the end of the game you are genuinely interested in their actions and story decisions.
I appreciated the attention to detail that allows you to customize both the difficulty and the game experience: active pause, different speed controls, highly configurable hotkeys, customizable general difficulty on top of the ability to replay maps on different difficulty levels (which actually play differently, instead of simply increasing the number of enemies or turning them into sponges). And then there's the Game+, which may just be even more fun to play than the normal game - if you can survive it. Plus, there's the sheep. Good luck with that. ;)
With its 30+ grindable main levels, the endless levels, a couple of different endings, a Game+, side missions to unlock and many interesting achievements, there is a very generous amount of content there for the price. Plus, a full HD/60 FPS upgrade is coming soon, for free, with redesigned graphics (the one aspect of the game that many may find lacking), so what more do you want?
Maybe what you want is Defender's Quest 2, which is expected to come out some time in 2016 - giving you plenty of time to finish playing 1 first. :)

Table Top Racing: World Tour is a kart racer with a Micro Machines aesthetic. Unfortunately, it's not an entirely memorable one. It's obvious the devs were trying to make something special here, with the admittedly pretty visuals (probably the best thing about the game) and the exotic locations, but after a while everything starts to blur together.
+The small car list is at least made up of vehicles that handle quite differently from one another.
~Some decent environment variety that sadly gets recycled quite a bit through the single player
~Weapon wheels give some sort of pre-race strategy, but not enough IMO.
~Music is okay at first, but you'll want to mute it pretty quickly. (In my experience, Forza Horizon music is a great replacement.)
-The game doesn't penalize you at all for using the Boing weapon wheels to jump over entire sections of the race track(s), which makes the game a cakewalk if you get those wheels too early.
-Multiplayer has been dead since day one, so don't bother if you're looking for a solid online experience.
As a single player kart racer, it's quite competent with some decent weapons-based racing to be had. Take a look past the gorgeous exterior though, and the hollow interior shows itself. It's an average racer in search of a heart that other games have.
If the above doesn't bother you, get it at a steep discount on sale. Otherwise, there are other games that do what this one was trying to do, but much better. If you want a great 90s style arcade racer, try Toybox Turbos or Redout. If you want a kart racer, Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed is still the best on Steam. And if you end up playing this anyway, whatever you do, DON'T buy the DLC. Each DLC makes the game worse in different ways.

This is purely a gamer's review, someone who's enjoyed horror, survival horror, action, and rpg games.  I am not a fan of the series, or of pencil and paper rpgs.  I have played unmodded, with only the unofficial patch.  EDIT: you fanboys can downvote me all you want, this is still an objective and accurate review.
Interesting story, that.  As it turns out, even though this game was released 10 years ago, with the developers apparently and immediately dropping support for it, people are STILL churning out both patches and mods for this game.  That should pique your curiosity at least.
Let's get something obvious out of the way.  Even with the patches, the graphics are pretty rustic.  Bugs are STILL legion.  You'll be able to ignore that with the atmosphere, but there's no denying this was a small budget enterprise in 2004.  With the unofficial patches boosting things up to higher resolutions, you may have terrible omnipresent screen distortion along the top edge, amongst various other snags.
You pick your vampiric clan and one of several back-histories, which determines your beginning stats and primary 3 vampiric abilities.  You can have the game distribute the points for you via questionnaire, or do it all yourself (which I did).
The game takes place in several small (and I do mean small) areas packed with buildings and npcs.  At first you'll wander around lost (the only maps are on bus stops and in sewers), but exploring is part of the fun in a game like this.  Several missions will have you venturing outside the city via cab to special areas that you cannot access afterwards.
Being a vampire, of course you have to feed on blood, and you can't let humans see you do this.  You have a system of 5 strikes which can be violated any number of ways, such as feeding with witnesses, allowing evidence of vampires to become known (sometimes objects, or dialogue choices), to random butchering of the cattle.  In the same way, being discreet can sometimes earn you these marks back.  The concept is neat, but fundamentally flawed, and in any case completely avoidable by simply not being a terrible player.
The story isn't overly predictable, and the game has a strong cast.  There's an undeniable atmosphere here, and I believe it's that undercurrent and plausible mythology that keeps the fanbase going.  There are certain people who have latched onto this game and will not let go, for various reasons.  The dialogues are lengthy and varied, and occasionally influenced by your specific clan type and certain vampiric traits (seduction, intimidation, etc).  However, there's no getting around the fact that you are basically an errand boy the entire game.  It's a little more plausible being the new vamp on the block and everyone you meet being centuries older than you, but the game never steps outside of this formula, not even once from what I've seen.
The combat is clunky, at best.  You could call it challenging, or cheap, depending on your viewpoint.  For my run, although I made sure I was fully stocked on firearms, I stuck with melee weapons, which may have altered the difficulty.  There's also a stealth system, with stealth kills if you're directly behind enemies, but don't expect too much.  AI is functional at best, even with the occasional wallhacking.  During one boss battle my enemies implanted themselves into walls and I had to start over.  The combat camera (3rd person view) is surprisingly fair, if a little squirrely.
Doing sidequests helps combat (and everything else) in the form of acquiring skill points, but the truth is you will never feel like a badass.  I played through spamming two primary abilities, superhuman speed and some form of intimidation to lower enemy's combat stats.  I know the Gangrel clan can transform (but I've heard it's underwhelming), another one can make enemies commit suicide, still another can turn invisible entirely.  The vampiric clan differences are pretty broad, and are wasted on the combat here.  Using your abilities consumes blood, and if you don't feed often enough or have enough blood to start with you run the risk of frenzying.  You'll get massive stat boosts, but be unable to control your character for the time being.  Obviously if it happens in public, this is bad.  Some clans are more prone to this than others, but it never happened to me.
Even with everything I just said, I'd still recommend the game - if it weren't for the endings.  Several glaring plot holes are present regardless of which of the five endings you get - which really aren't five endings, more like three and two variations.  All of them are at least vaguely unsatisfactory.  The game does a terrific job of building up, and you're always interested to see which fictional creature turns out to be real next, but the endings just flop out.
As engaging (if slightly predictable) as the game's atmosphere and events are, there's no feeling of reward for actually reaching the various mediocre endings.  If they were all different from each other, or at least interesting, I could recommend this game in spite of its flaws.  But they aren't, so I can't.

So why isn't this game good?  I've played tons of rhythm games and this one has 'decent' music, but has no real assemblence of something you could nod your head to and say: yea, this works in a rhythm game.  It simply doesn't and the input is bad.  Now to meet anyone that says: maybe you're just bad at rhythm games, maybe I am, but I the music alone is not motivating and doesn't telegraph much of a downbeat let alone figuring out the count.
The game tries extremely hard to be hip and ironic.  Using references of date♥♥♥♥♥♥ crystal meth, and getting stabbed by a hobo in less than 1 minute to get you to say: YEA, THIS IS HIP!

I love rhythm games. Stepmania used to occupy all my time when I was younger, but this game is just so messy. Casting spells then waiting for them would create awful timing where you'd end up having to defend yourself by the time your spell appear, so you'd have to stagger your timing, and failing a spell will punish you with reallocating your timing between attacking and defending to regenerate your mana. To make it worst, each fight is a timelimit based on the song's length so if you get to a choppy start, you're pretty much screwed. Timing is everything with rhythm games and for me there's just too much to keep track for me to enjoy actually playing the game.
Plus, this game is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if your play style involves two hands.

This game, as an RPG, keeps you on your toes. The crafting system and leveling system is well-balanced, but a lot of grinding is required to be able to match up to later boss fights.

A story about my uncle is a short, sweet hidden gem of a game where you play as a nephew of your adventurous uncle. While you traverse the levels, the entire story is being narrated as a bed time story by your future self. The premise is this: you basically enter your uncle’s cabin and find a special suit he uses to go on his adventures, except this one was specifically tailored for you. You strap it on, and propel yourself through each level, gaining stronger abilities as you move along. I’ll save the rest for you to enjoy, and enjoy it you will.
It’s a first person platformer but with very addicting mechanics. It’s not like anything I’ve played before. There’s just something amazing about soaring through caverns and caves with your crystal-powered grapple gadget.
This game may seem all nice and fluffy but don’t let it fool you, it is actually quite difficult, which I actually enjoy. It’s nice to have a challenge, you may get annoyed at some parts but it just makes completing it even more satisfying.
This is probably the biggest thing this game has going for it. It’s like you’re immersed in this book where you get to reenact the story. I love it, and I don’t even like story-heavy games or books for that matter, so it just goes to show.
Although this isn’t my cup of tea, I still put it here as there are many others who like speedrunning. If you’re one of them, there’s no reason not to get this game.
The story, though being fantastic, is way too short and you almost don’t want it to end. It takes less than an evening to complete the game. Sure as I mentioned earlier there’s speedrunning, but apart from that, there’s nothing much.
Although $12.99 isn’t a lot for a game, I don’t think this game has enough content to support its price. However, when there’s a sale this game usually gets a massive discount and is just a couple of dollars, it is definitely worth it at this time.
Although I think the graphics are quite stunning, the character models are almost something straight out of a nightmare. Albeit, this is an indie game, so I’ll cut it some slack.

The game has an interesting story, but I feel like the control scheme is poorly done. Enough so that I find it distracts from just enjoying the game. To explain, you have a sprint button, a jump button, a super jump button, and a grapple button. Super jump takes a couple moments to charge so you have to hold it down for a bit or it does nothing. The regular jump button makes you jump the moment you press it but it's not a huge jump, and doesn't seem to do anything if you hold it down. It just feels like to me that the jump buttons should have been combined into one. Tap the button to do a basic jump, and hold it down to do a super jump.
Furthermore, the regular jump is A on a controller something I feel is very intuitive, but the super jump button is the top right trigger and the sprint button is the top left trigger. Grapple is the bottom right trigger. It just feels wrong that the super jump feels like the jump I'll most likely be using most the time but is also a button that is pressed with the same finger as the grapple button. But it's not like I can just switch the controller layout so that the super jump button is the A button, because you still need the regular jump for hoping over little things.
Perhaps for some the control set up seems natural and fluid, and they go running around jumping and grappling onto things like in the trailer. But for me it feels counter intuitive and instead of feeling like I'm gracefully jumping through the sky I'm instead having to think about exactly what buttons I want to press to do something.
With a game like this, I feel it VERY important that the control set up feel instinctual, and I feel it fails in this. Sadly Steam only lets me either recommend or not recommend a game, so I have to go with not recommend. I trust though that if you've reached this point in reading the review though that you understand my primary complaint is the control set up. If you are all right with games with strange controls or you don't feel that the set up described sounds strange, perhaps this game is for you.

When it came out, I paid the full price of $60 at launch, plus $12.99 for each new faction and $3.99 a pop for a bunch of commanders. I come back now, only to find British Forces added, $12.99! Ethan Carter is a beautiful game. Every five feet I wanted to stop and take a screenshot but at the same time the screenshots don’t really do it justice, as the combination of visuals, sounds, and music really make the experience. The soundtrack is exquisite, haunting, and often ominous. It adds to the sense of wonder during exploration and keeps you on edge as you anticipate how Red Creek Valley’s secrets will present themselves next.
This game really excels in creating atmosphere. There was a major sense of foreboding any time I needed to leave the beautiful country backdrop and go inside. It didn’t matter if it was a Church or a mine, just seeing a doorway made the hairs on my arms stand up. At one point I stood frozen at the entrance to a crypt, knowing there was something to find down there, but dreading descending into the darkness. Tension is maintained through the whole experience. Even just walking through the lovely environments, listening to the haunting music, I was often startled by sudden narration or other sounds.   It maintains constant eeriness, without getting overwhelming. There is only one sequence in the game where you are in any real danger (though death has very little consequence). On one hand, it seemed a little out of place to have an immediate, rather than psychological threat. But on the other, it did amp up the game’s intensity and added a sense of urgency that was otherwise missing.
Gameplay is very simple. This is a first person exploration and mystery game. You can walk, run, crouch (though I found only one place I needed to crouch in the game), and examine or pick up objects. I really enjoyed the puzzles. You weren’t given much direction but everything was logical and the solutions made sense. The major puzzles involve solving murders. You examine the scene, which usually involves the body, the weapon, and a few other key elements. Once you’ve examined everything and put things in their rightful places, you can ‘communicate’ with the body of the victim, which sparks a new puzzle. Vignettes will appear around the crime scene and you need to put them in the correct order so you can reconstruct and watch what happened. Every murder you solve tells you a bit more about the story. There are also some non-murder puzzles to solve, and I found these even more compelling. A favourite of mine involved discerning truth from illusion as you explored an abandoned house. As you solve these puzzles you discover things like Newspaper clippings and stories written by Ethan, which flesh out the narrative.
The overall story is well told – this isn’t about simple murder, there are hints of a greater darkness everywhere. The game raises a lot of questions but doesn’t answer them all. I’m okay with this, as some things are best left up to our imaginations. The voice actor for the main protagonist does a solid, if not exceptional job. He conveys the paranormal detective aspect well, but his lines are a little one-note.
In a few ways, Ethan Carter reminded me of Murdered: Soul Suspect. Solving the mysteries and inspecting clues can be similar, and stylistically there some overlaps. However, unlike Murdered, Ethan Carter isn’t confused about what it is. There are no tacked on action sequences. The game promises exploration and mystery solving and that is what it delivers.
I have very few complaints about Ethan Carter. Sometimes parts of the game world felt a little too large – going from one end of the map to the other required a fair bit of travel time. This was a good thing while I was first exploring, but if I needed to backtrack it felt like a bit of a time sink.
The vanishing of Ethan Carter is one of the most attractive and atmospheric games I’ve played. It maintains an amazing amount of tension throughout, without going into full horror game mode. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys exploring and narrative gaming experiences.

I played Civ for lots of hours, days and weeks offline, so they are not logged on Steam. Actually, I am the original Civ fan from the first Civilization game (1991). Greatest strategy game. Infinite replayability. Nice graphics, atmosphere and amazing symphonic sountrack.
However, the developers could have added much more features to the gameplay, cause nowadays Civilization is basically the same game as the first Civilization (1991), just with up-to-day graphics in 3D.
I personally would like to see MUCH more detail in all the aspects of the game, more complexed city building, politics, culture, research, war and diplomacy, and more automation to avoid micromanaging (but that should be up to the players choice though, only when wanted by player, and still to be available to micromanage on demand). Diplomacy could be much more realistic.
The first Civ game (1991) had some nice feaures which are no longer in the game, such as city landscape view and palace building in the capital, ministers changing their look-outfit depending on the era and regime. Those features would be nice to add back to the game. It is always pleasant to see the detailed results of you country building efforts. I would add more features to that. The map view could be also more close to real life, with ACTUAL scale and look and of all the things there, and also more chaotic and less geometrically perfect-aligned-formatted (like in real life), less copypasted, with more unique looking features every time (sandbox/procedural-generated look according to the conditions on the map = geography, climate, time o fthe year, weather, terrain development, damage-pollution, civilization current status). Basically, it would be great if you could see you civilization and units like Google-maps terrain and street view. That would only benefit the game, I think.
Btw, I don't like the cartoonish-casual look of Civ 6 at all. This is a serious game in it's core principle, and I would prefer it to look PHOTOREALISTIC. I think, most of the Civ fans would agree on that.
