Well, now that I've achieved all achievements I feel that I should contribute and review this game!
This is the first time I've played a game like this and it was actually a pretty good experience overall, especially since this game was Free-to-Play!
The first thing I noticed and liked about this game was how it has full voice acting! The voices seemed to portray the characters in the game pretty well and provided the player with an immersive experience. But even though overall the voices were a pro for me, there were times when I felt the voices got excessive and annoying but I learned that it can be countered by just disabling the feature or just clicking through the dialogue. Another thing I loved about the game was how each "romance target" had a different story to tell. There were some overlays in history between the Demon Brothers but overall they each had different reasons for doing the things they did. Also great background music! I found the music pretty catchy in this game (especially the ringtone).
Some things I did not like as much was some of the art, how some parts of the story didn't go into enough detail, and the repetitiveness. Well the characters seemed slightly disproportionate and there were some people in the game that I thought looked like a mutant (the teacher) but I didn't expect too much out of a Free-to-Play game. The creator of the game provided a lot of cut scene art though so even though it wasn't amazing, it still provided players with a source of visual aid for the verbal descriptions and dialogue. So even though not great, still better than nothing at all. Also I felt like the story had the potential to become something better but because of the objective of the game (seduce everybody), everything was just glossed over and never really dug into. I mean at times I just felt information was shot at me and that I never really had the chance to digest it. If the creators went more in depth and explained some of the story, I felt the game would have been even better (I learned there was a sequel so its possible that they'll go more indepth on the story then). Last thing I thought was a con was the repetitiveness of the game. It is kind of to be expected since most of the individual characters' plots touch upon others but I still can't help but find it tedious to read the same thing over and over and over (I'm talking about the parts that aren't skippable but are still the same for almost all the characters (like the pre-ending dialogue.)
Overall
Pros:
FREE!
Voice acting included
Background music
Interesting story
Cons:
Some of the art
Not going indepth on story
Repetitiveness

Great Game For Younger Gamers
*A lot of my reviews are written for parent with younger gamers (4-7 years) and this is one of them*
This is basically your run-of-the-mill "kart racer". And that's pretty much why I bought it. My kids are at that age where they like video games but the only ones they can play with any skill are games with simple controls like racers. So I picked this one up on a recent sale and it seems like it's a lot of fun. It's not a very complex racer, utilizing only a few buttons on a standard Xbox 360 controller, which is a plus for younger children. Most of the cars seem to handle the same and while this may turn off mature race fans I doubt most kids and more casual racers  will mind. One thing that stood out to me right away was that the pysics are a little wierd; instead of feeling like your car is moving the game feels like the car is stationary and everything else (background/track, other cars) is moving around it. Anyone who's ever played an old SNES "Mode 7" game like F-Zero will know what I mean. But this isn't a bad thing, it's just something that takes a second or two to get used to. The cars are all pretty cool looking but have limited visual customizations which is sort of a minus for younger players who love to change their cars looks. One nice thing is that most of the cars can be fully upgraded with limited amounts of effort which will give younger gamers a real sense of accomplishment.
As far as everything else like graphics and music/sound goes it's servicable; nothing special but nothing deal breaking either. All in all If you can get this at the $10 range (I paid about $7 for the game and the DLC) and you have younger race fans this is one of the better Kart Racers out there and I reccomend it.

I'm not normally a fan of Vampire games, but I picked up this one upon recommendation by a friend, and holy cow is it good! Important points include:
1) There are violent encounters you can turn into diplomatic ones, if you're very diplomatic.
2) There are stealth encounters you can turn into shoot 'em up encounters, if you're inclined.

This is a great game! If you can get it to work.
That's right. Before buying VTMB, you should know what you're getting yourself into. The game was never finished; it was released as an imcomplete, buggy, broken product - and that's what it still is, even today. Teams of modders have been working on it to either fix as many bugs as they could or even to rebalance and redesign it and to install one of the unofficial patches is, after installing the game to your hard drive, the very first thing you should do; but even so, be prepared for a world of bugs, crashes, google searches, .exe replacing, .cfg tweaking and so on.
Let me tell you about my experience with this game. I bought it. Then, I installed Tessara's gold patch which, supposedly (and I have no reason to think otherwise) does an amazing job at fixing all the imaginable problems this game was released with. Then I had to find a way to make the screen resolution acceptable (not 1024*768, this isn't 1999 anymore). Then I was on the street and I noticed a loss of framerate, so I tweaked the .cfg file to deactivate meteo effects. After a couple hours I reached a beach and the game started crashing, forcing my computer into sleep mode. I couldn't get past that beach. Later on I found that the sea's texture was making my comps go bananas so I went for more .cfg tweaking. Then I played a couple more hours and the AI, suddenly, disabled itself - meaning, NPCs froze in place, making the game completely unplayable. Then, as I was looking for a solution, my comps started crashing again.
That was it. I decided to wait a year or two for the (unbelievably dedicated) teams of modders who were working at fixing this game, and uninstalled Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines.
Now don't get me wrong - some people (with Tessara's help in any case) are able to play VTMB just fine. I was able to play for like 5 hours and it was great - dark, immersive, great attention to detail, thrilling game system, great infiltration sequences... It feels like Deus Ex all over again. It feels like a pen & paper experience where I'm alone with the game master. It feels great.
But it's ♥♥♥♥ing unstable. It's broken. Anyone considering purchasing this game should know that there's a risk that it won't work at all, that you'll spend as much time fixing it as playing it. Buying this game is a gamble - you're risking your money here.
But, again, when it works, whoa, guys - what a ride!

Wonderful game, with some amazing ideas. I very much recommend it, as it belongs in the RPG Hall of Fame, despite all its shortcomings.
But remember: for all intents and purposes, this is an Early Access game, that never got finished. It lacks general polishing and bug-fixing, and the endgame was pretty much just tossed there, to have an ending at all.
It will offer 25-30 hours of great fun, playing as a vampire, with a very very good RPG system under the hood. This game truly excels when doing what Vampire: The Masquerade is all about: keeping up the Masquerade, while going about your vampire business.
The system forces you to be mindful of keeping your vampire existence hidden from mortals by the way of Masquerade Violations. If you commit an act that reveals you as a vampire (feeding in public, using obvious vampire powers in public, telling humans about your condition), you lose one such point, and if you lose them all, it's Game Over.
The RPG system also rewards going the non-violent way in quests, as there is no experience awarded for killing things, only completing objectives - often giving higher rewards for not killing anyone. This mechanic, combined with the fact that combat is a horrible click-fest, makes it well worth it to pursue other ways of completing the quests, and using violence only when absolutely necessary. Right up until the end-game, situations where violence is the only way are few, and well placed. Going without leveling up any combat skills is a viable (although challenging) route to take right up to the "Hell at the Hotel Hallowbrook" quest during the end-game. And that quest also happens to be the part where the game pretty much starts falling apart.
I keep mentioning the end-game, and for good reason: it is astonishingly bad. While up until this point the game is all about giving you choices, by the end it turns into a mindless action game with boring combat, and even more boring and repetitive boss fights. The only way through is by fighting, so all the points in Persuasion, Seduction, Stealth and other skills turn completely useless, and you are forced to kill waves after waves of enemies... The last hours of the game might as well be another game completely, and a bad one at that.
My recommendation would be to play the game until you meet a taxi driver that keeps asking questions, answer him as you want, then go on YouTube and watch someone else suffer through the horrible mess the game devolves into. That way you get to enjoy all the wonders of the game, and also get to skip 1-2 hours of mind-boggling stupidity, that has nothing to do with the game you've been playing anyway.
Another recommendation would be to download and install the Unofficial Patch - that fixes a lot of bugs, fixes broken parts of the game, and generally brings Bloodlines closer to feeling like a finished product.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is far from a perfect RPG experience. That being said, those who can overlook it's bugs and simple combat can find an engaging and refreshing take on the vampire genre.
What Vampire does well is create an oustanding amount of compelling and interesting classes with rich backgrounds drawn from various forms of Vampire myth, as well as well written dialogue and interesting quest-design. While this may not excite the common RPG player, Vampire enthusiasts will enjoy the rich world created to explore. The various "Bloodlines" serve as both the class system as well as a twist on character's story and how they interact with the world. A noble Ventrue vampire will find manipulating vampire's of lesser bloodlines easy, while the insane Malkavian will be forced to spread mania to acomplish his or her goals. This all leads to a considerable amount of replayability amongst the different builds and bloodlines.
Unfortunatly Vampire isn't without it's problems. Combat can become repetetive, especially towards the later end of the game where non-threatening enemies appear by the truckload. Bugs are relatively routine, though only one was game-breaking to the point that I had to use console commands. I did have to use an unnofficial patch from a third party site to even get the game to function on my computer, and even then I found myself having to alt-tab in order for the game's visiuals to display on the screen. Lastly visuals in the game are rather dated, but considering the age of the game, this is something the user should overlook.
While Vampire won't stand out to anyone not interested in the World of Darkness, any curious Vampire enthusiasts should consider picking this game up, it's well worth it's minescule asking price. 8/10

A Story About My Uncle, A first person platform focused game with a wierd sci fi fiction tale. The story follows a Nephew who is asked by a relative of his for a story, the man feels compelled to tale of an  adventure he once had as a young boy, one day when visiting his uncle, who had always taken him to travels and journeys around the world. His Uncle, a  renowned and ambitous scientist in many manners. Upon arrival to the uncles house the boy in question discovers that his uncle is missing. Furthur investigating leads the child to discover more mystery than he had always dreamed for. realms, locations that have yet to be visited by man, Following the clues left by his uncle, The boy sets out to discover the whereabouts and fate around the mesterious journey the uncle had set out on. The narrative is conveyed from the boy as the adult to young girl, the girl will promply interrupt the story the Man is telling of his childhood journey when a question isin her head, or she may state a thought, which adds more to thoughts as to where or what this tale really is.
Gameplay, over the course that is layed before you will jump a lot, given an item early on in the game you wiill be using it to tether yourself to objects,(most likely a rock), to propell yourself through the air, the game will for the most part not ever  hold your hand, delivering a lot of immerssion for the player to discover where and what to do next. Playing the game I felt some trial and error was happening throught most of the gameplay scenarios handed to you. A checkpoint system is mostly generouse, very few momments where you felt annoyed by the need to recontinue some elements of your journey. I never found any reason to complain, logically the mistakes i made were from my own doing. The game itself being relatively short, tries it's best to give the player a diffrent way to traverse the enviroment to feel a more fresh feeling towards the platforming, rather than desighning what you see at the beginning of game constantly, though you'll find that the game will always keep older platforming, "routes", around the entirety of the game, while constantly bringing forth new ones so that the feeling of repitition is hardly there. You'll as well will be given  "upgrades", that will help you greatly as well add the diffuculty.
Final thought this game is fantastic! I won't say any more in fear of spoiling the whole wonderous tale that you'll have to platform through to reach the conclsuion. I personally think the story is very thoughtful as well the game itself being aware of own challenges. The cheaper you can get this game the better, however if it's twenty, im really not sure what the price is. I would still recommend the purchase if you have that to spend.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an extremely well put together puzzle/adventure/exploration/mystery/horror game.  Its world is a joy to explore. The environments are so well put together I was contantly wanting to see what was around the next bend or through that grove of trees or in that house.  I took a ridiculous amount of screenshots.  It just seemed that after I took a few steps there was something else that I had to take a picture of.
The music is beautiful and the subtle transitions as you move between environments are very well done to adjust the mood of the game at a given point.
The story is really interesting and I wanted to just push on until I had solved the mystery of what was going on and had transpired in the valley before I got there.  It is one of those rare stories that stays with you after you finish it and you find yourself thinking about it for a while after you are done.  Really a great and well made game.  I highly reccomend it.

You just explore by yourself and if you find everything you were supposed to find, then good for you, if you don't no one cares, you'll still get to the end eventually. I absolutely love this game.  Some of the most fun I've ever had.  But honestly I have trouble even continuing playing knowing that the developers have no intention of continuing to develop and support the game.
Yes they roll out very small bugfixes and patches every so often, and they released a silly gun and some capes for "Liberty Day" this past month and a new shotgun back in march I believe, but they have explicitly stated that they will not be adding new "content" of any sizeable measure.  This means new enemies and planets.  And while the game is very fun, with gameplay that cannot be found in any other game, all this potential is being wasted by developers who refuse to continue to support the game.
This is especially sad since the game has been criminally underrepresented due to a lack of advertising.  The game deserves to be popular; the gameplay is incredible.  With some substantial content updates and advertising it would be a game that would last for years and years with a devoted, hardcore player-base.  Why can't they add new content though?  A recent statement by game designer Patrik in response to a reddit post asking "Will be there any chance to add new monsters/boss?" said "Probably not, we are starting to reach the technical limits of some of the consoles."
So, because this game was ported from consoles, the PC version is getting shafted.  No more content worth speaking of.  And the player-base is dwindling because of it.  So while I'm not prone to advise people against buying games because the games are dead and/or dying, I fear that this one will be irrelevant in no-time because the developers are moving on and leaving Helldivers in the dust.  And it makes me incredibly sad, as experiencing this gameplay was phenomenal.  It was something that I wanted to master and share with a large, thriving community for a long time to come, and to be excited about when I could have new content to introduce new challenges and possibilities to this incredible gameplay.  It's a shame, but I can't recommend the game.  Especially not at this price tag with developers who are jumping ship.

I am so tired of people comparing this to Starship Troopers.
This game is like Starship Troopers. Launch four squishy humans onto a merciless and wild alien planet, and raze it to hell trying to stay alive. Squad play is where it's at. The higher difficulty planets provide the MAXIMUM entertainment, as long as you have the gear to survive them. Being overrun by a ferocious alien horde, titanic behemoth beetles, or blasted into oblivion by a Cyborgian tank is where the game shines. Four Helldivers vs insurmountable odds.
And then the beat kicks in.
You can Lone Wolf the game as well, if you so chose. At higher level planets, you might actually consider the solo Stealthy play. Equipt with a fully upgraded UAV(which displays enemy patrols and SAMPLES*) and DISTRACTOR BEACON(draws all enemy patrols towards its location), you can send the aliens running one way while you sneak around the opposite direction. I conquered the Bug's Homeworld solo and earned the yellow bug cape(ACCESSORIZE!) that way. Sometimes, you can't rely on players to get it right, so going solo into the pits of Hell alone can often be the best move.
*SAMPLES = Upgrade Points. Each weapon and STRATAGEM(special weapons, vehicles, items, turrets, bombs called down from the sky) has a small upgrade tree. 10 SAMPLES = 1 Upgrade Point. You find SAMPLES scattered across the planets. Get the DLC that contains the UAV(RANGER DLC $2.99) and upgrade it to level 3(max lvl) so it will display all enemy patrols and reveal all SAMPLE locations on the map.
It can seem repitious after awhile, the gameplay only changes by what choice of STRATAGEMS you bring(together with your team). Tackling the hardest planets generates the most challenge, which IMO = maximum fun.
Also, Friendly Fire is always on, so try not to kill your teammates.. as best as you can.

Reason to pay Helldivers:
- Smash TV/Starship Troopers style Action
- Massive inventory of weapons
- Awesome co-op mechanics
- Loaded with dark humour
- The Chaotic Glory for Democracy

Table Top Racing: World Tour (TTR from now on) is a racing game that takes place on…..well, what do you think? Tables of course!
Kart racers have been around for eons, but what about…..car racers? Y’know, kart racers with real-looking cars? I suppose that’s what I’d describe TTR as. It feels like a kart racer yet the vehicles have the appearance of realistic cars, vans, or trucks. Normally I’d talk about gameplay first, but hey, why not graphics this time? Let’s switch things up!
So, the game has a sort of realistic look to it, like I mentioned earlier. The tracks all consist of a table (or what generally looks like somewhere in a house) with various household objects (food, bottles, etc.) spread around the track/table. As you drive your little cars around you can then knock a lot of the stuff on the track over, which is pretty fun. The cars themselves are just a mix of realistic-looking race cars and knockoffs of cars from pop culture (the Breaking Bad RV, a “fauxrari”, etc.). Everything in the game looks pretty crisp and polished overall, so graphically I definitely have no complaints.
Now onto the gameplay. Here’s where things are both good and bad. See, the game basically consists of you driving your little car around a track over and over until you win. That’s….basically it, however there’s a small variety of modes to mix things up. From the main menu there’s “Championships”, “Special Events”, and “Multiplayer”. Championships is the meat of the game, and it’ll last you about 5-8 hours or so depending on how skilled you are at racing games. Within Championships you’ll find 6 different cups with a variety of events to choose from. These events are one of a few different game modes (Combat races where you can use powerups, pure/no weapons races, a “pursuit” mode, elimination, time trials, drifting, and a “get x lap time” mode), which helps to keep the gameplay from getting too stale. On top of that, there’s collectable coins scattered around each track in some interesting hidden locations so even if you’re terrible at the game it incentivizes you to collect them and use the money they give you to upgrade your car (or buy a new one) and get better.
The Special Events mode is basically a variety of events, like in Championships mode, yet there’s some very minor twists. It’s just extra content I suppose. I never got to try out the multiplayer unfortunately (no one was playing online), so I can’t comment on that mode.
Generally I enjoyed my time with TTR, but what did I dislike? Well, to start, the tracks. There’s…..5 of them. That’s slightly remedied by the slight variation given to them during certain events (I believe the game refers to each track’s variations as “track A”, “track B”, etc.), but after playing what is basically the same track over and over it gets a bit old. I’d have really liked to have seen
tracks, not just the same 5 ones over and over with tiny changes here and there.
Secondly, the game’s handling feels weird, at least to me. Maybe this is just a personal thing but it felt like on every turn my car would either hit a wall (at least initially) or just barely make the turn, while the AI seemed to make turns at full speed just fine. Now granted, with handling upgrades on the best cars in the game it’s not too bad, but when I had first started playing it was definitely frustrating watching myself hit walls on almost every turn. I think the speed of the cars is pretty fitting but their handling could definitely use some work,
Beyond that, there’s not a whole lot to talk about with TTR. It’s fun I suppose, and pretty well-made overall. Err…...oh wait, that’s right - the music. It’s uh…..well, I think some people will enjoy it. Personally I thought it was mostly generic hip hop/electronic/dance stuff, so sometimes I just felt like muting the game and turning on my own music while I raced. However, I feel as if it’s not terrible, but simply “tolerable”, if that makes any sense. Also there’s a song that says “be drunk” repeatedly. I….I don’t even know.
Table Top Racing is a pretty solid fast-paced racing game with powerups. There’s a lot to like here, from the lovely visuals to the decent amount of variety in both customization options and game modes. Despite my problems with it, primarily the small number of tracks and some weird  turning problems (which are fixed with vehicle upgrades), I honestly really enjoyed playing this game. Bravo, developers - you’ve made a pretty great little racer!

Defender's Quest starts off as a pretty simple tower defence game with a goofy fantasy story and basic presentation, but then you start getting deeper into the game, unlock all the character classes and upgrade your characters more, and you find that there is actually a ton of depth and playability here. What's more, it never loses its intuitive and elegant design as it becomes more mechanically complex, and the game does a fine job of presenting you with a tough challenge but essentially giving you all the tools you need to overcome said challenge. Success is not determined simply by grinding to level up your characters, but rather by finding a way to better manage your resources until you find the optimal way to succeed.
This was one of my sleeper hits from 2013, and it's one of my favourite tower defence games on Steam, up there with Defence Grid: The Awakening and Plants vs. Zombies. It's a great starter tower defence game and introduces less experienced players to its mechanics in a very manageable way, but it also provides the depth and strategy that you just won't get from most of the free flash-based TD games you can find online. It's a fresh take on the genre and its very well executed...just don't expect to be too engaged by the cutscenes and character interactions that break up the combat missions. They're occasionally funny, but often rote and unnecessarily long. But that's just about my only criticism of the game - everything else is rock-solid.

My biggest issue with the game, as it happens, is that the various random events -- random drops, percentage to succeed/fail at crafting -- can be frustrating when luck is not on your side. Metro 2033 is a linear first-person shooter set in post-apocalyptic Moscow. The people living in Moscow live underground in old metro stations, while mutants roam on the surface. In addition, there are communist and fascist factions waging war against each other. You play as Artyom, who is sent to find help in defending his home station from attacks of supernatural beings called the "Dark Ones". The story of the game is very good, despite being relatively simple. There is also an alternate ending, which is unlocked by doing certain things during your playthrough.
The game can be played in two different modes, spartan and survival. The latter is, as you would imagine, a more survival-focused mode where you have to scavenge for supplies and there's a larger emphasis on stealth, whereas the former is more action-focused. I chose to play it on survival mode, because it's more in line with the setting and the theme of the game. There are also four different difficulty levels: normal, hardcore, ranger and ranger hardcore. In addition to deadlier combat, most or all of the HUD is disabled on the ranger difficulties, which really enhances immersion in my opinion. Unfortunately, those difficulties limit the amount of guns you can carry to 2 (3 on easier difficulties), which felt a little too restrictive. There are also no tutorials on ranger difficulties, which meant I had to figure out a lot of things myself. It wasn't a huge issue for me, but having tutorials on all difficulty levels definitely wouldn't hurt.
One of the things the game really nails down is the bleak and depressing atmosphere, which occasionally borders survival horror. It manages to paint a picture of a hostile world where there could be something dangerous around every corner. That is largely thanks to great art and sound design and often claustrophobic levels. The English voice acting is unfortunately not on par with the rest of the sound design, but that can be avoided by using Russian voices with English subtitles. The atmosphere, along with the interesting setting and game mechanics, like having to manually charge your flashlight or change gas mask filters, really help with getting immersed in the game.
The gameplay consists of fighting mutants and humans and scavenging for supplies in the metro and occasionally going to the surface to do the same thing. When fighting humans, you have the option of using a stealth approach if you wish. For a stealthy approach, you can use throwing knives and stealth kill or knock out people, in addition to silenced weapons. The enemy AI is fairly smart, although they may sometimes have trouble spotting you when you’re clearly in their sight. Unfortunately, stealth isn't really an option when dealing with mutants, which is a shame, since nearly half of the game consists of fighting them. Luckily, the enemy variety is pretty good and you have to use different techniques to deal with different mutants.
The gunplay feels pretty good. The weapons handle well and have a good amount of kick to them. There are a fairly large number of different weapons and they differ enough from each other. There is also some weapon customization: you can buy various attachments for your weapons from some metro stations, but the system is fairly limited.
The biggest problem I have with the game is its linear nature. There isnt a lot to explore and there are barely no side objectives and you’re often just forced down a tight path. It didn’t ruin the game for me, but i wish there were a bit more side activities, options to explore or multiple paths to the objective.
All in all, Metro 2033 Redux is a great game, despite its shortcomings and it’s one of my favorite games in recent memory. I definitely recommend this to everyone who likes single-player FPS games.
At the end of the day it's a dull corridor shooter with pretty poor enemy AI that feels very console'ish. The atmosphere is pretty well done though.

Metro 2033 Redux stands out in its survival horror genre. From stunning visuals to its intense gameplay, Metro 2033 Redux gets an outstanding score of 9/10.
The visual content in this game is one of the best I have seen. The amount of detail from start to finish is simply unbelievable. If I run the game at max settings, the main menu runs at 30 FPS on a GTX 1070. Why? As I said, the visuals from start to finish are simply amazing. I had to lower some post-processing settings in order to triple my FPS.
One thing to note is that the game is very hard. A mistake I made was to first play the game on Hardcore difficulty - probably because I'm pretty experience in the first-person shooter genre. I completely underestimated the survival aspect of the game. Bullets are very scarce (literally), and you will have to keep looking at your stopwatch to keep track of your gas mask filter. You will have to manually wipe the blood off your gas mask and manually charge your flashlight and some guns.
The story is simple yet very entertaining. It's one of those rare games that will make you read random scribbles just because you can't get enough of the story.
The audio could have been perfect if it weren't for the voice acting. Imagine a group of drunk Germans trying to imitate the accents of the Russians in the English language. A Story About My Uncle is a fantastic game. It's a bit short, but to be honest, I would rather have a short, high-quality game than a long, low-quality game.
I really enjoyed the first-person gameplay in A Story About My Uncle, and I think the devs did a great job with the mechanics. Games like Mirror's Edge and Dying Light have always been enjoyable to me, and I think A Story About My Uncle is actually better than them in some respects. Take Mirror's Edge, for instance. When you could really land jumps and time everything right, it felt
- like you were flying. In A Story About My Uncle, you get this feeling much more often. Sure, sometimes you get stuck on a puzzle, but for the majority of the game, the movement is fantastic.
This game is visually fantastic as well. The world that the devs have constructed is absolutely gorgeous, and I loved the architecture of floating structures, the glowing caves, and the enormous mountains. I feel like a lot of modern games have lost the ability to project that objects in-game are
, but A Story About My Uncle does it very well.
As far as my complaints, there are few. I noticed many people complaining about the last parts of the game being awful to navigate, however I did not have any trouble with it. Personally, I would have liked to see the final bits of the game be a bit more visually perfected, as the previous bits of the game looked measurably better. The other problem I had with this game was the voice acting. Let me say that this is VERY FORGIVABLE, but I still felt the game would have been better, had there been better voice actors (and maybe more emphasis on narration in general).
Overall, A Story About My Uncle is a very fun, beautiful, and interesting game. As I said, it's a bit short, so you might question paying full-price, which is understandable. However, if you think it's worth it, you should definitely give the game a try.

Dying light takes place in city areas in Turkey, where there is an outbreak that causes its residence to become infected with a virus that causes them to become flesh-eating zombies.
The protagonist is Kyle Crane, a GRE agent, who on a mission to Harran, (which in real-life was a real city.) Once there, he finds that the remaining people survive by keeping high on buildings and structures to keep from harm’s way, as well as fighting with improvised melee weapons and a few firearms. The parkor elements work on the same premise as the game that children play whereas the couches are land, and the rug is lava. In Harran, many of the infected cannot climb things well.
Sadly, there is no female player option, which is odd given that women do parkor in real life. Though, the way women are portrayed in the game otherwise won’t likely anger most women. The game takes place in a foreign country, but I did not find the game exploitative or racist, as the main character does care for the people, who are portrayed with depth, from good to bad. The characters speak with varied accents, many Slavic and Australian, but still some remain absent. Your mileage may vary.
As this is a melee combat survival game, the game-play is quite brutal. At times, the blood effects are presented in a Hollywood, akin to the movie “300,” that makes me wish for a bit more realism. With that stated, I applaud the absence of health meters over most enemies because not knowing the health of your opponent adds another dimension to game-play. Damage indications, such as missing limbs and multiple arrow impailments teach the player to remain aware for clues instead of using a brain-dead health meter floating over their heads.
As a survival game, most of combat deals with tactics. If you can take in the scene, and deal with things in the proper order you will likely live, whereas in expansion: The Following, things become quickly out of hand.
The climbing in the game is so well done that the daily grind for objects actually remains fun. There are a lot of player controls in this game, but once you learn the movement, the player moves with more freedom and body awareness than most games. If you are afraid of heights, you will either love or hate this game. For me, when I do fall, as surprised as I am, I still know the reason why. With that stated, the movement is lacking in clear ways to climb down from things—without jumping or using the grapple.
The player “lives” in an apartment building, but can set up other safe-houses across the city. The player can buy and sell things, sleep, and stash things to numerous to carry. There are several skill trees for the player to advance up, or really down in this case. The weapons take damage, wear, and break, though most can be repaired. It would have been neat if the weapons had “pain-skins” or in this case “wear-skins” that gave clues to their condition.
The player spends a lot of time looting apartments for useful things such as food parts, and commodities like coffee. Many things can be used to augment weapons, or sold to salespeople.
Graphically, the game is not so much stunning, but what they have done with it, is at times stunning—if not beutuiful: to watch the set set in Harrran. The engine does a multitude of effects very well. The atmospherics are not over the top, but natural. The rain is done so well that I wish it rained on some days. Surface traction and misery would have been nice game-play dynamics, but were not included. Originally, several effects such as chromatic aberration and film grain were mandatory, fortunately, these were patched to be options.
The game is demanding on a computer but not impossible. The game was just playable on low settings at 1920x1080 resolution on a 6-year old 2600k with a GTX 570. My new GTX 1080 plays it at DSR super-sampled 4k no problem, with all of the options. Players will want a lot of anti-aliasing because there is a lot of straight lines in a city. Aniosotropic filtering helps the distant clarity. There is a strong relationship between viewing distance and performance. With a GTX 1080, I want even farther detail settings.
The game features day and night cycles. Most of the zombies are not too aggressive during the day, but at night they will hunt you. Most do not climb well, which validates the whole parkor thing, as long as I don’t think too hard. During you have a creepy sixth sense or “survivor sense” to see the presence of the zombies. There are also redundant “spotted you” indicators over them, which probably should not have been added. This game can be quite scary at times.
Many of the infected are drawn to loud noises, making what firearms there think-before-you-use things. In places, the firearms are largely necessary; in places they will only make things worse.
You will also encounter various thugs some of which a sided warlord named “Rais,” who is very unpleasant. Unfortunately, Dying Light, suffers from console’itus in places, having the traditional “boss” style fights, which go so far as to ask the player to use new keys, not practiced elsewhere. There were a few timed quests, which I hated, not only for their difficulty and the need to repeat them, but for also needlessly pulling out of my character for a numerical value.
The player also helps various other people, by going on side-quests, which for me, were even more enjoyable than the main “boss” dealings with Rais. The protagonist meeting interesting characters added to the game, giving meaning to why Crane is helping them. Many of the side quests were enjoyable; a few were meaningful, deep, and dark. I wish there were perhaps ten more side quests, or even a small downloadable quest pack for the same area.
Most of the voice acting was done exceptionally well. I wish the thugs had more varied lines. The music is done well, does not become obtrusive, but does not stand out either. The textures and shaders are done well enough so coming close to things do not spoil things for the player. Many of the buildings are self-similar, but well designed. If you live in the United States, things seem just different enough in Harran to offer the player an excursion.
Overall, I enjoyed Dying light. While it does offer a good amount of gameplay, because of the environment they have created, it makes you want more. I look forward to trying it in co-operative.

My first sleeper surprise this year.  Hardly anyone sings praises of Defender's Quest, with its basic visuals, repetitive music, and seemingly cloned gameplay.  I'm sure other games have tried combining RPG and Tower Defense (just as Puzzle Quest did with RPG and match 3 puzzles), but I was sucked into this game quicker than I imagined.  The story is dumb but you come to like the silly dialogue and characters, and the stages tend to change just enough (at least on higher difficulties) so you have to keep on your toes.  Some levels will remove your archers for example, while others may force you to prioritize on certain enemies rather than the collective.  This is a great game for people who enjoy Tower Defense with the loot collecting and skill customization of RPGs.

This is a great tower defense game with lots or RPG elements included.  Instead of towers, you have heroes you position along a path to defend your leader.  As these heroes fight, they level up and can be built into different styles of tower depending on the skills you take.
Pros
- Lots of good tower defense gameplay
- Lots of well done RPG elements so you can modify each hero and personalize your play style
- Good story and interesting characters
- Lots of great items to equip to make your heroes (towers) even more effective
- The game rewards replay of older levels on higher difficulties by giving your heroes (towers) more experience and the ability to unlock special items
- Lots of replay value with all the difficulty levels and all the things that can be unlocked.
- Challenging maps that sometimes require you to think outside your normal setups.
Cons
- Older graphics
- Gameplay can be repetative if you're just interested in the story
Overall this is a great game that I would highly recommend to an RPG or tower defense enthusiast. The game gives you the option of both relaxed gameplay and very challening maps if you want them.  (It also rewards your party for completing said maps.)

I always heard great things about Sequence, how it mixed elements from your typical RPG with rhythm game mechanics in a very unique way. I don’t know why I didn’t picked it up earlier, probably because I wasn’t sure if I’d actually like it but truth is I bought Sequence on the Steam Autumn Sale of 2013. Well, it turns out rumours were right and my suspicions were correct. The game is great, it possibly has one of the best soundtracks I’ve ever heard on an indie game and the arstyle looks absolutely beautiful with some nice visual effects. The combat relies on a typical rhythm match game, where you have to press each key at the right time and it’s probably better if you don’t try to press the keys when you see them on the right spot but when they coincide with the music “beat”. The combat screen is divided in three different fields, the Mana field which everytime you match a certain key you regain mana and mana is used to cast spells, the Spell field where you need to match keys everytime you activate one spell and if you miss one key of the combo the spell casting cancels and you still loose your mana and the last field is the Defense field in which everytime you miss one of the keys on this field, that key will deal damage to you. That is about it for the combat, everytime you beat an enemy you’ll gain experience and loot, each enemy can drop three different items and those items are either equipables or crafting materials. The story takes you to a tower where you’re guided by a girl named Naia via an intercom and she explains to you how everything works and that you need to reach the top of the tower which has 7 floors and in order to proceed to the next floor you need to find the required materials to craft the key to unlock the door for the next floor and also defeat the guardian of each floor at the start of it, from what I understand these battles with the guardians are considered boss battles. On each floor you have a safe room where you can equip yourself, craft new items and spells and also learn and practice your spells and also this is where you’ll unlock the door leading to the next floor and where you can choose to battle enemies, from what I saw there’s three different enemies per floor.  I’m gonna be honest and you can probably see by my playtime according to Steam, I only reach the second floor and I’m currently fighting the second guardian but I’m pretty sure II won’t play Sequence anymore, not because I don’t like it, because I really do, but because I’m extremely bad at rhythm games and I found the battles to be rather frustrating for me, which might end up with me taking alot of time in order to beat the game and that kinda makes me sad because I’d love to experience the whole story and unfold the mystery behind Sequence and its world, from what I’ve saw thus far the story seemed to promise but I disliked the voice acting in this game but I do believe you can turn it off on the options menu if you don’t like it either. Sequence is certainly a very unique game and a very good one indeed, but like I’ve said, if you’re not good at rhythm games you’ll have a hard time with it, eitherways you should totally give it a try, it is totally worth your time and money but unfortunately it’s not my kind of game.

You wake up in a room with no recollection of how you got there. The last thing you know you were getting ready for bed and now you're here. A girl over the intercom tell you you're in a tower with seven floors and that you have to get to the top to get out. That's it. Oh, and by the way, you have to fight monsters and floor guardians in rhythmic RPG-ish-style battles. Are you confused yet? I was.
This game features four difficulty modes and I have to admit I played this on the easiest setting, which for a rhythmically challenged person such as myself was hard enough on the last couple of boss fights. You are free to change the difficulty around in the beginning, though, since you can switch up until the third floor.
The gameplay consists of fighting monsters by switching around three different 'fields'. There's a defensive, mana, and offensive field where you need to correctly push up, down, left, right according to the sequence they come down in. The trick is in juggling these three fields, since you're not able to play them all at the same time. When notes (I'll just call them that) come down in the defensive field and you miss them, you gain damage. To damage the opponent, you need to cast spells and hit the right notes in the spell or offensive field. To regain the mana you spent by casting spells, you need to go to the mana field where hitting the notes restores mana. There are quite a couple of spells in this game, ranging from healing spells to direct offensive spells to damage over time. At first it can be a bit confusing, but it does get easier over time. I personally played this game with a controller and often found myself pressing the wrong buttons when in a rush to reach the right field, causing me to miss notes. For me, the controls as such were something to get used to, but maybe it's easier when playing with a keyboard.
After each battle you gain a certain amount of XP and there's the possibility of getting items. While XP is used to level Ky, the protagonist, up, it is also used as a currency. On every floor you are given a couple a recipes you can use to synthesize items, gear, and spells. In order to do so, you need to invest some XP into the synthesizing process, a little more if you want a better change of success or a little less if you want like gambling. Spells can be learned by synthesizing scrolls and then 'using' the scrolls - again, with XP. You then need to finish one of the songs with a certain percentage of correct notes or a certain combo streak. The spells learned can then be put into your ring of spells, which starts out with two slots but increases to six as you progress in the game.
Now, the music. The music was the high point of the game for me, as most of the tunes were catchy and didn't really annoy even after a reasonable amount of time spent playing. Outside of the battles I cannot recall any kind background music, though I'm sure it was there. Just not memorable. The sound effects were all right, nothing much to say there. The voice acting on the other hand I really liked. I think the characters sounded real enough, though the script was a bit of a hit or miss at times: I think the topics of conversation and references made might not be everybody's cup of tea.
And last but not least, the story itself. So you start out with only knowing you need to get to the top of this tower with seven floors and that your shepherd, Naia, will guide you through via intercom. I won't spoil the story, but you won't find out much more than that until the end of the game. The ending itself, while explaining everything, felt a bit disappointing to me. If this game had relied on the story for its success, instead of the gameplay and banter among the characters, I don't think it would have worked out.
All that said, I do recommend this game if only for the fact that it's so cheap and quite a lot of fun. It's not a very long game, it took me a small ten hours to complete from A to Z, but the fun to cost relation definitely says that if you're thinking of getting this game you should give it the benefit of the doubt.

Voice acting, okay. Probably would have been better if there were a director of some sort, but everyone used professional equipment.

Anyway, it's free. I didn't have too much fun playing, but if it sounds up your alley, give it a try. Personally, I would rather buy a professional visual novel if it means an entertaining story and good art.

Mainly group based, it has a good matchmaking system that lets you literally drop in on someone with a drop pod and get right into the action. Or you can make a pre-made group and plan out your entire mission before launching. All this, for Super-Earth.
There are a large amount of weapons available, most well balanced and almost all viable, useful, and easy to use. (Point the loud end at the enemy), with plenty more called in 'stratagems' which range from defensive turrets to airstrikes, to supply drops. There is plenty of variety should you feel like playing with a different style for a change, and it's all viable. The only thing is that you may need to upgrade your items a bit before they reach their full potential.
Upgrading items is easy enough, with the upgrades clear on what they give you, and not too hard to get. You find samples during missions and 10 of these become one research point. It's fast enough to be noticeable progress, but also slow enough that you don't get to just unlock everything and then ignore it.
There are three different kinds of enemies, all with recognizable themes while their mechanics are different enough to be interesting in their own ways, requiring slightly different tactics or loadouts. The game's theme is excellent, with some small bits of humour in the over-the-top Super-Earth and the player character's zeal in spreading democracy. A few very well made one liners and a great overall wholesome fitting theme works well for pulling you in and giving the game a great identity that is worth coming back to.
With missions seeming to be randomly generated, the ability to drop in on any game or to team up with friends while using a varied, well balanced arsenal puts Helldivers firmly in the category of "Good games". Without any noticeable flaws and gameplay that keeps you entertained, it is certainly worth it.

Table Top Racing: World Tour is a mini-car/kart racing game in a similar vein to Mario Kart, that is to say where you have a small sized vehicle collecting power-ups to use against your enemies as you race around the small track. The visuals are great, but in my opinion, the sound track leaves a lot to be desired.
In Table Top Racing: World Tour you find yourself driving miniaturized versions of what could very well be real world cars. These mini-vehicles fit right in with the littered table top racing theme. Much of the debris lying around the track can be knocked out of the way. The racers can strike them as they drive around the course at the cost of only a minor loss of momentum. While there are really not that many varieties of tracks available, there are plenty of different race types to make up for it. Sometimes a lack of variety can be a bad thing. It could get boring with the same old, same old, but when it comes to racing games, knowing the track is the best way to give yourself an edge. Having fewer tracks to memorize allows you to spend less time crashing during unexpected sharp turns and more time winning races.
The game is divided into different cups, two cups per tier, and three tiers total. As you progress through the cups, more race modes will become available. I won’t go into an exhaustive list of every race type, but I will name a few of the more interesting ones. Battle Cars is the default mode. In it, it plays like Mario Kart. You race around the track trying to come in first place while using weapon pickups to slow down your opponents. Your enemies can also use those weapons, so you will have to be ever vigilant to maintain or improve your position in the race. There is also a more vanilla race mode that is just purely about racing skill rather than using cheap tricks to give yourself an edge. Drift mode is a fun mode; in it you try to slide around corners as fast as you can without hitting the walls, maintaining the drift until just before you lose control you straighten out and drive sensibly again. In Drift, you are not against other opponents; you simply are trying to beat one of the top three track scores in order to earn your bronze, silver or gold stars for the mission. There are the time trials which are similar, race against the clock to score the best lap record or best course completion time. There is also a cat and mouse style mode. You are the cat so to speak, and your goal is to catch up to the much faster mouse and pounce on it, or in car speak, ram into it. You do this through clever and creative means such as using your boost at opportune times and taking short cuts. At the end of each cup is a multi-race event that requires you to do well in each of the races in order to move on to the next cup. There are other modes and multiplayer, but you get the idea, there is plenty to do.
Each tier of racing comes with four car options. When you first start the game you can only afford to buy one of the first two available for the tier. Once you earn more by participating in races, you can either opt to buy a different car or upgrade the one you have. Each car will have different balances between their speed, acceleration, handling and armor. You will want to figure out which stats are more important to you when purchasing the car. Just because that one car has more slots for speed, it might not accelerate all that well so you might not actually get up to full speed all that often. The customizations don’t end here though. The wheels on the cars can be customized as well. The wheel customizations have a variety of effects and unlike the other car tuning upgrades, you unlock them once and you can use them on all cars you own. For example, you can equip wheels that cause you to earn more money from using weapons on enemies. You can also use wheels that give you a shield against some weapons, or even turn your wheels into weapons. There are others, but basically this adds a whole extra layer of strategy and fun to the game. Lastly you can paint your vehicles. I don’t believe painting them really has any kind of effect other than a cosmetic one. Odds are you better off sticking with stock until you have bought everything else you need.
Visually, as mentioned, this game looks great. It isn’t cartoony like Mario Kart, it actually looks somewhat realistic. The mini-cars really suit the “you are racing on the top of a table” style of the game. The random household objects and foods lying around as you drive through the various environments enhance the table top feeling even more. Overall, the visuals are very well done for the game. There were not even any graphical glitches that occurred for me, not even minor ones.
The sound on the other hand, that is something to talk about. The sound effects are your standard racing ones. Nothing really stands out there, but you don’t exactly want random nonsense sounds when racing around, you want to hear those standard sounds. The sound effects therefore are perfectly fine. The sound track on the other hand… well I read in other reviews people really like the sound track for this game. That’s great; I can see people liking it, but it was far from my style of music. Not wanting to be harsh, I would still have to say, the sound track is the kind of music that I typically wouldn’t actually class as music. It’s pretty much all remixed breakbeat (a kind of a funk/hip hop/electro/dubstep/techno blend). It’s the kind of music typically played at raves and other parties that I try to avoid being invited to. I tried my best to endure it and actually caught myself almost sort of liking one of the music tracks, but I realized that was just the Cognitive Dissonance kicking in. Luckily, you can turn off the music without losing the sound effects and play your own music if you are so inclined.
Overall, this is an excellent power-up racing game with tons of customization options and plenty of race varieties. The only real detractor is that I dislike its soundtrack immensely. Some reviews agree with me, others say it gets you into the racing spirit and mood. So hit up your favourite music streaming site, look up remixed Breakbeat and give it a listen. If your ears are not bleeding too heavily after that, go out and purchase this game!

Fun quirky little game, with a bit more emphasis on 'little'.
Content-wise, it's relatively sparse. There's little to no background story for each car and track. I wish the devs expanded this a bit further each track and rival that bit more special. A few extra lines of text helps a long way.
There's not that many track variety, and what track it has is dynamically limited to simple doodad physics. I was hoping for course-changing events (think Split/Second's PowerPlay) with animations that would incite shock and awe. Sure, it has doodads everywhere on the track affected by physics, but it just doesn't have that much of an awe factor, just cuteness. Oh, and more secret areas in tracks please, like RC Racer from the Playstation.
Finally, there's the racing element. I know it's suppose to be an arcade racing game, but personally I think this level of arcadeness can be dull really quickly. I wish that there's more gamified/cartoonified elements of real-world racing in the game here. Some examples I could think of are:
- quick tire wear (loss of grip after 5 or so laps, maybe have a 20-lap endurance race?)
- quick fuel consumption (in the same line of thought with tire-wear, varies with each car)
- component damage (too much crashing into others, damage to overall performance)
- track rules (not sure how this can be implemented, but a quirky full-course yellow and a stop-n-go penalty would be amusing)
- pit stops (complements the tire wear and fuel consumption)
Mind you, I'm mostly a sim racer when it comes to a car race. I'm not asking for this game to be a sim, I just wish that it has some elements of a sim, but make those elements exagerrated and quirky, especially when you consider the vibe that this gme is giving out.
There's a sale as of this review, so... eh, I'm enjoying it.
Forgot to mention: music selection is dope. Needs moar.
More stuff I forgot to mention: the aesthetics, I like it, a lot. Think of Road Trip Adventures from PS1. The cute, chibified cars are back and they're so adorable! Also, I like the resolution choices and how it still remains full-screen. What I'm getting here is that low-end PCs (like laptops) can play this game at reasonable frame-rates.

Scorecard:
Full review with screenshots:
Usual Unity quirks; no exclusive fullscreen support. No launcher to change monitor selection; doesn’t save the last value so it will return to Monitor 1 when launched. Fullscreen toggle on F1, disabling the standard Alt-Enter. There are a few unskippable intro logos, and can't be disabled in the configs.
Toggles for AA/DOF/V-sync, and a few levels of Ambient Occlusion (which seem unoptomized and impact performance heavily) can be changed mid-race, while volume sliders (SFX and Music) only show up in the primary options menu. Excluding the AO, it supports unlimited framerates and should be easy to run, though at a solid 120FPS, I noticed off-and-on stuttering more or less depending on the track. Seems like a v-sync or borderless window related confluct; it doesn’t seem to maintain the fluidity that such a high framerate should offer.
Renders wider than 16:9 properly, but the HUD contorts and loses a few elements, and the menus UI become essentially unusable. No FOV adjustment (default didn’t bother me) but there are 4 camera distances.
Two preset button configs for controllers (trigger vs face button brake/throttle), with almost full rebinding (excl. menu navigation inputs) for the keyboard. Controller bindings are intuitive and the menus responsive, with a few small issues. Vertical menus don’t loop around; you see this when exiting the game as it’s at the bottom of the list, and they left the PS4’s “Trophies” button in which now does nothing.
The event menus need work; championships use a larger grid with 2 layers vs horizontal event cards for Special Events. Having all of the event icons and star ratings, and the event cards are good, so a side-by-side approach would have worked better for both, unifying all of it. One pro; it stores your skin/wheel/upgrade selections per-car, saving some time.
6 modes to play [ Races w/ & w/o weapons (7 AI), Hot Lap (the best single lap within a time limit), Time Trial (time to complete x number of laps), Elimination (each lap removes car in last), Pursuit (catch up and bash into a car that starts far ahead of you), and Drift (points increase the longer you keep a combo, holding a combo lets you continue past the timer) ] on 20 track routes through 5 locations. Tracks feature a number of shortcuts locked behind objects and elevation, accessed via the 8 familiar weapon pickups (forward only, more effective after picking up a second) and 6 unlockable wheels with offensive/defensive/movement capabilities.
I have a knack for racing games so this may be skewed; I found the majority of the game to be far too easy. Handling is F1 with heavy traction control. Without the dedicated drift wheels, there’s almost no slide and there’s no handbrake, nor does there seem to be a way to lose traction and force an overseer with the throttle. Most sliding happens after jumps just before a turn, as you’re allowed mid-air rotation. The opposite of drift-focused arcade racers, you’d expect following a proper racing line to be key. It doesn’t seem to carry enough momentum for that to be enough of a factor, especially for the low and medium tier vehicles; I didn’t find them to be all that engaging to drive. The game only finds itself with the highest tier, and I’d quite like another faster beyond that.
Shortcuts make certain challenges dramatically easier, and range from elevated sections accessed by jumping (on cooldown) with the Boing wheels, large gaps that can be cleared the same way, and hidden jumps/paths behind objects opened up by the second stage of all weapons except boost (breakable objects have a pink sheen). AI ignores all of it, so they aren’t often necessary.
The most fun I’ve had has been in the Drift mode. With the right car (some better than others; their drifting potential is listed on car selection screen) it isn’t too difficult, and is very satisfying as you slide through the turns with a lot of control, but have to plan ahead in a way that you don’t for standard races. You get a similar feel by using drift wheels for other races, but that’s usually a hindrance as you don’t have much control over the grip to prevent sliding on subtle turns, and there’s no acceleration advantage coming out of turns (like other arcade titles with drifting) that would help balance it out.

They adorable car models are honestly the most detailed and polished I’ve seen from this genre, and their designs are so appealing to me that I’d genuinely be interested in buying physical models. The surrounding aesthetic has a few rough spots, but uses a nice variety of shaders and materials. The colorful lighting is basic but sound, but the cars lack distinct cast shadows in some of the indoor locations, and the outdoor Junkyard and Egypt locations lack ambient lighting that would mimic the indirect sunlight, making shaded areas darker than they should be.
The UI and HUD feature an odd selection of fonts/styles, though it’s functional outside of a lack of feedback concerning lap counts and position. A larger, color-coded position counter would be great along with at the very least a “Last Lap!” pop-up.
This video below (not mine) is a solid example of what the game has to offer. My favorite handling/sounding car, running a time trial on a medium complexity track. Competent players will maintain the lead often, so other cars aren’t a factor when not playing vs humans.
The generic electronic soundtrack was hit or miss; a “Skip Song” button or a list of toggles would have been welcome, though most will want to listen to their own music. The effects and engine sounds are surprisingly well done for an indie team. Most of the cars seem to have unique engine profiles (the exotic cars being particularly satisfying), and the collisions are a mix of the light plastic clacking of a toy car, and a variety of materials (porcelain, tin, thick metal, wood) matching the objects littered around the course. There's very little in terms of ground/tire materials or environmental reverberation. The engine sounds are great, but I've had prefered them at about twice the volume and abrasiveness.
A simple little game with a charming aesthetic (mainly for gearheads who appreciate the heavily inspired car designs and recognize the iconic skins) and matching sound effects, but unfortunately also features some odd choices that leave a bit to be desired. It boils down to the lack of a custom/free-play mode, raw speed (and thus challenge) in all but the late-game vehicles, and polish concerning some of the map physics and UI. Fixing these problems should be feasible, I just hope the upcoming DLC comes along side and not in favor of refinement of the base game.

Sequence is a great little rhythm game. The primary gameplay consists of you switching between 3 DDR-like boards during battles with monsters and opponents. One for defending against their attacks, one for gaining mana, and one for casting your own spells. The system works really well and each battle is set to some outstanding music (including a number of tracks by Ronald Jenkees).
There are some RPG elements including a levelling system, crafting different weapons, armor, accessories from monster drops, and the ability to customize your usable spells. All of this is tied together with a decent plot and some cringe-worthy voice acting, but it's not enough to detract from the game.

Edit: Changed name from "Sequence" to "Before the Echo".  It was, at one point, called Sequence.
Before the Echo is a simple, yet fun rhythm game.
The plot isn't the greatest selling point of the game, but if you approach it as a riff off the Guitar Hero or Rock Band style game it is very enjoyable.  The music can start to feel a little repetitive at times, but the songs are enjoyable if you like the style.  Ronald Jenkees did the vast majority of the songs in the game, and many are available on his youtube channel for some samples.
Your goal is to reach the top of a tower, while combating monsters with spells that you cast in a DDR style mechanic.  To complicate things, there are three "areas" that you have to swap between and work in- one for casting, one for regenerating mana, and one for defending yourself.  Winning a battle nets you some XP, and possibly up to 3 items.  The item drops and crafting mechanics seem designed to extend the length of the game, although I rarely felt like I was grinding unnecessarily.  There is something to be said for the practice associated with grinding drops and XP to burn on crafting, as the transitions in difficulty can feel a little rough here and there, and some of the spell casting sequences can take a bit of time to really feel natural.
The mechanics do feel contrived, but the game itself lampshades that fact.  Before the Echo doesn't take itself too seriously, and that is a good deal of the charm.  The music is great, and the art has a nice look and feel to it.
I have not tried playing with a controller, but the keyboard interface is simple enough to use that I don't think a controller is a requirement.  I was able to finish the game (including the "hidden" ending) on Medium difficulty without too much of a struggle.  I briefly toyed with the harder difficulty but I found that I enjoyed the game on medium enough that I didn't continue down the harder path.  The differences in difficulty seem to be entirely based on the number of symbols necessary to complete a sequence, and higher difficulties make more use of the two buttons at a time patterns (up+left, down+right, up+down, left+right) instead of just single inputs in order.
Overall, I think it was a fun game, worth a playthrough, and something I go back to from time to time just to play specific songs.  Worth the price of admission.

"We'll see about that." That's the phrase that begins Half-Life 2: Episode 1, the sequel to Half-Life 2. What's the relevance of these words? There are interpretations but no one knows exactly what it means. What I am sure of is that this is a very good sequel because it makes a good use of the elements that it inherits from Half-life 2.
The plot continues directly from the ending of Half-Life 2. The quality of the narrative in this continuation is still as good as in the previous game. Everything we experience at the surface covers something that's more in depth, that's a element that is present not only in this game but in all the Half-Life games. We'll never fully know the reason of why those things are happening, we'll only know what we can see through the eyes of Gordon Freeman. That's a sensation I won't ever be able to remove from my thoughts. I love knowing that there's something else behind all, but I hate to know that I'll never get an answer to my questions. It's a blessing and a curse at the same time.
The same as Half-Life 2: Excellent controls, movement, gunplay, and physics. The enemies are varied and the situations too. In fact it's due to the good use of the elements to create interesting and fun situations that this sequel doesn't fall into boredom, even with the absence of new elements and mechanics.
In this sense it's almost the same as Half-Life 2. Despite the year in which it was released, it was still visually impressive. There isn't a big jump from Half-Life 2 but there's an increase in the details of the textures and small improvements in the lighting. I don't have much more to say, the game is excellent visually.
The incredible composition of the predecessor is continued in this game and it's incredible. As in the previous two games, each piece of the soundtrack is good on its own and is used at the right moments in the game, thus creating incredible, thought provoking, atmospheric moments, or tense battle moments. The SFX are mostly reused from Half-Life 2 so they are still just as amazing.
In conclusion, this is a very good sequel, however it's thrown back a little because of the lack of new elements or mechanics. Still, I personally enjoyed Half-Life 2: Episode 1 a lot and I recommend it to anyone who likes Half-Life 2 or is interested in playing the complete series.

A terrifying and difficult post-apocalyptic shooter with an incredible story.
Note: This game says I've played this game only 15 hours when in reality it's almost 40 from multiple replays. Not sure why it says that.
This game is a mix of post-apocalyptic, stealth, linear FPS,  and survival horror, and is easily one of the best examples of all three, with an incredibly dark and lonely atmosphere.
You play Artyom, one of the survivors who escaped nuclear war in the Moscow subway system and have now rebuilt society within it. Every train station is a compact city, the pitch-black tunnels are mutant, or bandit-infested nightmares, and the surface is an abandoned, hostile wasteland where the air is unbreathable, requiring the player find and use air filters, which expire on a timer, adding to the feeling of urgency and desperation. The shooting is supremely satisfying, and incorporates well with the stealth mechanics. You fire a variety of cobbled-together hand-made weaponry, which add immeasurably to the immersion of the game. Ammo is scarce, so exploration, looting, conservation, and stealth killing are essential to survival. The game currency is scarce military-grade ammo, which can be shot through certain weapons. This means, in certain desperate situations one might shoot their meager savings to save their lives, adding consequence to player choice.
The game is a linear journey through several dark subway tunnels and through derelict, destroyed surface cities, where mutants, bandits, Neo-nazis, and Commies are a constant threat. This game reminds me a lot of the STALKER series, in its unforgiving difficulty, dark and oppressive atmosphere, and shear fear factor. The mutants, though perhaps not quite as scary as the STALKER ones, are definitely chilling. There are few game experiences as hair raising as hearing the howl of the wolven watchmen on the surface, hiding from the giant winged "demons", staring down the hulking simian librarians, or the scuttling, giant-shelled spiders which can seriously go straight to hell forever. Seriously though, screw those guys.
The story is compelling, featuring Artyom as he leaves the safety of his home and travels across the Metro to warn the Ranger corps of the impending attack of the Dark Ones, mysterious post-human mutants with incredible powers. Along the way he meets a cast of interesting side characters, each representing a different aspect of the dark, post-apocalyptic theme. The story moves through different twists and turns which lead to a satisfying ending.
The game also features one of the most nuanced morality systems of any game. Not necessary good vs evil but pragmatism vs benevolence, from what I can tell. Look up a game guide on it and you'll find no one is quite sure how it works. You know you've done something right when your morality system can't be quickly explained on a game guide.
However, the game isn't perfect. Like any FPS, there are turret sections, obligatory stealth, and QTE's, although I must say I found that this game had the best and worst examples of these things, and they are far from the majority of the game. Also, I had frequent issues of clipping. Enemies would charge at me and clip halfway through my torso like a mutant centaur that attacked me from within without me able to respond. Also, the game can really chew through frame rates on certain systems, as the graphics are no slouch.
All in all, a must have for fans of FPS, hard core survival horror, and post apocalyptic, as is its sequel, Metro Last Light.
