Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines was originally released November 16, 2004 It was developed by the ill-fated Troika games and published by Activision. Unfortunately, this was also the release date of Valve Softwares magnum opus, Half-Life 2. Vampire, like Half-Life 2, made excellent use of the Source Engine developed by Valve. However, since this game was using the brand new Source Engine, it was not allowed to release before Half-Life 2. This alone made Activison decide to "crack the whip" at Troika and push the release date to that of Half-Life 2. Ultimately, this lead to the game being riddled with bugs at release.  Troika, unable to find funding, laid off all of it's employees in several waves over time. Despite this, several employees developed a patch for the game without pay. Three weeks after the games release patch 1.2 released and official support of the game was shuttered. Despite this, even nearly ten years later, this game is still supported by fan patches developed by Wesp5. This review is written based on experiences with fan patch 9.0
Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines is a video game translation of White Wolf Publishings table top rpg, Vampire: The Masquerade. By translation, I mean this in an almost litteral sense. The game mimics the table top rpgs systems exceedingly well, right down to the way the character sheet works. You are actively encouraged through out the game to actually play your role in the twisted tale that is woven for you.
Humanity, or the lack thereof, is one of the key features in the game. Can you (your character) pretend to still be human, integrating yourself into society, while being a Vampire. Killing an innocent on the streets will make you lose a humanity point, further driving home the fact that you are a supernatural beast. Lose too many humanity points and you may frenzy if you run out of the games main resource, blood. Going into a frenzy unleashes the savage beast within you, temporarily causing you to lose all control of your character. One of the other key elements of the game, The Masquerade, challanges you to act human. If anyone sees you doing anything that a Vampire normally would do (using magick, feeding on an npc, etc,) you lose a Masquerade point. Losing these is an astoundingly bad thing. Did that Npc see you feeding on a bum? Yep, and they ran to the cops, you my friend are now being hunted. Sure, losing one point only gets the police on your tail, they are nothing compared to you, you're a damn vampire. But, begin losing more (up to six) and you will have Hunters (one of the games antagonists) or even other vampires after you. The systems from the table top RPG are translated so well into the game it is astounding.
So, I just explained some of the systems in the game, while that is all well and good, an rpg would be nothing without a good story and good mechanics to tell it to you. You begin the game with a questionaire of all things. This decides which Vampire clan you will play as. Will you be a melee powerhouse Bruhaj, or will you be a magick centric Tremere? Maybe a stealthy Nosferatu, or the absolutely (literally) insane Malkavian. After a thorough quizzing and assigning points to your character sheet the game begins. Your character is in the throws of passion with a vampire from which ever clan you picked (or were assigned) from the questionaire. You are turned, and are essentially born anew as a vampire.
I will be absolutely honest here, this game, it has some of the finest writing, and voice acting, I have ever encountered. I really have to commend Troika for the stellar cast they gathered. A few examples of the voice actors in the game are, Steve Blum (Cowboy Bebop), John DiMaggio (Futurama, Adventure Time), Phil LaMarr (Pulp Fiction, Samurai Jack) and Kathryn Cressida (Tarzan, Dexters Laboratory). All of the voice actors do a phenomenal job of playing the characters they were assigned, you actually believe these characters are apart of a living, breathing, world. The entire game feels as if it is alive. Bums wander the streets of LA, hookers propisition you, cops make your life hell and get in the way. Even politics play a roll in this game.
So, the story, is not just a story about your character, it's about the world of Vampire: The Masquerade. From the charismatic leader of the Camarilla, to the "all too happy to be a vampire" Smiling Jack, Troika crafted a story that not only grabs you, but makes you care about what is going on. I don't want to spoil anything of the story, even giving cliff notes of it would be doing a disservice to the reader. This story is one you must truly experience for yourself.
The gameplay of Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines may seem familiar at times, after all, this is a story driven RPG. You can play in first or third person, but I recommend a healthy mix of two. While first person mode takes away a good bit of perephrial vision, it makes the experience all the more personal. Speaking to npcs, you are given fully voiced and written dialog, with (for current times) pretty standard RPG choices. Depending on how your character is developed, you can get special dialog in the form of persuasion, intimidation, and even mind control. While it doesn't seem like anything really special now-a-days, back in 2004, this was pretty damn spectacular. The combat, to be honest, is the weakest part of this game. I am by no means, putting the combat down, it is a fully functional, working combat system, that, at sometimes, is a little bit wonky. Transitioning from first person gameplay to third person, at first, is a little jarring, especially if you're fighting with a melee weapon and casting certain spells. Doing this, the game keeps jumping back and forth between third and first person view, and can make combat a little more difficult than it should be. The only black mark that I can find that makes the game even slightly frustrating is the slight bit of downtime you have when casting spells during combat while using a gun. If you're trying to fight enemies while using a firearm and casting spells, the game delays you being able to shoot, reload, or even cast a different spell. This kinda breaks the immersion of the game at times, because it makes fighting certain enemies incredibly frustrating, more than once I had to take a break from playing because fighting the same foe for twenty minutes was grating on my nerves. (Though, this is a slight disclaimer, I was playing a Tremere, the heavy magick using class.)
There is still so much I can say about this game, but, I don't want the review to be exceedingly long. Yes I wanted to be thorough, but, all I really want to say is that Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines, with the fan patch 9.0, is an absolutely astounding game. The patch, in addition to making it work on Windows 7 and 8, actually adds back in some content that was missing from the base game. I really have to give it to Wesp5, he really has brought this game back out of the shadows and gotten it the attention it deserves. I cannot recommend this game enough, it is truly, one of the finest games I have played in ages.
I give Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines a 9.5 out of 10. The wonderful story, voice acting, and general gameplay make this an absolute treat.

An original approach to story design and a nice take on tower defense, Defender's Quest places you in the role of Azra, a librarian who gets epic powers to fight the otherwise invulnerable undead.
The story has been designed from the ground up: taking the game mechanics of upgradable towers who gain experience to become stronger ("like an RPG"), a story to fit the mechanics has been devised. Quite like when you were presented with the task of making up a story and including certain words or characters, only Level Up Labs made a game out of that. The benefit is mostly avoiding pitfalls growing out of weird game mechanics. IMHO, while the story did not blow my mind it is still very fine and the result works quite well.
So, like any tower defense, you defend a place from creeps that have different stats and abilities by placing "towers". In this they're game characters who have their own class and the associated, developable skills, i.e. attacks, buffs and debuffs. Azra summons them up and places them into the labyrinth in suitable locations. Every character is useful and has their role: to spell it out no one works as an instakill device against everything. The enemies always follow shortest path towards Azra, so you can plan accordingly even when some enemies can swim. Finally, if the troops fail, you can beat the horde back with spells. Everything uses kills for money.
On the world map, you move along a linear path that sometimes diverges for sidequests. Every space is either a level with attacking waves of enemies or a town where you can buy weapons and armor and recruit troops. Story advances in every space so you're never bored unless getting stuck in a difficult level. That does not happen often, for the easy levels are really easy and you can even go to casual difficulty and/or set experience and money gain to 3x normal for faster leveling up without any penalty. You do get better rewards for higher difficulties, and to master a level it has to be beaten on extreme: this always rewards you with a special item granting the incentive for beating them all, if the associated achievement won't do it alone. You can also return to beat the levels again after you've grown in strength.
When the levels run out, there are several "challenge" levels to beat, two of which are of endless type with ever-so stronger incoming waves. After beating the game you can also give it another go with NG+ that is more difficult with monsters getting additional special abilities. NG+ also adds several additional sidequests and its own version of the challenges.
While the flash graphics aren't eye candy, the music is engaging and the residing mechanics will let you enjoy the game for several tens of hours. However, trying to beat every level perfectly can become tedious, for the levels get tougher and tougher as you advance. Typing this, I've yet to beat the last few levels on extreme. Still, I would heartily recommend the game for tower defense fans: I sure got a blast with it. I especially recommend going for the Hero Mode+ challenge (and to lesser extent the Hero Mode++).

These vehicles handle superbly. I prefer to use my Steam Controller, but the controls are simple enough to work with any device. The wide variety of vehicle models includes standard super cars, hippy campers, and pickup trucks. If you’ve played the Disney Infinity 1.0 Cars Playset, you’ve seen how the fantasy addition of not-so-standard race cars can amp up the laughs, adding a much needed jolt to the fun factor in derby type racing. But, these cars each have their own set of strengths and weaknesses added to the cosmetic beauty of the car to create an addictive collectors  aspect to the game much like that of collecting Matchbox cars for children. Personally, I can’t wait to earn the Fauxrari. But, the availability of other upgrades may forestall that acquisition.

Comical sounding names for tires like: bling, boing, and shield let you know right up front what these tires can do for your ride. The boing tires are one of the more expensive to earn with the in-game currency, but give you the ability to alter typical game physics in a more satisfying way, and allow you to reach more hidden coins and shortcuts. The Bling tires, aside from the ascetic benefit, cause you to earn more money from races, though they don’t really help you win. There are quite a few tire options. Adding more would definitely be better, of course.  But, there are also cool paint jobs you can earn, and of course the leveling up of abilities, like acceleration, max speed, and handling.
The race tracks are atypically short for most of the kart racers I’m familiar with, more in line with standard stadium race tracks length-wise. There is no stadium feel here, however. It feels like being a kid lying on the floor of a garage, racing your Matchbox cars between old car parts and cans of transmission fluid. Or, like racing your hot wheels around the diner counter past the napkin dispenser. So, there is quite a bit of nostalgic pleasure derived from the game no matter who you are. But, the myriad of objects to drift into, collide with, and knock off the track, along with the ability to careen over the edge of the table adds the pleasure of riding the bumper cars.

If you enjoy the thrill of mastering all the championship trophies, and exploring the special events, then you will simply love the gameplay of multiplayer, which is where the real meat & potatoes of the game is found. You could spend many hours in single-player racing against the AI, but eventually you will want more than the scaling of typical AI races. Multiplayer becomes more of a competition, and a friendship forming opportunity. Though there is no co-op yet, MP certainly lends itself to teaming up against your opponents. The game could certainly benefit from that option.

If you have ever played a game like sonic all-stars, Mario kart, f1 all-stars, rc revenge pro, diddy kong racing, crash racing series, modnation racers or little big planet kart you would love this game. I have played all of these titles and adored them, same story with table top racing. The game has superb graphics and quick loading times between races, and runs smooth as silk on my three-year-old slow laptop. While reviewing this game a new update came out so I asked Playrise Digital on their website question form the new features and the team responded hours later.
There are 6 championships or 'Cups' to complete and several special races which may require certain wheel types  and cars to participate. The vehicles are divided into three tiers/categories; Amateur (Cult Classics), Pro (Street Racers), Expert (Super Cars) which have four different vehicles to choose from in each category. From the base game there is five different style of race tracks (tables) but four variations of the course. Each car can be upgraded in top speed, acceleration, handling, armour as well as choose from four styles of paint and seven different styles of wheels. Each wheel is unique and gives a different attribute to the car; Standard, Drift (For Drifting), Bling (For Bonus Coins/Money), Sheild (Force field around the car), Centurion (Spike Wheels), Boing (Allow your car to jump/bounce and reach coins on some tables) and Peace Bomb (Disarm weapons). One thing to note is when you buy the wheels which are fairly expensive, you can use them on everyone car without having to rebuy. Opponents do not have weapons wheels until the Expert difficulty cups however, opponents may have weapon wheels in special events.
There are seven different types of events; elimination (last car standing), time trial (quickest time over a set amount of laps), hot lap (quickest lap), Combat race (Race with power ups), pure race (Race without power ups), drift (race with drift wheels for drifting) and pursuit (catch up to a slower car and tag). In combat race there are several power ups; Acid, Rocket, Tracking Rocket, electric pulse, boost, bomb and ice beam, which once you pick up two power ups you get a special upgraded power up upon reaching Pro difficulty. The cars in the game generally handle with ease, however the cult classics are a challenge to turn. The opponents are extremely easy to beat in the first two difficulties but the game gets more challenging later in the game, especially the pursuits. The game also has online only multiplayer which I find impossible to find a server in Australia, the game allows the creation of one though. While typing this line I found one server and played, there was a slight jagged feel when controlling my car although this may be an internet issue for the other player. However, at this current update there is no local co-op multiplayer aka split-screen, which is a real disappointment.
If you decide to purchase the 'Supercharger' DLC you get three additional championships one each vehicle tier, four additional cars, one extra track 'Can Ya Dig It?' and 16 extra special events. Included is a great drift car which will be useful if you struggle with the drift events like myself. Please do note if you want to play with some people online you need this dlc. The game features upbeat, electronic dance music which adds a nice feel to the game with a nice variety of 17 tracks by WES SMITH which you can listen to on soundcloud:
.
Conclusion:
Table Top Racing: World Tour World Tour by Playrise Digital is a great indie title to play with friends or alone with a nice selection of vehicles, customizations and maps. The game does lack variety of tables, however I do not mind this as the game is highly addictive, and will provide at least 10 hours of fun. It is now your turn to decide whether a $20 USD price tag is a good price for the game.

Sequence is a rhythm RPG, which is, in and of itself, an interesting concept. It delivers this with surprisingly unique gameplay, an interesting story, and an excellent, albeit limited, selection of music to play along to.
In terms of gameplay, it's not unlike DDR in that you have four arrows that you have to hit to the rhythm as they reach the bottom of the screen while music plays in the background. However, the similarities stop there. Combat involves rotating between three screens: your damage screen, your mana screen, and your spell screen. The damage screen represents incoming attacks from your opponent, and each arrow missed on this screen will result in your health taking a hit. The spell screen is used for all of the abilities in the game, where you must select what type of spell you want to perform and then hit every arrow in that spell for it to succeed. The mana screen grants mana, for casting spells, with every arrow that is hit. As a result, the game turns into a very interesting experience where you have to time spells so that you don't take too much damage, and prioritize each of these screens so that you can keep yourself alive and deplete your enemy's health bar before the song ends.
When a battle concludes, loot is dropped. This loot can be used to craft specific items on each floor, such as new weapons and equipment, a key to get to the next level, and a few other secrets that are best observed within the game. Especially towards the end, there are some very interesting items that can be crafted, and a lot of secrets and hidden content. I highly recommend crafting every item in the game, waiting until after the credits, and then exploring a bit more based on what you learn. This game quickly becomes intriguing, and knows how to deliver on it.
One point of criticism I have for this game is that, if you're looking to craft all of the items in the game, it can get a little repetitive. Each enemy has the same song every time you fight them, and when you get close to the end, there are a few items that have pretty low drop rates. Having to repeat the same fight fifteen times in a row, as a result, can get a drab. Luckily, it's not the exact same pattern of arrows every time, and the gameplay is engaging and fun enough that I didn't find this to be much of an issue, but it is something worth mentioning.
If you're a fan of rhythm games, Sequence brings a twist on a traditional formula that makes it feel almost entirely new. I'm glad I put in all of the time that I did, and I think a lot of people would be surprised at how much they enjoy it.

This game is basically DDR (on a controller/keyboard) mashed up with an RPG. If that sounds like heaven to you, then you're in for a good time. You battle monsters by completing sequences of notes, swapping between three different 'tracks' to attack, block, and charge up mana.
The only major problem with this game is that it is *extremely* grind-y. To move past each level, you will need to craft a key, which requires collecting multiple items dropped from the monsters in that level. The monsters will only drop the items some of the time, and multiple items are usually required so you might end up fighting the same monster (and playing the same song) several times in a row. To make matters worse, crafting the items you need costs XP (meaning more battles to earn it back) and has a chance of failing (meaning even more battles to find all those items again). Playing the same song over and over again gets old very quickly.
Overall, this is a good game for rhythm game fans, but be warned that it can get repetitive.

TL;DR AT BOTTOM!
Wow. A serious negative review for this game, crazy, right? Wait, wait! Hold on - I can see that cursor dropping to the downvote button, but I insist you take off the rose-tinted and glasses hear me out.
This game is inferior in nearly every single way to EA's Battlefront - and EA's Battlefront 2. Why do I say this? Well, before I proceed to list the cons when compared to EA's version of the series, how about I list the pros and the neutrals first?
PROS
+ Heroes are relevant to the map
+ Clone Wars (Negated with EA's BF2)
+ Mods (Although, a game shouldn't be rated on it's mods, as those are user generated, not dev generated)
+ More maps (I suspect this will change in EA's BF2)
+ Singleplayer campaign (Aaaaand changed in EA's BF2)
+ Space battles (Once more, EA's BF2)
+ 64v64
NEUTRALS (Subjectives)
* Class based gameplay (Once more negated by EA's BF2)
* Stamina system
* Galactic conquest, a sort of... weird splice between strategy and the normal game (It's not really that great)
* No pick-ups
And with those out of the way, we move onto the...
CONS
- Zero progression
- Floaty, horrid gunplay
- Lightsaber fights come down to one thing: who can stunlock the other first
- Heroes are dished-out to the top performers of a team, making the unstoppable even more powerful
- Graphics are aged
- Sound is aged
- Animations are horrible, to the point of being broken at times
- Gamespy
- Heroes have a max of two or three side abilities, only one of which is useful in most circumstances
- Lack of atmosphere, Dagobah doesn't feel spooky and mysterious, Hoth doesn't feel cold
- Most classes are useless, there is no need to switch it up when you can easily get fourty kills as the basic soldier
- Individual soldiers are only rarely map specific
So, yeah. That's that.
TL;DR This game is inferior to EA's Battlefront(s) in every way save for content.

Tower defense is not at all my jam, but Defender's Quest adds enough other stuff (and pulls of the defense part painlessly enough) that I've ended up really liking it. I'm only about halfway through, but, well, I was only expecting to dip my toes into it when I launched it today, and instead it ate up most of my evening.
Essentially it's tower defense game with RPG mechanics and a story. Like, a proper story, that gives most RPGs a run for the their money.  That and the RPG mechanics give an attachment to your characters (who act as the "towers"), and a sense of progression, that make this game so much more than most tower defense games. The game seems to reward focusing on a small but powerful party, and I just find "making my friends way better at murder" more rewarding than "build a bunch of catapults." Also, it's pretty funny.
There are a few problems; the art for the cutscenes is pretty bad (although the pixel art in battle is pretty charming.) Some of the humor falls flat or, more often, breaks character. And adding the pointless subtitle didn't make the name any less generic. Still, it's overall a fun and addicting experience.

Yo dawg, Did you wanna fight for FREEDOM, DEMOCRACY, AND THE SPACE-AMERICAN WAY?!
Well, then this game is for you! With a neat satirical backstory, HELLDIVERS puts you as a member the elite titular taskforce, designed to be (literally) dropped behind enemy lines and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥Up.
With and interesting mechanic of being able to call in Stratagems via the radio, there is a twist to the usual "Airdrop inbound" mechanic quite a few shooters use. You see, you want that extra ammo pack or auto turret? You gotta put in a code, Contra style. Granted, the code is given to you on the bottom of the screen benath your mini-HUD (more on that later) but the catch is you gotta put it in quickly whilst being under heavy fire from deadly Cyborgs, or Space Bugs.
Now, the real bread-and-butter of of this game is the co-op factor. Don't get me wrong, you CAN play this solo, however it's gonna get really difficult. Like i said before, you are LITERALLY dropped behind enemy lines, so it's juts you, your team, and whatever stratagem beacons you packed in your bag. When playing Solo, you get a certain amount of Auto-Reinforces, which means if you die, you can get dropped right back in. You start out with just one, but you can earn more via completing objectives, holding a maximum of two. When playing cooperatively, however, you have to call in a Reinforce Beacon, of which you have unlimited uses, but it is on a (albeit short) cooldown, not to mention the whole, y'know, deadly Aliens/cyborgs shooting at nearly the whole time. One of the more well designed things about this game is that, like a lot of other good coop games, you can see the status of your team on the bottom of your screen. This show information such as what weapons are equiped, how much ammo in reserve, how much in the mag, etc. if you die, that information disappears and it just shows your name with a little skull next to it, and pressing any button will wiggle the icon and put the words "request to reinforce" above it. Expect to see a lot of that in game.
As for how difficult/challenging the game is, it can be pretty tough, especially going solo. Because you are meant to be infiltrating enemy strongholds, there is a sort of "stealth" mechanic about it. And yes, that's in quotes for a reason. When you first drop in, the enemy is unaware of your presence, but there ARE enemy patrols about, especially around objectives. When an enemy spots you, you have about 1-2 seconds to kill them or stun themk to keeo them from sounding the alarm. When the alarm is sounded, all hell then breaks loose. Bigger, badder enemies start spawning and depending on the difficulty rating of the mission, some of them are heavily armored and definitely require team ccordination to take down. You can run, and the alarm will reset, but be wary of that area, because baddies don't despawn, only respawn.
As for the difficulty itself, there are 12 difficulty ratings in game from level 1, "a dive in the park" to level 12, "hell dive." Difficulty does not affect base damage or rresistance, so you can take your dinky little lvl 1 rifle into a lvl 12 zone and still hold your own for a little bit. What difficulty DOES mean, is that Bigger enemies will spawn, and once you get up there, you're REALLY gonna want some anti-tank weapons to take on those guys.
Now as i said before, you CAN technically do the whole game solo, but like i said previously, you're gonna want some AT weapons/stratagems to back you up. the highest i would feel comfortable doing solo is maybe lvl 6, and that's at the very max level, but then again, i'm a casual skrub who needs to Git Gud.
Adding on to the coop factor, the game has several sectors and battles in overall "wars" in which we fly to space and wreck alien house. To determine victory, every time a player/team finishes a mission, it adds "influence." The higher the community influence, the further you push in that Factions sector of space, the further you reach the Homeworld, which has many more baddies, but quite a bit of good loot and exp.
As for leveling itself, it doesn't quite work they way most games do. Yes, as you kill things and complete missions you get exp, but that really only unlocks "perks" which are usually passive buffs to your character, such as faster sprint speed, faster stratagem deployment/racharge, etc, and also the occasional gun.The way you earn upgrades for your weapons/stratagems is by collecting SCIENCE! now where do you get science? well, during a mission you can find glowing yellow "research samples" and every 10 samples you earn a Research Point, which is used to upgrade weapons and stratagems. You DO earn a research point for every level, but that's not really a reliable way of getting reasearch.
Now, i know what you're thinking, "Midget, this sounds like an amzing game that's perfect in every way! i'm gonna throw all my money at the screen RIGHT NOW!" But HOLD UP THERE FRIEND! There is a problem here, and unfortunately, there is a Pay To Win aspect of it. That's right, the more money you throw at the screen, the more likely you are to find success in your missions! Now what do I eman by that? the game itself is about 25$ but there are some DLC for it that provide items. And not just cosmetics, either. For Instance, there is a perk called "All Terrain Boots" which means you no longer have your speed inhibited by Snow or Water, but to get them, you have to buy the "all terrain pack" (or something along those lines, can't quite remember the name of it atm) and there is NO way to earn them normally in-game. Having a tough time fighting Cyborg tanks and hulks, or those nasty, heavily armored bugs? then just shill ou $5 for the Entrenched Pack, and get a nifty Anti-Tank turret and mow em all down! also not earnable in-game.
So as fun as it is, this apple is a little bitter with that knowledge. That being said however, even without your super OP tank murdering turret (seriously the thing is ridiculous) they still have an INCREDIBLE base game here, and is massively fun, especially if you can get 4 people to work and communicate together. It is seriously the most fun i've had in a game in a long time, and is definitely worth the money.

I don't know if Arrowhead are geniuses or they got lucky with this one, I haven't played their other games... but Helldivers is, in my opinion, a masterpiece.
It's a game about situational awareness, quick thinking, and self control.  It can be brutally unforgiving, but also allow you to pull a win out of the messiest of situations, which can be very satisfying.  It's fun when you've got a very tight squad flawlessly executing missions, and it's fun when the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan and everything starts going wrong.  With full friendly fire, and tremendously powerful tools at their disposal, Helldivers can be their own worst enemies.
The graphics are excellent, and the animations superb, with great attention to details.  You see your character (and your squad mates) crouch down to type strategem codes into their computer.  You see them stop and open their map to find objectives or check on enemy locations.  All of these little details not only add to the great feel of the game, but also communicate what your squad mates are doing at all times.  The use of Strategem Codes is quite clever and tests your ability to think (and type) quickly under pressure.
With 3 very different enemy forces to fight against, a nice variety of terrains, and a big toy box full of fun stuff, I keep coming back to this game, and expect I will continue to do so for a long time.
The game isn't flawless, however.  There are some balance issues, for example:
1. Certain weapons and Strategems are used far more than others because they are simply better at their job.  Still, there are plenty of viable choices so that you won't ever be pigeonholed into using 1 best loadout.
2. Bosses give way too much 'Influence' toward the war effort, compared to normal missions.  This leads to some people 'gaming the system' in order to get on the leaderboards.  While ultimately the fault of players doing it, it's supported and even encouraged by the game due to this massive imbalance.  I don't care so much about the leaderboards, but it kinda undermines my sense of contribution to the war effort to see players gaining 10x as much influence per time spent playing as I can do by just playing the game normally.
3. Retalliatory Strike missions are much more difficult than normal missions of the same level, and there is no way to bypass them.  This can make solo play frustrating when a planet that you could normally complete on your own, comes up with a Ret Strike mission which is much harder to do alone.  Also, I find Retalliatory Strike missions to be less fun than regular missions.
4. As enemy factions are eliminated in the war, they become unavailable to fight against until the entire war is over.  When I first got the game, it was several weeks before I was able to fight against the Illuminate, and also unlock certain gear that only the Illuminate offer.  It's a part of the game though, and I hesitate to even mention it as a negative, but it was a little bit annoying when I was a new player.
5. I'm not crazy about the individual DLC prices.  I bought the game bundled with all DLC, which was a fair deal and I don't regret it.  However, buying the DLC one at a time will get very expensive.
None of these issues are enough to spoil the game for me... but I thought I ought to mention them.
Also, while the Helldivers community isn't
the greatest, I've seen some reviews here stating that the community is completely toxic.  I do not agree.  When I'm not going solo, I find plenty of good natured folks to play with all the time.  There are, of course, jerks like you'll find in every online game.  And Helldivers has it's share of elitists.  I've been kicked from a game for 1 'accidental' (killing a team mate) that I really didn't think was my fault.  But these are the exceptions, not the rule, in my experience.
A few tips for new players:
1. Learn the 'Reinforce' code (the one that brings back fallen team mates) and practice it until you can input it without thinking.  You can call in Strategems even while downed... but beware, they will drop to the ground if you die before throwing them.  This can be a
thing... if it's an Air Strike you just dropped on your squad.  This can be a
thing, if you are the last of your team to fall and you are holding 'Reinforce'.... it will drop when you die and you will 'Reinforce'
as well as your fallen squad-mates.
2. If you buy only one DLC, get the Terrain Specialist pack.  The All-Terrain Boots are pretty much mandatory for Snow Planets if you are joining multiplayer games with strangers.  You
do Snow Planets fine without them, especially if you use the jump pack, mechs or vehicles... but do not be shocked when you get kicked from a multiplayer game for showing up to a Snow Planet without the proper footware. (I won't kick you, but some people will)
Personally, I bought the DLC Bundle with everything and I don't regret it, even though there are things in there that I never use now (there's a motorcycle?!?!).  I went through the list and by my count, 9 of the 14 DLCs have very good and useful items that regularly find their way into my loadouts.  If I had bought only those 9 piecemeal, it would have cost more than the Bundle.  I do like to mix things up, so you may find fewer useful items than I did, but then you probably won't know until you try them.
3. Use your map frequently, to stay aware of enemy patrols even before they come on screen.  Against Cyborgs, the
red dots are IFVs (tanks).  I only just learned this myself a few days ago.
4. Don't fight what you don't need to.  If the objective is completed, move on.  There is no point staying to kill enemies, unless those enemies can keep up with the party (most won't be able to) or you happen to have a "Kill X number of enemies" objective on that mission.  There is no reward for killing enemies, unless it's an objective of the mission.
5. Be aware of how the camera works.  All players in the game share the same screen.  The further you move away from your team, the more you limit everyone's view of their surroundings.  When you aim down sights away from the party, you further pull the screen in the direction you aim.  It's best to stay close together when possible, so everyone has a clear view of their surroundings, to spot those scouts and eliminate them before they can sound the alarm.
I can't really take credit for all of these tips.  I'm sure I read at least some of them from other fans of the game... but I feel these are the most important things to know, going in.
Helldivers is one of my all time favorite games.  I hope you'll enjoy it as much as I do.

This game relies a lot on team coordination. It has a great balance between requiring skill and upgrades. High level players can play with low level players pretty easily, if they want to. Helldivers is a top-down tactical twin-stick shooter, similar to games like Alien Swarm and Red Solstice. It is also 4-player co-op, which is really where the fun lies.
Gameplay-wise, it consists of going to various planets to do randomly generated missions such as escorting, fixing, bomb-disposal etc. The zones themselves are fairly small - and are normally just a large square where objectives are placed randomly on the map. You get to unlock weapons and "stratagems" as you progress in RPG-like fashion. It allows for a fair amount of customisability - allowing you to equip your character with weapons and stratagems that you like or to compliment your team.
At the start of each mission you are allowed to outfit your character and select a drop-zone. The game features a multiplayer "hub" area in the form of a starship bridge where you can buy upgrades and customise your character before starting a mission. The missions themselves are generally quite enjoyable, if a little "samey". As a co-op game it shines.
Graphically it looks very polished and runs well at high resolutions (such as 4K) even at maximum settings. The crosshair is a constant PITA though, it's barely visible when you are not aiming and causes severe disorientation.
Unfortunately, it suffers from one very major issue: the missions you are allowed to play are determined by the community as a whole. As players across the world do missions it will occasionally lock you out of areas completely, until the "war has been won". This has happened several times for my team, where we all sat down on a Friday night, ready to play, only to find out we can only repeat one mission over and over again until such time as the game goes back to square one again. This is a real shame - and completely ruins the game.
If it wasn't for the above, my score would jump up two points. As it stands, the game can be really hit or miss depending on when in the month/week you decide to play.
(would be 8/10 if not for the "community progress" issue and crosshair mentioned above).

A fantastic game in which all of the mechanics have been honed to perfection. The DDR Max-RPG hybrid system works flawlessly, the voice acting is top notch, and the dialogue is great. Little touches such as being able to spend experience points to increase synthesis success, having a practice mode to work on your timing, and more are all done well. The hand painted enviornments look gorgeous, and the character and enemy designs are great, although a couple of the later enemies are palette swaps of the early ones. The soundtrack is great, with several catchy songs you'll find yourself humming in the shower later. Unfortunately, the number of tracks is rather limited, and each enemy is assigned only one song, but the songs are still good enough that they don't get annoying. The only flaw I can find is that there is no free play mode, as at this point I have reached such a high level that even the hardest battles only take around thirty seconds to win. Still, its hard to fault a game for not letting you replay it enough, so I'll conclude by saying that this is the single best indie title I have had the pleasure of playing on Steam. A fantastic game that should be enjoyed by all.

Before the Echo (the game was known as Sequence previously) is an interesting RPG. The game plays like Dance Dance Revolution with the notes divided into 3 separate note tracks running concurrently on the screen for casting spells, defending against attacks and regenerating mana. There is a quirky story to pull you through to the end but what won me over was most definitely the music tracks behind the gameplay.
I can't really gauge how difficult it is to play for beginners to the genre due to my many years of playing rhythm games from Stepmania, Guitar Hero and my current timesink of Osu!. Anyone who has played such games should find no problems however with adapting to the mechanics.
Due to the RPG nature of the game, it can become a grind for specific items to drop on the monsters which are used to craft items needed to progress in the floors. The game does not come with any additional content beyond the story that I am aware of (I played mostly at release back in 2011).
Before the Echo wasn't the most challenging game personally but it sits in my game library as a comfortable purchase when I look back over two years. Give it a go if it is on sale but just be aware it may not be fun for everyone; the usual disclaimer case for most games in the rhythm genre.

As a RPG and Stepmania enthousiast, this would seem like the perfect Indie game for me. And indeed, it was fun to play. It was unique. It was something fresh. And being a RPG fan, I am used with doing repetitive things in order to get that one rare drop.
One warning is that even casual gamers who would like to simply play the game and go through the story, might still face some moments where they have to engage battles over and over to get that last item for a recipe. Bite through it, the way you make story progression is quite slow in itself. Ronald Jenkees kicks♥♥♥♥♥ but not after the 6~7th time in a row. Yeah, having only one fixed song per enemy doesn't get you on your toes that much.
On sales it's usually just one buck, so hopefully no buyer's remorse after you've even spent an hour at it.

I HATE rhythm games. They're tailored to those with ludicrous skills and timing and don't ever quite grasp the concept of balance very well.
I don't hate Sequence because it at least tries to be a bit more generous while still failing to grasp an equitable balance of difficulty. I found most of the experience enjoyable because it's an RPG and it uses interesting mechanics so despite my implied ineptitude, I could apply strategy and grinding to bypass obstacles. It has great audio composition (being a rhythm game, I'd expect no less) and an interesting story. It alludes to a sequel that has yet to come at the time of this writing and the game's been out for some time, but I would probably enjoy it too.
I played the game on the medium difficulty and found it challenging, but fun. That broke down when trying to learn the last spell where the difficulty suddenly went to extremes. Because there's an achievement dependent upon successful acquisition of this spell, I found it necessary to replay the entire game on the easy difficulty and still found myself frustrated by the difficulty leap at the same point. Even when I reached the target I was given, it still would not give me the spell because (while not indicated at all) I had to exceed the target. If you want to complete the whole thing, play on easy. If you don't mind missing the achievement and finishing everything else, play on medium. If you hate yourself and your life, there are two even harder difficulties. Enjoy!

Okay, first of all, i have to mention that my 1st impression from this game was that this game, tries its best to be the Revolt - why not that game was(still is) 10/10 toy cars racing idol, so let's see if they made it or not:
+Visuals - contains high-quality graphics, backgrounds, cars, tracks - everything is good.
+OST - rare example when the game has modern music mixes and all of them are good, you are not getting bored listening to them they are well made. Big plus.
+ Time consuming - a lot of races in the story mode + a lot of special challenge missions + multiplayer, I wasted like 7 hours to complete 1st 3 campaigns.
+- 1st *problem* I faced playing this game - the difficulty is just low - story mode is very easy to complete, every single competition was completed within 1 to 5 minutes at best with 3 stars - so this is good for casual gaming, and not so good for those who loves a challenge.
-Only 5 maps for a ton of races, you know after like 10-20 races you understand that your a are rolling over the same places over and over again :| DLC contains 1 more map well then
-Not so many cars - you have 4 cars for each class 3*4 - 12 in total, and most likely if you will play as I do - you'll just pick the best car in its class - so you will most likely use only 3 because you have to pay coins for unlocks and upgrades. DLC contains 4 more cars with another car class.
-Weird collision physics - When you collide with cars and obstacles, your car acts very weirdly :|
-The last problem for me - call it personal - this game is about toy cars racing normal world BUT it does not feel like you are driving a toy car. It's more of a driving REAL car in the world where everything suddenly became enormous big. Maybe its engine sounds, maybe its turning feedback I cant say for sure, but this feeling still exists.
Short conclusion - as a racing game this game is nice for casual gaming, not a big challenge, also kind of fun to derp with your friends, can't say there is much of content but they are making DLCs with cars and tracks so I think after some time this game will become big enough to become something like Revolt.

Table Top Racing is a very aptly named game, because you race around on various sorts of tabletop surfaces. I'm not sure about the World Tour part, though I did see an American Flag in one level and a Union Jack in another, which I guess are flags corresponding to different parts of the world. Four out of five words is pretty good for a title.
Now I couldn't really make my mind up on whether I liked this game or not. I spent an extra five or so hours more than I feel this game deserved trying to decide. The graphics seem to lend to an illusion of this game being much better than it really is, at least for me as someone who enjoys racing games quite a bit. The flaws to the game and total lack of documentation on certain game features lend to my depreciating opinion on the game.
I know a lot of people will compare this to similar games on Steam like Toybox Turbos or Super Toy Cars and I'd definitely put this on a similar quality level. The graphics are much better but the gameplay lets it down a fair bit.
The handling model is incredibly simple and doesn't interact at all with the physics. If your car is acting under physics, whether you hit an object, got rammed or just landed after a jump, you have no control over your car until that stops. You have very mild 'air control' which is the same level of control you have while on the ground. This means the most powerful weapon in the game is ramming someone from the inside on a corner and makes the handling feel very inconsistent. Not to mention, the physics system itself isn't perfect by any means after landing from certain jumps or even little bumps in the track I've had my car rocket in total random directions. The very simple handling model and poor physics implementation means the meat of the game, the actual driving, is very hit and miss. I could forgive it if the game didn't force jumps on every track but every long race I was just constantly in fear of the next jump destroying my chances of coming 1st.
The AI doesn't offer much challenge either, none of them take any shortcuts, they all follow one racing line and drive at set speeds and only ever fire their weapons at you. This means the best events become the Time Trials, Hot Laps and Drift Events since all of the Combat Race style Events are braindead easy provided the physics don't screw you over.
This in itself wouldn't be a bad thing either, but there's no Single Race mode, you can't pick any of the tracks you've raced on, pick a mode and some settings and have some fun. You have to race on their preset events, whether they're in the Championships or Special Events. There might be a track you really want to drift on with your favorite car, but unfortunately you're not able to.
They're working on local multi-player, so perhaps this could come in a future update, but as of writing this review, this feature's not in the game.
There's also a lot of undocumented features. Lots of weapons in the game counter a weapon and are countered by another. Like bombs attracting Heatseeking Missiles or the Electricity blowing up the Bombs. Some of the pink glowing things on the side of the track are Shortcuts which can be opened by hitting them with a Level 2 powerup, the things that aren't shortcuts usually toss some debris on the track. There's a boost start you can use at the start of the race somehow which was recently added in an update. There's also a lot of little things on the tracks you wouldn't be able to find out without making a serious effort to. Like the orange GO! Sushi signs on the Sushi shop track actually being little doors you can drive through. Or the Circular Saw on the Workbench track actually hiding a shortcut you can take. I understand some of these things are meant to be 'secrets' but if you have some shortcuts highlighted and others not it doesn't really make sense. It's just confusingly inconsistent for no real reason. The level 2 weapons are also locked at the beginning of the game for some reason so you don't even really know they exist, which means things like shortcuts are unavailable to you as well.
Now the Drift Mode for the game, even though I've been decidedly negative about it this whole review, I found to be quite enjoyable. The DLC also adds an AE86 that's 'Legendary' for drifting, so I spent a good amount of time sliding around in the few available drift events I could use that car in. I'd personally say it's the best part of the game even if it's limited. There's also another great undocumented 'feature' in that a lower handling rating makes a car drift better. Especially useful on cars with lower drift ratings and high handling ratings like the Supercars.
Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game just because I hate the way the physics are handled. For a casual racing game player, once you start racing on the more difficult tracks I could see the difficulty spiking way up, especially with all the hidden things that aren't really common sense. For someone more experienced, the game won't challenge anything except your patience with the poor physics. A little more effort and it could have been a brilliant game.

Table Top Racing: World Tour is a mini car racing/combat racing game. This review is coming from someone who is not a fan of the racing genre and I tend to avoid racing games. This game however is an exception to that as it is extremely fun and very entertaining. It’ll remind you of Mario Kart, F1 race stars, those old Hotwheels games etc. The game is very polished and I was surprised how good the production quality is for an Indie game.
The graphics are very good, you can change settings to low, medium, high and ultra, depending on your system specs you can adjust accordingly. As it’s a table top racing game, the maps are filled with all sorts of stuff such as huge pool balls, spray cans even sushi plates and such, the cars are those cute small cars with huge wheels and they look adorable.
The game features upbeat, fast paced, techno-ish soundtracks which are very suitable for racing games as it’ll keep you pumped up. There’s plenty of tracks so you won’t get tired of listening to the same tracks over and over again.
The gameplay consists of, well, world tours of racing. You have 3 categories of races, there’s the “Amateur” level which will have the cult classic cars such as the Volkswagen beetle lookalike, Ford Mustang, Mini Cooper etc. There’s even a camper van called “Braking bad” which I thought was a hilarious reference to, you know, Breaking bad. Then there’s the “Pro” level which has street racer cars such as Nissan 350z, Skyline even a Range Rover type of car etc. The last but not the least is the “Expert” level which has super cars like Ferrari or “Fauxrari”, McLaren or “McHandful” as the game tells it. All the cars’ names will be different than their original counter-part I guess due to licenses and other such legal matters.
The cars’ physics and feel is very arcade-y as it should be for a table top racing game. The cars handle fine and have plenty of upgrades/paintjobs/bling-bling rims etc. There’s quite a few customizable items to unlock. The cars also have special wheels/rims which affect your car e.g. there’s the Spartan blade rims which will damage the other racers’ cars when brushing against them. Every time you win or lose a race you will get coins and the 3-star system which will give you stars depending on how well you did on that race/event. You can use these coins to buy new cars or upgrade your already bought cars. One car in all 3 levels are unlocked for you from the start, rest you will have to buy with coins. There’s a lot of stuff which can be bought with coins, paintjobs, wheels, performance upgrades etc.
You have a bunch of different types of racing modes available such as racing with power pickups, time trials and best lap time modes. The maps are small enough and most events have short races which are usually 1-2 minutes long with 3-5 laps. There’s plenty of themes like of the maps like a workshop theme which will have all those car parts lying around, sports theme such as pool stuff, kitchen theme with vegetables, sushi etc.
You can also get power-ups in races such as speed boost (sort of like nitro), rocket, bombs etc. The usual type of power ups available in any combat racing game. The AI is pretty good and will try to screw you over every chance it gets.
There are 3 types of racing levels, or leagues. Each has 3 tournaments which you can beat and get the trophies. The multiplayer mode is pretty dead, as of writing this review I could not find anyone playing online but then again it’s morning where I am right now so I guess people will be on at night time (as is usual for me with multiplayer games). You can also play with friends so if your friends have the game you can have plenty of fun with this game with friends. A short best lap mode race video can be found below:
The game looks very nice and is pretty fun to play. If you like racing games, you should get this game. There’s not many multiplayer people playing so do watch out for that. The music is awesome and the graphics are very neat looking, gameplay is fun and will have you playing more and more to unlock more stuff.

Note: This review is for the redux version, which is a free release from The Astronauts if you've purchased the original that I'm reviewing. The redux version improves the save system, updates the engine and improves the experience. I liked the game so much that I installed the original game since the redux version won't allow reviews on Steam for some reason. Ignore the 9 mins played noted here - I played 7+ hours of the redux version and finished the game.
Review:
This game doesn't rely on cheap scares to cause the overwhelming sense of dread as you explore. Atmosphere, visuals, relative lack of jump-scares (there's 1, and a good one) and complete lack of fighting make this a great game. Also love that the game doesn't hold your hand. You figure it out on your own and that's part of what makes this game so enjoyable; being scared and not knowing at all what's going on. The only regrets I have are that there isn't an option for 3rd person (I got motion-sickness from playing in 1st person. Turning off blur, head bob and bloom helped), and that I have now beat the game. I hope The Astronauts make more games like this, and look forward to them!

This is the story of my 5th run in FTL.
My ship was a Model-A Engi Cruiser called "The Asskicker". It was a fair ship, dependent on drones and an ion weapon that tore through enemy shields. It was crewed by Human Pilot-Captain Tina, Engi Jorl in engines, and Engi Nazi manning weapons. Tina was brave and determined, always trying to live up to her position; Jorl was tough, short-spoken, and hardworking; and Nazi was quiet and unsettling most of the time, except when doing his job, at which point he was quite enthusiastic. Over the course of their journey, the crew was augmented by Human Shields Specialist Charlie, who was the bravest man I ever knew. His Repair skill got to level 2 by the end.
The Asskicker breezed straight through several Zoltan- and Engi-controlled sectors, visiting every distress call it picked up until the true urgency of the situation became apparent (and 4 distress calls in a row turned out to be pirate ambushes). Eventually, the crew started skating straight past the opportunities to do good deeds.
At one point, the mission was almost failed when the Asskicker was boarded and half the systems were disabled, but a last-ditch stand by the crew in the Medbay repelled the attackers and saved the ship.
The Asskicker and its crew were a force to be reckoned with -with not a single casualty- right up until the final boss, at which point they were absolutely curbstomped because Tina believed in making a beeline through every sector, forgoing  many opportunities to upgrade the ship.
At one point in the final battle, Charlie was seriously injured, but the O2 generator was down. Jorl was sent to fix it, but Charlie was too brave, went in, and was almost killed. It didn't matter either way, because Jorl then died trying to fix it, and shortly after the ship and the rest of the crew fell to missile fire, dooming them to an eternal grave in the infinite blackness of space. The battle was lost, and the Federation doomed, but I didn't care about that. I only cared about the deaths of my heroic crew.
I've had 27 runs since then. I've had many Asskickers, of various makes and models. I've had many Tinas, many Jorls, many Nazis, and even a handful of Charlies. I even beat the game on Easy mode for the first time earlier tonight. But I will never forget the crew of my 5th run.
Get FTL.

Metro 2033 is a fun, easy-to-pick-up single player shooter experience. The story is quite simple (a 'coming-of-age' story in a post-apocalyptic world) and it captures what it could be like when a nuclear even occurs and remnant of humanity is forced to live underground.
Combat is pretty straightforward - left-click to shoot and right-click to aim down sights - with a simple stealth mechanic (i.e. enemies will not see you if your watches 'visibility indicator' isn't lit up).
The story is linear but has some intense moments. In the Metro 2033 world, humanity isn't the apex predator, so there's a lot of hide-and-seek and survival segments. It also presents moments where you debate the morality of your choices.
I recommend this game, but get this on the cheap.

**NO SPOILERS*
Into-
This game is based off a best-selling novel also called Metro 2033 and therefore I would consider this a story-based shooter rather than an action-based shooter.
Plot-
Metro 2033 is a post-apocalyptic first person shooter based on the aftermath of a nuclear war in Russia.After the nukes mutated creatures (simiply called mutatnts) forced the survivors into the metro  to create towns and cities for a new life underground.
You play as Artyom in Moscow in the year 2033 who has been given a task of seeking help from the Polis Rangers (A sort of  police that protects the metro from constant mutant attacks which have left Artyoms home city devastated.
Graphics -
A realistic approach to a gloomy railway civilisation really sets out the mood of the game. Dark shades are prevalent throughout the world with the reds of fires and civilisation a sight for sore eyes in-between cities.
Ive seen comparisons from the old Metro 2033 and the redux and let me tell you the remaster was significant enough to make the original  obsolete in comparison. Extra lighting effects, anti-alliasing and texture reworks are just a few things you can expect from the redux.The meshes arent out-dated and have aged well with particle effects from fires from grenades and water from rivers satisfying, but not satisfying enough.

7/10
Sound
Radios playing relaxing acoustic music are one thign i will definitely take away from this game. The music progresses great from cheery bar-music to eerie subway or exploration music to pure ambience for when you are truly alone.
8/10
Gameplay -
The gameplay mechanics in relation to lroe are refreshing to say the least in comparison to the "generic" shooters these days.Instead of the overused objectives or mission overlay that shows up in most shooters, holding an assigned key brings up a clipboard  that has Artyoms notes for his objectives, an accompanying lighter to brighten up the text is pulled out as well. As insignificatnt as this sounds, this simple element really blends into the atmosphere and enivorment of the depressing and chaotic world that is Metro.Guns are the weapons of choice in Metro and come in a range of choices that suit any play-style to run-and-gun machine guns to cowboy-revolvers to the sneaky poison gas=pressured gun.
Traps are put in smart places to be repetitive, yet keep you on your feet however their was not enough ammo for the constant onsalught of mutants and I constantly found my self dying to a forced reload out after all my weapons are out of ammo.There was also too many controls for placing gas masks in, changing filters,melee,grenades,torch and night vision many-a-time i have been confused on which but to press which lead to my death.

7/10
Story-
Without including spoliers the story is quite thrilling , with twists and turns around every door.Though some elements weren't explained at all and left me scratching my head for a character to jump in and explain all the mystical events though this could be because the books are a series.Notes are left throughout the world to help explain Artyoms inner thoughts and the world.World building has been well fleshed out with reasonable explainations for the events and clear displays of the effects that the devastation has left on society.
6/10
Length,Replayability and Difficulty
This game has a nice length with myself clocking up 13.1 Hours in one run.I did'nt have to retry a level more than 3 times and it was clearing implied what the game wanted you to do at most points with a few hiccups namely an infamous little boy spider web scene.The game itself isnt too difficult,even on ranger mode(Hard), finding ammo is the most challenging part of the game you will find, but if you save up bullets(the currency) running on empty should be a rare occurance.The game could have definately of had an increased mode for us hard-core gamers out there.The game is quite linear in itself and isnt that replayable, personally i would get bored by the third playthrough as the levels are designed with literal and figurative "tunnel vision".
7/10
Collabrative Enjoyment factor
8/10
Total Score-42/60 70%
Conclusion/TL;DR
Despite its flaws, Metro 2033 is one of the better novel-based games.What it lacks in innovative gameplay mechanics that are overwelhming and level design, it makes up for story,atmosphere and lore. I wouldn't reccomend this game for those looking for a sense of achievement from their games.It felt more like a story then a games at times, ironically. However it has a certain niche that would appeal to a plethora of gamers out there and I would insist on purchasing the Metro Bundle if you fit into this group.

INGREDIENTS
2 SERVINGS
1 lamb, brain
1 tablespoon vinegar
2 eggs, beaten
1⁄2 cup flour
1⁄2 cup onion, sliced
1 teaspoon salt
2 tablespoons parsley, separated
1 teaspoon extra virgin olive oil
1 tablespoon lemon juice
DIRECTIONS
Place lamb brains in a bowl with cold water for at least 2 hours. Change the water every half hour, until the brains are thoroughly cleansed.
Place brains in a saucepan with fresh water, add onions, salt, vinegar and 1 tablespoon of parsley.
Bring to a boil and then immediately remove the brains and place in a paper towel to drain.
Cut into four pieces and season with a little olive-oil, lemon juice, and parsley.
Roll the brains in flour, dip in egg, and fry in a skillet with oil, over medium heat for 7-8 minutes.
Enyoy!

Helldivers is a top-down tactical twin-stick shooter, similar to games like Alien Swarm and Red Solstice. It is also 4-player co-op, which is really where the fun lies.
Gameplay-wise, it consists of going to various planets to do randomly generated missions such as escorting, fixing, bomb-disposal etc. The zones themselves are fairly small - and are normally just a large square where objectives are placed randomly on the map. You get to unlock weapons and "stratagems" as you progress in RPG-like fashion. It allows for a fair amount of customisability - allowing you to equip your character with weapons and stratagems that you like or to compliment your team.
At the start of each mission you are allowed to outfit your character and select a drop-zone. The game features a multiplayer "hub" area in the form of a starship bridge where you can buy upgrades and customise your character before starting a mission. The missions themselves are generally quite enjoyable, if a little "samey". As a co-op game it shines.
Graphically it looks very polished and runs well at high resolutions (such as 4K) even at maximum settings. The crosshair is a constant PITA though, it's barely visible when you are not aiming and causes severe disorientation.
Unfortunately, it suffers from one very major issue: the missions you are allowed to play are determined by the community as a whole. As players across the world do missions it will occasionally lock you out of areas completely, until the "war has been won". This has happened several times for my team, where we all sat down on a Friday night, ready to play, only to find out we can only repeat one mission over and over again until such time as the game goes back to square one again. This is a real shame - and completely ruins the game.
If it wasn't for the above, my score would jump up two points. As it stands, the game can be really hit or miss depending on when in the month/week you decide to play.
(would be 8/10 if not for the "community progress" issue and crosshair mentioned above).

One of the hardest parts of writing any good review comes from writing the review itself. Every person has their own appeal, games they like and dislike, and reasons for those likes and dislikes. Not every game a reviewer will play will conform to those likes or dislikes, and a review must still compose himself and present a fair and balanced review in spite of his personal thoughts. I bring this up because it is very difficult to talk about Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines (hereafter referred to simply as ‘Vampire') without delving into the subjective elements it presents without sucking all the emotion and personality from the review and transforming it into a technical overview of the game itself. As such, I have divided this game up into two sections, an objective and a subjective one. But first an overview of the game itself;
In Vampire you play as a young person living in L.A. who has recently been transformed into one of the undead. Upon your indoctrination you quickly come to discover that the vampire society needs to be very secretive about how they act so as to keep the public unaware of their actions. Before long, though a sarcophagus which may or may not house the remains of a very ancient and very powerful vampire is uncovered and the various vampire clans in the city all begin a secret war of cloak and dagger tactics, each trying to recover the sarcophagus and its contents or deny them to others for themselves, all while trying to keep their very existence secretive from humans.
Firstly, for the objective. The game is VERY well designed and it shows in its game mechanics. Serving as a action RPG with elements of The Elder Scrolls (except less open, confining the player to four primary districts that are fairly small and multiple dungeons) it is solid right from the get-go. From the beginning you are forced to select one of a series of vampire clans, each offering its own unique set of bonuses, abilities, and disadvantages that will end up shaping how you play. I, personally, ended up going with Clan Ventrue which focuses a lot on persuasion, but can't feed off of animals and can only feed reliably on upper-class humans. Someone else may end up with Nosferatu which can't raise their appearance at all and has to avoid being seen at all by humans for example.
The gameplay itself is fairly solid with most of the controls being very tight and having almost no real problems beyond a few glitches (which I will cover later) which I can't blame on the controls. One of the interesting things is that, instead of leveling up stats like strength and such, the player instead levels up various skills and abilities which, in turn, affect stats. This can cause for some very interesting outcomes where a character may choose to level up a skill they don't intend to use at all to bolster another skill which they do, in fact, use and results both in a large amount of flexibility and interesting builds as well as a drive to experiment around and see what else can be done.
Another interesting thing is that players do not gain experience from killing enemies in the slightest, but rather from quest completion. This puts an added drive to complete even simple sidequests as the added experience is the only way to make your character stronger.
Lastly, there are two special meters that will need proper attention. The Humanity meter and the Masquerade meter. A large focus of the game is the focus on struggling against the vampire urges and keeping ones self ‘human' despite needing to drink human blood in order to survive. Certain actions can cause players to lose some of their humanity and, as the gauge lowers to 0, it can result in them becoming utterly feral. Meanwhile, keeping the humanity high can result in a weaker vampire who struggles with their new nature. Additionally, keeping ones actions as a vampire secretive is very key and, every time a player is caught being a vampire in public, it costs them on the Masquerade meter. They start with a set amount of chances and, if those chances ever all disappear, game over (going feral wastes a chance). This puts an added focus on keeping ones nature as a vampire truly secret and staying human as going feral at the wrong time on a player who didn't try to keep hidden can cause an outright loss.
Visually the game is fairly solid as well. While, sadly, you won't be able to delve too deep into the many complexities of polygon count, it very successfully manages to convey the feeling of the World of Darkness (the world as a vampire sees it). Vampire does its best to drive this home too, but manages to back it up with some solid displays. While they may look a bit dated today, there is a HUGE difference between ‘dated' and ‘bad' and this is most certainly not the latter.
There are some problems with the game though. First off it seems to revel in giving vague directions and not giving you anything resembling a quest-marker. While this wouldn't normally be too bad of a thing it is very easy to end up lost and unsure of where to go or who to talk too, especially if you stop playing the game for a week or more and don't remember the location of an important NPC with the lack of a map (aside from some bus-stop signs) driving the annoyance home. But, more overbearingly, is the glitches. There are a LOT in this game, and they are NOT of the minor kind. These are the kind that can destroy a game and leave it unplayable. Hunting down a patch and/or activating the command console may very well be a requirement for this game.
And now for the subjective. This is a dark game. A VERY dark game to say the least. The game makes sure to reinforce this with such locations like abandoned hospitals, scummy apartment buildings, sleazy motels, brothels and night clubs galore, and death around every corner. The streets are almost never clean and are littered with trash, bums and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s seem to be the most common ‘professions', and so forth. People looking for a game about sparkling vampires, or even just ‘normal' vampires may find themselves off-put easily. This is a very dark and pessimistic game, and it ended up causing me to rethink about how to score this.
To say that this is a bad game simply because it's world is so scummy and grim is shortselling what the game does right. In any other setting where you can count the number of people who are ‘good' on more than one hand this probably would have been an amazing title. However, this game does not hide for even a moment that this is a grim and depressing world. People not looking for this sort of thing specifically can very easily end up becoming disguised and/or offended by it. Even the ending of the game seems to love rubbing in just how dark this world is.
As a result, I feel it is VERY important to look into the game before buying it and deciding if you wish to play a game like this. While it can be enthralling for people who revel in its darkness, for those people looking for even the tiniest ray of light and hope, they would be better off searching elsewhere.
In summery: while a solid game that is mired by some technical problems, its subjective aspects and story may simply be so off-putting to a player who does not enjoy its dark and grim world as to not make this game recommendable on a whim. If you buy this game, you should know what you're getting into, because this game is in no way shy about tossing you into the shadows.
My pricing: For someone looking for a dark game: 15-20 bucks. It's very solid, if a bit dated and dealing with bugs.
For someone not: Avoid at all costs. Remember, this is a game where it is possible to lose because you couldn't pretend to be a human being instead of a blood-sucking monster well enough.

Nifty little game.  The price tag is a bit high considering dollars-to-entertainment, compared to what we've come to expect, but overall I have to recommend this.  I got it on a Steam Sale at $6.00 and was not at all disappointed for the 5 hours it gave me. However, when I consider that this may be a brain-child for future endeavors, and think that this idea is a test-drive for future titles, I think, "Well, let's see how far they can run with this," and that makes the price fair.
You play in first-person as a paranormally-gifted investigator who is resolving a weird case involving a town that is basically abandoned except for a family that is killing itself off as a result of mysterious "force" prompting weird behaviour from within that family.  The plot and theme unfold as it goes, and this is one of those adventure games where you could watch it as a movie and feel satisfied afterwards.
In the process of going through the game, you investigate murder scenes, and you - the protagonist - have the ability to commune with the dead. In order to do so, however, you must reconstruct the clues and environments that led to that death. Having constructed the clues and "recreated" the moments before the death, you then have to determine the order of events. When you can do that, the story of "that death" is revealed, and in the telling of "that death" you get a better insight of the whole of the plot of the arching story.
It is a really great and new idea in adventure gaming and murder-mystery solving premise, and the way it's implemented is novel. Throughout the pieces of the puzzles you are challenged, with no hands-held, to work it out on your own. The puzzles, if you don't use an online strategy guide, will keep you guessing. At least some of them. By the end, you (or at least, I felt) will feel like you were part of the story.
Amazing graphics. There were a few times I turned a corner or walked through a "path" and had to call my wife over to admire the "unreal" engine. The soundtrack is great. The voice acting is more than sufficient. By the time I was done, which was all-too-soon, I felt the 5 hours I spend was well-worth the sale price.
A few gripes: There is no "auto-run" feature, and much of the game involes running around trying to find the next "death" scene. No hand-holding at all is fine, but it was about like playing Crysis where you can spend hours just crawlling through the forest wondering if something is going to happen. Having to hold "shift+W" got old really quick.
Also, there are no clues to point you into the next direction. Once you solve a "murder," nothing says, "Go here next," so of the 5 hours I spent playing this many minutes were spent randomly wandering the landing hoping I didn't miss something. I get that--showcase the graphic engine, extend the length of the average playthrough--but some sort of "go here next" system would have been appreciated.
Minor gripes aside, a great little adventure that I highly recommend if you get it on sale,  If you appreciate a good murder mystery, adventure game with intellectual puzzles, or even just an arching good story. Hopefully,  the Astronauts will keep up the skeer.

reminds me of The Sims, except that instead of building a house and managing your characters' home lives, you're building an office and managing their work. It's an interesting idea, and the game has a lot of charm to it with its low-poly pastel graphics. Unfortunately, I can't recommend the game because I just didn't find it fun. Outside of the building aspect, most of the actual "gameplay" is just clicking around in menus to assign employees to teams, prioritize projects, load-balance servers, etc.
Perhaps the issue for me is that I'm a software developer in real life, so the game reminded me too much of actual work, but I kind of felt like I was "playing" an Excel spreadsheet. There are many different systems to learn and manage, to the point that it's a bit overwhelming, but no matter how well you play the game your impact seems to be limited to making numbers and bar graphs go up or down.
I almost feel bad writing a negative review, because clearly the developer has put in a lot of effort and paid great attention to detail in designing the game's many systems. But personally, I would have preferred fewer but more engaging game mechanics. I wouldn't call
a bad game; as other reviews show, if you're the type of person this particular style of game appeals to, then it's very well made and you'll probably enjoy it. I thought I was that kind of person, but I guess not--at least not to the extent required by this game.
