TL;DR AT BOTTOM!
Wow. A serious negative review for this game, crazy, right? Wait, wait! Hold on - I can see that cursor dropping to the downvote button, but I insist you take off the rose-tinted and glasses hear me out.
This game is inferior in nearly every single way to EA's Battlefront - and EA's Battlefront 2. Why do I say this? Well, before I proceed to list the cons when compared to EA's version of the series, how about I list the pros and the neutrals first?
PROS
+ Heroes are relevant to the map
+ Clone Wars (Negated with EA's BF2)
+ Mods (Although, a game shouldn't be rated on it's mods, as those are user generated, not dev generated)
+ More maps (I suspect this will change in EA's BF2)
+ Singleplayer campaign (Aaaaand changed in EA's BF2)
+ Space battles (Once more, EA's BF2)
+ 64v64
NEUTRALS (Subjectives)
* Class based gameplay (Once more negated by EA's BF2)
* Stamina system
* Galactic conquest, a sort of... weird splice between strategy and the normal game (It's not really that great)
* No pick-ups
And with those out of the way, we move onto the...
CONS
- Zero progression
- Floaty, horrid gunplay
- Lightsaber fights come down to one thing: who can stunlock the other first
- Heroes are dished-out to the top performers of a team, making the unstoppable even more powerful
- Graphics are aged
- Sound is aged
- Animations are horrible, to the point of being broken at times
- Gamespy
- Heroes have a max of two or three side abilities, only one of which is useful in most circumstances
- Lack of atmosphere, Dagobah doesn't feel spooky and mysterious, Hoth doesn't feel cold
- Most classes are useless, there is no need to switch it up when you can easily get fourty kills as the basic soldier
- Individual soldiers are only rarely map specific
So, yeah. That's that.
TL;DR This game is inferior to EA's Battlefront(s) in every way save for content.

Summary
Metro 2033 Redux offers a new and unique experience for players. It cleans up most of the problems that the first one had and made it better.
Story
You play as Artyom, who must get to Polis to warn about the immediat threat of the dark ones and gain support from the council. But your journey isn't a simple one as you go through the Reds, Bandit and Nazi camps, while helping other station with their mutant problem.
Gameplay
Plays as your standard FPS shooter with some survival elements. With linear elements, you can explore places to gain more items, in which you'll need to do if you don't want to run out of the ammo or gas masks in particular section like the dead city. Currency (Miltary ammo) will keep you supplied throughout your journey with weapons customisation adding silencers to laser sights to help you aid in your fights, grenades and medkits. The combat is very standard, with some stealth elements incooperated in it. The player can stealth kill or even avoid entire fights throughtout the game (Against human enemies) and turning off lights is favourable as it will help you sneak better.

However the hit detection for mutants seems very random. You could kill a mutant with a 2 shotgun blast at close range, however when you do it again, it may take 4-6 even if you get them in the head. There is alot of hand holding, so you don't feel isolated all the time. There some sections which you are by yourself, however most of the section especially towards the ends, you mostly with companions and they are doing most of the shooting for you. I rarely shot in these sections and watched as the AI did most of the work.
Sound
The atompshere of this game is brillant. Its captures the esscense of being stuck in a dark metro. Places like the Market, where it was populated, felt buzzing! The unique conversation that everyone was having around you was amazing and gave you insight of the world. Contrast that to where your alone, its terrifying and the dark atompshere makes you check corners for any mutants.
Game: 9/10

if i were to describe the gameplay its something like an rpg, except the combat has been replaced by tower-defence. each character you meet that joins your army can be placed down on the map, then it will attack with whichever move is off cooldown at the time. it speaks for itself that you have to place these "towers" in an tactical superior way, so they help each other kill the revenants (zombie type mobs with a variety of mechanics such as, but not limited to, attacking back, being able to swim,..).
RPG:
despite this being part rpg this does not contain any "choice" as regards to storyline (except maybe 1, though its very clear which one is superior). you do get to pick traits out of trait trees and make every character unique in its fighting style. also you can equip all your characters with weapons and armor (except the last kind, though you will understand when you get there). different weapons do no have different boons, the more expensive ones simply do more damage. same goes for armor, the more money it costs the more defense it gives. the customizability is in the trait system, definitely not the equipment system.
tower defense:
each tower is unique, and at the end of every match you get xp and perhaps a trait point (lvl up) to decide how you want to build it. you can improve your tower during the match though, with the match currency called spi, this will give him/her access to more moves. you can not block paths, or build any kind of obstruction to make the mobs change course. this is one of the tower defense mechanics that is missing (can't have it all).

I bought this game before it was greenlit after seeing a WTF is... about it. Played it start to end twice in a row and had a blast all the way thru.
For those uninitialized: Defender's Quest is a Tower defense with heavy RPG elements. Your "towers" are characters you recruit thru progress of the game. You level them up and give them skillpoints and equip them with weapons and armors. Your characters will be with you the entire playthru and level up with your character.
The goal per usual is to stop the enemies from reaching your "pool" and taking away from your life. This is done thru set mazes where the monsters have to follow a premade maze, so sorry, no mazing for you that like to build your own mazes in TDs. You progress thru a gameworld where you can face each stage in three various difficulties, the harder it is the better the reward. You can also backtrack to previously defeated levels to try it on a harder level or just grind for gold/xp for your characters.
The game also offers a fairly interesting story with alot of written dialogue with some pretty nice graphics to go along. The steam version also features updated graphics to the game which makes the game feel apropiate for the pricetag.

While fighting monsters you have three "rhythmus screens" you can switch freely between: the mana screen (only for regeneration of mana), the defend screen (block attacks to avoid damage) and the spell screen (match the combination to attack with your spells). Watch a gameplay video to get a better impression.
As a sidenote you can not choose the music for the game. It is preset and there are "only" between 10-15 playable songs. Personally I found them quite enjoyable . Also you need to grind a tiny bit during the game in order to gain experiences and the right items. If those minor things are no problem for you I can only recommand this game to you.

I'll be frank: sometimes, my sarcasm meter gets a little low, and I play the odd otome for the purpose of snarking my way through it. Though a lot of people enjoy otomes (which is perfectly valid), I personally tend to enjoy making quips and commentaries about the game more than the act of playing through it. However, I don't usually expect to actually enjoy an otome... this is exactly what happened with Seduce Me. Though there were some aspects I didn't enjoy, I was surprised to find myself really enjoying the game and a few of the romances!
Cons:
-The formula for how to romance your chosen LI is pretty simple/entirely the same for every character... not terrible, but I generally enjoy more personalized character paths (ie. trying to think of what reaction would suit this character best, as opposed to "get as close to them as possible and take every chance to be romantic as you can").
-The voice acting is a bit hit-and-miss. I thought some characters were voiced very well, and others were a bit spotty.
Pros:
-CONSENT CULTURE! I LOVED seeing how much consent was brought up in this game, and I loved how the Protagonist is ALWAYS asked before the sexual scenes whether she actually wants to do it or not. Regardless of your LI, they will let you know that it's no problem if you aren't into it. The sexual scenes are completely optional- you can complete the romance without doing them!
-The story, I thought, was more interesting than most of the other otomes I've played.
-Some of the later scenes with your chosen LI are actually very sweet- I even found myself going "awwww!" a few times!

TL;DR: Cliché characters, disjointed story line and romance and no sex in a game about freaking sex-demons but at least it's free.
This game had an interesting premise but unfortunately it leaves it at that. There are a few saving graces but they are not enough to actually make me recommend the game. Let's start off:
Cons:
- Characters. So who's your favorite? The 'bad boy'? Maybe it's the 'smart and sensible' one? Or perhaps 'Baby Spice'? Point: you dislike stereotypes? You'll dislike this, from the Mary Sue main character to the predictable enemies.
- Story. Two half-baked parts that have either little or no connection (it's the latter, there's none, ZIP). It's like they wrote half the story and then changed their minds, quickly wrapping up the first and introducing the second.
- Sex. There are five sex-demons (who literally consume sexual energy) living in a mansion with a teenage girl. I can think of seven different ways for that to go down, off the top of my head. PG-13 is NOT one of them. Potential: WASTED.
- Romance. I expect a game relying on romance to do so, well. This...doesn't. I made a choice about eating food and whom to help and then I found them in a room and we started making out and now he loves me...that doesn't happen when you're sober.
- Harem. Be it male or female, I just don't like it. I love options but they have to be properly implements, this is just lazy.
- Writing. Creating a setting and backstory is all good, info-dumping is not. I cannot remember what the first 5 minutes of the game was like because it was a ton of exposition which had nothing to do with the actual story. Unfortunately, they drop the ball on some of the more relevant aspects, simply showing them without exploring.
Pros:
- Premise. They set up things that sound really intriguing and with a little more depth could have been great.
- Voices. The voice acting is not top stellar but it's solid and fitting.
- Price. It's free, this is a major plus.
- Length. It's well paced and not too long.
In conclusion the game is free so it's not a major loss but it's just not reaching even half of its potential.

One of the hardest parts of writing any good review comes from writing the review itself. Every person has their own appeal, games they like and dislike, and reasons for those likes and dislikes. Not every game a reviewer will play will conform to those likes or dislikes, and a review must still compose himself and present a fair and balanced review in spite of his personal thoughts. I bring this up because it is very difficult to talk about Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines (hereafter referred to simply as ‘Vampire') without delving into the subjective elements it presents without sucking all the emotion and personality from the review and transforming it into a technical overview of the game itself. As such, I have divided this game up into two sections, an objective and a subjective one. But first an overview of the game itself;
In Vampire you play as a young person living in L.A. who has recently been transformed into one of the undead. Upon your indoctrination you quickly come to discover that the vampire society needs to be very secretive about how they act so as to keep the public unaware of their actions. Before long, though a sarcophagus which may or may not house the remains of a very ancient and very powerful vampire is uncovered and the various vampire clans in the city all begin a secret war of cloak and dagger tactics, each trying to recover the sarcophagus and its contents or deny them to others for themselves, all while trying to keep their very existence secretive from humans.
Firstly, for the objective. The game is VERY well designed and it shows in its game mechanics. Serving as a action RPG with elements of The Elder Scrolls (except less open, confining the player to four primary districts that are fairly small and multiple dungeons) it is solid right from the get-go. From the beginning you are forced to select one of a series of vampire clans, each offering its own unique set of bonuses, abilities, and disadvantages that will end up shaping how you play. I, personally, ended up going with Clan Ventrue which focuses a lot on persuasion, but can't feed off of animals and can only feed reliably on upper-class humans. Someone else may end up with Nosferatu which can't raise their appearance at all and has to avoid being seen at all by humans for example.
The gameplay itself is fairly solid with most of the controls being very tight and having almost no real problems beyond a few glitches (which I will cover later) which I can't blame on the controls. One of the interesting things is that, instead of leveling up stats like strength and such, the player instead levels up various skills and abilities which, in turn, affect stats. This can cause for some very interesting outcomes where a character may choose to level up a skill they don't intend to use at all to bolster another skill which they do, in fact, use and results both in a large amount of flexibility and interesting builds as well as a drive to experiment around and see what else can be done.
Another interesting thing is that players do not gain experience from killing enemies in the slightest, but rather from quest completion. This puts an added drive to complete even simple sidequests as the added experience is the only way to make your character stronger.
Lastly, there are two special meters that will need proper attention. The Humanity meter and the Masquerade meter. A large focus of the game is the focus on struggling against the vampire urges and keeping ones self ‘human' despite needing to drink human blood in order to survive. Certain actions can cause players to lose some of their humanity and, as the gauge lowers to 0, it can result in them becoming utterly feral. Meanwhile, keeping the humanity high can result in a weaker vampire who struggles with their new nature. Additionally, keeping ones actions as a vampire secretive is very key and, every time a player is caught being a vampire in public, it costs them on the Masquerade meter. They start with a set amount of chances and, if those chances ever all disappear, game over (going feral wastes a chance). This puts an added focus on keeping ones nature as a vampire truly secret and staying human as going feral at the wrong time on a player who didn't try to keep hidden can cause an outright loss.
Visually the game is fairly solid as well. While, sadly, you won't be able to delve too deep into the many complexities of polygon count, it very successfully manages to convey the feeling of the World of Darkness (the world as a vampire sees it). Vampire does its best to drive this home too, but manages to back it up with some solid displays. While they may look a bit dated today, there is a HUGE difference between ‘dated' and ‘bad' and this is most certainly not the latter.
There are some problems with the game though. First off it seems to revel in giving vague directions and not giving you anything resembling a quest-marker. While this wouldn't normally be too bad of a thing it is very easy to end up lost and unsure of where to go or who to talk too, especially if you stop playing the game for a week or more and don't remember the location of an important NPC with the lack of a map (aside from some bus-stop signs) driving the annoyance home. But, more overbearingly, is the glitches. There are a LOT in this game, and they are NOT of the minor kind. These are the kind that can destroy a game and leave it unplayable. Hunting down a patch and/or activating the command console may very well be a requirement for this game.
And now for the subjective. This is a dark game. A VERY dark game to say the least. The game makes sure to reinforce this with such locations like abandoned hospitals, scummy apartment buildings, sleazy motels, brothels and night clubs galore, and death around every corner. The streets are almost never clean and are littered with trash, bums and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s seem to be the most common ‘professions', and so forth. People looking for a game about sparkling vampires, or even just ‘normal' vampires may find themselves off-put easily. This is a very dark and pessimistic game, and it ended up causing me to rethink about how to score this.
To say that this is a bad game simply because it's world is so scummy and grim is shortselling what the game does right. In any other setting where you can count the number of people who are ‘good' on more than one hand this probably would have been an amazing title. However, this game does not hide for even a moment that this is a grim and depressing world. People not looking for this sort of thing specifically can very easily end up becoming disguised and/or offended by it. Even the ending of the game seems to love rubbing in just how dark this world is.
As a result, I feel it is VERY important to look into the game before buying it and deciding if you wish to play a game like this. While it can be enthralling for people who revel in its darkness, for those people looking for even the tiniest ray of light and hope, they would be better off searching elsewhere.
In summery: while a solid game that is mired by some technical problems, its subjective aspects and story may simply be so off-putting to a player who does not enjoy its dark and grim world as to not make this game recommendable on a whim. If you buy this game, you should know what you're getting into, because this game is in no way shy about tossing you into the shadows.
My pricing: For someone looking for a dark game: 15-20 bucks. It's very solid, if a bit dated and dealing with bugs.
For someone not: Avoid at all costs. Remember, this is a game where it is possible to lose because you couldn't pretend to be a human being instead of a blood-sucking monster well enough.

Bloodlines is a flawed gem of a game, it had a troubled as hell development and it really shows. The game is a buggy mess, but thankfully fans have patched out a lot of the bugs so make sure to get the Wesp fan patch before you play. To sum it up Bloodlines has some of the best atmosphere, writing, and actual roleplaying in an RPG and it still really holds up to this day. There's multiple solutions through missions and each vampire clan have their own unique skills to solve them, i.e. Nosferatu can turn themselves invisible, Tremere have powerful blood magic, and Malkavians can drive people insane. Sadly, the game falls apart in the end with some horrid forced combat sections (So make sure you have a good combat build going, though just cheating through it is totally fine) but it ultimately is a game worth playing because there are still way too few RPGs that are like it.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an adventure game developed by The Astronauts that puts the player in the shoes of detective Paul Prospero as he visits the American town of Red Creek Valley to find clues about the disappearece of the titular Ethan Carter boy, only to find the town long abandoned and filled with mysterious murder cases.
The videogames takes place in a huge map the player can roam freely. In this map there are several points of interest that clue the player in a murder that was committed on the location: your objective each time is to examine the surrounding area for clue and put all the pieces together or simply explore the place, solve a puzzle of some sort and uncover a tale left by Ethan behind. As the developers inform you on starting the game, no one is holding your hands here, so you can "solve" the various "puzzles" in any order you wish or being one just to drop it and come back later. It's a walking sim- hey wait, come back! It's actually a good one. The world is scenic and beautiful, but it doesn't feel completely inert like, say, Everybody's Gone to the Rapture. It's interactive to a fair degree and the environments change enough to keep you interested. The story's a very slow-burn kind but again, unlike some games, it makes perfect sense and manages to cultivate a seldom-seen kind of slowly creeping terror even though there are only few dangers - I guarantee by the time you're actually at risk of death you'll be shaking in your boots, fueled to press on only by how interesting the story's gotten at that point.
It's a fascinating world to explore, and it manages it far better than other, similar, games. I'd recommend this for everyone with patience, and especially for writers - there are a few interesting literary themes in it.

Gone North Games proudly introduces us to their debut project A Story About My Uncle. An atmospheric first person puzzle platformer that will keep you engaged throughout.
Jumping straight into the options menu you'll find it to be sparse. Resolution and VSync options are available and you also get an FoV slider. More advanced optons are absent and you're stuck with only two options for Detail Level. 'Medium' and 'High' and you also get a Texture Quality option. That's about it.
However this does not mean the game isn't beautiful. Built on the Unreal Engine this game has one of the most amazing set pieces I've ever played in, with vast caverns and floating mountains.

Really not much to say. Voice acting was amazing. Ambience was spot on. And the soundtrack? Top notch and absolutely beautiful. Big props to Santiago Ferrero on such an amazing job. The OST really is the highlight of this game.
I won't spoil much. Basically you are the protagonist telling a bedtime story to your daughter about how you embarked on an adventure in a fantastical land on a journey to find your uncle. Total playtime was about 5 hours which felt a little short. Considering the amount of retries I had to do to complete a section of the game.
Gameplay consists of you using your grappling hook and long jumps to swing between platforms and ledges. You also get a pair of rocket boots which is awesome. Timing and reaction is incredibly important in the later stages of the game. As you embark on a journey to find your uncle you are taken through dark caverns, floating mountains and ice caves. Each stage is beautifully designed and nothing feel the same.
A beautiful atmospheric puzzle platformer with and endearing story and amazing soundtrack this game is definitely worth your money if you dont mind the short gameplay time.

An excellent game that asks you to set your mind off to another dimension, really. This experience felt so soothing. The controls are responsive and the music is atmospheric.

By now everyone knows this game. Who cares, if you don't, you're about to. Because this is one of those games that you shouldn't think twice before hitting "buy".  It just hits all the right keys. It's challenging, fun, entertaining, engaging, immersive... it just has it all. It has endless replayability thanks to the totally random galaxy you'll find each time you play, and the fact that you can unlock a good ammount of ships and ship variations - and each one plays differently. Add to that the dozens of weapons you can unlock (some of them really fun, there's nothing like setting a whole enemy ship on fire and watch'em burn!) so gameplay on top of fun is varied.
There's not a fixed way to win it, there are multiple strategies you can go for depending on your ship, the resources you find and the way you want to play. It's got three different difficulty settings, so you can adjust for how much of a challenge you want. Easy is...not that easy in fact, at least not if you're new to the game. Normal is a real challenge. Hard is mindboggingly tough. So choose how much of a hard time you want to have and just have fun.
Seriously this is one of those games you just MUST have. And if you're still in doubt go check any of the hundreds of Let's plays in youtube with this game...because on top of being ridiculously fun to play...it's a hoot to see others playing it.

While Tower Defense games are not my top game genre, this one won me over.  Excellent game play, engaging story, challenging maps to resolve.  Replayability on higher difficulty levels.  Cartoon graphics just right.  Silly conversations, well, silly and fun.  Acquiring and upgrading of your crew is easy and trying different strategies and arrangements one of the game's best aspects.  Whether you're new to TD or a fan, this game is highly recommended.

An exceptionally fun take on the Tower Defense genre of games. The sprites are neat, the music is okay, and the dialogue is spectacular. If you don't hate Tower Defense, buy this game; it's likely one of the best iterations of the genre on the market.

If one were pessimistic or dismissive, it would be easy to look at this Tower Defence game and dismiss it for being generic and dated-looking. However, that would be doing the game and the developers a real disservice.
Granted, the 16-bit style is one you're either going to like or not, but it is executed very well indeed, as the use of colour is very done so that it remains pleasing on the eye and never jarring. The execution and balance of the game overall is very polished, and belies the developers' size - it really appears to be well-tested and difficulty is a very smooth and progressive curve.
Pacing is similarly excellent, and it definitely evokes that magic "just one more go" response. The icing on the cake is the story, which is nice and humorous without being too cheesy or vulgar, so it greatly appeals to a wide audience. As comedy is a very difficult thing to write, they have done a fantastic job here; it's very tongue-in-cheek, and it fits the game perfectly.
The meat of the game lies in having characters as your "towers" to place on a map. You can purchase extra characters to a maximum of 6 of each, and level them individually. The range of characters are well-defined (such as straight-up brawlers, archers, mages, healers, and even big ol' dragons), and afford some forethought as to their placing on the maps.
The length of the game is good, running at a good few hours minimum, but with the added replayability of New Game+ and more. Whilst the game might seem a little high for something that looks like an old game, it is well worth money, as it will entertain you from start to finish.
For fans of the genre, this is a must. Even for casuals, it's highly recommended.

This could have been a good game, but it wasn't. It starts out great - It's got stunning visuals, fun platforming action, passable narration and characters, and a story I actually kind of care about. The world opens up in a breathtaking way, and you start to get the sense that the most interesting part is just around the corner.
And then, there are the ice levels. Endless ice levels. You leave behind the stunning world of the early game for what seems like an eternity of drab, monotonous, completely visually homogeneous ice caves. The puzzles become increasingly frustrating and poorly planned out, the story development all but stops in its tracks, and any drive you may have had to finish the game dies, frozen to death in an infinitely tedious, perfectly homogeneous icy wasteland as you wonder: who thought it was a good idea to pad out the game's playtime with this absolutely meaningless garbage? Who thought it was okay to put such care into crafting an interesting and immersive early game only to ruin it with a sloppily cobbled-together grind of a late game? And will they ever be held responsible?

This game gives you absolute freedom on how you run your software company, you can either be a lone dev who only takes contracts and company deals, or you can choose to be Bill Gates and make the next Windows OS and make billions off of it.
Some players might find the micromanaging in the game a bit tedious but I really enjoy it.
There are mods out there that adds furnitures, and new types of softwares. You can also share the buildings that you made which is pretty neat.  The dev of the game is responsive to discussions and is clearly passionate about the game, which are traits that in my opinion most early access devs do not have. He also has a Trello map(found on the Discussion page) which lists what is next on the updates.
The only cons I can think of is that the game lacks an endgame, after you have billions in the bank, you can pretty much just buy out all the competitors and that's basically how you "win". Also, players who are new to the simulation genre might find the first few hours tedious and the tutorial might be vague to some players.

COH2 is a bittersweet affair.
The base game and gameplay is excellent; it is an improved version of COH's wonderful squad based tactics and vehicle combat, but it's split up into as many parts as SEGA could get Relic to create. COH simply had 2 expansions, Opposing Fronts and Tales of Valor which your could have bought with the base game for $100 MSRP, at release.
COH2 has no less than 6, as well as dozens of DLC commanders and skins. The base game with minor expansions cost around $140, and the commanders would cost you nearly as much if you wanted them all. The skins I can forgive as they are cosmetic, but the commanders introduce new units and capabilities that ABSOLUTELY RUIN THE MULTIPLAYER.
Take the Soviet Industry Tactics commander for instance, that gives you the capability to slam out T-70s and T-34s out so quick, the enemy barely has time to deploy AT guns. Or the Elite Troops Doctrine, that allows you to pay for veterancy in troops, as well as a Tiger Ace. Do you want the have the ability to use this against your opponents? You've got to pay extra, of course!
This simply is unnacceptable, and I can't recommend anyone pay for such a shameful pay-2-win scheme.
Now, with my gripe out of the way;
COH2 has a great Soviet single player campaign, and the Ardennes Assault campaign is fun, although it has less personality being somewhat more freeform. I enjoyed all the missions from Case Blue, but haven't tried Victory at Stalingrad or Southern Fronts.
I really, really, really wish they'd had a German compaign like in COH's Opposing Fronts. It was a favorite of mine, as well as the British Campaign. The fact that COH2 doesn't have anything more than a Soviet Campaign and American campaign in the style of Warhammer DOW Black Crusade is dissapointing. The Brits, Ostheer and Oberkommado West are completely left behind.
As for the multiplayer, it's solid and fun. It allows for only 2 game modes, Victory Points and Annihilation, but games are typically fierce and fair. As long as you can ignore the unfair DLC commanders, you'll enjoy it.
Overall, COH2 is a great game, but flawed by SEGA, an evil DLC loving publisher. It makes me sad that Relic fell under their corrupting and vile influence, but at least their games are still mostly intact. Without the disgusting DLC commanders, I'd give the game a 8.5-9.0 out of 10. However, with the current dispicable DLC situation, it's only a 7.5. Still a recommended game, and one of the best of the modern RTS games, but dissapointing for afformentioned reasons.

An excellent tower defense/RPG.

Defender's Quest is a novel rpg take on the tower defense genre. That in and of itself would make an interesting game, but the designers saw fit to include an interesting story to explain away the game mechanics as part of the plot. While the central theme of plague and the risen dead is dark, the dialogue between characters is lighthearted and oftentimes funny. Such a combination of serious undertones and bright interplay amongst the characters helped me enjoy the game quite a bit.
Insofar as the actual mechanics are concerned, this is not a "maze building" tower defense game. The enemies will come in waves along pre-defined paths with limited placement for your defenders (the towers, essentially) available. Defenders can be upgraded by "boosting" them through five levels which unlocks any abilities they may have earned through levelling and a rudimentary talent system. Speaking of levelling, this is where the rpg mechanic comes into play; every level gained by a defender gives you talent points which you can use to tweak the character and gain new abilities. While the talent system is very basic, it does give you a feeling of satisfaction to distribute your points when a defender levels or you gain access to a new class.
While there are only six classes of defender to use in the game, the customization inherent in the rpg progression system means there is the possibility of some differentiation. Additional defenders can be recruited in towns across the game's story map, wherein the plot is advanced and new battlefields are opened up. In battle, these defenders are placed with the same resource you use for upgrading, but recruiting new defenders gets progressively expensive with the game's story mode currency (won through battle). That same currency is used for equipping your defenders with weapons and armor, so there is an opportunity cost. As additional currency can be won by going back and fighting harder versions of prior story mode battles at any time, you never truly feel strapped for cash.
As the game is 2d, the question isn't whether the graphics are advanced, but how good and cohesive they look. Cut scenes to advance the plot are drawn with a style which gels extremely well with the battle sprites and look pleasing to the eye. Opinions on art styles will vary, but the cleanliness and cohesiveness of the game's visuals can not be denied. There are no sloppy looking sprites in this game and your defender's colors can even be customized to a limited degree to further suit your tastes.
Unfortunately, while the animations of your defenders (and especially that of a certain antagonist at the very end of the game) are fluid and pleasing to watch, the animations of the monsters which you are tasked to kill are very basic and stilted. Still, most of the time said monsters are drowning in a sea of pleasing damage numbers as your defenders are chopping them to pieces, so perhaps some gamers will be able to overlook this as I did.
According to steam, I was able to extract 13 hours out of this game and there are still bonus challenges to complete and a new game plus mode to experiment with. Whether that is worth the price of admission is a decision that I encourage you to weigh carefully if you would normally pass up a game based on length: it is lovingly crafted and an enjoyable experience that I can recommend to any rpg fan, even those who aren't familliar with tower defense games.
The long and short of it: 8/10, buy it.

Tied in my mind with Defense Grid for best tower-defense game to date. Where Defense Grid's strength is the perfect distillation of the tower-defense formula, Defender's Quest remains toe-to-toe with it because of how it radically adapts the basic idea of tower-defense -- deploying stationary defenses along a path or series of paths -- to work with a highly original fantasy setting and a set of solid RPG-like mechanics. The presentation, while not sophisticated, is incredibly appealing, and the writing is nothing short of superb.  It's also endlessly replayable, and the New Game + mode actually gives you a reason to do so.
Highly recommended to everyone, tower-defense fans and non-fans alike.  As with Defense Grid, If you're a fan, you will like this; if you're not already, this stands a good chance of converting you, and if it doesn't, then you never have to wonder about another tower-defense game again, as you'll know it's just not your bag.

I don’t like real time strategy or tower defense games, you can’t out click a computer and they usually cheat.  So it’s seem odd that I would even buy this game, let alone log 196 hours (wait, how many? I’m not even done with the Play+.)  What made the game appeal to me was the RPG element.  I like RPGs, it’s reassuring to know you can grind and level up to make up for your lack of skill and intelligence.
The game offers 25 stages plus bonus levels that are all replayable (didn’t realize that’s not a real word) at not just different difficulties but also with a different mix of enemies.  There are only six characters (towers) but each has 10 or so skills which adds to the variety.  There are 19 enemies including repallets (figured that wasn’t a real word) and five bosses.
The best part is the characters.  The dialogue and interaction is engrossing often hilarious.  The replay mode unlocks Azra’s diary with extra (also hilarious) insight to her background and the other characters (SPOILER ALERT!! Slak knows how to read and write.)
In conclusion (that never gets old,) Defender’s Quest: title too long is a great mix of tower defense and RPG.  Most importantly, it’s fun.  If you had to pay all 15 bucks for this game, it’s worth it.  If it should happen to be on sale around Thanksgiving or Christmas (or whatever other holiday you celebrate on your fast track to hell) you’d be a fool not to buy it (unless you’ve got something better to do with 196 hours, like work.)

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is a flawed old PC gem and here's why:
The game features several different player character classes or clans as they are called in the game and picking any of these changes the way you play the game, some more than others of course but also changes how NPCs treat you. After beginning the game you're free to develop your character any way you please with some skills only choosable by some classes.
The graphics are dated sure, but back in the day they were fairly good and in my opinion they still hold up, however mods have been made to update the textures. The music is alright and does most of the areas justice, it has everything from rock in a seedy bar to more eery pieces as you explore possibly haunted houses. The voice acting is fantastic for it's time and it is still great and invokes everything from sexy to silly.
With great free roaming and plenty of side quests to entertain what could possibly be flawed? The gameplay, the gameplay has it's ups and downs. It's fun to create a character and watch them grow but the combat never really gets much farther than button mashing, especially if you make a melee character, some boss fights are almost impossible if you haven't leveled at least one ranged weapon and a lot of quests can be solved by simply killing somebody although to the games credit this will have consequences.
To sum up, Vampire: TM-B has fantastic atmosphere and a world that feels fun and alive. The gameplay does have its hick-ups but it is well worth the money, especially if you pick it up during a sale.

The Vanishing Of Ethan Carter is a newly released mystery themed first person narration developed by indie developer The Astronauts. Though this is the first release by the newly formed developer they are built up of very experienced developers and The Vanishing Of Ethan Carter certainly passes off that vibe. The game plays out with you, Paul Prospero, walking throughout the small village of Red Creek Valley. The core of the game consists of you going through the town solving each murder mystery that the town has to offer, which is quite a few for such a small place. Since the core of the game is it’s story, I’m going to write this review without going into details on the story, so rest assured this review will remain spoiler free.
So like I said the game plays out as a first person mystery solver. The game begins with the text “This game is a narrative experience that does not hold your hand” and that is about the most definitive statement I can say about this game. The game is totally open world and will not give you any guides or hints about where to go or what to do. This is nice in the sense that you are totally free to explore the world and solve mysteries as you stumble upon them. As you explore you’ll notice items that seem to be missing from scenes. As you explore the world you’ll often find the missing items scattered around so that you can investigate and pick up the items. When you finish putting a scene back together you are able to open a portal into another dimension to explore and discover the secrets of what happened in the world. Exploring the story was interesting and though it felt like a good bit of the story didn’t quite fit in at the time of discovery, after further exploring and really examining the environments the pieces all came together. The story is really the reason to play the game. Their really isn’t much action, and you will spend almost all of your time exploring, examining and then walking to your next location.
Luckily walking around the game world means you get to view more of the environments. The Vanishing Of Ethan Carter has possibly the best graphics I’ve ever seen in a video game. I mean the world is truly astonishing and is incredibly realistic. There were a number of times I actually had to stop playing, to admire the fact that what I was staring at was not a real life picture. And with the exception of one location, a mine, all were very unique yet realistic in their design. Not to say that the mine wasn’t well designed, but compared to the rest of the world the rocky maze like mine just seemed rather boring. The titles sound effects were not nearly as well done as the games graphics but quite honestly I found myself so indulged in the visuals of the game that I very rarely focused on the sound effects.
Finally the ending of the game is one that I really enjoyed. The ending doesn’t explicitly say what happens one way or another. This works especially well because The Vanishing Of Ethan Carter leaves the story open to certain speculations. The end is left for you to sit, think about the events of the game and determine how it ends. Additionally the amount of small details you’ve paid attention to can actually have great effects on how you interpret things which can ultimately lead to an alternate view on the ending than you would have had otherwise. Unfortunately The Vanishing Of Ethan Carter is very short at roughly four to five hours to complete and because of the way the story plays out replay value is limited.
8/10
PROS
• The best visuals seen in recent years
• Small details that can effect the way you see the ending
• Very well done open ended ending
CONS
• Story is only about 4-5 hours length
• The design of the mine level

The first thing you notice about this game is how outrageously pretty it is, especially for a game from a small independant developer based in Poland. It comes as two versions, an 'original' version which runs in Unreal Engine 3, and a 'Redux', which runs in UE4 and has various functional improvements, as well as graphical upgrades - although I couldn't spot them! I played the UE3 original version as I found it performed better on my machine.
The awe-inspiring visuals also help create the incredibly dramatic atmosphere which keeps this narrative based game gripping throughout its roughly 4-hour story. The developer states from the outset that this game does not "hold your hand", and they aren't kidding, there are no restrictions, no clues, just the player and the environment. The background music is suitable eerie, and the dialogue is well written in such a way that gets the story across clearly.
Speaking of the story, without giving too much away, this is one of those games with a moment of revelation, when a penny you didn't even realise was suspended, drops. Only one other game I can think of pulls off a plot twist quite as well as this, and that is the 'Would you kindly' revelation in the first Bioshock.
My only complaint about this game is that it did have a tendency to crash on certain scenes, but the developers are active on the Steam forums, along with what seems like an enthusiastic community willing to help out where they can.
Highly recommended if you want a short, very well produced thriller that will keep you thinking about it long after you finish it.

After 57 hours on this game, there are some points that I feel everyone should know going into it.
Company of Heroes 2 isn't a bad game. Not at all, in fact. The gameplay is a lot of fun, the core mechanics of the game prove to be challenging, intriguing, and very in depth. It is a fantastic representation of small scale battles set in World War 2, and the varieties of armoured vehicles and infantry will keep you interested. The Commander system is fun, as is the intel bulletin system. However, many of the commanders that prove to be the most interesting are all pay DLC, so that can be a deterent for many players. The cover system and squad systems, similar to Dawn of War 2 and the original Company of Heroes, have proven to be an enjoyable take on RTS games. The Campaign mode tells an interesting story, but if you, like myself, know anything about the Soviet Union's struggle against the Axis, you'll notice many irregularities, and indeed insulting if you are Russian, with the representation of the Red Army and the NKVD. Apparently, according to Relic, Soviets just LOVED firebombing their own men and villages!
However, the glaring problems with this game come into full view on multiplayer. The Allied and Axis teams simply aren't balanced. Wehrmacht and PARTICULARLY the Oberkommando factions are hands down better than the other teams; it seems that Relic thought the German warmachine was unstoppable in World War 2! Axis tanks, infantry, and support weapons are simply better than Allied counterparts; a Panzer IV can easily destroy T-34s, Oberkommando Infantry guns (small artillery pieces) perform 5x better than many other mortar pieces, unless you drop huge resources on heavier artillery guns to counter them. German infantry equipped with Panzershreks, when fielded enmasse, can shred through the opposition if they are supported correctly. Tigers, Panthers, and the larger Axis tanks, once they are on the battlefield, spell the end for the opponent easily.
The other problem I've ran into a lot during multiplayer games is the community itself; many of my fellow players are uncommunicative, unsupportive, and incredibly rude. Many times, if my side is struggling, my comrades will then berate me or whoever else is apparently not pulling their weight, making for an incredibly unenjoyable gaming atmosphere. No camraderie will be found here; if you enjoy sociable historical settings, I recommend something like Civilization or Total War, where most people enjoy playing with other history buffs. The 'competitive' nature of this game is a farce when its already so poorly balanced, and many players act like losing a casual match is an insult to them! To quote one player 'I'm not having fun, unless i'm winning'; expect this attitude every game.
So in all, I enjoy playing Company of Heroes 2. However, I do not enjoy playing it Multiplayer. I will continue to play missions and against AI opponents, but I doubt I'll be spending much more time online with other players. If you want an enjoyable World War 2 RTS, I'd recommend you check out the Blitzkrieg series. If you REALLY want to play with other people, well, good luck, and god speed.

Buy This:
If you love tower defense
If you love 8 bit era RPGs
If you enjoy a humorous adventure starring a bunch of misfit heroes.
Defender's Quest is another tower defense game with a few twists that put it above the curve. For starters, rather than building soulless towers that you have zero attachment to, you employ RPG style characters to defend your "Librarian." These characters can be named, stylized (to a slight degree with color options) and then leveled the more they're used. They each even have a system of perks that can be unlocked through the course of the campaign. You can employ as many as you can find the dosh for, but each requires "mana" to be deployed in battle. This is a finite pool that is replenished by killing baddies. The maximum mana you can have increases as your librarian levels as well, so in essence it is a clever way of keeping the player from throwing 70 towers up at the start of a new mission and steam rolling.
The game also has a pretty humorous story line, and memorable main characters. There's unique items you can unlock for your favorite minions, and even a brutally hard Game+ mode if you desire even more once you finish the campaign. With such a low price point, this is a must have for people who like old school RPGs, tower defense style games or both.

I know most people will just thumb down this review without even reading it because its just one of those games where its the socially acceptable thing to love it unconditionally.. But i know a great game when i see one and this is not one of them. It is not a bad game by any regards, but it is certainly not the cult classic all the reviewers had made it seem.
Its very cartoonish and arcadey and a majority of the game is spent going from A to B in mini city-like towns doing mundane quests for random NPC's with tons of loading screens inbetween. I would say 90% of the game is running back and fourth between loading screens and 10% is actual combat.
The combat consists of an awkward free mouse aiming spam-clicking action onto your enemy as fast as you possibly can. Every time you hit an enemy you either knock them down or send them flying in an overly-dramatic sideways barrel-roll through the air.. It is laughable to say the least. And you will notice right away that there is no depth to the combat mechanics at all. The block is way too slow and unresponsive to be deemed worthy of any use in combat. It is also impossible to do any sort of stratgy like circle around your enemy to get behind them because they always face you no matter how fast you try and run around them..And there is no way to prepare for an enemy attack because it  occurs instantly and the game shows no animation to let you know the enemy is lifting up his arms to attack. It just happens instantly when you get near the enemy.  Not to mention the silly damage numbers that float above their head with each strike. It's is just a very hard game to reccomend to anyone over the age of 12 as it is extremely cartoonish and bubbly.
Quests..some very long, very carried out, and not very specific in what you have to do. Many times you are forced to look up a walkthrough online just to figure out where to go. Each quest requires a lot of backtracking (check your email, go back to your haven and check your mailbox, go back and talk to so and so again) Not to mention that these extremely long quests only result in a mere 1-3 exp reward which is very frustrating considering you need at least 8 exp points to unlock anything worthwhile.. The only leveling up that seems to make any difference is lockpicking and hacking because strength, melee, and brawl seem to change very little in terms of the physical damage i do to my enemies.
And the gun combat.. The gun combat takes the trophy for the worst gun combat i have ever seen in my 15 years of gaming. The first time i used my revolver i walked up behind an enemy, aimed it at the back of his head at close range, and when i fired i saw huge yellow letters that said "10" listing the damage amount that my shot did.. The enemy than said "Ouch" and turned around and started punching me, i than shot 5 more times and each shot showed huge yellow damage numbers. I than had to ditch the gun and just kill him with my fists. It is just so arcadey and childish. Not to mention ammo is extremely scarce.
For a vampire game you would think it would be raw, mature and gritty, not bubbly and cartoonish.

Hi there! My name is Claire, I am 26 years old and from Denmark. I have over 20 years of gaming experience. I do all achievements for the game before I review it. So my review truly reflects a 100% completion of the game.
Eventhough my reviews are quite long and extensive, I try my very best to keep them as spoiler free as possible.
Remember to take everything I say with a grain of salt, as it is just my subjective opinion. Hope you enjoy! :3
Metro 2033 Redux falls into the genre we know as a modern First-Person-Shooter. You play through a linear world where you interact and experience whatever the game sets out to show you. There is very little exploration and alternative paths to take. Thus it is more akin to games such as Call of Duty, rather than oldschool FPS' such as Doom or Duke Nukem.
The lack of player exploration allows the game developers to create some truly awe-shocking and atmospheric moments, both through it's gameplay but also its story. This is in my opinion Metros strongest quality, and will be further expanded on in the Story section.
It is clear that Metro 2033 Redux wants the player to truly feel immersed in the gameworld. This is very evident if you look at how the game handles its game mechanics.
When you enter the post-apocalyptic Moscow you have to wear your gasmask because the air is toxic. You, as the player, have to manually put your gas mask on. You also have to monitor your gas mask filter on your watch. Once your filter is running low, you have to equip a new one, or you will simply die.
The same goes with your flashlight. You want your flashlight turned on almost all of the time because the game is very dark, especially in the deep abandoned places of the Metro. However your flashlight has to be charged by the player manually, by taking out a DIY charger and pumping a new charge into the flashlight.
There are many instances of this mechanic in Metro 2033 Redux, and I thoroughly enjoyed it a lot. It not only makes you much more engaged in the gameplay, but it also adds a clever level of fear as your flashlight potentially runs out of power while being chased by monsters.
Throughout your time in the Metro you will encounter a variety of weapons to play with. All of the weapons feel distinct from one another, with the exception of a few of the assault rifles which in my opinion didn't have much of a different feel to them. You are able to customize your weapons with different scopes and handles etc. I feel that this was not expanded on well enough. There simply was not enough upgrades for it to feel very meaningful.
Metro 2033 Redux has a TON of stealth sections. Atleast if you play them "the way it's intended" because you are able to run and gun your way through all stealth sections of the game. The AI in Metro 2033 Redux is probably the worst AI I have seen in many years. You are able to literally walk right past NPC's that seem to be looking directly at you. Yet on the other hand if you end up getting spotted by just one person, the whole area suddenly knows where you are and will hunt you down until you either die or kill everyone in the area.
I wanted to stealth my way through the game, so when I got spotted I had to restart to the last checkpoint as there was no way for me to reset my "stealth". This felt gimmicky and is not the way you want your stealth gameplay to work.
It took me 9 hours to complete the game on Survival mode, and only 7 hours on Spartan mode. I would recommend Survival mode.
You play as Artyom, a young man from one of the Northern Metro stations. Your station has been under attack by the mysterious "Dark Ones" for a while, and your station needs help. You set out on your way to the capital of the Metro called Polis to help your station. On your long road through the Metros web of stations you will encounter many different people and maybe more disturbingly... Many different monsters.
I don't want to spoil anymore than that, as the story is truly one of the selling points of Metro 2033 Redux. The whole game is  built up around a best-selling novel called Metro 2033 by Dmitry Glukhovsky.
While the game is very linear it makes sure to give you a lot of dialogue that helps you understand the world you're in. I feel like they could've easily elaborated on the story a lot more. Although there is an expansion called Metro Last Light which I haven't played, which supposedly expands on the whole Metro universe.
While the game is a few years old now, it still has absolutely jaw-dropping graphics. The polygon-counts may not be the highest we have ever seen in a game, but Metro 2033 Redux has something most games desperately wants. It has soul in its graphical fidelity. By that I mean the metro stations looks run down. The people in the metros look ragged and dirty. The weapons look home-made, which most of them are. The disfigured faces and dismembered bodies of the people who died on the surface frightens the player of what to come.
I always felt that no matter where I looked in Metro 2033 Redux I would be looking at a convincing piece of a post-apolyptic world. I never lost my sense of immersion, because everything seemed just right for the world I had been placed in.
The lighting effects in Metro 2033 Redux is some of the best lighting effects I have ever seen. A lot of care and detail went into the lighting effects and it is a clever decision, because you spend most of the game in very dark areas where you can really show off some amazing lighting effects. The game even goes so far as to use this lighting mechanic when you fight some of the monsters in the Metro.
With that being said the facial animations of some, if not most of the humans in the game are not very good. They don't look very convincing in my opinion, but I think it boils down to the game being a few years old. I actually found some of the human faces much more scary than the monsters. :P
The background music of Metro 2033 Redux is okay. I didn't feel like it was anything special, and I didn't stop and listen at any point in time. I think this was intentional by the game developers. They didn't want big musical scores booming in the background. They wanted their music to compliment their two strongest factors of the game. The story telling and the atmospheric immersion. If this was their intention, I think they hit it spot on.
The game uses sound to communicate to the player if they are about to be spotted during stealth sections. This is nothing new, but it works quite well in Metro 2033.
The gun sounds are okay without being anything special.
The sounds of the monsters range from okay to very good. The very good sounds from the monsters were the skittering of spiders crawling into holes behind you, or the distant howl of a Nosalis (A big mutant creature). These sounds were very useful to the game, as they helped to create tension and immersion.
I played the game with the english voices, and the voice-acting in Metro 2033 Redux is not that great. It is acceptable without being good. It is not bad enough to be a problem though, with the exception of the kids voice acting, which is just downright strange in my opinion.
You can buy Metro 2033 for 19.99€ or your regional equivalent. You can buy it as a bundle with Metro Last Light.
It frequently goes on sale on Steam, and I would recommend you to wait for a steam discount before purchasing.
Metro 2033 Redux is a very atmospheric and immersive FPS game set in a post-apocalyptic world. It has average gunplay with some clever added mechanics through the management of gas masks, filters and your flashlight.
It has a great story with two different endings.
If you even remotely enjoy linear and story driven FPS games you should give Metro 2033 Redux a chance.
I give Metro 2033 Redux 8 out of 10.

What more can be said of a series that has produced sleeper after sleeper of a turn based genre that it practically invented? Sid Meier’s Civilization 5 seeks to answer that question. This time around, there are some simplifications in some systems and increased complexities in others and with the Brave New World DLC, new systems of victory, technology, and trade have been introduced.
Overall this game plays very much like any other game in the Civ series. You settle a city, explore and find your neighbors, vanquish barbarians, research technologies, decide on cultural policies, religious platforms, and eventually pursue a victory condition. Victory conditions range from killing everyone else, a.k.a. domination, to more peaceful pursuits such as science, cultural, or diplomatic. Other civs in the game will be pursuing these goals too of course, so it’s up to you to sabotage their efforts any way you can.
Most of the challenge in Civ 5 comes from the early to mid game where most civs will get knocked out by military action, backstabbing, and clever political maneuvering. After that, it’s more of a micro-management sim where you spend most of your time hitting “next turn” until whatever research, wonder, or weapon finishes. Basically, once you start to pull ahead of the other civs, the rest of the game becomes a bit of a cakewalk and I wish there was some sort of system in place to detect this and expedite a victory condition instead of dragging it out unnecessarily.
Regardless, Civ 5 can be quite the time sink (in a good way) and you should expect to spend a few weeknights just to finish one regular sized game. The added DLC plus the variety in civs gives you plenty of replayability, and if you happen to have a very patient friend, there’s even multiplayer to consider.

This game has given me 3 years of joy, even with its flaws. I just cant seem to put it away in favor of other games.
It has been my game of choice since the night of release in june 2013, and I dont see that changing anyitme soon.
To address common issues:
The balance can be bad, but only at the highest levels. Before that point, its a matter of learning how to play.
The bugs can be NotLikeThis FeelsBadMan too, but for the most part relic is currently actively working on or has fixed alot of them, there are no game breaking bugs at the moment.
The game is still regularly patched, so if there are issues they are usually fixed.
The optimization, well dont play on a potato and you should be fine. I never had an issue with optimization. During my first year and a half of play, I played on a ♥♥♥♥in' potato laptop and I had to run the game on minimum. This is a super addictive tower defense game.  Take on the role of a Librarian who is thought to contract the plague and tossed into "the pit" a canyon seperated from the rest of civilization where plague victims spend the rest of their days. Like other tower defense games you need to protect the goal from hordes of invading enemies with units or towers that you place along the pathways to destroy the enemies.  However, unlike other games, this one has a story, and your characters stay with you, level up and grow along side your main unit. I possess this game for a little more than half a year now and played it to level 50 with 2-3 achievments left to be unlocked. My steam friendlist exploded of helldivers players.
In my oppinion helldivers is a perfect game, but perfection also implies limitedness.
After you played the 3 bosses, retaliation missions (really small maps where you have to hold out wave after wave) and normal missions on helldivers level you will have seen all there is in this game. Still i found much fun after weeks comming back again more than once. So i consider the replay value very high, the game is casual and its very easy to dive back in again.
There is some humor in that game, which is very alike to the humor and setting in the movie starship troopers. The soundtrack fits perfectly and very often one will find himeself immersed into movielike situations, jumping into the escape shuttle in the last second surrounded by bugs biting into your behind.
Gameplay:
You play allone or in a team of max four ppl. The view of the map is shared and no one can run allone out of the screen. If you run to the right edge, your teammate will have no distance on the left to view whats comming. Its a teamgame with friendly fire, which can lead to hilariously insane action. Teammates firing can kill you, resupply send from spaceship can slay you and the escape shuttle can squish you.
You can play allone though (then you'll have 3 lives which increase after every successfull missiongoal), which is good too, because it can leave room to a more methological approach, where a team sometimes dramatically increases the chaosfactor. If you play allone, other players will eventually join unless you set the game to private.
There are 3 factions in the game. Bugs, Cyborgs (a kommunistlike society) and Illuminati (squidlike entities based on esoteric tech). Players collect factionpoints, each time a team succesfully wins a map. With 50 points, a boss can be challenged. If the boss is killed often enough by all players worldwide, the faction is permanently defeated, untill the other factions are defeated too. After the whole war is won by all players, superearth government states for example that bugs produce oil and leading moral experts conclude, that it would'nt be right to kill them. Then the factions turn again gainst superearth and the cycle restarts.
One advice:
Buy the version which includes all DLCs. Do not save 10€, because you will really regret it very very soon. I cannot say this explicitly enough.
The first time, that you are playing on a wintermap (which is quite common) and don't have all-terrain-boots from the Terrain Specialist Pack, you will curse, that you're always last in the team or can't run away from the enemies fast enough. I saw once a player without DLCs complaining in a game, that this is pay-to-win. Bulls.hit! The community of players have asked the developers over time to add content like vehicles, mechs, weapponry to the game and they did. That additional work has to be repaid and the price cannot be fixed forever to that of the primary game without the extra effort. Enough said.
Conclusion:
This game was my best buy of 2015 gameswise and even when i play less im still grateful for the good time i had with it. This is a game i would even buy as a present.

*Warning, you will need to follow a good set of bug-fixing texture packs in order for this game to even be considered functional. Word of warning, this review is based on after all the necessary patches are in place.*
Despite my warning above, Vampire: The Masquerade-Bloodlines is a FPS/RPG hybrid unlike anything I have seen in most games. The game shockingly has a lot of  replayability in terms of sure story and content. First off, this game manages to bring alot of the V:TM mythos into the story and it manages to have alot of interesting ideas and story-branching that it can get you to replay the game with a different clan just to see the difference. There is alot in V:TM Bloodlines that is worth playing, but that is only if you are truly willing to get the patches necessary to play it. I for one, am glad that I bought this since the game has alot of great characters, story, world-building and more. The only cons I have are the clunky combat system and stealth as it is clearly broken on several levels. Despite this gripe, I would highly recommend this game to any RPG or Vampire fan for the effort that was sadly rushed by Acitivison, as the game's poor sales resulted in the the closing of Tokia Games Studios in 2005. (R.I.P)

A beautiful, story-based game with a perfect soundtrack.  You can tell it's doing a lot of things right by the sheer tenacity of the trolls in the community hub.
Given the passion of the trolls, you can correctly infer that the game is about in-depth exploration, not fighting.  If that sounds appealing, you'll likely love this game.  However, it should be noted that the game DOES have exactly one area with a real, traditional, troll-approved monster roaming around.  It's an unpleasant desgin choice, given how well the rest of the game is tailored to the exact sort of player who would hate that.  On the other hand, if this is a concern of yours, please note that you can easily look up the details of this in advance.  (Not immediately.  The game itself will quite directly warn you when it's time to do so.  Spoilers can be kept to an absolute minimum.)  If you do research the area before heading in, the challenge of avoiding the monster is fairly minimal.  I did exactly that and never "died."  Also, note that the penalty for this "death" is minimal.
Aside from that, this game was amazing.   Go for it.

If you like DDR-esque games this could be a good choice for you.  It has good writing and passable voice acting to go alongside it.  The gameplay is novel and has some tactical depth to it as well.
It is however a very obvious straight console port.  Without an analog stick you cannot preview spells before casting them, making it difficult to tell when you have enough mana without simply memorizing the mana costs.
Another negative is the fact that it has no volume controls in the game at all, and the sound effects are kindof terrible.  The music seemed okay I guess.
This is an awesome rhythm action/rpg hybrid.  Totally worth $5, or you can wait for it to go on sale.

Metro is a great game series, and it really shines on this next gen hardware. The story of the Metro and Artyom is an exciting thriller, and if you have not played it, now is the time. The story engulfs you, but not with huge explosions and jaw dropping action. However, it is the atmosphere of this universe. The characters, the feeling of sneaking past mutants, not knowing whats around the next corner, and the visuals (especially on next gen). The first time you exit from the darkness of the Metro into the nuclear wasteland of Moscow the feeling is incredible. The outside is not any safer though as the wasteland is covered with mutants, and you survive by gas mask to keep safe from the toxic air. Metro has a very special feel to its game play as well. The series does an exquisite job of balancing the survival aspect without making you beg for ammo after every encounter. Redux also gives you the option to play the game like a more fast paced FPS like Call of Duty by choosing the games "Spartan Mode" which is good if you do not prefer the survival aspect of the series. Weapon upgrades like adding night vision scopes or making your double barrel shogun a quad barrel also play a big part to the game play. While not unique the upgrades do feel like a nice addition to some already pretty solid gun play. The different enemies and situations Redux throws at you will also allow to take full force of your weapon arsenal, whether its a silenced pistol, an LMG, or flamethrower. Even though Redux brings a lot to offer the Metro can be repetitive sometimes. The game also broke at certain points while playing as I could not advance because of game script not working or invisible walls but these problems are nothing that can't be fixed with a patch. Metro Redux is almost a perfect game, and right now one of the best games to play on next gen.

If you are not musically challenged, you should play Sequence, it's currently the best (and only) Rhythm RPG out there.
It plays like any DDR-like game, where arrows fall down the screen and you have to clear them on the beat of the music. But instead of one stream of arrows, there are three: the HP stream, where every missed arrow causes you to take damage; the MP stream, where every hit note regenerates some MP; and the Spell stream, where you have to hit every note to execute a spell successfully.
The dialogue is clever, the art is gorgeous (although it uses sprites), and the item descriptions are hilarious (example: Broken Pencil [Utterly Pointless]). Best of all: it's only €3,99, and even as low as €0,99 during sales. Buy one ice-cream less this year and get Sequence.

Defender's Quest is a simple turn based tower defense game.  Defenders are set up on a grid, and enemy units follow a path to the goal.  The units are well balanced and versatile, and the enemies return the favor.  You can set the pace of the battles at anytime, from a complete pause, to 4x "get this over with" speed.  You also have the option to control the difficulty to be as easy or as hard as you prefer.  Harder the challenge, the bigger the payoff.  Real strategy players are going to find the regular game a little too easy, but the game does offer unique challenges for the elite.  Gamers new to strategy games will find it very welcoming.  It is a game for every level of gamer, from casual beginner, to advanced tactician.

The game is an old-school four colour CGA graphics platformer. It is also rendered in such a way that it simulates playing on an old CRT monitor. And then there is the crazy futuristic option of playing in the sixteen colour CGA mode!! Whaat?
Sorry, I'm overly excited because this game is epic! I mean, when I dowloaded it, I thought... I can't expect much from a free game, can I?
Boy... I didn't even realize how much I missed these old-school platformers with their monotone computer sounds, and their evil, unforgiving mechanics.
Basically you traverse numerous rooms, all connected, named differently, sometimes with a hint of what you should/shouldn't do, or a bit of sarcasm. You collect power-ups that in time will allow you to go further, higher, or deeper. You keep moving back and forth, through the same rooms, to check how your new found power-ups will help you to move forward.
Which is actually pretty horrible for me, since I have no sence of direction and spacial orientation. I keep getting lost, and forgetting where I'm supposed to go. And believe me. This game is difficult enough without a problem like that.
It is very challenging, you will get lost, you will die continuously (just because sometimes, you have to die to figure out what you should do), and sometimes you will scream out of frustration. There are areas where I died about 50 times before I could move a step forward... and then I would die anyway.
If you are curious what could kill you, there's spikes, and flames, and crabs, and jellyfish, and water, and loads more. Generally, most of the game can kill you, and will kill you at one point or another.
If you miss your old-school 8 bit platformers, with their old-school merciless nature, you should give "You have to win the game" a shot. Especially since it's free to play.
Also there's a cat mode.
And YOLO mode, that's also there.
Basically... you have to win the game. Well crafted, addicting, old school sidescrolling platformer. Nothing I have found to dislike this far!

While it requires a fair amount of modification to be playable on a modern PC in 1920x1080 resolution, the game itself is quite fun.  From a technical standpoint, it still feels like a (really good) Quake total conversion, but given its release date that can't be helped.  It does a decent job of using the Storyteller system (you have a character sheet similar to tabletop Vampire: The Masquerade and assign dots to attributes and abilities in similar fashion), though like any video game it isn't nearly as brutal as its tabletop counterpart.
More than anything else, it makes me wish that someone, perhaps Rockstar, would make an open-world World of Darkness game.  Regardless, it's easily worth $5 as long as you're comfortable locating and applying patches.

This is not Twilight. This is not Dracula. This is not Anne Rice. This is not Buffy. This is World of Darkness... and a masterpiece.
Vampire: TMB's world is mysterious and complex, rich with lore from White Wolf Publishing's WoD tabletop games. The quests are memorable, characters desperate, locations varied, and character customization extensive. It is easily one of the best written RPGs ever published, right up there with the Fallout series.
I would blindly recommend this to anyone remotely into verbose games. NPCs have very unique insights into the world they live in, and constantly share their philosophies with the player (the voice acting is excellent). Naturally, anyone who finds themselves bored after a few paragraphs of hearing NPCs talk should skip this game.
Edit:
I should have probably also mentioned that although VTMB's writing is stellar, there is also quite a bit of combat. The game strikes a nice balance between letting you feel like a ridiculously overpowered rampaging creature of the night, and a mere shadow of other, elder vampires: some fights will be hilariously easy (especially against human foes), others will be tremendously difficult (high-level supernatural enemies, yikes!). Character creation and levelling up is very comprehensive, and should be a joy for anyone who likes putting thought into how they will play the game.
Please note that the game was extremely buggy when released, and is moderately difficult to run on modern PCs. See here for post-installation instructions:
Shoutout to modder Wesp5 for keeping this game playable even 10 years after its original release!
