HALF-LIFE 2: EPISODE 1<
The sequal to half-life 2 came into the scene in 2006. Episode 1, formerly known as Half-life: Aftermath, was the beginning of the new episodic style valve was realeasing new installments. This would give fans what they wanted without having them wait years and years for another game but with some understandable sacrifices. The game was a hit for fans of the previous installments and brought some new tech advancements into the game such as better lighting. The plot takes place right after the end of Half-life 2 and doesn't waste any time getting back into the meat of it.
PROS:
-The story is very well paced and put together very nicely as all the others. You play as Gordon Freeman again during the aftermath of the citadels destruction. Not spoiling the rest in case you haven't picked up a copy in the many years its existed.
-The environment is very immersive as it is a long seamless road to the end of the game with, as the definition of seamless implies, zero cutscenes or immersion breaking interruptions.
-The gunplay involves the same chaotic weapons from half-life 2. The arsenal available is pleasently loud, very powerful feeling, and quite fun to use when eliminating the enemy as per tradition.
-Dialogue breaks are few, far between, and about a minute each if you even count them as such.
-Same engine as hal-life 2 to no surprise but with very few legitimate puzzles to get your thinker going.
-As with half-life 2, the ending is satasfying and closes things out with a nice bow ribbon.
CONS: (Not even half-life is safe from sin, sorry) Please note that i am extremely aware that this game is sorta old.
-Controls feel less floaty than half-life 1 but there's still some slip n sliding.
-The combine is a painfully easy enemy throughout the entire game and even when their ranks change.
-Various visual bugs and other graphical anomalies give the game a kind of rushed feeling.
-The games puzzles and other logic based conundrums are bonehead easy and will just seem like annoyances on successive playthroughs.
-Not much of a con but i found it quite odd that gordon gets his crowbar more towards the end dispite being his iconic weapon of choice.
This game is about as much of a must have as half-life 2. I picked the entire series up in a frantic buy in a summer sale and it was worth it. To me the episodes wern't very replayable, they arn't very exciting to play again and not very memorable. The games main critisim is it's length which is somthing that i fully agree with. I wasn't aware of half-life 2 at the time so i wasn't one of the masses waiting anxiously for this to drop but i think the length was perfect. I feel as if it went any longer it would have outstayed its welcome and become a bore. I certainly would'nt skip the game for fans just coming in but if anything it's textures for gmod if you don't have much interest in it.

It has very decent modelling tools, and, considering only convenience of modelling process, I would recommend it over most of the other 3d software (and definetely over Blender).
But! Even most common commands like extrude and edge extend can act really buggy. Everything CAN go the right way, but pretty often I got some weird unwanted geometry like doubled verticies and faces, cuts, and sometimes extrude just splits geometry in two parts. And that's really a pain. I've tried reinstalls, nothing helped. That's the biggest issue.
Second is polycount limit for the export. If you don't have modern PC and you've applied freese tessellation and got more than 100k polys on one model - you're screwed, cause retopology process in Modo consumes a lot of resorces. Also you won't want to store levels in Modo Indie, because when it gets more than 100k polys you'll have to export it in parts. And if, for example, you need the level in Zbrush, it'll take you 5-10 minutes to import a part, save it as ZTool, import next one etc. and then mush them all together.
And you really want to export thing out because of the third issue - pretty slow and really unintuitive render system. Even though it support substance files, it's shader tree with the texture order is a real mess.
I haven't tried rigging and animating in Modo Indie, but I have heard negative opinions about it, and I myself have a bad feeling about it.
So it's a one big advantage and several big disadvantages. I think Modo Indie still could be useful, but I would recommend   renting it for a couple of months to find out if it works for you, not buying.

This is a really good software package, and a great price. It's worth learning, but there is a learning curve from other softwares. This is like a mix of Blender, maya, and mesh lab. If your familiar with Maya you can set your viewport navigation to it so you won't lose a lot of productivity in adjustment process. You should have an excellent gpu I'm using gtx1070 8gb, and 16gb ram.. One problem I've come across is the FBX format. Modo can't import FBX from maya. It's using an older version? It kind of tangles up some workflow. I need to send maya to ue4, and export from ue4 then import to Modo. Basically have to do this with Blender also. Pivot tool is excellent, and sculpt tool is excellent. I would definitely purchase the perpetual bundle license if it were not going to be a forced steam client package. I would love to see a standalone flatpak bundle for Linux available for purchase.

I got this game entirely by sell trading cards, and for $1 it is worth it. There is a campaign that took me about and hour, and the standard skirmish vs ai. The campaign is more of an extended tutorial, with some skirmishes to test out the stuff you learn.
The design of the game is really simple, but the game is incredibly deep. You have access to 4 types of units that have distinct roles and I found it necessary to make all of them in every game. It's not the lazy kind of RTS where every unit does the same thing just with more health and/or damage.
The gameplay is really well thought out and balanced. The goal of the game is to capture 75 percent of the territory on the map, which you do by using your Sentinal unit. The sentinal can capture territory and structures by moving over it, but it cannot attack or move through enemy units (or be killed). This means you have to use other units to attack enemy units and clear pathways, as well as block the enemy sentinal from moving through territory, at least until they send units to attack yours.
There is also online multiplayer, which unfortunately no one is playing anymore, but what can you expect from a pretty much unknown indie game that's 2 years old. If anyone wants to play the multiplayer let me know, I really want to try it.
Fun cheap and has a lot of depth to it.

After watching the trailer, I immediately realized that this is a very interesting and concrete project. Without thinking twice, I bought and rejoiced, because it weighs only 300 mb.
I downloaded, I was happy again, I began to receive training. But later, realizing that this is the whole beauty of the game, I was stuck and continued to master the complex management (well, that there are hotkeys). The first thing I would like to say is that this is a very long and detailed training in many stages and battles with the computer. Each explanation is accompanied by a mini-game where you dictate to study new techniques and new "objects", which in the future you will fight. These "objects" you have to create with the help of the barracks, which, in turn, feed on special sources of energy. There are several types of "items": some - ordinary pawns, other guards, third strong fighters, and the rest - excellent snipers. Even in the game there is an object that allows heroes only in one direction, which makes the battle even worse.
After several such explanations, you get into the game using a computer, where you need, with the help of the aforementioned "assistants", to grab the necessary number of fields. Over time, things get complicated. Of course, you can follow exactly the same way as your opponent, but that will not be enough to win. You will need to create a brain opening tactic (or simply) with which you will win.
Plus enough in this game. The first plus is the idea itself, the second is unconditionally graphic, because it relaxes, and the third plus is the soundtrack, the fourth and fifth are gameplay and entertainment with friends, because the battles in this game, especially with a friend, are quite spectacular.
But in this game there are minuses. For an inexperienced player, there are "protracted" situations when playing with bots. That is, the effect of the slogan "our rounds lasts no more than 5 minutes" in such situations collapses due to the fact that you can get into a tactical or strategic stupor. The game is very well balanced, you can not crush the enemy by the farm, you will be saved only by competent tactics, which at some moments can reduce the dynamics, causing the player to "slow down" the action and think about the next move in the game, and thus the round can drag on 10-15 minutes. It all depends on the ingenuity of the player. But experience in the game as a result can deny this flaw.
Some of them may call the controversial setting of the game - a kind of fantastic "underwater" or "bioworld" is at first a little scary, as long as the player gets used to the mechanics of the game.
Interloper - a good network puzzle with unusual gameplay, suitable for the break.
With all this, the game dragged me over 51 hours. But for those who just want to spend time pleasantly, I advise you to immediately copy several packages to yourself and friends. Due to the fact that I can not immediately find a network fight 9.5/10.

It plays like any DDR-like game, where arrows fall down the screen and you have to clear them on the beat of the music. But instead of one stream of arrows, there are three: the HP stream, where every missed arrow causes you to take damage; the MP stream, where every hit note regenerates some MP; and the Spell stream, where you have to hit every note to execute a spell successfully.
The dialogue is clever, the art is gorgeous (although it uses sprites), and the item descriptions are hilarious (example: Broken Pencil [Utterly Pointless]). Best of all: it's only €3,99, and even as low as €0,99 during sales. Buy one ice-cream less this year and get Sequence.

Sequence is a fun but simple DDR-style rhythm game with just enough uniqueness to keep the 10 hours it takes to reach 100% completion interesting. Its voice acted narrative, level-up system, and loot and inventory elements help it rise above its fundamentally repetitive nature. Several NPCs have some really great dialogue, which kept me eager to push through to the next story scene.
It would have been nice to have a lot more variety in the music, but thankfully the handful of tracks, especially Ronald Jankee’s work, are all great. Considering only two people made the game (and it only cost me $1.25), Sequence was and is a memorable experience worth playing.

The combat system is just amazing. It adds purpose and depth to the already tried and true DDR formula. Unfortunately this game suffers from what I call Indie syndrome. Iridium simply could not afford the polish needed to fully realize Sequence's potential. The RPG elements could have been more robust and it would have been nice to have a larger catalog than just one artist. However these shortcomings do not take away from the experience, making this a must buy.

I must say, I am a fan of RTS games and this has to be one of my favorites! The game itself is odd in the playstyles that you have to use to win/loose, but overall its fun- especially with friends. I'll quickly list the Pro's and the Con's and move on with life.
Now starting out with the game itself the Singleplayer is something you want to stay away from, since it's disgustingly inaccurate in a sense of historical terms and how the Soviet troops were treated, essentially it's a pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥ ON THE OTHER HAND the multiplayer is pretty nice with the maps and gameplay styles that you'll have to use depending which side and country you are on. The maps are consistantly different which is good in a successful RTS game.
Now back to the gameplay styles and statistics as I stated before its all up to who you are, Axis or Allies. Depending who you are you'll have to take many things into context including the map, which commander you've chosen and who are you allies (If not playing 1v1). Continuing with that communicating is a major thing since if you are trying to do a spear push to middle point and your the only one doing it, that's pretty bad teamwork. Along with saying that the Allies are VERY WEAK if you are in a 2v2 or above match and you do not work together, since if you think about it The Big Three (US, UK, Russia) worked together to push the Germans back and end the war? Well it works the same in here, if you have a US and Soviets and they try to independently take points it can work, but without helping each other in the late game they will truly and utterly get massacred and loose.
Now the technical things, the AI can sometimes be stupid, but it works and isn't as bad compared to many other RTS titles out there. The DLC is really nice and pretty good, but the prices I think are way to high- get them when they are on sale instead of full price. Then within the game are the micro-transaction ♥♥♥♥♥ which but don't leave out, skins, commanders, faceplates, and bundles! Which are all over $5.99 and $5.99 is the cheapest the 'bundles' come in. Also majority of the time within the game it is Axis sided if you don't know what your doing- as in if you make one fatal mistake there goes the game. It's weird.
In total however the game is truly worth the buy, especially if it's on sale! The game is full hours of fun with or without your friend playing in a PVP manner. The DLC's are also worth it if you get tired of playing only Soviets and Wermacht, but the drops you can get after playing a game can spice things up with the abilities that they have to offer. So yes I rate this positive since it is truly a fun WWII RTS Game.
Have fun, and happy hunting!

The game has pros and cons; it just depends on what you like.
Pros:
Easy, amusing story; easy to pursue love interests; replays take minimum amount of time; lots of replay value.
Cons:
Cliches abound; Art is mediocre in "cutscenes" and sometimes downright disproportionate; some of the story branches literally do nothing for the overall story, introducing new characters for no reason other than to have them disappear; some story choices don't make logical sense, considering the type of character we start with.
Game takes place over 48 to 72 hours (storytime) and then has a flash to the "distant" (three months later usually) future. All but the heroine's singular stories are very easy to follow through fairly obvious options and after the first couple of playthroughs you can get through a story in thirty minutes or less if you would like, making it a fairly easy play. There are a few timed questions but they pose no real challenge, even if you fail them you can rewind the story to a certain point. (I have done this at a point where the heroine was being attacked and manage to dodge after I'd already failed the attack before. Might have been a glitch, but it happened.)
Overall, it's very difficult to immerse yourself into this story because the timing is weird... you know someone for two days and suddenly you're so in love you'd die for them? But it's interesting and as a story enthusiast, it's fun to examine every facet of the story.
Be warned, there are a lot of visuals that are cringe worthy and I don't mean gorey or offensive. Some of the art is not very proportionate or even in following with a character's appearance. A lot of the "nudity" is very tasteful and there are ways to the "good ending" without the nudey scenes but just the same, I'm looking at my completion gallery and each boy has just as many akwardly drawn scenes as he does appealing.
Strangely, the girls are drawn fairly well, save one very strange anatomy shot from underneath where you're supposed to be looking at a buxom woman from a laying down position and she's standing over you... but her body and face are drawn so weirdly that it's jarring, but there is no LGBT nudity or any such thing, despite that one of your love interests is a succubus. Take from that what you will.
POSSIBLE SPOILER!
Considering we start with a character who is chastised, molded and beat down (literally) by her family, I find many of the choices she makes two days after moving out of her house to be forced (if you want the best ending anyway). Upon knowing what it is she's dealing with, our herione must at least twice in any given storyline aggressively confront two people she knows can and will kill her with a flick of their wrist. Martial arts be damned; her personality is not a "fiery" one, or totally stupid and beligerant, no matter what you choose in previous segments, so why force these "options" on the player? A lot of people call Episode One the weakest Half-Life game there is. There are better, sure. However, that way of putting things makes it sounds like HL2: Episode One is God damn worthless and you should skip it. As I usually do on my reviews I'm gonna start talking about the biggest problems the game has, then move to it's good parts, that way you have a big idea of what to expect.
First and foremost, the lenght. It's no secret that Valve kinda messed up with the episodic way of dealing with the episodes, however this one feels shorter than Episode Two and it goes by too quick. Worse still, a good chunk of that time is spent running around and talking instead of doing more creative things as the rest of the episode does. I feel like an extra hour would have made the game extremely better and also make the people who call it the "weakest" HL game change their minds.
Second, the price. Half-Life 2 is a very complete experience and it's worth 10€ on Steam. Episode One? 7€, despite being way shorter. Did someone mess up the price? I know that back then HL2 used to be priced at 20€, and at that price it would make sense to have Episode 1 at 7, however right now I would drop it back to 5 or less. Might look like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ thing to pick on, but you gotta understand, lots of people here are poor as all hell.
Third and last problem I see on it is the lack of extreme set-pieces. Look at HL2: You have the airboat section, the buggy section, controlling the antlions, fighting some guardians, the amazing fights back at city 17... Episode 1 has a lot of enemies, but only two amazing encounters, one of them being
It just doesn't compare, and it's probably why it feels so underwhelming.
However, looking past that, what do we got? An interesting but short followup to the story.
Something I do love about this is the bigger focus on Alyx. For a decent chunk of it, you actually need her for more than just talk and open doors. HL2 used to change the gameplay all over the place to add variety and Episode One doesn't it to that much, however turning Alyx into the one dealing damage and turning you into a support role for a while is great and works wonders.
Some of the scenery showed a big leap on graphics between HL2 and Episode One, something that should be mentioned. City 17 is actually quite impressive in it's devastated, ruined state and the citadel falling apart is also cool. Makes me wonder why wheren't that many amazing things to look at in HL2.
Also, the set pieces are less in here, however the ones you have are quite cool. Specially the
It was an amazing way to end it, and the music only made it better.
Lastly, the enemy AI did get some changes. For once, now the combine drop from rooftops in surprise attacks instead of going in big groups around the city. You also get to see roller mines a bit more, and get to see the stalkers up-close, which I think only appear at the end of HL2 and you don't even do anything with them, they're just on the background.
Is Episode One a good game? Yeah, but it's short as all hell and will go by fairly quick. It's main reason to exist is just to link the great HL2 with the great Episode Two, sandwiched to death by superior games. It's good and it's fun, but you'll probably like Episode Two better, so I would suggest, as usual, to get them all on a big sale. Though it does offer some replayability with the achievements, sure as hell the single bullet one is fun as hell to do.
TL;DR Edition: A short sequel that got squished by the game that came beforehand and the sequel it got later. Not a bad game, but short and lacks the exciting parts that made HL2 and Episode Two so God damn fun. I would recommend buying it, sure, but try not to spend too much money. You might play it once or twice and then just move on to better things LIKE IT'S AMAZING SEQUEL.

While fans of the White Wolf game will enjoy this RPG, fans not familiar with the setting will still enjoy the experience.
Set in modern day where vampires walk among us.  You take the role of a newly turned vampire. You can't just willy-nilly go on a wanton blood bath, as breaking the masquerade can have severe consequences (perma death).  There is some politics involved as you soon learn that not all vampires see eye-to-eye on everything.
Game itself is skill based, but left up to the player as to what they want to do.  Want to charm you way through a lot of conversations avoiding combat as much as possible?  Sure.  Want to skip the talk and let the bloodbath begin?  If you want to.
There are multiple endings, something we see more common now but was somewhat rare back in 2004.  So the game has a high replay value as you can join a different vampire clan and go a different route politically.
It's too bad that CCP's World of Darkness MMO was cancelled, leaving this game as the showcase for White Wolf's world.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a beautiful looking game that tells the story of Ethan Carter and the relationship with his family in a very interesting and engaging way. It's important to realise that is more an interactive visual novel than a straightforward adventure game. It has more in common with games like Dear Esther and Gone Home than Gabriel Knight and the Black Mirror series. But the inclusion of the puzzles and the way the story is told, sets it apart from these games. Compared to traditional adventure games, the game is fairly short. It should take you about six hours on a first playthrough and less than half that on a second playthrough. The replay value lies in the story and the way it's told. Once you've reached the end you'll see everything you've experienced in a new light. On a second playthrough you'll  have a much better understanding of the 'real' story and pick up on dozens of subtle clues that you probably missed the first time around. Once you've finished the game it's worth to scour the forum for more information about the story of the game. There are a lot of interesting theories (some confirmed by the creators) and links to in depth interviews with the creators. These forum posts are full of spoilers so don't bother with them until you've finished the game. I'm serious, don't, you'll spoil the surprise. Besides the engrossing story I also really liked the psychic detective puzzles, seen in one of the videos above. They're unique to this game and I wish there would've been more of them.
I recognized a lot of my younger self in Ethan (though my family was much nicer and didn't get killed) and that really helped to draw me into his world and his story. So if you're also a little like Ethan Carter, and you were reading horror, detective, science fiction and fantasy books at a young age and loved to write stories yourself, you should really play this game.

Well, it was kind of annoying downloading this game and then finding out there's a Redux version but that's neither here nor there.  So if you're wondering if I beat it with the puny amount of time it said I played it, I did, but I beat it with the Redux version and I'm posting a review on the normal version because it won't let me write a review for the redux.
Positives: Beautiful looking game but more importantly a very interesting story.  I really enjoyed it.
Negatives: I have two big negatives.  The first is somewhat intentional.  The game tells you there's no "hand holding", which kind of sucks early on because you have no idea what you're supposed to do.  You walk around a fairly large map and you might come across something.  Or you might not.  If you do it might say "Sense" but nothing happens.  What does that mean?  I have (well had) no idea.  For example, I wish the first part would've just said "Not enough... I need more clues before I can fully sense this.  They must be around here somewhere."
You see something interesting and inspect it.  Words come out (thoughts; really neat), but then words start flying out in repitition.  What does that mean?
Meh.  I appreciate the attempt to not "hand hold" but it would be nice if things made a little more sense.  Because of the lack of "hand holding" you could easily move on when you're not finished.  You might not have a clue you were "done" or not only to find out in the end you didn't finish (but luckily it allows you to go back to finish things).
But that leads me to major problem #2.  Wandering around until you come across something.  They make the maps a little too large for item hunting IMO.  There's parts where you can walk a fair ways out and there's nothing there.  And that's kind of neat in a way, but also very annoying in a way (sucks to find out you were combing a large area for... nothing or walking a long distance only to realize you shouldn't go there yet).
Some game examples of this (no spoilers don't worry):
You need to find the 5 traps in the first part.  I didn't realize this was how the game worked; I only found 3 and moved on.  Later, I returned to find the other traps.  One I found relatively quickly, the other took me forever.
There was also this part where the puzzle required you to explore a secondary location first.  I spent a LONG time trying to figure out the key to the puzzle until I finally looked at the walk through and found out I was supposed to visit another location further down and map that location out first.  D'oh.
In the end though, I quite enjoyed the game.  It had a fantastic atmosphere and a very interesting way of story telling.   Play if you like occult style mystery stories.  Dont' play if you want action.

Let's start off with the good side of things.
The graphics, in short, are the best you can witness at this point in time. It is really a stunning looking game. I'm really surprised I can't actually smell the environment through my screen because it looks so beautiful. 10/10 - This really sets a bar, and simply needs to be experienced to be believed.
Sound design is also exceptional. All the music and other auditory cues are timed very well and create a good atmosphere. I do feel that a lot of games get this right, though. Having played other games where atmosphere is important, I think developers realize that you just can't build a good immersive game without the proper auditory cues. This game makes great use of its music, sound effects, and just absolute, dead silence whenever necessary. It creates a very eerie atmosphere indeed.
The story is very intriguing itself. It's got a nice, Bioshock level twist at the end. I do have to say that I expected this game to be a bit more focused on the "horror" aspect, and I found the story undermines it a little bit. It's hard to explain this without actually spoiling the story, but needless to say, I felt fairly confident that I'm unlikely to be in any actual threat, or at least the threats are going to be rather infrequent. It's not a bad story, though, in fact quite the contrary, it's a good story told very well. It just happens to miss the theme that I was expecting from the game. It's still very chilling as it progresses. It's just that you as a character are not participating in it, just observing it.
Now on with the negatives.
Steam will show that my play time for this game is about 3 hours or so. That's how long it really took to get through this game. Why is it so short? It makes it feel more like a minigame than a full fledged title. This short play time really makes me wish that the developers actually cut down some of the time they spent on the graphics and sunk more of it into creating an actual game. Pretty graphics are all well, but I want a good game.
And that's another thing. This game can well be called an Eerie Walking Simulator. It's very minimalistic in almost all content that actually matters. It's a great experience, but it's so hard to actually call this a game. I think I would have felt no shame in just watching someone play it on youtube. It would spare me some of the backtracking if I just happened to miss one of the puzzles in the world, having to go back to it just to unlock the final narrative. I do like the fact that no one is holding your hand, however, and the fact that the world is, for the most part, open even if there is little of it.
Overall, the experience is great, and the quality of execution is superb, but because of that, quantity suffers greatly. At 3-5 hours, you can easily finish it in one sitting even if you take your time to explore the environment.
I'll recommend the game, but only if its on sale. I give it 7/10, just because of its length and the small amount of stuff to do in it. Despite the shortness, it's got a great story, great graphics, and great sound. If you can't get it on sale, watch it somewhere on youtube because it's worth at least that much.

One of the most visually impressive games around, made even more amazing by a new, remade version with an updated engine and some of the original versions annoyances supposedly ironed out. I haven't played the redux yet, but it comes packed in with the original game for new and past purchasers, which is a very nice move on the developer's part.

I'd almost recommend this one just for the enjoyment of wandering around looking at stuff, and I'm not the sort who usually cares about graphics. Realistic backgrounds meet strange fantasy elements to make for a very distinct look and feel to things. It really is like playing a dream sometimes.
But prettiness aside, there is also a mystery to be solved here. It's quite a dark one, involving murder, cults, and other things I won't spoil. It all wraps up in a way I found a little unsatisfying, but it's still a compelling narrative to follow. Which is good, because narrative is all he game really has going for it in terms of game stuff. Exploring, some fairly simple puzzle solving, and piecing together the storyline is all there is to keep you busy in the fairly short playtime, but this one's much more compelling than the usual narrative-only games, with some wonderful twists and surprises in store for you as you explore. A brilliant RTS board game, with a nice presentation.
It's minimal and with a straight forward concept. You can finish the tutorial and learn all the mechanics within an hour, however it can take quite a while to actually wrap your head around it and do everything in real time.
The visuals, audio, and overall atmosphere is pretty relaxing, but at the end of the day, this is still a micro-heavy RTS game, so it can get really intense.
You have to control your main unit to capture map territory while also juggling with 4 different types of sub-units with effects like path blocking or lane clearing. There's also unit-producing nests, unit-converting nests, and power generators to power your nests. So it's an area control game, with lots of multitasking between all the different units and tasks at hand, while also trying to counter your opponent.
There's about 10 different maps to play which adds to the variety of possible scenarios and strategies.
This game has online multiplayer, however all servers are dead. So if you want to play this with actual people, get the 2-pack and find a friend to play it with.
Great game if you're willing to invest the time to master it.
Matches play fast so it's definitely recommended for RTS fans who want to take a quick break and practice their micro.

I've been using MODO indie for a bit now, and over all, I do enjoy it. It's a great modeler, the UI is one of the best and most intuitive you can find. As far as its modeling goes, I can't really fault MODO for much. However, it can be a bit buggy at times, crashes a bit, but that's gotten a fair bit better over time and crashes happen less these days... but, still happen at a fairly consistent rate. That said, MODO tends to be somewhat good at picking up where you crashed out.
My biggest gripe is the FBX support is limited to 2015, which is pretty much two years behind standards... so, for those of you who want or need full FBX 2016/2017 support, it's not happening here. I suppose that is fine for simple projects, but not for those who want complete shader/material/light/animation exports, etc.
All in all, I would still recommend MODO for those who want to do very small scale indie development, it's pretty keen. And while I still kinda recommend MODO Indie, the FBX export is showing its technology age... and while I absolutely love MODO Indie purely as a modeler.... I'm on the fence if in this day and age, it's worth the typical price tag for a Indie package.

As PC users, we're very used to seeing the word "unplayable" thrown around in Steam reviews. More often than not, this is a far cry from the truth, with users simply being picky and spoiled. This is not the case with MODO Indie 10.
Oh my god, the bugs. From "You have no undos left", despite my prefs being set to 100 undos, and not having used a single one of them, to broken symmetry, double polys, and the like. It is broken on PC. It is broken on OSX. More time is spent correcting the program than actually modelling in it.
It crashes, it hangs, it freezes. It UNINSTALLS ITSELF. "Save early, save often" is not enough here. You're left having to choose to save after every move, knowing full well that if you save, there is a very real chance that it may just crash and corrupt the file during the process.
"Contact support!" I hear you say! As other users have pointed out, MODO does not see Steam users as actual customers. You'll get a generic email back telling you to check the forums. If you find anything in the forums related to your problem, more often than not, it's just other users saying "Same problem here, please fix."
As a student at KCAD, our entire class is required to use this program, as the local Underbite Games insists that it is the industry standard. Again, this is absolutely not the case. If you're a student, get Maya for free. If you're anybody else, get Blender for free. There are so many superior options to this broken, rudimentary program.
UPDATE: After saving after every major move, the program glitched out, undo stopped working, so I tried reloading to my last major change. I loaded it to find out that the program had not, in fact, actually saved since my initial project save. Hours of work, lost. The save dialog would open, and the overwrite dialog would pop up, but it has not saved since I had barely started on the project.

I will start by saying that the only good thing I can say about Modo right now is that they gave me the ability to rent and not buy.  If I bought this outright I would have been extremely upset.
I cannot remember the last software package that so regularly crashed on me as this one, and no matter how mundane the task or even the complexity of the current working mesh(es).  Rendering an image?  Crash.  Open a file?  Crash.  Go from vertex selection to polygon selection?  Crash.  My work system is a 2015 iMac Retina system (32 GB), so I suspected that maybe the macOS version is neglected.  Firing it up on my FX8350 machine seemed to offer no respite.  That means I really cannot blame either macOS or Windows.  I hoped this was a case of a sh*t port to macOS, but I experienced problems on the Windows machine similar to those on my iMac.
Worse, is that whenever I try to use the UV mapping utilities, I often get a spinning beach ball of death, forcing me to quit the program.  Over and over.  This happened even more frequently on the Windows machine than on my iMac.
About 50% of the time I finish baking a normal map, Modo inputs cease to respond although I can grab window bars and move those windows around.  Other than that, nothing responds.   It's Russian Roulette each time I bake a normal map or even switch from layout to layout.  Yet another instance where I have to Force Quit the application, losing any and all work since the last save.
It illustrates what a number of us refer to as "Microsoft engineering" where stability is sacrificed in order to meet demands from accounting/marketting for new (and often marginal) feature additions.  It's always a good idea to save frequently, but my Modo experience has taken that to a whole new painful level.
Modo's Game Tools will allow mesh exports so long as the format is FBX, which I find grating.  FBX is a confusing mess of a format that I feel was designed solely to inflict pain and confusion upon others and I go out of my way to use nearly anything else.  I understand that maybe this layout is geared for UE4 or Unity developers, but It shouldn't be very hard to allow for exporting to Collada or vanilla OBJ.
My biggest issue with Modo has been rendered artifacts when baking normal maps (especially over curved surfaces).  My normal workflow was always to generate a low and high polygon mesh inside whatever package I'm using and get Substance Painter to generate the normal maps for me.  The Indie version restricts mesh outputs, forcing me to use the baker provided.  And it regularly generates artifacts which have to be corrected in Photoshop.  That is, unless I part out my meshes to get below the polygon limit restriction and assemble the final object using another program so that I can generate new maps with Substance Painter itself.
Another pet peeve of mine is installing new materials in the Asset directory.  Unless I'm reading the readmes wrong, it's a bit of a pain to add new items in.  Guess what happens to me when things aren't installed right?  That's right, Modo takes the opportunity to show it's displeasure and crashes on me.  Maybe the development team for Modo should take a cue from Substance Painter's approach to drag and drop into the shelf for asset addition.
I have to say, Modo does feel like a beta release product most of the time.  This experience has left me paralyzed in a sense.  I'm not sure I want to risk renting Maya LT because chances are high it could easily be as frustrating.  I also don't feel like paying a monthly fee and still not own any software.  At least with Modo, they offer it up for a good competitive price.  Especially when the costs of other suites often involves limbs and kidneys.
The modelling approach is different from others in the past (Rhino, Cheetah3D, 3DS) and will take some getting used to.
The new addition of procedural modelling could be interesting.  Just worried it's just another opportunity for Modo to keep crashing on me.
The workplane approach is a bit reminiscent of CSG packages like Solidworks and handy in some situations.
Sculpting is fun and could offer up a (much) cheaper alternative to ZBrush.  There is something to say about something that can generate high polygon mesh, retopology, baking and UV mapping inside one program.  It can also rigged up figures and so on.
Modo would be better if "crashes per hour" was not measured in double digits.  Would I recommend this?  I wanted to love using Modo, but it makes it difficult.  The final price won't just be the sticker price but the instability that comes with it.  If one were to take precautions and obsessively save work, then a person might never see a better deal.
___

There's a very intriguing meta aspect to the game that only shows itself if you're interested in getting ALL of the achievements. However, I thought what the developer did was novel and impressive, and quite reminiscient of the Portal ARG, but on a smaller scale.
Overall, this is one of the best Indie titles in my game library, and i've got a lot of respect and admiration for what Sequence is, and managed to do.

I did enjoy this game for what it was: free.
That being said, of course there were things I would have loved to see in the game that were not present, and some things I would change. Then again, I can't complain because this game was, like I said before, free!
What I liked:
- The whole game was voice acted, besides he character you play as.
- Most of the game was visually appealing!
- Most of the characters had some character progression.
- Some of the scenes were quite funny or touching.
- Sam in general. His art style and his voice. I also think he had the best voice actor.
- I like how you can hang out with your friends more if you want, instead of the sex demons.
- Timed events from time to time that give a sense of urgency in urgent situations.
What I disliked:
- If you played through the game once, the other playthroughs felt like a big rinse and repeat process. For exsample, with no spoilers, if you make out or have the dirty-nasties (ya know... the sex) with your incubus of choice, nothing changes besides the name. You'll have the same encouter with Sam as you do with Damien. This was a bit upsetting.
- Some of the characters seemed like a different art style, or maybe they just looked odd... maybe it wa just me haha.
That's all I can think of at the moment. Once again, I'd like to let you know that this is a free game, and I would have spent some money on this; but instead I got it for free. Supposedly, the makers are in the process of making a second that will be pay to play, but if it's as good as this game was and works out the rinse and repeat problem I stated earlier, I'll have no problem paying to play it!

I enjoyed Saints Row IV, but it's reached whatever stage is beyond shark-jumping. SR3 hit just the right notes in my book while this one began taking the goofiness to a point where it's no longer effective- it's sort of like how too many CG effects in movies make them all seem unspectacular. For example: there are a lot of cool vehicles in the game but why bother driving them when you can fly?  I guess this is where Saints Row decided to be the true anti-GTA and fully endorse the id vs the super-ego and it works but only goes so far.
The plot is hit or miss. The villian was very well voice-acted and hits the right notes but there's a fanservice theme throughout the game that gets old- callbacks and references that overwhelm everything else. Characters from early games that are one-dimensional and dated. The movie references also feel like they're a bit much but are fun in small bits.
The gameplay is fun but at times over-complicated. The 'powers' that are added (think magic or the force) unbalance the normal parts of the game completely and so demand difficulty spikes to add any challenge (or the arbitrary removal of said powers). The weapons are fun as well and range from boring but practical (shotgun) to bizarre and niche (plunger-shooting-gun... with farts).
The best part of Saints Row IV, I think, is the way it handles co-op. It's a shame there's no options for 3 or 4 players but understandable since SR4 opens the entire game to 2-player co-op (unlike games that half♥♥♥♥♥it like Far Cry 4). It could be done a little better by setting up a actual role for the 2nd player but it still works great and is a model for how co-op should be handled in these games.

Okay, so I don't remember buying this game, it just showed up in my library for free, so I figured the least I could do to make up for that was write a review.
The story was short and sweet, with a good soundtrack to go along with it. The mechanics were solid and effective; actually, they were fun to use (for the most part), which surprised me a little bit. I can't say it's everything I would wanted from a game with grapple hooks, but I'm probably a bit more demanding than the average person when it comes to grapple mechanics. That being said, I still enjoyed using it, it felt like I was going exactly where I intended with very little practice, which is exactly what you want a movement mechanic to do.
But the thing that stands out most to me about this game is the purely beautiful landscapes. Everything is perfectly lit and the world feels almost magical. Also, they managed to make it obvious where you have to go without making it seem like there's only 1 way direction you can go. All in all I'd say the level design was top notch.
Unfortunately character animation wasn't amazing, and the voice acting wasn't perfect either, but that didn't take much away from the overall experience.
So, would I recommend you buy this game? I'm not sure, it would depend on the person. I wouldn't recommend it to people who aren't comfortable with first person controls, there's a decent amount of semi-fast-paced aiming that needs to be done. I also wouldn't recommend it to people who don't have a lot of expendable cash, because at $13 for 2.5 hours of gameplay there isn't much value to time spent.
But if you're comfortable with general FPS control and have enough spare money and are looking for a fun experience? I would definately recommend this game.

While it looks great and has a good soundtrack, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, as a "first-person story-driven mystery," failed to keep me interested in its story. A lot of the storytelling decisions seemed questionable to me. I absolutely loved the setting in the beginning, but the story made me shift from eager to explore to wanting to just get through it.

Do you like story? Stunning environments? Brain teasers? Games driven by exploration, gathering of clues, and mystery? Then this is for you.
The world itself looks gorgeous, with the only thing that could make it any better being 4K textures. The weakest point is probably the character models, as they don't seem to quite fit in the hyper-realistic environment. Most of the time however, you're simply exploring the environment, so it certainly isn't enough to take away from the experience.
Big thumbs up, hope The Astronauts are looking at making another game in the same vein.

(Please note I've played 12 hours of the newly upgraded "Redux" version)
Absolutely fantastic. I'll get the obvious out of the way first: It's one of the most vibrant, visually beautiful games I've seen in a long time. The new "Redux" upgrade version especially brings the environment to life and the accompanying soundtrack compliments with its haunting score. But the story is where the game really shines. The narrative puts you in the shoes of a detective on the search for a missing boy, the titual "Ethan Carter". As you progress, you come upon clues that you must piece together to solve various crimes that all tie together with the disappearance. Without spoiling the story, everything comes together into an ending that you really don't see coming, and so makes the impact all the more powerful.
However, the game isn't without some (minor) flaws. The puzzle mechanic involved in piecing together the clues is obscure. You are literally warned that there will be no hand-holding on the learning curve and that's pretty accurate. The first puzzle will likely require some Google-Fu to get the hang of how the mechanics work. But once you've got the idea, the rest are pretty self-explanatory.
The game is also not always as linear as it may appear. Some of the sequences you need to complete in order to finish the game you risk missing because they require you wander the forest around you, with no real guide as to what is expected. But helpfully, you'll be supplied a fast-travel system near the end to help you re-trace anything you may have missed, so it's not a huge problem.
Those minor nitpicks aside, it's a great game with a memorable story. Definitely recommended.

Let me begin by saying that I really enjoy this game. I'm the last person anyone would think of as enjoying otome/VN games, but trust me, I do. This one is probably one of my favorites - unfortunately, there are some definite cons.
For example, I have seduced all five of the demons now and each make out/final sex scene was copied and pasted with the name changed. I was disappointed; with James (my first choice) it made sense, but moving on to Matthew and having it be exactly the same was a bit off. I figured each character had different quirks that would come into play in the bedroom, but they don't.
Another con is the inability to date Malix. I'm sorry, he's probably my favorite character next to Matthew and I was excited to romance who could be considered the antagonist of the game (mostly, anyway). I know this is unrealistic, but you can't stop me from dreaming.
There are a couple of small other cons that aren't particularly worth addressing. I will say, as someone who has studied Latin for four years, I was unable to translate a word from that one part of Damien's story (logiatur) and could not find it online. I tried looking for the root as well. If anyone could tell me what it is, I would be grateful as I have all the other words.
Let's move on to the pros:
The incubi are all cute. Your friends rock. There are a ton of romance options (though not as fleshed out as I would have liked).
I enjoyed the voice acting. Sometimes, it was a bit weird, but most of the time it was decent and I wasn't pulled out of the story by any weird noises.
The art style is cute and I like being able to go into the gallery and see the pictures from the stories.
Including unlockable bloopers was a great idea.
I mean, most things about this game are a plus. The plot is interesting, there's a ton to do, and each boy's fight with Malix made me squeal.
As usual, I'm taking way too long to describe a game, so I'm going to sum it up for those who don't want to spend ten years reading a review:
Even with its repetitive lines for each route you take, this is a solid visual novel that makes up for what it lacks with a fantastic base and a good plot. I would recommend this to anyone who wants something to kill a few hours. Also, there's cute incubi boys you can romance. Also, the game is free, so there's no real reason you shouldn't check it out.

I needed something to replace 3DS Max since I only had the student edition (which cannot be used commercially), I cannot afford a subscription, and it was unstable and prone to crashing my computer, so I looked for alternatives; which is where MODO came in.
Modeling in MODO Indie is very easy, once you know how to work your way around in the program. You also have the ability to texture, UV unwrap (which I found quite easy to do compared to other programs I've used, by the way), render, animate, and even paint on the mesh directly.
You also have the option of remapping the keys in order to make using the program a customizable experience, and even has a number of preset options which mimic other programs; an option for 3DS Max was a godsend for me, but there's also options for MAYA, Cinema 4D, and more, which makes learning the program quite a bit less intimidating.
There are a few shortcomings and limitations for MODO Indie, however. The biggest ones are that it uses its own file type (called .lxf) for saved meshes, so it's impossible to open meshes made with MODO Indie in other programs without exporting it to another file type. This is where its second biggest limitation lies: meshes with more than 100,000 polygons cannot be exported at all. It may sound like a large number, but trust me, it really isn't. This is fine if you're working on a video game by yourself (since real-time applications only use low-poly meshes anyway), but these two limitations make it very difficult to share work between team members. Additionally, scripting is not supported in MODO Indie, although I've yet to encounter a situation where this proves to be a major setback. Thankfully, those are the only major limitations, so go nuts with the animating, texture mapping and UV-ing!
There is one issue I encountered with the paint tool, though, and it's that the texture I'd painted on became darker and darker each time I reloaded it. This is easily solvable by simply using a separate program for painting on textures, though, and MODO is primarily a tool for modeling, anyway.
Those limitations aside, MODO Indie is a very powerful modeling program, and is very reasonably priced for what it is.

Monogon Games are the developers behind Interloper that saw its release on 21 May 2016. The game is an RTS in its most pure form. The primary objective of the game is to gain control of each map. There are both single-player and multiplayer modes. Because the game is founded on the most simplistic of RTS rules it serves as a fantastic gateway into the genre. Therefore, if you have ever wanted to play an RTS but have felt uncertain as to whether you would enjoy it or intimidated by the big names then this may be the game for you.
The single-player campaign mode starts with a well-presented and implemented tutorial. The game goes through each of the fundamental mechanics that the game is built upon. It is very thorough while affording the player the opportunity to make mistakes along the way. For each mechanic, there are two levels. The first teaches the player the mechanic with the second making the player put the lesson into action. If, at any time, it seems like you have screwed up you can forfeit and restart the match. There is no penalty for doing this and you shouldn't feel bad if you have to restart once or twice.
Once you have completed the tutorial it is time for you to discover one of the facts of the game. That is that the individual matches or rounds themselves are only intended to last for approximately five minutes or so. I have seen comparisons of Interloper being the RTS equivalent to Hearthstone. It is primarily in the simplicity of gameplay and the anticipated shortness of matches where I believe this to be most fitting.
This places a significant importance on the opening moves of each round. You can quickly find yourselves in a potential match determining position. The simplest mistake early can have those types of consequences. This is both a strength and a weakness of the game. It is a strength because it rewards players who are able to implement successful strategy immediately. However, it is a weakness because matches tend to go one way or the other extremely quickly. I have yet to see many matches where the player who got out of the blocks quickly didn't end up winning the game. This is in regards to games that I have played myself as well as watched.
There are two very identifiable weaknesses on top of the early gameplay often determining the winner of a match. The first of these is that the game requires greater numbers in online play. Although I enjoyed spending time with the campaign the AI can only go so far. The multiplayer games are fast and furious fun when you can find a match. The other problem that I have with the game is something that can be easily solved. That is that I'd like to see a greater number and variety of maps. There are currently thirteen that can be played with. If this number increased to about twenty that would be fantastic.
Interloper makes fantastic use of Steam's features. There are trading cards (9) and achievements (20). The title also makes use of the Steam leaderboard system. Furthermore, the game also makes use of cross-platform play.
Interloper should appeal to many people. Firstly, f you're a fan of RTS games and don't have time to play those that seemingly take forever to play then the short matches here should appeal. Secondly, if you haven't played an RTS and are unsure as to whether you would enjoy it then you could definitely do much worse than trying your luck with this one. You may just open yourself up to an entire genre that is bursting at the seams with outstanding titles.

Interloper is a unique, beautiful and fast-paced RTS game in which you control a tribe of alien fish with the goal of capturing more territory than a rival tribe of alien fish.  Your main character is a Sentinel, which is immortal and can capture territory or go invisible and intangible.  Each map contains certain structures that can be captured.  Assemblers produce Drones, provided they are connected to a Power Source.  Drones are quick little creatures that can block the path of Sentinels and can attack other Drones.  There are also Foundries, which also require a Power Source and can convert Drones into Specialist Units such as Defenders (cost 2 Drones but have 3 HP), Snipers (cost 3 Drones, and have 1 HP, but can shoot enemies at a distance), and Destroyers (cost 4 Drones and have two arms that can be used either to attack or defend, but recharge over time).  And that’s about it.  The player who captures 75% of the territory wins.
This is one of those games that has the perfect balance between simple rules and depth of gameplay.  You do not need to memorize the stats and abilities of dozens of different units, know the full implications of different technologies, or spend hundreds of hours playing or watching game mechanics videos to understand the subtle intricacies of the game.  You can learn everything there is to know about the game in 1-2 hours, then test your skills against either the AI or other players online.  Interloper is a game of quick thinking, reflexes and strategy in which skill beats dedication and no strategy will always win.  (You may form a strategy which will usually win if you always play against different players, but once someone learns your strategy, they can come up with one to beat it.)
Features:
-	Unique, beautiful, and somewhat surreal atmosphere.
-	Single Player Tutorial/Campaign that walks you through the basics.
-	13 skirmish maps where you can play against AI or other players.
-	Public Online Multiplayer matches with a ranked leaderboard.
-	Private Online Multiplayer matches in which you can challenge your friends.
-	4 difficulty levels of AI and 4 behavior types, as well as 7 handicaps for an additional challenge.
-	Replays of all your matches are automatically saved, and you can optionally upload them so that everyone can see them.
-	Option to play skirmishes against the AI or watch replays while in the public multiplayer waiting queue.

In first impressions, A Story About My Uncle is an absolutely beautiful looking game with really solid mechanics that add together to make a wonderful game to play, and it lives up to that moniker as "a wonderful game to play".
The visuals look absolutely stunning and the game is a whole boat-ton of fun to play through. If you ever screwed around with +hook in Quake servers, or even the unreleased official Q3A grappling hook, then you'll be right at home. This is an entire, single-player campaign video game based around such a Quake-style grappling device. To back it up, the player is equipped with a "super jump", that allows him to bound across long gaps or up large heights, and later recieves a pair of rocket boots that allow you to shoot through the sky letting you traverse even further distances without grip. This is probably the updates the game has recieved talking, but unlike many reviewers I never ran into an instance where the platforming solution I chose dissallowed me from continuing. If a solution was wrong, it was extremely obvious. You could even game with platforms that weren't meant to be landed on to recharge grapples. (You get 3 grapples per jump, but it builds you up to that point throughout the first level.)
A quick note on the level design: There are a few "waiting puzzles" were you have to time your grapples to when a rock comes to you to use the momentum to your advantage, but these disappear pretty quickly. Later puzzles with moving parts have enough grapple points to be more like "momentum puzzles." Otherwise, the level design and gameplay is nearly flawless.
That's why I kept playing the levels, over and over again, looking for unlockables and seeing if I could 100% it plus achievements. It's
to play.
Hope you've girded your loins, because that's all the praise this game is getting. I'm really not sure how to begin this next paragraph, so let's right out say it.
This is truly ironic for a video game where "story" is the title's first non-article word. It's practically painful. The story follows an unnamed protagonist who visits his uncle's house one day after a long time with no contact. Inside, he finds a powered suit and launch pad that send him to another planet with mysterious flora and strange inhabitants as he searches for his missing relative. This is told through the framing device of our protagonist in his old age telling the story back to his daughter as best as he can remember it.
There's nothing to examine here. He's looking for his uncle. Nothing will stop him. That's the whole story. The sheer simplicity of the
story here makes all the attempts the game makes at detailing itself and making itself coherent moot. When it does attempt it, the game falls flat on its face.
For example, there's a very big bit about an outcasted group called "The Strays" who either left or were banished from a village encountered early in the game. Much later, you finally get the chance to meet some strays. You say hi, your NPC friend exchanges some banter, and then you leave.
There's a language The Strays have, and it's 1:1 to the English language. Translating them explains nothing. Only jokes and pointless phrases that are so generic they could've been fit anywhere else in the game at any time.
The voice acting is shoddy. Nobody seems to have put any effort into saying their lines beyond the intensity I would expect from an Edutainment game from the early 2000s. The best actor plays Fred, who only appears at the end of the game for a grand total of one scene.
Elements are introduced and then are not explained. The writing is so terribly written that it really shines how terribly plot-holey it is, not to mention the dated memes peppered about here and there. (20% Cooler, anyone?) There's so much that didn't give me any sort of closure.
And that's just coming off the top of my head. I wouldn't doubt there's a ton of other inconsistencies and confusing instances one could come up with as to the quality of the game.
There are sets of unlockables, 5 per level, that add little jokes to how you play the game. There's a "Goat Mode" which makes the character's grapple beam be a Goat Simulator-style Tongue, and make the character spout annoying Goat noises whenever you do anything. Did you laugh when I mention that? I didn't think so. The only unlockable worth anything is "Beam Color", which you obtain after 10 unlockables. After that it's just the unfunny Goat Mode, Midas Mode, which is kind of cool, but makes it hard to identify things like Power Crystals when swinging since they turn Gold instantly and stop glowing, and Acrobatics mode, that makes your camera swing around wildly when you jump, making the game completely unplayable.
My last complaint about the game is the inconsistent animation. It looks like the budget ran out about half-way into the game. Everybody all of a sudden moves so stiffly and expresses only basic emotion in their face, when in Maddie's first appearance she has lively facial expressions and body movement that really brings across any sort of emotion. Maddie herself is an annoying little brat, but her animation was stellar. Suddenly the quality dropped off the face of the earth for everyone. What happened? The modeling is pretty bad too: Even on highest detail settings, Maddie's face (amongst all the other frog people) looks disgusting.
So, verdict: The game is an absolute
to play. However, it is too short and WAY too poorly written to really make it a game I would reccomend. If a modding community can spring up and create a series of awesome levels to go along with the game, I'd probably recommend it. But A Story About My Uncle itself is not a very good video game. I can't reccommend it in good judgement.

FOR THE DEVS:
This game would improve by offering more granularity to the statistics that are viewable to the player and maybe a calculator that is part of the interface. I've been a user since the original MODO Indie (801) and I'm still a huge fan.  Previously, I came from Maya LT, but after trying the demo version of MODO, was excited to see it come to Steam in an Indie offering.  I think it's well worth the price and would highly recommend it to anyone interested in 3d modelling.  If you're on the fence, grab the demo version from The Foundry's website and take it for spin.  Once you've used it for awhile, come on back here and pickup the indie version.
Some caveats before you buy -- be sure to checkout the restrictions on the indie version listed in the details.  While it's nearly identical to the full version, there are a few things that may impact your decision, mainly the Python scripting is disabled (meaning a lot of external plugins that rely on scripts aren't going to work), and there's a 100k polygon limit on any FBX/OBJ file you export.  Personally, I haven't had any major issue with any of the restrictions.  The 100k polygon limit just means I bake my normals in MODO and export the low-poly version, which is what you probably want if you're doing game development anyway, and the missing scripting isn't as big of an issue as it used to be since the newer versions of MODO include a lot of the functionality that external scripts added.

I have a background in Blender and Maya since 2010, started using Modo Indie 801 in 2015.
Modo is an amazing package of tools which you can utilize from start to finish in your modelling process. It features great tools to speed up your process, and has a neat, tidy and customizeable UI. The Foundry has wisely placed the most common tools in easily accessable hotkeys and menus for quick access, and the tools are amazingly functional.
Before I updated this review, I had some compaints about there being some problems with baked texture compatability with other software. This has been fixed in Modo 10, with the introduction of the Game Tools. We now have a what-you-see-is-what-you-get workflow with multiple shaders available, ease of exporting, ease of vertex normal editing and improved baking tools.
There still are times I wish I could simply export the high poly model out and bake the normal and ambient occulsion in the Substance Suite, but baking those two in Modo is fun and easy enough now, so I can easily live with it.
Enjoy Modoing!

I've used many products over the years, 3ds Max, Maya, Blender, and now Modo Indie 901.
I think modeling overall is pretty fast and is what most people talk about when you think of modo.
However, the problems arise when you start to get into creating a skeleton and binding it to the mesh.
I have never worked with software that is so painful to use in this area. Whole features that don't work such as
mirroring a set of bones over. or in the case that you did get symmetry to work it only works during creation. When you have to change the bones later symmetry no longer works.
Bascially Bone creation becomes a very 'Eye-balled' process where you can't even guarantee that the bones are symmetrical.
When you start weighting all this, Half the menu's that are in the documentation dont even match what you are seeing. You are left trying to figure out why you can't see a menu, or get access to something that is supposed to be there.
It becomes a very 'Eye-balled' process once again.
For a payed program there seems to be less documentation than that of Blender.
I can't realistically see using this to create any game for production. Too many core features that were 'Put' into the app as 'Working' and effectively don't work at all.
If your on a tight budget, just start learning Blender since its free.
If money is not an issue, 3ds Max would be my recommendation.
If you're somewhere in between Maya LT is a very good option for indies.
I believe all those options are far better than Modo indie 901.
I've already sunk money into the original Modo indie and the expansion 901. At this point I'm giving up on this software

This is a fun game, but you have to go into it with the understanding that your skill level will plateau after about 5 - 10 hours, but that does not mean that you will be able to ever win the game except by sheer luck. You can lose from lack of skill, but you cannot win from skill. I have repeatedly lost on the final boss because I never got good weapons all the way through the game. Due to the way the shield system works, it is really helpful to have lasers that fire lots of shots. On one playthrough, I got a bunch of these and just totally dominated everything. On many other playthroughs, I didn't and lost.
In general, the weapons are really imbalanced, in large part because all of the missle and bomb weapons require missles, which are in short supply, so you can't use very many missle weapons. This forces you to use laser weapons most of the time. However, once you start using laser weapons, you probably want to jettison missle weapons because laser and missle weapons don't have great synergy (although there are ways to make it work), Most of the weapons are worthless and it's annoying to find stores in the game thathave three terrible weapons for sale. I think I will look for cheats that will give me higher odds of getting useful weapons and completely remove the terrible weapons.
In spite of these issues, I think it's a fun game and would recommend trying it out. But wait for a sale.

I'm going to be straightforward; I love this little game. Fast-paced, very easy to learn, and quite difficult to master.
I only have two main complaints:
- Not enough people on Multiplayer
Multiplayer is a lot more fun than A.I., once you've managed to completely squash the four different expert A.I.'s, but there's simply not enough people on to play on multiplayer all the time. But once more people see the game and enjoy it, more people will be playing and it's an upward spiral from there.
- Maps
Don't get me wrong, the maps are well-balanced and perfect for match-ups, but there's only 13 of them. If there were some element to allow us to make maps, or for the developers to simply make more maps, that would leave me very satisfied. Since there are very simple components in the game, having a map-maker seems like a challenge that can be (relatively) easily accomplished.
All in all, I highly recommend this game. As an RTS player looking for a more simplistic strategy game, Interloper has done the job quite well.

There are very few times, when developers create a game with such an engaging story, GREAT atmosphere, incredible graphics, beautiful music score, interesting puzzles and a ♥♥♥♥ing amazing yet oh so saddening twist. Yet The Vanishing of Ethan Carter has all of that and more.
You play as Paul Prospero, a supernatrual detective that investigates supernatrual cases. This time, he has arrived in Red Creek Valley after receiving a letter from Ethan Carter, inspiring him to journey there. Once he arrives tho, he knows that this is a dark place, filled with secrets and mysteries.
Story wise, this game features many tie-ins and symbolisms you can come across. These elements help you to really think about the story as you progress (and also way after you have beat the game). The way the story is told, makes you intrigued and interested in what will unfold next in the story. The characters are diverse and well done, in terms of voice acting and the way they act in general. They feel authentic and adds several layers to the story. I mentioned that there are also some symoblism in the story. They add these to represent the characters throughout the story, to make it all feel tied in and complex (in a good way that is). The symbolism itself is really well designed in that sense that it describes the characters, symbolically and makes them seem more human. Which solidifies just how well designed the characters and this story is.
This game had a very eerie nad haunting tone for the largest portion of the game time, which was executed in a delicate and clean way. The lonliness, the darkness and the sadness, each of these elements being represented so perfect in the music and the sound. Wether it would be the howling of the wind or the splash of the waters. Either way, this was definetly a headphone-worthy experience, to say the least.
But, does this game have good graphics? To put in perspective; For a good amount of the gametime, I found myself on several occasions just screenshotting the sheer beauty of the landscapes this game offers. Every single detail is well designed and even breath-taking at times. Add to the fact that there are also NO bugs or whatsoever that I encountered and you got yourself a well crafted game. The developers really took their fair share of time to perfect the looks of this game to the fullest and the same can be said about the performance of this game. Maybe a lagspike here or there. But who cares, it is not an abselute need for this game to have a perfect framerate. This game is not fast paced, you do not need to have a perfect framerate all the time, though it would add to a better experience with the game I guess.. Oh well.
When it comes to the score, there are mainly two aspects of it. Sadness and darkness, this adds to the tone of the overall experience. Which is something I cannot describe by words, the music itself features such strong emotions of various forms, it has so many shades, so many nuances. Take my word for it when I say: Mikolai Stroinski is a wonderful composer. Listen to Ethan's theme and you will see just how amazing the music in this game can get.
Gameplay-wise, this game is rather simplistic yet creative. There are mainly the "search for clues" type of gameplay alongside the "complete the puzzle yourself" added with some creative and different elements which I will not get too much into. Now there are no problems with these types of gameplay. However when it comes to puzzels in games, it is rather critical to acess some form of hints or something alike those lines if you were to be stuck in some spot, yet in this game you do not get a lot of help or aid. However it is important to note that the gameworld is not extremly big, so this issue really is not that much of an issue. The game also features some horror elements and also one perticular horror like sequence (depending on what you refer to as "horror"). And I wont lie tho, that sequence scared the ♥♥♥♥ outta me..
And the twist? Well I will not spoil it, but I will say this: You are not prepared...
In the end, this was an abselute blast of an experience! I loved every single moment of it, from the exquisite story to the fantasticly well composed music all the way to the eerie and haunting tone throughout the game. The flaws in this game: none. Well there is one tho.. It ends.
Would recommend this game? ♥♥♥♥ yes

Piggy Poggy Pog is a masterpiece. It is easily the greatest thing I've had the pleasure of playing in my life. The game has a glorious soundtrack, boasting a plentiful amount of no songs. As for the story, well, it's the greatest I've ever seen. The game takes place in a post-apoccalyptic world, where carrots have suddenly turned poisounous. On your farm, your unsuspecting pig friends have continued feasting on these delicious carrots, dying in a matter of days. During the gameplay, you are alone; nothing but you, the devilish evil carrots, fiendish spikes that are there, a strangely ominous barnyard looming in the background, strange floating bricks that may have some hostile intentions, and a shed lying on the other side of each stage. The game teases your brain with highly explorable levels, each of which are exactly 1 screen in length, allowing for high amounts of exploration, while also opening the opportunity for speedrunning due to the explorative yet streamlined experience. Each of the 12 levels makes you think: What would the best route be for going about this stage? The gameplay is also a perfect ten out of ten. You move the pig (named "Poggy") through 12 fun-filled levels, each about a minute in length, making an attempt to escape the farm you are trapped on, so you can get into the wilderness with the fresh foods your tastebuds adore so much. However, blocking your escape, is a locked door. This door is unable to be opened, because you are a pig. Not only that, but the door is sentient. If you attempt to move through this door, than you will meet an untimely and gruesome fate. However, this door will open on one condition, for you see, the door has a strange addiction to Nuts. It loves nuts. It can't get enough. It wants those nuts inside itself, nuts are it's favorite meal. Its sexuality is questioned often, due to its lust for nuts, and most stores refuse to sell it some of its favorite nuts. The door also can't move, it's a door. The door will only open if Poggy can get it some♥♥♥♥♥♥ so Poggy must go around each of the twelve stages, collecting nuts. If Poggy can collect all of the door's nuts, it will open, allowing for the pig to help yet another sexually confused plank of wood, and continue his quest for survival. You can move Poggy using the arrow keys, but why would you want to? Pressing the jump button allows you to jump, so you can ascent vertically up the stage, of which there are twelve, and collect more precious nuts. You will have to avoid the deadly traps, consisting of spikes, the door, and of course: the atrociously villainous carrot plants. The difficulty is spot-on, hitboxes are in questionable locations, allowing for plenty of death, and adding a small element of trial-and error. If so much as a pixel of Poggy even slightly touches a pixel of any part of the hazards, you're going down.  Platforms move up, down, left, and even right at the speed of light, allowing you to keep you on your toes, and keep you wanting to show the game that you are good enough to beat its wonky hitboxes and conquer the strange jump physics of Poggy the pig. The game lasts about 10-15 minutes, allowing for maximum fun, and the replay value is high. I won't spoil what you get for beating the game, let alone completing it, but I will say that there needs to be a patch that if you beat the game fast enough, then all the platforms will be wearing bikinis. All in all, Piggy Poggy Pog gets the highest rating possible, of a 11/10. TSS Studio is amazing for producing this wonderful game, and I cannot wait for it to be ported to the Nintendo Switch so I can experience this game's amazingness on the go.
