This game brought me back 10 years, scouring Newgrounds for dating sims and accidently stumbling into the 18+ section. Good old times!
You are Mika Anderson, an 18-year-old high school student with two best friends who is not on the best of terms with her father. You were really close to your grandfather, though, who passed away recently. He owned a famous toy company which is now without its CEO, and your dad is pushing you to become the new CEO against your wishes. And then it turns out that your grandfather left you his big mansion after he died...
Amidst all the family drama, your dad insists that you move there, and so you eventually do. And that's where the fun begins: five beautiful boys show up, claiming to be incubi, pursued by a devil and his posse. An entirely different demon lady with an agenda of her own also shows up, desperate to lure the incubi back to their world, and you are caught in the middle!
+ It's a free game!
+ It has many save and skip dialogue options
+ There are some slightly steamy scenes (let's say 16+)
+ You can romance both guys and gals
+ With such a large selection of romance options, someone will probably strike your fancy
- The art can be annoyingly off in terms of perspective/proportion
- The protagonist's thoughts can switch from simple & short to ENDLESS amounts of unnecessary purple prose
- The voice acting is okay but a bit cringeworthy
- All the text/dialogue for the steamy scenes is the same, save for a few variations
- The story is more or less standard for a simple supernatural dating game
In the end, I'd say that if you enjoy visual novel/otome games, you should at least try it -- I mean, it's for free! Just don't expect top notch quality. Playing through all the different romances/endings does give you a nice perspective of the story, even though some questions are never fully answered.

The creators of "Magicka", "Magicka: Marshlands" and "Magicka: Holiday Spirit item Pack" asked themselves "What if we took everything that made Magicka a kind of interesting experience for both gamers
and redid it with a PS4 interface in mind, removed the time consuming storyline and interesting locations, and set it to the theme of L. Rob Hubbar's Starship Troopers". Then they outsourced the whole thing to their low paid interns and let the Magick happen, if you'll pardon the pun.
The imaginative result of these mad lads is sure to cinch this year's Nobel prize for literature. Let your mind conjure up this scenario:
In the far distant future, mankind battles among the infinite expanse against ruthless enemies whose only goal is our eradication. In this forward-thinking hellscape, wars are won not only with space laser guns, but more importantly by escorting
to their space bunkers, across millions of worlds and at the expense of billions of lives. Sometimes, just to mix things up, you will be asked to perform a geological survey which involves standing next to a flag for a minute. Other times, you'll be asked to capture a point which oddly also involves standing next to a flag for a minute. But both of those are ancillary and only to facilitate the more expedient delivery of future space briefcases.
If this sounds too good to believe, trust me. Because one really interesting feature is that the game tracks the global number of bullets fired, lives lost, enemies killed, and "space briefcases securely delivered".
The real question is not how fast you should buy this game, but how much of the DLC you will buy. My suggestion is to take out a second mortgage immediately. You only Yolo once, as the kids say.

This review is going to go against the grain... but it's my honest opinion here.
This game is a 2-d, Top-Down resource management game, that gives you variable resources, sporadic choices, and a forced up-tempo on-rails-like experience.
By itself, the game system is not all that hard to figure out.  You get scrap, which is your main currency, to buy crew, supplies (like missles), and upgrades to your ship.  You then fly from star to star fighting for or chancing upon more scrap and the occasional item or crewmate addition.  You are forced to keep moving forward by a "Fleet" chasing after you, so there's a constant pressure to not get caught by them.  If you do, you're almost guaranteed serious damage to your ship or a game over.
So what's the problem then?  Its the difficulty.  Which has nothing to do with strats or skill.  Its comes from the randomness.
Random encounters.  Random events.  Random upgrades.  Random sector maps.  Random... just about everything.  You can have the best strats in the world, but if you don't get the breaks you need in bumping into the "right" stuff, you WILL fail.  Every time.  In fact, failure is a lauded feature by the more zealous players of this game.
Also the final boss... it's the "Rebel Flagship"... and must seriously be a troll move by the developer.  You can have the perfect ship, with all the stuff that can wreck any other ship you encounter in the game... and just about beat it... when all the sudden it supercharges its remaining weapons and wrecks your ship.   Super frustrating.
Lastly... the graphics look like something from a 90's PC game (think Ultima VI).  I guess that adds charm for some.  To me, it seems dated.
I guess one real positive from having low graphics is that the game has little to no loadtimes or overhead for interface speedbumps.  Its all pretty much point and click, and is a fast play.
So if you like bashing your head on your desk every couple hours in abject frustration... play some FTL.

Can I recommend this game, even after all the patches, updates, and a significant play time? Nope. Company of Heroes 2 - its fun if your for it, but there are many nagging issues and unaddressed complaints that keep this game from greatness, or a recommendation on my part. I will try to outline these issues below.
1. Too much DLC and Pushing. I hate buying something only to have what I bought try to sell me something. It makes the product I purchased feel incomplete, like I was taken by some scam artist and sold an upgradeable half game. I have owned products that use DLC in the past, DLC I have purchased and felt good about. COH2 is the opposite.
2. COH2's shoddy - incompleteness. The menus feel dated, the match maker is troublesome, and there is no good system to fix an afk player. The menues are something straight out of Medival Total War, clunky, dated looking, and poorly explained. The match maker has had a hard time getting me into good, balanced, close games consistently. Its a 50/50 shot as far as I can tell - 50% of games I either own/get owned with ease, 50% of them are really fun, enjoyable, workable games that make me think. I would say 25% of may 2v2 to 4v4 games have been ruined (RUINED) by an AFK player on my or my enemies team. There is no way to remove the player, or bring someone else in.
3. No map selector, or for that matter, player voting. They removed winter from the online mode...i personally enjoyed the diversity a good blizzard could bring. Players cant vote on maps. Players cant vote to extend a match, a real trouble when you find one of those rare "close/fun" matches. It would be nice to have the option to vote to extend a game, and thus, extend the fun.
4. Developers are focused on balancing the game, not on making the game fun/enjoyable. This is my biggest complaint, as it relates to many of my previously mentioned issues. Many commanders (the player chosen-form of army specilization) were changed/nerfed for the sake of perfect balance, but along the way, many commanders lost their unique flares, and some really stand-out-unique army builds (no retreat, anyone?) were lost and homoginzied into one well balanced goo. After some time, it feels like wild concepts for play style were thrown out the window in favor of "blank is OP nerf the pants off it!" I would much rather have a fun game then a balanced one, and while I feel there is a perfect medium between the two, COH 2 has trended too far towards the later for a long time.
5. Developers promised a fix to the warspoils system. Year on, no fix, nor mention of a fix. Again, I feel used, cheated, and lied to.
6. Community is good (forums), but a lot, lot of people you play with can be complete bags. Just mean, mean people who curse your very soul for not doing exactly what they tell you too, or insta-rage quit as soon as they lose a squad. 'Buck em.
Well, thats about it for my complaints. The game is quite good, probably my favorite, when it's good.... - its just that half the time, its really bad, and isn't getting any better. Would I buy COH 2? Only after I read the reviews, saw no mention of DLC spam like it is in this game, and didn't hear a bunch of people b*****g about "blah blah op nerf buff blob hakz stuppid game".
I play games because they are fun, COH 2 is only half that.

It is an understatement to say that this game is great.
This game is unlike many of its genre. While other World War Two RTS's out there have similar characteristics to this game (And likewise), this game is unique in its own right. The voice acting for one, is fantastic, and unlike any other game I've played. The look and feel of the game is great as well, but I'd say the thing that takes the cake with this game is the gameplay.
Before I start to sing the praises of this game, I will first tell you the things that you might not like about it.
Number One - DLC. There are five different playable armies in this game, but only two of them come with the game itself. The other three you have to pay for, and that can be a little annoying. There are other things that come in the form of DLC, such as different commanders for the different armies; different vehicle skins; different missions; etc, all of which you have to pay for if you want them.
Number Two - Online Gameplay. While I don't play as much online as other people might, I can tell you that there isn't really a balancing system in place in terms of player skills, meaning that someone who is Level One could get matched up against someone who is Level Forty-Three.
With those out of the way, it is now time for the things that you will likely enjoy about this game.
Number One - Gameplay. You do not have to just play online. There are modes that allow for battles against A.I as well as battles that allow for just you and a friend. Or if that style of gameplay is not your cup of tea, there is a Campaign to play as well.
Number Two - Unlike other RTS's out there, you do not have to level up to acquire different units. (Almost) Every unit that you can train is available with that certain army.
Number Three - The Perilous Moments. If I were to choose one thing I love about this game the most, it would be the experience you get from it. The feeling of finally being able to break the enemy line or winning against a really tough opponent just fills you with joy. Even in defeat, there will always be that feeling of perserverance that will linger with you from game to game.
The Bottom Line is, I feel that this game is great and well worth the money (Though it does come on sale during major steam sales typically), but only if you're willing to be patient and learn it. If you do, it will be one of the best World War Two RTS's you've ever played.

Tentative thumbs up for this game.   Lovely graphics, easy to interpret layout, and rules you can pick up inside of 5 minutes.  Really the most minimal and simplistic a RTS game can get and still be entertaining.  Very short rounds, clean graphics, and intuituive interface, all making for a fast paced strategic game.
... Unless you have the misfortune to end up in a stalemate reneacting the Cold War with your arms buildup and end up in a round that lasts for 40 minutes.  Which I did.  It pays to not think like an AI in this game, it seems -- Hence the Tentative Approval.
Definitely get it if:  You need a time-filling fast paced game that you can quit without feeling bad; you have a "use it, abuse it, lose it" philosophy to your gaming habits; you have a friend to play against in multiplayer.

Vampire the Masquerade Bloodlines is a simply sublime title by Troika. It was the third and final title they ever made before kicking the bucket.
You play as a newly formed vampire in a "World of Darkness". You choose between several clans, from the rebellious Brujah to the insane Malkavians. Each clan has their own stat differences and NPCs react to you very differently. Especially if the player plays as a Nosferatu, you are treated like a hideous monster and cannot stay around human NPCs without them running away from you. The gameplay is solid and acts as both a first person shooter and a hack and slash.
Most notable is the atmosphere of VtmB. It features very well made map design that is riddled with side quests in it's city hubs. Believe me when I say this game takes a while to complete, and is very rewarding once you do it. It is also replayable due to how much of the game changes depending on what clan you play as.
It runs on a beta version of the Source engine. The version it runs on is actually more primitive than Half Life 2. As a result the game is fairly buggy due to it's rushed development. However like all of Troika's games there is a large fan community that has released an unofficial patch that fixes most of the issues.

Combat is real time but based on stats (weapon damage + your skills). You have some vampire powers also to use. Boss fights can be a drag, but are not really that bad. A Story About My Uncle is a decent game if at all.

-Nice environments

A lot of people seem to wanna say that the story is good.  I personally don't think there's much here.  It's kind of painted like a children's story, which, I know that's kind of the point, but it's hinted at that it's based off of his actual experience.  The dull narration doesn't help, especially where he replaces his own words with his narration.  You can hear the voice actor try to get into the script in some parts, but you can't really feel much there for the most part.
Now, why would I ever suggest this game?  Well I'd say it's a nice game to try if you have the money or see it on sale like I did.  5 dollars for 2-4 hours of pure fun was pretty nice to actually see in a game, and when I say fun I mean that type of fun you get from enjoying the game mechanics.  Being able to zoom around and trying to not fall to your death is a simple idea for a game but this game does throw in some nice ways to get around.  There's no ground breaking puzzles, or anything like that.  The environment did look pretty nice, too, and that's all that really mattered.  There was just one or two frustrating parts from time to time because a level or two might have been glitched and never patched.  Otherwise, solid gameplay.
One day, I'd like to see some DLC for levels because I really liked zooming around and all but the game is a bit short.  Like I said:  only 2-4 hours of gameplay and that 4th hour is really pushing it.  If you can get past dull narration and an odd story though, then I'd really recommend trying this game.

I can't say I enjoyed my time with this game. It's confusing, and everything you make starting out will be horrible quality. You and your employees will randomly sit there doing nothing, even when you have a contract to complete, or software to develop. I have no idea why they're doing this, and the game doesn't clearly tell you why. There's no clear way to increase your skills. Unlike other, similar games (from Game Dev Tycoon to even Game Dev Story) where you'll naturally become more skilled from projects you complete, you seem to stick on your poor skill level with Software, Inc. Overall, the game is obtuse with how you become better. It feels like in many ways the game strives for realism, but goes past the point where it should've stopped. Your software won't sell, you won't make any profit, and it just creates a frustrating and confusing enviroment. Even with tutorials out the wazoo (pretty much everything you click pops up with a tutorial), the game doesn't give you a clear path to success. I don't ask for the game to hold my hand, but just give me clear paths and steps I can take to get towards some amout of "success". I don't want to be forced to put a ton of hours into a game just to get remotely good. Other, similar games didn't ask this of me. They showed me that with every project my in-game skills would grow and improve, leading to better projects, more money, and a clear (though not always easy) path to success.
I was really interested and curious about this game, but my expectations were no where near met, which saddens me greatly. I wanted to like this game so much. The videos I've seen of it make it seem so fun. But, in practice, I'm left dissapointed, especially someone who's budget doesn't allow him to constantly buy games.
Maybe one day the game will be good, or at least good to me (my opinion in very much in the minority here). After all, this game is still in Alpha. I hope to give it another try, one day. As for now, I'm afraid to say the game is simply a dissapointment to me.

As someone who's been playing Dance Dance Revolution emulators on PC since 2003, I drooled at the chance to try this.  I was not disappointed.  In the same way that Puzzle Quest was a role-playing adventure using Bejeweled as its combat system, Sequence is a fun, genuinely hilarious quest that has you playing DDR to represent combat.  This is a lot more creative than it sounds.  You're faced with three streams of arrows; one for offense, one for defense, and one for regaining mana used to fuel your attacks.  Constantly shifting between streams, organizing your list of spells, and seeking out rare materials for crafting new gear is made even more fun by the top quality music, great voice acting, and a script that is much funnier than you'd ever expect.  The $5 price is yet another reason you should add this to your collection.  Don't pass this up.

This is the most amazing modeling software I have ever seen - even for a newbie / anti-talent like me - normally, I can barely draw a circle (I'm a games programmer). After a few hours, seeing some very good tutorials available on the official and third party sites, I am confident I can do anything - from models and mechanical structures to environments.
My first day in MODO - my first 2 hours actually - following a tutorial I messed something up, and I had to redo everything all over again, and I was able to retrace my steps in a few minutes !!! It goes so fast that it never crosses your mind to give up, because everything you do is a huge waste of time, and the results are riddled with errors and asymmetries anyway – useless for any decent commercial project. How many times did you get that feeling, trying to use a new software, and seeing the modest results of your best efforts?
How many times have you seen presentations about how great and easy to use a program is, only to hit a brick wall after you got it, and realize that you will have to pour weeks and months of hard work into it before you get some half decent result that, as a first attempt, will have to be remade anyway from scratch, while you are wondering if you have what it takes - a perfect memory, some rare talent that only some goblins have, and an impossibly steady hand that allows you to move and place everything with the accuracy of an industrial robot?
Well, MODO is nothing like that - the interface is simple, intuitive, everything is automated, processed directly with numeric values, and with a few simple commands you can create things that are incredibly detailed. So far I have been building the inner workings of a car – steering, transmission, suspension, things that are rather industrial-design oriented – isn't details and devices that appear to work what everybody wants? Now that I think of it, some degree of realism must exist - many components really need to work since game engines are physics simulations, and if you just attach 4 wheels to a tin barrel, instead of a car you will end up with a shopping cart moving really fast – good luck trying to stay on the road and steer it properly.
MODO proved to be everything I hoped it would be. The Foundry has all the best movies you have seen in recent years in their portfolio, and if their software is not enough for you to succeed, then nothing is. We are lucky that they gave us, the little guys, the slightest chance to even touch their software.
So non, je ne regrette rien, and neither should you.

This review is going to go against the grain... but it's my honest opinion here.
This game is a 2-d, Top-Down resource management game, that gives you variable resources, sporadic choices, and a forced up-tempo on-rails-like experience.
By itself, the game system is not all that hard to figure out.  You get scrap, which is your main currency, to buy crew, supplies (like missles), and upgrades to your ship.  You then fly from star to star fighting for or chancing upon more scrap and the occasional item or crewmate addition.  You are forced to keep moving forward by a "Fleet" chasing after you, so there's a constant pressure to not get caught by them.  If you do, you're almost guaranteed serious damage to your ship or a game over.
So what's the problem then?  Its the difficulty.  Which has nothing to do with strats or skill.  Its comes from the randomness.
Random encounters.  Random events.  Random upgrades.  Random sector maps.  Random... just about everything.  You can have the best strats in the world, but if you don't get the breaks you need in bumping into the "right" stuff, you WILL fail.  Every time.  In fact, failure is a lauded feature by the more zealous players of this game.
Also the final boss... it's the "Rebel Flagship"... and must seriously be a troll move by the developer.  You can have the perfect ship, with all the stuff that can wreck any other ship you encounter in the game... and just about beat it... when all the sudden it supercharges its remaining weapons and wrecks your ship.   Super frustrating.
Lastly... the graphics look like something from a 90's PC game (think Ultima VI).  I guess that adds charm for some.  To me, it seems dated.
I guess one real positive from having low graphics is that the game has little to no loadtimes or overhead for interface speedbumps.  Its all pretty much point and click, and is a fast play.
So if you like bashing your head on your desk every couple hours in abject frustration... play some FTL.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a Sci-Fi Action-Adventure Rogue-like Open World Procedurally Generated 2D Space Indie Game about getting data to the Federation, and avoiding the Rebel Alliance on the way. It sounds great, right? Well, I have great news! It really is. So, if you have anger issues, a short temper, or are easily attatched, don't buy this game. Your crew will expand and deflate over the course of the game, and you have tiny control over that. You have to deal with keeping your systems online and intact, keeping enemies off your ship, random attacks, keeping your shields up, keeping your crew alive, putting out fires, fixing breaches, having a supply of missiles and fuel, and not going into Rebel territory. Oh, and did I mention, once your whole crew dies, the game ends? The goodies are rng, oh and role playing. My entire game was MASSively EFFECTed when Kaiden and Ashley died trying to fix our oxygen supply, then Shepard completed it with like 10 health, then ran back to the med bay to heal up. He went on, until just a few beacons later he finds a rebel scout fighting him, and then the scout flew off and left Shepard with low health an extremely damaged ship, no oxygen, fires everywhere (and the scout left troops on my ship), a destroyed medbay, no shields, no weapons, nothing but the cockpit unharmed, and a doomed Shepard. It was bad when they lost the SR3 and the SR5, but nothing was as unstoppable as the third sector, battlehardened SR6. This game is insane. If you love role playing games, buy this. Oh, if you want tobe a one man unit, just send your crew to the airlocks, and open up the doors. Then you'll be experiencing a REAL RPG. This is no Star Wars. (unless you want it to be) Goodluck out there. Be prepared, and don't get attatched to your crew. They'll die sooner or later. For sure. Just to know when.

For its small price it's a good enough game. It's a pretty simple RTS with just 4 types of units. The graphics look good, the sound and the music are ok, too. You color tiles of the field by moving around your main unit, and capture buildings which produce new units, upgrade those units to 3 other types (sniper, guard and melee fighter). The game tends to get somewhat chaotic, as units may take unexpected paths (e.g. if a one-way gate is in their way, which may not be immediately visible) or travel to locations where they will die simply because you forget to update rally points for the building which creates new units. The game is pretty hectic, and actually reminded me Herzog Zwei (it was the first ever RTS game, released on Sega Megadrive a year or so before Dune 2). The campaign is pretty short, just 18 missions which I completed in a bit over half an hour. Only the last mission was difficult and required a retry because the enemy starts with a few control points already. Skirmishes are relatively easy, even with AI set on "expert". Other than that, there is multiplayer, and since it's an indie game and it surely doesn't have millions of active players, there is no one online to play against. You may try playing skirmish and give AI some advantages like faster movement speed or extra units and so on.
Again, for a $1.5 or something I got it on sale, it's fair to play it for an hour and basically see everything it has to offer. Somehow it reminds me games on iOS or Android, e.g those where there are bases constantly growing small dots and you send half of those dots against enemy bases. It's a bit more complex though. If you're bored and want some interesting but short experience, grab this little RTS for sure. I'll surely keep on my PC for rainy evenings.

Here's a strange melding of RPG and rhythm game that shouldn't work as well as it does.  Though I believe the game would be a hard sell to most players based on a description of its gameplay, I also think that's a shame.  Sequence is a wholely unique and worthwhile experience.
Calling Sequence a role-playing game is accurate but also potentially misleading: RPG elements like experience gathering and equipment crafting are a substantial part of gameplay, but, outside of rhythm sections, you'll only be navigating through menus.  There is no exploration and very little to do outside of rhythm battles and item creation.  While this sounds shallow (and perhaps, on the surface, smacks of dumbed-down, "casual" game design) , there's plenty to do thanks to the clever design and balancing of Sequence's underlying mechanics.  The music is great, too! (Though I do wish there was more of it.)
Highly recommended for rhythm fans.

But for just 5 bucks, it is hard to complain when you getting something unique and quite addictive, if you're into what it has to offer that is. The story is bland and the menus are simplistic but Sequence offers an intense, one-of-a-kind battle system that will leave you wanting more. It even supports the dance pad accessory!
Pretty fun stuff.

Puzzle Quest is to Bejeweled as Sequence is to DDR. Sequence is a dungeon crawler / RPG of sorts in which battles are done in DDR-like matches. Of course, arrows are hit with keys instead of a dancepad. The twist is that there are three different playing fields, and you have to switch between them. One regains mana as you hit notes, one blocks incoming damage when you hit the notes, and one is for casting spells. It's an interesting concept, and while it's done very well, it still seems to be amateurish. I'm glad I played it for a bit to get a good idea of the game, but it's not worth the grinding to continue.

I liked it a lot. It's hard to put a finger on why because I don't like RPGs or scrolling rhythm games (especially of the directional arrow variety). Definitely worth checking out. Surprisingly the whole game was made by one guy who is also the voice of the protagonist (and all the art/design was done by one girl).
Sequence is a very fun game, and it's great for only $5!

A week ago i'd never played Metro before, besides a brief go on the xbox one. I bought it cheap along with last light not expecting much but I was pretty surprised by it. Metro 2033 is a very good single player game, with a wide but not over-the-top selection of weapons and mods, good resource management and some pretty nice gritty graphics. Some have likened it to a Russian response to Bioshock, and having replayed the game I have to agree. There's some pretty well thought out questions of morality, and even when dealing with Nazis and Communists the "right thing" never seems very cut and dry.
I must admit that besides achievement hunting I don't see this game having too much replayability, but with a decent size campaign (I took my time and finished my first playthrough in around 8-9 hours) I can hardly fault it. I must also admit that some elements of the morality system seem flawed, with "moral points" required for a good ending being earned through rather random events, to the extent that I would be willing to bet that most people aiming to achieve said ending would have a hard time doing so without the use of online guides. Perhaps that's just me though.
Regardless of these cons Metro 2033 redux is a solid game, and I would definitely recommend it to any fan of the Bioshock series, and for that matter any gamer interested in post-apocalyptic themes or survival horror. 8/10

Half-Life 2: Episode 1 is the first in an unfinished, yet concluded, trilogy of games in the post-launch of Half-Life 2 to continue the storyline similar to the execution of the Blue Shift and Opposing Force expansions of Half-Life 1 with one continuity. These are as much of expansion packs in the epilogue of the Half-Life 2 campaign as they are an entirely new game broken into parts. Episodic models of the mid-2000s did not have as bad of a reputation as they do nowadays with the idea of unfinished games, and the episodes of Half-Life are example of the benefits of its model as well as the possible downsides. As much complaints people have with Episode 1 due to its length and its linearity that focuses on the well-executed scripted levels of the base-game like Ravenholm and Nova Prospekt, EP1 manages to take the best parts of the gameplay of HL2 into a game that does a better job masquerading its tutorials as they shifted the focus on the combat rather than the puzzles.
Before we continue with the review of Episode 1, as a reminder I will not be discussing the recent leak about Half-Life 2: Episode 3 until we get to the end of the Half-Life 2: Episode 2 review. This review mainly serves as a retrospective view of Episode 1 to follow-up my review of Half-Life 2, so if you want my thoughts about that section of the game or the end of the series then it’s best to read the review associated with it. EP1 should be remembered not so much as embodying the pitfalls of episodic models that may begin strong/weak or that rely on its future iterations for closure; instead, it should be remembered of how these stand-alone expansions can refine the mechanics of a finished game and continue the development of the future of a series by recusing their assets.
Episode 1 begins immediately after the events of Half-Life 2’s ending where instead of fading off into obscurity yet again for the G-Man’s plans Gordon Freeman and Alyx Vance are rescued from one dire situation and put into another. The two of them must escape the Citadel impending on its inevitable collapse by going through the bowels of the Citadel tower and escaping through City 17 from its remaining trainyard before the portal to the Combine’s home world opens again. Immediately following this minor victory is where the game ends the first episode at another cliffhanger ending that has become a staple of the series that leaves the player desiring another adventure for Gordon Freeman.
Something that has become more apparent with each chapter of the original Half-Life 2 and its episodes is that every level can be condensed down to one sentences about each level, and the series of chapters would read off as a synopsis rather than the full-scale story itself. EP1 is perhaps the most blatant of these set-ups as the game constantly paces the player with the simple objective of escaping the city with various deviations in the player that could be read off from the script as, “Gordon and Alyx were _____ when suddenly….” This isn’t so much a complaint about the obvious set-up of these level designs but it showcases how rather deceptively simple these campaigns are as the player is always given a clear direction and a current obstacle that makes every moment punctuated like the end of a sentence. What this really tells is not that the campaign itself needs to have an engaging storyline with complex narrative tricks but that structuring a Half-Life game is really closer to a bullet-list than a plot-structure where the level-design and gameplay obstacles are the main attraction.
This is perhaps why as short and sweet as EP1 is compared to the base game and EP2 are structured it’s why replaying EP1 is always a worthwhile turning point of the series because the level-design and set-pieces are as memorable as Ravenholm. Similar to Ravenholm and other linear levels of Half-Life 2 the sequences of EP1 are moment-to-moment obstacles that range from using the charged Gravity Gun to deactivate a reactor without guns to scavenging between a pistol, shotgun and gravity gun with Alyx in the bowels of the tower amongst the zombies and Antlions. These obstacles are largely combat-focused, including the puzzles themselves such as closing Antlion holes with cars, as well as working with Alyx and the other resistance members to fend off the waves of Combine as the remaining people make their escape. The result makes for a much more engaging experience than the many physics seesaw puzzles of the original game, and what was simply another excuse to get Gordon back on his feet yet again is one of the better sections of the entire Half-Life 2 experience.
Other than the brevity of its campaign and its somewhat formulaic composition of an experience, the only bad things about Episode 1 itself is that it’s more of the same except more polished and more geared towards its combat, which are not bad things compared to the slower sections of Half-Life 2. Even the narrative elements, though few and far between compared to the base game and Episode 2, are condensed down into the only notes needed for the player to follow along that expands upon what players know about the lore of Half-Life. Compared to the insignificance of the first Half-Life expansions and how poorly Blue Shift was as a stand-alone title, EP1 does more to redeem itself from the ire of its fanbase. Perhaps the only thing it is guilty of much like Episode 2 is that it is doomed to repeat the same mistakes with its ending of holding the player’s attention long enough for a future sequel to continue where it previously left off and bringing up story-arcs that will likely never be given an in-game resolution to reward the player’s patience of the wait.

Helldivers is a good game. It has great game mechanics, graphics and sound. I can see how many people have tons of fun with it and understand its good ratings.
But I personally didn't enjoy it. And if you are also a casual gamer looking to play this game with a couple of friends on your couch every now and then, it might be not for you either.
The main problem is that it's stressful. Every mission feels like a survival marathon with enemy troops running at you constantly. I absolutely hate the "alarm" system. If you don't clear certain enemies off the screen fast enough, they call an alarm which spawns more troops. This is nothing new, in many games you have these "necromancer" type of enemies but usually those are rare, easy to kill or take a lot of time to "summon" more enemies. But in Helldivers, the most basic troops call for help constantly.
Yes, we (my coop partner and I) sucked at this game. And yes, I believe that once you get the hang of it, you'll be able to kill those guys before they call for help, but I don't like this mechanic.
Compared to Magicka, you can't goof around in this game. If you kill your team mate (accidentally, of course! :)), you'll have a problem (and he'll probably be angry). In Magicka, if you do those kind of things, you simply die (laughing hard) and respawn at the last checkpoint. In Helldivers you'll have to go through several "Mission Summary" screens until you can finally restart the whole mission. That's frustrating.
And regarding the "stress": Stress can be very exciting in games. One of the best examples is L4D. There's nothing better than yelling "Get out of there, now! I'll hold them off! RUUUUN!" at your team mates and getting out of a tight situation (or maybe not). But then you'll have time to breathe again, scavange for items and simply blow some heads off from zombies standing idly at the wall - you know - relax a little.
Helldivers is constant action, and keeps you challenged all the time. It always requires you to do several things at once without giving you some time to breathe.

Usually don't stray away from Command and Conquer with RTS. But I decided to give it a shot, all in all a good game. Fun with friends, and if you're an RTS fan, you should get comfortable fairly rapidly.

First and foremost: This game is free, so it's already going to get a positive review from me.
Second: It legitimately deserves a positive review.
I did enjoy this game, regardless of it being free. The plot is decent. Not spectacular, but not awful, either. It did give me a major case of the feels at points, which I consider a good thing. For the most part, the writing for the characters is good. It gets a little cliche at points, but considering it's an otome game, and there's only so much that could be deemed as 'original', I didn't consider this a bad thing. Some of the voice work is very nice, quality work. The game is short, but when dealing with visual novels with multiple endings, I generally view this as a good thing.
The cons are heavily in the artwork for me. It definitely felt rushed and unpolished, like the art staff ran out of time and submitted their rough work in. With more attention to detail put into the art, and perhaps more time, the game would feature something more pleasant to look at. That said, I liked the gradient effect that some of the characters had. I would have liked to have seen it carried over to each of the characters for a more uniform style. And, some of the voice work isn't as good as the rest. Some of it was bad acting, but some of it seemed to be poor equipment being used.
Overall, I liked this game, and played through two routes. I suggest playing it if you enjoy otome games.

One of the best platformers I ever played.
The game is a bit akin to VVVVV as the graphics are pretty simple, and the adventure is about exploring different rooms connecting together. There can be some rooms full of dangerous spikes or moving enemies, but the checkpoints are very frequent.
The game can be quite hard at times, but the controls are so responsive that it's a real pleasure (even in the air the player is in complete control, and there are thankfully no inertia or sliding effects as in Super Meat Boy). Several gameplay abilities can be unlocked through the game, such as the double jump and the wall jump. Once in possession of both of them, it feels awesome.
One gripe I have with the game is  the lack of a map (although you can get one in your browser, check the steam guides).
There are different graphic styles, with more or less colors, and the borders of an old-school CRT monitor, adding to the charm.
Since it's free, I recommend anyone that likes platformers to give this gem a try.

Long name, incredible game. Quite possibly the best game I have ever played. I have reached the final boss several times, but only finally got around to giving him his Final Death today. Taking around thirty hours, this is a game complete with an amazing story, interesting characters, cool powers, and the most legit vampire's I know of. The basic story begins with your 'embrace' - where you become a vampire - and continues as your rise in power and prestige, until you are causing the events, rather than reacting to them.
Each of the nine clans you can choose from have different abilities. They could be considered classes, similar to other games, but they aren't usually wildly different. Most of the change is in the player models, and the powers - each clan getting two powers from a pool, and a third unique to their clan. But there are enough differences to make replaying a possibility. For example, the Nosferatu are hideous, and as such cannot seduce people for blood, and instead have to suck on rats in the sewers below the streets, while the Ventrue clan is the opposite - they cannot drink from rats due to their nobility. Another is clan Malkavian; each and every one of them is insane. Incredibly, they have 100% unique dialogue, opposed to other clans having a few lines or opportunities each, and can engage in some interesting tangents - such as having a conversation with the news reporter on TV.
While the vanilla version is very buggy - due to the developers being rushed in their final stages - most of these issues can be resolves with the fan made Unofficial Patch, which is a must-get if you plan on playing. It's not the prettiest game either, with some pretty terrible animations at times, but all this is forgiveable in the face of such a wonderful experience. The game uses Valve's source engine (an earlier version of the engine Titanfall is built on), and was released on the same day as Half-Life 2; and though the models in the game are by no means of equal quality, they are attractive in their own way, and help nail the bleak, horror/noir atmosphere.
If Firefly was a game, it would be this one. While the themes are not at all similar, it is the kind of game that when someone brings it up in conversation, or you read about it on the net, you pretty much have no choice but to reinstall and have another crack at it.
10/10. I honestly cannot think of any way to improve it, other than give the devs more time to improve a couple of the cutscenes.
P.S. ♥♥♥♥ the haunted hotel. The game isn't all that scary, the hotel always gets me.

This review is going to go against the grain... but it's my honest opinion here.
This game is a 2-d, Top-Down resource management game, that gives you variable resources, sporadic choices, and a forced up-tempo on-rails-like experience.
By itself, the game system is not all that hard to figure out.  You get scrap, which is your main currency, to buy crew, supplies (like missles), and upgrades to your ship.  You then fly from star to star fighting for or chancing upon more scrap and the occasional item or crewmate addition.  You are forced to keep moving forward by a "Fleet" chasing after you, so there's a constant pressure to not get caught by them.  If you do, you're almost guaranteed serious damage to your ship or a game over.
So what's the problem then?  Its the difficulty.  Which has nothing to do with strats or skill.  Its comes from the randomness.
Random encounters.  Random events.  Random upgrades.  Random sector maps.  Random... just about everything.  You can have the best strats in the world, but if you don't get the breaks you need in bumping into the "right" stuff, you WILL fail.  Every time.  In fact, failure is a lauded feature by the more zealous players of this game.
Also the final boss... it's the "Rebel Flagship"... and must seriously be a troll move by the developer.  You can have the perfect ship, with all the stuff that can wreck any other ship you encounter in the game... and just about beat it... when all the sudden it supercharges its remaining weapons and wrecks your ship.   Super frustrating.
Lastly... the graphics look like something from a 90's PC game (think Ultima VI).  I guess that adds charm for some.  To me, it seems dated.
I guess one real positive from having low graphics is that the game has little to no loadtimes or overhead for interface speedbumps.  Its all pretty much point and click, and is a fast play.
So if you like bashing your head on your desk every couple hours in abject frustration... play some FTL.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a Sci-Fi Action-Adventure Rogue-like Open World Procedurally Generated 2D Space Indie Game about getting data to the Federation, and avoiding the Rebel Alliance on the way. It sounds great, right? Well, I have great news! It really is. So, if you have anger issues, a short temper, or are easily attatched, don't buy this game. Your crew will expand and deflate over the course of the game, and you have tiny control over that. You have to deal with keeping your systems online and intact, keeping enemies off your ship, random attacks, keeping your shields up, keeping your crew alive, putting out fires, fixing breaches, having a supply of missiles and fuel, and not going into Rebel territory. Oh, and did I mention, once your whole crew dies, the game ends? The goodies are rng, oh and role playing. My entire game was MASSively EFFECTed when Kaiden and Ashley died trying to fix our oxygen supply, then Shepard completed it with like 10 health, then ran back to the med bay to heal up. He went on, until just a few beacons later he finds a rebel scout fighting him, and then the scout flew off and left Shepard with low health an extremely damaged ship, no oxygen, fires everywhere (and the scout left troops on my ship), a destroyed medbay, no shields, no weapons, nothing but the cockpit unharmed, and a doomed Shepard. It was bad when they lost the SR3 and the SR5, but nothing was as unstoppable as the third sector, battlehardened SR6. This game is insane. If you love role playing games, buy this. Oh, if you want tobe a one man unit, just send your crew to the airlocks, and open up the doors. Then you'll be experiencing a REAL RPG. This is no Star Wars. (unless you want it to be) Goodluck out there. Be prepared, and don't get attatched to your crew. They'll die sooner or later. For sure. Just to know when.

A week ago i'd never played Metro before, besides a brief go on the xbox one. I bought it cheap along with last light not expecting much but I was pretty surprised by it. Metro 2033 is a very good single player game, with a wide but not over-the-top selection of weapons and mods, good resource management and some pretty nice gritty graphics. Some have likened it to a Russian response to Bioshock, and having replayed the game I have to agree. There's some pretty well thought out questions of morality, and even when dealing with Nazis and Communists the "right thing" never seems very cut and dry.
I must admit that besides achievement hunting I don't see this game having too much replayability, but with a decent size campaign (I took my time and finished my first playthrough in around 8-9 hours) I can hardly fault it. I must also admit that some elements of the morality system seem flawed, with "moral points" required for a good ending being earned through rather random events, to the extent that I would be willing to bet that most people aiming to achieve said ending would have a hard time doing so without the use of online guides. Perhaps that's just me though.
Regardless of these cons Metro 2033 redux is a solid game, and I would definitely recommend it to any fan of the Bioshock series, and for that matter any gamer interested in post-apocalyptic themes or survival horror. 8/10

Episode 3
Dearest Player,
I hope this letter finds you well. I can hear your complaint already, "Gordon Freeman, we have not heard from you in ages!" Well, if you care to hear excuses, I have plenty, the greatest of them being I've been in other dimensions and whatnot, unable to reach you by the usual means. This was the case until eighteen months ago, when I experienced a critical change in my circumstances, and was redeposited on these shores. In the time since, I have been able to think occasionally about how best to describe the intervening years, my years of silence. I do first apologize for the wait, and that done, hasten to finally explain (albeit briefly, quickly, and in very little detail) events following those described in my previous letter (referred to herewith as Episode 2).
To begin with, as you may recall from the closing paragraphs of my previous missive, the death of Eli Vance shook us all. The Research & Rebellion team was traumatized, unable to be sure how much of our plan might be compromised, and whether it made any sense to go on at all as we had intended. And yet, once Eli had been buried, we found the strength and courage to regroup. It was the strong belief of his brave daughter, the feisty Alyx Vance, that we should continue on as her father had wished. We had the Arctic coordinates, transmitted by Eli's long-time assistant, Dr. Judith Mossman, which we believed to mark the location of the lost research vessel Borealis. Eli had felt strongly that the Borealis should be destroyed rather than allow it to fall into the hands of the Combine. Others on our team disagreed, believing that the Borealis might hold the secret to the revolution's success. Either way, the arguments were moot until we found the vessel. Therefore, immediately after the service for Dr. Vance, Alyx and I boarded a helicopter and set off for the Arctic; a much larger support team, mainly militia, was to follow by separate transport.
It is still unclear to me exactly what brought down our little aircraft. The following hours spent traversing the frigid waste in a blizzard are also a jumbled blur, ill-remembered and poorly defined. The next thing I clearly recall is our final approach to the coordinates Dr. Mossman has provided, and where we expected to find the Borealis. What we found instead was a complex fortified installation, showing all the hallmarks of sinister Combine technology. It surrounded a large open field of ice. Of the Hypnos itself there was no sign…or not at first. But as we stealthily infiltrated the Combine installation, we noticed a recurent, strangely coherent auroral effect–as of a vast hologram fading in and out of view. This bizarre phenomenon initially seemed an effect caused by an immense Combine lensing system, Alyx and I soon realized that what we were actually seeing was the research vessel Borealis itself, phasing in and out of existence at the focus of the Combine devices. The aliens had erected their compound to study and seize the ship whenever it materialized. What Dr. Mossman had provided were not coordinates for where the sub was located, but instead for where it was predicted to arrive. The vessel was oscillating in and out of our reality, its pulses were gradually steadying, but there was no guarantee it would settle into place for long–or at all. We determined that we must put ourselves into position to board it at the instant it became completely physical.
At this point we were briefly detained–not captured by the Combine, as we feared at first, but by minions of our former nemesis, the conniving and duplicitous Wallace Breen. Dr. Breen was not as we had last seen him–which is to say, he was not dead. At some point, the Combine had saved out an earlier version of his consciousness, and upon his physical demise, they had imprinted the back-up personality into a biological blank resembling an enormous slug. The BreenGrub, despite occupying a position of relative power in the Combine hierarchy, seemed nervous and frightened of me in particular. Wallace did not know how his previous incarnation, the original Dr. Breen, had died. He knew only that I was responsible. Therefore the slug treated us with great caution. Still, he soon confessed (never able to keep quiet for long) that he was himself a prisoner of the Combine. He took no pleasure from his current grotesque existence, and pleaded with us to end his life. Alyx believed that a quick death was more than Wallace Breen deserved, but for my part, I felt a modicum of pity and compassion. Out of Alyx's sight, I might have done something to hasten the slug's demise before we proceeded.
Not far from where we had been detained by Dr. Breen, we found Judith Mossman being held in a Combine interrogation cell. Things were tense between Judith and Alyx, as might be imagined. Alyx blamed Judith for her father's death…news of which, Judith was devastated to hear for the first time. Judith tried to convince Alyx that she had been a double agent serving the resistance all along, doing only what Eli had asked of her, even though she knew it meant she risked being seen by her peers–by all of us–as a traitor. I was convinced; Alyx less so. But from a pragmatic point of view, we depended on Dr. Mossman; for along with the Borealis coordinates, she possessed resonance keys which would be necessary to bring the vessel fully into our plane of existence.
We skirmished with Combine soldiers protecting a Combine research post, then Dr. Mossman attuned the Borealis to precisely the frequencies needed to bring it into (brief) coherence. In the short time available to us, we scrambled aboard the ship, with an unknown number of Combine agents close behind. The ship cohered for only a short time, and then its oscillations resume. It was too late for our own military support, which arrived and joined the Combine forces in battle just as we rebounded between universes, once again unmoored.
What happened next is even harder to explain. Alyx Vance, Dr. Mossman and myself sought control of the ship–its power source, its control room, its navigation center. The ships's history proved nonlinear. Years before, during the Combine invasion, various members of an earlier science team, working in the hull of a dry-docked vessel situated at the Aperture Science Research Facility in Michigan, had assembled what they called the Bootstrap Device. If it worked as intended, it would emit a field large enough to surround the ship. This field would then itself travel instantaneously to any chosen destination without having to cover the intervening space. There was no need for entry or exit portals, or any other devices; it was entirely self-contained. Unfortunately, the device had never been tested. As the Combine pushed Earth into the Seven Hour War, the aliens seized control of our most important research facilities. The staff of the Borealis, with no other wish than to keep the ship out of Combine hands, acted in desperation. The switched on the field and flung the Borealis toward the most distant destination they could target: Arctica. What they did not realize was that the Bootstrap Device travelled in time as well as space. Nor was it limited to one time or one location. , a fun and challenging cooperative twin-stick shooter. Developed by the same folks who brought you Magicka, Helldivers takes that hectic and often self-destructive action, refines it, and mixes it into a cynical science fiction setting. You're trapped on one screen with your fellow divers, and absolutely nothing is safe as you helldive to one planet after another, handling missions for the future of Super Earth!
Your bullets, your bayonets, and your hellpods do not distinguish between friend and foe. One moment you can be gunning your motorcycle, the next you might slip into a crevasse. Your enemies are three different species - Cyborgs, Bugs and Illuminate - and each of them will challenge you in a different way. When you land, you're fighting for Super Earth, and by the time you're waiting for pickup, you're fighting to survive.
Each Helldiver is entitled to their own loadout, which consists of a primary weapon, a stratagem, and four skills. These skills afford different pieces of equipment or ordinance you can call from space to assist you in combat - you might request a flamethrower, an ATV, or a tactical nuke. The requisition system is the special sauce, forcing you to input command sets at tense moments to get what you need, including recalling Helldivers who have fallen, often before your own bullets.
The core game has had a number of free updates, and provides a good selection of equipment, but the DLC just take it further. Different DLC focus on different specialties, so you can pick and choose what enables you, as a Helldiver.
If Helldivers has a fault, it is that the game is both challenging and social. The active player base is modest but strong, and they’re eager to meet new recruits! You can play it with your friends locally, or online, or even mix the two.

I think this game is a great addition to anyone's steam library, and I will continue to play HELLDIVERS™ for hours to come.

TL;DR
i really love this game, but feel it gets repetitive too soon.
my first review was a thump up, and i would switch back if devs were to give some more love to the game:
c'mon, on pc it's been released less than an year ago!
FULL REVIEW
with Helldivers was love at first sight:
- gameplay a la AlienBreed / AlienSwarm
- nasty coop features ( friendly fire, killer drop pods, shared view )
- frantic pace
- awesome graphics
- StarshipTroopers inspired humour
- mechs and capes!
but "hope is the first step to disappointment".
GAMEPLAY & REPLAYABILITY
- no story mode, just a massive online campaign ( love it though ! )
- unfortunately after the initial excitement, quickly becomes clear that the whole game is the same missions repeated over and over, just shuffled a little.
- missions themselves are
repetitive ( hold the position while nailing arrow key combos),
bland ( carry an object from point A to point B. i grew to hate briefcases! )
and out of contest ( why disarm a mine field of yours on an enemy planet ? who did put all those random facilites in random places and WHY?!!! )
- enemies are not challenging at all:
with bugs just avoid patrols and enjoy a boring trip across the map;
with cyborgs be prepared to be senselessly ambushed by tanks falling from the sky! ( or glitched into the scenery )
too often you're so overwhelmed that run is the only option;
though the real fun is dying in stupid ways!
PROGRESSION  & CUSTOMIZATION
- poor character customization: you can change aesthetics choosing helmet, armor and cape ( love it! ) from a limited selection though, and you cannot even change colors!
- poor character progression: levelling just unlock weapons
- weapons are not so many, and after you figure them out you will end up using always the same 2 or 3 weapons ( e.g. there is no point in wasting a stratagems with delpoyable ammo when you have infinite laser )
- it's nice to be able to upgrade weapons; would be even better to mod them, in a non linear fashion.
- almost all DLC contents are pretty useless, the few worthing the price are must-haves
MISSED OPPORTUNITY
Helldivers is a missed opportunity:
it lacks of
- immersion
- gameplay depth
- replayability
played with friends is real fun, but you'll get fed up really quicky;
once unlocked every weapon and stratagem there is no motivation to play further, grinding the same old anonymous missions.
procedurally generated maps are a great way make a game replayable, but then something should ensure engagement and purpose:
- tactical choices
- customization
- or even mere collecting urge, by levelling, modding or unlocking
achievement.

War.
Eternal. War.
This is the tale of my friend and I's survival. A tale of slaughter, of endless carnage, and of fear. Running from the iniveitable.  Let me begin by saying this: Never underestimate your foes in this. For they WILL prove you wrong. Let us begin...
It was a dark and stormy night (It was actually a quite fine day), and there i was, talking to my friend on Skype. Suddenly, we had an idea. "Let's make a game in Civ 5 of you and I against Japan!" I said with glee, thinking of an easy victory and wonderous in-game glories. "Sure, dude." Responded my friend. And we booted up the game. I chose Germany, he chose America. We decided on a map of the entire world for our battlefield. Japan was then selected as our foe to our team. And we hit play
Little did we know what was to come.
It started off peaceful, randomly spawning across the globe. Me in North America, my friend (lets call him A) in Europe. We immetidately sent our scouts on a search for Japan as we readied our respective armies and researched for tech upgrades. Generations passed, the seasons passed. Then, around the bronze age did i find Japan. They were in Canada, surronded by tundra and mountains. "This'll be easy, but let's just build up our forces, A." I said over mic, moving troops to my northern border in anticipation. "Sure dude, let me send some spearmen over." Repiled A, joy oozing from his lips. 5 turns later, IT began.
I had found little resistance at first, and i even conquered 2 cities with A's help! The war was good and victory was certain. But then we approached Kyoto, and the invasion froze. We couldn't push up, for they were more advanced and had muskets. So we pulled back and reformed our soldiers around their conquered cities. Their people revolted, so I had them razed. Killed them all for their defiance. That was a mistake. When A and I reached the age of gun powder did the REAL WAR begin.
They struck back, the A.I with a anger I didn't expect. They pushed back my forces from the ruins of their conquered cities, and pushed me to my very border. Then they began their southern campaign, conquering the my city of Hamburg, then Munich on the west coast. I panicked, and had my entire army, settlers too, flee across the sea to Europe. We were given all of Russia by A to rebuild. I checked the coast of NA to see Berlin make her last stand, holding on for 5 more turns with her own army units I'd produced. We had reached, us and Japan, the Industrial Era. But only 3 turns later did Japan inavde Europe, to get at A's holding.
By this time, A and I had gone all out. We became WAR, and so did Japan. We fought and fought, killed and even dropped nukes to stop them. But we couldn't. Europe fell after about 13 turns, i think. A retreated into the Urals, where we spammed forts and dug in.
We held Russia and North Asia for about 7 turns till we had to have another exodus. This time was to China and south Asia. I settled the island of Japan, A got China and India. Due to much more resources here, we reached the Future Era. But so did Japan.
Our final stand was in 2065 A.D. All we had left was two cities, one each on Australia. There, we turned every piece of usable land into a fort, and dug in for the final time. We had Giant Death Robots and Mechanized Infantry in every place we could fit. But out on the ocean, Japan was there. They OWNED the seas. For hexes around our island fortress were ships of EVERY kind, from transports shipping Mechanized Infantry to Battleships. It was a final stand....
OUR FINAL STAND.
Then the game ended, and we won by a slim point margin.
A good end to the Eternal War.

Typically I am not interested in playing these "Walking Simulator" games. However, after trying this game on a friend's computer for about thirty minutes, I decided to buy the game myself. I will avoid narrative spoilers--aside from a comment on these types of games' take on stories--yet I will give a starter's guide for getting around some annoyances of the beginning part of the game (and a certain achievement).
That's the gist of the gameplay. I think out of all the games trying to attempt this format (i.e. any Chinese Room game), this game is almost perfect with its execution. Mostly because the game has some few challenging puzzles and gameplay changes to keep things interesting.
The narrative is not given to you; it's rewarded for exploring and solving puzzles. More importantly, there is a cohesive feel to the story that you can follow, even out of order. Even though you will most likely play out certain events in a linear manner, there is enough player-choice involved to make the experience feel like a geninune mystery.
Besides walking, you, a supernatural investigator, have the ability to piece together clues by setting up the situation as before and watching them unfold. There's even a part of the game where you have to play out events in a specific order inorder to get the straight story. (Similar to Murdered: Soul Suspect, except without the unnecessary stealth). This puzzle--as well as the final puzzle of the game--are the weakest aspects, in terms of gameplay, but the paranormal ability really does immerse you as the protagonist and it makes sense of certain strange things that unfold in the game.
You also have some basic puzzles that require you to wander the nearest area for clues. Sometimes everything will be located in the same room; other times,  the one thing you need is located somewhere else because, reasons. The game has one or two old adventure-game like issues of puzzle-pieces being hidden for the sake of artificial time-lengthening. But, thankfully, most of these puzzles are done right and they're logical without being too obvious.
The usual structure for this game is: Find new area, search for clues or solve the puzzle, then solve the paranormal investigation.
And as you walk around the countryside of Red River, you'll have time to contemplate all the things you'll find along the way, hear little bits of conversation from the protagonist, and experience random stuff you didn't think would happen. The general room of thumb for knowing when it's safe to move on: If you have found the Ethan page or got the achievement, you can go somewhere else.
I'm going to make this brief. I get why this game is set-up the way it is and how the mystery is unfolded to the protagonist. But, please, can we have more stories that have us engaged or doing something with the actual plot? We can still discover things and explore without being detached from all the interesting bits of the stories.
This game gets a pass because it does something creative and comes up with some believable explanations for how you experience the story. I'm by no means calling this game's story original. I think it is a well-executed, neatly made game and story. As with most mystery-stuff, you quickly get diminishing returns (in this case the first hour and a half were the peak). FTL is fun until it isn't. No amount of planning or careful allocation of resources can save you from being destroyed in one battle simply by being unlucky. I have had 6 rounds (of 12 shots each) all miss. In a row. That's 72 misses without hitting anything, including shields. (Easy difficulty, btw.) FTL also sucks time away. The game makes you believe you have a chance for a while and then reminds you that, in fact, you are completely at the mercy of some number generating algorithm. Then you start over thinking that it was a fluke and you really did have a chance. If you want to throw away a bunch of time, you're probably better off reading a book.
The best part of this game is idea behind it.
FTL is most fun before you start playing, when the entire (in-game) galaxy is at your fingertips and you actually think that you may succeed. FTL is most fun before you realize that clicking randomly almost gives you the same chance of victory as thinking every move through thoroughly.
--> The music is pretty darn good, and may well be my favorite aspect of the game.
-> If you want a game where you feel like you are being treated fairly do NOT play this. FTL WILL make you miserable.
-> If you want an excellent time killer that you will be restarting every 45 minutes after feeling like you've had an involuntary colonoscopy, then this is for you!

I'm not strongly into tower defense (TD) games, but this game does away with some of the downsides of tower defense games which bother me. Your towers are characters you gain as you progress in the story, or purchase at various points. Your team protects your summoner, and both the characters and summoner, gain XP after each battle (win or lose, although that can be adjusted). If the game becomes too hard, you can replay an earlier level for extra XP / scrap (the game's currency). However, replaying levels is not grindy-feeling, since each level can be played at three different difficulty levels, which is a different than just the same monsters with more HP (for example, sometimes there are additional spawn points and sometimes the monsters have additional bonuses). (And if you really don't like redoing levels for XP and scrap, you can increase the gain of each of them.)
Unlike some TD games, there is no pathing manipulation: the squares the characters can be placed on are different than the creeps' travel squares. That doesn't mean that character placement is permanent: it is sometimes useful to remove and re-place characters (especially in boss levels or the bonus levels available during the second playthrough).
Speaking of the second playthrough, that isn't just the same monsters, but more HP. Usually the second playthrough monsters have additional abilities, such as attacking your characters as they walk by, or become temporarily immune to non-area damage. The second playthrough also allows purchase or unlock of the best weaponry. Another nice touch is that switching between the first and second playthrough is just a matter of returning to the menu; your entire party and loot remains the same. (I worked a bit on the second playthrough, got stuck, went back to the first playthrough to do some of the harder difficulties of the levels, got stuck, went back to the second playthrough, et cetera.)
Besides your party characters, the summoner has a few spells that unlock while progressing through the story and can be increased as the summoner's level increases. These spells can help out during tight spots in earlier levels, and are pretty much required for the hardest levels.

This game creeps and puts you on edge without anything campy or over the top. The game does a great job developing an unease, making the player feel as if they are a tresspasser in a land where things just are not quite right. The graphics and sound are beautiful bringing to life ancient forests, dilapidated structures, and artifacts of industry gone by the wayside. I really enjoyed wandering the map.
Which you will have to, because there isn't a lot that is intuitive about "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter." Players who enjoyed the old "Myst" series will find some nostalgia here, but the puzzles are not as deep, and often, knowing whether you are in the puzzle is half the puzzle.  Once you solve your first major puzzle you will discover the pattern they take, but too often, the missing piece I needed to solve something was obscure, or worse, something I considered but just didn't do in the right order.
Never the less, I enjoyed "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter." I recommend it with a little hesitation, as it isn't for everyone.

As a short-time veteran of turn-based strategy games, I personally and highly recommend such players, both fellow veterans and newcomers, to try out Civilization 5.
The game itself is simple, yet complex. The game is crafted in a way that a child could play it with skill, and still be used as a medium for game-winning strategies, competative tournaments, and historical reenactment (although not up to par with RTS games in terms of historical accuracy.)
Overall, the game is an ode to human evolution, the glories and blunders of the past, war and peace, and the problems we face both in the modern age and in the future.
tl;dr: Just try it, dammit. You'll have a good time, even when on a losing game.

I was hesitant to click the "Yes" button and recommend this game.
I've been a fan of Civ for a long time, but recent versions have taken tactics and strategy largely out of the game. And some of the things I dislike have been problems in just about all versions.
Things like:
- Triremes doing damage to battleships (Or any archaic unit doing damage to modern, armored units). I don't care how any times you shoot a crossbow at a tank, you won't do any damage, unless you consider chipped paint as damage.
- Aircraft have been crippled. Can't recon with aircraft?? Really?? Can't bomb units in cities?? Really?? Can't attack specific improvements?? Really?? And on a related theme as the first point; how can swordsmen, or any non-missile unit, do damage to an aircraft??
- Why aren't riflemen and related units considered ranged units, but primitive bows are? And primitive bows have the same range as artillery?? Really??
- Why do other civs denounce you or declare war on you when you've been super-nice to them, and given them all you can?
- Why can't you trade technology?
I still play from time to time because I enjoy the concept, but really, the idiotic limitations and impossible things get so frustrating.

You Have to Win the Game is a 16-bit platformer that has exploration, adventure, and tricky platforming. The game plays on a television screen that bends the game and adds more realism, while not hindering the player in any way.
You Have to Win the Game plays in a similar style to VVVVVV, with the obvious difference of jumping instead of flipping gravity. Most of the power-ups you get are behind bosses, and the only time you are forced to start over (other than dying on YOLO mode) is to grab a LOSE 'power-up.'
Overall, You Have to Win the Game is a retro platformer while still keeping a realistic and nostalgic feel (both the television and the game). I would recommend for players who liked VVVVVV, but thought it was too linear.
The only thing I would like to be added to this game (aside from bug fixes) would be a level editor.

I should start by saying I'm not a Star Wars fan (did not know what a Hoth or a Wookie was before this game). In general, this is a great cheap (both on money and resources wise) game. Rather fun to remind you of the olden FPS games, and if you are boosted by nostalgia (especially if you come from the PS2 game) this can actually improve your experience by introducing XL mode (a very fun mode I might add). Part of the gameplay reminds me of Battlefield 2 (one of the good ones, I'd say) and it's generally most of the same thing (run around, capture Control Points, have heated fire battles, rinse and repeat). Then there's the Space Dogfighting mode which incorporates space battles (really fun) where you either destroy an entire ship from the outside, or infiltrate the inside and do the same.
The AI can be stupid at times, standing around getting shot and shooting from the hip to the distance (shotgun classes suffer the most here) but if you're a hero they tend to focus you down more often, which is sort of realistic (as realistic as a still wookie may be) given you can wipe any class with your basic attacks.
One downside I'd have to say is that battles feel pressured against you. Wherever you may go, battles seemed to be turned against you. Be this space battles or ground battles based on tickets (or reinforcements), your side seems to lose unless you have a ridiculous K:D ratio. That said, battles can be pretty intense when you try to keep it up. I just wish you could set the reinforcements/tickets higher so you could have longer battles, but as it is you can have maybe 15-20 minutes? (I pretty much play Hoth, this is the average battle time).
And I should It runs well, though sometimes it may have its quirky piece of code and outright crash. Nothing too often (for my little playtime anyway), but everything's in order in my side (running Windows 10). It should, theoretically, work in given order.

Certainly motivated by survival, Artyom trudges through the Metro, while the ethereal, horror, and the depravity of man fares as good company.
Metro 2033 is quite a game; and as a game that's several years old as of this writing (2017), it stands strong against other atmospheric, linear-story-based first person shooters. At times, the presentation of scenes are so satisfyingly immersive from the incredible ambient soundtrack and visual effects, you'll feel, literally, behind the mask as Artyom. And it's through the mask you understand what the "Metro" really is; the Metro is but a thread of this interestingly told story that weaves factions, supernatural, and mystery into not-just-another post apocolyptic video game.
While the atmospheric effects are often tremendous (fog, smoke, lights, enemy animations), a few nitpicks: some character animations are comparatively stiff. Addditionally, but not related to visuals, but another notworthy nitpick, some of the notebook writing is poorly done.  As you journey through the Metro, you will pick up journals that act as story descriptors to the events you're experiencing, but many of these have typos, etc, which can be distracting. These aside, the voice-acting is mostly solid, especially considering the dub in English is all spoken by Russian sounding actors - impressive.
This is a fairly short game, as well. At a campaign length of 8 or so hours, the varied and interesting gameplay will be over before you know it. Fortunately for you, there's a sequal that's easily as good, and both can be picked up for under $10 during various Steam sales. Pick 'em up together.
