The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an adventure game which was released on PC in mid 2014, and then later released on the PS4 in the summer of 2015.
This is an open world style environment where you have very little guidance on where to go or what to do. You are left to your own devices and to progress in the game. There are a number of puzzles which you must find yourself and pretty much solve with no aid at all. Some of the puzzles are pretty hard to even locate. All of the puzzles are solved by using paranormal abilities such as sensing where objects are in the world or assembling a time line of events of the past.  This was my favourite gameplay mechanic in The Vanishing of Ethan Cater, you essentially have to work out the order of events that led up to the murder of a character. This is done by seeing small memories throughout the world and then just ordering them by assigning them a number by walking up to the memory. This really makes you think about the events which have taken place, and some of them can be quite shocking!
The graphics in The Vanishing of Ethan Cater are absolutely gorgeous, easily one of the best looking games out there at the moment. The game runs in the Unreal engine 3, and the developers have really pushed it to it’s limits here. There is a wide array of graphical options in the menu, allowing you to customize it how you want. All of the graphical elements are perfectly designed. Sunsets, water reflections, foliage, all of it looks almost has a photographic realism to it.
Plot wise, this game has a very interesting tale to tell; I have to admit, it took me at least 15 minutes or so for me to really understand what was happening but after that I was fully immersed and engaged in the story. You will see plenty of twists and turns right until the final credits.
The Vanishing of Ethan Cater is fully voice acted to an extremely high standard; all of the sound effects are really well made too, such as the sounds of the forest, lakeside noises and other ambient sounds that go unnoticed, unless you actually listen out for them.
As this game has some moments in it where you have no idea where to go or how to progress, I had to resort to the use of a walkthrough, many people who read my reviews will know that it is something I have to do on a regular basis for this genre of game. Saying that, even with the use of a walkthrough, there are still moments where you have to put a lot of thought into the puzzles. There is also only one  “enemy” in The Vanishing of Ethan Cater throughout the whole story, and I was a little disappointed that it wasn’t made to be a more challenging encounter than it was,  since you could easily navigate your way around it with ease.
The open world in which The Vanishing of Ethan Cater is set in, is giant, and you can find something interesting to look at everywhere you turn; there are tons of different letters, journals, books and signs to interact with to get even more depth from the story. You won’t really encounter any other characters in real time though, all of the other NPCs you find will be when you are using your paranormal abilities, so there isn’t any real character interaction going on.
This game took me just under three and a half hours to complete; I feel that to be a perfect length for any adventure game like this, as it allows for a plot to be formed, fleshed out and resolved in a timely manner.  Bear in mind, this was with a walkthrough for the majority of it; if you are going in blind, I would estimate you are looking at a five or six hour game.
I started out playing The Vanishing of Ethan Cater on a 4K resolution, and whilst it was playable with the majority of the settings on full, I still had the odd frame rate drop when I was looking in a direction which had a lot to render, such as over the dam. When dropping the resolution down to 1080p, the frame drops stopped and I was able to continue playing at a smooth 60 FPS.  The game does have full controller compatibility, however I would recommend you use a keyboard and mouse for this game, just because it’s first person and a mouse makes controlling so much easier.
In conclusion, The Vanishing of Ethan Cater is a very nicely presented adventure game; whilst it doesn’t have any really fast paced action moments, it does have some intriguing puzzles and well throughout story behind it. You will also get to see one of the best looking games to date, and that is something which you should not miss out on.  I won’t go as far to say The Vanishing of Ethan Cater is a must play for a PC game, but I will highly recommend it, just because the game has very little, if any negative points, and everything else is done to an exceptionally high standard.
1) Stay away
2) Only recommended when on sale

Amazing game with brilliant graphics, was a ton of fun to play through. I like to think that I'm pretty decent at solving puzzles myself, and have played/read Professor Layton, Sherlock Holmes, etc. for most of my life, but The Vanishing of Ethan Carter took being a detective in a game to a whole different level.
A few quick things about the game, and then you can be on your way:
-This is not an action game. There is no shooting, ducking behind cover while the building you just escaped explodes, or anything like that. It's more ambient and thought-provoking, making you think about how to solve /this/ puzzle, how /this/ from earlier might've tied into /this/ part, etc. (in fairness, there is 1 grenade in the game, but you don't throw it at anyone/thing)
-Takes about 6-8 hourse of gameplay to beat the main story, assuming you look up the occasional guide for when you get stuck/confused (happens more often then you might think, trust me). Probably longer than that if you don't use any guides, but I wouldn't know.
And that's pretty much all I have to say.
TL;DR, it's an ambient mystery game, has a short-medium length story-line, and has one part that's kinda creepy (though I haven't played enough of that kind of game to judge very well).
Anyway it's a great game, pulls you in very effectively, is lots of fun, and even has a plot-twist or two thrown in there as a bonus. Definitely worth the money.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is not your typical game.
It is VERY barebones when it comes to game mechanics, keeping the interactions of the player character to movement and an interact-button, but what it lacks in mechanics, it more than makes up for in visual beauty and sense of exploration.
You are dropped into a eerie, beautiful land with one objective, find Ethan Carter, and how you go about it is completely up to you.
This game offers nothing along the lines of handholding, you are given free reigns to just wander, and figure things out.
It rewards the inquisitive, and punishes the unobservant by making interactable objects seemlessly a part of the world.
At many points in this game, I had to stop and just appreciate the beauty of the world around me.
I heavily recommend this game, it is quite the experience, even though it has it's flaws and doesn't have that much to do,  you can easily spend hours jsut walking around and looking.

My first impression of the original 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter' was not positive. I was not pleased with the unfriendly checkpoint autosave system, the general lack of clear instructions, and the linearity of the game (to trigger the autosave points) despite the game claiming it doesn't hold your hand. While I was very impressed with the beautiful graphics rendered on the Unreal Engine 3 and the game's use of music and ambient sounds to set the spine-chilling mood, I quickly gave up on it.
The Astronauts then tweaked the game based on gamers' feedback and updated it to run on Unreal Engine 4. I decided to give the game another chance, and I'm glad I did. The improvements that the designers made resulted in a more playable game, mainly because of a better autosave system. The claim of not holding the player's hand remains an issue for me because to me, in order to get the most out of the game narrative-wise, the player should solve all puzzles, perhaps even sequentially, so he/she can see how all events and character motivations fit together. Without some form of hand holding, looking for the next puzzle at times feels like looking for a needle in the haystack. If it weren't for a published walkthrough, I would have missed two sets of puzzles altogether.
Nitpicking aside, the revamped autosave system means no need to backtrack to save your game as in the original version, and that itself makes the redux version more playable and less infuriating to play. Furthermore, the graphics in the new version are GORGEOUS. Never have I spent so much time taking in-game screenshots. Thank goodness 'Ethan Carter' is full of quiet moments that allow you to soak in its gorgeous vistas.
'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter' turns out to be more supernatural than I anticipated. It feels tonally inconsistent at first, but as the player unravels more of the mystery, this inconsistency starts to make sense even thought one particular scary part sticks out like a sore thumb gameplay-wise. Overall, 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter Redux' feels and plays like a really good M. Night Shyamalan movie, and it has won me over with the improvements the developers have made. I highly recommend those who gave up on the original like I did to give the game another try.

Helldivers, the hardcore twin-stick shooter that borrows ideas heavily from 1997's cult classic, Starship Troopers.
It's a good game and a whole lot of fun, but you need friends to play with.  When you have three friends with you playing this, the propensity for hilarity to ensue is extremely high.  Friendly fire is always on, and you can even crush your fellow Starship Troopers with your pod as it comes down.  Planetary missions can quickly devolve into a risky game of "Tag, you're it".  It's even MORE fun if you make a drinking game of it.  Anytime someone dies from friendly fire, take a swig.  Got crushed by an incoming pod?  Drink.  Fell off the map to your untimely death?  Down the remainder of the bottle.
It takes a lot of coordination, but once you get the feel of the game, it gets easier.  There is a wide array of weapons, skills and stratagems to choose from.  Prior to a mission, you choose your loadout, including both primary and secondary weapons, perks, and the all important stratagems.  Stratagems are player activated skills that are on a cooldown and are limited in number, but can be extremely powerful.  From free-firing turrets to mechs, strats are almost a necessity in order to complete the more difficult missions.
If you decide to purchase this fine game, do yourself a favor and pick up some of the DLC, because you're likely going to need them.  They add much needed firepower to your Helldiver.
The visuals, sounds and gameplay are terrific, but there is a reason it's labeled as hardcore: It can be very difficult unless some strategy is used between loadouts.  Also, you can't just go off on your own when playing with friends - because there is one camera view and all Helldivers have to be on the screen.  It can be annoying, but it makes the game that much better, because it ramps up the difficulty.  You have to be aware of your fellow 'Divers and just where in the hell they're shooting.
I picked this and all of the DLC packs up when they were on sale, and so far, it's been worth every penny.

Star Wars Battlefront II (Soon to likely be called Star Wars Battlefront II: The Good One) is a classic Star Wars game many fans have fond memories of.
But does it hold up?
...Well, duh, why would most of the reviews be positive?
The gameplay is as smooth as Lando, and tight like a chain around Jabba's neck
It may look it's aged as well as Yoda, but that's to be expected with a game that is over 10 years old (which in game development time may be a couple hundred years).
The music is what you would expect, it's Star Wars.
The story... Is slightly more entertaining than C-3P0 lecturing you, but there much more for the singleplayer than just the campaign, like galactic conquest and instant action. But really, instant action and the multiplayer are the real meat for the game.
It is certainly moddable, which can add even more value than what you get here.
All around, it's a solid game, while having aged, is still very enjoyable and relatively cheap to get and pretty much runs buttery smooth if you can get it running, which should not be much of a problem considering we live in the future.
Basically: It is literally better than the EA reboot in pretty much everywhere where it really counts. And I'm willing to bet it will still be better than the sequel of the reboot.

Bugness Level:  2/10 | Barely any bugs.
World Design: 5/10 | Not much "Backstory" or "Theme"

Game Writing: 4/10 | Barely any story.
Level Design: 10/10 | I LOVE THE ART STYLE! Simplistic, yet complicated at the same time! <3!
U.I. Design: 8/10 | Great, but sometimes hard to find things that are buried in lists.
Audio Design: 2/10 | Basically no audio. I recommend listening to some on YouTube, Spotify, iTunes, etc.
Replayability: 9/10 | If you replay it, it is almost a different game every time.
Learning Curve: 7/10 | Shallow learning curve, but a lot of depth. I recommend watching lets plays on this as a tutorial.
Game Feel: 9/10 | Calm and relaxing in some parts, but hectic in other parts.
Price: 9/10 | Worth the money, Totally.
Development Speed: 6/10 | Updates don't come out very often.
Update Quality: 8/10 | When updates come out, they are usually packed full of content, as can be seen on the Trello.

I should start by saying I'm not a Star Wars fan (did not know what a Hoth or a Wookie was before this game). In general, this is a great cheap (both on money and resources wise) game. Rather fun to remind you of the olden FPS games, and if you are boosted by nostalgia (especially if you come from the PS2 game) this can actually improve your experience by introducing XL mode (a very fun mode I might add). Part of the gameplay reminds me of Battlefield 2 (one of the good ones, I'd say) and it's generally most of the same thing (run around, capture Control Points, have heated fire battles, rinse and repeat). Then there's the Space Dogfighting mode which incorporates space battles (really fun) where you either destroy an entire ship from the outside, or infiltrate the inside and do the same.
The AI can be stupid at times, standing around getting shot and shooting from the hip to the distance (shotgun classes suffer the most here) but if you're a hero they tend to focus you down more often, which is sort of realistic (as realistic as a still wookie may be) given you can wipe any class with your basic attacks.
One downside I'd have to say is that battles feel pressured against you. Wherever you may go, battles seemed to be turned against you. Be this space battles or ground battles based on tickets (or reinforcements), your side seems to lose unless you have a ridiculous K:D ratio. That said, battles can be pretty intense when you try to keep it up. I just wish you could set the reinforcements/tickets higher so you could have longer battles, but as it is you can have maybe 15-20 minutes? (I pretty much play Hoth, this is the average battle time).
And I should It runs well, though sometimes it may have its quirky piece of code and outright crash. Nothing too often (for my little playtime anyway), but everything's in order in my side (running Windows 10). It should, theoretically, work in given order.

I will mark whether I like something +, dislike something -, or am neutral +/- as I write the review.
You start as the founder of a software company in a standard sandbox enviroment +/-. You can choose the difficulty, speed of gameplay, starting funds, starting time period, traits, and skills of your founder +. You are able to set a basic appearance for the founder, but this is clearly not a focus of the game +/-.
You cannot customize the size/capabilities of the competition outside of the basic difficulty selector -. This games does not simulate real companies and products, but it does realistic simulate technical progress +/-. That means you won't find Microsoft or Valve in the game. On the plus side, this means the market is unique to each playthrough, vastly improving replayability +.
Once you set up your world, the game will simulate a number of years before your start date. This creates a background market (operating systems and some other various basic programs are already on the market) in the game...the software industry does not spring out of nowhere +.
You start off by designing your office which can be a challenge in your first game +/-. The building interface is reminiscent of the Sims and is very intuitive and the interface flags things that you might have forgotten (temperature control, for instance). The office is fully 3D, and you can make very impressive multi-level structures +. Because of the time dilation, office optimization is much more important in this game than in real life (takes a lot longer for an employee to get somewhere than in real life) -, but that is par for the entire tycoon genre +/-.
You make profit generally by releasing software or doing contract work for other companies. The game accounts for personnel management and some basic asset handling (insurance, your stocks, pension, investment in other companies, and your distribution vector). This kind of stuff is information heavy and marks it as a more serious management game compared to a casual simulation (which is a + for me).
The nuts and bolts of the game is in balancing your cash flow so that you can produce software in a timely manner but also somehow pay for your employees in the mean time. This appears to be an accurate portrayal of the industry from an outsider's perspective (I am a banker, not a tech company developer in real life) +.
Personnel management is well developed. Employees are individualized with looks, traits and compatability. They can be assigned to teams, request raises, get sick, come in late and go to training/education +, There is an HR level in the game that can be automated which means hiring/firing/assignment/raises etc can be delegated to in-game employees. The same exists for project leads which allows you to scale your business to the dozens or potentially hundreds of employees and not be -as- bogged down in micromanagement +.
There is a basic R&D component in the game, centering around patents +/-. The implementation at this point is not very good -, but it is a new feature at the time of this review. Otherwise, tech progress is a function the game year and not otherwise controllable. At this time, research is not a major part of the gameplay -.
There is a large selection of software types and the 'features' that make them up. The more features, the more powerful the product, but the more time it takes to develop. Software Inc. does a very good job in tying together the various kinds of software you develop together +. For example, you use your visual and audio editors (or license another company's) as well as a game engine to produce a game. This is quite natural and lets you enjoy intermediate products (editors, for instance) as well as the more well-known end-user ones (games, etc.) +.
Marketing exists in Software Inc., but only in a basic fashion. You can choose your vector (internet, radio, etc.) and simply pour money and manpower into it +/-. This is being fleshed out to include timing releases with marketing in the next update +. There is a similar gameplay depth in running servers and your own (abstracted) store. In the next update, physical distribution (printing your software onto media to be shipped out) is also being added to the game.
The difficulty curve is inverted. It is quite difficult in the beginning and becomes easier +/-. While this is similar to reality, games tend to avoid this. It is too cheap to scale your company -. After your breakthrough release, the game is easy -. The other gameplay scales fairly well and plays interestingly at both the one-person company level to the I don't know the names of all of my employees level +.
The structural and world graphics are nice enough for this level of game +/-, but are not comparable to larger budget sims (Planet Coaster for instance). In particular, character models and animation are still quite weak -, but they've improved significantly recently +. There is a feature to save layouts for buildings in game, which is a massive + for replayability (if you don't want a unique office in every game), and there is a function for copying individual rooms if you want to copy/paste standardized designs in your structure(s).
Software Inc. supports mods and the workshop +. Because the gameplay design is in flux, gameplay mods are usually broken and the community is small -. Most 'mods' are office designs -.
Sound quality in the game is not memorable +/-. If there is music (and I don't think there is), I can't remember it at all, even after a lot of hours -. Audio production is clearly not a goal for this game which is reasonable for the genre +/-.
It is very bug-free for an EA title, but bugs do exist. Stability is no concern in this game +. Because it is developed on Unity, it is not ever going to be greatly optimized -, but the current state of optimization is sufficient for its scope +/-. It is too heavy for its weight, but that doesn't make it a heavyweight game, so to speak +/-.
There is no tutorial/campaign mode -. It is pure sandbox, so if you are expecting a narrative or progressive objectives (do this, do that!), this is not the game for you. I never play the campaigns in tycoon type games myself, so this isn't a concern +/-. No campaign means you are thrust into the thick of it, relying on the interface to teach you the game -. It wasn't a big problem for me, but for players who are not genre-savvy, it could be a concern +/-.
This is an EA game run by a single developer made on Unity. Be aware of this if you buy this game +/-. That said, the developer is both industrious and transparent (has a public development Trello). In other words, you don't need to trust the developer. You can check on his progress at any time and make your own judgment. Because of these traits, I have great faith in the developer +. Just Google Trello and Software Inc. if you want to check it.
At this point, the developer could release the game and abandon it and would be a decent game that I would recommend +, and in its current state can give many players a good cost/hour ratio. This is a safe purchase in that sense +.
Software Inc. is a good game. It shines as an example of a successful single-dev EA game. However, the genre has weak competition and is not well developed. There are some game development simulators out there, and I enjoyed Mad Games Tycoon, but it is a different class of game. Software Inc. feels and plays like a PC game. The other ones feel and play like console/mobile games, if you understand my comparison. If you want a more streamlined, casual/arcadey simulator, this may not be the game for you. Software Inc. is more akin to Football Manager in a genre full of FIFAs (+ for me).

You wouldn't think I'd like Sequence, given my proclivity for RPGs, sandbox games, and turn-based strategy.
You might, however, change your mind, not only because I led my review by saying 'you wouldn't think', but also because it is pretty much an RPG with the mechanics of a rhythem game. Which sounds sort of repellent when I say it that way, but I'll just reiterate how great it is.
For one thing, the combat mechanism is ingenious, forcing you to choose between offense, defense, and the ability to actually do anything, meaning that you can't just turtle up, you have to be doing multiple things at once. This is complicated by restricting you to a certain time limit to resolve your combats. When you factor in the occasionally crippling difficulty (especially if you joined me in suicide and started on the hardest difficulty setting)..♥♥♥♥♥♥s hard. Which is great.
For another thing, it has a pretty decent story behind it (and not a few dramatic twists), and some quirky ARG elements behind one of the achievements, which I thought was a fun touch.
Of course the RPG elements are only in the sense that you can 'level up' and 'have an inventory', but the decision between taking levels and ensuring crafting successes is another cool touch.
I highly recommend this game if you like games with a solid story, and even more if you already like rhythm games by themselves.

With unique gameplay and an engaging story, Sequence is a gem among indie games. The intelligent, fully-voiced story, great visuals and soundtrack and the interesting blend of two otherwise distinct genres make this game more than worth its price.

War.
Eternal. War.
This is the tale of my friend and I's survival. A tale of slaughter, of endless carnage, and of fear. Running from the iniveitable.  Let me begin by saying this: Never underestimate your foes in this. For they WILL prove you wrong. Let us begin...
It was a dark and stormy night (It was actually a quite fine day), and there i was, talking to my friend on Skype. Suddenly, we had an idea. "Let's make a game in Civ 5 of you and I against Japan!" I said with glee, thinking of an easy victory and wonderous in-game glories. "Sure, dude." Responded my friend. And we booted up the game. I chose Germany, he chose America. We decided on a map of the entire world for our battlefield. Japan was then selected as our foe to our team. And we hit play
Little did we know what was to come.
It started off peaceful, randomly spawning across the globe. Me in North America, my friend (lets call him A) in Europe. We immetidately sent our scouts on a search for Japan as we readied our respective armies and researched for tech upgrades. Generations passed, the seasons passed. Then, around the bronze age did i find Japan. They were in Canada, surronded by tundra and mountains. "This'll be easy, but let's just build up our forces, A." I said over mic, moving troops to my northern border in anticipation. "Sure dude, let me send some spearmen over." Repiled A, joy oozing from his lips. 5 turns later, IT began.
I had found little resistance at first, and i even conquered 2 cities with A's help! The war was good and victory was certain. But then we approached Kyoto, and the invasion froze. We couldn't push up, for they were more advanced and had muskets. So we pulled back and reformed our soldiers around their conquered cities. Their people revolted, so I had them razed. Killed them all for their defiance. That was a mistake. When A and I reached the age of gun powder did the REAL WAR begin.
They struck back, the A.I with a anger I didn't expect. They pushed back my forces from the ruins of their conquered cities, and pushed me to my very border. Then they began their southern campaign, conquering the my city of Hamburg, then Munich on the west coast. I panicked, and had my entire army, settlers too, flee across the sea to Europe. We were given all of Russia by A to rebuild. I checked the coast of NA to see Berlin make her last stand, holding on for 5 more turns with her own army units I'd produced. We had reached, us and Japan, the Industrial Era. But only 3 turns later did Japan inavde Europe, to get at A's holding.
By this time, A and I had gone all out. We became WAR, and so did Japan. We fought and fought, killed and even dropped nukes to stop them. But we couldn't. Europe fell after about 13 turns, i think. A retreated into the Urals, where we spammed forts and dug in.
We held Russia and North Asia for about 7 turns till we had to have another exodus. This time was to China and south Asia. I settled the island of Japan, A got China and India. Due to much more resources here, we reached the Future Era. But so did Japan.
Our final stand was in 2065 A.D. All we had left was two cities, one each on Australia. There, we turned every piece of usable land into a fort, and dug in for the final time. We had Giant Death Robots and Mechanized Infantry in every place we could fit. But out on the ocean, Japan was there. They OWNED the seas. For hexes around our island fortress were ships of EVERY kind, from transports shipping Mechanized Infantry to Battleships. It was a final stand....
OUR FINAL STAND.
Then the game ended, and we won by a slim point margin.
A good end to the Eternal War.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a detective game with some of the hardest puzzles, but will you want to play it ?
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a story driven game made by the ex developers of Bulletstorm. This is a heavy departure from the other games they have made.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter puts you in the shoes of the paranormal detective Paul Prospero. Paul get's a letter from a boy named Ethan Carter who say's something strange is going on at Red Creek Valley and he urges Paul to come here. As soon as we show up we find out something is not right about this place and it's up to us to figure out what happened to Ethan Carter.
Gameplay is really simple. It's a walking simulator, but you actually have to figure out puzzles to figure out what happened to Ethan and his family. This goes from collecting clues to putting together a crime scene to play back a flashback and to find out how that crime was committed.
The soundtrack to this game is phenomenal and the sound effects are amazing too. This game just begs you to play with headphones on. It's a great soundtrack and it's worth purchasing on it's own.
Graphics are absolutely phenomenal. When I first played the game I took some time away from the game just to look around the scenery, it's that good. If you want some nice looking screen savers than this game is surely for you.
Some of the puzzles are insanely difficult as the game doesn't hold your hand from start to finish. It's all up to you to figure out the mystery of the Vanishing of Ethan Carter. You don't take any notes so it's up to you to remember everything you saw and read.
The game took me around 4 to finish and I found it just the right amount of time to complete this game.  Apart from that there's not much replay value. This game is a one time experience. Some of the crime scenes and the ending pack quite a punch and you won't get the same effect the second time through.
I didn't encounter many problems. The only problem I had with the game is a micro stutter when I played through the mine section, but apart from that I encountered zero problems.
Now this is one thing I wanted to address and that's the Ancient Gods puzzle in the mines. This is a spoiler for anyone who will want to play the game so I'll try to keep as less spoilery as possible. You have to find and inspect 4 dead bodies in the mines to get clues so you can open a door.
It took me an entire hour just in that section which annoyed me the living hell out of me. But I guess that's just a rant and not a problem with the game.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a phenomenal experience. I can't recommend the game enough. This game is a must own for any adventure game fan, detective fan and a mystery fan. This game is one of my favorite games of all time and is worth the full asking price. I give The Vanishing of Ethan Carter a 10/10

When I was about 9 years old I dug through my brother's locker while he was away at college.  It was an old brown wooden locker with large hotdog shaped handles and the lock had finally given way after years of pulling on it when no one was looking.  It popped open with a quiet squeak, and inside was a giant tangle of tennis rackets, socks, a few ribbons, a couple of  award plaques, old t-shirts, some stinky cologne shaped like a turn of the century automobile, and an old rusty tin.  The rusty tin caught my eye.  I secreted it away in my room and shut the locker.  The lid gave way with a bit of rust and inside were items that I still find fascinating to this day.  Old comic books.  Really old.  Older than he was, dating from the 30's, 40's, and 50's.  It must have been handed down to him from my grandpa or grand uncle, I never found out.  They were aged and nearly falling apart.  Inside them were stories of horror, alien attacks, secret people under the sea awaiting to attack, detective stories, ghost stories, and a distinctly remember a giant sea monster attacking a guy in an old diving suit that looked like something out of Bioshock.
It was with that type of fascination for discovery that I felt completely taken in by The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.
You are Paul Prospero, a detective looking for young Ethan Carter.  From the moment you step out of the tunnel, the graphics pull you in and narration starts.  It's not frivolous.  The dialogue has a will of it own and the mystery keeps you in the dark about what is really going on.  You start out finding clues and small side stories.  Each story takes you on a mini journey.  There are puzzles involved and clues to be sorted out in chronological order.  Generally, these fairly are straightforward and the hardest part really is figuring out how to get to the next clue sorting mini game.  Followed by those are cut scenes of your clues in order blending into the game quite well about a very devious evil that pressures Ethan's family.
Among all this are some of the best graphics I've seen in a game.  And I found myself taking more and more screenshots.  Stared at some trees for almost 5 minutes.  Left
the river running in game and just sat back to enjoy the environment with my eyes closed for the sound experience.  It's serene. The backdrop to all these dark missions, is the most relaxing background I've come upon.
And the missions are a reasonable difficulty level.  Nothing is right in front of you, yet not hidden from sight.  I'd say it's just right.  Ok, well that crow did take me ages to find, but besides that I thought *pacing* was set very tightly to a good groove.
Gameplay is straightforward with clicking on certain items that glow with inviting text, but you *do* need to complete certain events in order to move forward.  If you get stuck, you might have overlooked something that has to be done first.   You won't need to combine many items or keep an inventory, it's elegantly simple in it's design.
The ending does come a little quick.  Yet, I had no feelings of "aww, that's it??!!".  If anything I felt like it came to a very satisfying end.  And I played the ending a few times just to see it again.  You'll get about 3-5 hrs out of it depending if you go quickly or search every nook and cranny like I did.  And sometimes I'd just let it run for the hell of it as background scenery.
When I was done I found I was missing a few achievements.  Those are not easy to locate without a guide.  However, I do not advise looking at a guide until you have finished the game.  You will get so much more out of it that way.  This is a wonderful story, or rather set of stories.  Hidden away in a secret locker inside a tin.  Waiting for the lock to give way. 9/10.

Star Wars Battlefront II (Soon to likely be called Star Wars Battlefront II: The Good One) is a classic Star Wars game many fans have fond memories of.
But does it hold up?
...Well, duh, why would most of the reviews be positive?
The gameplay is as smooth as Lando, and tight like a chain around Jabba's neck
It may look it's aged as well as Yoda, but that's to be expected with a game that is over 10 years old (which in game development time may be a couple hundred years).
The music is what you would expect, it's Star Wars.
The story... Is slightly more entertaining than C-3P0 lecturing you, but there much more for the singleplayer than just the campaign, like galactic conquest and instant action. But really, instant action and the multiplayer are the real meat for the game.
It is certainly moddable, which can add even more value than what you get here.
All around, it's a solid game, while having aged, is still very enjoyable and relatively cheap to get and pretty much runs buttery smooth if you can get it running, which should not be much of a problem considering we live in the future.
Basically: It is literally better than the EA reboot in pretty much everywhere where it really counts. And I'm willing to bet it will still be better than the sequel of the reboot.

This game, is awesome.
It's a very refreshing aproach to the classic visualized RPG genre. It combines the best aspects of "Tower Defense" games and what's usually considered rpg-elements (even though I disagree on the common definition of what these are). The game itself doesn't give you much freedom of movement in general, you just kind of advance to one point of the story to the next, but that didn't actually bother me, surprisingly.
One of the nicest aspects of the game is the option of giving every single one of the characters your group gets a name of your choice. There's always some dialog, main char asking "What's your name?" and you get a prompt asking you for a name, which is then used throughout the rest of the game (and can be changed if desired).
The game puts you in the shoes of "The Librarian" (her name will be asked for first) who has the unique ability to summon her allies (regular fighters, archers mages and the like) into a "spirit realm" where the undead, which make up the bulk of the enemies encountered in the game, can be actually made re-dead for good.
Therefore she's the one who needs to be tower-defended. The army of defenders consists of six different classes of units which can become six of each type (additional characters can just be recruited in towns for ingame scrap). They all level up and have skill that can be improved by the player with each levelup.
The dialogues and the general story is actually quite good and really really funny, all the characters are quite sympathetic and just lovely insane.
Also, the game has a neat turn when it comes to playing it a second time (new game+) because the second playthrough mode actually adds several new sidequest, an upgrade option for the unique weapons found during the first playthrough and a simply hilarious journal, which recieves entries every now and then as the journey progresses... extremely funny =D.
Even though the game seems to be a finished release, I gather there's still people working on it, so it might even get additional content updates.
Definitely recommended.

This game was the first otome I ever played, and having successfully gotten me into otomes, I'm a little grateful to it.
Pros:
1. Several choices in guys, even lesbian options.
2. Doesn't treat the protagonist like a virgin flower and lets me make choices about what I want to do sexually.
3. Protagonist has a family, something of a personality, and a past.
4. Nice music.
5. The voice actors do okay.
6. You don't have to have sex with the guys to get the good endings, which I approve of.
Cons:
1. The art is very young and cartoonish--like someone who wants to draw anime but is just starting out. Talking generally with the boys it's fine, but the art pages you collect are disproportionate with people missing eyes and having huge heads or distorted bodies.
2. The writing is again very young, and the author could use some practice. There's tons of repetition, rambling, awkward phrasing, and a lot of melodramatic pondering about "souls" and "hearts" etc.
3. The storyline is all very odd--five dudes show up in your house, one kisses you, you let them stay. You go to sleep A LOT. They fall in love with you in a week. What?
4. No one talks normally. The female friends are all overly enthusiastic about everything, the guys tell you everything you want to hear, and everyone calls you "princess" or "love" or "my love" so that it gets weird.
5. There's a strange sexual assault vibe in one of the storylines (Damien) that I found to be a bit disturbing.
6. One of the guys (Matthew) looks like a little boy, acts like a little boy, but you can still romance him. Bizarre. Could not complete the storyline.
So it's not a terrible game. I played it to completion, got all the achievements, and found it to be not a waste of my time. I recommend trying it out and supporting the people who made it. They may go on to make bigger, better otomes in the U.S. which we sorely could use.

If you're a Stepmania and/or DDR addict, I won't recommend this to you, cause you already own this game.
For those of you not quite as addicted to keyboard-dancing:
pardon me, 'Before The Echo' (lawsuit trolls forced them to change the name) is a rhythm game, but with a catch--and added RPG elements. The controls can take some getting used to, especially because a certain kind of multitasking is required of you in all battles, but you'll quickly pick them up. They're fully customizable to suit your own preference--which you will be glad for, as the highest difficulty will have you crying for mercy at times. That said, there is something incredibly satisfying about the combat system, and that certain something is what has made me return to this game multiple times, eventually beating it on the hardest difficulty setting with no little satisfaction.
Gameplay aside,
Before The Echo manages to weave in a nice story with likable characters, with some of the most natural-sounding dialogue I've heard in years. I loved its sense of humor, found everywhere from dialogue to item descriptions. Without spoiling anything, the ending had me both widening my eyes and laughing at the same time.
The music is above-average, as it should be for a music-based game. Some songs are better than others, and there's definitely a few earworms in there.
Long story short: why haven't you put this in your cart yet?

Interloper is a beautifully executed, fantastically original take on the RTS paradigm.
This game does away with all the pomp and bloat of contemporary RTSs and presents a concise, compact and expertly balanced competitive tactical scenario.
We have a top-down view of a largely grid-based map, each player commands a single primary unit which is used to capture terrain and buildings. Capturing around 70% of the map wins you the game.
There are three buildings. Assemblers build a second type of unit: Drones. Drones are front-line defensive and offensive soldiers, blocking the primary terrain grabbing unit's path and thereby forming defensive front-lines and, with the benefit of numbers, destroying the opponents front-lines and opening gaps fro the terrain-grabber. Foundries consume drones to create three more specialist units which have varying advantages over drones and increase the tactical depth many-fold. Both these buildings require power from captured Power Sources, the third building type.
Despite its simplicity, the range of scenarios you can run into over different games, even on the same map, are diverse and thrilling. The majority of games are fast-paced land-grabs initially and evolve into high pressure management of various choke-points and front-line standoffs. These games favour the bold, the tactically nimble and the quick thinkers. Oftentimes a slower paced pseudo-stalemate can arise from these frantic situations where both players gain a stable foothold on the map and foster similarly powerful defensive lines and economies. Such stalemates, however, are no less tense, no less exciting and no less tactical. Indeed, any foothold you think you have gained may be at risk of crumbling dramatically in the face of a smarter opponent.
Ultimately, Interloper is a breath of fresh air in the RTS genre. It has the potential to become a fantastically balanced and meaningful competitive game if the multiplayer scene kicks off. It is a RNGless, pure-skill game much like a real-time Chess and it shares Chess' beautiful dichotomy of being mechanically simple yet tactically fathoms deep!
If you're looking for THE new kid on the competitive RTS block, buy this game now, buy copies for your friends, come join our burgeoning community at
and come meet the small but wonderful development team who ACTUALLY talk to us and ACTUALLY play the game with us! With the excellent competitive following this game is sure to foster, it will soon be a force to be reckoned with!
Happy Interloping!

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is eerie.
Let's start with the story. You play Paul Prospero, a paranormal detective answering fan mail from one Ethan Carter, a 12 year from Red Creek Village, WI. When you arrive, you realize something is awry as you find a railcar with blood sprayed on the front and a pair of legs not far behind it. The rest of the corpse is nearby. Now you get to investigate and look into the dark world of the Carter family and you start to realize just how insane they are. Without spoiling anything, let me just say that the further you progress, the more you'll realize about what's really going on.
On the technical side of things, the graphics are stunning. I mean, perhaps some of the best graphics in a video game I've seen to date. The atmosphere is, as stated, eerie. The plant and tree life are highly detailed. The water looks amazing. Basically, everything looks amazing. Even the sun, you don't get terrible sun shafts, instead the sun shines naturally, it's great. Gameplay is rather simple, you explore for clues and put together pieces while uncovering memories.
I really liked this game. It's short, but once you uncover everything, it's kind of shocking, but at the same time not that surprising.
9.2/10

I'm going to recommend this, even at full price, but please know that this game has a serious flaw. Yep, you guessed it, the auto-save system. I read the other reviews mentioning this but didn't think it'd be a problem. Well, I'm here to tell you it's a HUGE problem and very frustrating.
You see, other games that have the auto-save feature save frequently...you may not think so, but compared to this game they do. I wouldn't mind this type of save system if it saved relatively often. With well over an hour play time, however, it's only saved once....and that one save was about 10 mins into the game! Since it's so wide open and mysterious, you have to spend a looong time walking around, looking for clues. I solved the first puzzle (hence the one save) and then began making headway on three other "quests" for lack of a better term. Although I was making progress, I was getting a little bored of all the walking, so I decided to exit and come back to it later. Out of curiousity, I went right back in to see where it would drop me and I was waaaay back AT THE BEGINNING!! So, I've played for 1.8 hours (of a supposed "4 hour only" game) and only the first 10 mins have been saved with NO WAY of being able to save manually. This is a great, intruguing game, and although I do recommend it for the experience alone, you should know about the attrocious save system going into it.
My advice? If you want to take a break from the game, leave your computer on and just Alt+tab it. After you've completed enough of the most recent "quest" you will notice it save your progress. Like I mentioned though, the quests are long and they tend to drag out. Completely a quest is the key since it won't save automatically until you complete it. You can't do 90% of a quest and expect it to save...I learned the hard way. You can't merely travel a certain distance, to reach a "checkpoint" triggering a save. There are no checkpoints, it saves based on quest/puzzle completion only. If you have to, download a strategy guide to help when you get stuck or stumperd, it will move along the save system that much faster.
Overall, this is an excellent, creepy, mysteriously beautiful game with a Twin Peaks vibe. For a review on the actual content, there are other reviews that sum it up better than I could at this point. It really is as stunning as it looks in the videos. BUY IT, but plan to accomodate the crappy save system.

Take the post-apocalyptic environments like from Fallout, mix it with FPS sneaking and shooting like from Assassin’s Creed, and top it off with an awesome story and progressive levels like Half Life.
14 hours on first playthrough, I was bit overwhelmed by the environments and controls, missed a lot of interesting stuff but did spend a bit of time exploring everything I could.  When I first started, the tutorial messages flashed up and from the screen so quickly that I didn't figure out how to recharge my flashlight until near the end of the game :)
Upon finishing the game (both endings) on my first playthrough, I thought to myself "that was fun, let's do it again."  I can't remember any other game that I'd ever done that with before - so it says a lot about the entertainment value here!!!
I played through the entire game again on a harder difficulty and on Spartan, which affects many of the game mechanics, and enjoyed it immensely, now that I knew my way around and understood it better.  I spent another 10-12 hours on the second run, then the remaining hours were spent chasing down achievements or sitting idly in the menus while paused doing something else.
Metro 2033 has a fantastic story that draws you into it (on the same caliber as Half Life), lots of spooky levels to explore with varied and interesting enemies, many interesting scenarios to work your way through, and top-notch atmosphere, made up with terrific (and chilling) music, sound effects, voice acting, and detailed level design.
Like Thief or Assassin’s Creed, you can fight your way through or sneak your way through much of the game – but what I like is that the game doesn’t necessarily force you to take a specific path.  It’s a thoughtful game with great soul, and is definitely worth the price of admission just for the story itself.   I’m looking forward to playing Last Light next.

So Metro 2033 Redux is a beautiful game with stunning graphics, and decent physics. You'll spend some of your time staring at all the rust covered metals, strewn across the game, and saying - "Wow! thats the most Beautiful rust covered metal i have ever seen." So be prepared to get angry at your graphics card, then sell it on eBay, because Metro 2033 Redux will, in all probability, will completely obliterate your graphics card.
That being said, enjoy this game, if you can, because its worth a try.

Metro 2033 is a definite must-play for anyone interested in atmospheric shooters. Beyond the nice gunplay there's a surprisingly great stealth system that makes ample use of the fantastic lighting and the comparatively smart enemy AI. Many levels can be played both without alerting anyone and by mowing down everything that gets in front of you, which adds a great amount of player choice to the otherwise linear levels.
Perhaps the biggest achievement in my eyes though is the fact that Metro 2033 creates a world that feels extremely believable even though the premise is rather outlandish. The surroundings cycle between comfortable and hostile constantly, but what never changes is the fact that all of the levels are incredibly gorgeous to look at. The lighting, the animations, the overall stupendous attention to detail give the dreary tunnels and lively metro stations a feeling of authenticity that I've never seen before in a videogame. I even died multiple times because I was concentrating on framing screenshots instead of fighting off the deadly mutants.
I played this on Ranger Mode for the "ultimate immersion" and I'd highly recommend this experience to anyone. The combat gets very tense since everything - including you yourself - dies in only a few hits, so fights are often decided very quickly and violently. If you've got a good idea of where the enemy is and a nice bit of cover, you'll probably steamroll them. Should you lose control over the situation though (and that's definitely going to happen), you'll get ripped to shreds just as quickly. Especially while you're in the ruins of once-great Moscow you'll have to manage everything you do very carefully. Ammo is scarce, enemies are numerous and your time is limited since you need short-lived filters for your gasmask to survive on the surface; Everything comes at a certain cost which keeps the tension high throughout.
Even the story is interesting and kept me engaged to the very end. From my perspective, this game succeeds at just about everything and it gets a very easy recommendation from me.

This was definitely not the case for Metro 2033. The story grabbed me in an interesting story, and even after completion, I didn't want to leave the ruins of Moscow, or the depressed communities of the underground.
The story is definitely one of the strongest parts of this game, and combat, gameplay, stealth, resource management, and exploration keeps the game flowing steadily. A few times my heart was racing as I stared into the eyes of a monster called the Libraian, who attacks you if you look away from it. The atmosphere of an apocalypse is incredibly strong, and one can't escape the tension by staying in the tunnels either. Gangs such as Nazis are at war with your people, and sometimes opposition cannot be dodged.
All in all, Metro 2033 will force you to stay alert, and protect the people you love from the mostrosities and demons of a frozen nuclear wasteland that is Moscow.

Interloper is an innovative, fun, and deep yet balanced game for anyone who's into RTS games.
Though it might seem slow and overly simple at first glance, there's actually more depth to it than any other RTS game I have ever played, and I was very happy to find that there were maps
special units because they actually made it too complex for me in the beginning! I'm sure that RTS veterans should be able to find tonnes of different strategies for each game, and - though also fun for beginners - the game seems to be targeted more at that (more serious) audience.
The best thing about all this though, is that matches take so little time, so you're inclined to try again and get better at the game in a Spelunky-type fashion, instead of feeling like you just wasted 2 hours playing a lost game.
What I'd like to see in the future (and from what I gather on the forum this
coming) is a 2v2 or 4-player free for all game mode, so I can play with more friends to see who is the best strategist. I think that would also make the game a lot more fun to more novice players - and it's a great way to introduce your friends to the game without immediately having to crush them.

Hi everyone! This will be a pretty long review: i will try to consider both the base game and the DLCs and i will give you my personal opinion about some complains that can be easily found in other reviews. I am italian, so sorry for any grammar or sintattic mistakes.
First, something about me: i played this game for 1100+ hours with all the factions and i know well game mechanics and units; i consider myself a decent-to-good player (i am NOT a pro player), i played the first 300 hours only against AI, then i start play against humans. I have a really bad internet connection (so i always have lag :( ).
Before going into details, i summarize my opinion here for those who do not want to waste a lot of time reading reviews: overall i find this game really good and enjoyable but i warn you that relic always tries to convince you to pay for more things, so i recommend you to buy the game when in sale (it is often at 75%) with the western front armies expansion (USA and Oberkommando west factions) and the british forces expansion, they are worthy and the game experience is a lot better if you can play all the five factions.
I also recommend you to see some gamplay on youtube so you could have an idea of the tipe of game.
Now, details:
-The gameplay is almost the same of CoH1 with better graphics and better ui: you have to cap the territories of the map to have resouces, you have a true sight feature (you cannot see thruought a higt wall or a house, so you can hide some unist behind corners to surprise the enemy and to flank positions unnoticed). The map is fully destructable and you have to use the directional cover of the objects in the map to protect your infantry.
-The base game includes wermacth and soviet union as playable factions, a russian single player campaign and some teather of war missions. Compared to CoH1, the campaign is not that good and some of you could find disturbing the fact that russians are not presented as heroes nor strictly good guys (while in CoH1 USA, germans and brits where always heroic and good guys in the campaign).
The teather of war are solo or coop missions against ai with russia or germany set during operation Barbarossa; they are divided in challenges, that are strange missions (like kill the soviet officers in the map using only snipers), and ai battle, that are common skirmishes with restricted tech tree (based on the year of war) and sometimes some bonus/malus to carachterized the battle (for instance, the enemy has a bonus fuel income but you have some at support at the start of the match). The teathers of war are not balanced, the ai at hard difficulties will cheat brutally, also since the start of the game units have been patched a lot of time but the teather of war where not adjusted accordingly, so some are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ You could buy three addictionally teather of war, but i do not think tey are worthy, even on descont.
AI skirmish are good, you can play a victory point game (you have to hold some key territories on the map) or an annihilation game (destroy the enemy base).
The core of the game is automatch against real players in victory point games from 1v1 to 4v4, i strongly recommend you to spend some time against the ai to learn the basics before going against people, the matchmaking is not always fair and you could be send into battle against veterans that will crash you in 10 minutes.
-The automatch is based on ranks that are given to you after 10 games of a tipe with a faction. Note that all different combination of friends in a match is consider separatly, so you will have to play 10 games with the same people and the same side (allies or axis) before starting to have balanced match; the first ten math are casual, you could have to play against noobs or pro.
The level of the player (1 to 300) is NOT involved in automatch, it is only a meter of how many time you have played the game (often, until level 100 people are not good players, but someone could reach level 300 playing only vs bots, so he will be a noob nontheless).
ONE IMPORTANT THING: A DECENT PLAYER IS FAR BETTER THEN THE BEST AI IN THIS GAME, SO DO NOT THINK YOU ARE GOOD ONLY BECAUSE YOU CAN EASYLY BEAT AN EXPERT AI AND DO NOT THINK YOU CAN HANDLE A GOOD PLAYER, AI IS SOO STUPID.
-You can buy three more playable faction: USA, OKW and UKF. I strogly recommend that you buy all those factions, the game experience is far better if you can play more different factions and, even if you want to play only one faction, knowing the enemy is always usefull. These expansions are worthy even at full price, but there are often 75% off so wait for a sale.
-You can buy a sigle player USA campaign, Ardenne Assault. If you really like single player, you can find this good, but it is NOT worthy the 50€, even at 10€ it is still a bit overpriced. It does NOT add any content to multiplayer, saved for some bullettins (see below if you do not know what they are) and some vehicles skin.
-During the game, you have to choose a commander from a roster of three that you brings in battle with you. Commanders will unlock addictionaly special units, useful abilities and off map arty or airplanes to destroy your enemies.
You have a default roster of commanders when you buy a faction, then you can buy addictional commanders in the in game store. Despite the fact that someone says that the buyable commanders are too powerful and you have to pay2win, this is NOT true. There are some buyable commanders that are really good (and some that are crap), but the basic commanders are good too and if you are a good player with good micro you can win every match WITOUTH ANY premium commanders. Most of the premium commander have the same abilities of the basic ones mixed differently, some unlocks new units but you can win also witouth them.
All commanders suits a specific tipe of gameplay, choose them wisely and buy only those that suits you, but i repeat: you do not need them to win if you are a good player.
The cost of the commanders are pretty higth, wait for a sale.
In the in game store you can also buy cosmetics (vehicle skins and faceplates). They are overpriced, do not buy them unless if you really want that specific camo, then wait for a sale.
-At the end of all matches, you can drop one ore more war spoils: these are COMPLITELY CASAUAL drop (it does not matter if you have played well or not) and you have a chance to drop skin, faceplates, bullettins (really small bonus that you can give to your army at the start of the match, like +3% accuracy ecc, not that useful) and even commanders. The chance that you drop a useful item is REALLY LOW, if you want a skin or commander do not wait and buy it, you will recieve a lot of doubles (double bullettin can stack for greater effect) and there is NOT yet a craft system to transform your doubles. If you are luky, you can drop for free some good things, but the war spoil system is bad to encourage you to spend more money.
-A final thought on balance and patching: relic patches this game often; i find the patches overall really good, but often you have to expect more then one patch in a short time because sometimes they create some bug or give unintentionally a bonus to one unit and they have to repatch it. There is the possibility, for the major patches, to try out the changes in the beta and to give a feedback. In my opinion, in fact of balancing relic hears the feedback of the players.
You will find a lot of comment and reviews in witch someone cries that one side/faction is OP or that one unit is OP. DO NOT BELIEVE TO THEM. If you read carefully, the same units and factions are consider both OP and UP: this is mainly because when someone loose a game it is simpler to blame an OP unit than himself.
All units in the game are different and to be effective must be used correctly. If played correctly, all factions are pretty balaced.
All in all, i strongly recommend this game to all.

If this were something you had to pay any sum of money for, I might be more hesitant about recommending it, but given that it's, well, free, it's really worth checking out, if only for the side story.  I've only played one route so far, and I may update this review upon going through a few more, but let me briefly outline my two playthroughs.  Mild spoilers may be ahead, but I'll try to stay as vague as possible:
Playthrough 1
Went totally serious on this one.  Dove in blind, no spoilers.  Played as I might have acted in real life (well, minus the crippling social ineptitude, of course) or, rather, in a way that was actually attempting to win.  Wasn't sure who I was going for at first, but I very quickly pegged the personality tropes of most of the romance options.  Posh Boy, Mean Boy, Flirty Boy, Boyishly Charming... Ended up going with the one I was the least certain of, who I was debating back and forth between 'shy/quiet boy' and 'secretly creepy with some hardcore repressed issues.'  I won't spoil which one it was, if either, but overall, the whole story just felt kind of bland and predictable.  Oh, that's their past?  Definitely didn't see THAT one coming.  Oh, so-and-so knew such-and-such and did the thing with the other thing?  You mean I wasn't supposed to have figured that out already?  The main route, at least the one I play, didn't really seem to do a whole lot to subvert your expectations, and I have to say, I wasn't THAT impressed with some of the dialogue my character was getting.  The relationship felt very sudden and rushed, and I found my immersion broken by disbelief.
Playthrough 2
Stopped trying to win.  Deliberately picked all of the options that sounded the worst.  Didn't get close to anyone.  Skipped through all the dialogue I'd heard before.  Ultimately ended up getting what I'm convinced is the most interesting route in the game.  No joke, I actually regretted the stupid name by the end of it because I'd actually gotten invested in the story all of a sudden.  The story WITHOUT the Trope Troupe.  It was a satisfying conclusion.  Stuff happened.  Information was learned.  Why wasn't I getting this level of storytelling in the main routes?  It's one thing to keep some tidbits to the side to encourage exploration, but this honestly felt more like the True Ending than any of the others.  Not only did it leave me eager for more to the story, but it answered the most plot threads, put me at the side of the most interesting character, and made me as the player feel like like a part of a bigger and more interesting story.  Talk about bizarre.  Not that I'm complaining, but it just seems bizarre.  It almost felt like this was the story the author was actually interested in telling, but someone demanded that they fill the main one with predictable tropes and forced them to bury the quality stuff where only a few adventurous souls would find it.
In any case, I reiterate that this game is free, can be downloaded quickly, and doesn't require a huge time commitment.  There's really no reason not to play at least one or two routes.  The voice acting is a little shaky at times, some of the writing is clunky, and some of the art is a bit on the cheap side, but, well, you can't argue with free.  For what it is, it's pretty decent, and while it's very flawed in many ways, I'm glad I did it.  I'll probably try to finish the rest of the routes, too.  I just hope they're a little less, err, obvious.

Vampire: The Masquerade-Bloodlines is a game fraught with problematic issues. Most egregious of its sins is the combat, with the melee combat being the equivalent of Grand Theft Auto: 3 fist fighting without the targeting feature, and the first-person shooting element handling like the first Deus Ex game, in the sense that your character cannot hit the broadside of a barn without staring at it for a full two seconds. Oh, and most of the boss battles are borderline broken, especially a particularly grating fight towards the end of the game, involving an amorphous horror (anyone who has played the game will know EXACTLY what I’m talking about). Stealth in the game IS broken, as not even the fully upgraded invisibility power will stop certain enemies from knowing precisely where you are at, although they might not attack you during the cloak.
Despite all of these flaws, I still found the game to be quite entertaining. Though the shooting bits are reminiscent of Deus Ex, so too are many aspects of this game. There are some fun dialogue choices, particularly if you play as a Malkavian character, and the game presents you with multiple paths to accomplish the various objectives. Fans of the pen and paper game will find that the experience system the game utilizes is faithful to its sire. While you cannot customize your character physically (appearance is determined by vampire clan), the ability upgrade system allows for some flexibility in regards to what kind of skills your vampire will excel at, with most of the skills being desirable at one point or another during game play. Mainline quests will almost always culminate in some sort of ridiculous boss fight, though, so remember to put some points in combat skills from time to time.
I would recommend this game for anyone who enjoyed Deus Ex, as there are many parallels that can be identified between the two games. Also, if you liked the White Wolf pen and paper game, you’ll probably find Vampire: The Masquerade-Bloodlines to be a fun experience. The game is certainly long, so you’ll get your moneys worth on game play time, even at its current retail price. I picked it up on sale during the 75% off deal, and am more than satisfied with my purchase. If you happen to see it on sale again, and the flaws that I mentioned don’t discourage you, snatch it up.

I would love to reccommend this game to everyone. You have no idea how much joy it would bring me to tell every PC gamer I know that there was another great Action RPG they never played. I want to like this game. I realllllllllly do. But I just can't ignore the fact that this game has problems, and I mean ALOT of problems. I'm not even going to touch on the fact that the game is basically unfinished and even modded out the bum, still glitchy as all hell. This game is HORRIBLY unbalanced in terms of RPG stats. Good luck finding any ammo if you built a gunfighter, cause a word of advice, in the first 3rd or so of the game, there isn't any. Good luck earning money to buy armor so you don't die from so much as a gnat brushing past your shoulder, because there isn't any. Money, I mean not gnats. Combat feels extremely clunky and unsatisfying. You can be an all powerful Vampire decked out with powers and holding a shotgun and easily takes down by a thug with a knife. While there are multiple solutions to problems, there arent enough given the large amount of skills present in the game. And don't be surprised when your silver-tounged computer whiz gets locked in a room with a giant blob monster you have to defeat. A blob monster only weak to edged weapons. As far as Action RPGs go, I would much more highly recommend Deus Ex, Fallout 3, or System Shock 2. Those games feel all around more complete and you aren't gritting your teeth the whole way through. However, I can definately see why it's considered a cult classic and beloved by a section of PC gamers. The RPG elements, while unbalanced, are incredibly deep and allow you to build a multitude of characters (even if most of them end up completely useless). The way the game immerses you into the rich setting and intresting story is really something to behold. Character Interactions in paticular are well done and allow you to complete conversations with completely diffrent outcomes, adding to replayability. It's just a shame the game was rushed out or it could've been one of the greatest of all time. But execution counts for everything, and unfourtanetly, this Vampire stepped out into daylight.

I like Tower Defense games, and I found this to be an enjoyable entry in the genre. There's a lot of management options throughout each battle: the ability to cast spells, to recall and replace units for better effect, and upgrade units on the fly. There are time acceleration/deceleration options to reduce the grind if you've got an efficient unit setup and just want to get the battle done, or for if things get intense and you need to suddenly micromange your setup.
You can also modify the experience bonuses/penalties for the game so that, if you don't have a lot of time to play, you can compress the game progression to reduce the grind even further. Frankly, it's an elegant and user-friendly setup for even the most casual of gamer.
The RPG element to this one is a nice twist, and there is a decent amount of replayability via the New Game+ mode.
But if there is anything which truly makes this game shine, it's the writing.
This game has made me laugh until my lungs protested, and has resulted in my replaying the game multiple times just for the dialogue.
I highly recommend it even at full price. And if you see it on special, grab it immediately.

Now that we have real reviews I wanted to give this game a better response.
As a long time tower defense player, I have to say this game is in the top 3 of all time. I'll try to explain why I love it so much, and why I'm so excited for the sequel that was recently announced.
Mechanics
This game provides somewhat traditional mechanics if you're familiar with TD games. Players can build units on the perimeter of the path only, so there is no blocking/routing mechanics to worry about. Unit's have different attack types that are better and worse for some situations
What is unique about this game is that units level up in a persistent manner between levels, allowing your units to grow over time, This included an entire skill tree for each class of units that can be customized to your play style. Additionally, units have a weapon and armor equipment slot and the game does a good job of making this meaningful by introducing rare equipment a bit later in the game.
Levels are replayable so you can grind your team a bit if you feel a little weak or would like to beef up a bit before a boss level. To compliment this aspect of the game, each level can be played on different difficulty levels, which provide bigger rewards at the cost of a higher difficulty. This aspect of the game kept me going back and trying to beat my records and old levels in order to get some of the better rare gear.
Lastly, the game features a fast forward mode which is a welcome sight for those who play a lot of tower defense games. It really helps grinding out those later levels.
Story
It's rare for a TD game to have an in-depth story, but Defender's Quest does a great job with this. It's not ground breaking, but it certainly sets a nice tone and even introduces a bit of moral dilemma that plays into the unit mechanics later in the game. I won't spoil it, but I will say that the level of narrative impressed me, and kept me engaged until the end.
Graphics/Sounds
All standard stuff here. You can look at the screenshots and get an idea of what you're into. In general I'd say that the graphics do a good job of matching the needs of the gameplay, and the animations are smooth and crisp even during hectic late game levels. The graphics change into a pleasant style during story segments and do a good job of relaying the emotion and facial expressions of the characters.
Summary
All in all, this game really scratched a Tower Defense/RPG itch that I'd been craving for a long time. If you can pick the game up on sale and like TD games I'd recommend buying it without hesitation.

This wasn't too well received by fans, mainly due to its length and the fact that it's all setup and no payoff. The concept of episodic gaming was pretty new at the time. The low price now, and the fact that you can play Episode Two right after if you like, means these aren’t big problems. It’s not bad, but it’s also not great. Maybe it’s just because I’m comparing it to the legendary Half-Life 2, but something is lacking.
On the surface at least, there’s very little that's new here. Most levels feel like they might have been abandoned during HL2’s development, and then adjusted slightly for this Episode (though I’m not saying that’s actually the case). No new locations, just new areas of locations we’ve already been in. No new weapons. There’s hardly even any new assets. There’s one new enemy... But, that’s it.
This episode has a focus on Alyx, her character development, and teamwork with her. They succeeded at that, and her AI is a lot better than the normal friendly NPCs. Or at the very least, she isn’t a burden. Since she’s such a great character, it’s a welcome change to go through game alongside her. It also took a darker tone (and darker levels in the literal sense) than HL2, which was originally supposed to be a darker game, and they were probably trying to explore that a little with this episode. So there are new things here, there’s just not a lot of substance to it.
Still, its 3-4 hours of your time, and it leads into the fantastic Episode Two. It's a perfectly adequate game, it's just not a very adequate follow-up to Half-Life 2.
