Fans of genres more Lovecraftian in nature will find themselves at home in this title, though I've seen it disputed in discussions here on Steam, so I will clarify: If you are familiar with Lovecraft outside of the Cthulhu Mythos (and even that, to a smaller degree is captured in a tale), there are some very notable atmospheric relations here that any fan of occult science-fiction will be able to pick up on. Without spoiling too much, if you imagine the protagonist of this game to be something of a young H.P. Lovecraft, perhaps you will see a more direct correlation.
MOVING ON!
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an absolutely beautiful game, with an abundance of textures in scenery that contribute to full-scale immersion that bring me back to travels I've personally explored out in nature. If you're able to max out this game and its offerings of visual options, please do so. The subtle nuances in tracking, texturing, reflections, and light filtering make it an entirely different experience altogether. I don't think I've stopped to take so many pictures in a game.
Similarly, the audio spectrum of this game weighs in just as heavily as its graphical counterpart, with ambient nature sounds that lends the atmosphere its heart; whereupon, the soundtrack gives it a soul. I wouldn't say the soundtrack on its own is by any means the greatest soundtrack I've heard in a game, but it does a great job of bringing the mood without working against the background sound effects (which I find to be one of the more important elements for this explorative-type game).
The gameplay is relatively simple, there aren't any difficult control layouts to remember. You walk, and you click. There is a lot of ground to cover in this game, so I wouldn't recommend breezing from path to path in search of the obvious, or you will miss a lot of what this experience provides the player. In my total time playing, (11-13 hours at typing this?), I think I could say that I covered every inch of the map in 8-10 hours of gameplay.
The gameplay mechanics as far as puzzles and interaction goes is pretty straightforward, if you're willing to take the time to take the visual cues offered to you. As most of this game is meant to have you solving a mystery, I personally like that it doesn't hold your hand and walk you through "how to" solve any of the puzzles. The game starts, you're in the woods and you're there to figure out what happened independently from the get-go.
The game is comprised of several mini-mysteries. I can't say specifically how long they each took me to complete, but because of the lack of a proper save element in this game (that I will expound upon shortly), I would recommend completing this game in the same way that you would approach reading a book-- by "chapters." It isn't what I would call "linear," although, it does follow a loose-woven path and so not every area is open immediately to explore-- some puzzle-solving will be required to open buildings and paths.
The game is branded in some places as a "horror," although I can only think of one time I was horrified because I am a person who loves to hate jumpscares. There is only one occurrence of that in the entire game, and the puzzle is relatively simple... just something pants-shattingly petrifying about knowing a spoopy monster is going to pop out at you. People that hate jumpscares will hate this tiny part of the game. It didn't ruin it for me, but it was so unexpected that I couldn't properly solve the puzzle without running and clicking, hoping for it all to end.
The worst criticism I've seen this game receive is that you can't drop-down and save it. You have to reach a point or engage an event where the game will auto-save; however, there is a workaround if you really need to log. Most of the solved events (most notably, places where you've emerged from solving a mystery) have an item that triggers an auto-save, like reading a certain document. Not perfect, but if you need to go in a pinch, there you go. This is why I would say gauge the time you want to spend on this game and play in "chapters" or story-by-story.
You shouldn't NEED to backtrack too much, unless you plan to 100% this game, as one of the achievements is actually a partial bit that didn't make it into the whole game, it's on you to go back and put that all together. (It's not an entirely rewarding achievement if you're content otherwise.)
After completing the game, I can say I'm moderately happy with my experience playing. The characters were not amongst the best written, but the protagonist more than makes up for it in his constructed tales as they unfold the story. I can't say that I would play this again anytime soon, due to the length and the simplicity of the puzzles, but I did enjoy playing it through the first time.
As far as monetary value, I know I got this game on sale, maybe for 10 bucks? I'd definitely pay $10 or $15-- $20 is a stretch, but if I sit and really consider how much heart went into this game, I would if I knew how much I'd enjoy this game.

First Take: It is a good, great game & it comes highly recommended! I found that the "Redux" version fixed the things that I thought were bad about the original Metro 2033 in a satisfactory way. The storyline is excellent, like Activision's CoD:BO2, & the gameplay is fun & engaging. The gun customization mechanic is neat & makes sense. The monsters are sufficiently scary such that there is definitely a dark feeling to it. That being said, it won't get to you the way that the new DOOM4 will, but then again that is a high-budget game from 2016 made by Id Software, so, there you have it. There isn't anything satanic or any cruddy factories in it, so, that's something
Comparisons: much like Resident Evil 6, it has sort of a sci-fi/horror/adventure feel to it. It is in first-person perspective, not third-person like RE6, so there's a difference there. Half-Life 2 by Valve is even more sci-fi inspired than this title. Metro2033Redux is MUCH better than the absolutely terrible Enemy Territory: Quake Wars game. It is much like the germanic Wolfenstein: The New Order, but with a more inspirational tone whereas Wolfenstein:TNO is more of a "Nazi-Killing Commando" kind of FPS.
Age: it holds up well for something that came out in 2010 (2014 for the redux version) as there is a good & engaging plot. I believe it is based on a book. Much of the game takes place in the twilight hours of the day, the evening. Anyways, it is coherent & makes sense & there are impactful rewards to making it long-term through major chunks of the game, unlike in Valve Inc's CS:GO which feels the same throughout. That's not so terrible as it is very well thought out, in any case, but that is not as satisfying in the long haul.
Rating: 10/10 Stars, well worth getting, especially nowadays as it can be had for essentially nothing ($20 or $10 or something like that, not a whole ton). It is the best story-driven FPS of that vintage that I have ever played. Go get it! It goes well with a Monster energy drink & a McDonald's #1 Meal. After a long day on the clean room floor it is nice to play something fun & adventerous. My girlfriend thinks I play too many of these but oh well, they are a good time.

I would go far enough to say this game is culturally insensitive. And then some. LIke holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is it culturally insensitive. This one doesn't go out of it's way to say the Werhmacht or SS Panzer Divisions were okay and did nothing wrong but in fact seems to go the opposite direction entirely for Soviet Russia. And the campaign suffers for it, greatly. The cutscenes between missions are essentially about how war is pointless, bloody and horrific. This is kind of a weird message for a game that is literally glorifying the people who fought in the battles in world war two. Where the previous game's campaigns seemed to have this air of grim necessity, we're not so different you and I but we just happen to be on the wrong sides kind of deal between the factions presented, not necessarily glorifying war but definitely not advocating peaceful solutions.
This is my problem. The whole notion of war sucks is kind of hard to put across when your whole game is prominently featuring war. It's especially hard when the game is essentially rewarding you for being good at it in most cases. I say most cases because almost every campaign mission in the Russian campaign pretty much ends with "you lost" or "you were supposed to lose here" or "your effort was pointless."It emphasizes that no matter what you do your decisions are going to equate to tens, hundreds or thousands of lives lost. It showcases your superiors being incompetent or unfair in setting your objectives. This is an interesting thing that doesn't seem to appear in a lot of war games, the fact that you always have someone you answer to when you're in an actual military.
As frustrating as it is as a player, it's somewhat admirable as a story writer. I just think it's the kind of message that would be better suited for a movie or a novel or something.
Oh wait, they did that, it's called Enemy at the Gates. There's not a single moment where the Russian campaign every deviates from that movie's portrayal of the red army. CoH has never really been 100% historically accurate but really?
The other funny thing is the American campaign is a complete 180: it emphasizes the importance of carefully managing your troops so they don't die, as you have a little counter that represents how many troops you've lost over the campaign thus far.
So, to recap, this game is saying the following: WW2 America is good and can do nothing wrong and cares about the lives of it's men, WW2 German Army and Nazis are just answering the 'call of duty' if you will and represent an effective fighting force full of people who might be good but are just caught up on the wrong side, and WW2 Russia is grossly incompetent, doesn't care about it's losses and sometimes actively causes them by shooting whole squads of men in the middle of combat for 'cowardice' (like retreating slightly) and is apparently perfectly okay with all of this.
So the campaign is annoying. The American campaign is slightly better. If you can get past that or just play it skirmish / online it's a fairly fun RTS and will serve nicely to replace CoH1 as the obligatory WW2 themed game on your steam list. Oh yeah, and the Co-Op mode missions are less annoying because they have less plot and are specifically a thing unto themselves, which is cool.

RPG elements mostly revolve around your towers leveling up in a persistant way.  In addition you buy things like weapons and armor for your towers. It has the same fallbacks as other TD games, monotony being the main one.  You have to grind out levels and money to make yourself more powerful, but the game has an awesome options menu that gives you the option to speed up exp gain for units in and out of combat, as well as speeding up monetary gain, all without flagging yourself as a cheater, or denying yourself awards. The Room Two is a great little puzzle game. While it is somewhat short like its predecessor (You'll most likely finish it in a few hours), the experience of the game itself is worth the small outlay, especially during Steam's sales.
Graphically, the game is visually beautiful. At times, the graphics of the game can be distracting as you find yourself admiring the detail of the environment and objects within. One tip though is the game does not select the graphic detail with respect to your computer so be sure to crank up the graphics quality when you start as it defaults to the lowest setting.
The game is relatively straight forward but will make you think a bit. Unlike the first one, this game feels slightly less linear in its approach to solving the puzzles, whereby the contents of the room contain multiple puzzle pieces, whereas the first focused mostly on the boxes on the tables. This game had me stumped only once but that was because I missed a somewhat subtle hint as to something I was missing, after clicking everything else in the room multiple times.
The story itself I felt was rather bland and somewhat pointless. It sort of tied it all together but after a while of working your way through the puzzles, it veered more towards noise than engaging.
In terms of puzzles, you will need to think outside the box a few times and be sure to explore the environment around you. They aren't all difficult; some are somewhat easy. All the clues are there in front of you, sometimes (frustratingly) staring you right in the face.
If you enjoy puzzle games that don't hold your hand the whole way through, you'll enjoy The Room Two. If you haven't played The Room (first one) either, pick both of them up and enjoy the ride.

I'm not saying the game is bad but I personally just can't get into it. The game is played by you making jumps from one system/planet to another while the rebel fleet chase you down, which is fine but each jump can literally be game over and so its a glorified mine sweeper.
Its a game someone can watch you play and it will seem exciting but the reality is that the base concept of the game is dull and the metagame of maximizing scrap so you can run the typical build order also dull for example;
No matter what, if you are in sector 1, then get 2 shields.
Sitting still against an enemy that has no hopes of getting through your shields, is a good idea for skill level ups.
Kill everyone and everything because then you get more scrap.
So on and so forth.
I don't feel like I need to adapt to whats going on, just that I am going through the motions again and again. Every single time I deviated from the 'plan' such as trying a new weapon or going for a different build order, I get killed. As long as I do the same thing over and over during the early turns, I will be fine. You don't even need to take my word for it as if you are reading this on steam then you can just go to the guides section and they will explain exactly the same thing. It is the illusion of choice because there is only 1 way to build your ship in the early game if you want to survive the late game.
The games music drones on comepletely ignoring current events and is otherwise unremarkable. I don't feel like the USS enterprise or other space fantasy captains, the music sounds disjointed from the game and just sounds generic. Normally I wouldn't point this out except for the fact the soundtrack is sold seperately, save your money.
You need to get scrap in order to do aything such as upgrade your ship or buy shop parts, but those are random so you can only buy what you are lucky enough to get, just like a deck building card game. I don't really mind because that is also the nature of rogue-likes but what I do mind is that you can die very quickly in sector 1 because your
jump is a rebel ship that just
to counter your ship perfectly. Its rare but it does happen. Later on after sector 1, enemy ships seem to just "randomly" have subsystems that perfectly counter your build which also leads to the wonderful metagame of gaming the game and that seems to be all the guides and all the videos I watched about this game. If you want to deviate from the cookie cutter build then you just have to 'trick' the game and that gets really boring.
The last boss is the perfect example of 'gaming the game'. If you kill the crew in regular fights then you win. Against the last boss this isn't the case, instead the last boss gets
! So instead you kill everyone except the one person who mans the lasers because lasers can't hurt you if you have your shields up meaning you can kill that form of the last boss at your leisure.
Last boss has 3 forms by the way, because why wouldn't it. No you don't heal in between rounds, its a 'rogue-like' so its supposed to be "hard". The game has potential and free DLC was also made for the game which is always great. Overall I recommend this game simply because if you don't like the game, you will very easily find out very, very quickly in time to get a refund and if you do like the game then you don't really care what I, or anyone else says. For me personally I would like it if the game encouraged experimentation. So many builds or weapon combos are just going to get you killed and its infuriating that such suicidal options are even incuded.

I had much higher hopes for this game, and was definitely disappointed by the game, but it's still not a bad game. I was hoping for a game with mystery, atmopshere, adventure, excitement, horror, paranormal, etc. This game was less than I expected. You basically spend the game walking around solving puzzles and searching giant environments for a few objects, just like other adventure games. There is really no player interaction and really any action at all. There is 1 tense/scary part and that is about it. The game feels quite empty.
I did love the atmosphere. The visuals and feel of the area are some of the best I have ever seen, and this game was made for screenshots. The areas are varied and the graphics are decent. The crime solving can be fun sometimes with observations made by your character. Sometimes solving the order of events and finding objects can feel intuitive and you enjoy it. Other times the scenes used for the order involve a person standing there by themselves, or 1 scene has a new person none of the others do, and since it's just a still you cannot possibly gain an idea of what happened enough to put things in order. The game does this with clues. Sometimes you have to wonder off in a tiny area to find something. Like adventure games, if you don't find all the puzzles, and every object/clue and trigger every event, you can't beat the game. This means you'll prolly use a walkthrough, because of how big and open environements are, and there is no help from the game at all. The game says it doesn't "hold your hand" but in reality they are just being obtuse and  poor with some object placement and scene solving just to make it harder for no reason.
The game is short. The story is interesting to begin with and you are invested in what happens, and without spoiling anything, the ending is kind of a dud. So the best part of the game is the environment and visuals, with some interest from the story. The gameplay is the same ol boring item find/puzzle solve of an adventure game, with walkthrough needing for some parts, but does have a few new novel mechanics to use.
Touching story, looks fantastic, doesn't overstay its welcome, great sound, intuitive and non-intrusive puzzle gameplay; the Vanishing of Ethan Carter gets my recommendation.

I bought this game during the Steam Summer sale of 2016. I've had my eye on this game for a while and finally pulled the trigger. I got the game + all dlc bundle and it was worth it! It's not necessary to have all the DLC but it does give you more options for weapons and stratagems (defensive / offensive support call ins).
The graphics are really nice and the game runs very smooth. You can play alone, with friends or just join a mission that is already started. It's like most games where there is a leveling system in place. You're character levels up with all the XP you gather from missions. Through leveling up, you earn weapon and stratagem unlocks to use in game. You also gather up "research points" which are used to unlock weapon add-ons or used to make any of your stratagems more effective (or stronger.)
There is friendly fire to be aware of where you aim, shoot, throw grenades or stare your vehicle because you will end up killing a friendly. Neither party will lose any XP for friendly fire but you do have to call in reinforcements and during heating battles on the higher level missions, it becomes a chore trying to get to a safe enough spot to call in the reinforcements.
Overall this is a really fun game to play. I do suggest getting the DLC, although it isn't needed to play with others. Just adds to the overall experience of the game.
My one issue with the game so far is the fact that you can't run off screen from the other players and do your own thing or just because you need to retreat from the enemy in a different direction from your team mates. So you're essentially bound to the same area as your team mates and can't wander off.

Rhythm game meets old-school turn-based RPG. This is every bit as peculiar as it sounds. The music is slick, much of it licensed from capable hands such as the wonderful Ronald Jenkees, and the gameplay can be quite punishing on higher difficulty levels. I would recommend playing this game witha controller, and indeed have not checked if it is possible (or enjoyable) without.
You'll be switching between three sets of scrolling DDR style arrows: one for incoming damage that is blocked by accurate hits, another (typically containing the most difficult pieces of the song) recharges your Mana pool on accurate hits, and a third for spells. Spells are cast with the right analog stick, which (after a delay) sends down a specific rhythmic snippet that changes it's tempo to fit the current song (the specific direction of arrows changes every time you cast, and the difficulty level also changes the spells, making the more complicated versions of the same basic rhytmic idea).
The game has you madly flying between these screens to defeat enemies before the song ends--it's one wierd, wild ride and it's well worth it. Battles are tense and fascinating, and there's a lot of room for varied play styles in your spell collection of choice as well as a lot of room for growth within the broad difficulty span. There's even a practice mode where you can just play through the full songs in a more standard rhthym game format. Highly recommended.

It expands on what Civ 4 did correctly and got rid of many of Civ 4's flaws.
Unfortunately, the AI is a massive failure. I've lost units to City-States and barbarians more often than the normal AI, which is kind of disappointing. The AI literally never uses aircraft and their navy is often dismal. Turning up the difficulty sometimes gets me outmanuevered politically, but the AI military remains decrepit. This is a far cry from Civ 4's sneak attacks, world wars, and battleground regions. I can fight 1v8 against the AI and win. Easily. How is that reasonable?
When I tried to mod the game's AI, the modding feature crashed the game at random. I own all the expansions and patches so you would expect this to be fixed.
All in all it's a great game but with a massive deficit. If you like city building, road planning, political battles, etc., then perhaps give it a try. But if you like warfare and tactics like me, this is probably not the game for you.
P.S. I purchased Civ 6 and its AI was somehow even worse.
2017 UPDATE:

The game is quite old, so the graphics are not all that. You will also need to download a fan-made patch to make it work properly, but once that's sorted the game works just fine.
You get to choose one out of seven clans, your gender, and if you want - a backstory. All of these will have an impact on your playthrough, and gives you a lot of diversity to play with. Each clan has different abilities and traits. Sadly, you don't get to customise your appearance though, it's set by your sex and clan.
The dialogue options allows you to voice your opinion, often in a rude way. The game gives you the options you need to go around and be an a-hole to everyone, and you can of course lick butt if that's more of your style. There will also be unique dialogue options based off your clan, stats and abilities.
As you play through the game you will eventually be part of a story of politics, intrigue, and the fight for power and gain in the city. You will get to choose through your actions the outcome of this struggle, which I found very satisfying as you can make the ending of the game directly reflect your opinion on the conflicting factions of LA. There is no black and white answer here, as all these factions could be considered bad in different ways.
All in all it's a good experience, and I highly recommend it.

*note: as of when this review is being written, my steam profile says i have 0.2 hours in the game.  I have played the disk version for well over a thousand hours, and only own this game on steam because it was part of a humble bundle i got.
Everyone has the game that makes them into a pc gamer.  Maybe you occasionally played some mario on your family's nintendo console, but there is the one game that makes them realize how awesome video games can be.
For me, that game is Star Wars Battlefront 2.
Allow me to explain the road to me playing this game.  For at least a year, I played the original Battlefront weekly at my church's youth group.  Some there who had played this said the second was so much better, and that i should play it sometime.  My first experience playing The second battlefront came when my family visited our cousins in Malaysia.  My cousin owned it on ps2, so we gave it a try.
My first reaction to this game?  I hated it.  My 13-year-old brain thought it added too much, making a simple and fun game into a nightmare of random buttom-pushing.  I didn't change my mind on that untill that next year, when we visited my cousins again.  I tried it woth cousin again and for some reason,  I loved it!  I started to appreciate the new content; the heroes, the new maps, the story mode.  I loved it so much i bought it for pc.
Once i started playing in mid-july, it was all I did for the entire summer up untill the week before school started, when i bought some more star wars games because of how good this was, but i'm getting ahead of myself.
You may be asking, how did this game, with only 26 maps and 5 game modes, keep me coming back for a month and a half?  The answer is mods.  This game is the best example of a thriving mod community;  if you check the moddb page for this game, there are still tons of mods being created.  The mods make this game into an epic experience, from the overpowered republic commandoes in the battlefront: republic commando mod to the KOTOR era, maps and heroes from the conversion pack.
In short, buying this game is a must for anyone who likes epic games with a lot of content.  It is my favourite game ever and is the reason I am a gamer.

I absolutely love Defender's Quest Valley of the Forgotten. When I read tower defence rpg I was a little lost. I have never heard of the two being combined and wondered how it could be done.
The rpg side of this game is based around the story of Azra; Azra is a royal librarian who found herself in the forgotten zone - a plague ridden part of the kingdom and things went crazy. Along the way Azra met people to aid her in her journy to find out what is going on. People like Slak and khetti (names can be changed I kept them default though). the players met along your journy become your towers and placed in a standard tower defence way, slak for example is a berserker who slashes and slaughters light hp targets, and khetti is an archer. The characters are leveld up over time so the player can equip them with gear and put points into skills such as slaks flurry to hit 5 targets at once.
Now back to Azra; since the game revolves around her what role does this librarian play. Well in combat you are summoned to the spirit world to kill the plague ridden posessed citizens. Azra levels up with your characters so she can cast damage spells, buffs, and heals to your people during combat. The heal is very advantagous because your people will die. . . HOWEVER they can be resummoned. To prevent deaths one of the options is to equip them with armor which can be purchased and unlocked at certain points in the game along with other mercenaries.
overall I rate this game 5/5  due to the 5 dollar sale price during steam weekly sale and the unique story and combat. The game also supports the steam workshop so that you can continue the game with player made levels which I have not tried yet.
For the cons of this game I have not found any but some players might be turned off by the non applicable voice acting, all of the narrating is texted out.

This and Last Light Redux are probably two of the best games I've ever played.
I will be honest, the gun sounds are pretty bad. And also the gun animations in survival mode look like they've just been slowed down to half speed instead of actually changed. And I'm not going to pretend that the stealth is any real challenge. The graphics are aging just a tad. Oh, and you have to edit a config file to change the FOV.
But that's pretty much it.
I wanted to start off by outlining the differences in plot between 2033 and Last Light. 2033 feels more like this grand adventure you're going on - find the mysterious Spartan Order, destroy the Dark Ones, and save humanity. Last Light focuses on you discovering the true effects of your actions and eventually turns into a quest for redemption. The result is heartbreaking - playing both games back to back (which I highly recommend) was probably one of the most emotionally draining experiences I've had in my life.
This game (henceforth, "this game" means both 2033 and Last Light combined) has the best atmosphere I've ever seen. Half Life 2 comes somewhat close. The game does an incredible job of illustrating the level of hopelessness and despair humanity finds itself in, with people being slaughtered in scores by mutants they cannot possibly defeat. You will find a child crying over his uncle's dead body, you will be part of a station's last stand against a horde of mutants, and you will find the dead bodies of other humans littered across the wasteland. The game also shows the other side of the Metro, where people can get a few drinks at a bar and have a good time. All of this is reflected in Artyom's diary, conveying his internal thoughts in a way that adds so much more to the game.
I also wanted to talk for a bit about Ranger difficulty. Despite sounding very basic - no HUD, less ammo, you and enemies do more damage - it honestly adds so much to the game. The first time I played this game was via family share on a friend's account. I initially decided to opt out of Ranger mode. I got about 1/4 of the way through 2033 and Last Light before I decided that it just felt like a regular FPS. So a couple years later I decided to give it another chance, this time playing on Ranger mode. And it honestly changes everything. It feels like you're really there, mainly due to the insanely good atmosphere, which also makes the story and setting that much more believable. The game simply feels like it was designed from the ground-up to be played on Ranger difficulty.
Some smaller things. While the guns don't sound good, they do feel good. They have a somewhat realistic kick which makes shooting mutants and enemy humans feel meaty and realistic. Items are hidden well, which requires you to spend some time scrounging for ammunition and gas mask filters. The scarcity of ammo requires you to sometimes be stealthy or sometimes just run away from enemies, which adds to the atmosphere even more. Some of the weapons are very unique - some of the crazier ones include an LMG refitted to fire shotgun rounds, an automatic harpoon gun, and even a (rare) railgun.
If you can only buy one game right now, I would say buy Metro 2033 so you don't spoil it's storyline by skipping to the second game in the series. If you can, buy both games and play them back to back on Ranger difficulty, as it is absolutely worth the 30 dollars.

Remember company heroes online? This is pretty much the same game with the same nuiscances. faction inbalance, worse graphics then original coh+expansion. and loads of annoying cashshop content.
Cut to the chase. Most people will play for this for multiplayer. Currently the multiplayer gameplay is very unbalanced especially larger 4vs4 maps. This has to do with simply with faction units. Tank destroyers are easier to destroy then soviet halftracks. Vetted conscripts gets blown to bit by volkgrenadier with 2 bazookas. Ally Snipers take 7 seconds to fire taking them ages to kill support units they are designed to kill, its a joke.
The huge unit balance issues forces you to use specific doctrines which are commanders you can purchase in the cash shop or be lucky enough to find in game. So if your playing Soviets you literally have to go commander that gives you shermans as all your tanks are useless even your unique special tanks wgucg are essentially inferior german panther tanks. If your playing American you have to go commander that gives callopies because the german strategy in this game is simply spam bazooka infantry then tank.
And thats one of the main problems with coh 2 is that it encourages blobbing and spamming 1 or 3 units, Company of heroes franchise differentated itself from other rts franchises like starcraft in that it wasnt a macro spam blob game. Which ultimately makes for boring gameplay. Gone are the epic plays and comebacks of company of heroes where for example your playing axis and decide to build tier 2 volkgrenadies with heavy machine guns to kill a rifleman spammer riflemen right outside your base.
Unit balance issues is one of the reasons coh 2 has worst gameplay then its predecessor but the second reason is that they removed lot of secondary structures like bunkers or mines you can build and tied them to specific factions. Also capturing points for attrittion purpuses is dumbed down and pointless in this coh as everyone gets the same manpower rate and cap.  These core changes to the game dumb down the gameplay and get rid of what made company heroes unique compared to other rts games.
I suggest not playing company of heroes 2 and install instead old rts games like lords of magic 2 or age of empires xD. Cheap games on steam and simple fun where you only have to spam like 2 units.  Because thats essentially what your doing with coh 2 but without the annoyances and loss of dignity as a former coh fan.

This is actually a very interesting RPG game. It has DDR-style arcade action which is well distributed in a very challenging format between protecting yourself, casting spells, and regaining mana; all done separately. The first few monsters weren't so tough to battle, but after the next couple levels in, it gets right down to pure skill and let me tell you, it gets rough. You need to be on your feet and have good hand/eye coordination to get the right buttons down quick enough.
Oh yeah, and the music isn't half-bad either.

If I had heard someone say they were going to make an RPG that used Dance Dance Revolution as a combat system, I would have checked to make sure someone hadn't switched out my coffee for decaf, because there's no way something like that could actually happen.  And yet, this game exists.
I'm not going to lie, there is a bit of a learning curve at first, but once you adjust to the (surprisingly smooth) concept of managing three different DDR boards at once, all in different fashions and priorities, the game really flows well.  The story is interesting, and the descriptions and names of the items you get really show how much the developers enjoyed making the game.  Speaking of the devs, they read the credits at the end, which plays out as more of a DVD commentary than a bland credit list.  This was actually the first time I've really cared about a credit sequence for anything, ever, so props to them for that.

Twin-stick shooters have a special place in my heart. My first one was Geometry Wars on the Xbox 360. Yes, it was free. And the trial version if I'm not wrong (damn that thing was last played years ago). But I liked the frantic action and the deceivingly simple controls. Which is why I was interested in this. Picking up Hero Siege fairly recently got me back into these type of games and I didn't regret picking this one up. Very fun mix of furious blasting of alien scum and a bit of team coordination make this an enjoyable experience. Graphics are cool too, with it's own unique artstyle. I liked the whole idea of "dropping feet first into hell" ala Helljumpers from Halo. Badass and packing huge firepower, but still human and fragile. The guns and weaponry are awesome, and offer a selection to send the enemies to hell. There's also vehicles like mechs and tanks. Another thing is the button minigame implemented when you want to activate something, kinda like a mini para-para kind of mechanic. Up, up down down on the D-Pad...That sort of thing. Which means under fire you're supposed to do this.... Damn. The pressure's on. With only an hour or two on the clock, I can't criticise the grind some of the guys here bash the game on. So far so good.
One major aspect of this game: Friendly fire. Not only from others, but yourself. Sending a pod down? Mind the impact. Your boys letting loose a hail of gunfire? Might wanna duck. Evac dropship inbound? Stay clear. So many ways to die other than getting torn apart by enemies.
TL;DR if you wanna be a badass ODST and send the enemies of mankind packing through sheer firepower get this game. Bonus points if you get your mates in on the action too. The 4 man squad system is perfect in its size. Just mind the bump.
Gaunlet-esque gameplay with fun customization for different playstyles and many different missions to grind through. This game can get incredibly difficult and they fully embrace the friendly fire.

While it could be properly considered a "Walking Simulator" TVOEC plays more as a crime/supernatural investigation where the player is actively involved in searching for clues. All plot elements were properly foreshadowed if you found the right "readable elements" and is a pretty engrossing while not being too-short or too-long.
The creators have claimed to have been inspired in some elements by the Lovecraftian Mythos, and I can definitely say that it delivers on that promise.
Price point: While a little high, would you see a movie about a paranormal detective solving an X-File in a small northeastern town? If you'd pay for the movie ticket at that price, you should pick up the game as well.

Half-Life 2: Episode One begine right where Half-Life 2 ended, and continues the story of Dr.Gordon Freeman in City 17, however, this time, the priority remains to escape the city following the events of Half-Life 2.
With updated lighting and AI for deuteragonist Alyx Vance, and expanded usage for the Gravity Gun, Half-Life 2: Episode One continues Half-Life 2's usage of advanced graphics, physics, music and writing to create a game that is both rich in gameplay, plot, and emotion. Like its predecessor, it uses training techniques to allow for a more fluid experience, and utilizes the game's physics engine to a full. With excellent performances by its cast, it's able to greatly explain the story of Gordon and Alyx escaping City 17.
With an excellent soundtrack composed by Kelly Bailey, the game becomes even more action packed, and the act of blasting zombies in an infected hospital with a shotgun becomes far more enjoyable, and the scene of fighting infected Combine soldiers in the underground becomes more threatening.
The game also includes Developer commentary in the form of a commentary mode that allows the players to listen to the developers' thoughts on everything from map design to character and scene writing, and includes all variant of Valve Employee sharing their thoughts on the game.
If I had to say I had any issues with the game, I'd have to say that it's fairly short, while Half-Life 2 is around 12-15 hours long, Episode One is around 5 hours long. That's not to say it's a bad game for that, though, as the story and game runs at a certain pace that allows for it to be enjoyed to the fullest; Replaying the game with the knowledge of how short it is doesn't damage or reduce the enjoyment of playing it, as Valve injects a great deal of fun into the game so there aren't many moments or time that is wasted, and every minute is used to its fullest.
If you enjoyed Half-Life 2, and want more, I greatly suggest you buy the Half-Life Complete Steam bundle, preferably during a Steam Seasonal Sale. The bundle consists of this game and every other Valve-released Half-Life title, and is an essential for a fan of Half-Life.

tl;dr This game is awesome if you like online co-op and are willing to pay for some DLC.
1. The bad part: the base game is fine for a brief bit of co-op fun, but if you want the game to have any lasting potential some of the DLC is
. In particular you will need: Ranger, Pilot, Demolitionist, Entrenched, and Terrain Specialist. The game is playable without these, but you will really struggle on the harder difficulties. I think that's a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥ of the developers to do, but if you're okay with the extra cost then it's definitely worth it.
2. For some reason when I bought this I assumed that this was a linear story-based action game like Magicka. It is not. It's more like Left 4 Dead where you just jump in for a few standalone co-op missions. You can play it single player, but it's really not as fun. The game sort of has a structure with its "galatic war", but that has almost no impact on the game other than deciding which enemy factions are available to fight.
3. The online community is surprisingly friendly and helpful. I've had almost no trouble with toxic players or trolls. At first I only played single player and local coop because I generally find random internet people annoying, but now I always let random players join my games and it pretty consisently leads to fun experiences.
4. The unlocks are a bit of a grind. Judging from my progress so far and from my friends who play I'd estimate that it takes about 120 hours to unlock everything (if you have all DLC). The saving grace is that you choose what to unlock first and the list of "essential" unlocks is actually pretty short, so it really doesn't impact the game that much. I'd estimate that you can unlock all of the really awesome items by about 40 hours, but most of those are only essential at the highest difficulties, which you'll need to work up to anyway.

I usually don't like RPG's in the slightest.  The idea is cool: you get to create a character (whether it's based off you, a friend, an alternate persona, or a total joke), hurl them face-first into an adventure and circumstanes out of their control, and you go about it your own way.  The problem is you really only usually end up as the valiant hero or a cartoonishly evil villain (who still, all evil aside, mostly does what the hero would have done, until the final cutscene, at least).  Bloodlines does something different.  It throws you straight into a world where it's everyone for themselves.  There are no good guys, and hell, there really aren't any bad guys.  There's you, some friends (if you even care to have any), and a bunch of greedy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who are willing to stop at nothing to get their way, and you just happen to be in it.  In order to surive, you're going to have to claw your way up the rungs of vampire society, using whatever powers and connections you have at your disposal.  The big dogs boss you around, and you have to bide your time to either take them down or join their side.  In short, this game is GRIMY, and I love it for that.  Just that fact got me to overlook any sort of bugginess (sp?) as well as the out-dated graphics.
Not that the gameplay is bad, quite the opposite.  You don't get experience for killing enemies at all, you just get it for completing assignments (there are special bonuses for doing things a certain way on some missions, and I actually think, funny enough, you CAN get a bonus or two for murdering EVERYBODY).  This means you can talk, sneak, fight, or even hypnotize your way to victory.
You can even be completely insane and have conversations with your television.
No.  Seriously.  You can.
If you're looking for a RPG whose story is dirtier (not essestially darker, as in swearing every five minutes coupled with unnecessarily dramatic ultra-violence), whose feel is raunchier, and its overall mindset is cynical and snide, than this is the game for you.
Just make sure to look for the patches.  It is time consuming (and rather neccessary), but a quick Google search will get you on the right track (all the patching is my only real gripe with the game, tbh).

This is my review on the 1st of the 2 Metro Reduxes.
The gameplay in this game is quite fun. The menus throughout this game are simple and easy to use, so swapping weapons or throwables, or even checking the amount of time left you have on your filters is a breeze, which helps when you're on the battlefield. The weapon combat is fun as all hell. Pick up a gun, and fire, just be sure to watch your ammo. On harder difficulties, the ammo for some weapons is much more rare than others, so ammo conservation is key. As the ammo is rare, the currency,(coincidentally ammo), is also rare, which increases the need for the ammo conservation. Getting back to the gunplay, the weapons are good, there are a great deal of weapons to choose from, some bad, some good. The customisation for weapons may be limited, but the upgrades that do come are brilliant, as they can sometimes be the difference between life and death. Sometimes, when you run out of ammo, you are forced to use your throwables, be them molotovs or pipe bombs, they are sure to get the job done. No matter where you are, you are bound to find them, so stocking up is recommended.
You are artyom. Born days before the apocolypse started, taking most of humanity with it, you were moved into the underground Metros, as many others were to seek refuge.
With this, the story begins, and you travel to polis to report the situation in Exhibition. The game ends as it begun, with a cutscene, and you close the game. You proceed to open Metro: Last Light Redux for the second half of the story.
The graphics in this game are brilliant, With a good computer, you can easily run this. Some textures are good, some bad, and there is one setting that brings down the FPS heavily on any computer, and that is the SSAA. That ♥♥♥♥s your FPS harder than a Dump Truck running over your foot. I keep forgetting about this option when I reinstall the game, so be sure to take some time to lower it. There isnt a set balance to what looks good and what doesn't, it randomly changes, sometimes all good, sometimes all bad, sometimes in between. The Good and Bad dont have much difference though, so a low setting can look as good as a high one, with FPS to spare.
Overall, I would recommend this game, and the Sequel, Metro: Last Light. A solid 8.5/10 for this one folks. I appreciate your reading, and will recommend my Second review of the series on the afforementioned

Helldivers is a one-to-four player, top-down twin-stick shooter that cleaves itself from average title in the subgenre with its heavy emphasis on squad tactics, careful aim and preperation. It's a slower, more methodical kind of twin-stick game. You have a large degree of control over your character in-game beyond just moving and shooting: you can sprint, dive to prone, use simple voice commands (yes, no, wait and go) and even pick yourself back up when you are downed if no one else is nearby. Allies can shoot over you safely while you are prone, and you will avoid incoming fire and some explosive damage. Careful management of your resources is necessary: You have limited reloads for your guns and you even lose the ammuntion left in a magazine if you reload before one is empty. This PC version of the game is an excellent port, adding text chat, better netcode, and other quality-of-life improvements not present in the original Playstation versions, and includes the three free content expansions.
You are part of the Helldivers, the elite shock troops of the comically imperialistic federation of Super Earth, deployed via drop pods behind the lines of a galactic war to spread "managed democracy" to humanity's enemies: the Bugs, the Cyborgs, and the Illiuminate (in ascending order of how annoying they are to fight). The game lacks a true story mode, instead being based around procedurally-generated levels with a random assortment of simple objectives, such as capture a point, escort civilians, or destroy a key enemy structure. While on missions, you can find pickups that add to your "research count", every ten adds one point that you may use outside missions to purchase permanent upgrades for your weapons and gear. Once all objectives are complete, or at least resolved, an extraction beacon becomes available that once activated, will bring in an escape shuttle after a set timer.
Helldivers has a whopping twelve difficulty levels, from "A Dive in the park" to "Helldive", with each level increasing the number and types of enemies you face, as well as the number of objectives to complete, research pickups to find, and experience earned. You have a considerable arsenal at your disposal thanks to a number of DLCs and unlocks earned by leveling. You can carry a pistol, primary weapon, one perk, and a choice of four "Strategems", call-ins activated through directional button inputs, almost in the manner of a fighting game move. I'm not too fond the input mechanic, but their variety and effectiveness is unquestionable: support weapons and equipment that you can pick up and use, artillery, air and orbital strikes, deployable bombs, vehicles including mechs and APCs, and defenses such as automated sentry guns and minefields. There are so many loadout options that each player in a game can equip a completely different setup. Some cosmetic customization is available in the form of different helmets, armors and capes, and you may also choose your diver's gender: this effects only voice lines. You are always grey with yellow trim however, to contrast your enemies: greenish with orange highlights for the Bugs, dark greys and red for the Cyborgs, and whites and blues for the Illiuminate.
Much like Arrowhead's Magika series, friendly fire is an omnipresent problem and accidental team kills are commonplace. Not only can you be shot by your teammates, but you can also be crushed by incoming drop pods and even the escape shuttle! Most of the time it happens so suddenly that it's more comical then anything else, though there is a report function in case people are doing it deliberately. You always have an extra Strategem available that will respawn any currently dead squadmates via drop pods. Watch where you're standing at all times!
There is also a sort of metagame wherein each mission you complete with all objectives completed, all players escaped, and/or minimal deaths adds to a score taken from all players in the game, counted towards control of galactic regions. When the players reach an alien homeworld or when the aliens attack a regional capital planet or Super Earth itself, a special timed event begins where the players can take missions on that world for double experience rewards. If the players earn enough points in the alloted time, the aliens are defeated and their world is taken, knocking them out of the war for its duration, or a human world is sucessfully defended, preventing loss of a region. The war restarts when all three alien factions are defeated, or if the aliens conquer Super Earth. It's not a huge deal of a mechanic, but it's a nice extra layer.

PROS:
-Still has online multiplayer via Gameranger
-Epic gameplay and amazing visuals/atmosphere for 2005
-TONS of content
-REAL space battles (Not dumbed down like EA battlefront)
-4 Factions with 24 classes total (admittedly a lot are similar)
-Many additional races including Jawas, Ewoks, Tuskan Raiders, Wampas, Geonosians, and Gungans (And yes you can play as them)
-Decent campaign that makes you feel like a Clone Trooper/Storm Trooper
-2+ person vehicles (You haven't been tense until you try to land a gunship with 6 people into an enemy hangar)
-About 20 heroes (including Yoda, Darth Maul, Grievous, Chewbacca) and the ability to have a heroes only mode
-Beautiful music with Star wars's best tracks
-Amazing replay value (many of us played over a thousand hours of this on the PS2 before switching)
-The ability to relive the movies and watch stuff like AT-STs getting crushed by logs, taking an AT-AT down with tow cables, get eaten by a rancor, fall into the death star's garbage pit, and many more.
-HUGE quantity of mods with more still in development
-Quality of mods is excellent, adding new maps, missions, and classes, while also improving graphics and lighting
-MODDED MULTIPLAYER!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
-High gameplay depth. Gives the first impression of a basic shooter, but against other players and swarms of bots it will take all of your skill and gamesense
-Can be played however you like. Got 15 minutes until you have to leave? Play a quick skirmish in Princess Leia's starship. Want to get lost for hours? Play the campaign, conquest, or online. Just feel like messing around? Try Hoth on endless mode with 500 bots
-Simply put, far better than EA Battlefront and it's many dlcs, all for a tiny fraction of the price
CONS:
-Not many people on at one time, although usually enough for an all out war on Hoth or Mos Eisley. Expect to see the same faces and make friends in the BF2 community
-Graphics haven't exactly aged well. Mods will do their best with new models, HD textures, and better lighting, but it won't look like new Battlefront
-Getting it to start can be a bit annoying, fortunately there are many guides written
-minor audio bugs, music will occasionally loop/glitch for a few seconds
If you like Star Wars or games in general, grab your blaster, lightsabre, pilot helmet, and fusion cutter. And may the force be with you.

So i bought this game on sale for $3, more like 4, and also recived all the DLC that was relased for it. For the price i paid and the quality of the game i am not dissatisfied. Although i could sum this game up to be a funnier version of GTA it does have a wonderful charm to it. Normaly i wouldnt like to play games like this but becuse of the special sale and what i read in gameinformer when it was a hot release i decieded it was worth giving a whirl. It starts off a little slow with what i would consider 3 intros but each one builds on the next and in a way makes sense. Dont try to think about the plot too much. It also makes several referances to it's previous games and to several others that i found quite humorus such as metal gear solid.
gameplay wise it's sort of like Dead Rising without the wide customization on weapons but numerous customizarion on the outfits, styles, and looks of your gang. And a fairly stright forward customizable character sytem. You have a couple of cool instant kill moves you can use to obliterate weak enimes which feels OP in the begining. A fair selection of weapons keeps you entertained in how you kill your enimes my personal favorite is  the christmas themed dubstep gun.
I liked the earning money based on how much of the map you controled. Logining in and seeing that i have spending money to purchase my guns always left me feeling a little excited to be able to get the upgrades i wanted without too much grinding.
their are tons of side missions and things to find: audio recordings, statues to destrory, vehicles to hijack. races to master, assasinations, rampages, data clusters. etc. Easily found myself spending nearly all night playing and sometimes did. Has that perfect rhythem of 'just one more' on your way to and from quests and wanting to see what the next tid bit is.
The common downfall of these neat games is always when you finish them because you wanted more. you feel like it was just warming up and you were learning about each character and starting to like them when the game desides to finaly finish. Granted this is not completley bad as it doesnt wholey disapoint but just leaves you wanting more. Much like Brutal Legend.
Overal i'd give it a 4.2 of 5 just because it was really fun playing through the first time but i dont see much replay value. I may go back and complete everything but I already am at 91% complete and have finished all the side and story missions.  I also have more game time than steam says I do, dont know why my in game time says 25 and my steam time says 19 but for what i paid i am happy. The sound track is great with  plenty of inuindos and cliches to revel in.
for $15  its not a bad game i would maybe recomend gerring it at 10 or less just so you don't feel too cheated on the content. Not becuase it doesnt have much but because it is not so easily replayable and that price also covers the DLC mostly because the DLC only conrains two actual conributions to the game other than costumes or cars.

I had already played this before it was greenlit and I'm just waiting on a friend to replay.
For starters, this visual novel is free while having VOICE ACTING! And let me tell you, the voice actors are awe-some! (and James Brown Jr. does such an awesome job, I couldn't believe it when I heard it!) Now that's already something from the get-go.
It has a good enough plot, with the silliness of an otome VN nevertheless ("So why did my heart still feel so heavy...?" gee idk maybe he passes JUST YESTERDAY?!), mixing slice of life with supernatural/fantasy. You can change the protagonist's name, if you're into that. The story mixes also humour, fluff, a bit of mystery, and a bit of sadness in a right amount of doses. It is well-written in the overall, though there's some slight mistakes.
There's 6 datable males, 3 females. The sprites are adorable, and I love that they didn't follow the trend of going for anime-style art in the end. AS for the CGs, they could use some work in the anatomical department. There's one in which when I saw Mika I screamed "SHE LOOKS LIKE A WITCH!", and that one in which her butt really creeped me out! But I heard Alejandro Saab say there a problem with the first artist and the current one had to do everything with little time.
The extras feature bloopers, aside from the classic CGs' gallery,  which are absolutely hilarious! I also enjoyed the ost.
Overall, I believe this game is completely worth your time. I enjoyed myself plenty. It's only too bad that the human date routes seem much smaller in comparison, like there's not as much depth to them.
BUT if you don't like reading, visual novels aren't really for you - though there's a book for everyone out there, and VNs make it easier for people who get bored reading, to actually do so and enjoy it.
P.S.: Simon Tabby!!! <3

I've just 100%'d this game, and since the Steam Sale is on and it's on sale, I figured it was time to write a review. Given it's my most played game on Steam with 100+ hours.
So, basically, a group of mad swedes got tired of blowing up turkeys in dungeons in their previous game (Gauntlet), and  decided to make a title about what would happen if Donald Trump took over the Earth and created a new world order dedicated to bringing freedom to the galaxy. Ever watched Starship Troopers? Ever read Starship Troopers? It's sort of a mix of that, but on a twin-stick shooter that emphasises team work and trains you to take Friendly Fire seriously.
Gameplay is essentially drop onto a planet, accomplish objectives (which range from escort civilians up to blow up AA batteries), and GTFO. Sounds simple? It is. But it's done with so much panache and style that you can't help keep playing - case in point being my play time. Despite being a PS4 port, it controls perfectly with M+K and the engine used outputs graphics that look crisp and detailed, with hilariously cheesy (but effective) music. It can be played single player or co-op with up to 3 other players, and shifting between is seamless and slick. This game is the work of some exceptionally talented devs.
While it has no story to speak of, where it excels is pretty much everywhere else. You have three opponent factions - the not-Zerg (Bugs), the not-Borg (Cyborgs) and the not-Protoss (Illuminate). Each faction approaches combat differently and they're all fairly satisfying to fight - you rarely get sick of fighting in this game as if any faction bores you, you have two totally different ones to face. Weapons and kit - particularly with the Deluxe edition with all the DLCs - are *amazingly* varied. The list runs basic machine guns and lasers all the way to toxic sludge throwers, nukes, mechs, drones and a host of things besides, you won't easily get bored.
This game rocks. Get it. If you don't it means you hate freedom and are possibly a communist.

Dying Light is a great zombie game.
Of course I might be biased since I like everything to do with zombies in general but having zombies in it is far from the only thing that makes it great.
The first thing that stands out to me is how well the game implements parkour. Many people compare it to Mirror's Edge and it's certainly on par, if not better: you can freerun on rooftops, dive into water, climb almost any ledge without breaking stride. That combined with the sense of danger when being chased by the faster and more terrifying zombie variants makes it a really immersive experience.
Speaking of zombie variants, that's another thing the game does well. When you first start out, you encounter almost exclusively the slow and "normal" type of zombies so that you can get comfortable with the game and get used to using the urban terrain to your advantage. But as you progress, you encounter at least 5 more types of zombies, each with their unique strengths and weaknesses.
Now for the negatives, I can name but a few. Firstly, the story could've been a little better but, to the game's defense, almost every gimmick there is has already been tried in the zombie genre. Another thing is that the game can get laggy during the more intense scenes or cinematic cutscenes if your PC is at or below the recommended settings.
But these drawbacks are far outnumbered by the things Dying Light does very well and that is why I wholeheartedly recommend it.

The Vanishing Of Ethan Carter is a game where you play as a psychic detective who is investigating a case in Red Creek Valley. It's a forsaken and gloomy place where tragic and mysterious events have unfolded which you have to put together piece by piece. Like in a good detective story, we have a narrator, the protagonist Paul Prospero himself, as he reflects on his previous cases and the little that he got to know from the letter from a boy called Ethan Carter. The storytelling is superb in this game, the scrip is very well written and the voice acting is true to life. Every sentence said carries a meaning and enhances the whole experience.
Now, the thing that got me jumping off my stool with this game were the graphics. The beauty of the scenery is breathtaking. It's this lush overgrown countryside in early autumn where the trees have red and yellow leaves on them already but the weather still holds. All the time there's a light breeze which makes the trees and grass sway in a lazy manner and they found just the right sound to go with it. I could literally start sensing the odours of the countryside, that's how powerful the experience was.
The gameplay is simple but original. You interact with some items and pick up others but the way they're connected with the psychic abilities of Paul Prospero makes it a whole new experience. The puzzles are tough at times and need focus, I even made notes on sticky paper here and there to keep track, but at least they fall in the same box and have a sense of consistency to them.
If the beauty of scenery is something that matters to you then I highly recommend this game. If it doesn't, then it's still loaded with good puzzles and a kickass storytelling. Highly recommended.

The half baked save system is checkpoint based, and the checkpoints only keep track of completed puzzles, if you quit or run out of the puzzle area before completing the puzzle you have to redo the same damn puzzle from the beginning. Took me about five hours to finish this game, probably spent over half that time just running across the landscape, because that's the only way to get anywhere. There's no quick travel system of any kind until you get to the end of the game, and even then it's only one way travel.
This game is not worth anywhere near full price, and it's not worth the sale price I bought it at (66% off).

I'm old.
I've played 'Pong' on a Saba Videoplay console, 'Pac Man' on an Atari VCS, 'The Hobbit' on a Sinclair ZX Spectrum, 'The Castles of Doctor Creep' on a C64, 'Defender of the Crown' on an Amiga and hundreds of other games on consoles, home and personal computers.
Like I said, I'm old.
Up to this point, I've NEVER played - no, experienced - something that intense like 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter' (TVoEC).
This game made a lasting impression on me and I still think about it, although I finished TVoEC months ago.
For me, as a fan of old Stephen King, David Lynch and H. P. Lovecraft works, this game was a revelation. It created the perfect mood, the right atmosphere, with amazing graphics, an ingenious soundtrack that creeps into your subconscious mind and the strange feeling of pleasant but spooky loneliness.
Yes, the riddles might be easy to see through for an experienced gamer and let's be honest, TVoEC is not a very long game. But this doesn't have to be a disadvantage. I for example prefer a typical 6-episodes season of a British TV production over a 22-episodes season of e.g. an American or a German TV production in general.
Those 6 episodes are packed with just good stuff and I enjoy watching them again and again, whereas 22 episodes often contain unnecessary fillers.
In other words, I prefer quality over quantity. Maybe because I’m old.
‘The Vanishing of Ethan Carter’ is a high quality game.

I can't wait to see with what ‘The Astronauts’ come up next.

Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten is the definition of a hidden gem. The game is amazing, but criminally overlooked.
The game plays something akin to a Fire Emblem: Tower Defense where stat and character growth elements are mixed with strategy and storyline. Acquiring new gear for your party (via extra challenges) as you progress through the story arc elicits the same feeling of excitement, joy and wonder I had when I was a child exploring Final Fantasy for the first time in glorious 16-bit. The music is genius in it's simplicity, the graphics are a throwback to the olden days, and the story is interesting from the get-go.
If there's fault I can find within the game it's that the difficulty balance in some of the stages leans too heavily on the easy side (when set to normal difficulty in-game). I find myself pining for an extreme or endless mode, or better yet, a colosseum with extremely rare equipment and rewards.
Buy this game; It's going to amaze you.

Defender's Quest Vallie of the Forgotten is my (new) favourite of this genre.
Through an intricate story and and choice in game mechanics, it manages to combine Tower Defense with a human element, something I didn't even know I missed in the genre, and a distinct RPG feel.
Besides the rich story (which is, you know, rare for these kind of games) this game has a very nice and original art style, clear game mechanics and overview, extensive and incredibly intuitive controls, and an awarding difficulty.
It's weak points are probably the low resolution, which unfortunately doesn't upscale very well (as of writing),  but I've found this to be a minor point at best.
With the original content, and a New Game+ mode, this game is definitely worth buying, especially for this price.

Long time VN/Otome lover, and as far as F2Ps go this is a TOP. NOTCH. STORY. I recommend it to any lady who enjoys the genre.
You play as Mika Anderson (first name negotiable) and you can end up with one of five gorgeous Demon men, a nerdy Human dude, a sexy Succubus, or one of your two best friends. That's a lot of routes for a F2P game. Lots of room for story development, too. (Like how does one go from romantic demons to their best friend? Who knows!)
The Good:
-- Great selection of characters to 'romance.'
-- Unique cast of characters from red-faced Devils to evil squirrel plushies.
-- Backstory is developed throughout the different routes. It's clear that to "complete" the game you need to play all of them. That's how you get the whole story. Otherwise you'll be left with many questions after playing for 10 hours straight like I was.
--  The whole Demon-lore story was presented in the least cheesy manner at a VN author's disposal.
-- The love is cute. Each relationship has its own quirks.
-- Soundtrack is phenomenal.
The Bad:
-- The worst parts about VNs with numerous routes are the scenes and texts that overlap between routes. I understand this author has done a lot of excellent work on Seduce Me and I LOVE what they've done, but each of the characters' "Seduce me" options could've been unique to the character and create the sense that the protagonist was experiencing that character and not *generic character sex scene description.*
-- The love itself feels hasty. I attribute it to the fact that Incubi feed on passion and can stimulate emotions, but it's still a bummer.
-- Many ineffectual decisions throughout the game.
-- Protagonist is boring. Like LOZ's Link boring. But at least he has a sword.
This game gets a solid 8.5 on the grounds it's an absolutely incredible F2P game and gives so much more than you could hope for out of a F2P. Consider donating to the author. This is very strong work.

If you liked Room 1, or are debating which one to get (why not both, they're relatively cheap, especially on steam sale), Room 2 delivers a richer experience.
Room 1 has working your way to the center of a central object, and the environments change very superficially.
Room 2 is more "Myst-like", where you'll time travel to various rooms (crypt, lab, ship, etc... that kind of stuff). In those rooms, you are given more freedom... it's still point and click, but each level now has multiple points of interest, so you'll need to between areas to solve puzzles. This makes the game feel less linear -- while you can still click around on everything to solve, it's a lot less effective this time around since each level has more and more "things" for you to interact with, so your critical thought will be important.
One level felt like a bit of a cop out:
.. the achievement pops and gives you a "sometimes less is more" type message, but don't call it it's own "chapter". I suspect that area was too ambitious, and the dev decided to just cut it short. With that being said, even with that level omitted (or if you consider it a narrative section where you do literally 2 things to beat it), the rest of the game has more than enough.
Also, it was odd that this game didn't pick up where the Room 1 left off, rather it kind of reset you in a new person. I know in this "universe" there are probably infinite rooms, and parallel timelines (all that time travelly stuff), but it would have been nice for the story to continue, considering in this game, starting with a new person, and jumping from zone to zone doesn't really achieve any more .
Once again though, you're not getting "The Room" for it's storytelling, you're getting it for it's overcomplicated contraptions that you can unravel and feel like you're in the DaVinci code or something alone those lines.
The Room 2 is comparable in length to the first, (perhaps a bit longer), but it's definitely a step up, which is promising, since if the dev continues to up the ante like this, the series could go far... or just keep making more of these, why not.

TL:DR adding golf to the Worms universe has actually worked quite well here and has made for a fun game
Full Version:
A pretty good spin on the Worms games usual formula, this adds golf into the mix. You have the familar 2D maps but this time instead of battlegrounds they're golf fairways and greens. You simply aim your shot, hold down the button to power it up and release to take the shot. The fun part comes in the different power ups and obstacles the game gives you. As you play you unlock power ups such as reverse gravity or rocket boost. The different levels also have stuff like cannons and portals that can help you navigate the ball to the green.
There are 4 courses with 18 holes or levels each. Each course has a different theme with Brittania, pirate, cemetary and carnival themed courses. Each level has collectable coins and crates which can be used to unlock stuff to customize your worm golfer.
Good points:
-a fun twist on the Worms games formula
-some great level design that offers a decent challenge
-the power ups give you some much needed help while the obstacles also add to the challenge
-has hot seat multiplayer which is great for some local co-op
Bad points:
-the collectible coins feel a bit pointless as I ended up with loads of coins despite not really trying to collect them. Yet every level has loads which need to be collected to 100% that level
-more courses would have been nice.

Even though tutorial messages can't be skipped, turns can't be started almost immediately and coins are a grind to get, it's a pretty fun golf game.
The game is a bit too slow for co-op, though.

Worms Crazy Golf is, as the title suggests, a golf game in Team17's Worms universe. It is not a serious golf game, like for instance Tiger Woods PGA Tour or Links, but a more wacky 2D golfer keeping with the series comical tone and graphical style. Supposedly it is a sequel to the 2004 mobile game Worms Golf, but who cares, right? The object of the game is to complete each hole on par or below par with its par number. If you fail to do so you have to play the hole again. There are three courses (four with the added mini expansion Carnival Course) that contain 18 holes each. Once in awhile you get to play extra challenge levels where the object can be to keep the ball in motion for a certain time or to pop all balloons, etc. These challenges are quite fun and can be a good break from the normal levels.
As you progress in the game you unlock power-ups, a couple of which make the game a little too easy. Well, the power-ups combined with the fact that you can steer the ball mid-air by tapping left or right will result in a few hole-in-ones. Some levels have wind and magnetic fields, which ups the difficulty a tad. The levels also contain greenskeeper worms, sheep, bats, moles who steal the ball, and old ladies who strike the ball with their handbags. You collect crates to unlock things in the shop, such as hats or different colored balls, and you collect coins to buy these accessories. The only accessories that alter the gameplay are the golf clubs, so these are worth getting.
If you're unlucky, the ball can get stuck inside the ground, though it rarely happens. And if it does happen you can just restart the hole. The game is quite short and can easily be completed in one sitting. Hot seat multiplayer is available for up to four players in true Worms tradition. I found the game pretty enjoyable, a lot better than the puzzle spin-off Worms Blast, but still lacking something to keep it from being just another Worms sidetrack.

I've just 100%'d this game, and since the Steam Sale is on and it's on sale, I figured it was time to write a review. Given it's my most played game on Steam with 100+ hours.
So, basically, a group of mad swedes got tired of blowing up turkeys in dungeons in their previous game (Gauntlet), and  decided to make a title about what would happen if Donald Trump took over the Earth and created a new world order dedicated to bringing freedom to the galaxy. Ever watched Starship Troopers? Ever read Starship Troopers? It's sort of a mix of that, but on a twin-stick shooter that emphasises team work and trains you to take Friendly Fire seriously.
Gameplay is essentially drop onto a planet, accomplish objectives (which range from escort civilians up to blow up AA batteries), and GTFO. Sounds simple? It is. But it's done with so much panache and style that you can't help keep playing - case in point being my play time. Despite being a PS4 port, it controls perfectly with M+K and the engine used outputs graphics that look crisp and detailed, with hilariously cheesy (but effective) music. It can be played single player or co-op with up to 3 other players, and shifting between is seamless and slick. This game is the work of some exceptionally talented devs.
While it has no story to speak of, where it excels is pretty much everywhere else. You have three opponent factions - the not-Zerg (Bugs), the not-Borg (Cyborgs) and the not-Protoss (Illuminate). Each faction approaches combat differently and they're all fairly satisfying to fight - you rarely get sick of fighting in this game as if any faction bores you, you have two totally different ones to face. Weapons and kit - particularly with the Deluxe edition with all the DLCs - are *amazingly* varied. The list runs basic machine guns and lasers all the way to toxic sludge throwers, nukes, mechs, drones and a host of things besides, you won't easily get bored.
This game rocks. Get it. If you don't it means you hate freedom and are possibly a communist.

Helldiver gameplay as a twin stick shooter feels responsive. The smoke and bullet trace to the enemy animation made your gun have an impact when shooting them. What helldiver is famously known is for their difficulty. Friendly fire will always on, mech can kill your friend with two step, and even the escape shuttle can crush your whole teammate.
The game also have a stealth mechanic, in which you need to be careful of enemy patrol. If the patrol spotted you, they will call reinforcement. Their reinforcement is endless, which mean if more patrol spotted you, more alien will show up.
You will play as a helldiver, your job is to protect your earth from three kind of alien that want to destroy the earth. The earth will be strike from three alien at the same time, so you need to think which one you should eliminate first from the war. If one of those alien get to earth and we failed to defend it, the war will be lost. The war is a community effort, which mean everybody help the invasion from the star they earned from mission. Higher difficulty give you more star which can make the war faster. What happen if the war ended? there will always a new one ;P
The game have a unique air support called strategems. Strategems can be the difference of life and death of your team, escpecially in higher difficulty. Strategems can call mech drop, drone, ammo, equipment, and even a nuke. When equipment strategems is called, it will drop a pod that will crush anything (your teammate also) on your marked area. While the airstrike strategems will fire anything on your marked area. I remember killing my teammate while he is riding a mech with an ammunition drop.
The critic I have is boring map and repetitive mission. The map seems to consist of dessert, snow, and jungle. Because each mission is about 10 minutes, you will get to see the same map and mission over and over again. So I hope they will add more map soon.
It also got local coop which is awesome. You can play with keyboard and your friend on controller.
