I'm old.
I've played 'Pong' on a Saba Videoplay console, 'Pac Man' on an Atari VCS, 'The Hobbit' on a Sinclair ZX Spectrum, 'The Castles of Doctor Creep' on a C64, 'Defender of the Crown' on an Amiga and hundreds of other games on consoles, home and personal computers.
Like I said, I'm old.
Up to this point, I've NEVER played - no, experienced - something that intense like 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter' (TVoEC).
This game made a lasting impression on me and I still think about it, although I finished TVoEC months ago.
For me, as a fan of old Stephen King, David Lynch and H. P. Lovecraft works, this game was a revelation. It created the perfect mood, the right atmosphere, with amazing graphics, an ingenious soundtrack that creeps into your subconscious mind and the strange feeling of pleasant but spooky loneliness.
Yes, the riddles might be easy to see through for an experienced gamer and let's be honest, TVoEC is not a very long game. But this doesn't have to be a disadvantage. I for example prefer a typical 6-episodes season of a British TV production over a 22-episodes season of e.g. an American or a German TV production in general.
Those 6 episodes are packed with just good stuff and I enjoy watching them again and again, whereas 22 episodes often contain unnecessary fillers.
In other words, I prefer quality over quantity. Maybe because I’m old.
‘The Vanishing of Ethan Carter’ is a high quality game.
This is a game for your heart, not for your heart rate.
I can't wait to see with what ‘The Astronauts’ come up next.

TVEC is an extraordinarily immersive game that succeeds by providing the player a fascinating abandoned world to explore. The landscape and buildings seem to be of a time and place one can't easily pin down, though the setting is somewhere in the modern day USA. I was reminded of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. by lonely hills, forests, and tunnels that may or may not be haunted. The supernatural exploration detective game Betrayer comes to mind as well as the paranormal investigator protagonist combs the terrain for clues.
The story is hit or miss. I had a hard time buying into the story, but I was familiar with the type of tale being told. The incorporation of certain horror literature elements were rather well done but it was the interpersonal family dynamics that weren't as convincing as they could have been. The "twist" ending (depending on your point of view) wasn't very profound and the idea of ghosts "letting go" alternately fascinates and bores me. It was done reasonably well in Betrayer, dealing with cursed souls, and handled rather clumsily in Murdered: Soul Suspect, which over-relied on the concept.
2017 EDIT: After replaying the "Redux" version (the exact same game story wise), I'm just as disappointed with the story - white working class kid wants to be a weird nerd but everyone is mean to him. lol. Pretty visuals though.

TL:DR
The Room is better than The Room Two. They are nice puzzle games with beautiful graphics and worth your money (1,69 for 5 chapters).
I started out playing The Room. It has nice puzzles. It had 5 chapters, which was acceptable, because the game was worth 1,69 on Steam Sale. I loved the graphics and the sophistication of the puzzles. It really gave me moments where I scratched my head and thought: "Well that's done, now what? Let me look around for some clues." The briljant graphics gave a relaxed atmosphere to work on the puzzles. The beautiful graphics also ensured that some compartments would stay hidden and made you look for clues or anomalies. I have a feeling that The Room has a lot more potential and that there are a lot more possibilities for harder puzzles.
The Room Two on the other hand has different priorities. I don't think the developers where aiming on the puzzles, rather on the storyline and the mystery behind the Null element. Two things that give me that impression: the graphics, which are less compared to The Room, and the sophistication of the puzzles. A lot of times when you unlock some part of the puzzle in The Room Two, the camera just pins you to the place where you should put the accuired piece. I find that very linear and straightforward.
So definetly a good game, with a lot of potential. The developers should go back to The Room and take that as a basis and concentrate on more sophisticated puzzles with more layers. With more divers pieces, one creates difficult puzzles, because it all seems random and chaotic. It could also eliminate the linearity of some puzzles.
So 10/10 for The Room
and
7/10 for The Room Two

You play as a random mook in the most iconic battles in Star Wars history, which included such battles like: Geonosis, Hoth, Endor... Mygeeto... P-Polis Massa... very iconic.
Battlefront II is usually the more well remembered of the original Battlefront series, it placed 5th in video game sales according to the NPD of 2005 and is “The best selling Star Wars game of all time.” According to this case of the Playstation 2 version I found lying around. It was also the second most played Multiplayer Xbox game in 2007 and “really good”  according to the strange man sitting beside me.
Battlefront II is a first or third person shooter akin to Battlefield 1942 or Battlefield 2,
. You take the role of just another soldier on the battlefield, and it is your duty to make the other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s die for their countries while taking as many strategic points as possible until the time limit is reached or the enemy runs out of respaws.
There are four factions to play as.
The Grand Army of the Republic: An army of Jango Fett clones led by Jedi who have objectively the coolest weapons and armor in the series. You can't argue, because I'm great.
The Confederacy of Independent Systems: A Separatist movement that fights the Republic with the help of a Droid army funded by literally the most evil people in the galaxy. Wink Wink.
The Galactic Empire: The most iconic aspect of the Star Wars universe with legions of Storm Troopers and nerds nobody cares about.
And the Rebels: The bad guys.
Each faction is set to their timeline in multiplayer, so the GAR always fights the CIS and the Rebels always fights the Empire.  From here you go on a 64 player battle royal in an attempt to not get shot in the face or slapped in the head by some loser with a space sword.
Fightyside part 2 also has two major additions compared to the original 2004 release. One of the most advertised aspects of the game was the implementation of space combat. In space combat, two sides in capital ships try to destroy the other with the use of the ships main cannons, fighters, bombers, interceptors, and boarding parties with the use of transport crafts.
The mode is competent enough and the ships feel great to control even with a mouse and keyboard, but don't expect the mode to replace Star Wars: X-wing or Tie Fighter. For a map set in space, the warzone feels rather small in comparison and the mode is usually over too quickly to actually get invested in the mode.
The other big feature was the addition of hero characters to the game, with Jedi and sithlords being the big selling point. After achieving certain goals, you have the option of enlisting the aid of a hero, which you take control as and tear apart the enemy, though you usually just end up wiggling around until someone shoots you in the face with a rocket launcher.
The problem with this mode is just how stiff some of the characters feel, especially the force users, especially more since I just got off playing Jedi Academy before playing this game and I'm use to flexible jeddy characters.
Battlefront II also offers an improved single player experience.
Journals of the 501st is a story mode where you play as the infamous Vader's fist, the most recognizable clone troopers and later Storm Troopers in the series. The story mode takes you from the middle of the clone wars all the way to the Battle of Hoth, using multiplayer maps and adding extra objectives to give it a more narrative flare.
The mode is competent, but it will only last you about two or three hours if you aren't dragging your butt across the ground.
The other single player mode aside from the obvious Instant Action is Galactic Conquest. In GC you pick one of the four factions who have to fight their respective rivals for dominance of the galaxy. Once again you go from multiplayer map to multiplayer map and fight for control, only this time you keep the planet on the GC map and use the resources gained from your victory to buy new classes, power ups, and fleets so you can attack more than once. When your fleet and an enemy fleet meet over a planet or an area, the game starts a space combat map where you can destroy the enemy fleet and remove them from the map.
It's like a very basic grand strategy game, but it's neither complex enough or engrossing enough to keep you for very long.
Honestly, it's still fun and feels great. If the aged graphics aren't your cup of tea then there are a few graphics mods that improve the look a little bit.
Unfortunately, official server support shut down some time ago, and the single player doesn't really hold up for more than a handful of hours.
But, fortunately, a little birdy told me there are still ways to get multiplayer working and servers with players that are still up to this day, you just need to do a little bit of digging.
Unfortunately again, the most populated server is heroes vs villains, which is a janky, boring, and ultimately lamer version that Jedi Outcast's or Jedi Academy's multiplayer. But if you can get people together for your own server or to commandeer one that is playing the game the way it's meant to be played, then you're in for one hell of a time.

Personally, I enjoyed it.  It's a simple relaxing solitaire game.  The music is soothing and Christmas-y.  Quite a lot of levels which lends itself to the one-more-turn syndrome.  And these levels add just enough variety not to make it too repetitive.  Different levels, based on the different card locations and number of shuffles lends a bit of strategy to where in the layout to focus one's matches.
It's not without it's flaws though.  Card clicking can be frustratingly non-responsive and takes a bit of getting used to.  And the most annoying thing for me was the "Earn 1,000,000 coins" achievement which actually means you need to gather a total of 1,000,000 coins at the same time.  I mistakenly spent a lot of coins on upgrades and had to grind 100,000s of coins just to finish the final achievement.  If one is conservative with upgrades, you'll hit 1 million coins well before the finish at which point you can start spending like crazy to finish the last levels and get the "Use XXX Upgrades" achievements.
Overall, despite it's flaws and simplicity, there is quite a bit of game time to it which made it worth it's asking price for me.  Not going to say it's a "must buy" or anything like that.  It could be more polished (see flaws above), but I enjoyed at as a nice casual game.

Now I played the old Metro 2033 game and this Redux and I have to say the Redux is truly worth the name Redux.So many issues with Metro 2033 have been fixed ,graphics are beautiful,they even added some parts to levels so you can be sure its not just a reskin of the old game.
The entire metro story is incredibly unique , with the people escaping from the fire of the nuclear missiles,animals and such that did survive mutated on the surface and you do meet alot of them , the settlements people created in the Metro , the makeshift weapons they use to defend themselfs and of course - The Dark Ones.Creatures that are still pretty unclear to me,i believe they are humans that survived the war and mutated into something better , into a better race , into Homo Novus , a next step in the evolution.
In my opinion Metro isn't that scary as other horror games , but it is still very grusome ,the things you will see are defenedly not seen in other games that usuallly only have bad jumpscares as their way of saying they are horror games.
The scaryness of the Metro and the surface world is the psychological effect, the choking and depressed atmosphere outside because it makes you think what people have done to a beautiful world,and the even more dark and depressing atmosphere of people underground barely surviving from selling food and weapons for before-the-war-made high quality bullet cartridges.The weapons people use have this makeshift feeling to them.And it just feels like its made somewhere in underground.
The main character Artyom is also written pretty well , although he is silent troughout the game ,he still writes his journal and thats where you see how he thinks , is he scared , what he is going to do.He is very brave,and I mean he really is because the creautres he meets and the challanges he faces look impossible from the beginning but he always finds a way to reaching his goal.The other characters Artyom meets are very interesting aswell,but in my opinion Khan is the most interesting one , and my personal favourite side character.In 2033 you will see how Artyom transitions from nobody to a elite Sparta Ranger.And it shows that if you want to achieve something big you will have to go trough Hell to reach it , but when you do you will be so satisfied that you reached this goal.
I have to point out that both 2033 and Last Light have beautiful soundtracks that you should have a litsen for yourself and then you'll realize why I am saying this because it makes no sense for me to explain why it matches this game so good.
As I said , the game is amazing and I as a huge fan of the old Metro 2033 game gotta say it is more then worth the money you pay for it.And i also advise you to buy Metro Last Light with this because if you don't play Last Light with this you are missing out a lot.

Short but sweet.
Using a minimalist approach The Vanishing of Ethan Carter can take off the numerous training wheels common in game design today such as nav beacons and HUD while still remaining brief and effective.  Good writing makes the story worth following and interesting to unravel.
Mechanically it's closer to games like Myst or Robot City than Dear Esther for all its brevity because The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is actually a game like Robot City and Myst and not a pile of bad prose shoved down unwitting players' throats like Dear Esther.  The puzzle mechanics are straightforward and interesting, not rocket science but not condescending either.  The usual question at the heart of each one is 'how did these things come to be as they are now?' and it reinforces the thematic importance of imagination as escape from the quotidian.  What looks at first like an abandoned town turns out to be more, then more again.
I was frankly amazed at how their techniques managed to yield such impressive results in the aging Unreal 3 engine.  There are very few moving objects in the game but the world as a whole is incredibly detailed in a deliberate fashion.  Art direction ties well into the macabre mechanics involved in reconstructing various characters' personal histories and the sense of a day frozen near magic hour is both visually stunning and a massively important plot point.  It really does feel like every piece of the game fits in a larger sense.
The only mechanical gripe I have is the lack of manual saves.  I recommend switching to the Polish audio with English subtitles.  The voice actors just seem to deliver their lines with a more natural sense of conviction in Polish.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter won't resolve the 'length versus quality' debate but it does put a solid marker in the 'short but well done can be worthwhile' camp.
Give it a look if you like first-person exploration-oriented puzzle games or just interesting experiments in design backed up by solid execution.

I wanted to like this, you know. A Very intriguing setting, as I really like mysteries and the process of uncovering them. But for me, the Vanishing of Ethan Carter fell a little short. I won't debate the price of it or existence as a game. I won't go very into this. Probably.
The world of Vanishing of Ethan Carter is absolutely stunning. I noticed I spent most of the time just looking at the beautiful landscape, seeing the love and work put into this. I felt like I was physically there, in Red Creek Valley, my feet at the grass and running on the dirt roads. Atmospheric isn't an adequate term to describe it. Never before I have been so immersed. It isn't even the realistic style behind it – I can get immersed into a world made of pixelated graphics or simple colors. It's really hard to say what pulled me in. The soundscape, perhaps.
Oh, the music in this is very lovely and also very creepy, carefully put in the right places. I felt delighted every time the music started playing.
Collecting notes and miscellanous items throughout the game was interesting to say the least. I'm a sucker for those, always yearning for knowledge and the game lore. And I really loved the fact you start the game with "We won't hold your hand" type of text. It felt like a challenge, and I was thrilled.
The mechanic behind solving the murders was simple and often times I felt like the puzzles weren't very challenging (with the exception of the mine caves because hahah, I wasn't prepared for that......). In the beginning I was a little at loss what to do but I got the hang of it pretty soon. I won't debate the easiness of puzzles though, because everyone experiences them differently. At this point when I fully understood what the game wanted from me (this was probably at one hour point) I felt like a part of the game's charm stopped. I didn't feel challenged anymore, I didn't feel
anymore.
Where the world was immensely immersive, I found it hard to learn the characters and actually to get interested in them. Even at the end I felt nonchalant, even towards Ethan. They felt hollow, like ghosts which is ironic. The voice acting was good, so there is no problem in that. I would say the problem is in the setting because the narrator is an outsider. You're not being given information purposely – but as he has the power to experience the last moments of dead people, shouldn't there be some way to experience it a little more thoroughly? This is just my opinion but as a really empathetic person this is weird that I didn't get to feel as much as I wanted to.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter has a way of immersing people but not enough. Like I already said in the beginning, it falls a little short. It never rises to the excellent category, at least for me. The space scene was amazing though and I will give it its well-deserved credit. The game begins strong but ends up toning itself down too much.
And no, I'm not saying you shouldn't buy this game despite giving it a thumbs-down. Everyone feels differently, experiences differently. Maybe you will like this more than I did.

Truly an incredible game - an intriguing story, gorgeous graphics, and a very immersive soundtrack.
And while the graphics and the music are award-worthy in and of themselves, the story is where this game really shines.
You piece together the story of what happened in Red Creek bit by bit, through notes, stories, and the memories of the dead, and while the true meaning behind it all is hinted at, the ending is a real surprise, and a satisfying one, at that.
The storytelling is smooth, keeping you interested in the fates of the Carter family up to the very end.
Yes, it can be easy to miss some of the clues - backtracking is not only possible, but expected. And yes, the save system can be a nuisance. But these are very minor issues, and do not at all interfere with the telling of a truly memorable story.
I can say without hesitation that this game deserves a solid 9.5/10. Well worth the price.

This solitaire game has a very low completion rate without using any cheat mechanisms (which you will have to buy for ingame currency per each use).
Despite having a timed mechanism (match faster to grow your combo multiplier), the game has a very annoying 1 second delay after every match during which you can't click any other cards so if you're too fast and clicked the card right after the match and didn't notice that it didn't register (the selection highlight is barely noticeable), you'lll be very confused.

A nice casual Christmas-themed solitaire game.  Though the gameplay is different than Faerie Solitaire and games like that.  In this one you click on match pairs of the same number.  Your goal is to get all the gold special cards.  There are 3 bonus abilities you can use:  Shuffle, Undo, and Wild Card.  You can buy them in the in-game store with the coins you earn by playing, or occasionally you get a free one by matching a card with an asterisk (*) on it.
There are 2 difficulty levels, and 12 groupings of 10 levels each.  In the easy difficulty you can replay any level you want any time.  In the hard difficulty you have to replay from the first level in each group.  Each group has a different background (though some are just a mirror image or a smaller portion of a previous larger one).
You can change the image on the card decks any time, even mid-game.  This is especially helpful on levels with a dark background or light background where you want a contrasting color to see the cards easier.
Note to achievement hunters:  If you want to get all the achievements then I recommend you NOT to purchase any bonuses in the store, because one of the achievements is to earn one million coins.  And if you keep buying stuff then it will take longer to get than achievement.  It took me about 30 hours to get all the achievements.
The music is very nice and pleasant.  It changes and shifts so that it doesn't get boring.
Minor bugs:  One level has a black background; whatever the image is supposed to be, it does not load correctly.  And occasionally a bug will happen when matching one of the * cards where it magically collects all the gold cards even though they are still buried.  But that's a bug in my favor so I'm not complaining!

I have a love / hate relationship game.  From my perspective, you have a game that is very much like the original Deus Ex in terms of choice by in-game actions or conversations mixed with a compelling atmosphere perfect for the location and time period of the story.  Being able to make various choices or alternate routes of completing goals is awesome.  The 90s pop / gothic vampire cults imbued in Southern California culture is convincing and enjoyable.
Unfortunately, there are some design decisions that prevent it from being the same great addicting experience that is Deus Ex.  The combat is lousy.  While Deus Ex has aged in terms of gunplay, there are at least mechanics to perform instanteous lethal kills or knockouts.  While stealth holds up with human foes, it is somewhat hindered in my point of view by the third person perspective that is forced when equipped with a melee weapon.  When firing at an aware NPC, the combat feels similar to a bullet sponge FPS with no ADS.  Think Halo.  This would not be a problem if you did not get forced into critical situations requiring combat, however, there are boss fights that must be completed throughout the main quest.
Combat aside, the game has trouble with pacing.  Some times you can become stuck trying to find an item or clue that will set you off on the next thread of the main quest.  While tinkering around the world is enjoyable, being lost in 90s computer records is not great.
Anyways, I think this game should definitely be played.  Buy it when on sale and dedicate 6 hours of game time before calling quits.  Also, spending time with a character creation guide to make the most of your skills and vampire powers is advised.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is one of the most suspenseful games I've ever played. I can't say it's "scary" or even "atmospheric." It's just suspenseful. You're dropped into an almost vacant world, a chillingly empty mountain region where a boy named Ethan Carter is attempting to challenge a supernatural entity called The Sleeper, which is taking control of Ethan's family. You as Paul Prospero must find out what happened to Ethan and his family by examining the town and tying the mystery together, ultimately discovering the truth.
It's difficult to say why this game's story is so superb without spoiling its phenomenal ending, but I encourage players to see it through to the end. The struggles of the Carter family go far beyond the supernatural, and the ending feels so tightly crafted, that it'll stick with you long after the credits roll.
The mechanic of examining areas for clues and deducing a crime scene event by rearranging chronologies in the right order is great. It's admittedly a bit easy and succumbs to trial-and-error a bit too much, but it's an interesting way to approach a mystery. Some parts of gameplay are a bit more standard in puzzle design, but the constant shifts in aesthetic keep things fresh. The save system, however, is all based on auto-save, and with long periods of walking between parts of the map, it can become exhausting. A better-implemented quick save or even a manual save feature could've remedied this.
I also must say that this game is beautiful. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter's hauntingly isolated mountain scene is so perfectly presented with varied environments and a few surreal spirals to keep things interesting. Voice acting is equally good, as Ethan's tense family dialogues exhibit sincerity and desperation to survive. Know that it's a pretty demanding game technologically. Mid-range PC's and lower might find some technical snags along the way, only reinforcing the amazing technical prowess of this game.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a short game, a fleeting yarn being bent, but it'll stick with you for a long time. It's a mystery that begs to be solved, and with such a creative merging of story and gameplay, it's near impossible to forget.
Pros: Gorgeous graphics, creative blend of story and gameplay, excellent voice acting
Cons: Save system is pretty convoluted, large world can demand lots of obnoxious backtracking, short length

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter: In-depth Review
Game release date: September 22, 2014
Review date: July 23, 2015
INTRO
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an amazing game. The story is intriguing, the gameplay is unique, and the graphics are hands down some of the best in the history of gaming so far. The product is not without it's cons; however, it is still a polished and compelling game overall.
STORY (spoiler free)
You're a paranormal detective who journeys to a place called Red Creek Valley to find a boy named Ethan Carter, who sent you fan mail that intruiges you to invesitgate some of his claims. When you arrive, you find out that a strange evil has claimed the town, and an adventure of mystery, horror, and hope ensues.
Overall, the narrative is solid, if not a little too vague at times. But with that said, it keeps you immersed throughout the entire experience, and is one of the defining factors of the game.
GAMEPLAY
The game is played from a first-person perspective. As usual, you're basically just an invisible floating head, which means you can't see your hands, feet, or any other part of your body. Levers and switches seem to move on their own. Items are picked up by invisible your invisible hands. While this is a minor gripe, I think it would have made the game much more realistic.
Primarily, you explore a decently sized open world map, solving puzzles and searching for clues on what to do next. The pacing is brilliant, that is, until you have to backtrack over large distances just because you missed a small element. By the time I reached the endgame, I had to go back and complete other "missions" because I'd so easily missed them as I passed by. This is another minor gripe, as the game itself tells you that it won't hold your hand throughout the experience. Keep your eyes sharp. But hold onto your seats as well, as there are some jump scares. The puzzles are relatively easy, but most require a ton of thinking.
Traversal is almost entirely by foot. There's a zoom function for taking DOF lessened screenshots. and a sprint button (which you'll be holding down almost the entire time). There's also a neat easter egg which either requires you to have the knowledge of the steps before hand, or blind luck to solve it.
GRAPHICS
By far, the game's most defining quality. My jaw hit the floor when I first booted up the game, and there are plenty of "wow" moments throughout the adventure. Almost every environment looks spectacular, and the level of detail is incredible. Textures are photorealistic, and looks amazing coupled with cinematic effects. Character models are also extremely detailed. The entire world is designed to give you that surreal-dream-like feel, and it pulls you into this virtual world. It's insane.
Also take note, the game is running on the Unreal 3 engine, pushed to the limits. Performance is great, but as always, comes down to what rig you have. An update which upgrades the engine to the breathtaking Unreal 4 is in development at the time of this review.
OVERALL
While I recommend this to everyone, don't buy it expecting Call of Duty or Skyrim. This is a puzzle solving, story heavy, visually stunning experience. It clocks in pretty short though, I completed the game in around four hours, and that was with a lot of restarting and general goofing around. But don't let that sway you into not buying it. It's well worth the asking price, and unbeatable during sales.

I do love civ V, but why do I and what has this game offer to you?
Civ V is a round based strategic game where you are able to choose between a big variety of nations (18) (43 with all dlcs). Every nation comes along with different and unique advantages such as (certain buffs/abilities/troops). Your goal is to build your empire, you might choose to get few big cities or many smaller ones. You are also free to establish your own policy you adopt by gaining culture. You may focus on building wonders to gain powerfull buffs that will help you improving your empire in many ways, or you seek out for war to conquer cities all over the world. You see Civ V is a game of a wide range of opportunities.
Moreover its friendly "cartoonish" graphic style with those bright colors gives you a far more pleasant feeling, than other games of this genre could ever provide.
Unfortunately - and this is the only critical thing I can point out - to get the full satisfaction and enjoyment, you need to purchase at least the two major dlcs (Gods and Kings/Brave new world) otherwise you'll have a proper game but you'll never find out how much more enjoyable it can be.
So... before you spend 30 euros for an over-average round based, bright colored, "family friendly" strategic game, you might consider the opportunity to get far far more out of it, by spending 15 euros more and buy the complete bundle.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Saints Row IV is an open world action-adventure video game developed by Volition and published by Deep Silver. It is the fourth title in the Saints Row series. In the game, the playable character is the leader of the 3rd Street Saints, a street gang that has become the world's most powerful and popular organization, and must fend off an alien invasion after becoming President of the United States and receiving superpowers. The player is free to explore their environment while completing main and side missions at their leisure. The game incorporates elements from science fiction video games and films, and continues the series' reputation for over-the-top parody. It was released in August 2013 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360, and was later ported to PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Linux in 2015.
The game was Volition's first after its sale to Koch Media in early 2013. The supernatural and superpower concept for the game started in Enter the Dominatrix, a cancelled expansion planned for Saints Row: The Third, which the team expanded into Saints Row IV. Volition later released a "director's cut" of Enter the Dominatrix as downloadable content for Saints Row IV alongside How the Saints Saved Christmas, other weapons, costumes, and vehicle packs, and a standalone expansion, Saints Row: Gat out of Hell (which serves as the epilogue to the story)
Similar to previous Saints Row series games, Saints Row IV is an open world action game with third-person shooter elements wherein the player is free to explore the environment and, at their leisure, play story or side missions. As the leader of the Saints, a street gang that has become the world's most "powerful and popular" organization, the player is elected President of the United States, receives superpowers, and fends off an alien invasion. Most often the player will engage in shooting and racing activities, though other activities vary from fighting crowds of zombies, shoot-outs in tanks, side-scrolling brawlers, fights against supersized, daikaiju energy drink cans, and using a dubstep gun to interrupt 1950s Americana. The player-character receives elemental powers and superpowers that greatly increase their jump height and running speed, such that the player can hop over buildings and outrun vehicles. The elemental powers include abilities to shoot fire and ice projectiles, telekinetically toss things, and create shockwaves upon landing jumps. As the player progresses through the game, they can optionally upgrade their abilities and weapons skill tree by using collectible "data clusters" scattered around town. If the player becomes too rowdy, the alien race's police analogue will intervene. As in previous games, the player-character's look and feel is entirely customizable via a robust character editor feature.
The game is set in a nearly identical simulation of Steelport, the fictional city setting from Saints Row: The Third, though individual story missions have new, custom-designed levels. Saints Row IV's story parodies science fiction video games, especially Mass Effect 2, as well as films like The Matrix and Zero Dark Thirty, and other "nerd culture". Some story missions are propelled by individual characters' existential crises, as each Saint character is stuck in a personal simulation of their own hell, and must be rescued by the player.

One hint about the game that works for all of the levels  and especially the last level: don't just concentrate on your aim, but concentrate equally on your rhythm as well. This game is a cross between Dance Dance Revolution / Stepmania and Puzzle Quest.
If you reacted to that sentence with "hey that sounds cool," this game is for you. Not certain? Still worth a look.
Playable with the keyboard, a gamepad, or a dance pad (which I really want to try one of these days), the basic gist of the gameplay is hitting arrows in time with a beat a la DDR. For the Puzzle Quest influence, this has an RPG story where you beat monsters to collect items and proceed up a tower. You flip between three "boards": one board's arrows are attacks aimed at you, and clearing the arrow defends against the attack; one board will regenerate your mana; a third board is active when you cast a spell, and nailing that sequence means your spell succeeds.
The dialogue is refreshingly snarky, and fully voice-acted.
The all-important question: how's the music? Very good, and there's a solid variety too. At least, variety within the style - they're all going to be a bit dancy-technoey.

Seduce Me the Otome is a visual novel game that revolves around you, the granddaughter of a toy company mogul, and the stories of five incubi. Each of the incubi has their own distinct personality, and you have your choice of one of them through each play through of the game.
So, pros and cons!
Pros:
- Each character is fully voice-acted except for the main character.
- Each character is well-written, giving them their own distinct personality and quirks.
- The story is very interesting and I personally got very invested in it, and all of the little minutia that is involved with each of the characters.
- The game is pretty short, making it more inticing to replay and get other character endings.
- There are female romance options.
- It's free.
- Main Character is pretty kick♥♥♥♥♥and isn't (always) a damsel.
Cons:
- You can tell a lot of the voice work isn't professional. There are a few characters with low-quality voices. (But this doesn't detract from the game, IMO.)
- The two female romance options are your human friends, and you'll miss most of the plot involving the incubi if you choose to romance them, making it less likely that you'll want to romance them. (Some succubi being in the main group might have helped this.)
- It's hard to understand what to do to get some of the character's perfect endings. There's lots of "stats" that you can keep track of during the game (Character love, and I think there's a "good" and "demonic" stat as well?), and I don't really understand how they all work together towards what ending you get.
- The game's quick ending leaves some plot holes and glosses over some stuff that happens after the second chapter of the game (but I don't know if some of these will be addressed in the sequel):
-
-
-
All of this being said, I really enjoyed Seduce Me the Otome, and I'm very much looking forward to the sequel, and seeing if  it answers any of my burning questions!

I LOVE this game.
The story is brilliant and very emotion-inducing. It's made me cry in both ways, of joy and of sadness. The characters are oh-so memorable, always making me smile and have the feels. And while it took me so long to finally unlock all the endings and artwork, I still enjoyed this game to its fullest.
If you do not want spoilers, do not read the rest of this review.
I find Mika's situation to be fairly similar to my own, always being expected to do great things. I love her character design and personality in this story...
As for Suzu and Naomi, they are memorable friends and it's fun to identify with them.
As for the incubi, OH MY GOODNESS. They're so fun, and I have to say they're very well developed characters, each going by a specific archetype but still have depth and meaning to them. I especially like James, Erik, and Damien. Although I can't say I'm a fan of Matthew's childish nature or Sam's bad-boy attitude, I still love them both. Erik makes my heart melt with his charms, James makes me feel important with his leadership role, and Damien makes me feel emotional with his tragic story.
I'm serious, I think I'm in love with all of the incubi.
As for Diana... I love her, I hate her, and I love to hate her. She's amazing and sexy and OHMYGOD, but she's also aggravating and I love that about a character. I love it when a character can pull off being two opposite extremes at the same time.
I don't know about anyone else, but Diana is my choice if I wanted any single one of them as a romantic partner.
And to be honest, I don't really dig Andrew, but he's cool.
As for second tier characters like Malix, Eris, the Demon Lord, Lisette, K, and others, they're really fun to see interact with Mika and the cast. They definitely add to the story and I would have loved to see more of them.

TL;DR - Great little indie game if you are interested in running a software company, simulation games and/or just like to geek out on building a nice little (or huge for that matter) office. Not for the more action- or graphics oriented gamer and not too much of a challenge to be had (if you're decent at simulation games that is :P).
This is a great example of one of those little gems out there made by indie developers. Software Inc. currently already has quite enough options and variety in what is essentially a sandbox game. With the basic starting settings you begin with a few thousand bucks and the tools to use those to build yourself a tiny room/garage with a table and computer. Your ingame avatar then starts hammering at his keyboard alternating between developing new software titles and doing some contract work, because the latter pays a lot more bills at the start. It's impossible to compete against the pre-existing companies out there at that moment. You start getting some consumer recognition, improve your skills, hire some employees and proceed to take over the (entire?) software market if done right. You do this by out-earning your competitors and buying all of their stock and do a hostile takeover (netting you their intellectual properties along the way). It's fun, can be quite engrossing (with a bit of roleplay, because otherwise it's all just managing sliders and figures) and is worth it's current € 14 (or regional equivalent) pricetag. In terms of gameplay, the game starts off telling you that it's not going to hold your hand, which it doesn't. this is a double edged sword in my opinion. On one hand, you don't have some clumbsy UI detracting from the immersion of the game. On the other hand, the games definition apparently includes: Explaining controls, explaining your abilities, explaining why you are wherever it is you are, letting you manually save and letting you view an inventory(or notebook system....or map). So, in the end it's kind of cool thatyou have a nice clean screen to enjoy the visuals of the game, but that also means that if you quit playing for a few days and forget what you have collected, or what you were trying to do, yer pretty much up a creek without a paddle.

Worms Crazy Golf is a light hearted mini-golf game that holds up well in both single player and local co-op.
You’ll know if you want this game. Either you enjoy the Worms series and/or enjoy mini-golf games. It features 4 full courses with a good variety in level design and difficulty. I won’t go into this point much, as like other mini-golf games, there will be traps, obstacles and power ups along your way to creatively finish the hole and gather all the collectibles.
Collectibles! Each hole has 4 objectives. Collect all the coins, get par or better (required to unlock the next hole), collect the crate and get a high score (usually more than 100k). Figure that in to 72 holes and that’s a lot of collectibles. It does provide a good challenge and gives the game some replay value as far as single player is concerned.
You can either play by yourself or up to 4 people in local co-op (sitting at the same computer). There is no LAN option for multiplayer.
I think it’s worth saying they put out an entire course as free DLC. Always nice to see that.
I had two minor complaints that I’ll expand on.
First was the constant zoom in on the player at the start of each hole and also during different strokes. The default camera is too close so I had to constantly zoom out so I could see where I was going on any particular hole. I wish it either saved your zoom level or had a slider option for “default zoom level”.
Second were the animations between shots. Where your worm would either scoot over to the ball or be transported. These became fairly annoying to sit through constantly. I would have loved an option to either speed these up or disable them. It would have made gameplay much faster. This is especially noticeable when playing a multiplayer game.
On to the pros/cons
+Graphics are nice, sharp and vibrant. Scales well to 1440p
+Smooth 60fps throughout
+Fun courses, well designed
+Good multiplayer (local co-op only)
+Replay value
+Collectibles to extend game length
+Free DLC
+Music & sound effects repetitive
+Zoom reset after each hole and after some strokes
+Animations between shots are slow
This is a great, casual game you can pick up if you or your friends are bored. The $10 asking price isn’t too bad considering the replay value is there with multiplayer support and if you want to complete all the holes 100% it will take a good amount of time.

This is the most universally appealing party video game I have seen yet.  I haven't tested it on a wide range of friends and family yet but, so far, it has great potential.  As good as my old 3-D Ultra Mini Golf game was (dead now because Sierra stuck this 32-bit game behind a 16-bit installer), and as good as Worms always is, Crazy Golf appears to work with a random group of people better.  Probably because it is less golf like than 3-D Ultra and easier and more widely appealing than Worms.  "If you don't already love earthworms, then surely you must love mini golf.  Right?"  That was probably the pitch at Team 17.
What is missing from the multi-player mode, however, is more mayhem.  This is surely due to the primary focus of the game being the single-player mode with the multi-player mode looking like an afterthought.  To add insult to injury, the different golf clubs, balls, and even hats, are locked up until someone decides to waste enough time in the single-player mode to earn enough coins to buy them all.  Sheesh.  Why do multi-player games do this?  I am continually annoyed by games I buy solely for their multi-player features only to find gear and characters and vehicles locked up in some irrelevant single-player achievement adventure.
Specifically, the mayhem falls short by strangely turning off the explosions and destruction seen in single-player mode.  What is particularly odd about this is that players don't interact in multi-player mode anyway.  So what, then, is the point of making the playfield indestructable if each player already gets their own copy of the playfield?  I suspect various ideas were play tested and nixed but I, at least, would prefer an option to turn on a destructable playfield and interactions with the worms and balls of other players [okay, that just sounds bad -- but such is the hazard of writing about Worms].  The current rules of non-engagement are good for many crowds, I am sure, but some of us prefer more chaos in our social engagements (see this for more discussion on mayhem and games:
).
So what! if a player gets stuck in a crater created by another and has to take a penalty to get out.  So what? if another worm or ball gets whacked by nearby players or their projectiles.  Isn't that what mini golf is about?  Croquet like?  Is was in my family.  Sure, I can see where parts of the game would need to be tweaked to make the game destructable and still playable (such as probably turning collisions off on the green), but those things can be worked out by the right creative minds.
Another thing I would like to see is the ability to play with friends online but, given the focus on single-player, I'm not surpised this is not here, and falls under Too Much to Ask.
Oh, yeah, fix that DirectX 9 depency already so that it installs smoothly with sound support on Windows after XP, and so we don't have look up the solution in the forums.  D'oh!!!
Regardless, this is a great party game in multi-player mode and well done with some good attention to detail.  Now, if I can just find some cheat codes to unlock all the gear.  I'm shaking my fist at you Team 17!

Saints Row IV is an open world action-adventure video game developed by Volition and published by Deep Silver. It is the fourth title in the Saints Row series. In the game, the playable character is the leader of the 3rd Street Saints, a street gang that has become the world's most powerful and popular organization, and must fend off an alien invasion after becoming President of the United States and receiving superpowers. The player is free to explore their environment while completing main and side missions at their leisure. The game incorporates elements from science fiction video games and films, and continues the series' reputation for over-the-top parody. It was released in August 2013 for Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 3, and Xbox 360, and was later ported to PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Linux in 2015.
The game was Volition's first after its sale to Koch Media in early 2013. The supernatural and superpower concept for the game started in Enter the Dominatrix, a cancelled expansion planned for Saints Row: The Third, which the team expanded into Saints Row IV. Volition later released a "director's cut" of Enter the Dominatrix as downloadable content for Saints Row IV alongside How the Saints Saved Christmas, other weapons, costumes, and vehicle packs, and a standalone expansion, Saints Row: Gat out of Hell (which serves as the epilogue to the story)
Similar to previous Saints Row series games, Saints Row IV is an open world action game with third-person shooter elements wherein the player is free to explore the environment and, at their leisure, play story or side missions. As the leader of the Saints, a street gang that has become the world's most "powerful and popular" organization, the player is elected President of the United States, receives superpowers, and fends off an alien invasion. Most often the player will engage in shooting and racing activities, though other activities vary from fighting crowds of zombies, shoot-outs in tanks, side-scrolling brawlers, fights against supersized, daikaiju energy drink cans, and using a dubstep gun to interrupt 1950s Americana. The player-character receives elemental powers and superpowers that greatly increase their jump height and running speed, such that the player can hop over buildings and outrun vehicles. The elemental powers include abilities to shoot fire and ice projectiles, telekinetically toss things, and create shockwaves upon landing jumps. As the player progresses through the game, they can optionally upgrade their abilities and weapons skill tree by using collectible "data clusters" scattered around town. If the player becomes too rowdy, the alien race's police analogue will intervene. As in previous games, the player-character's look and feel is entirely customizable via a robust character editor feature.
The game is set in a nearly identical simulation of Steelport, the fictional city setting from Saints Row: The Third, though individual story missions have new, custom-designed levels. Saints Row IV's story parodies science fiction video games, especially Mass Effect 2, as well as films like The Matrix and Zero Dark Thirty, and other "nerd culture". Some story missions are propelled by individual characters' existential crises, as each Saint character is stuck in a personal simulation of their own hell, and must be rescued by the player.

Helldivers is a fun game from the makers of Magicka. It is similar to Alien Swarm, but it has randomly generated maps and more humor. Missions are short but get longer as difficulty increases, and there are clear moments of low and high tension which keep the game interesting. At the end of each mission is a 2 minute extraction sequence kind of like the equivalent of a Left 4 Dead finale.
Each planet has a pattern of patrols crossing through it with some randomness. If a patrol spots you, you have a couple of seconds to kill it before it sounds an alarm and summons stronger enemies. It is technically possible to get through a mission without sounding any alarms, but I haven't done it yet.
Like Magicka, human players are  very powerful, with each player bringing 4 "stratagems" to each mission. A stratagem can be airdropping ammo supplies or it can be calling in an airstrike, or almost anything inbetween. I personally enjoy bringing a Guard Dog drone, which flies around and shoots at enemies (it has a quick reaction time, which helps me against the patrols). in addition to the 4 chosen strategems, each player gets a reinforce stratagem that resurrects dead players and any mission-specific stratagems like a metal detector for sniffing out mines. Because of the resurrection stratagem, death in Helldivers is not a big deal, and most of the time a player is not out of the game for very long. Also like Magicka, a mission is failed if all 4 players die without calling for reinforcements, however.
Two key differences between Magicka and Helldivers are:
1) In Helldivers, it is relatively easy to know when and where your attack is  going to hit. Killing friendlies is easily avoided most of the time, and few of the attacks are going to wipe the party. This allows for more consistent, less annoying gameplay, imo.
2) The writing of Helldivers has a theme with a bit of a smaller scope (making fun of Starship Troopers, mostly) but there are less references to internet memes.
I consider both of these differences to be, on the whole, positive.
Missions are randomly generated and each completed mission adds to the Community Influence in the galactic campaign, which is an aggregate function of all Helldivers' efforts in the war. As players spread managed democracy across the galaxy, they approach the home planets of 3 alien races: the Illuminates, Bugs, and Cyborgs. Each faction has its own sector of the galaxy, and the playerbase as a whole must balance their efforts to make sure that none of these factions gets too close to SuperEarth by completing missions in each respective sector.
There isn't a ton of plot, but there is some lore to read up on if you're into that sort of thing, and the Helldivers occasionally spit out gems like "Say 'hello' to Democracy!" while blowing up a planet with orbital strikes or stomping on things in a Mech resembling the Dreadnoughts of Warhammer 40k. You also unlock cosmetic customization options as you progress through the leveling system, and some of them look pretty nifty. Your cape is the most important item in the game, as it will flow magnificently behind you as you twirl in place.
Occasionally there are connection issues. A friend of mine seemed to be disconnected from the game any time we failed a mission. Other players have reported black screens. Once I saw, through a screenshot of someone else's game, an objective spawn outside of the bounds of the map. Personally i haven't experienced any issues other than seeing my friend disconnect, and I consider the game to be pretty playable in its current state (5/17/2016).
If I have a major complaint it is that the game forces all players to share a screen. This is the era of internet play and I don't need that nonsense. I have died a few times because I got stuck around an objective off screen and couldn't see. It isn't a huge deal in terms of enjoying the game, it's just an archaic design decision that gets in the way for players who are not playing local coop.

This game requires a bit of investment to figure out its nuances, but when you do, there's a beautiful (if somewhat small) world to explore with pieces of a good story hidden all around.
GAMEPLAY: WSAD control scheme. It's simplistic, without combat, platforming, or anything much beyond walking and examining objects to solve puzzles. This game says at the beginning that it "doesn't hold your hand" - which is very true. There's no map (until the end of the game), no journal to keep track of puzzles, no hint menu, and no indication as to how to do the puzzles. This may sound frustrating, and was for me - but when I figured out how to do each puzzle, there was a "eureka!" moment that made it all worthwhile. Without giving much away, puzzles generally consist of using paranormal abilities to recreate scenes from the past by placing a few key events in chronological order. It's a neat way of using game mechanics to further the narrative.
A problem here is the save system - it uses an autosave, but you never seem to know just when it autosaves. It doesn't deal breaking, as you may only have to do part of a puzzle again and the world isn't very large, but the uncertainty is irritating.
VISUALS: The valley looks beautiful, especially when you're on the dam or rail bridge and can get a commanding view of it all. It's lonely and serene, without so much as any wildlife to disturb it. It's bright and colourful, with some nice lighting effects, from the sun, moon, and fire. Unfortunately, there's not much to see beyond the puzzle items you'll find scattered around. This is especially problematic indoors, as there's little in the way of debris, decor, etc. to admire.
AUDIO: A slightly ominous score gives off the vibe that something sinister has occured in the valley, but without being so oppressive as to comprimise the beauty of the valley. It almost seems as though it's fine to pass through and even explore a bit, so long as you don't stick your nose into too much.
The voice acting is believeable, and the oily drawl of the protagonist is especially memorable.
NARRATIVE: This is what makes this game shine. You play as a paranormal detective who has been summoned to Red Creek Valley to locate a missing boy, and on the way, find out how he disappeared. The story is revealed in small chunks after each puzzle, and gives you enough at a time that you can begin to piece it together. A big part of the fun is thinking you know what's going on, coming up with your own theories, and then awaiting the next plot point to see if you were right. An added bonus to this is the way puzzles are used as an integreal part of the story, as they really have you think about the events in order to progress. When all is revealed, you won't be getting anything incredibly deep, but it's a creative murder mystery of sorts that keeps you guessing.
If "walking simulators" and puzzles aren't your thing, I doubt you'll enjoy this. Furthermore, the game isn't overly long, so the $22 asking price might be a bit steep, especially if you're on the fence.  However, it's well worth a purchase for those looking for some decently challenging puzzles and a story to work their minds around.

This mysterious first-person adventure game is a beautiful and bizarre experience that I enjoyed very much once I wrapped my head around the style of gameplay.  The player moves through an enormous world while investigating unknown events that occured there, gradually revealing a story in chunks at a time.
Even as soon as the first scene loads, it becomes apparent that the game does not plan on helping you figure much out.  The story progresses only when you manage to figure out certain nondescript sequences of events that are required to move the game forward. There are no loading screens, and you are left to wander in a quiet forest and valley of intimidating size and detail until you figure it out.  This is not a miserable thing, however, because the graphics are fantastic, the sound effects are incredibly lifelike, and the score is perfectly fitting.  When the realization hits you that you've figured out exactly what the devil that one critical action does that you've been hung up on for so long (and when it actually helps), you can progress with relative ease.  Once you learn to speak the language of its concepts, the game becomes much more enjoyable.  Dare I say it reminds me of
because of that? Again, not a miserable thing despite the possible implications.
The graphics and game engine really are astounding.  The forest areas are so realistic in composition to real life, it's like the developers took a photo somewhere in the most picturesque forest known to man and animated every minute detail of it.  Not only that, the architectural design of the buildings and props is astute as well.  If one can find flaw in this game, it is most likely not going to be in the visuals.
The story itself is very interesting and clever once you get used to its delivery.
is well worth the experience.  It is consistently interesting and engaging throughout even when you are not sure what needs to happen.  This game deserves the praise it gets.

1980 - Have your founder grind through contacts for your first year or two to get some cash in the kitty. Take a few months off to get educated.
1982 - start your first serious development project by hiring a 2-3 staff, a couple to help your founder develop and code, plus a marketer to hit the phones so the thing actually makes money. Rinse, lather and repeat.
1984 - work out that your teams are much happier and more productive if you make one of them a Lead and make the team have meetings and co-ordinate their efforts, and most importantly, get to know each other's most shameful secrets. ("I liked the ewoks!" - *gasp*)
1986 - one of your titles (probably 2D or 3D editor with innovative features) takes off and now you can afford a dedicated team to create an operating system while you have other teams working on smaller projects - mostly sequels to your hit to keep the cash coming.
1990 - Your first OS does well enough to make a reasonable profit, but it's definitely niche and only used by people who've heard of the internet. Start working on Version 2,
1992 - you have enough people working in your firm that you need several cooks to keep them fed. Hope they like spaghetti bolognese.
1995 - Congratulations, you are Microsoft. Commence driving your competitors to the wall until Apple gets Steve Jobs back.
I bought this as EA a while back, it was a bit barebones but the potential was there. Fortunately, development has continued and I am now pleasantly surprised how "sticky" the game is now since I've gotten back into it (October 2016).
There's quite a bit more meat on the bones, and is now pretty compelling as what is basically an office sim - if you work in a office, you can pretty much set up. Software just happens to be the product your worker drones. It is quite dry, but is also cute in its own way. It seems a little more free-form, in that once you get the cashflow working you can set up several teams working on different projects at various stages. (By this point I'd say the UI/UX could use a few quality of life improvements, as you start having to scroll the job list to keep track of it all, but it's really not too bad as is)
I guess if there's one element that could do with some balancing, it's the end-game progression which can hit you pretty quick and the monetary challenge just goes *puff*. But then you can build an enormous office full of drones and commence world domination. The 3D modelling is representative rather than realistic but to me, it's just about right between eye-candy and performance, given that you could potentially employ hundreds (I haven't really pushed the limits yet!).
Of course, this is still in Early Access, so there's probably more features and improvements to come. For instance, maybe more variety of furniture and building objects (although the building system is really quite flexible since you now build things at weird angles), a little more sophistication behind the economic and technology models, although these probably need a tweak more than an overhaul.
There's also a pretty decent modding scene on Workshop, with a bunch of furniture, building blueprints, as well as new software and even hardware types that you can develop just in case vanilla doesn't give you enough to do.
So def recommend as it is already pretty solid, although I would like to see more stuff added to it.

This game keeps getting better and better.  Been playing for months and I can't put it down.  There are plenty of great touches that make the game a classic.  I love the overall campy/Starship Troopers feel to the game.  But, instead of just bugs you also have to fight the technology of the Illuminate and the gun-toting armor of the Cyborgs.  It is a war against 3 races in a number of interesting environments (forest, snow, desert, and volcanic).  You play the game as a team of up to 4 players.  Your mission is to complete several multi-objective missions in order to secure a planet and help all Helldivers gain a foothold against each of the enemy races in an overall war.   If the community neglects any one race, it could quickly overcome Super Earth and the war is lost.  But drive forward through multiple systems and the Helldivers can conquer the home planet of any of the races and knock them out of the war.  Knock all 3 races out and the war is won.  Along the way, your player gains experience and unlock stratagems and weapons.   Stratagems can be called down throughout the battle.  They can provide support or devastating attacks.  But calling down a stratagem is no simple tasks as you need to complete a series of up-down-left-right key combinations to call it.  This means taking your eye off the battle with possible fatal results.  Losing focus isn’t the only way to die.  Your teammates can accidently shoot you, a drop pod can land on your head, a volcano can dump its lava all over you, or you could fall off the edge into many of the bottomless pits on many maps.  At times there seems like a 100 different ways to die.  This can be tough on players new to the game.  But, this is indeed where the real challenge lies.  There is nothing more satisfying than a perfect Hell Dive accomplished with an experienced team.  The community has been great.  A game like this lives or dies based on the number of in-game idiots.  But, my experience has been very positive.  I’ve added more Steam friends playing this game than any other in the last 5 years.  Finally, the graphics themselves are plenty adequate for this type of game.  But the sound quality is EXCELLENT.  Environmental sounds and weapons fire are extremely well done.  The cinematic score does an excellent job of building up the excitement when the action is hot.  I don’t ever remember a game where the musical score did such a seamless job of building suspense and excitement.  This game tastes better than a “cup of LiberTea!!”.  Don’t miss it!!

Metro 2033 is the video game adaptation to Dmitry Glukhovsky's eponymous book, detailing the struggle of humanity to survive in a lethal world created by a cataclysmic war.
The Redux edition of the game carries several changes to its presentation, graphics and art design, level design and gameplay, and I find most of these additions to be very welcome.
Immersion is this game's strongest card, and it delivers it even from the main menu, which is rendered in great detail as a 3D space, and various desk items and screens light up depending on your choice. Being based on a best-selling book, it also has a head start in the plot, dialogue and character development departments.
From a technical standpoint, Metro 2033 already looked sharp: high detail shadows, high resolution textures, Analytical Anti-Aliasing for a crisp image, volumetric particles, and one of the best lighting engines I've seen. It turns out the dark, cramped confines of the Moscow metro provides the perfect opportunity to bring the best lighting your engine can handle. The Redux version not only manages to look even better, but even runs better on a wider range of hardware: I can enjoy faux-4K ultra quality at a stable 60fps on my desktop, while my laptop is content with 0.5x upscaling and medium settings.
The artistic side hasn't been neglected either, as there's now a much wider palette of faces and appearances any random human can have in the game, making it less likely to see the same face on two different dudes. The other creatures have been given an upgrade, as well, so they look really good while scaring you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and then disemboweling your character.
Where it fails somewhat in the graphics department is the animation: it is moderately better than the standard Metro 2033, but you still have moments of floaty character movement, weird camera gliding, and other such oddities when cutscenes happen.
Sound is a mixed bag overall, and my greatest gripe with the game overall. The music, all in all, is good. It fits the atmosphere and kicks in when needed. Spoken voice lines are just a tad underwhelming. The sound effects, however, are for the most part stock sound effects. Generic revolver firing sound, generic lion roars for some monsters, and even some environmental impact sounds (concrete, wood, glass) are exactly like the ones from Half Life 2. I can't not pay attention to them, as they disrupt my suspension of disbelief even for a split second.
Gameplay is a mix of First Person Shooter and Survival Horror. Fittingly for a post-apocalyptic game world, whenever you're not sneaking and shooting around, you're looting whatever you can for the much needed scraps of ammo that also double, in one case, as
Military Grade 5.45mm Rounds, in a pinch, will make short work of most enemies, but then again, you'll be literally shooting money. Your arsenal of firearms go from the mundane revolvers and real-world rifles, to submachine guns clobbered up from bits of other guns, revolving shotguns made from bicycle parts, a heavy machine gun adapted to fire shotgun shells, and various ball-bearing or arrow firing pneumatic and electromagnetic weapons.
There is a minimal heads up display on the lower difficulties, but steeping into the Ranger difficulties cuts down even those sparse elements, leaving you reliant almost entirely on memorisation of your resource amounts, as well as on your vision, breathing and heartbeat for your current status. Your waypoint is shown by bringing up a dossier, with its compass (or the included lighter's flame) pointing towards your next objective. Even some of your weapons have diegetic "readings" for remaining ammo or pressure, most notably the Kalash, thanks to its always visible translucent magazine.
As difficulty increases, supplies and ammo become increasingly scarce - expect no more than 1 bullet per stripper clip you find on Ranger Hardcore, for instance - merchant transactions work more and more against you, and everything deals more damage and takes less pounding. A second-long burst of weapons fire or two claws from some monsters will become enough to do you in.
Direct combat almost always comes at a loss on higher difficulties. Thankfully, you have a revised stealth system in the Redux edition, where instead of only being able to avoid or kill enemies from the shadows, and having a gradual visibility system that didn't quite work well, now you only have a "you can be seen"/"you can only be seen when literally in someone's face" display on your watch, and you can also just knock out enemies with hilarious punches, chops and elbows to the neck or face.
Also, that very good lighting system? It works wonders to scare the crap out of you with things that you can't see, but can hear!
Redux also brings forth Metro: Last Light's weapon customisation system, making it so that instead of scrounging for an exact weapon setup that suits your needs, you can just install the desired weapon mods, within monetary reason of course.
It's not a long story, and it doesn't have to be. You'll be looking at between 7-12 hours to complete the game, depending on your skill and chosen difficulty. I will say, though, that the Metro games
It perfectly encapsulates the dog-eat-dog nature of the new world humans live in, and creates a sense of tension and fear that becomes absent when you have an abundance of resources and the means to recover from a failure.
As a part of the Redux Bundle, Metro 2033 Redux is absolutely worth your time. The original, while still flawed, was a great game in its own right, and with this update it is a hearty recommendation. For the $8 I spent on the bundle, it is a must buy.

These are not always the most fresh of ideas, but they break the pace of the various puzzle-box mechanics and add a layer of interest to the existing underlying plot. There's also the added atmospheric benefit to the game coming from that shift.
Furthermore, the game features greater interactivity with the rooms, and even has some nicer comments added at the end of each chapter (compared to the generic blurb at the end of each chapter in the first game).
Finally, the game wrapped up a first story arc for the series, with a nod at games to follow (The Room Three being out there for smartphone owners, of course, but not yet for desktop computers).
