This is a difficult game to review - in a good way. :)
*Note - I am writing this reviews as a slightly prejudiced and a huge fan of plot driven adventure games, a person who was, you could say, "raised" on classic adventure games, such as the cherished Broken Sword, Lucas Arts' Monkey Island, Full Throttle, legendary Grim Fandango, and Gabriel Knight. I also have experience with more recent adventure titles, such as Agatha Christie games, Fahrenheit: Indigo Prophecy, and various lesser known indie and non-indie titles from all eras of adventure games.
The game begins with a warning (now I'm keen on thinking of it as more of a product disclaimer, literally) - - -
"THIS GAME DOES NOT HOLD YOUR HAND."
(Implying: Don't curse our names while waving your fist around if you find that fact annoying while playing, as you have been rightly warned) :D
And it's true, all the way.
Let's start with the game itself.
This game is beautiful. Period. One of the most detailed, nuanced and stunningly jaw-dropping visuals I have ever seen in a game, not just within the adventure branch.
You are inserted deep in Pennsylvania countryside, and as it's seems, and it's fall. The most nostalgic part of the year. You play as Paul Prospero, an experienced, observant and world-weary detective who "specializes" in supernatural stuff. Prospero's voice acting and
internal monologues are very well-done, and quite badass IMHO, and even if there isn't that much voice acting
in the game, the main protagonists come off as pretty well-rounded.
You are investigating the disappearance of a young boy, named Ethan Carter, who had sent a cryptic letter to
Paul Prospero's (your) address, warning him (you) of his upcoming disappearance and strange events happening in Red Creek Valley, in Pennsylvania.
Well enough for a plot, and there are many more things for you to discover. The story is layered, emotionally charged, quite original,
and takes you for a ride in some unexpected directions. And that's a good thing. Admittedly, I have not yet finished the game, but I am working on it. ;)
The game revolves around A LOT of exploration in your environment and surroundings, looking around for objects
or traces of disturbance, and trying to "reconstruct" what happened at that place, some time ago.
Our world weary detective Prospero also has supernatural powers, as he can literally "reconstruct" a crime scene,
by seeing murder victims, collecting objects associated with the incident and placing them where they were during the time of the event/crime/struggle, etc.
Takes a while to get used to, although I believe it's an innovative and well-utilized approach.
Soundtrack is excellent, soothing most of the time, mysterious and intense when it needs to be - and helps very much to tell the story in it's own way. Every specific location in the game has it's own theme; which only adds to the overall excellent atmosphere of mystery and exploration.
The game is very atmospheric - while not exactly a "horror" game (although there are a few REALLY good scares, belive me), best description that would fit would be "supernatural thriller" - think David Lynch's Twin Peaks series , and Lovecraft's or maybe Robert Louis Stevenson's supernatural fiction, combined with a soothing and meditative stroll
through the woodland outbacks.
You are free to explore the game at your own pace, and in your own way. You can solve the puzzles in any order you see fit, and that is quite good.
Freedom of movement and exploration in the beautiful outbacks is quite generous, too.
So, what's the problem, you may ask? What makes this gripping, atmospheric and emotional story a tough one to review, and to recommend?
Well, it's like this...
There is <NO> inventory. Nothing. Nada. Rien. Zip.
Also, no compass, and no map whatsovever. No way to get your bearings. The map isnt' that much of a problem, really - because you can get around pretty fast and it's not that tough to get your bearings, and it also makes a good orientation practice.
The complete lack of inventory is a bigger problem, given that you do have to collect some important items in the game,
and there is no way to see or examine them further once you've collected them. So, you better remember well what you've picked up and where. I know that it's supposed to make the game feel as an "artistic" and unique experience, different from other adventure titles, but it makes sense for an experienced supernatural detective to maybe, just maybe, know what he has in his coat and pants pockets, right? Right...?
But the worst thing of all (and this doesn't affect all gamers/reviewers equally, but it did bother me quite a bit) - the wacky, counter-intuitive and unhelpful saving system.
There is NO way to save manually. The game does have autosave function - but ONLY after the game decided that
you have "made progress", reconstructed a crime scene, reached a place of importance, or something like that. On the plus side, you can't "do" anything wrong, or in the wrong order - you are completely free to play the game in the order you wish, no need to worry about making "mistakes" that will be saved and block you from advancing, or things like that. Although, do expect having to collect some items again and to play through some areas again if the game did not autosave.
As I said, it doesn't bother everyone - but it bothered me. Not enough to give up on the game, no way, but still; certainly not a plus IMO. Did the developers make it that way to make us work harder on puzzle solving? Or just a ploy to "extend" the game experience?
You be the jugde. :)
Graphics are stunning, true - but if you want the game in full detail and lag-free, you better have a decent current-gen graphics card, and minimally 2GB RAM. This is also not often seen in the tradition of adventure video games; hardware demands. While not staggering, they are higher than with your usual adventure title. Truth be told, graphics and visual experience  justify it at least to an extent.
There is the possibility of a lagging, which is also a minus - try changing the "camera smoothing" option, and if need be, get rid of anti-aliasing and some other stuff. Even though I can play it decently with an incredible amount of detail and in high configuration, it still sometimes lags just a bit with my GeForce GTX650.
Do I recommend this game? That's a tough one. I have hit "thumbs up", but only because it was mandatory. :P xD
Why?
Because, as with most things in life - it depends. :)
If you want an emotionally rich and mysterious story, and you want to get lost in the woods (this game is good to tun to i
you're stressed or tense, it comes as a soothing experience, trust me), this is the right game for you.
If you like  slow-paced, meditative and mysteryious experience, this is the right thing.
If you enjoy a lot of quirky and offbeat dialogue with many characters in the game (similar to LucasArts classics), then it's not the best choice. If you enjoy faster-paced adventure games with some guidelines, you might try looking somewhere else.
As for the price range, I would suggest grabbing it if there's a Steam discount available.
I would even recommend it to newcomers to adventure genre - honestly, it might even sit better with newcomers
than veterans, because it is a fair departure from most of the other "cult" status titles.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter brings something new to the beloved adventure genre. How successful it is?
Get lost in the woods and solve the mystery for yourself! :)

First of all this game looks incredible, the landscapes look very realistic. The atmosphere is eerie and broken, not like game broken, like something happened so grave that it rent the land itself. You can feel something is wrong from the moment you start, and it lingers after you finish. Unlike most mystery games, you actually feel like a detective piecing together bits and pieces of an event that changed this entire small town.
Secondly, it's short as hell. I didn't even clock 5 hours and I notoriously leave my games on while I break or eat, that's about half a telltale game. It was a complete experience and I'm not regretting my purchase, but I mention length because I wanted MORE. The game has such a massive, beautiful setting with so many nooks and crannies that, in most games, would contain content of some sort, easter eggs or notes or something. I scoured every inch of the area like I always do and it actually paid off once early on, I found a thing that had no use, then from then on, nothing. After a couple hours of disappointing nook after disappointing cranny, I simply stopped exploring and pursued the main objective--the only objective.
Thirdly, this game has more rocks than any game ever made, probably any piece of media ever made, probably inch for inch more rocks than earth itself. The ground is made of rocks, the horizon is all rocks, the forest is made of rocks, the buildings are made of rocks, there is an entire sequence where you're underground with nothing but rocks. This could have been called Rock Quest or Rock Story because just as you think "there couldn't possibly be more rocks around this corner" you turn the corner to find the largest rock you've ever seen. It's not good or bad, they are very pretty rocks, very well designed landscapes, but I think the sheer volume of rocks in this game is a bigger mystery than the Vanishing of Ethan Carter.
In short, nice game..

is an indie game made by The Astronauts studio. This is a story-driven mystery game where you control a private detective named Paul Prospero, exploring and discovering several clues by communicating with the dead and seeing visions that help him locate a missing boy and discover the mistery behind a dark force lurking in Red Creek Valley.
In terms of gameplay, its a game with very simple mechanics, yet they work perfectly in it with many enjoyable puzzles that will engage you into the game. There is not much more to discuss in this aspect since this is a story-driven game, but I can say that everything gameplay wise works in favor of the game, and its experience, which overall focus on exploring beautiful scenarios for clues that help you solve the mystery around Red Creek Valley, while having a great sense of freedom that differenciates this piece of art from other linear story-driven games.
Longevity is pretty small since I completed the game in about 3 hours, but somewhat expected since this is a story-driven game. Yet you will certainly spend some more hours into the game just by wandering through the astonishing environments present in the game, as by taking several screenshots since this is one of the most beautiful environments in game history in my opinion. The only two downsides of this game are really the length and the few autosave locations present in the game (no manual save feature either).

This is an extremely important category in this game since, like I said before, it is a story-driven game. And boy, how good it was! This is an extremely powerful and interesting story making the game extremely captivating. The writing is very smart, it is amazing to see a game with such smart writing and dialogs. This game also uses complex themes in its story in a very interesting and sometimes unpredictable way. The pacing of the story is top-notch too as the mystery unravels slowly till you reach the end. I also enjoyed the ending very much, it was an amazing conclusion and I am sure most of you will love it to.
Moving on, lets discuss the graphics. They are amazing! A-M-A-Z-I-N-G! This is one extremely gorgeous game. The environments are simply breathtaking. If you like taking screenshots, you will do it all the time in this game. Absolutely insane the level of detail and spectacularity present in the scenario. It is so good that it makes you wanna visit a place like the Red Creek Valley in the real life. With amazing views like it has, the exploration part of the game feels extremely good, instead of feeling like a chore like in some other games.
Sound-wise I do not have any complaints either. The soundtrack is a perfect fit, as the sound effects. Voice acting was very good too, did not seemed like it was an Indie game at all.
Performance was great in my medium specs rig (you can see it in my profile). I played it in my 1440x900 resolution with almost every graphical settings maxed out (you have plenty of them to tweak in the game laucher) at 60 fps, with very few drops to never less than 50 fps.
8.5/10
If you like story-driven games this is a must-buy. If you are looking for a game with amazing graphics this is also a must-have game. An amazing tale that revolves around the supernatural with a powerful story and a beautiful world to wander around. The small longevity may make you doubt about the value of this game, but even from its base price this game is one to have in your steam library. Have fun wandering through Red Creek Valley.

★★☆☆☆ - "Average at best, Id give it a miss"
PROS:
- Visually stunning, the game is beautiful. The textures are incredibly detailed and realistic and theres a atmosphere similar to that from Naughty Dog's 'The Last of Us'.
- Room changing and Maze puzzle. This game has two terrific puzzles which whilst not difficult, worked brilliantly. The latter provides a cheeky little scare also.
-Soundtrack completely sets the tone and reflects on the areas you visit and helps with immersion.
CONS:
- Puzzles, I only mentioned two cause in my opinion they were the only ones. For a game heavily labelled with the genres 'Mystery' and 'Detective' its completely unjustified. The detective elements are shallow as hell, they're almost insulting. At first with the traps I thought the game had pulled me into another world but I soon realised it simply tells you where to go with images not hard to work out. When you start the game it tells you, 'We will not hold your hand'..this is a lie. Whilst they are no checkpoints or mission icons the mystery elements give you everything you need without allowing you to solve a thing. There could have been real clues to make you think and lead you to the next area but instead you're told by a series of words and in some cases you line them up using the camera.
- Story, this just about makes a Con cause reflecting back I did actually want to know what was going on, but do I even now? Not really, its so vague and difficult to understand not because its complicated but because its such a daft premise and it has a terrible ending.
- Choose the Order of the events..okay so this is the games main mechanic. What happens if you guess incorrectly? Nothing. You try again. In some cases its insultingly easy and the stances or animations are nothing, they feel like they're put in just to make up time and gameplay. Frogwares recent Sherlock Holmes instalment 'Crimes and Punishments' has this mechanic however it only utilises it on 3 occasions during the game and its done better. That game is made out of repercussions of decisions, mini game puzzles, interrogation and real detective elements.
- You feel like you achieve nothing, I didn't feel in control of anything as a detective, its more of a walking simulator like Dear Ester and more importantly like reading a book. Theres nothing wrong with that other than its not what is says on the tin.
- £14.99 for 4 hours of gameplay, no thanks. Thankfully I paid £3 and thats all its worth I'm afraid.
VERDICT?
Its important that I inform you I planned on giving this a recommendation when I set out with this review, for the first time I have change my mind whilst writing. Thats how on the fence I was, however on reflection this game has a real lack of substance and in my opinion lies about its detective elements and about offering you a difficult thought provoking experience without much guidance. I was totally disappointed with this game.

This a nostalgic and fair but difficult puzzle platformer I would say belongs in the masocore category (but again, it's fair, unlike some other masocore games such as I Wanna Be The Guy). It's really hard, expect a thousand deaths on your path to the end of the game, where you invariably will lose the first time because you haven't figured the magic word out yet. So you're started from the same place again without your power pickups, where you get to play through the whole thing again in a try to figure the answer out. If that's not enough for you, you can run the game in a cat form, with only nine lives. Or in the YOLO mode. And after that there's a harder remix of the levels for you to try out, again with the earlier mentioned modifications if you find that too easy...
Aesthetically, the game hits it's spot. It's got that CGA monitor, scanlines, big pixel, CRT bending, effect to it that looks really authentic. Or if you want to upgrade to an EGA monitor, you can do that, too. If you want to turn off the CRT screen effects, you can do that. The controls are really responsive and smooth, with one little nitpick from me - if you're using a controller, for this kind of platformer I really would like to be able to use the D-pad for movement instead of just the left stick. The premise of "Seduce Me" is wonderful, and it could have made for an exciting dating sim. However, that interesting plot is overshadowed by confusing, unrelated subplots, cut-and-paste romantic dialogue for each of the incubi, a lack of character development, gaping plot holes, and a villain (Malix) who manages to be more interesting, well-rounded and fun than all of the main characters combined. One of the main issues is that there are too many characters, and those characters constrained to being common archetypes instead of actual people with relatable emotion.
Some of the choices are outright bizarre, others are essentially meaningless. There are very few moments that have any emotional weight. And all of the romantic options, save for Andrew, are simply unrealistic. Let's be honest: Mika falling in love with a demon she's known for a few days and has absolutley nothing in common with isn't just unrealisitc, it's actually kind of creepy. Even the romantic entanglements with long-time friends seemingly come from nowhere.
For every instance of poor writing, there's a glimmer of quality entertainment. Some of the voice acting is unintentionally hilarious, some of it is genuinely decent. But this is not a good visual novel in the slightest, and I'm actually surprised this was successfully funded. If you're looking for some shallow entertainment for a few hours, free of cost, I would recommend this- if you're looking for a decent romance, however, look elsewhere.

A very fun top-down shooter mostly based on teamwork and cooperation.
In HELLDIVERS, you are essentially the human race settling in a new home planet for what is called Super Earth. However, there are 3 factions that call for war and you are required to fight them in order to liberate their sectors to gain peace amongst human and other species.
+ Large variety of equipment and "stratagems" (Call-ins that can provide support or bring in a piece of gear). There are a lot of weapons that you can choose for certain types of missions or if you're wanting to change your style. As for stratagems, there is also a large quantity of those that you can chose and a type for each different scenario, also has substitutes if you have yet to unlock the one you want.
+ 3 different factions/species you can fight against. (Unless that faction has been defeated)
+ Enemy patrols can and will call for back up if you are spotted and haven't wiped out the patrol. Wiping out the patrol before they can send a signal will prevent their back up and you can continue on your merry way of completing the mission. However, allowing the patrol to signal for reinforcements will cause you pain and misery in the higher difficulties.
+ Very basic controls, stratagem call-ins require you to do some button smashing, but it's fairly simple. Until you screw up, that is.
+ A long ongoing war that will continue regardless if you lose or win. Losing requires for the WHOLE community to not play or to be so horrible that they manage to lose the entire sector, which allows the enemy faction to invade your home planet. On the other hand, winning will be a long, hard journey of triumphing multiple missions in order to claim important cities and sectors alike.
-+ Large amount of DLC. Can be see as a con as some DLC are not worth getting or if you're a not into paid DLC. However, you can get all of the DLC if you want to support the devs or get the Digital Deluxe Edition whenever it goes on sale.
-+ Small Stealth aspect, it's possible to avoid any conflict, but you better be looking on your map every 5 seconds and lie on the ground whenever you spot a patrol passing by. Be aware that suppressed weapons won't hide you. Learnt that the hard way.
-+ This can be seen as a con or a pro. The camera is based on the entirety of the squad, forcing you to stay with the team. Also causes issues when the team is horrible at placement, causing you or someone to have a VERY limited view.

Starting off as a struggling developer working out of a 3x2 'shed', reluctantly doing contract work to fund my own pet project, ultimately to be disappointed by the traction of your first and second releases, dealing with exorbitant development licenses just to be able to build your software for the latest and greatest operating systems, and paying for game engines and image editing software and the like. A little later, one of my projects finally catches a few thousand peoples attention, and I make 100k profit from it; enough to increase my office space, add a few creature comforts and take on a likeminded individual to help me with version 2. By the time we complete it, operating systems have moved on, and the money we spent on licenses is all for nought. Fortunately, we are able to port it to the latest version of the OS (at a cost, naturally!).
Fast forward 15 years, and I now employ 40 people including a dedicated design team and support team, and not only do I do my own software, I design, test, support and server host for a range of companies... many that I have bought shares in when they were new in the market, then helped to succeed (or fail... in order to buy a particularly juicy piece of IP from them!.). I have a bunch of team and project leaders to help me delegate and organise; I can't do everything myself!
I even have my own software distribution system, and now my ambition is to become the next Steam. ;)
As I said, it's a pretty deep game, with research, OS and engine dependancies, porting of software, marketing, trading IPs, stocks and shares etc as well as the people and resource management you expect. Not to mention the freeform building and furnishing of your offices, which gives it an additional and very personal sort of 'The Sims if you were micromanaging their work instead of their lives' vibe, rather than just manipulating a bunch of stats.
Your employees are surprisingly complex, too. They have personality, skills, learning abilities, laziness, likes, dislikes etc that affects their interactions and efficiency as a team. I have employees that I actually hate - that the rest of the team hate - but they're so darn good at their jobs I put up with them. The fact that individual employees can evoke this kind of reaction rather than just being 'some generic employee' is testament to how well this game plays.
So anyway, the fact that you can do all of the above within the confines of a £10 early access game is extremely encouraging and though I'm not sure what else there is to add in an already well rounded game, I'm sure it can only get better.
tl;dr: I'm always cautious about early access but if you like micromanagement business sims, this is as good as they get and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it.

I cannot begin to describe how boring and tedious this game was to navigate.
Notice that I didn't say play.
While there appear to be some inventory management puzzles, these merely amount to a checkpoint system. Go click on one thing, watch a bunch of words circle around; then, go click another thing. Some of these things that you click give you puzzle pieces of larger visions. But collecting all the parts of these visions involve long meanders across very similar looking terrain. It is all very green or rocky, or occupied by dilapidated structures and abandoned buildings, but all so very empty.
The stretches between finding something, anything, to interact with are painfully long and litter the aforementioned overgrown and homogenous landscape. Now don't get me wrong, the settings are very pretty and detailed. The music creates a sense of foreboding and mood. The sound is composed of subtle authentic sounding forest noises: wind rustling branches, distant lonely birds and so on.
There is a large amount of real estate to traverse and you only have two speeds of travel: excrutiatingly slow and merely painfully slow. There is no fast travel; though, for reasons I never discovered, you can crouch.
I thought maybe the crouch move would be for some stealth elements or to get into low places, but since I encountered not a single other soul and didn't go inside anything other than a train car, I couldn't figure out a purpose for the key other than simulating my character napping from all the boredom.
Probably the most absurd moment is right at the beginning when the game announces that it won't be holding your hand. Immediately, anything you encounter simply involves holding the mouse button and then words swirl on the screen quite literally telling you what to do. (i.e. Old train engine with a connection for a crank? Go find crank: check.)
Not holding my hand, as best I can tell, is a reference to the sprawling, mostly empty, landscapes that you must travel without the aid of an automap function. Wandering in circles hoping to bump into the next thing I'm suppossed to stand in front of and hold a mouse button to activate isn't my idea of fun.
The voice acting is good, but the few things that the narrator (presumably your character, though I didn't hear/see that definitively stated) are noir platitudes. The character talks about working hundreds of cases as a detective, but we don't get any details. The character talks about the darkness of the locale, but no sense imagery is used. The narrator mentions going to the 'other side' and leaving parts of himself there. Beyond leaving his automap there, I had no idea what that really meant or why I should care.
In the end, I simply dashed around as much of the environment as I could. The few locations that looked even remotely interesting or promising were closed, gated or had no obvious mean of approach, which seems like an appropriate metaphor for experinecing this 'game'.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter sounds nice and looks pretty, but it is vapid and empty, grasping at mood and a random and distant scattering of things to click on, instead of providing any interesting characters and the promised narrative experience.

You Have To Win The Game, besides being a blanket statement that applies to all games, is a wonderfully charming free to play retro platformer. The game is practically a love letter to the old platformers on the ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64 like Jet Set Willy and Fantasy World Dizzy. It's a breed of platformer that could be called "open world". Instead of distinct, linear levels, these platformers are usually just one giant, sprawling level. The game gives you an objective, usually several items to collect, stuffs the level full of checkpoints, and then sends you on your merry way. You Have To Win The Game follows the formula to a T, right down to the EGA graphics. For those of you who are somewhat ingrained into the indie game scene, you may be thinking that the description I gave sounds an awful lot like another C64-inspired indie game. You'd be absolutely right! You Have To Win The Game bears uncanny similarities to Terry Cavanaugh's indie masterpiece VVVVVV. Both are difficult, retro platformers with checkpoints, exploration elements, unlockable areas, no health bars or lives system, and rooms with distinct, often clever names. That being said, You Have To Win The Game is more similar to the actual games it's trying to pay homage to. Now, both games are great in their own rights.
VVVVVV is one of my favorite indie games EVER. You Have To Win The Game unfortunately doesn't emulate what makes me love VVVVVV. Now, I can't vilify a game for not being similar enough to another game that I enjoy. Both are great games and are worth your time. Both set out to do different things, and both accomplish what they each set out to do with flying colors. Where as VVVVVV is a mind bending, acid trip of a platformer, You Have To Win The Game is a slower, thoughtful, more casual experience. That is not to say that it is a casual game, but instead is to say that you can play it with less commitment than VVVVVV. You Have To Win The Game is far less difficult than VVVVVV and also skimps on the story, so you don't have to be as invested when you play it. Even with the difficultly scaled back, It still provides a rather meaty challenge. So, those who have never played Mario before should proceed with caution. The gameplay is nothing that hasn't been done before. In fact, it's about as run-of-the-mill as you can get. But the level design and difficulty is enough to keep the game interesting. My biggest gripe is the omission of a map screen. I realize that the developers are likely going for accuracy here, but the open world nature of the game makes it rather easy to get lost and the absence of a map makes it even worse.
While the gameplay in You Have To Win The Game is nothing new, it was the game's visuals that made me fall in love with it. I'm no expert, but the graphics appear to be completely accurate to the capabilities of an early 80's IBM PC. They are sweet, lovable, charming, and give the game that sort of quaint retro feel. The game uses two color pallets, a 3 color CGA, and 16 color EGA, the two most common pallets of the time. The game also allows you to add in emulated screen curvature, video artifacts, color bleed, and scanlines that make the game look like it's being played on an old computer monitor. They can all be turned off if you'd rather play the game pixel for pixel without the old monitor feel, but I feel it loses something if you do. It gives an incredible sense of retro-activeness. If you didn't know, you easily be fooled into thinking that you are playing a real, honest-to-God, PC platformer from the 80's. The graphics will disarm you with their charm and give you a big, warm, 8-bit hug. The sound design is sort of lacking, though. The game has no ambient soundtrack, which I suppose is accurate. I can't really comment on the sound design in detail, though. It's hard to really form an opinion when there are about 4 or 5 sound effects and nothing else. I suppose that those sound effects are all the game really needs, but I would've loved to see a quirky, lovable soundtrack.
All in all, You Have To Win The Game is a rare, free to play gem in the generally murky swamp that is Steam. It is a game that will make you fall in love with it from the first moment. While not my favorite platformer, You Have To Win The Game can definitely hold its own in the ring against a game like VVVVVV. And considering the fact that VVVVVV isn't free, You Have To Win The Game is worth more penny for penny. It is a game that you will love.
PROS
+ Charming, quaint visuals
+ Retro feel
+ Provides a decent challenge
+ A bunch of cool, retro monitor options
+ Full USB controller support
+ Completely, 100% free
CONS
- No map screen
- No soundtrack
- Can be a bit too easy at times
- Easy to get lost
I Give It a 8.9/10

I'm gonna put this paragraph first because I feel this could make someone change their mind about buying this game. A Story About My Uncle is one of those that was literally made for speedrunning and it does have a time trial mode. Searching for the best shortcuts and choosing the best moves to overcome certain obstacles, planning and executing the perfect run is much more exhilirating than the basic gameplay. If you enjoy that sort of thing, you can significantly stretch the 3-5 hour average playtime. On the downside, there's only a handful of maps so you can grow bored with it pretty quickly.
Now, I'm rather bad at platforming so it probably took me significantly longer to play through the game than almost everybody else and there were a few times I had trouble navigating myself through the 3D environment as well as a few times when I knew what I had to do but had difficulty executing it. All that sprinting, jumping and basically flying can be very exhilirating but since there isn't any other aspect to the gameplay (except the speedrunning potential), you may feel unmotivated to get through the more difficult/annoying bits. If there were other puzzles and a more extensive (and compelling) story, it would be an epic game. As it is, it feels more like a promo.

This is an AMAZING game. It is an RPG Tower Defence. Instead of towers, you have a party of people, which are put in to 6 different classes. You only get a max of 6 of each class, so placing them on the lvls more important than other tower defence games.As a bonus, everyone in your party gets XP even if they were not put out, which makes getting those lvl 1 guys you just got up to a lvl that they can be helpful much easier.
Each party member has their own lvl as well, and each class has 5 different skills they can use in total. However, when on a lvl, you must 'boost' them to get access to the high lvl skills. This, in turn, makes the game very strategic. Do you put a few of your people out, and boost them to Max at the start, or do you put more people out, and only boost them to lvl 2 or 3.
If you like Tower Defence games, and are looking for a challenge, then this game is right up your ally. And, as a bonuses, the story as actually pretty dam good too. XD

I love this game. I have several (many!) like it, because I love these kind of management games. This, however, is a cut above the rest already! It's surprisingly deep and seems extremely well balanced for realism; and I do have some experience of this, since I am a software developer for real (yeah, I know... I play a fictional software developer in my free time, now, too!)
Starting off as a struggling developer working out of a 3x2 'shed', reluctantly doing contract work to fund my own pet project, ultimately to be disappointed by the traction of your first and second releases, dealing with exorbitant development licenses just to be able to build your software for the latest and greatest operating systems, and paying for game engines and image editing software and the like. A little later, one of my projects finally catches a few thousand peoples attention, and I make 100k profit from it; enough to increase my office space, add a few creature comforts and take on a likeminded individual to help me with version 2. By the time we complete it, operating systems have moved on, and the money we spent on licenses is all for nought. Fortunately, we are able to port it to the latest version of the OS (at a cost, naturally!).
Fast forward 15 years, and I now employ 40 people including a dedicated design team and support team, and not only do I do my own software, I design, test, support and server host for a range of companies... many that I have bought shares in when they were new in the market, then helped to succeed (or fail... in order to buy a particularly juicy piece of IP from them!.). I have a bunch of team and project leaders to help me delegate and organise; I can't do everything myself!
I even have my own software distribution system, and now my ambition is to become the next Steam. ;)
As I said, it's a pretty deep game, with research, OS and engine dependancies, porting of software, marketing, trading IPs, stocks and shares etc as well as the people and resource management you expect. Not to mention the freeform building and furnishing of your offices, which gives it an additional and very personal sort of 'The Sims if you were micromanaging their work instead of their lives' vibe, rather than just manipulating a bunch of stats.
Your employees are surprisingly complex, too. They have personality, skills, learning abilities, laziness, likes, dislikes etc that affects their interactions and efficiency as a team. I have employees that I actually hate - that the rest of the team hate - but they're so darn good at their jobs I put up with them. The fact that individual employees can evoke this kind of reaction rather than just being 'some generic employee' is testament to how well this game plays.
So anyway, the fact that you can do all of the above within the confines of a £10 early access game is extremely encouraging and though I'm not sure what else there is to add in an already well rounded game, I'm sure it can only get better.
tl;dr: I'm always cautious about early access but if you like micromanagement business sims, this is as good as they get and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it.

Despite being early access, I already feel like I've gotten my money's worth for this game and given the development roadmap and frequent updates by the developer, I'm confident that this game is just going to get better. I haven't had a game pull me in like this for a while, it's a lot of fun.
The building tools are fantastic, allowing effortless construction, merging of rooms, moving of furniture (with clever grouping of items - ie. move a desk and the chair, computer, phone all move with it). You can build multiple stories and below ground, customise styles and colours, copy and apply styles, it really is one of the nicest building tool-sets I've used, there seems to be a way to do everything from the simple right click menu. The only time I had some trouble with them was when I enclosed an outside area by adding other rooms and couldn't understand why it wasn't behaving like a room should, but once I realised what the problem was I simply used the wall tool to trace the room and could then manipulate it properly.
I really like the variety in the approaches, there appear to be lots of ways to play the game, specialising in different kinds of software, buying and selling IPs, researching new technologies and licensing them, running hosting servers for other companies, as well as a few others. My first software company specialised in making video games (in fact only RPGs and Adventure Games) but I'm really excited to start again and try a completely different approach. It will be interesting to see how many are viable ways to run a successful company.
The tutorial popups are a nice touch, as a lot of early access games throw you in the deep end with little to no guidance of what you should be doing. They're certainly not perfect, and there were definitely times when I was confused about certain aspects and wished there was a little bit more information, but it was definitely helpful when just getting started.
Being early access, there are of course parts of the game that still need to be further fleshed out, there definitely could be more feedback on exactly why certain things fail to sell as well as perhaps adding ways to do market research or see market trends. A lot of the things I felt were missing or incomplete (like software expansions) are already on the development road map for inclusion in future updates so plenty to look forward to.
I wouldn't normally recommend an early access title unless you really wanted to support the developer and help steer development/find bugs, however in this case I think you'll already be getting a fun game on top of that.

So this is a roguelike game, a bit of RPG, a bit of exploration, and a fair bit of strategy & tactics. Expect to die, like, a *lot*. Not just during the early game - even after dozens of games and several victories, you'll still die sometimes. That said, this is one of the few games where a loss is pretty much as enjoyable as a victory, because the sequence of random encounters create a really colorful adventure, with ups & downs, epic fails and wins, and everything in-between.
Oddly, a lot of my fondest memories from this game relate to some of my major screw-ups... Like the time when I accidentally left the airlock open for just a tad bit too long, suffocating my entire crew... or when I activated the cloak just a moment too late, and got torn to pieces in the last stage of the bossfight... or the time I put off the doors upgrade, telling myself, "hey, this is a civilian sector, I'm sure nobody will try to board my ship here!"...
All in all, this game is highly recommended!
( btw I put in 200+ hours into my other copy, don't let the steam time count fool you... ;) )

I'm gonna put this paragraph first because I feel this could make someone change their mind about buying this game. A Story About My Uncle is one of those that was literally made for speedrunning and it does have a time trial mode. Searching for the best shortcuts and choosing the best moves to overcome certain obstacles, planning and executing the perfect run is much more exhilirating than the basic gameplay. If you enjoy that sort of thing, you can significantly stretch the 3-5 hour average playtime. On the downside, there's only a handful of maps so you can grow bored with it pretty quickly.
Now, I'm rather bad at platforming so it probably took me significantly longer to play through the game than almost everybody else and there were a few times I had trouble navigating myself through the 3D environment as well as a few times when I knew what I had to do but had difficulty executing it. All that sprinting, jumping and basically flying can be very exhilirating but since there isn't any other aspect to the gameplay (except the speedrunning potential), you may feel unmotivated to get through the more difficult/annoying bits. If there were other puzzles and a more extensive (and compelling) story, it would be an epic game. As it is, it feels more like a promo.

The story could have been interesting if they developed it a bit more. As it is, I feel it's only there so you wouldn't be swinging through otherwordly caverns just for the hell of it. The storytelling concept has been proven to work before and I find the dialogue between father and daughter rather sweet as opposed to some other people, but I do admit that the voice acting is terrible.

Released in 2004, This game is obviously dated, so don't go in with high expectations. However, I still have to say that the devs did a great job of making faces expressive, that really stands out even compared to todays games. Or maybe its different enough that that stands out. It works for me.
The gamestyle (not neccesarily gameplay) feels a lot like Deus Ex. Deus Ex is a FPS with RPG elements. VtMB goes farther with the RPG, and I think the result is better. RPG Points are awarded for completing quests, and there are enough attributes to work on that choosing your next upgrade takes some serious thought. Thought in a FPS/RPG?
I'm usually critical of in-game economies, and this one is sorta silly too. What does a Vampire really need? You can sell your junk at the pawn shop, but aside from some obvious items, the game isn't forthcoming about what items might be mission-critical. Other things are strange; I have this girl's belongings, and she's still - undead, so why can't I just give them to her? The inventory system is clunky but not infuriating, and it doesn't distract from gameplay. Controls for the Vampire powers or disciplines or whatever could be better.
The stories in the quests (there really aren't side-quests, just kind of a sea of mini-quests between you and Objective) are surprisingly good. I like to be in a story that someone worked really hard on. Combat is just "all right". Gunplay certainly pales by today's 'normal', and there are problems with melee. I was supposed to damage something on the floor, and even though I had a ginormous fire axe, I couldn't seem to do whatever was appropriate for an infuriating 10-15 minutes. [Likewise this is an early game (Source engine) where you can manipulate (move around) objects in the game, and the items show the collission detection issues of the early games that did this. You're going to drop something in the hallway - just because its so big, then trip on it repeatedly. Very annoying.] What really saves the combat is the ginormous fire axe, and the fact that you can jump on a near enemy and just drink him dry - if he fails a defensive check.
If you can condescend to play a 2004 title, and can suspend your disbelief just a little, VtMB can be highly entertaining. I recommend playing as a Malkavian(?) vampire. They all suffer a curse of insanity, and this manifests in your dialogue choices. Its not what an insane Vampire would say, so much as a really drunk classical studies scholar at an academic party, but it does make the game more interesting. Even friendly characters say "Oh no. You're a Malkavian, aren't you? I'm not going to understand a thing you say, am I?"

This game is a buried gem. Activision rushed this game into release about halfway through the development. The result is somewhat painful as far as bugs and glitches go. For me, the game wouldn't even start on its own, and when I initially tried to play it, I uninstalled and felt regret for buying it on my boyfriend's recommendation.
A few months afterwards, I installed it again while I had a craving for RPGs. Here's the single key to enjoying this game: go and download the unofficial patch, and make sure to select the patch plus during the installation process. A large amount of the game's content is in unactivated code. The patch is regularly updated - the most recent update was this year, last I checked - which fixes all of the game breaking bugs and readds content that wasn't quite finished or activated.
The game? Great. The lore is excellent, which most of anyone who has experience with the Old World of Darkness universe would know. Even if you're not, the game is a great introduction. I wasn't a huge expert before I started playing, but a few hours in, I pulled up the wiki and simply started reading. The writing is quality. The characters are memorable, and it's hard not to feel about them; usually, if they're not Beckett or Jack, that feeling is indescribable loathing. The quests are so interesting, you feel a need to go out and find all of the ones avaliable. The environment offers many areas to explore and makes you want to explore them.
The only two things I would say aren't perfect about the game are the graphics and the combat. The graphics, naturally, are as dated as the game, and they haven't aged well. I honestly enjoy them because sometimes they're literally laughable. The combat is charmingly schizophrenic, in that you're never quite sure what you're doing, nor what you should be doing, but gosh dang if the results aren't fun. The combat difficulty jerks up and down with little in game conceivable reason, and initially I was confused, but then I realized that the difficulty wasn't based on game mechanics. It's based on lore. If the game makes you fight vampire hunters, no matter at what point you're at in the game, the fight's going to be very hard because vampire hunters in the Old World of Darkness are damned near impossible to kill.
It's a great game, and I think that if lore, missions, writing, and plots are your thing, you should play it. However, don't buy it. Pirate it. A larger company - I think it was Bioware - bought the company that made it and fired everyone who worked on it. Your money would be spent paying the people who ruined the chance of a second game.

Saints Row IV (or SR4) is quite possibly the best game I've played in recent years. Yes, it is easy, and yes, the graphics engine is the same as SR3, but the game is fun. And it takes advantage of the fact that it is a game to justify all of the tropes that are in games.
The opening for the Saints Row games are ever more elaborate, like the James Bond movies, but unlike James Bond, SR4 steps up its game as you go along. It starts you off in the same drab corridor shooting galleries that every other first-person and third-person shooter needs to do nowadays, and then completely turns it into its head once the story gets going. And yes, the there is a story, and it is excellent.
The customization is great, and if you're not happy with your character, you can change everything about them during the game itself. There's no need to do a restart. And your character isn't a silent protagonist. He/she has a voice, and it isn't just to grunt randomly during combat, but to snark at the world around them. It's so great to play a character that doesn't have their head up their rear-end, and enjoys what they do.
It's not a perfect game, and there are problems:
1. It's easy. That's not something I usually complain about, being as bad at gaming as I am, but it really is pretty easy.
2. There are a lot of side-missions, and 100-percenting will be frustrating, especially if you come across "that one mission" that you hate. And you will want to 100% to unlock everything.
3. There are so many guns and so many vehicles, but once you get your super-powers, you will most likely ignore them, which is a shame.
4. Your "homies" are really good, but you will usually only call them out to hear their banter.
But let's face it, these are quibbles. I can't recommend SR4 enough. Never mind GTA, this is the sandbox game to play.

The first half hour of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter may feels more like a tech demo than a game. You will wander around the stunning environments wondering what you are supposed to do, but the gameplay is in there waiting for you, but, as the title screen says, this is not a game that holds your hand. You are left to work out gameplay elements yourself, and the open nature of the environments means that you may well walk straight past the first couple of puzzles without realising. There's no avoiding the fact that, without looking at a walkthrough, you will spend a lot of time tracking back over the same terrain looking for things you might have missed, which can be frustrating, as is the lack of NPCs to interact with (pretty much all characters in the game are only introduced via flashbacks). Nevertheless, the game has plenty of character and suspense and the puzzles are engrossing enough to keep you engaged throughout the relatively short story.
If you are looking for action and instant gratification, this is not the game for you. If like the idea of exploring a beautifullly rendered solving mildly challenging puzzles, give this one a try. There is certainly enough to suggest that a more ambitious and fleshed-out sequel would also be worth a look.

Actually, the word perfect, describes the game well. Everything in it is perfect. The story, the setting of the abandoned village in the middle of mountains, the soundtrack, the voice casting, the technological visual marvel, the game mechanics to solve the mysteries, the mood.
The only downside that I can see in the game, is the lack of save functionality. The game has auto-save in certain key-points, normally after completing a sub-story. For one side, I didn't get frustrated by it, since the mood and involvement the game creates, you just want to keep playing it. But it can be troublesome if for some reason you need the stop playing and you are in the middle of something.
Hope to see more games like this. Maybe it revitalize the genre of point-click adventure games, following this game steps.

A slightly odd little title that uses the Worms licence as a flimsy excuse to deliver a simplistic 2D golf game. For what it is, it’s highly polished, with great optimisation, visuals achieving a fantastic level of detail, music complimenting the theme of each course, and solid gameplay mechanics that deliver consistency as well as playability. Course design is mostly a success, and encourages risky play - hitting a ball at top speed against a solid wall high above you, for it to bounce back off towards the platform opposite and come to a stop inches away from the flagpost, is a satisfying experience, albeit one that grows old quickly. The game features achievements, which is a great incentive to play, but collecting all 29 of them will probably prove too tedious for all but the most dedicated gamers.
Think of it as the Worms variant of Windows Solitaire - fun to play idly for a few minutes, then you’ll want to shut it down and do something else.

Unlike most games of this genre it isn't just going from left to right, there is a 3D element in play too as you can be heading up or down along a path as well, so it isn't quite linear, which opens the door for the a bit of exploring if it appears there are two paths you can take.The HUD is perfect in its simplicity, top par is your health, bottom bar is your energy (which is tied to the player's ability to block or fire a weaspon)

Playing normal difficulty, there is a nice even flow, where you have to learn and master all the basics, as knowing when to dodge and block can often be a determining factor being victory and defeat, by the end of the 3rd stage, a player should have all the basics down solid (at least in theory)

"In a journey through distant and unknown galaxies, you play as the members of the Zheros squad: Mike (strong, awkward and dim-witted) and Captain Dorian (agile, smart and ready for anything). Your mission: defend the universe from the evil Dr. Vendetta and his twisted plan to mutate every living creature in his trusted minions. In single player or in co-op mode, you can rely on your punches, using a rich selection of combos, and on powerful hi-tech weapons, but if that was not enough, a strong and destructive mech will come to the rescue in the most dangerous situations..."
Ah, yes… another retro-styled throwback – another beat ’em-up battle of furious fisticuffs. Here we go again! Zheros, bring it on. I’m ready to blow stuff up, jump around, and mash my punch button combos.
The first bit of news is that the game is good to go from the off; I plugged in my PS4 controller and all the button hints immediately changed in recognition. The early stages are easy to get into but not so undemanding to cause a collapse from boredom after five minutes. Gameplay is a mix of easy, intuitive and hard to master in just the right ratio. How do I know this? Well, there was a big grin on my face the entire time I was playing. A few points there then. (DING!)
Zheros is very good at what it does, with a well structured and nicely polished design, but sadly it fails to deliver as much fun as it appears to promise. I may just be incompetent, but the timed Level Five took me four attempts to complete, each try lasting around five minutes. I challenged a friend to complete the same level, and he is still trying - I have no expectations of hearing back from him any time soon. Also, be warned, checkpoints refuse to save when quitting and dropping in and out is impossible; levels have to be played start to end. Sometimes retro is slightly too retro.
I was a bit frustrated by unskippable, stupidly difficult enemies – to kill certain opponents in timed conditions the buttons were simply not responsive enough, which was not helped by the weird, unchangeable, control mappings. (Note to developers: please avoid mapping a quick-response button to a trigger control!) Add in a lack of cues for the timing of button-presses and LEVEL 5, yes LEVEL 5, was as far as I ever progressed in my hours of solid Steam time.
The graphics are, however, very colourful and engaging, and honestly, quite pretty; the look of Zheros will not bore and the graphics and art style fit the gameplay beautifully. As impressive as it looks, though, there are only two worlds to explore - if I had ever made it past the first one. A positive though,  is the soundtrack, which is fast, aggressive, and motivational.
And then to the plot, which could be sketched out in full on the back of the proverbial packet of cigs. Frankly, there is no real reason for the slug-fest between the forces of good (all TWO of their best soldiers!) and Dr Vendetta, surely the daftest super villain name since Dr Evil and Sir Bonetopick, who were both clearly unavailable when Zheros was being developed. So plot points… more like flop points!
So where does that leave me? Well, there are no user-designable levels and I can confirm there never will be – because I emailed the devs. There were a few joystick issues in menus [scrolls being detected twice etc...] but all things considered this is actually surprisingly adequate for what it is and how much it costs.
To sum up: If you want a simple, well made, bug-free beat-em-up then Zheros is the game for you, provided you can get past the first level. However, if you came searching for a sense of humour, or a plot of any kind… well… your princess may just well be - dare I say it? - in another castle.
7/10

ZHEROS gets a 4/5. Overall I enjoyed the game. It had goofy and quirky characters, nice galactic feel to it, and a ton of different combos. It did take a little while to get a nice variety of enemies because they show up one at a time, but I kinda enjoyed watching their little introductions. The first half of the first world felt a bit repetitive, but after that the levels started having their own design and uniqueness to them.
-Graphics: Very nicely done cartoon graphics. I did get a bit of a headache when I first played the game though. That camera shake was just too much for me and I normally don't have  that kind of problem with games. Thankfully you can change it in the settings and I brought my camera shake down to 20% and turned the depth of field off.
-Sound: Extremely up beat music made to amp you up.
-Story: You are a couple of galactic police officers trying to take down Dr. Vendetta and keep the galaxy safe.
-Single-player/Multiplayer: Single player and has local co-op. Unfortunately you cannot play online because I recommend having a friend to play with. Not only does it make the game more fun, but when you go down they can pick you up. In single player mode you will have to start at the beginning of the level or the last checkpoint. However, in co-op mode the RP is not evenly distributed between the two players so one person can easily end up weaker than the other.
-Controls: Very nice and you can change them in the settings. I highly recommend having a controller as it makes it easier to perform those combos and if you play with a keyboard you'll have to look at your controls setting since the tutorial will give you controller keys but not keyboard keys.
-Setting: The futuristic type music fits perfectly with the galactic settings.
-Characters: There are two characters to choose from. Mike is your basic meat-head who just wants to punch things. Captain Dorian is agile and fond of kicking. She also does a slam move that just makes me cringe because she lands in a split... ugh.
-Gameplay: Fun and full of minions to beat up. If you ever forget how to do a combo you can pause the game and look and the combo list to refresh your memory.
-Customization: Can't change a characters looks, but you can distribute your RP between combos, shield, or gun after each level.
-Dialogue/Well Written: There's really no talking in this game, just punching, kicking, shooting, and the grunting that Dr. Vendetta does instead of talking.
-Tutorial: The first couple levels are pretty basic. They go through which buttons do what (On the controller, for keyboard you need to look at your controls) and introduce enemies and traps.
-Other: I wish the beams and pillars in the foreground went transparent when you moved behind them, but that's just a small gripe. Enjoyed the additions in the background of little robots repairing stuff or being locked out of a door.
-Worth the price tag: I'm always in the mind set of catch it on sale. However, this is a pretty good beat-em-up so for fans of the genre I say go for it. Another positive is you only need one copy since it's local co-op.

When it comes to videogames, you can never have too much
. This is an underappreciated element of videogames, and let me tell you why: Most developers simply don't have the time. No matter the era, developers are constantly faced with impossible deadlines. Basically, not every "i" is going to be dotted, nor will every "t" will be crossed. However, if developers had the time to make even the slightest adjustments, they could turn a good game into something even better.
Since this is a review, you already understand where I'm going with this. Zheros is a nice beatemup. It has a solid foundation, some good ideas, and it can be pretty entertaining. However, this is a game that deserves a good polishing. The problems with Zheros could be measured in fractions and decimals. These issues are so slight, so miniscule, that people are liable not to notice them, but they'll still realize that something's wrong when they're playing the game. They'll say things like "What?" and "That doesn't make sense." or maybe just "Bullcrap!"
Jack and Dorian are a couple of Zheros out to stop Dr. Vendetta from doing evil things. Dr. Vendetta? I guess Captain I'mABadGuy and AdmiralBoneToPick weren't available. Anyway, the two playable characters team up to deliver fists of justice to a massive number of aliens and robots, over the course of 18 levels. Despite being a beatemup, this game is fairly long. Many of the levels can take more than 10 minutes to beat, some even as much as 30! In the time it takes to beat one level, you could probably play through the entirety of
, or some other classic arcade brawler. Needless to say, it's greatly appreciated that progress is saved, after the completion of every level.
With the beatemup genre, we can expect at least some level of repetitiveness. Thankfully, Zheros does its best to keep things interesting with a large variety of enemies to battle. Jack and Dorian also have a wealth of combos they can perform. To add to this, the good guys can deflect both bullets and blows with a well-timed block. The brawling itself is serviceable, and it's fun just pounding baddies by the dozens. However, as you progress through the game, you're also liable to notice all of the little problems. At first they feel like nitpicks, but these complaints add up and start tearing away at the game. Allow me to share with you some of the issues that I've run into.
A lot of the enemies have melee attacks that are hard to read. The most common enemy is a small robot. Aside from firing their laser rifle, they also kick and swing their gun at the player. In the heat of the fight, it's never really clear what they're doing, and their range is so short you'll hardly be able to tell they're doing anything. Other, even smaller robots on wheels are harder to focus on. They rear back and do a lunging attack, but the lack of movement doesn't help them stand out. It's also annoying that the heroes drop everything, just to kick the bombs that these "dog-bots" drop. Kicked bombs don't suddenly explode and damage enemies, they're just moved to a different spot.
What you're more likely to notice is all of the damage you'll take while on your back. Certain larger enemies are capable of doing knock-down attacks. When they gang up on you, they can knock you to the ground, then continue hitting you. There's nothing you can do about this. It's a rare occurence, but if their attacks are timed at the right moment, they can deplete your health fairly quickly. While you can also knock the enemy down and continue hitting them, the larger foes can block your attacks at random. I've had my attacks completely deflected, even when the foe was lying down! Some other enemies will repeatedly dodge your moves, which is also annoying.
When enemies aren't randomly blocking your attacks, they can do a fantastic job at countering you. While the game would probably be too easy if your attacks had all of the priority, I'm of the camp that believes in "some is better than none". Your combos will get stuffed by enemy attacks at a constant rate. When foes group together, you'll find that it's extremely hard to get some moves in to spread everyone out. On the other hand, I think this aspect of the game adds a little depth. Beatemups are really enjoyable, when you have to work for those openings in the enemy's onslaught. Although, I also think that the heroes should yell "OUCH!" or "OOF!" when they take damage. Even when they're getting pummeled, Jack & Dorian don't utter the slightest grunt.
In level 1-8 "The Shelter", there is a section where you have to hit a button. This button causes a shutter to close, which keeps intense heat from sapping your health. However, this shutter re-opens in just a few seconds, which isn't enough time to get more than a couple punches on a huge cyborg bullman. This is one of those moments where two seconds, yes, two additional seconds of closed-shutter time, would have made that section far more manageable. Instead, you're going to be constantly distracted by the shutter, and trying to babysit it while also not being obliterated by one of the toughest enemies in the game.
Then there are the bosses. I didn't really enjoy fighting these clowns. Most of your attacks just don't do much damage. I had the most success with the Y, X, X, X, X, X, etc combo. Oddly enough, I had the least amount of trouble with the final boss, and that's because his attacks are the only ones that can be shut down by the block. The other two bosses require liberal use of the dodge button, and even that isn't guaranteed. On the brightside, there are plenty of health items, and the bosses don't do an excessive amount of damage.
What's telling about most of these complaints, is that all of them could be fixed via minor adjustments. Let's say that some attacks give the player 1 or 2 frames of invulnerability, or allow them a half-second to recover after being knocked down. The second boss would ever-so-slightly pause before their double axe-handle, allowing the player enough time (if they're paying attention) to get out of the way. The player should be allowed a distinct audible cue when their hero is getting hurt. These are all little things, the ones that are most likely to be overlooked, but they have a sizable impact on the game.
Despite my many complaints, Zheros is a perfectly serviceable way to spend a weekend or two. If you have a friend to play co-op with, then it's all the better. If you're flying solo and are prone to aggravation; consider sticking to the easy difficulty. This game's polish deficiency will cause you to repeat some headache-inducing sections, and there's no way to change difficulties, without restarting the entire game. That said, if you do decide to tough it out and play on normal or hard, you could eventually become accustomed to the wonkier aspects of this game. It might take longer than it should, but this game will "click" for you, if you allow it to.

This game is an exciting and innovative team based shooter. The progression system is great. You are always unlocking new stratagems, vehicles, and weapons. Different planets grant new equipment when completed as well. I have played 20 hours and I am hooked. The aesthetic is similar to starship troopers, terminator, or Alien. Space marines dropping onto a planet to deal with hordes of bug or cyborg enemies. There is a lot of customization possible in regards to your weapon, your perks, and the stratagems you can call down during a mission. Friendly fire is a reality and you can easily kill your friends or yourself if you're not careful. Death is cheap though your allies can bring you back in 10 seconds if there is at least one of your teammates left alive. Missions are varied assassinate targets, capture areas, sweep minefields, activate oil wells etc. Stratagems are also varied call in an automated minigun turret, an air strike, a flamethrower, jetpack etc. Most of the DLC is cosmetic or of equal power to stuff already in the game. You do want the all terrain pack if you are going to play the upper level snow missions though. It probably should have been included in the game, but the game is relatively cheap at 20 dollars, so an extra 2 dollars isn't too bad. One last thing is that the game makes you feel totally awesome. You're a helldiver restoring democracy to the galaxy. You have your own ship, your crew idolizes you and you bring with you insane amounts of firepower wherever you go.

Look, you've got a story called "Seduce me," so why does it take forever to actaually get onto the stuff involving members of the opposite sex?  I followed it for about 30 minutes (which was about 28 more than my intuition told me), and it was just dire.
This is dirt-cheap game production.  I could probably program this, and I'm certainly no expert.  But it's a way to pass the time.  It could be a lot better.  The story is not just utter crap, but the most amateurish writing I've seen in a very long time; elementary-school standard.  The characters are absurdly stereotypical.  The choices offered to you are few and far between, and seem to have no impact on the storyline at all.  Is there any reason why the characters couldn't be personalised?  Instead of asking simply what name you want your character to have, why not ask about skin colour?  Hair colour?  Hair style?  Facial features?  Straight or gay?  Hell, why not ask if you want your character to be male or female,  adjusting the story suitably?  And given that it's hardly a gripping storyline, why not just cut to the chase and get onto the seduction bit?
Which isn't much of a seduction bit.  Why not have a choice about whether your character is going to kiss him or not?  And with the kiss, why not have a choice about whether to do it again? push him away? drag him off to a bedroom? do it right there in the foyer with his brothers watching?
This game could be a lot of fun, and seriously filthy!  With more frequent choices that actually affected the story, it could have been a lot more entertaining.  As it was, it's like a young girl's English homework, with a few pics and sound effects attached by her big brother, who's in a high-school omputer class.
But hell, if you're bored and don't fancy paying out for a new game, it kills time.  I wouldn't say anything better than that.

Saints Row IV (or SR4) is quite possibly the best game I've played in recent years. Yes, it is easy, and yes, the graphics engine is the same as SR3, but the game is fun. And it takes advantage of the fact that it is a game to justify all of the tropes that are in games.
The opening for the Saints Row games are ever more elaborate, like the James Bond movies, but unlike James Bond, SR4 steps up its game as you go along. It starts you off in the same drab corridor shooting galleries that every other first-person and third-person shooter needs to do nowadays, and then completely turns it into its head once the story gets going. And yes, the there is a story, and it is excellent.
The customization is great, and if you're not happy with your character, you can change everything about them during the game itself. There's no need to do a restart. And your character isn't a silent protagonist. He/she has a voice, and it isn't just to grunt randomly during combat, but to snark at the world around them. It's so great to play a character that doesn't have their head up their rear-end, and enjoys what they do.
It's not a perfect game, and there are problems:
1. It's easy. That's not something I usually complain about, being as bad at gaming as I am, but it really is pretty easy.
2. There are a lot of side-missions, and 100-percenting will be frustrating, especially if you come across "that one mission" that you hate. And you will want to 100% to unlock everything.
3. There are so many guns and so many vehicles, but once you get your super-powers, you will most likely ignore them, which is a shame.
4. Your "homies" are really good, but you will usually only call them out to hear their banter.
But let's face it, these are quibbles. I can't recommend SR4 enough. Never mind GTA, this is the sandbox game to play.

So this is a roguelike game, a bit of RPG, a bit of exploration, and a fair bit of strategy & tactics. Expect to die, like, a *lot*. Not just during the early game - even after dozens of games and several victories, you'll still die sometimes. That said, this is one of the few games where a loss is pretty much as enjoyable as a victory, because the sequence of random encounters create a really colorful adventure, with ups & downs, epic fails and wins, and everything in-between.
Oddly, a lot of my fondest memories from this game relate to some of my major screw-ups... Like the time when I accidentally left the airlock open for just a tad bit too long, suffocating my entire crew... or when I activated the cloak just a moment too late, and got torn to pieces in the last stage of the bossfight... or the time I put off the doors upgrade, telling myself, "hey, this is a civilian sector, I'm sure nobody will try to board my ship here!"...
All in all, this game is highly recommended!
( btw I put in 200+ hours into my other copy, don't let the steam time count fool you... ;) )

I know that I probably have no right to even consider giving a review on a game when I have barely played an hour of it. Despite me only having played just a little over an hour of Metro 2033 I can tell you this... The 1.1 hours that I have played is enough to make me want to delete the game and never go back to it. Since the release of Metro I have been keeping an eye on it. It always looked interesting to me, but not interesting enough to buy. Despite it being a good game, I didn't know (personally) any of my gamer friends who owned it. Nor did I ever hear any one ever tell me how freakin exciting and awesome Metro is. In my head I pictured a game with "decent" graphics, and "decent" storyline. I don't buy "decent"... I buy "out-of-this-world", "ridiculously brilliant", or "crazy innovative" games. The only time I buy "decent" is when the game is on sale for crazy cheap and prey that when I play the game it will be everything but "decent". This has only happened to me a couple of times. The first time was with The Witcher 2. I bought it shortly after I built my first rig. Way back when I barely knew anything about PC gaming. Heck, I had only been a mamber of Steam for a couple of days when I saw The Witcher 2 on sale for something like $2 or $3. I watched the trailer, thought it looked pretty cool and decided to go ahead and try it. I figured that it was going to be a "decent" game... It was only $2. Man was I wrong! That was when I realized how much of a gem that Steam truly was and how smart that I was for decideing to get into building computers and make the switch from console to PC gaming. The second game was Far Cry 3. I bought it for I think $10. I had no idea what the game was about. Just that a friend of mine suggest I pick it up. He said for $10 it was a steal... Thats all. No details... He just told me to trust him. So I did and I bought the game also thinking that it was going to be decent. Again I was totally blown away! In only 2 weeks after I built my first rig I had bout 2 of the best games I have ever played in my life for less than $20! I was hooked... I have built several rigs since then. Each better than the last.
Now I am playing games on a rig that dim the city lights when I turn it on... Theres nothing it can't handle. This brings me to this review. Now that I 100% know what I am doing, every now and then I try to find me another game that will blow me away like TW2 or FC3. Let me just say that ever since FC3, I have yet to find a game $10 or less that is that good. I was really... REALLY... Hoping that Metro 2033 was that game. Unfortunately for me it wasn't. A lot of gamers say that you can't possibly know a game is good within the first hour... BULL$HIT!!! I know if a game is good usually with in the first 10min. From the start I knew I was going to have problems... Remember I said my rig dims the lights when I turn it on and there isn't a game it can't handle. Well Metro 2033 doesn't seem to play well @ 4K. I'm running an ASUS Maximus VIII Hero, Intel i7-6700k, 32gigs of Corsair Dominator LED DDR4 ram and 2 x NVIDIA GTX 1080s. The game is being pulled from 4 x 240gig PNY XLR8 SSDs set in RAID. Since I built my rig there hasn't been a game yet to stump it... Except Metro. I figured it would be a newer game that would shake my rig up, Not a 2 year old remake of an older game. Durring my first 5 min of the game I noticed that the sound was extremely off. NPCs in front of you soulded like they were behind you and NPCs behind you sounded like they were in front of you is the best way I can describe it. Its actually a lot deeper than that, but the sound problem is so strange that I can't really explain it. All I know is that when Hunter was talking to me it sounded like he was whispering while some guy somewhere on the map was yelling. Despite the sound the people look weird. The lost little boy looked like a little boy body with a mans face. The graphics are drab and boring. Everything is brown and grey. I know its taking place in a subway tunnel after a nuclear war but c'mon. The talking was so boring that I almost fell asleep. To me it's like The Godfather movie (yes I do not like The Godfather)... Interesting plot but put togeather in a super boring way.
I am sure to the right gamer that this game is awesome. I am sure that on a different rig there woudn't be any problems (although my rig is top-notch I know that there are other rigs that are better. I know that rigs with parts less expensive than mine can run 1000 times better, its all in how you built it and the combonation you use). For me the game didn't get it. If the game doesn't grab me in the first 10min (realistically about 30min) it's not gonna hold my attention period. Metro 2033 didn't do it for me. It's to slow. Don't get me wrong... I do enjoy a slow and supenseful plot that makes you think... but only if it starts off with a bang and then slows down in the middle.

I found this game through the recommendations from others. There was a lot of high praise for this game. And it is a very good one at that. For those of you who do not know this game is about exploration and adventure with a little bit of puzzle solving thrown in.
The beautiful open world was a great choice. I often found myself staring out into the distance into the scenic view this game often presented you with. The story flowed quite well despite being a free-range, do what ever you want whenever you want type of game.
The one thing I do stress is to have an open mind going into this game. They say this game doesn't hold you're hand. And it really doesn't. I found it a bit frustrating at times, not knowing what to do to complete a puzzle. They are generally  well laid out and the answers are usually fairly close to the questions. I think this is the one thing I struggled with the most. But that's my own problem. Just beware of that and try to think things through rather than just going with the flow. Because there really is no flow.
Overall, it isn't along game at all. 4-5 hours is all it will take you to complete this game. And damn those 5 hours are worth it.
