I read some other reviews and I think when it comes to Seduce Me the Otome the question of whether or not you will enjoy it depends on what you are seeking from a visual novel (VN).
For me, I love stories and specifically i go for the serious hotty character and the sexy hotty character.  In Seduce Me the Otome I did the James Path with a strong though at first to doing the Damien path.  I turned out doing Diana's path after finishing James.
At the time I came across Seduce Me, I had finished several paths in Cinders (which IMO is a great VN).  I was working on a stat based VN and a another very involved VN, so I really wanted another story but i felt tied to the others because of the cost of many of the VNs.  When i saw Seduce Me was free, I was all for trying it.
Also I did some Steam streaming of this game and a few people popped in and out.  One being the creator.  She was nice and seemed very excited to see her game being streamed.
Now here's where I will be a little lighter on the criticism, being that it's a free game yes i would and have recommended it to others.  I could be wrong, but i actually believe this project was Seduce Me's creator's venture into the VN world.  It's a kickstarter and while we know there are a lot of kickstarters that are amazing and on par with the big name professionals, we know there are many more that are works in progress at different levels.  With that in mind, i enjoyed the game for the time I spent on it regardless of whether it was on par with the other VN titles around on Steam (that again cost money).
Then again, i like trying out things and this was entertaining to me.  There's a fight scene where i did it two different ways and having my girl kick butt was very satisfying and hilarious.
I played the game before the achievements came out so i will probably replay James and Diana to get some achievements but I am curious to get a few of the others.
The overall question i ask myself about games is whether or not i felt it was a waste of time to play.  If lose interest and have to take a several month break to get the willpower to play it through, then I will have issues.  If i can play through and get at least one path completed, I'm satisfied.

My previous review reflected my experience with the game. Unable to play, no answers from support.
Since then, the bug or problem that was ruining matchmaking has been fixed, so it's now easy to find matches again.
So, bugs apart and old problems solved, the game itself is a good offering, specially if you enjoy playing games with friends. You control your soldier and have to do missions "fighting for Democracy" in space. You can do them alone or with friends in squads of 4, matchmaking itself is good and fast to find you a game to join. Each mission drop offers a sequence of different field objectives that you then need to endure and fullfill, fighting hordes of enemies trying to stop you. There are 3 different enemy factions, with different units and abilities. Each of those races has a home planet. Progress is linear, you progress through missions untill you get to that homeplanet and cvomplete all missions.All of these are done as a community, with players having several common goals, with constant on-going events. As soon as a war cycle ends, a new one begins starting over. Each time you can either win in spreadintg democracy to all the alien worlds, of get defeated and extinguished, as aliens conquer our home planet.
Individually, as a player, you control your character in a top-down view, you can choose your loadout before each missions, and gained XP allows you to unlock better weapons, armor and equipment for your soldier. The game is light, fun and easy to understand, requires some skill and good timing analysis to decide when to use what from your inventory.
All in all, I'll finish as I started. If you have friends to play with, it can be quite fun. If not, you can still have fun while matchmaking with randoms, since there is a rating system for players, and generally people are friendly and do try to play the right way. See a few videos to check if you like the gameplay.

Zheros:
~~~~~~
Mike and Captain Dorian are members of the intergalactic team called, “Zheros,” which combats crime in the universe. This time, they are facing the evil Dr. Vendetta who wants to mutate every living creature and transform them into his minions. This is definitely not going be a walk in the park; it will be a challenging mission for “Zheros!”
Zheros is an action / 3D beat’em up game where you play either Mike or Captain Dorian from the Zheros squad in single mode, or you can play with someone else on a local co-op mode. This game is absolutely frantic from the start. You will face several types of enemy as you progress into the game. The most comment one will be the white robots with a triangular shaped head, but you will encounter other really tough ones like the “Space Cow”. As in all good beat’em up games, you have to maximise your combos to get as many points as you can. On top of that, your character will have a shield to protect him/her from projectiles and punches, as well as a mounted gun on his/her forearm to use if you are in a pickle (they are plenty in this game)!
Collect all the golden tokens by destroying the orange boxes and do not forget about the golden star; there is one hidden in each level. At the end of the level, you will be able to see how many tokens you have collected and how many RP’s you will get for them. You will need RP’s to upgrade Mike and Captain Dorian’s abilities; more moves, better shield or more damage with your mounted gun.
Also, there are blue, green and red cylinders; the blue one will help you with your ammunition and the green one will regenerate your health. All I can say for the red cylinder is shoot at them when your enemies are close to them…hehehehe, BOOM!
Levels will also have obstacles, electric grids, lasers and more.
I really enjoy the 3D cartoonist graphics in this game and the animations are fabulous. The levels are fun and challenging. The controls are really responsive. The soundtrack will keep you pumped and help you to beat the upcoming levels.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great 3D cartoonist graphics
-	Fun, fast and frantic gameplay
-	Really good animations
-	Plenty of moves
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	RP not equally distributed in Co-op mode
A great, fun and fast 3D beat’em up game to have in your library. Highly recommended!
8.5/10

ZHEROS is a side-scrolling brawler type game with a twist as it has a more 3D perspective to it.
Right off the bat as I watched the opening cut scenes it gave off a Saturday morning cartoon serial quality which I loved as I reminisced about all those shows I used to watch. The developers of ZHEROS have a great sense of humour as some of the cut scenes are hilarious and priceless. :)
You battle your way through the sci-fi setting using brute force or some occiasonal weapons. You want to to try and maximize your combo moves to boost your score. I really liked the way the controller layout in the settings illustrates with pictures exactly what each button will do for you so you can pick it up almost instantly and be an efficient brawler right away.
As you make your way through you can continue to develop your characters skills and improve their abilities. I have played with Mike only so far and I'm quite happy with his current skill set. You will also unlock some weapons and gear as you work your way through the levels.
While the combat is challenging I would have liked to see more from the computer AI as I find the bulk of your battles is just facing ever increasingly larger mobs of minions that come at you in waves and this can get to be a bit repetitive after awhile.
Visuals are very impressive and again I liken it to a saturday morning sci-fi cartoon which I love. Music and effects are upbeat and well suited for this type of game.
There is no online multiplayer but there is a local co-op which I'm sure this would make it even more fun but unfortunately I haven't had anyone here to play with yet but I will get my son to try it out with me when he comes home this weekend.
Overall I have enjoyed this game to date and it has served as a trip down memory lane for me as well. Even if beat'em up games are not your thing I encourage you to try this one as the story, humour and visuals might be enough to change your opinion of the genre.

If you love beat-em-ups, there is nothing much to say except that Zheros is a must-have.  The gameplay is very satisfying and I'm sure you'll fall in love once you start playing.
As I mentioned, the gameplay is very satisfying.  Overall the combat is solid and very well done.  It is your typical light attack, heavy attack, but with some other goodies mixed in such as being able to actively dodge, blocking/parrying enemy attacks, and you can shoot enemies with your sidearm.  There are a variety of combos that you can pull off by stringing light attacks, heavy attacks, AND your ranged weapon, each combo has it's own unique style to them so you won't get bored watching the same thing over and over again.
Also you have an energy bar, using your ranged weapon will slowly deplete this gauge.  The bar will regenerate slowly over time, but can be refilled quicker by finding energy pick-ups.
Lastly there are two characters you can play, their fighting styles are different from eachother, one is more punching-oriented while the other kicking-oriented.  Nonetheless, both are very refreshing to play.
The level design is somewhat linear that are broken up into fight segments, where you have to defeat all enemies in an area before you can proceed.  Throughout the levels there are collectible items such as health pick-ups, energy pick-ups, and coins which contribute to your overall score.  you can find these in crates in which you can break open.
A nit-pick I have with the game is how some fight segments are too short mainly due to enemies being too squishy.  Honestly it's not that big of a deal, but if I had to say something this would be it.
As for the price-to-hours ratio, I'd say it is decent and you will definitely get more hours than it is worth, or definitely break-even.  The gameplay is good enough though so you'll for sure get your money's worth, especially if you're playing with friends/partner/wife/husband/kids.  From a singleplayer standpoint, the value is still there and you will for sure get your money's worth, it may not be as much as playing coop though.
Overall very great game, you don't see very much
beat-em-ups nowadays, but then you have Zheros which came in guns blazing showing that this genre is still alive.
I hope this review helps you in deciding whether to purchase this game or not.

Zheros is a generically beautiful Sci-fi brawler that is only really exciting when there are two players on the sticks. If you play it solo it’ll feel more like a tech demo than an actual game.
Zheros is a game starring a Macho Man and a lithe and flexible Female as they beat-up the robots of an evil genius. The story is told through small cutscenes that completely lack voiceover. There isn’t much to the story besides these two people that want to beat the crap out of a villain… so no worries there.
Zheros contains some fantastic graphics with a Science Fiction backdrop. What you can expect is a beautiful brawler with fast and responsive combat. The combat is all about punching and kicking various robots in the face with a variety of combo strings and air juggles. Increasing talents will unlock more elaborate combos to perform on the various enemy types in the game.
The backgrounds are dominated by constant moving parts like a rich Sci-fi skyline. The combat in the foreground tends to be a bit too moderate in comparison. When playing alone the characters tend to face off against a small amount of opponents in short waves. The robots take a lot longer to dispatch and the combat becomes tiresome even after only an hour of play.
When playing solo, the enemies lack the aggression we’re used to in older more rambunctious 2D brawlers.
Once another player has stepped up to bat, the game changes to a hectic brawl of life and death. Players will be on their toes constantly as they face endless waves of enemies. The combat bumps up significantly with two-players and it’s usually a battle of attrition to try and survive. It’s much more thrilling to play cooperatively as the enemies tend to keep the players on their toes.
I have two things I don’t like about cooperative play. First, it’s only local-coop and since this is the best way to play the game… it’s a strange omission. Secondly, the only way to obtain talent points is to pit the players against each other. The player with the highest score earns the most RP and the player with the lowest score earns none. This stops the second player from earning skills to increase their combos and damage, which in turn makes that player weaker in the long term. This is counterintuitive to a cooperative style of play and is damaging to them team dynamic.
In conclusion. The solo game is all about short bursts of combat in rather boring environments that don’t look much different from the last. However, once two players are involved in the brawl the background disappears among the waves of enemies trying to destroy you. To be honest, Zheros is a game that can only truly be played cooperatively. Playing this game solo is a bore, but with two players you’re in for a slightly interesting experience. Since the game is local play only though, I’d wait for a sale unless you have a friend that’s always on hand.

Allow me to just talk for a moment. LucasArts made about fifteen games, I think. When the original 2003 Star Wars Battlefront came out, it was an awesome game that allowed you to be part of the fight. I spent so much time in my childhood playing this game, and I could not have had more fun getting home from school, hopping on the computer, and shootin' the hell out of some droids. In between the first and second original incarnations of the game, a few versions of a Real Time Strategy game were released, as were other games I am not aware of. While SWB_2003 was available on console, these ones were not, due to their control scheme or game style. This game is the second incarnation of the SWB series. This featured updated models, new maps and updated ones to those that were already in the game. While some maps were somewhat scrapped or lost in time between the 2003 game and this one, some new ones were added, and they were just as fun. One of the most awesome features of the new game was a spaceship mode where you flied in space. Incredible Addition to HL2**
There is no way to undercut this DLC. It is absolutely phenomal and even a casual visitor (such as this reviewer) will likely relish every moment spent playing it, quirks and all. Any return to the Half Life universe is most welcome. This installment begins with the player loading in at precisely the moment HL2 ended. As you can imagine, this only helps deepen the immersion of the journey.
The story of Episode One is the driving force, and well it should be: storytelling seems to take on a new prominence, even for Valve. HL2 was one of the first games in recent memory that made so complete and compelling use of NPCs to really advance the story. The writing, direction and pacing of the story not only continues to be first rate: it actually gets better. That didn't seem possible given how utterly fantastic HL2 is, but Valve found a way to do it. Facial animations are unreal (remember, this DLC originally came out in 2005-6) and the voice acting is incredible. AND THIS IS A FREAKING SHOOTER. If this genre is supposed to inspire the feelz, shouldn't it be limited to excitement and anticipation? Not an emotional rollercoaster of tension, fear, relief, wonder and suspense?
Speaking of being a shooter, the level of difficulty is increased accordingly. While not insurmountable, those players who had been looking for more of a challegne should be pleased: Episode One returns players to a time when combat decisions matter. More use of the functions of the HEV suit (flashlight, oxygen, etc) and some good puzzles/lateral thinking help here, as well. Also, there is noticeably less ammunition. It's no longer possible to blast your way through EVERY problem encountered. A bit of finesse (or fleet-footedness) will be required.
**But for all these changes, there were some struggles. At times, it feels as though Episode One shines a spotlight on some of the things HL2 struggled with. It was very cool to learn more about Alyx and watch her character develop. It was far less cool to watch her do virtually everything of consequence in the game. As a player, it's frustrating to have nearly every action (for story or game play progression) require NPC input. At this point, we've watched Gordon Freeman (the only 'theoretical physicist' who can single-handledly take out entire teams of Recon Marines, Delta Force-level goons, previously unknown armored alien vehicles like Striders and more) solve every problem thrown at him. To 'need' someone else to open every door for him, or tell him where to go seems a bit... contrived. Forced. Less fun. Advancing the goals of humanity was, until this point, a task left almost entirely in the hands of one person. But suddenly, someone else is required to help. It also seems a disservice to Alyx, as she is strong and capable. Does she really need Gordon to do these things? No, and that makes the relationship seem insincere at times. In those moments, it's not about seeing Gordon and Alyx struggle and grow together; it's about having a semi-emotional vehicle that attempts to justify itself as a means to shoe-horn the story forward.
Regardless of the criticism offered in this review, it must be remembered that this content is still well worth the investment (in finances and time). That statement is true of any addition to the HL franchise, be it episodic, stand-alone or even only tangentially related (Portal, et al). Similarly, even with these few subjectively negative oberservations, Episode One is a part of one of the best, most powerful and enduring franchises in video game history. Not only that, but it is part of an amazing progression in storytelling, as well. Conceptually, the HL universe is compelling and completely engrossing. This DLC continues in that tradition beautifully... even if that beauty is marred by a miniscule, nigh-on microscopic blemish.
8/10. Incredible. Episode One is head and shoulders better than many of its peers in the FPS genre. Peers that are full-fledged, core/base games that take tens of hours to complete, not a DLC/add-on that takes a mere handful of hours to play through.

is a casual, wacky game that focuses on strategy and puzzle-solving in a silly cartoon atmosphere.  Do note: it is certainly more reminiscent of other trajectory-based games, like
, rather than any other actual golf games.  If you like silly, simple, trajectory-based puzzle games then you will probably find this enjoyable.
To keep things fresh and crazy as you play, different in-level obstacles and utilities (explosive sheep, cannons, teleporters, and such) make appearances in the various levels.  There are also unlockable power-ups which you can equip and use to manipulate the movement of the golf ball.  Using these things, you will find there are various ways to solve each level.
Besides just beating the par (in strokes), there are also 20 coins and 1 crate to be collected in each level.  You collect the items by causing the golf ball to move through them.  Everything is cumulative, and you can take as many strokes as you need to collect everything.  So with time and patience you can easily collect everything without having to worry about hitting a wall due to skill level.  There is also a score threshold to beat on each level, which can be reached by taking crazy shots with a lot of airtime and that cause many explosions and such.  There is an achievement for completing all objectives on every course (minus the DLC course).
Of course, there are some minor annoyances inherent in the gameplay.  For example, I found it mildly obnoxious that some of the animations couldn’t be skipped; most of them only last a few seconds, but over the course of playing it starts to get old having to wait after every shot before you can take the next one.
is a very casual game.  Once you have access to the power-ups, it’s pretty easy to ace every level with a “hole-in-one.”  The pleasure of the game comes from its silly, easy nature, so don’t expect mind-bending puzzles.  Anticipate approximately 5 hours of gameplay to “beat” each course; if you want to complete all objectives on each course, then that number will probably rise exponentially.  If it sounds like something you would enjoy, get it for a price you are comfortable with and give it a shot.

What an absolutely brilliant game!  I really enjoyed its predecessor, The Room One with it's crazy supernatural atmosphere and beautiful graphics, but I have to say The Room Two is even better!
I wish I could tell you what the story behind the games are, but all I can say is that you have a curious friend who is also travelling the dimensions and time... He's leaving you notes, and pulling you to a door back to your own world, from which you seem to have been locked away from since the first game...
Each 'room' is a puzzle, with lots of hidden switches, knobs, turntables, symbols and all sorts.  You have to find the right sequence of things to do in order to progress.  It's a bit like one of those chinese puzzle boxes, but where anything in the room might be part of the lock.   There's some logic to the puzzles, so you're not left wondering too long about each puzzle.
The game has a lot of hints in the design of the objects, the texturing and the way things are laid out, but if you do get stuck, there's a very nice little hint system that gives you a "light" hint, and then if you're still stuck after a few minutes gives you the option for a much more specific hint.    I only needed to use the 'light' hint a few times, because there was something I'd completely missed, but the system is very well done.
The sound, the music and the ambiance are perfect for each 'room'.  The rooms are very varied: There are locations such as a ship, a tomb, a victorian parlour and a scientist's laboratory.  Each centers around a table, which is set up as the focal point of the room-sized puzzle.
The game took me three hours or so to work through, and at no point was I ready to beat it to death, which is a good sign!  Normally point-and-click puzzle games infuriate me, but both games by Fireproof have been superb insofar as they don't punish the player at all.
At £4, the game was very well worth it...  Considering a movie ticket would be triple that amount for half the time it kept me engaged, I feel very glad I picked this up.

I use one ability (maybe 2) only on any given commander tree. I notice similar from our opposition. Occasionally a commander has an ability that is pretty strong (normally a off-map type call-down) and when they spam the commanders (everyone on the opposite team picking the same) and spam that ability it can decisively turn a game, which sucks...but thats just the nature of these crappy commanders.
They really wanted the commanders to be the micro-transaction of the game....which instrinsically meant they had to be dull, weak and boring or else the game gets unbalanced or pay-to-win...which is bad enough, but also due to lack of balance testing resources available for any micro-transaction system applied to game mechanics, it also means an occasional commander ability can produce unforseen results when spammed in big multi player games.
So...commanders suck. rest of game is good enough.
Going to recommend this game, but only on special (75% off)....and never buy any commanders. Waste of money. Just wait for the in-game rewards drop of one (rare) or use the in-game supply reward purchase (common enough, but accumulates slowly, oh-so-slowly, over time to purchase the commanders)

Cons:
- Story feels like an afterthought; it wasn't that well developed.
- Levels feel a bit repetitive.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter
"The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a first-person story-driven mystery game focused on exploration and discovery. As occult-minded private detective Paul Prospero communicate with the dead to discover the fate of a missing boy and the mystery behind a dark ancient force lurking in Red Creek Valley." Steam description of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter
Story (Spoiler free)
The story of TVOEC is outstanding. In the beginning you do not completely understand what is going on, but this is okay since that is what is intended. Later on you think you start to understand more, but there are still many things that do not seem to make any sense. The game finishes with a beautiful plot twist that makes you question everything you know, both in-game, and in real life! The characters you encounter all have very clear personalities and you can always identify with them. A improvement could be the clarity of the story. The plot twist was maybe not clear enough. I can imagine people being a bit confused if they did not get all things that have happened.
There are scenes, much like flashbacks, since you character, a detective, is reconstructing what has occurred. These are always very interesting to see, though I feel that sometimes it was hard to find who a certain person was. For example, in the first 'flashback' you see the older brother of Ethan, Travis. Travis also comes back later, but it can be hard to recognise him. What SHOULD have been done, is when characters speak, and you have subtitles on (Those were just english for me) then it should say the name of someone, next to what he is saying. Otherwise it can be hard to keep people apart if you are not very far into the game yet.
The games length is very short, 3 hours, then again, it only costs 10 bucks on♥♥♥♥♥ so don't expect putting 300 hours into it. The quality of this content is very good though. The story has a lot of depth, if they would have stretched it to make it longer you would have noticed. It would not feel natural anymore.
That sums it up to a 8/10 for the story.
Visuals
The game takes place in Red Creek Valley. The world has been created outstandingly. I can safely say that this is the most beautiful game I have ever seen. From the grass, to the particles, to the water. What could have even more enhanced the visuals were particles if you walk on the ground, and maybe being able to see your own body if you look down.
The visuals help compliment some epic scenes that would not have been as breathtaking without the impressive water effects.
The character designs have been done quite well. They look very realistic, but a downside is that the animation could have been done better. They are not as fluent and sometimes feel a bit clunky.
The world has masterfully been assembled. The few houses that you visit are very detailed and feel very realistic. The forest and the river seem completely real.
If you would take a screenshot of the nature in TVOEC, you could swear it was a picture.
The developers have done possibly the best job at visuals in any game I have ever seen, and that truly deserves a 9.5/10.
Gameplay
The gameplay mainly consists of finding clues, solving murders, and walking towards the next place of interest. The clue finding is very interesting and truly makes you feel like a detective. You have to step in the shoes of the people that you are finding clues about. Only then, you are able to reconstruct the scene and solve a murder. The controls for this are simplistic, and feel very natural. The murder sequences start with finding the body. Then you have to find the clues. As soon as you have all the clues, you can go into a 'sense' mode. In this mode you will find a one, or more, character(s) standing in a pose. You can then try to put the different 'snapshots' of the characters in the right order. If you find the right order you will see a cutscene of what happened at the murder.
The puzzles are quite interesting and can prove quite difficult.
There are some downsides in the gameplay. First being that exploration is not always well rewarded. In some situations you have to explore in order to find certain clues or find entrances to places of interest that you HAVE to explore in order to complete the game. However, in other areas, you seem to not get rewarded for exploring. You might think, oh, thats a nice piece of forest, whats there? Then you find that there is nothing there. I kept trying to exploring the areas but at the end I felt like it was getting useless.
Another flaw are the areas in between the main puzzles. It is sometimes hard to find where you are supposed to go. For example, when you have solved one of the murders you cross a dam towards the main village. You then, have the possibility to go to the right, and walk along the cliffs. You may think, I may find something over there! However, what will happen is that you will walk for around 15 minutes (if you don't stop) and find points of interest, but you will not find the place where you have to go until you finish your journey and end up in the village again, about 20 metres from where you started, because the place you had to go, is one of the houses. This makes it quite annoying to find where you have to go.
So, in conclusion, the gameplay is very good and a lot of fun, but sometimes the player could use a bit more of directioning if you don't want him to get confused. That gives the gameplay a 7.5/10, alot of fun, but not polished enough.
Conclusion (TL;DR)
In conclusion, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a beautiful short game. It has a outstanding amazing story, and possibly the best visuals in any game that I have ever seen or played. The gameplay is a lot of fun, but is not always polished and misses some things.
My final verdict, for The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an 8.5, a truly great game, almost a must-play.

But what an experience that is. This game's atmosphere is excellent, ranging from mystifying to creepy as you explore the derelict ruins and secluded countryside. The game's environmental graphics, ambient sound effects, and haunting soundtrack round off an excellent presentation that will likely remain unrivalled for quite some time. The character models and animations are a bit standard-fare and, while not bad, stand out as average when compared to the rest. The voice acting is fairly good, especially from the main character, whose voice provides occasional narration to the story.
If you've ever wondered what would happen if you blended some Twin Peaks and a little bit of Silent Hill and had an occult investigator serve as the protagonist, and then poured it into a nice cup of game: this game is for you.

So now to compare it a bit to Dear Esther, my de facto standard for good "walking simulators". Which is better at what areas?
Graphics -> Ethan Carter; this game is astonishingly gorgious at times, although the character models and animations are not as good as the landscape. All in all this might me the best looking game after GTA5 I have ever played.
Music -> Dear Esther; EC has some great tunes but Jessica Curry's haunting tunes seem to be in a league of their own... I rarely experienced music that tore more at the heartstrings than Dear Esther's.
Voice acting -> Dear Esther; EC's main character Paul Prospero's sounds great, but all the other characters are less convincing.
"Gameplay" -> Ethan Carter; this games actually has some puzzles and even a point at which you can *gasp*  DIE!
Atmosphere -> Dear Esther; Ethan Carter is beautiful, but lacks the melancholy soul Dear Esther presents. Basically Dear Esther's island is one big metaphore for your journey, while EC's woods and hills are seemingly just that: (beautiful) woods and hills.
Mystery -> Dear Esther; while both games have plenty of mysterious events and settings and good stories, EC has a pretty nice wrap-up in the end where most has been explained. Dear Esther remains ambiguous even after several playthroughs, which I like more.
Emotional impact -> Dear Esther; it basically wins because the overal presentation including music and writing is a more poetic experience; it thus affected me more than EC, although the ending of EC is also a really good one.
So once again: recommended, but not able to become my favourite "walking game" after Dear Esther.

This game is something that is very unfortunate. It has a seriously interesting world, that will imerse you regardless of whether you're a fan of gothic culture or not. It spins a vampire tale that is both interesting and enjoyable at the same time. The plot remains solid and tense up until the 75% mark and then it feels unfortunatly rushed. I ended this story, feeling satisified of the journey but the overal end just left me feeling like alot of choices I made didn't matter. This is of course, due to the game developer being rushed to finish the game on time and highlights of game gems such as this one, are unfortunatly not given the extra attention they deserved.
Gameplay is very similar to that of games like Deus Ex. You are allowed to tackle objectives in any way you wish, in fact the game presents you with a series of classes which almost define your playstyle from then on. And this isn't just a minor state boost ethier. Playing as a particular class for example, renders you unable to travel on the streets due to your inability to blend in. The consequence of this is that you spend most of the game in sewers eating rats, but have a massive advantage when it comes to any stealth encounter. This is one of the fantastic game design choices the games makes! Certain vampire classes have advanatges in certain areas. Some are good at meddling with humans, others are better at combat and violence. One class is considered insane, and has an entire dialouge choice to back it up in conversations.
Combat can be a little worse for ware, but it isn't unplayable. The broken AI, doesn't tend to put up much of a fight - especially in stealth sections. When you pick your class, you will find it difficult to progress down any other path. Stealth classes, tend to be killed quite easily if you try full frontal combat. Stealth isn't just a one off thing ethier, it is supported by stealth kills, shadow blending etc.
Overall, when you play this game - it is very difficult not to appreciate it, for what it could be and for what it is. I find it difficult to discredit the game up to the 75% mark. After that, things are obviously rushed, everything becomes more combat focused and you will find yourself struggling if you didn't pick a combat class. Before that though, is a game that definatly rewards player choice in both story and gameplay. It provide an interesting, immersive gothic world that will delight both those who enjoy vampire culture and those who don't, alike.

I honestly grabbed this as an impulse by and its actually quite good. Its pretty difficult at first but it gets easier. The best way I can describe it is like a Battle - DDR RPG... Or Puzzle Quest with DDR instead of Bejeweled.

If you love rhythm games, specifically DDR, then look no further. Taking rhythm to the next level, you are forced to pay attention to up to three separate flows of arrows at the same time..and all while keeping beat. Utilizing the Dance Dance Revolution style of rhythm game, these arrows shall be used for offense, defense, and recovery as you battle your way through foe after foe.
What can make it particularly exciting is that no two battles are alike: by using your spells at different times, you essentially 'remix' the steps within the song yourself, providing a somewhat-new spin time and again.
Of course, with a rhythm game, you want its soundtrack to shine, and Before the Echo does not disappoint. With a variety of techno-like beats providing you with sweet ear-candy, you'll find yourself swaying or bobbing to the beat as you work to defeat your foes.
We've had Puzzle/Bejweled meets RPG in titles such as Puzzle Quest, and now the rhythm genre seeks to remix..and so far, it's shining.

In the way that Puzzle Quest is an RPG with Bejewled for combat, Sequence is an RPG with Stepmania for combat.  Addictive, fun, absolutely worth the low price. Fantastic little gem that delivers beyond expectations. Haven't had this much fun since the original Transport Tycoon.
You're basically a developer / entrepreneur who's come into some money in the 80's / 90's / 2000's (all defined by you before you begin the game) to start a business - in the software industry.
You start off with building a little shed for yourself (similar to your first ever cave in minecraft) and begin coding away. A few contracts for other firms to gather some money and before you know it you're designing your first application. You market it, it sells somewhat decent and you find yourself with a load of cash and start dreaming bigger.
Fast forward to two extra offices and a mid sized team crunching away to deliver what you hope the piece of software that will put you on the map!... But.. things aren't going as fast as you'd hoped and that wad of money you got from your first application is waning dangerously low. In a state of panic you lay everyone off and try and finish the app yourself. It takes forever and you realise you're pretty much broke.
Put the project on hold - grab a few contracts - get yourself some leeway and back to the project! You manage to finish it in twice the time you would find acceptable but there it is anyway. Fingers crossed you do your marketing and release it.
You can't wait for the next day to pluck the fruit of the huge amount of work that went into this - only to find out it sold♥♥♥♥♥♥ Mental breakdown, angry muttering and a cigarette break later you decide to be laser sharp this time and bite on what you can chew. You open up the contracts menu - sell every other furnitare in the office and essentially start over again with a tarnished name.
Fast forward again a decade or so and you find yourself thinking if you should upgrade the OS that took the world by storm yet - or focus on cutting edge game engines?
Decisions decisions.

Okay been playing this a lot more with some oldtime coh1 friends. we all finally made the move over because the automatching in coh1 for 3v3 and 4v4 don't work due to lack of players. 2v2 is also pretty slim pickings in coh1. So anyway, thats the reason for the move, and the only reason for the move. coh1 is the better game.
But having started playing it a lot now, I can say we are having fun. My chief complaints is still the commander system. Commanders are still so boring. I use one ability (maybe 2) only on any given commander tree. I notice similar from our opposition. Occasionally a commander has an ability that is pretty strong (normally a off-map type call-down) and when they spam the commanders (everyone on the opposite team picking the same) and spam that ability it can decisively turn a game, which sucks...but thats just the nature of these crappy commanders.
They really wanted the commanders to be the micro-transaction of the game....which instrinsically meant they had to be dull, weak and boring or else the game gets unbalanced or pay-to-win...which is bad enough, but also due to lack of balance testing resources available for any micro-transaction system applied to game mechanics, it also means an occasional commander ability can produce unforseen results when spammed in big multi player games.
So...commanders suck. rest of game is good enough.
Going to recommend this game, but only on special (75% off)....and never buy any commanders. Waste of money. Just wait for the in-game rewards drop of one (rare) or use the in-game supply reward purchase (common enough, but accumulates slowly, oh-so-slowly, over time to purchase the commanders)

First off, I'd like to say that for some reason, Steam is logging my time incorrectly. I've easily poured several entire afternoons into this game trying to get all the possible endings/pictures. Way more than the few hours it shows. There will be some light spoilers in this review, but nothing too groundbreaking.
From a writing standpoint, plot wise, this game is amazing. To get a full grasp of the storyline, you have to go through all the different routes. You only learn certain details from each route, so getting all of them really allows you to piece the entire story together. It truly embodies the phrase "there are two sides to every story." When following any of the incubi routes, Diana seems like the enemy. But when you play Diana's route, the opposite seems to be the case. By following every option, you get a much more well-rounded perspective of the over-arcing situation. As you can imagine, this makes the replayability extremely high. There are a good handful of romantic endings (as is to be expected) but also a couple great non-romantic endings that are really empowering for the protagonist, and even a few endings where the protagonist doesn't survive. It's quite unique.
The characters are a lot of fun. You can choose to romance male characters or female characters, which is a huge plus. (I'm always up for lesbian options.) You also have the option of romancing the human characters. The human routes are shorter, however, which makes sense considering the demons are the main draw to the game. It's a shame though, since I find the human characters to be more interesting.
The protagonist is great. Several times I was presented with violent options, which was a ton of fun. Punching Sam, slapping Erik, bringing an entire beatdown upon Lisette and Malix; the protagonist is not some passive "damsel in distress" type like many dating sim protags seem to be. She definitely know how to hold her own in a fight.
The biggest critique that you'll see from most players is that the sex scenes are all basically the same. That doesn't really bother me at all, though, because I'm asxual and don't need fancy sex scenes. In fact, the scenes are optional, you don't need them to get the perfect ending with that particular character. (If you want all the pictures, then you have to do it, but you can just click right through the scenes since they're all extremely similar.) You only get the sex option with the five main demons, which is my biggest complaint. As I stated earlier, I prefer the human characters' routes, and it seems like they get the short end of the stick.
Overall, fantastic game. It's free, so you have no excuse not to at least give it a chance.

It may not be the longest game, it's rather short, but what it lacks in duration it adds in quality. The landscape, the atmosphere and the soundtrack are just beautiful and a pleasure to enjoy. Stunning graphics and really amazing design.
The story kept me guessing until the end and surprised me many times. It's a game full of subtle hints that are open to your on imagination, while still painting a very interesting picture.
The puzzles and tasks aren't very complex but really fun to solve. It's not the greatest challenge but it still makes you feel like a detective. The game has many fantastic elements in it, bending reality, so if you are a creative person you'll really like this.
Some people pointed out that there is no manual save option and that you have to wait for checkpoints. That is true, but the time from checkpoint to checkpoint is rather short, so that you don't have to play a long time until the next save. I'd say there's an autosave every 10-20 minutes, which is okay. Never had issues with that, and I usually don't have a lot of time to play.
TL;DR:
- It's a little short...
+ ...but what it lacks in duration it adds in quality.
+ Amazing graphics
+ Beautiful landscape and soundtrack
+ Interesting story with many surprising elements
+ Entertaining puzzles
+ Autosaves often
Hope that helped in your decision to buy the game. :)

I think they went too far on this one, somehow.
Don't get me wrong, the problem is not the plot or the characters, or that this game pokes fun at games like Mass Effect, the problem is that Saints Row IV strayed too far from it's predecessors, ditching the whole sandbox crime game and turning it into something that attempts to be a power fantasy, and while some loved it, i wind up hating it after playing for some hours, for reasons like :
* Why do i have to play a stupid puzzle game to take control of a store instead of buying the place or taking it by force like in the other games? If i wanted to play a puzzle, i would be playing a puzzle.
* The darker, grainy, color tone they gave this game make it somehow look worse than SR3. I know they were going to the "cyberpunk" look, but it just feels wrong
* All those powers the game gifts you with not only make your character uber strong but also makes many "mundane" stuff  completely useless, why i wanna ask for backup if i can crush the ground or use telekinesis? Why i even want to customize my car if i can jump taller than a building and run faster than Quicksilver?
* Yet, when the story calls for it, all your powers are REMOVED and you're left with your basics, which you probably didn't care for, cause you were flying and super/puching things up to that point. Why you do that to me game? You don't want me to have fun? Is that it?
* Instead of making side missions interesting they're all normal activities disguised of something more, i get that in 3 and 2 it was also like this, but here they overdone it.
* All the high-jumping-fastrunning-long-gliding action makes me physically ill if i play this game for too long.
* All those awesome customization options and yet a world so shallow to play in, really guys, why all the game must be inside of  a ugly darkened red neon shaded simulation?
* The game gets HARD if you don't grind on the side missions, you won't notice, because you'll be doing them anyway, to get the best the ending this game has to offer.
The game is not BAD, really, it's a pretty neat piece of digital fun, and i will finish it someday, somehow. It's just that SR2 and SR3 were so much MORE. More of everything, if S4 proved something to me is that even exaggeration must be done with moderation.
I really wished that IV was just an 3 with revised mechanics, bigger and crazier, What i got was this "i wanna be the super hero". Blergh, why they simply why didn't they call this a spin-off? I would accept the game better.
Know what? Stick to SR3 might have less customization options and none of the superpowers but heck, It's Awesome.

The good: Nice graphics, great attention to detail, it has a special type of charm, something between Sim City and being realistic. A lot of interesting details like room temperature. Good UI, you can clone entire rooms if you want.
The bad: Well, I really want to like this game but I can't. I can't find any real pattern within in. Sometimes you create something and you earn $5.000.000. Other times you don't. No feedback on what works or not whatsoever. The game is complex but this is not the problem. The problem is that 90% of the time, there are formulas you have no idea about working behind it.
For example, you can get the IP to a software that will earn you millions for a few tens of thousands. On the other hand, you need to pay millions for a software that generates virtually nothing. As a matter of fact, if you simply want to skip playing the game, just get some money through projects and buy IPs. The first time I've done this, I've made close to a billion in a single day.
Plus, I don't understand how it scales. I can get 100 programmers, 100 designers and 100 artists and put them to work on a single project but honestly, it will be just as fast as using five of them. Great presentation, great concept but the mechanics feel broken on a level I can't explain. I'll just stick to something else.

A story about my uncle is a very hard game to describe, it is one of the few games that has a fantastic balance between story and game-play.
The game-play is fantastic, it is a first person platformer with a fantastic “grappling hook” mechanic similar to what you'd expect from a first person Spiderman game, you will swing from place to place and eventually find new ways to get around, the game is linear, but by no means constricting, you can follow the path, but you can choose your own way of getting around the environment as well, in fact the game will reward you for doing so. The game is also very challenging, if you screw up you will not get much of a chance to recover, but fortunately the checkpoints are very generous and I never felt frustrated (ofcourse if you try to get the achievements I imagine you will go nuts as they can be absurdly challenging).
While most games have a storyline of “epic heroes” and “villains”, this game has neither, there is no combat at all and there really aren't any “enemies” in the game, honestly I found it to be a massive relief from all the violence from most other games (don't get me wrong though I still love those games but seriously, there are very few games without some sort of violence in them).
It is also not something like Gone Home either where there is very little “game-play” either. A story about my uncle is instead a simple story of a young man trying to find his uncle.... in an alternate dimension with a super suit that allows him to swing like it was Spiderman's birthday, deep stuff I know but it is literally a bed time story.
Sarcasm aside it's a very sweet story, and one of the few games in the past few years to genuinely move me, there may not be that much dialogue in the story, but it is honestly just the amount that it needed.
The game is very short roughly 2-3 hours long, which while very short, also has a lot of replay value (it's the length of a good movie and like any good game it left me wanting more), if you want a game with a moving story, great game play, beautiful graphics and an exhilarating feeling of soaring through the air, then I can only recommend a story about my uncle.

- The writing doesn't feel believable at times. Honestly, I felt no relatability to the MC. She started off with a strong personality dealing with family issues despite being an immature teenager, but seems to disappear when the incubi's plot comes in. In fact, she's suddenly mature and accepting of her situation right away with little inner conflict. I would have liked to have seen more of the MC's growth past her teenager self to the mature woman she becomes in the endings (such as more scenes with the MC talking with her parents, teachers, and friends).
- I felt no building chemistry between the MC and her love interest. It makes the romance feel unnatural when the incubi go from not understanding love to fully declaring their love. I think more filler scenes of spending time with the incubi as a family would have helped. Right, I'm going to go ahead and say that I'm not good at reviewing, but I figured I might as well give it a shot.
This is a top-down, co-op shooter with a whole lot of com- I mean, Democracy, weapons and even more silliness.
"What do you mean silliness?" you might shout out. Well, let me put it as simple as possible using a very simple technique:
4 untrained idiots + high tech weapons and armor + Droppable vehicles from tanks to mannable robots + Aliens + a whole lotta democracy.
= The biggest f*** fest I have ever seen.
You drop down, and the first thing any experienced diver does, it get whatever he needs to be prepared for the mission ahead. If all things go smoothly, everyone gets their stuff and they hop along merrily. But let's assume this is the worst case scenario.
You all drop down, just in time to have three patrols walking in on you as you exit your pods. You instantly get spotted, and thinking you have time, you call in your pod of equipment anyway. It seems to be going well, as the team have done the same and have started fighting back, things seem well. Until a pod kills two of your team mates at once, causing the third team mate to panick and get taken down by an unseen terror with tenticles the size of Hitler's railway cannon.
All of a sudden, you realize that the sh*t that is the alien enemy has now reached your waist, and you must think quickly. The first thing that comes to mind is to call in a beacon to call down your friends, so you run, leaving behind mechs, APC's and other usefull tools. You think you're in the clear, but instead of finding the brief pause you need to call back your friends, some lanky♥♥♥♥♥bug spits goo into your face, and you get devoures by what you swear was a giant pillbug.
This is basically just one of the SIMPLE ways this game can go from a "Dive in the park" to "Oh my god I'm not getting paid enough for this".
The game itself is amazing, and to maximize this, get some friends in on it. I have no comment for the DLC, sure it has some cool stuff, but most of it is cosmetic, I got it anyways because wtfn?
Buy it, you'll appreciate the f*ckery you get into while playing this game with both friends and randoms.

Sequence is an interesting game wich mixes DDR with rpg elements. As you unravel the curious story of Ky, a man trapped inside the misterious Tower, with no idea how he got there. The gameplay is rhythm based (in the vains of ddr or guitar hero), but you have three "lanes" between wich you keep changing in order to attack, deffend and recover your mana. Now, the game starts really pretencious about its own plot, and about how "different" it is. It is techno based and fits the mood of the game perfectly . Unfortunately, for the scope of the game, the soundtrack is a little too limited. There is a lot of grinding towards the end which exacerbates the problem, however, when you consider that the game was coded by one man, it is easy to forgive.
To sum up, the game is a steal at $5.

For a Worms game, this is oddly the cutest entry of the lot.
From the cutesy theme in the title to how happy all the worms are playing a nice game of golf instead of, you know... Trying to blow each other up like they normally spend their time doing.. It is an odd change of pace, but that doesn't make it bad.. I found this game rather charming, really.
Worms Crazy Golf is a game that takes the classic Worms system and combines it with golf to make a rather strange, if interesting, hybrid of 2D golf sim, where players try their best to smack a ball all the way to the hole in as few hits as possible, while trying to avoid more Wormish hazards such as mines, sheep, and even grumpy grannies, in time earning items that help make getting that tricky hole-in-one easier.
A game about 2D golf might not seem all that interesting at first, but once you give it a wack you find a humble pleasure playing this simple little game. Sadly, as fun as it can be at times, it does suffer from a flaw or two that holds it back from being a rather enjoyable game in the long run.
For 10 dollars, the content the game packs is rather meh, a decent player able to beat the game in a few hours. It might have some form of replay value, but it is rather humble in that area.
To make matters worst, the game suffers from an awkward balancing issue, being that one of the powers (Reverse Gravity) is by far the most broken item in the game. Upon earning it for the first time, it doesn't take a player long to realise that he can abuse it to get easy holes in one for EVERY course in the game.. I am serious about that, it takes all challege out of a nice little golf game, so if you are the kind of person who seeks a challenge, I suggest you avoid using it if you don't want to spoil your fun. For the egotist, however, it certainly does satisfy the desire for easy glory.
I suggest you wait for the game to go on sale for 5 bucks or so before getting the game. It is fun and all, but clearly not worth the current price offered.

As much as I really wanted to...I just found it difficult to get into this story. After two hours, I still couldn't care enough about the characters and plot to continue. The scenery is beautiful, and I love the concept but I just didn't click with this.

On the plus side, the game looks gorgeous, sounds beautiful, and is very well voice acted.  I won't elaborate on these, other than to say - look at those screenshots, they aren't lying.  I also like the investigative aspect; I appreciate games featuring detective player avatars ... that can actually detect their way out of a paper bag - Paul looks at evidence and actually comes to intelligent conclusions about what happened!
On the negative side, it was short, yet went on too long.  You can't beat the game without finding and solving everything.  Yes, finding, and some of the plot scenes are decently hard to find.  You can either (as I did) consult a guide, or play hunt-the-pixel in a 3d world.  Also, the investigations sometimes involve the same problem, hunting for all the hotspots in order to progress.
I also take issue with the plot.  Basically, it isn't very scary.
doesn't build tension well because the pacing is off.  You yourself are never in danger at all, so any tension would theoretically revolve around either a rush to save Ethan, or a burning drive to know what happened.  The problem is you barely get to know any of the characters, or see anything about their world, so it's hard to get drawn in that way.  The net effect is a moody story, but not really a very scary one.  Also, I did not really like certain spoileriffic aspects of the ending.

It took me maybe 4 tries to get a company to survive more than a year. Even bumping the starting cash from $10,000 to $50,000 it was impossible to get anywhere before ultimately going bankrupt. Eventually I hit upon a winning strategy, with a founder skilled at programming and another employee for design, cranking out constant contracts ($30,000 worth a month) and putting a few hours every day into a game. This was a really un-fun amount of micromanagement, having to click 50 different prompts to advance the contracts through the different stages of completion before the month whizzed by and I was bankrupt again. Eventually after like two years enough work had been done on the game to release it to 300,000 people, where it got maybe 3,000 sales and I was back to constant near-bankruptcy. I hired two cheap marketers and started on the same plan with more or less the exact same details, a programmer and a designer spending their spare time when not doing contract work working on the game. This time, with 2 marketers working non-stop before and after release, It made $8 million in a few months and at that point there was no real reason to keep playing.
This game is a chore until it isn't, at which point there's nothing left to do.

So, I'll go ahead and get this out of the way. Yes, I have played over 275 hours in this game, and yes, my review is still a thumbs down, but only by a slim margin.

Some of these changes are really great, but in its current state, I cannot recommend this game. The balance went from forgiving and inviting, to a perfect glass ceiling, in which you will not, no matter how well you play, reach in the billions of dollars as you could in previous titles. Sometimes, it takes me 10-15 in game years to reach $50mil, other times, longer. This frustrating brick wall, combined with new distribution systems, Sound - which is difficult to work around, resulting in several office rebuilds, and other new implimentations, make me think twice about recommending it.
There is a good game in here, I've seen it firsthand, but it's not where it needs to be. If/when the game changes, I'll be back to change the review! Otherwise, I can't recommend it in its current state of alpha 9. If the dev is on here, I'd love to talk about this in more depth, and offer some particular feedback to someone in a position to do something about it.

Metro 2033 is a well crafted game. Post apocalytic games like Fallout are normally set in America, so it is great to see a developer focus on Moscow instead. Unlike Fallout, the game is level based rather than open world. Most of the levels are quite linear with limited exploration, but there are several levels populated with bandit, Commies or Fascists that can be handled in different ways. The AI of mutant enemies is simplistic, but human AI is very good for a game. If you attack them openly with unsilenced weapons rather than use stealth to avoid them or quietly  take them down in a dark place, all nearby humans will begin hunting you down.
If you are intending to play the game, one thing to take note of is that there are 2 different endings, and the better ending if only accessible if you have a reasonably high 'karma'. You gain karma points by being generous, by approaching the dark ones, by obeying orders, listening to conversations in their entirety, by exploring, and by using stealth in certain situations rather than killing all humans in certain levels.
You will required at least 2 playthroughs to get all of the achievements, but you can get most of them in a single playthrough followed by replaying certain chapters.
I recommend reading the novel Metro 2033 first before playing the game. The outlines of the story are the same, but there are significant differences between the game and the novel.
I recommend using Reshade to tweak the graphics, particularly it's sharpening shaders, since Metro 2033 is a bit soft due to FXAA like antialiasing which you cannot disable.
Bugs: The game is quite stable and bug free, with a single exception. Sometimes the game would lock up when loading a new chapter. I do not know the cause, and had to kill the process using Task manager, and restart the game.
Suggestions for improvement: More weapons
Faster start (at the main menu)
An open world version of the game with an entire subway system to explore as well as Moscow above ground.

So, I'll go ahead and get this out of the way. Yes, I have played over 275 hours in this game, and yes, my review is still a thumbs down, but only by a slim margin.
My first review was incredibly brief, and positive. I liked the customization, loved the mechanics, and all together found the game a GREAT time waster. However, as this is an early access game, it has shifted in direction and evolved as updates have been released. Some of these changes are really great, but in its current state, I cannot recommend this game. The balance went from forgiving and inviting, to a perfect glass ceiling, in which you will not, no matter how well you play, reach in the billions of dollars as you could in previous titles. Sometimes, it takes me 10-15 in game years to reach $50mil, other times, longer. This frustrating brick wall, combined with new distribution systems, Sound - which is difficult to work around, resulting in several office rebuilds, and other new implimentations, make me think twice about recommending it.
There is a good game in here, I've seen it firsthand, but it's not where it needs to be. If/when the game changes, I'll be back to change the review! Otherwise, I can't recommend it in its current state of alpha 9. If the dev is on here, I'd love to talk about this in more depth, and offer some particular feedback to someone in a position to do something about it.

I've been playing this game since I think around Alpha 1.4, and the progress has been consistently top notch. The continutation of adding depth and the subsequent variation that provides is resulting in one of the best management simulations I have played in recent years. Add to that the fact that this is a one-man operation makes it all the more impressive.
I'm not generally a fan of the graphical style used here. However, that this is all done by one person makes it a sensible and pragmatic design choice, and I think it works very well.
I'd like to see some more options in the way of keeping track of employees, as I find that once I get beyond a staff of 10, I'm more focussed on building an overall cohesive unit, as opposed to perhaps focusing on the individuals within the team. I'd also like to be able to see what role a retired employee used to do, and perhaps have the option to increase their pension! I do feel bad when someone retires early on, and they're essentially left with a pittance compared to employees who retire later.
The development mechanics work very well, with the addition of overstaffed teams having a negative impact on the development of a given product. I love being able to create and expand my company office space, and I think the tools given to do that are very well implemented. I'd like to have more choice in terms of items and equipment, maybe with different brands, each with their own advantages and disadvantages, and perhaps even with employees preferring a certain brand. I'm going to say this right away,
is probably my favorite platformer of all time. Imagine Portal, only without the Portal Gun and you're Spiderman instead.
The core gameplay mechanic is your grappling hook, which you can attach to almost any surface to swing yourself through the levels.
combines thrilling, high-speed platforming with a beautifully crafted and detailed fantasy world and a captivating, though really short story. The difficulty scales very nicely throughout the game, starting off slowly and becoming quite the challenge at the end, but without ever feeling frustrating or unfair, or breaking the pace of the story. And for those seeking more of a challenge there are always the achievements, which in this game are really an 'achievement' to get. The story/motivation is pretty short and can be explained in two or three sentences, but it's more the presentation than the content that keeps you on track. And I absolutely love the main voice actor/narrator!
In summary, I can recommend this little hidden gem to anyone who has a thing for platformers and loves to admire gorgeous graphics with a slow-paced story. If you're in for a ~5 hour long adventure, you're definitely gonna have a blast!
-Gharren

It is indeed short. I searched every nook and cranny and took time to just awe at the environment and snap screenshots for desktop backgrounds and still clocked in at only 4.5hrs. So that is the biggest flaw, it really is short. Even when you take your time and move at the pace I did. Me being the penny pincher I am makes me wonder if it was worth the 7.99USD I spent. Closest thing I can compare it to is Amnesia: The Dark Decent and Dear Esther, but that goes without saying that it is an entirely different experience than both. Openness of the environment and its beauty compares but surpasses Dear Esther with ease. The story, storytelling, and voice acting rivals Amnesia. All the while it stays its own entirely unique experience. If any of that is making you interested at all I'd highly recommend it.
I would highly recommend not even consulting a guide if you get lost, just be lost. Nothing in this game is THAT difficult to find or solve and you will come around to it eventually. And the scenery is nice in the meantime. Avoid any spoilers of any kind as much as possible! The sooner you dive in and stop poking around about it, the more you'll get out of it. Skip the "lets play's" and guides, just get into it yourself like the old days. The unique experience you get from this game is short and precious, so enjoy it to the full extent by doing it all yourself!

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter offers a unique gaming experience by combining different genres into an impressive game.
First, we have the exploration layer: the landscape is a dreamy mountain valley, traversed by rivers and bathed in sunset light. The scenery is so beautiful that it will make you want to take screenshots of every single tree that you encounter. And when you think you just caught in one screenshot the nicest view there is in the game, you realize that if you move a bit sideways there's a completely different angle that makes the scene even more beautiful than the previous one. I spent hours just walking around and looking at everything, discovering sceneries of amazing beauty and marveling myself at the astonishing graphic detail.
But the game is much more than a walking simulator. The story unfolds as you explore the surroundings: it's the tragic story of a boy called Ethan that has gone missing. Playing the role of the detective Paul, you embark on this mysterious adventure of finding the boy. On the road you discover different clues and solve different murder cases associated to his disappearance, by using of your supernatural ability to sense things. The story has a way of keeping you interested until the end, with unexpected events along the way. The ending is not predictable, although not out of the ordinary either; but it's the kind of ending you least expect to have.
I would also advise checking a guide after you complete the game because there are a couple of vey enjoyable Easter eggs that are a nice addition to the main story and it would be a pity to miss them.
The story is designed as a thriller, there are a few scenes that might cause a bit of discomfort to some people: blood on the ground, mutilated corpses, spooky dark areas and a couple of jump scares. But it's not at all a violent game and the horror-y scenes are very bearable even for an easily startled person as I am.
The music adds a lot to the whole ambience of the game. It is dark in the sinister areas and cheerful in the lighted areas. The sound of the wind, of the river flowing, of the creaking floor when you step on it - all these immerse you even deeper in the whole atmosphere of the game.
The price of this game has been a bit too spicy for me (18,99€) if you consider it's shortness (4-5 hours for a complete playthrough) and I avoided buying it for a long time, but now after I played it, I understand that the price might justify the effort the developers put into creating this superb game. I definitely recommend buying it while on sale, at 75% off.

I had picked up SanctuaryRPG during a Steam sale a few years back. To be real: It was less than a dollar and I was feeling frisky. But after 70+ hours of playing this game, my thought is that the sale price is an insane steal. For the hours of entertainment and enjoyment that I've received from this game, I think the full price tag is worth it and I feel almost guilty for paying so little for a game I love so much. But hey, if you see it for 90% off (like it is RIGHT NOW... at least at the time of writing this) I fully recommend picking it up. That's value.
SanctuaryRPG is a text-based roguelike RPG where you choose from six different classes (each with their own strengths and weaknesses) and grind your way to gain levels and find gear. The premise itself is standard, but there is enough depth to the ways one can create their own character builds that make each new game exciting.
There are four game modes: Classic (permadeath), Softcore (respawns), Lunatic (go ♥♥♥♥ yourself), and Survival which is unlocked through beating the game on the other modes. Most of my experience is playing on Classic, though, I had the unfortunate idea to try playing on Lunatic mode and well… this game is out to kill you. There is no hand holding. You are not safe. Encounters, like most things in this game, are randomized. In the same area that you’ll find a mob that you can one-shot with ease, you will find something that will blind you and force you into a war of attrition before slaughtering you.
That sense of unease and fear can be a lot of the fun of this game though. It sucks to die after thinking up a new build idea and finding the perfect items (which are all RNG drops) to make it work, but there’s some charm in this game that has me throwing more and more attempts at it without ever feeling like it’s pointless. The combat is easy to learn and get into so starting fresh never feels like too much of a drag.
There are definitely some annoyances: because random is well… random, you’re prone to legendary drops that you’re forced to throw away because they have worse stats than some common sword you found at the start of the game. Crafting can sometimes feel pointless because the items you make are just as random as anything you can find from killing mobs (though it is an extra chance at loot). And the inability to hold any armor/weapons besides the ones that you are wearing can feel incredibly frustrating, though, it does make one more mindful of the gear they choose to pick up and forces the player to play and build around the items they find (which can make for some interesting characters).
The ASCII-style art of SanctuaryRPG is one of the features that initially stood out to me when I purchased the game and are one of many things that make the game unique. There is a lot of variation in characters, mobs, and environments that is achieved perfectly in this style and are well made. It serves to capture the setting and tone of this game which is very old-school and quirky.
It’s definitely a matter of taste. The screenshots give a good idea of what this game looks like (though, there are some very nice pieces of art that one gets to view as they progress through the story). Some people may be put off, but this game has its own niche that it fills and the ASCII-art continues that theme and charm.
Another fun part of SanctuaryRPG is the writing and the tone and universe it is set within. There is a lot of comedy throughout the game: a lot of silly and random (like the gameplay itself) events that have you milking ghosts, stealing weapons from hobos, or eating flying pancakes. Even in the creation of your character alone you are given an elaborate randomized backstory that sets the fun and humourous tone for things to come.
That said, SanctuaryRPG isn’t devoid of a narrative and it isn’t solely lolsorandom humour (not that I minded the more lighthearted parts of the game anyway). The main plot of the game, while seemingly standard, has your character fighting through places of the world and discovering more about its lore and people.Though, there aren’t many huge plot twists that will keep you awake at night or any moments that will elicit intense emotions.
The story gets the job done and there’s enough intrigue to keep you wanting to get to the end, though the worldbuilding is what I’d consider a stronger element than the plot itself. This game has an interesting setting that feature both dragons and low-technology weaponry alongside robots and portals. It feels like its own unique setting and while it does borrow many classic RPG tropes, it arranges them in fun ways that allows the setting to stand out on its own.
SactuaryRPG’s soundtrack composed by Rafael Langoni Smith consists of 64 chiptune-style tracks. Along with the ASCII-style art, the music helps to give the game both an old-school vibe and its own unique elements. There is a lot of variety in the soundtrack: from the soft and relaxing (Sanctuary Arp II: Title Screen) to dark and ominous (You May Be Experiencing Some Discomfort) to intense and triumphant (Sangue nos Olhos).
There are some really great and memorable melodies in these tracks. The music often serves as another driving force to make one want to continuing playing longer. There’s a thrill in getting into a fight, hearing a particular track and just knowing that you’re ♥♥♥♥ed. This is a game soundtrack that I’d actually recommend listening to solely on its own as well!
+Multiple ways to play/build your character
+Easy to get into, but plenty to master
+Unique artstyle
+Comedy-focused writing (which can be good or bad depending on one’s taste, but I’m personally found it entertaining)
+Decent world-building that gives the setting and world intrigue
+Melodic chiptune-style music
+/-RNG adds an element of surprise, but also annoyance
+/-Standard plot that gets the job done, but could have been expanded further (though, I admit that I enjoyed the game regardless of the story)
-Epic/Legendary weapons mean very little since their stats are randomized and often unuseful
-Crafting as well as some other features (such as the Temple or Library) can feel pointless since the same things can be achieved through grinding

This game is just awesome. A (Survival-)Horror, 1st-person post-apocalyptic shooter in the russian Metro. The characters are well written and actually help you during shootouts, the monsters strike fear in your heart while still staying mostly realistic, and if you can't get enough of the universe there's a sequel and 3 books (this game is based on the first one, it tells you in the loading screen, seriously read them if you liked it), and another game is planned for 2017.
The adaptable difficulty and playstyle are set up like this:
>Spartan mode (less survival and more bullets)
>Survivor mode (more suvival and less bullets)
Then you choose either Normal, Ranger or Ranger Hardcore difficulty. Normal being full HUD, easy enemies and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of stuff, Ranger is less HUD, stronger enemies and more survival aspects, and Ranger Hardcore means no HUD, all ressources are scarce and enemies kill you easily (every shot counts, but one or two shots actually kill an enemy).
Another special feature are "moral points". You steal some bullets from a beggar? You loose a point. You talk to your stepdad and say goodbye to your friends before leaving the station? You gain a point. If you gain enough during the playthrough you unlock the good ending, if not you get the bad one.
The annoying achievments I mentioned above are "Kill 50 humans with pneumatic weapons" or "Kill 100 enemies using revolvers". I don't use pneumatic weapons (because I want my gun to go "bang" not "phew") and I can't bring myself to using the revolver for an entire playthough. But aside of those most other achivments just happen while playing or are actually interesting, f.e. "Kill all enemies in the level Frontline" (There are two factions in two different camps, both blind firing at each other. It's pretty awesome.).
Also, pro tip: Once you're in the train with Khan, burn the cobwebs he stops in front of with your lighter. Don't get stuck like me and google like a idiot. Just burn all the cobwebs you see in the game, ♥♥♥♥ those spiders.
