As a fan of tycoon and resource management games, this immediately caught my attention and I sat and watched - the asthetic factor of the game and the sheer amount of things to do in it perked my ears right up. The first time I dove in, I went in with baited breath and expected to absorb just about everything it had in store for me within a few hours. I was dead wrong about that.
In fact, it almost bombarded me with micromanagement details, from the smallest character flaws of potential employees to a robust server system and a catalog of options on types of software to zone in on and carve my very own virtual niche in the market. It was everything I wanted, and much more. Almost too much more. An overwhelming sense of more.
It was a bit much, more than I expected, and I admit to not catching onto the learning curve until my second jump in.
Once I caught it, however, it's been non-stop.
So there is a bit of a learning curve to it, but the tutorials are nice and simple and helpful. For once, I caught myself wanting those tutorials, rather than letting my hand go to roam about on my own.
What an enjoyable game. The freedom and flexibility to either stay super small, a clique of "buds" that just crank out some indy games and scrape by, riding the waves of the popular tides and not making waves. Or a multi-billion dollar company churning out market-smashing operating systems and taking the world by storm - along with literally everything, and I mean everything, in between.
Can't stop. Don't wanna stop. Just want to keep on keepin' on. I want to do a game with this idea, or that principal, or start a new company to try a different venue all before even getting my hands dirty in my current one.

I'm going to say this right away,
is probably my favorite platformer of all time. Imagine Portal, only without the Portal Gun and you're Spiderman instead.

combines thrilling, high-speed platforming with a beautifully crafted and detailed fantasy world and a captivating, though really short story. The difficulty scales very nicely throughout the game, starting off slowly and becoming quite the challenge at the end, but without ever feeling frustrating or unfair, or breaking the pace of the story. And for those seeking more of a challenge there are always the achievements, which in this game are really an 'achievement' to get. The story/motivation is pretty short and can be explained in two or three sentences, but it's more the presentation than the content that keeps you on track. And I absolutely love the main voice actor/narrator!
In summary, I can recommend this little hidden gem to anyone who has a thing for platformers and loves to admire gorgeous graphics with a slow-paced story. If you're in for a ~5 hour long adventure, you're definitely gonna have a blast!

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: I sure can appreciate a simplistic platformer, and this game delivers on that front. It's the kind of game you could play on an Atari 2600 controller; all you do is move and jump. To say that this game is reminiscent to VVVVVV is one hell of an understatement; this game pretty much is VVVVVV, but without the flipping. Another thing that this game took from VVVVVV is the ability to make very simple, yet sometimes very challenging rooms. Note that I said challenging, not difficult; there's a vast difference between the two. The challenge of this game is akin to World 2 of Super Meat Boy; not too terrible and certainly manageable, but still tricky in parts, nonetheless. I also really dug the exploration aspect of it, and since the game won't last you more than an hour, you don't feel too overwhelmed by the world. My only complaint is the puzzle thing at the end. It really isn't necessary and instead feels completely out of place in a game like this. I would almost call it game-killing, as it made me feel so apathetic toward the game that I didn't want to complete it again. However, the other 99.9% of this game is still quite good. Definitely worth the $0.00 you paid for it (oh yeah, I forgot to mention; it's free). 8/10.
Story: There... really isn't any. NEXT CRITERION
Graphics: I really dug what they did with the graphics. Rather than going with a plain CGA palette, they also rendered the sprites on a mock-CRT monitor, phosphor glow included. It's really quite impressive on a technical level, and is definitely both more inspired and more interesting to look at than just a flat screen. Playing this on a CRT monitor would probably hurt some heads, but that's beside the point. They did a very good job here, and they deserve at least some props for what they did. 4/5.
Music: Man, where is the music? I know that we're going for an early-DOS era game, but even those had some sort of music. Even something simple I believe would have helped the ambiance. The sound is functional, though; I just wish that there was something more than just the bare minimum jumping sounds and the beginning fanfare. 2/5.
Overall score of 8/0/4/2; 7.0/10. I'd just pick it up for the sole fact of it being free. However, be warned that the puzzle at the end of the game may leave a sour taste in your mouth, as it did mine.

What really defines a "retro game?"
Sure, there are quite a few two-dimensional one-afternoon's-scope games out there with chunky, obvious pixels and "chiptune" soundtracks -- how I hate that appellation, much as I dig the genre itself -- and surely you've encountered buckets of 'em in your travels. They're clearly trying to appeal to a certain nostalgic market, but I find that many of these so-called "retro" games don't really understand what it is to which they're alleging to pay homage.
You Have To Win The Game has no such difficulty. It understands its audience quite intimately.
If you've ever played an early home computer platformer, with brittle, stylized art tiles on a sea of black background, stages rather than a scrolling continuous playfield, and that curiously fast twitch-timing that makes "simple" tricks hard to duplicate without a dead-steady hand, you'll recognize this one immediately. Fans of the Monty Mole games, Jet Set Willy, Montezuma's Revenge, Dark Castle, and other multiscreen platformers will be right at home. The CGA-style 'magenta and cyan' default graphics cement this port clearly as a PC game, though there's an option to step up to 16-color EGA graphics if you prefer. The PC speaker style sound effects, staggered hex-aligned pixels with faint scanlines, and bowing of the screen to a curved glass surface really drive home that this game is an artifact from a cultural time capsule, and the simulated monitor bezel around it completes the effect nicely.
Be sure to return the disk to its protective sleeve and file it away in its sunshielded flipcases when you're done with it.
The game itself is delightfully frustrating, prone to tease the player with glimpses of as-yet-inaccessible areas, to inspire mad curiosity about the only occasionally map-friendly physics. Many rooms map easily, yes, but some loop back on themselves, or take you to places from which you can't easily return by stepping back through the passage behind you. Some rooms are clearly designed to make you sweat and suffer, and suffer you shall if you want to earn that coveted 100% at the end. Be glad for the unlimited lives in the standard game mode -- you'll need 'em. (If you're truly crazy, try the Playable Cat mode for nine lives, or the YOLO mode for a single life.)
The game is an exploration platformer and a puzzle game. Without ruining its secrets, let it suffice to say that careful note-taking, mapping, and that sort of curious and self-reliant Eighties gamer mindset will serve you well. The sort of person who would prefer platformers to be purely feats of dexterity may be frustrated by this game's unavoidable puzzle elements, but I suspect anyone who remembers the games that inspired You Have To Win The Game will recognize that this was de riguer back then. There are certainly some moments of frustration to be had playing this game, some vexingly tricky rooms to navigate, but that's part of the fun of it, really. Anyone who's put together Monty Mole's Freedom Kit or played a Sierra game in which it was all too possible to end up in an unwinnable game for lack of an item acquired earlier is surely used to these frustrations, and the "sunrise moment" of finally getting past a tough room to see what lies beyond it is ample reward.
Curious minds will be left with many questions about the game world visited. The minimal, simple graphics and room names offer clues, but few answers, as to who you are, where you are, how you ended up here, why you're here, and what you're after. This too was part of the charm of these games, but I find myself intrigued by the landscape the game so simply depicts, and given such a large blank space where narrative and purpose would sit in a story, I find myself trying to imagine how this unnamed protagonist got here, to this dangerous world with its varied alien and Gothic imagery, and who the few named figures in the game are, or were.
As a platformer, it's delightfully tricky but not impossible. This aging gamer managed to achieve 100% after six hours of play, and six hours of play is quite impressive for a game of the era to which this one's paying homage. The game is well-balanced, too -- there are many optional challenges for completion that aren't strictly necessary to win. (I've seen five-minute speedruns through it.) There are some lovely challenges awaiting completionists, though, and the game does indeed reward you for your additional effort. Like every great exploration game, there are places you'll miss if you don't explore thoroughly, and seeing them all will take some real effort.
This is not a retro platformer for folks who simply like the idea of 2D games with chunky pixels. This is a love letter to the mid-Eighties home computer platformer, from the eloquent and unmistakably informed pen of J. Kyle Pittman and Pirate Hearts. This is a return to a lost era, and it is meant to bring back not only the look, not only the feel, but the entire zeitgeist of a bygone age of computer games. Tread reverently. This is a relic from an alternate universe's past, a living fossil. You can't meaningfully compare it to the games of today, at least not in capacity to rate it. Compare it to games of the increasingly distant past, and if you haven't played those games, play this one. It's a stellar specimen of the early days of home computer platformers.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter has the freedom and gameplay of Myst, which includes a rarely-seen-in-modern-games sense of wonder at the ability to explore the gorgeous landscapes while not being blocked by invisible walls or constantly yelled at to get back on track. It's an exercise in letting the player control their own pacing and progress, and it works marvelously.
The story and setting are channeling pure Alan Wake. And that's a good thing. The graphics are some of the best I have ever seen. High res textures and thoughtful lighting effects make it feel like you're walking through a carefully constructed work of art.
The soundtrack is phenominal. It's one of the only games I've played recently where I want to listen to the music outside of the game. Although part of the brilliance is the way the tracks change based on context.
Where the game suffers is in its saving system. You only get checkpoints after major puzzles are completed. This means that if you make partial progress on a puzzle and then move on to another and then another you won't have anything saved until you complete one, and then only that last puzzle is saved. When you load up the game the next time all that partial progress is gone. It's a befudling problem. On forums the developers have waxed ad naseum about how the engine (Unreal 3) doesn't easily support saving the whole state of the world. Ok...who cares? It's a weak excuse for a monstrous oversight. They obviously have the ability to create a save system outside the bounds of the engine, they just got lazy and didn't extend it far enough. If you can save the state of completing a puzzle, then you can also save each piece of the puzzle. There's definitely less than a hundred steps across all puzzles total, so even brute-forcing the system and manually checking each state would be a simple task for a single developer. I'm harping on this so much because loading up the game for my second session was one of the most jarring experiences I've ever had in a game. To have work I thought completed magically undone is not fun.
Another problem is the lack of a fast travel system. Having to walk everywhere feels great at first, but by the end running around to get to locations that can be many minutes apart with nothing in between gets tiresome. And it's very easy to miss things so it's almost guaranteed that you'll be backtracking. A lot.
The game can be a bit obtuse at times as well. If you happen to miss one tiny thing then completing a puzzle becomes impossible, and there are no hints, so you're just left wandering around the game world, knowing that you can't quit yet because your work on the current puzzle won't be saved.
Overall Ethan Carter is an excellent, immersive experience. It's thought provoking, chilling, and awe-inspiring at different points. It has flaws, but once you get past them it's a journey worth taking.

For instance, when you first start out, there are some fairly obvious indications towards clues which lead you to suppose this is a common precident, and yet later in the game with some of the more important clues, they are not evident at all so you could easy miss them. Beware also of back tracking to look for possible missing clues, as picking up objects at previous save points seems to erase your progress. The developers state that it is an "experience, in non-linear fashion" and for the most part this is true, but you will encounter the invisible wall syndrome quite frequently. Jumping off bridges or swimming in the lake is definately a no-no, no matter how hard you try.
A labour of love without doubt, and worthy of praise, but if you lack patience, stamina and a considerable attention span, you could find yourself developing a thousand yard stare.

Sequence is a classic RPG, except that combat is performed by out-DDRing your opponent. To defend yourself and cast spells, you need to press buttons in time with moving arrows, which move with the beat of the music. I figured I would like it going in, but it suprised me by surpassing my expectations.
Combat is fun. At any time, you can switch between three modes: defending yourself, casting spells, or gaining MP, and there are many ways to approach combat. There's definitely a lot to think about, and having a plan is more important than hitting every arrow. The one downside is that trying to get certain drops can be a grind.
The plot is a bit short, but the dialogue between the characters is amazing. This is one of the funniest and wittiest games I've played. The music is enjoyable, but it would've been nice to have more tracks. The art is pretty nice, for being 2D stills. And it's fully voice-acted.
This game could easily sell for more than $5. It's absolutely worth it.

Sequence, while short, is a very invigorating indie game.  The combination of music, defense, and spell casting merge seamlessly.  The arrows match the beat of the music making the experience feel almost rythmic,  Casting spells isn't just click and it's done, you have to execute a small sequence to complete it as if you were actually casting it.  To regain mana you can access a mana pool in which you execute an almost "Guitar Hero" esque sequence, each note giving back mana.  Lastly you can defend against enemy attacks the same way you cast, just on a different screen.  The three screen technique is not at all taxing, in fact it seems almost instinctive.  While adding to the challenge, it makes the experience all the more wonderful.  If given enough practice you can switch from all three screens easily casting, defending, and regenerating quickly and efficently --  which the game slowly introduces with tougher and tougher enemies.  Overall Sequence is a solid indie game.

"Hardcore" retro platformers have been making something of a comeback in recent years, thanks in large part to Super Meat Boy's success, and the DOS inspired You Have to Win the Game is the latest to join the batch of games designed to make you grit your teeth as you die again and again...in theory.
Putting you in a (mostly) nonlinear metroidvania world, you hop your way around exploring and collecting upgrades to progress further, to eventually do exactly what the title says. There's very little more to say in that regard as YHtWtG isn't trying to do anything new and knows this, acting more as a diversion than something you'll continue to talk about after the 30-60 minutes it takes you to finish it.
It plays decently, with functional controls that I didn't hinder my advancement or cause me any great difficulty, and is for the most part is fairly average at what it does. There is nothing particularly noteworthy I can say for or against it, but that's also because so much of the game consists of...nothing. Room after room I entered greeted me with rarely a trap or platform to be seen, allowing me to leisurely walk from one side to the other only to find much of the same waiting for me when I entered the next screen. There's little challenge to be found here aside from a few obnoxiously placed traps, but the lack of any map and the convoluted nature of the environment means a great deal of patience is still required to finish the game (less you fall asleep on account of the tedium of backtracking through every screen looking for the passage you missed). The lack of any soundtrack only adds to the emptiness, almost as if the developer was intentionally designing the experience to make you to feel cold and alone.
As a game that aspires to be something that twists your fingers into knots and causes you to curse your monitor in rage, You Have to Win the Game is a shockingly easy adventure that leaves little if any impression. I can't say it's bad, but for every second I spent playing it I had to ask myself: what was the point? If you have a likening for oldschool platformers and need to kill an hour, you could definitely do worse than YHtWtG, but I can't help but feel that those with more limited free time would be better off spending it elsewhere.

If you liked The Room, you'll probably like The Room Two. The puzzles are fairly similar, but your viewpoint is a little expanded. Instead of being closely focused on a single box/table at a time, The Room Two is really about the entire room your're in. In many cases, you can't completely solve puzzles by just focusing on one item or table - you have to move to other items or tables and solve puzzles over there to figure out your next steps. In theory, this should have complicated things, but I actually found that, in most cases, this made The Room Two a little easier than The Room. I relied on the game's hint system much less.
The ending was a bit of a disappointment, but, honestly, I wasn't playing these games for the story. The puzzles were still good, even though the story holding them all together wasn't that great.
Overall, I preferred The Room and its fascinating and beautiful puzzle boxes over The Room Two, but The Room Two was still worth playing.

If you ever wondered what it'd be like to run your own tech startup, then you owe it to yourself to get this game. Do not get this game if you aren't comfortable with failing and learning.
I was a bit hesitant to purchase Software Inc. because of the early acccess bit, but after browsing the game's official forums and the steam forums I can see that the developer pays attention to and shares information with the community. For being a solo developer, that's quite impressive and I'm glad that I can support him by getting his game.
Regarding the actual gameplay, it's essentially Game Dev Tycoon on steroids with the Sims, with micromanagement and far more complex mechanics. You will fail multiple times on your first few companies until you learn how to get off the ground and stay above the red. I enjoyed the learning process because I felt it somewhat emulated real life tech startups (failing multiple times to succeed).
Once you grasp the core mechanics and gameplay loop, you'll find quite a few interesting systems to interact with. Some of these systems are as follows:
1) A stock market (you can release stocks, buy out other companies, etc.)
2) Distribution networks (change who sells your software, online/brick-n-mortar, etc.)
3) Server management (some software will require you to set up a network for server access)
4) Employees/teams (build teams, assign work to them, train/management)
5) Research
6) Development cycle (design, alpha, marketing, beta, post-release support)
7) Mods (easy to mod due to developer support, almost anyone can mod XML files)
So yeah. Get the game if you're on the fence about it. It's a fantastic simulation game even in alpha with great promise and a developer who communicates with his community.

I wholeheartedly recommend this game.
It may not be the best first-person platformer I've ever played. It isn't. But it gets pretty close. The movement mechanics are really enjoyable, and you rarely get a jump that feels badly designed. The level design is good.
My biggest praise with the game is its overall universe design. It really tries to go for its own thing instead of settling in on "fantasy cliché #81672", it invents its own outlandish alien world, and that's something that video games desperately need, as those have been really scarce since the late 80s/90s. It misses the mark on a couple occasions, but the execution is solid and I would have commended the game even for just trying.
The "production value" has lows and highs. While the landscape is flat out gorgeous, the characters definitely have something weird about them. The good kind of weird (outlandish design that's not afraid of itself), but also the bad kind of weird (model and animation quality). Although animation-wise, I do like that for dialogue, the game went for entirely hand-animated the whole way through; there is no re-use of dialogue poses, and they never stand still, not gesturing, Oblivion-style.
My biggest gripe with the game is the audio. The voice acting is alright, nothing's really bad but nothing's really good either. The sound effects lack some "punch", some clarity (I'm especially thinking of charging the glove, which sounds really weak). I thought it was really weird that the sound of wind in your ears when going through the air at high speeds was so faint. More atmospheric sounds could have REALLY enhanced the experience. And then there's the music... or lack thereof. There is almost no music, which in itself is not necessarily a bad thing, but it really feels like it should have been there. The lackluster ambient soundscapes make its absence all the more noticeable.
My first reaction to the game ending was that it was pretty short, and that I wish I'd seen one or two more locations in this magical world... but on the other hand, it's good that the game doesn't pad itself or overstays its welcome, and lasts just the right length before making all that grappling and jumping lose its charm.
This is unlikely to happen at the time of writing this review but I wouldn't mind seeing some DLC that expands on the world, maybe from the point of view of the uncle. That'd be pretty great!
If I had to assign this game a rating, I'd say 8/10. But despite its flaws you should absolutely buy and play this. NOW.

A Story About My Uncle is a narrative exploration about a man relaying an adventure he had as a child to his daughter in the form of a bedtime story. In the adventure, he put on an "adventure suit" his uncle built for him and tampered with a device his uncle left behind that warped him to...somewhere else; the game doesn't really tell you where but it's also not important, so for all intents and purposes he was taken to "another world", one that is mostly constructed of impossibly floating rocks ala Avatar's "Pandora", or for bigger nerds "Zendikar".  Since his uncle used to adventure out into the world all the time and used to send postcards back, the fact that he hasn't been heard of in several months got him thinking that maybe his uncle ended up in this unusual world, and so he sets off to try and find him.
Mechanically the game is played as a first person platformer, in which the kid in question walked into the device wearing a modified version of his uncle's adventure suit, which allows him to charge up a "superjump" and is also equipped with a grappling hook that gets upgraded very quickly to handle multiple mid-air grapples which also cause the game's difficulty to spike very quickly since it's expectations of what you can do slightly outpace your ability to get used to the awkwardness of trying to fly with a grappling hook without hitting the things you're latched onto.  The Floating Islands bit of the world design allows for the jumps to get pretty crazy and combined with the grappling hook also make a lot of the jumps fairly lengthy, but they also require you to have a pretty good understanding of momentum and how to make it work for you while in mid-air.  It's not an easy game by any stretch.
As you travel through the game you'll meet a few characters, see a few significant landmarks, and are given small quantities of backstory via strange objects left behind regarding the relationship between the uncle and his nephew.  All that being said, the actual narrative isn't especially deep nor is it anything terribly surprising; you can guess most of how things are going to play out right from the beginning, and while there are surprises they aren't the sort that make the story any better so much as make the world around it more diverse.  I may not have gotten a lot out of the story, but the world construction was very imaginative and full of vibrancy, even in the darkest of places.  And even though the story wasn't anything really special, the conversation around the story between the father relaying the story and the daughter listening and interjecting made the experience feel quite genuine.
Would I recommend it?  Yeah, but not desparately.  It's a neat game with some great scenery in a cool location, a story that isn't bad but maybe a little simple, and the game ends before it has a chance to get too stale, but getting there will probably require a fair chunk of trial and error.  If it's on sale, definitely get it.  Otherwise you have to ask yourself if this is your sort of game: If you like difficult platformers and beautiful scenery from what feels like a very small team of developers, you'll probably enjoy this.

HELLDIVERS is a fantastic coop game that is filled to the brim with challanging PvE scenarios that require real teamwork to overcome. But that does not mean the game is without faults, or that it is a game for everyone.
Couple areas of concern... "Consolization" or whatever people call it nowadays, really hurts this game. incase you were not aware this game was only on PS4/PSP/PS3 of quite some time, and like many other titles have done in the past, when the game is ported to PC or other platforms its missing things that are more or less requred for PC gaming (i.e. graphics settings). Queing into games is affected as well. All players must load a map before each mission starts. On the PC these screens have loaded for 5-10mins when connected to a full team of 4 people with PCs of varying speeds!! This is simply an issue that does not exsit when playing on Playstation.
By the way this game is not easy. There is progression in the game as far as equipment and skills to unlock but a higher level will not make you more powerful or resilant out right. The real thing you need to succeed is good old teamwork and cooperation: LOTS OF IT. Friendly fire is most definitely ON at all times and really shapes the way the game is played. This leads to countless occasions when HELLDIVERS teeters on the line between difficulty and frustration.
Would you like to know more??
HELLDIVERS is awesome when it works they way its intended to. Oozing with Starship Trooper themed action and humor; Its never felt more satisfying to hear patriotic music over guns blazing while spreading Managed Democracy In the name of Super Earth. The entire HELLDIVERS community works to beat the game together with every completed or failed mission affecting the war effort against threats to mankind.
Im doing my part... Are you??:TR:

Alright, So this will be the first review i've written for a singleplayer game that i've completed completely. As you can see I got over 20 hours into this. You might take a lot longer to complete it. I rushed to the end because I was engaged.
Let's break it down in a couple categories:
Graphics:
I've never played a Saints row game before but from what I can tell it's the same as Saints row III with the same engine. At least this is what i've been told. The game looks nice and the light effects are well done. Game isn't realistic looking and people should understand that before buying the game. This game isn't about spectacular graphics. But overall it does the job well and fits the theme, 7/10
Story:
The story is a fckin mess. A good mess though. The main antagonist is extremely fun and hateable, wich is what you want from a antagonist. The dialogue is spot on with cheeky references. Lots of fun little minigames like a 2d side scroller and overall the flow is extremely well done. The game doesnt drag on and there is a good pacing in there. Voice acting is I think with just the same actors as the previous games. In other words it's good. It works. I'd say a 9/10
Gameplay:
Now you've probably seen that you are superpowered, wich means you can run like Sonic and jump buildings etc. This leads to a overall extremely fun gameplay experience when traveling towards objectives. You still got your old saints row mechanics but these are basically obsolete due to you being so damn powerful by yourself. So calling your homies or driving cars with EXTENSIVE customization. Wich you should really check out it has a crap ton of options.
But the game does lose points for the overall lack of real challenges. I think I died twice in the entire game? And that is me just dicking around half of the time. Overall a fun experience 8/10
Audio/Music:
The game has a good game score, the radio stations have fun tracks but are a bit limited, and you'll quickly hear the same tracks over and over. The sound assets are pretty solid with alien rifles sounding like well.. alien rifles. The game does have licensed music wich makes it a bit hard to record or stream but for the most of us it wont affect us. 8/10
TLDR:
This is a weird take for the franchise, and with the devs saying this is the last we'll get for a while. Is it worth your purchase?
YES. The game doesnt cost anything, even the GOTC edition is cheap. You can get a lot of fun in the game with a bunch of activites to do. I might jump back into it and get some more of that good ol' open world mayhem. Because that's what this game is. Just you blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up and wrecking havoc. And I love it.
Game has a good Boss fight at the end as well by the way. And i felt actually accomplished when I beat the game. But needless to say. it does have the ubisoft open world syndrome (even though it isnt created by them). Wich means a lot of activities are not that interesting and are more there for just filler.
Overall score a 8.5/10

Overview:
The game is good, not much more not much less. This thing is straight up pumping with the blood of america at parts and its quite halarious to play. There are many satires on games including COD, Metal Gear, Streets of Rage, and even Space Partinoids. However, The game relies on its comedic value and out there ideas to keep it afloat really. The story is poor, the game while polished has some horribly annoying quirks to it that show up once in a blue moon, and the game time is padded by side quests.
If you get this game on sale then its absolutly worth it. However

A flawed masterpiece.
The game has its problems, that's undeniable.  It seems the development team ended up being punished by time constraints and ended up sorely neglecting the last quarter of the game; neglecting the truly excellent role-playing elements for more and more uninspired combat.  Fortunately, thanks to numerous community patches, the rest of the game has aged pretty well.
If you overlook the minor annoyance that combat represents, and the fact that the end of the game feels too brief and rushed, even with the significant amount of "lost content" added to it by the aforementioned  patches, then you're in for a real treat.
The atmosphere is outstanding; the game does an excellent job of creating an almost film-noir bleakness that typifies the World of Darkness setting.  At least two relatively early missions ratchet up the creepy into moments of true horror, and there is a constant air of menace that you'd expect from a game where you build a custom vampire and embark on the life of a creature-of-the-night.
The roleplaying elements are truly first-rate.  Some of the best I have ever seen, with characters that are unique, memorable, and fully formed.  The degree with which you can interact them is solid, and just a whisker shy of being superlative.
The skill-sets you can pick from strike a great balance between utility (being able to hack computer terminals for info, or lock-pick), social (seduction, intmidation), and combat.
The stealth system is solid, but not amazing – the obfuscate ability makes it pretty redundant for a couple of "clans" (classes) but stealth-kills are an effective tool in most situations.
The plot is gripping, although as I mentioned above the conclusion feels a little rushed; as if they ran out of time in the third act and just cut-to-the-chase.  The numerous side-quests are insinuated into the game subtlely, and in a way that makes completing them fun, rather than just busy-work you have to go through to get 100% completion or some extra XP and loot.
This game is truly a diamond in the rough.

Still, it provides a tight, well written RPG with many amusing elements

This game is a playable mystery movie. It is not about action, it is about watching the plot unfold as you solve puzzles. Your character has very limited abilities in the "movie" - you can walk/run, view things, interact with things, and crouch. Everything is in first-person view. There is no real "action" - you won't be shooting at things, or ducking, or anything like that. You will be moving from puzzle to puzzle in order to advance the plot.
Graphics are very pretty (Unreal engine), and when everything is turned up to max it can cause even a beefy system to jitter every now and then. Sound consists or eerie music and environmental sounds, all of which are good.
I find it hard to say if the game is good or bad... The very first words you see upon running the game tell you flat out that the game does not hold your hand. Simple puzzles are just that, but more advanced puzzles are not self-evident. If you like puzzle games, you will probably like this game. If you like playable movie games, you may like this game.
I like puzzle games (e.g., Portal, Portal 2, Limbo, etc.). I don't have much experience with playable movies, although the PlayStation Drake's series feel that way. This game just hasn't drawn me in.
One annoying feature of the game is savegames. The game only does saves at certain checkpoints, and those checkpoints, from what I can tell, are at the beginning of each puzzle. Some puzzles take a while to complete, so if you do 80% and then need to close the game, when you load the game up you lose all your progress. I really hate that.
As a result of all this, I won't give the game a global recommendation. If you like puzzle games and playable movie games, you may like this game. I would keep a walkthrough handy if I were you...
Rating: 3/5

Plot (don't worry no spoilers)
From what I can say. This was an abundance of emotions mixed in with WTF just happened! I really like the story and the background to WHAT actually happened before this nuke, who the characters were, what you were before this, and what you are fighting now. It seems that artyom has a gift from the dark ones that touched him in a certain yet unforgiving way. I could somewhat handle the graphics on medium-high but not that well; still overall nice graphics!
From what I could tell it wasn't a fast paced game, just short.
Surviving:
I really liked this aspect of the games. Usually in games like Call of Duty you would just Run & Gun but in this one you would have to take it slow in order to not die. There is an option for the run & gun option but I recommend NOT to take it as it takes away the main core aspect of surviving and feeling "immersed" in the game. Bullets are rare and you trade with fire rounds so you should be careful and save up.
Fighting system:
Fighting was great, I loved how you got blood on your mask if you shot near the enemy and you could just wipe it to the side, brings out the "I feel like I can do anything in this game" option. You can go stealth or all out in some areas, mainly all out guns but with stealth its a bit harder since they have dangling cans you have to avoid.
Overall: recommended on sale price because of short story

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic Banana-Bread recipe you've come to the right place.
Tips
No need for a mixer for this recipe! Clean-up is easy too, if you want,
you can mix everything in one bowl.
The best bananas to use for banana bread are those that are over-ripe. The yellow peels should be at least half browned, and the bananas inside squishy and browning.
Ingredients
- 2 to 3 very ripe bananas, peeled
- 1/3 cup melted butter
- 1 teaspoon baking soda
- Pinch of salt
- 3/4 cup sugar (1/2 cup if you would like it less sweet, 1 cup if more sweet)
- 1 large egg, beaten
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract
- 1 1/2 cups of all-purpose flour
Method
1. Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C), and butter a 4x8-inch loaf pan.
2. In a mixing bowl, mash the ripe bananas with a fork until completely smooth. Stir the melted butter into the mashed bananas.
3. Mix in the baking soda and salt. Stir in the sugar, beaten egg, and vanilla extract. Mix in the flour.
4. Pour the batter into your prepared loaf pan. Bake for 50 minutes to 1 hour at 350°F (175°C), or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean.
5. Remove from oven and cool completely on a rack. Remove the banana bread from the pan. Slice and serve. (A bread knife helps to make slices that aren't crumbly.)

Simply one of the best post-apocalyptic shooters I've ever played. If you like Fallout or S.T.A.L.K.E.R. you're sure to love this.
Amazing atmosphere, great gameplay, and fun gunfights. There's also a possibility of doing some "missions" stealth, if you like that. For a real challenge, play on survival and Ranger Hardcore. Played through the game that way and it was maybe some of the most challenging gameplay I've ever experienced at times, but when i finished the game it was amazing. Pretty sure I got the "bad" ending tho.
The only negative thing about the game is the karma system. There is no introduction to it in the game, so I never knew that beeing good was rewarding. Basically it works like this: If your good to people and avoid killing humans (even enemies) you get good karma points. If you do bad stuff you get bad karma points. The points determine wether or not you can get the "good" ending or not. I'm pretty sure I had no karmapoints what so ever, so I never got the option to go for the good ending.
I'll give it a solid 9/10. The karma system is the only negative thing in my eyes, but it's not gamebreaking at all. just be aware of it if you wish to get the good ending.

When I first saw this game, I was insanely curious and I just looked at the ratings, which were positive to 92 % and I thought, I'd just give it a try without further looking at any ratings etc.
Well, I finished the game within my first session playing it and here instantly comes the great, great downside: It's only 2 hours long, even if you play it for the first time and are a good player that can go through it without bigger problems. 2 hours. Well, additionally to that, there were some noticeable bugs and the "People" you meet (pretty early in the game) are... well... ugly as hell. The graphic of the surrounding areas etc. is amazing (Especially because of the great level/world-design), it's just the character models (and animations). But well, why do I rate this game as good? It's pretty buggy and "unfinished" and only pretty, you could say.
Well, first of all, this game offers amazing gameplay and an unique experience. It truly offers a journey, a journey in a new world, where you have to search your uncle. The story is good (but pretty predictable), the setting is very good, and the few dialogues that exist are at least believable. Except the last one, but adding information here would be a spoiler for the already short story.
Plus: This game offers options for speedrunning (Tracking your time and a level choice after beating it). Still, to be honest, this game is not worth 13 € in my opinion. Get this game when the price is reduced, or if you are into amazing experiences, or if you are a really ambitious type of human being.
All in all, I'd recommend anyone who could think he likes it, to get it, when it's price is reduced by 50% or more. This is an amazing game, but too short.

Episode One is a solid follow-up to the main Half-Life 2 game. The gameplay and graphics remain unchanged, and there is nothing wrong with that. The game picks up right after the explosion that ended the main game. The main goal of this "add-on" game is to escape City 17.
The first part of the game is enjoyable, particularly the portion with the modified gravity gun. There are few things as satisfying as yanking enemies from afar and throwing their ragdolled-bodies around. However, that part of the game is short-lived and ends after you complete a couple of puzzles.
The rest of the game feels like a brief glimpse into a "horror masterpiece." I often found myself running out of items to throw with my gravity gun. There were a lot of instances in which I had to crawl through air vents, stumble through the dark, and hide while Alyx shot at and killed many enemies. Despite these commonalities, this game kept me engaged with its solid pacing from start to finish.
The story is simplistic, and the achievements will add a little replay value to this game. I was able to complete every achievement on the first playthrough... so you can accomplish this feat too. For me, the citizen escort portion was the hardest portion of the game. At least, it was the hardest part until I realized that I could use the rocket launcher to kill everyone and everything. When I find time, I will probably go back and beat the game with guns-a-blazing. I'm sure the game will play differently if I do.
In the end, this "add-on" game can be completed in under five hours. It is a solid addition to the Half-Life lore, and the game does not strive to be too ambitious. Simply put, you should play Episode One shortly, if not immediately after you beat the Half-Life 2 main game.

Aesthetically superb and intellectually challenging, The Room Two follows in the steps of equally gorgeous riddlefest The Room, this time with a hint of a story.
We still get to assemble and use the famous eyepiece in order to access any not immediately visible parts of a riddle, but now there is at least one additional helpful component to it. The puzzles are more or less in the same vein, albeit slightly more complicated - not necessarily in their level of difficulty itself, but in that we are not confined to one single part of a "room". Instead, we are given full freedom to move within our surroundings (even pilot a boat!) and explore them in their entirety, as meticulously as we can.
Another (already mentioned) novelty in this new installment of The Room is a suspenseful as well as melancholy tale threading itself through the stages of the game. The basis of a similar element was already present in the original Room, but here it is much more (and better) fleshed out, keeping our interest alive until the last second of the gameplay.
Just one quibble - in a few of the puzzles, while what has to be done is pretty much obvious or logically deduced, the fact that the "camera" has to be positioned at a very specific angle for the hotspots to be activated, can sometimes be a pain (I got almost hopelessly stuck on a couple of instances). Besides that, The Room Two is a feast for the eyes and ears and a treat for the brain. Definitely recommended.

TL;DR A solid topdown twin-stick shooter where you deliver democracy, freedom and liber-tea by shooting everything, even your teammates. Controller recommended
~A game where you and 3 other people over internet or hotseat are sent out on liberating planets and conquering sectors by shooting, exploding, capturing, defending and delivering enemies and objectives alike.~
Lore shortly: 2084, man sets out on a space journey, finds 3 diffirent alien races; Highly technolygigly advanced Illuminate, Swarming Bugs and Super Earth Terrorists Cyborgs. Man tried to come in peace but aliens were not happy about humans entering their hood so they declared war. A massive 3v1.
Controlls are really simple and easy to learn. Left stick moves, right stick aims, one button shoots, other button reloads, prone button, weapon switch button, melee button, stratagem button, nade button and a sprint button. I've tried few matches on KB-Mouse, a bit more challenging but having a sight(while aiming a simple sight appears), WASD-movement, shift... You know the usual.
You start out with few starting items on vanilla. Assault rifle, pistol, some nades and 4-stratagem slots. As you level up your character you unlock more and more content such as; weapons, cosmetic armours, perks and stratagems. Many options... You can be a fire support medic, Mobile AT-man and my favourite; Engineer with an LMG. Vanilla version of the game has a handfull of base content but is recommended to buy the complete edition because of how much content it adds. It may sound like a bad decision but trust me get the complete edition if you can.
The galactic map. Shows you the progress of the current war. Each enemy faction has their sectors and inside them are 12 to 14 planets with difficulty parameters. Each planet adds Influence to that sector which enemy has the sector to themselves. Expample; A difficulty 9 planet, "Hard as H3ll." with 3 missions that have about 5-6 objectives, adds 9 community influence on that sector when it is completed but also there is a catch... Complete the planet with all players aboarding the extraction shuttle, all objectives completed(No failed objectives) and low death counts on players. Adds a multiplier to that 9. Completed with all players extracted adds 9 to the counter, completed with players extracted, all objectives and low deaths makes 3x9=27. 27 community influence from that planet added to the sector conquer meter.
As far as the gameplay goes, it's sometimes very fast paced, hectic and adrenaline inducing. Sometimes very slow paced, not much happens and there are very little enemies but that's war... As a twin-stick this game has screen sharing. Yes, you share the same absolute screen with other players... Even online. What this means that with complete strangers it's very difficult to say where the want to go or do. It might get irritating but i've already been okay with it ever since I started playing. On a subject of players... They can be nice, cooperative and helpful. And there's people who don't know what the F they are doing or seeing, complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, trolls or griefers... So very mixed player base.
Aahh... The sountrack. Orchestral master piece. Absolutely epic. The great feeling of achieving something. Fits this game nicely.
Closing words. Stunningly well desinged and produced game from the makers of Magicka. Love the scifi-setting, the great feeling of patronizing, bad@ssery and neat stratagem system. Solid gameplay with online or hotseat.
I give it 8/10. Has few connection issues but very minor.

122 hours in this game and what can I say? It's awesome. Some people will rag on the map. It's the same as SRIII. I get it. Really, I do. I guess it helps that I didn't play the third game and went in with no expectations of newness or greatness. Still, knowing that they doubled down on the setting doesn't bother me at all. It's great. The story and characters are superb. You actually really enjoy getting to know the backstories of your crew. There are little sound bites tossed in around Steelport which flesh them all out and make them feel like real people.
The gameplay is okay. The physics are only so-so. But SRIV isn't a simulation sandbox, it is through and through an arcade game. Don't expect any GTA IV-level interactions. Cars don't really weave or slide around, they just drive. Some are faster than others. The styling/vehicle/character creator... Okay. Rockstar, are you listening? USE THIS MODEL. It's 10x better than GTA in that regard.
Combat is good. It has a real flowy feel. Occasionally an input error would leave me stumbling, but for the most part that was my fault. I never had to fight the camera. Never found enemies stuck behind an obstacle or knee deep in concrete. And there's no other way to say this--it's basically a superhero simulator.
Graphics are serviceable. There's a weird pixel effect that cuts in pretty often. You can disable it with a mod. If it bothers you, do that. Everything else is pretty good for a 2013 game standard. Pretty much what you would expect for a AAA title.
Sound and audio. This game has one of THE BEST soundtracks I have ever heard. There's music in here that will have you singing along as your character tears up the streets in a hover tank, or glides through the air toward another objective. I would say 70-90% of the music in this game has found its way into my personal collection. The sound effects are alright. Though the things the people say on the street are pretty repetitive and dumb.
Overall, I would definitely recommend SRIV at a sale price of 29.99 or less. It's a steal at 19.99. Get the DLC bundle with the Christmas expansion and the Dominatrix. Both are worth the asking price.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a First Person Adventure Game where you play as a detective trying to resolve the case of Ethan Carter. To do so, you end up in a forest, trying to search for clues to retrieve the little boy.
First of all, the first thing that you will see when playing Ethan Carter is that the game is beautiful. A lot of work was done on the vegetation of the forest (as well as the buildings, the water, everything !) just to make it look as realist as possible. And it worked ! I found myself starring at some landscapes for minutes just because it looked so real.
Since you're a detective, you'll have to find clues and interact with some of them to be able to reconstruct the crime scenes. After you found every clue, you now have the ability to revisit the crime. To do that, there are 4 or 5 visuals and you'll have to define the chronology of the events. This aspect of the game is pretty easy and it's well done. The story is really interesting and you'll want to know what happened in this strange forest and why Ethan went missing.
"This game won't take you by the end".  In Ethan Carter, you're free to go wherever you go when you want. It's possible to miss some puzzles the first time and you'll have to come back later to do it (not sure if you have to do EVERY puzzle in the game to see the endgame). The puzzles are fairly easy. The only difficult part in my opinion would be finding a specific object when you have no clue about it's location. You know it's near but it could be everywhere on the ground.
I would definitely recommend Ethan Carter to everyone who wants to play a good adventure game which isn't too hard to get into. The game is relatively short (between 3-5 hours) and doesn't have much replayability but these are intense hours that were totally worth it !

Ethan Carter is not a very long game, but it is a very beautiful game - with a focus on narrative and exploration, on telling a story that you uncover in scraps and fragments before everything is explained.
In a lot of ways, at least as far as actual gameplay is concerned, it's something along the lines of Gone Home but with a heavier focus on puzzles. Not hard puzzles but puzzles that rely on simple problem solving, intuition, and at worst that can be worked through on trial and error: they may slow you down if you can't figure them out but it's always possible to just try until you finish so you can see the story through.
The only complaint I really have is about the lack of a clear and intuitive save system, it relies on autosaves and in some areas they feel pretty rare and leave you feeling like you have to finish another puzzle before it's safe to exit for the night.
im all for a cryptic game, but this went way too far in that direction.

I had about £3 in my Steam Wallet, and a few more £'s in my bank account. I was bored so I started browsing the store looking and hoping to stumble into a gem of a game.
Normally that doesn't happen, normally I stumble into another early access money-grab. But not this time, not at all.
I've been constantly surprised with the depth of this game, and what it has to offer. It's a fantastic simulation that will reward you greatly for paying attention to the information that it provides you regarding other companies and what people are using, software wise.
There's no dispute that the simulation is at the forefront in the game 90% of the time, but the workplace building is extremely easy, and intuitive to use. You can make some really nice stuff - especially if you check out the workshop beforehand for some of the mods that add additional decoration props.
The game tells you to build a place for your start-up company, and recommends taking some contract work to get a bit of quick money. This teaches you the ropes of how to manage your employees while they're working. Then it'll ask you to start hiring some staff, and to do this you have to pay for and manage an interview process, which allows you to choose a good fit for your company. Then it'll ask you to build some software, and oh boy, does the game open up here. You have to consider a bunch of things, like what competition will be releasing soon, how long it will take you to finish the software, how big your audience will be which is defined by what operating systems you choose to build the software for.. and I could go on. It's so in depth and if you love that kind of thing then this game is definitely for you.
Make sure you follow the tutorials at least once, as they'll teach you some vital stuff, it's so worth it when you get that first overnight million in the bank and it feels like you earned it because you were managing everything to earn it.
Another thing to note is the dev seems really active with the community, and is also building the game out with more features at quite a fast pace, which is fantastic and refreshing to see in the early access scene.

The gameplay of this game is not very exciting or impressive frankly, but the atmosphere that the game gives off with its beautiful backdrops and immersive music builds the intensity of the game nonetheless. TL;DR A solid topdown twin-stick shooter where you deliver democracy, freedom and liber-tea by shooting everything, even your teammates. Controller recommended
~A game where you and 3 other people over internet or hotseat are sent out on liberating planets and conquering sectors by shooting, exploding, capturing, defending and delivering enemies and objectives alike.~
Lore shortly: 2084, man sets out on a space journey, finds 3 diffirent alien races; Highly technolygigly advanced Illuminate, Swarming Bugs and Super Earth Terrorists Cyborgs. Man tried to come in peace but aliens were not happy about humans entering their hood so they declared war. A massive 3v1.
Controlls are really simple and easy to learn. Left stick moves, right stick aims, one button shoots, other button reloads, prone button, weapon switch button, melee button, stratagem button, nade button and a sprint button. I've tried few matches on KB-Mouse, a bit more challenging but having a sight(while aiming a simple sight appears), WASD-movement, shift... You know the usual.
You start out with few starting items on vanilla. Assault rifle, pistol, some nades and 4-stratagem slots. As you level up your character you unlock more and more content such as; weapons, cosmetic armours, perks and stratagems. Many options... You can be a fire support medic, Mobile AT-man and my favourite; Engineer with an LMG. Vanilla version of the game has a handfull of base content but is recommended to buy the complete edition because of how much content it adds. It may sound like a bad decision but trust me get the complete edition if you can.
The galactic map. Shows you the progress of the current war. Each enemy faction has their sectors and inside them are 12 to 14 planets with difficulty parameters. Each planet adds Influence to that sector which enemy has the sector to themselves. Expample; A difficulty 9 planet, "Hard as H3ll." with 3 missions that have about 5-6 objectives, adds 9 community influence on that sector when it is completed but also there is a catch... Complete the planet with all players aboarding the extraction shuttle, all objectives completed(No failed objectives) and low death counts on players. Adds a multiplier to that 9. Completed with all players extracted adds 9 to the counter, completed with players extracted, all objectives and low deaths makes 3x9=27. 27 community influence from that planet added to the sector conquer meter.
As far as the gameplay goes, it's sometimes very fast paced, hectic and adrenaline inducing. Sometimes very slow paced, not much happens and there are very little enemies but that's war... As a twin-stick this game has screen sharing. Yes, you share the same absolute screen with other players... Even online. What this means that with complete strangers it's very difficult to say where the want to go or do. It might get irritating but i've already been okay with it ever since I started playing. On a subject of players... They can be nice, cooperative and helpful. And there's people who don't know what the F they are doing or seeing, complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, trolls or griefers... So very mixed player base.
Aahh... The sountrack. Orchestral master piece. Absolutely epic. The great feeling of achieving something. Fits this game nicely.
Closing words. Stunningly well desinged and produced game from the makers of Magicka. Love the scifi-setting, the great feeling of patronizing, bad@ssery and neat stratagem system. Solid gameplay with online or hotseat.
I give it 8/10. Has few connection issues but very minor.

Amazing co-op shooter with high difficulty ranges that force you to employ and upgrade stratagems and group tactics to complete mission objectives. The game claims that it can easily offer up to 100 hour gameplay experience and while I would like to challenge that claim, I will not deny it entirely.
The reason its claim is questionable is because of the large potential in play styles and wether you want to play solo or not, which may prove to be challenging on high difficulty either way. This just goes to show how flexible the game could be and yet how refreshing it is when you employ random players which may prove to be more chaotic and difficult than playing solo.
And if there's a section where the game suffers, it's in the content department which DESPERATELY requires the attention of the developers.
This could be easily remedied by creating a player studio/modding kit to allow players to submit their own content which is to be implemented in-game. A not-very-demanding measure, imho, considering the potential Helldivers has if supplied with adequate content. But as it is, the game is a unique gem in the rough and it requires further polishing before it can even be consider a gold mine.

This is one of the best multiplayer games I've played.
The game's harder difficulties really encourage team work, a basic understanding of the game's wide variety of weapon / gear options, and awareness of how the other players are equipped and what they're doing.  Yet, somehow, it does all this without being overwhelming or intimidating.  I learned enough to stop being a team-killing rookie within the first few hours of play.
Another thing that anyone looking to buy this should know is this: even though single player is an option, it isn't really feasible beyond the easiest missions.  Because enemies can attack from anywhere, and because characters cannot turn around instantly, 3- or 4- person teams are required to effectively cover multiple angles.  This isn't like MAGICKA, another game developed by Arrowhead Game Studios.  I was able to solo much of MAGICKA.  But in HELLDIVERS, I got killed within a minute of trying a medium-difficulty mission.
Thus far, I've had minimal experience with jerk randoms.  A majority of random players I've encountered have been helpful and skilled.  The downside of this game's multiplayer is, like any multiplayer, you're at the mercy of public game availability.  During peak hours, finding a game is easy.  But if you're like me and your friends don't play this game, and you have a hankering to play at 3am or something, you're out of luck because there won't be any public games up.
Overall, I'm happy with this purchase, and I can see myself playing this game for a long while.

I dont think I have ever played another game like this. It took me a few hundred hours to really undestand the mechanics and then another five or six hundred hours to master them. The replay value is nigh endless, every new map is YOUR story. The AI is pretty good- even though it is fairly easy to hold off a powerful army with some micro'ing and composite bowman, I found the variety of fair-weather friends, traitors, competitors, (and even a couple allies,) to be a lot of fun.
How you approach the tech tree, and game, is largely dependant on your own style of play. Want to be diplomatic? In many ways it is easier to play a peaceful game than a militaristic one, which is super rare for any marco-managment strategy game. There is just so much potential in each game, and sometimes it is fun to simply reload to an earlier point and then see, like a divergent fork in the cosmic narative, that new save becomes a parallel reality. What if the Zulus hadnt betrayed Morocco, and you were able to form your religion and spread it to the corners of the world? In one you ended up a military autocrat battling enemies on all sides while desperatly keeping a cap on unrest and rebellion on the home front. In the other, you became a religous country preaching peace and diplomacy... using culture and religion to dominate the world.
This game was easily one of the best I have ever played. Ever. The variety of strategies and possibilities is really quite amazing. I give this game four and a half golden Shoggoths. And a silver Nightgaunt.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a detective-like game in which you use your paranormal abilities to solve succesive crimes in order to find Ethan Carter.
Being a fan of crime novels, H.P. Lovecraft, paranormal fiction, puzzles and detective stuff, I just can't stop drooling after finishing this game. Its open world has awing extremely realistic graphics, perfect sounds and an amazing sountrack which adapts to every place you walk in making you feel the exact way it wants.
The game difficulty is good for a avarage gamer and a bit challenging for a beginner. It has just enough guides to "follow" a path, which I thank a LOT since I really hate getting lost. (You have a general guide, although enough freedom to roam since it's an "open" world. Usually huge stones, lakes, trees and slopes define the limits of the terrain.) Still, I kept my game guide handy until I got the hang of it because at first it's confusing and in fact,  I realized I missed so much with the guide that I started all over again.
The amazing developers have some really crazy ideas which keeps the story interesting and just makes you ask yourself.. What the hell is next? The psychic powers are a reaaally nice add on to an incredible detective story. **spoiler alert** It also has a really unexpected, amazing yet hearthbreaking ending I can't get over yet.**
The playthrough is quite short. It took me 6 hours to complete, but the game is so absorbing I felt like it was a whole lot more.
The only detail I would highly criticize is the lack of player-saving option. You have to find and finish the next "scene" so you can save the game which is kind of frustrating if you have to go and therefore lose everything since the last auto save. I-1 for that.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is gripping, with fascinating graphics, perfect ambience, intriguing storytelling and a tragic storyline. If you like good detective stories, mystery and paranormal stories, this is for you.

Background: I'm a casual fan of Worms game, love everything about it.  I've played golf maybe 10 times or so in real life.  I picked up the game on a humble bundle.
This is one sweet game.  You have 4 18 hole courses to play in a 2d platform style.  You choose your club from a driver, iron, wedge or putter, each behave differently and choose your angle and how much power to swing it.
You have a few different objectives, you need at least a Par to progress, although later with powerups its common to get hole in ones.  You will need a great mix of strategy, powerups, planning, and luck to get it right.
There are 20 coins per level you can collect, these help you to buy other clubs, hats, balls, voices etc.  There is one crate on each level which is needed to help unlock items.  There is also a requirement to get a certain number of points, however this becomes the easiest/lamest to achieve.  If you get a hole in one, you get this straight away.  However in earlier levels I just aimed straight up and hit the ball out of the map repeatedly/or into the sea and got my skill score.
Getting all of these challenges on the normal levels will take some planning, but nothing is impossible.  Sometimes you need to wait till you unlock an ability later.
There are some seperate challenge maps, eg the "chip in" challenge.  If you get the ball on the green you get extra time in your countdown.  If you get it in the hole you get more time.  The "keep up" challenges are quite fun, you get only one shot and have to use land mines and other objects on the map to keep the ball moving as many times as possible, you can only choose one powerup to use until it runs out.
Most of the achievements in this game will pop normally just playing the game.
The best thing about this game, it was always fun, even when I was just smashing the ball straight up in the air.   A great casual game if you have 5 minutes or 2 hours.

Helldivers has a great soundtrack, it has fun mechanics and it has good art direction. The weapons are almost universally fun to use, the mechs and tanks really give you a kickass feel, and there are few equipment options that are downright bad.
So why am I not recommending this game?
The camera. The goddamn camera. It was designed for a hot-seat/friends-in-front-of-TV multiplayer situation, meaning that it just settles in the rough center of the group of characters. This keeps everyone together, which is good, however, the view area is painfully tiny, which is bad, and it is consistently the least fun mechanic, because the view area is so TINY that big enemies can barely fit in it alongside the player characters. When you die, it'll rarely be because you got outflanked or screwed up, it'll be because you got sniped by an enemy literally outside of the field of view or because you ran afoul of the view area and got trapped in a niche somewhere while enemies dogpiled you.
The camera works fine for singleplayer, but the game ramps difficulty too high for most people to play singleplayer beyond the very earliest and easiest stuff. If there's a patch saying they've improved the camera by the time you read this review, ignore it, get the game, you'll have fun. If there's not, heed the warning and don't buy it.

After the success of HL2, Valve made the design decision to release its sequels as episodic titles. This allowed them to capitalise more efficiently on rapidly improving graphical technology and dispense their content a lot faster. Released in 2006, Episode 1 is the direct continuation of HL2 which charts Gordon and Alyx’s treacherous escape from City 17. Technically, it attempts to improve and advance every aspect that its predecessor established.
The gameplay of Episode 1 is based almost entirely around the concept of you working in partnership with your AI companion, Alyx. This mainly involves Alyx following your lead and helping you during combat, but there are also several innovative sections which reinforce the idea of teamwork. These include a dimly lit area where you need to use your flashlight to illuminate enemies for Alyx to shoot; and a section where you need to clear Alyx’s line of sight while she supports you from afar with a sniper rifle.
She has been programmed to act as a support role, remaining reticent during puzzle sections and hanging back during ‘boss’ encounters. This feels like a well-balanced design choice as it allows the player the freedom to advance at their own pace and feel more of a sense of accomplishment at overcoming challenges.
The AI has seen significant improvements, especially in path finding abilities. Alyx in particular has had a substantial upgrade, giving her new animations for crouching and synchronised kill moves for a lot of enemy types. Enemy AI has also seen developments as Combine soldiers can now crouch and take cover more effectively. They have also been given a rope repelling animation which always looks visually engaging. The only new enemy type introduced is the Combine zombie, or ‘zombine’. They are an entertaining addition that adds a new threat to the undead portions of the game.
The puzzle sections are still relatively easy and should not take anyone too long to solve. Despite this, they are slightly more diverse than the simple physics based puzzles of the original game and still serve as an effective diversion from the combat scenes.
Graphically, Episode 1 has seen some major upgrades. Valve has adapted their Source engine to include new developments in HDR (High Dynamic Range) lighting, which was originally showcased in their Lost Coast tech demo. This really helps to elevate the presentation to a high standard; for example the shader effects used around the Citadel core still manage to impress me today. There have also been further advancements in facial expression modelling which helps bring some more personality to the main characters.
Overall, Episode 1 is a solid entry into the HL2 series. The main criticism that can be presented is its length; it is only five chapters long and can be comfortably completed in less than 10 hours. However, it is worth mentioning that there is also a developer commentary mode which provides some insightful observations if you are at all interested in the design process, or if you simply want to get a little more replay value.
Personally I feel that Episode 1 provides the least story enhancement of the series, which can make it feel more inconsequential. However, from a technical stand point it does improve on almost every aspect in terms of gameplay and graphical experience, and is a well-polished presentation that serves as a good stepping stone into Episode 2.

Compared to other popular gangbang themes, Saints Row is definitely not for everyone. Contrary to the “real world” like San Andreas or Los Santos where you rob a bank, steal a car, hang out with your friends, Saints Row 4 offers a world of super-man powers where practically everyplace you see can be visited or explored using your super power. Indeed, as the leader of the Saints, this time you enter in a simulated world, where your only goal is to fight your way through it and face the overlord Zinyak, an alien boss who invaded the earth.
+++: The storytelling inherits its preceding approach of absurdity. And this lore of absurdity can be reflected in the gameplay on almost every single way:
1.	You can create your character as ridiculously as possible. Funnier your character looks, more fun can be obtained by provoking with people with your designated taunting gesture. The creation of character will be actually more lore-friendly as you make your characters anti-traditional, which is not the case in a lot of RPG games that have character creation option.
2.	You will be able to level up and upgrade your ability, feeling the progress you make as you explore the world and complete missions. This feature is not had in a lot of open-world action gangbang games, even if the world is dynamically created to explore. But overtime as you cannot feel the progress you made during the gameplay, the story mode becomes boring to play.
3.	You will be able to use magic. Freezing people, stomping the ground, telekinesis… All of those abilities that seem unrelated to the real-world gangbang can be realized in this awesome simulated world of Saints Row.
4.	You will be able to play nudely.
5.	You will be able to fly like Batman and climb like Spiderman.
6.	You will be able to romance hilariously with your companions. Each companion has a loyalty mission with great story. Even if you haven’t played the previous titles, those companion missions will connect you better with you gang, really making you feel that you are a part of the Saints Row.
7.	Even though setting in an unrealistic world where you own superpower, the old-school Saints Row missions like Mayhem and racing is still retained and improved to allow you to have much more fun.
---: While playing this game, I do suffer from the anxiety of repetitive gameplay and the robotic simulated world with no dynamic interactions with NPCs. While I do understand that some of those features are intentioned (since it is only a simulated world), I do hope that the future Saints Row titles will hold more gameplay mechanics such as the GTA series, and much more interesting side stories that keeps the player interested.
I began to play this game after finishing Fallout 4, and I would say this is much more of an interesting game. Saints Row 4 has some really nice and innovative ideas of making a gangbang game. And what’s more precious is that the developers put those ideas into use, transforming them into some really awesome action-packed gameplay experiences. I am still 40% to finish this game when I wrote this review, and I feel that my journey has just started.

No matter what anyone says, this game is epic!  You start off in typical Saint's Row fashion by running around the streets, getting money and weapons and avoiding trouble until you're geared up... and then it takes you to a whole new level by giving you superpowers and setting you off on an unforgettable journey of revenge and humor.  It revives key moments of the franchise's history when you go to rescue your people, through dialogue, and through audio logs that you discover throughout the game as you unlock more content.  The vehicle selection is only a little limited, but the customization is pretty fun.  The alien tech you acquire can become potent gear with enough time invested into upgrades.  The character customization is top notch, from the actual appearance which you can change at any point in the game, to the clothing and outfits which you can change at any point in the game.
This game is truly an open-world sandbox experience that lets you do whatever you want short of plowing through buildings.  But you can jump those buildings in a single bound, so no worries there!  This game gets a rare 10 out of 10 from me, because I'm not going to count off for the occasional game crash.  Things just happen and that's okay.  This was originally intended for a console and the PC port has done very well.  I don't expect the transition to be perfect.
Yup.  10 out of 10.  Go play it if you're not a square.

What a wonderful surprise this game was for me, I didn't know anything about it when I bought it. A fair bit of warning, the game has a lot of violence and nudity. That said, it made me chuckle quite a bit with it's crude comedy. In fact, this is one of the most entertaining games I've ever played.
The game is set in an open world and in this world where an alien overlord has taken over the planet and threatens humanity. It is up to the mother trucking president of the United States to take care of business. Armed to the teeth, the president and his crew must kick alien butt.
Many fun mini games are incorporated into the main storyline, things like speed runner and puzzles. There's even some really fun references to old school video games, in particular the opening scene from Double Dragon was amusing.
Speaking of the story line, here is where the game really shines. I loved the dialogs and the actors did a brilliant job.
