Having previously sunk several hours into this game on the Playstation 4, getting Helldivers on here was practically a no-brainer.
The game is an interesting twist on the twin-stick shooter, mainly in that friendly fire is a factor in abundance, stealth is encouraged whenever possible, and ammo is always more scarce than you want it to be. Communication and adaptability are key to surviving long enough to complete your objectives, and while the game overall can be quite difficult, pulling off some of the more difficult missions can feel immensely rewarding. The controls are as tight as can be and the game's tutorial does a good job of filling you in on its intricacies too, meaning you never feel like you're actively fighting against the game itself.
Also worth noting is Helldivers' Starship Troopers-esque aesthetic and sense of humour, with hilariously over the top patriotism taking centre stage as you campaign against three different enemy armies that all embody some form of "threat to liberty" (especially hilarious are the Cold War communist Cyborgs).
That's not to say that Helldivers is perfect though. Some of the mission types can feel a bit at odds with the game's own mechanics (the arena battles are particularly bad for this, as the rest of the game actively encourages you to avoid combat when possible and is built around doing so), and a string of bad luck can sometimes leave you completely at the mercy of a large group of enemies that are unkillable without some kind of anti-armor weapon (which wouldn't be so bad were it not for the fact that incredibly few weapons can penetrate armor). Also, while this isn't so much a flaw as it is a bit of caution for potential buyers, the majority of missions in this game are virtually unplayable without bringing other people along, so if you don't have friends to play this with and are uncomfortable playing with people you don't know online, you'll likely want to give this one a pass.
All that being said, Helldivers is an exceptional time that'll likely give you tons of moments that you'll remember forever, either due to amazing victories or hilarious failures. At $20, the game is an absolute steal.

Mirror's Edge meets Dead Island. I guess this is the best definition so far.
Well, the story is always the same: a virus turns people in zombies in the fictional city of Harran, which now is quarantined and few survirvors remain in a city full of zombies. You're Kyle Crane, an agent from an agency called GRE sent to recover some files useful to recreate a cure for the virus. Cool. Plane.
But the way the game actually starts simply changes the perception of the story: When you land you get stuck on a tree with your parachute and the moment you fall you get bitten by zombies and saved by a couple of scouts from a group that has a refuge in a condo called "The Tower". You will soon find yourself in the middle between your duties with GRE and the need to help your saviours and their group following a story which could result linear nonetheless interesting and pleasant to follow
The miracles of the Chrome Engine 6... Well maybe they're not exactly miracles, even though it has been improved a little with the enhanced edition, however You will ALWAYS have landscapes, places, and little things to admire. Lighting will always give amusing sunsets or particular suggestive illuminations and the "real time" day-night will allow a more immersive and changing atmosphere by living the same city both day and (the more dangerous) night.
There are two main maps with further minor sections that have been created with lots of care for structure, locations and credibility of the places: the whole map has been shaped to be run through various paths, ground or rooftops, climbing sections, mattresses or landing zones to jump off high places or cable lines to run down fast and far; Each map has unique subzones, the tower, A bus station, a fishermen's village, highway, train station, bridges, squares, hotels, parking lots, whatever and each of these zones are credible. Of course, for developing reasons some elements are copy-pasted, but you will be overwhelmed by other elements added making each zone unique, such as desperate help messages on rooftops, posters, peculiar vehicles, and more.
Music is mostly made of synth notes that will accompany various situations, but there will be some specific themes that will nail in your head such as the intro, loading theme and the school raid. Those are some cool ful themes that really have some character and stick to your mind.
Here comes the most interesting part. Dying light is an FPS, a Survival with RPG elements, Horror.
With order: The game uses first person view and considering the situation your weapons wil mostly be sticks, wrenches baseball bats at the very beginning. Going ahead you will find lots of new weapons, knives, hammers, blades, bows and firearms of course.
You can loot around, you MUST loot around, because besides some random money to use by vendors you will find some components to use with blueprints (which have to be found as well) used to improve your weapons giving them some particular effect (fire, poison, lightning).
You can run all around the city climbing buildings to their rooftops, jumping down on mattresses and sliding down cables. This is one of the funniest sides of the game as it was for Mirror Edge. Of course a game like this HAS to implement a grappling hook!
The day goes by until the night comes. You can clearly see this happening "naturally" (read gradually, not "in less than 12 hours"), and when the night comes the nightmare begins: zombies will be higher in nunmbers and they won't be the only ones around. Volatiles are the "evolved" and way more aggressive evolution of the undeads, they run faster than you, they climb and fight hard and will be your worst enemy giving you the real sense of fear and respect towards the night.
Your only hope and resting point are the "safe zones". The Tower is the very first you find, as you begin there, but the maps have many safe zones that must be secured first, in order to be used.
There are abilities trees, through missions and zombie killings you gain experience until you level up and get points to spend there, giving Kyle new skills and actions or improving existent ones.
There are the usual story missions that allow the player to move on, and there are some secondary missions as well that can be played after the end in free roaming mode. There are ability challenges around the map, both fighting or parkour challenges. And there are some unmentioned quests such as the quarantine zones, which are usually the inside of a certain building where the player must kill all the zombies inside and loot some crates for some rewards. Worth your time both for the experience and the rewards.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, is a near perfect gaming experience despite coming across hundreds of flaws in most every aspect of the game, from the visuals, audio, optimization, rushed mechanics, poor save files, and so forth... Bloodlines suffers from a plagued development, and is far from finished, but comes across as a product both greatly entertaining and lengthy in gameplay. Utilizing the HL2 Source engine, Bloodlines is easily modifiable, and as such many fan made community patches are in circulation around the internet. I highly recommend downloading these patches for a more refined and polished gaming experience (although it is optional as the game is still playable all the way through without said patches). Bloodlines delivers exceptional voice acting, a grim and atmospheric setting, a fantastically agreeable soundtrack, a fair amount of character customization, and at times, a fair amount of role-playing choices, all for a low sum of 20 bucks, and believe me folks - with said amount of issues, it's still very much worth it.

Software Inc. has to be the of the most underrated games on Steam. I accidentally found it while searching for tycoon games and what a surprise it was! This is the best software development game I've played compared with Game Dev Tycoon, GamersGoMakers, Mad Games Tycoon etc.
What sets it apart is the simple graphics and the smooth interface. It is easy to learn the controls and build big impressive looking office complexes.
You start as the founder of the company starting to work on a few small contracts. From there you start developing your own software: Antivirus, games, operating systems, audio and visual design software, ect. As you grow, you can expand your office and workforce. It's entirely up to you how much you'd like to micromanage. You can assign team leaders and send them on HR and project management courses allowing them to hire and manage teams and their own projects completely independently. The game scales incredibly well as you expand your company.
Some might find the micromanagement a little overwhelming. This game was really well thought out and you have all the data you might need at your disposal.
It is early access so there are some glitches, and the game could do with more content. Most notably furniture is currently a bit limited, but that said all the necessary stuff is already there. There's also some minor balancing issues that will be sorted out later but nothing gamebreaking and nothing that will ruin your fun. So far the developer of Software Inc. has built a great foundation for what will probably become one of the most unique and fun management simulations on the market.
In the simulation/management genre, this game is right up there with the best of them.
- Great interface
- Level of micromanagement is optional
- Regular updates
- Workshop support
- Still Early Access
- Limited content
- Ballance issues

I helped fund this on Kickstarter and played the demo game back when it was first being promoted. The voice acting was the same throughout the two versions, not necessarily a good thing, however. It didn't feel like the VAs were given any kind of direction on how to portray the characters, so the vocal tones were contrary to the mood, at times, or depicted the characters as kind of stock personas, especially the friendgals. The writing was amateur in places, and purple prose in others, with no real happy medium between the two.
However, the background art did get a sharp improvement on the visuals, and the UI was greatly improved over the production time. Most of the character art also came through looking really great, if a little small. There was a certain issue with scrunched faces on Ms. Philips, Suzu, and Lisette, but most of the characters looked like they were part of the same universe, with equivalent proportions, and I think the new character artist will be put to great effect in future games, especially with a little more practice.

Is a game that orbit around cheats and god mode. Is totally different from previous Saint Row games. For example, once you get the gliding and running super-powers, which happens right at the beginning, all cars and planes become obsolete. Combat is perhaps way too easy too with all the regeneration and quite an endless bar health. It sort of Just Cause 2, but instead of being Spiderman, you are Superman.
But this doesn't mean that the game isn't fun. The game follows the previous saga in it characterizing making fun of the GTA-like games, but taking it to the extreme. You can shoot black-holes, you can abduct enemies, if you have the DLCs you can get into a diIdo rampage with Santa Claus.
Congratulation to the one designing the movement and controls for gliding and jumping because it feels and works great right from the start. The way it handle such unusual way of movement is outstandingly good with top notch precision.
The game lack some of the fun that Saint Row 2 had. For example, I haven't found another mission as fun as the shait truck which was in SR2. You won't get records for throwing people away, or for surfing on the rooftop of a car, or anything of the like. In the script there is also a lack of seriousness and more spoilers into the story would be very welcome. SR2 is still for me the best of the saga, to the point that it was at the same level as GTA:San Andreas.
The game is also "bug free", technically. Since the entire thing run in a simulation, and the simulation get glitchy randomly, any real bug that you may encouter won't look like it, and would appear to be just part of the aesthetics of the game.
For the next one, please take back Zimos at one of the main characters please.
Overall the game is good. I'm not sure if SR3 was equally good or above. And I think SR2 was way better than this one, SR3, GTA-I-II-III and IV, with the same level of SA and Just Cause 2.

I found that a customized Medium setting was perfect for me, everything still looked and felt extremely viscereal and realistic and I was perfectly content to leave it that way, coming from an utter graphics ♥♥♥♥♥.
The story was good, I won't say great but good. What makes it are the main character's very emotional and poetic journal notes that flesh out the world a lot more than is shown. I wish more detail had been focused on the political and personal aspects of the story, but ultimately I felt it tied the fantastic exploration into its premise perfectly.
The level design: Excellent. There is a linear path that is left to the player to navigate through. Go the wrong way, and you'll face the consequences. Get impatient and you'll want to quit for a while. But if you really pay attention to what you're doing, treat it like you would were you in the actual situation, you'll do great.
The combat was...... Egh. It was very smooth, and challenging. But enemies were extremely spongey in Survival difficulty, which I despise, and most weapons had too much recoil for what they were (the 5.45mm Kalashnikov which has less recoil than an AR-15 in real life ended up losing control in like 6 shots on full-auto). But besides that, no complaints.
The NPC interactions felt very sluggish and deliberately drawn-out. I can recall several instances where I would reach the end of a chamber and wait around 30 seconds for the NPCs to catch up after their scripted sequences gave up. In many cases where you would think "we need to hurry or we'll die!" some sequences just don't make sense and in lots of instances I would get angry at the fact that rusty locked doors are somehow obstacles when I have several weapons that could easily break the doors. This was the most jarring issue for me.
World depth was mediocre; you should have been allowed to explore a lot more than allowed, hear peoples' stories, spend your currency on more than just gear. Things like that. The few instances where we were presented with truly amazing places that warranted exploration and possibly side-questing were basically irrelevant due to the forced linear shooter layout.
Ultimately, I feel like they could have made a better RPG out of this than a shooter, but I did enjoy the experience, despite some serious annoyances. 8/10.

The mechanics are dated, there's a metric ton of bugs and the use of fan patches is absolutely mandatory, but all of that sketchiness hides one of the best RPGs of the early HD era, and the only worthwhile supernatural RPG on the market.
Aside from the abovementioned niggles, what you're getting is some of the best characterizations and voiceovers in the business, a fully realized chunk of White Wolf's famous World of Darkness setting, and the opportunity to play a shady type in a shady world, something that's typically been the province of the Deus Ex or Thief series.
You'll hate the rough mechanics, but you'll absolutely love everything else about Bloodlines, which is precisely why CCP's long-delayed WoD project has been under close scrutiny by fans of Troika's last production.

I think I would have found this game more compelling without attempts at storytelling. Although I love a good story, the execution of the narrative and dialog were both lacking. There was very little emotional payoff to the end to top off a consistently mediocre dialog/narration performance. The voice acting was at best believable, at worst downright awkward. Accents were all over the board and internally inconsistent. Fred himself was a decent performance, but only barely used. So, overall, a big 'meh' for the story elements. Although I will say, I did love the old-school whimsy of the environments. It's nice to see characters and landscapes that aren't designed to be dark, depressing and 'realistic', so full credit for that.
The gameplay, though... was quite good. The mechanics were a bit odd to me at first, but they built up nicely. The ending puzzles were suitably difficult, and even adrenaline-inducing. There was only one gameplay aspect which I found to be truly bad, and that's the dash jump. With absolutely no control, I often found myself just barely overshooting a platform because I'd been a little *too* careful to make the gap. That's a frustrating feeling. I think making the dash jump have far less control than a normal jump is a good idea, but at least let us move a few inches for a bit of fine-tuning (or design long-reach platforms with backing walls/rocks to catch the player from over-jumping).
Overall, I'd say if you don't mind cringing a bit at a mediocre story, it's worth a go.

For me, much of the attraction of this turn-based game is in the rich diversity of the weapons, armor, shields, charms.  Each item boosts 2 of 5 attributes (vitality, strength, intelligence, dexterity, or wisdom.)  Items have different levels of rarity.  They can have special prefixes giving boosts. Finding, buying or crafting these items is great fun, and as a character advances, the loot gets stronger.  Other aspects of the game (music, humor, depth) come together.  I will confess that while I play the game on Classic difficulty, I will occassionally go to the Steam data file on my computer and make a copy of the save files to a folder.  I understand that this is frowned upon by part of the gaming community, but I enjoy the game more having the backup.  My point here is that the game can be played in whatever fashion is most enjoyable to you.

Metro 2033 is a very atmospheric survival shooter set in the Russian underground metro system.
The first playthrough of this game is awesome. It has a real wanderlust to it that you don't get from most other games these days - It feels like a great adventure.
There's a good variety of difficulty options to accomodate every kind of player. The easier ones suffer a bit from bullet-spongery but the "Ranger" difficulties were just right for me - removing a ton of the hud for a more immersive experience and causing both the player and enemies to die in just a few hits. Ammo is also much more scarce on the Ranger difficulties which encourages proper scavenging, ammo conservation and making use of the game's excellent stealth systems and devices. The stealth only enhances the experience and doesn't feel dull and laboured like in some other games.
The game boasts a great story from start to finish and has a good balance of unsettling and creepy atmosphere with moments of relief, exploration and intrigue.
Overall, Metro 2033 sits happily on the shelf next to some of the best single player fps experiences I've ever played. Heartily recommend.

Let me start by saying this is a yes-ish recommendation. There are some key things that need to be said about this. First, it's not explicit what the audience is for this game. The graphics, dialogue, and actors diction make it seem like it should be for younger ages (6-12). Yet the puzzles, storyline (and theme of it), controls and gameplay all make it seem like it was made for a little bit older ages (15+). It also wasn't all that long. The time you see, 118 minutes, was 1 straight playthrough with minor amounts of messing around/exploring, about 45 seconds of graphical tweaking, and an average amount of deaths/failures. All this being said, I, at 19 years of age, can officially say I enjoyed this game. The gameplay was new enough to keep me entertained but not side tracked by the story. If you're a graphics junky, this may not be your game. Models and animations are somewhat lacking but this is an indie game and it wasn't the main focus (though the animations for your character were perfect! Couldn't have been done better). Overall, 8/10 on a professional scale, 9/10 on an indie scale.

HELLDIVERS is pretty cool, I guess.
Created by the team behind Magicka, a game that destroys friendships, comes another game that destroys friendships.
Set in the distant future of next Thursday, HELLDIVERS, as my Steam library likes to shout at me, is a game about humanity at war. You are a HELLDIVER, a type of orbital shock unit that gets into little pots and fired at planets like angry genocide bullets. Super Earth is in danger! Threatened on all sides by evil alien threats, the HELLDIVERS must lead the spearhead from planet to planet, conquering and annihilating all opposition in your way so you can indoctrinate and exploit your enemies harshly and go back to your way of life of being spied on by the government and using dead bodies as food.
Wait, are we the bad guys?
HELLDIVERS is a strictly multiplayer game, sure you can go in lone wolf but much like my ex wife, it kills most of the fun and forces you to live out your days living in your own refuse.  Unlike many games with a war narrative, HELLDIVERS is entirely about the war, where you and thousands of other players march from planet to planet and conquer them in the name of Super Earth, taking over sector after sector until you can reach your enemies home world and knock them out of the war for good. And when all three enemy races have a Burger King on their home world, the war is won and the game resets! Letting you and your HELLDIVER comrades start from square one.
But the real meat of HELLDIVERS is the actual game play. After picking a planet and the location of the planet you want to attack, you're introduced to a top down stick shooter with various objectives for you and your three squad mates to accomplish. Now, I'm not a fan of twin stick shooters, they are to me what Carlos Mencia is to comedy, that is to say they don't click. But I ended up actually really enjoying HELLDIVERS, all of the weapons had this very crunchy kick to them and it was satisfying to rip cyborgs and bugs to shreds under a hail of gunfire.
HELLDIVERS also has the advantage of letting you customize your load out, taking down with you not only perks and weapons, but also vehicles, defensive emplacements, and even tertiary support like air strikes and orbital bombardment. The game play compliments the war-time narrative, by making you feel like an actual fighting force rather than a hero unit with an objective.
Another thing that lets HELLDIVERS stand out from other twin-stick shooters is that it isn't a horde mode game. Many games of it's natures just have you mow down wave after wave of enemies until they finally get you, tallying up the wave you killed and giving you a score much like getting a gold medal with chocolate inside in elementary school for participating in track and field. While HELLDIVERS does indeed have a game mode like that, even that one has a kill limit. Your goal in HELLDIVERS is to complete your objectives and then escape the planets surface without being completely overrun by your enemy.
Even though I liked HELLDIVERS, I like it the same way you like eating fast food or smoking crack, it's good but you shouldn't be doing it all the time. Due to it's nature, HELLDIVERS is a very repetitive game, there isn't much variety in missions and all the difficulty levels do is add more objective while throwing more dirty alien commie scum ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s at you. But I don't think HELLDIVERS is meant to be played all day every day, more like you put a good number of hours in when you first get it, and after that you just kind of play it from time to time.
There are other things I can criticize about the game that isn't really the games fault. I played this game the whole of yesterday and it is really addictive. I love the concept and it is implemented quite well except there are many things that need to be improved.
Pros:
+ Really fun to play (one of those games where you look up and realise you've lost half the day.. and night)
+ Graphics aren't mindblowing but are fit for purpose
+ A lot more options and content then Game dev Tycoon
Cons:
- Gui needs serios work, why can't I shift camera angles with the mouse, everything is on the keyboard
- Some important info menus are missing, I can't find anything that shows a breakdown of my sales for the month
- Building mechanics are a little backwards and need improvement. Parking lots are laid down opposite to their icon for instance. You also cannot delete walls and you need enclose a whole square on existing walls before walls are set. Why can't I just lay a single section of walls, to create a passage way between two rooms for instance.
- Need more furniture and upgrades. There is too much of a gap between 1990 and 2000
- The interface for assigning teams to projects needs to be in a single screen, where you can drag and drop and see where they allocated/overallocated
- What about creating toilet cubicles.... why must I enclose each toilet with a wall?
- I don't understand/like the HR manager and Project Manager implementation, why aren't these separate roles like IRL
- I know the same is about Software, but why not introduce a Hardware manufacturing element (DLC maybe?). Would be fund to be an Apple/Microsoft and Manufacture the hardware to go with my Phone software/Console etc.
- Pricing: There should be a metric indicating public price sensitivity. Otherwise it's a guessing game. Perhaps you can commission a report to see what people think about your product and suggested pricing points?
- Time to develop should increase with better equipment, it doesn't feel like this every changes
- Servers never seem to keep up with demand and the wiring mechanic is screwed. Why can't they all be linked together, there seems to be some arbitrary limitation that is beyond comprehension?!!?
- Stocks: There has to be a better way to implement this. Also it would be cool to be able to take control of companies after you own more than 50% and set their objectives. i.e. what they can and can't make. I'd also like to be able to set their dividens level, some like in capitalism.
Don't let the many con's above put you off this game, it is really cool and well worth the money, it just needs a good few tweaks to make it awesome.

Summary:
Basic run-through of the game takes about 3 hours and it is very linear (ie. no side quests and limited exploration).  A very creative and beautiful murder mystery story.
Details:
This is one of the most creative and imaginative game's I've ever had the pleasure of playing!  The mechanics are extremely well designed, the story is engaging, and the environment is beautiful and immersive.  While it is a relatively short game (~3hrs) I imagine many people would play it multiple times to enjoy the puzzles and scenery.  I truly hope many more games are made using this same engine.

Many people hyped the game because of its great graphics so I bought it at steam sale. Here is my experience with this game:
The game looks pretty sweet. I expected a little bit more after the big hype about the graphic but the game looks good enough.
Very good! I really like the feeling while I walked around the world. Some people complain that the world is dead (for example no animals in the fortress) but I like that because it fits to the game atmosphere.
The puzzles are quite good! They are not too hard to solve but you have to think about what you have to do next. Good mix for casual puzzle player. Hardcore puzzlers may find the puzzles too easy.
The story is one of the most important points of the game. I enjoyed the tour but the ending was.. well it could be better. The story is also not that long. I completed the story in about 5 hours - without rushing. You can discover everything and you can also get all achievements in this 5 hours without having a time problem.
Not many. The elevators are the main source for serious bugs (glitching through the elevator) and also got some vision bugs at a cut scene but at all I didnt have many bugs found.
Well this game is more a interactive movie than a real game. It doesnt have real gamplay and you will spend a lot of time with just walking around.
Save points are badly placed. No option to save the game on your own.
After you finished the game you will have no real reason to play it again. There are no alternative endings. The only reason to start the game again is to get the achievements (you will get nearly all if you just complete the game).
In the end I have to say that the game is not worth 19€ because of the lack of content. If you enjoy games like this you should definitively buy and play this game but wait until it is on sale. Suggested price is 5-8€ in my opinion.

In the Vanishing of Ethan Carter you play as Paul Prospero, supernatural detective. Paul travels to Red Creek Valley in search of the titiular character, Ethan Carter who has sent him letters describing things no child his age should know of. To find Ethan, you must use your abilities of deduction to uncover the events that have transpired in the Valley.
The game possesses a simple premise that is well executed. You must find objects of interest and place them back into their proper places before using your abilities to piece together and replay the events. It is a interesting mechanic however, each mystery is solved the same way. This doesn't become an issue though because of the overall length of the game (which I finished in about 4 hours). Additionally, there are a few minor puzzles between these sections that do provide some more varied gameplay and require additional thought to solve. Finally, if you are looking for a game which will test your deductive skills with each mystery, this is not the game for you. One last thing to keep track of is the lack of ability to manually save the game. Instead, you will have to finish significant sections of the story before the game will auto save for you.
Though I do recommend this game, I do not recommend buying at full price. While an enjoyable experience it was a very short one. Additionally, the game provides no replayability as most achievements will be unlocked as you progress through the story and all of them are unlockable in a single playthrough. With all that being said, if you come across this game for a fair price I do recommend giving it a try.
Pros:
-Interesting Mechanics
-Beautiful Graphics
Cons:
-Short
-No replayabilty
-Little variation between each mystery
-Mysteries are not difficult
-No manual saves
Final Score: 6/10

I've had enough exposure to sci-fi games and stories to know what to expect from this simplistic little spareship simulator. Get a ship, buy upgrades, build up a crew, fly missions and OH MY GOD I EXPLODED.
A lesson this game teaches quite early on is not to get attached.
It went against so many of my natural tendencies. I want to clear all the sectors. I want to get all the upgrades. I want to take care of my crew and get them fully trained. Tough, says FTL. You have to make some very hard decisions. You have very little time. Bad things are going to happen to you. They're largely arbitary. You're going to have to asphysixiate your crew at least once.
It's very hard. It's very fun. The random number generator is not kind to you. You will probably die quite a lot. You will experience the ecstacy of having a rig that just chews through enemies and the agony of when the thing you were praying didn't happen happens and your (nearly) perfect ship goes up in flames.

You will die, a lot...
I can confirm that after playing more than 300 hours you will be a different man.
I recommend if you want to find your inner peace.

As a player that likes to only play games that let me have short bursts of fun, I heartily recommend this game. The action is awesome, the missions are short, the level of challenge can be adjusted, and it offers a true sense of accomplishment, even if you only complete a couple of missions at a time.
The game is about dystopic earth that is constantly at war with three alien races. Helldivers are commando units that accomplish short missions to advance in our fight for democracy on distant worlds. It can be to nuke a bug nest, reactivate a SAM site, defuse mines in a minefield, rescue some survivors. You get in, accomplish one or more objectives and get out. It can get repetitive if you spend hours of your day playing Helldiivers, but for people my age that have to do grown up stuff, it is perfect. The game reminds me of the old NES Guerrilla War, but this time you can kill your partner and ask for special equipment or artillery fire to be delivered wherever you want.
Helldivers multiplayer is great. People are nice enough to let you ruin their game without being too rude. Yeah, sorry about that guys, but I´m a slow learner. However, the game is not hard to master, and you can serve of great support once you learn how to use stratagems and not to kill your friends.
It lets you play cooperatively on your computer, which is a plus for me because I play with my GF and my kid without affecting the game of others. We have a blast with this game.
It also runs smoothly without being too demanding on hardware, and it still looks awesome.

I'm a little torn on this game. It has a number of good aspects, and bad aspects.
One of the good things about it is that it's a beautiful game. Even on all the lowest settings (Which I unfortunately needed to use to prevent the game from lagging) the game is breathtaking.
Secondly, the story is pretty interesting. Discovering what's been going on in this cut-off little town was worthwhile. I also enjoyed Ethan's stories scattered throughout the game.
Then, we get to the things I didn't really like. As many people point out, the game is VERY short. Admittedly, my own time is likely on the shorter side, since I used a guide to make sure I didn't miss anything, but even still there's only really a handful of things to do, which is a shame since it's a fairly sizable place for the amount of content.
The fact that I DON'T regret using a guide is also a bit of a shame. You see, in order to see the ending, you must complete all the little side-events. There's only a handful of them, but many of them are off the beaten path and EXTREMELY easy to miss, especially since there is no clue in-game really hinting on where to explore. (Well, until you reach the end and realize you can't unlock the ending until you find them.) In the beginning, the game admits it doesn't hold your hand, but when the only hints you get are at the very end of the game at the extreme far end of the map in a large world that you missed some well hidden events at the very beginning? Well, that's just unnecessarily frustrating.
The inability to save your progress on exit is more of an inconvenience than a terrible fault. Also, the mine maze part of the game was a bit of a detour in the game style... One I didn't particularly appreciate. (Even if the scene at the end of that event was pretty awesome.)
In the end, for the few bucks I paid for it, I'd say it was okay. If you'd like to try it out, I'd recommend waiting for it to be on sale, though, as you might not find it worth the full price.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a good Lovecraftian detective story. You play as a supernatural detective attempting to track down a missing boy. As you search for clues as to his disappearance, you wander through a stunningly beautiful and atmospheric environment, accompanied by an excellent soundtrack and a growing sense of dread.
Your psychic abilities make for an interesting game mechanic. You search around for clues (some of which will lead you to other clues), and then put them together to get a psychic vision of what happened. Some of these clues require solving puzzles, some of which are the fun kind of difficult to solve. These flashbacks build up the story behind Ethan Carter's disappearance. Building up this narrative by yourself is the central mechanic of the game: there's nothing to tell you what to do or where to go next besides what you discover in the story.
For the most part, the game is very good at getting you the information you need to figure out what to do or where to go next. In a couple places, though, sometimes the narrative fails to deliver a key piece of information, and you're left wandering around until you stumble onto the path forward. That can be unnecessarily frustrating, and after spending 20 minutes looking for the path forward it felt like the developers were intentionally obfuscating things just to pad the game length.
In fact, it's the length that's my biggest issue with the game. I finished it in only 4 hours (including all side quests), and there's nothing in the way of replay value. A couple of the main quest puzzles in the game don't have a lot of substance to them, so it takes only a couple of minutes to figure them out. For what is essentially a detective game, that's inexcusable. The game could have easily lasted at least another hour if the puzzles already in the game had been fleshed out and polished a little more.
In a way, this game still feels like it's in late alpha stage, and it's not worth the full $20 price. I'm glad I picked it up on sale, and if you're a fan of Lovecraftian/weird horror it might be worth the price if you can get it on sale.
Pros:
- Soundtrack meshes well with the game environment
- Beautiful scenery
- Good Lovecraftian horror story
- No hand-holding, progression is delivered through narrative
- A few puzzles that require some thinking
Cons:
- Extremely short (4-5 hours at most to do everything)
- A couple puzzles are extremely simple and feel incomplete
- No way to keep track of stuff you've found at the end of completed quests
- Path forward is sometimes extremely unclear
- Most voice actors have a stilted delivery
tl;dr: Something to think about getting if you're a Lovecraft/weird horror fan and the game's on deep discount. Hard to justify the full purchase price given how short the game ends up being.

There is a certain amount of affection I have for SanctuaryRPG.  Back in 2014 a young and naive boy was creating slighty cringy videos on a youtube channel that had but a few watchers.  Most people saw just another face in the crowd, another young lad attempting to reach fame and fortune through an overly saturated market.  Black Shell Games did not.  They saw an entertainer trying to be the cause of laughter and discussion but was lost in a sea of those exactly like he.  They took pity on this young soul and gifted him a copy of their newest game: SanctuaryRPG.
Three years later, they still remembered him and his weird videos (and disgusting goatee) and sent him a copy of their updated title, now on steam.
As you can probably tell, SRPG takes me far back into the areas of my life that I try to repress.  I remember the excitement of being approached by a developer about sharing their game with my small audience.  Words cannot describe the joy I found from that simple tweet so long ago.
The amount of bias I have for the game does not subtract from the absolute comedy and D&D like gameplay that the game provides.  SRPG is a exceptional example of early text-based adventure games and even surpases many of its predecessors in innovation.  Simple dungeon-crawler gameplay allows for more time spent of the development of the ASCII graphics, which look amazing.  Never has 1s and 0s looked so good.
The only negative thing I can say about the game is the monotony that is the combat.  I believe this to be a fault of the style rather than the execution.  As everything is text-based there is not much room for improvment or innovation when all you can do is select 1, 2, 3, or 4.  Even with special abilities and status effects, there really isn't anything good about the combat and I can only play for a few minutes at a time before boredom overtakes me and I desire something else.
In short, SanctuaryRPG is a perfect example of the bygone era of the text-based genre.  The story, music, and RPG components more than make up for any failure and fault of the combat system.  Casual and hardcore gamers have much to find and many hours to be lost in this beautiful dungeon crawler.
Pick it up now or on sale, either way is worth your time.

Helldivers is a top-down twin stick shooter from developer Arrowhead, on the surface this description is underwhelming but through a combination of diverse enemies and addictive gameplay it has the potential to be the very best in its genre.
On starting the game you are greeted with a slick recruitment video giving you all the motivation you need to drop into enemy territory. You are a Helldiver and that means making the safety of Super Earth your personal responsibility, using a huge range of weapons you will spread “managed democracy” across the galaxy one bullet (or laser or toxic goo or missile or fire etc…) at a time. It takes a very satirical approach to the messaging reminiscent of 1998 masterpiece Starship Troopers.
First up is the graphics, they are not genre defining and by no means the selling point of the game but Helldivers is pretty to look at. By utilising vivid colors and an almost cartoon quality Helldivers is easy on the eye, throughout my time with Helldivers I experienced no graphical or frame rate issues. Most impressive are the weapon effects, each weapon handles very differently and you can plainly see the time and effort that has gone in to the various animations. Bullets from a LMG spray across the screen with smoking shells flying and laser guns overheat with smoke rising from the weapon, it is this attention to detail that really gives this game an edge. The only weapon that left me slightly disappointed was the flamethrower, the first spews out in a steady stream rather than the sustained wide destruction you would want from such a weapon especially as the effects on all other weapons are done so well.
Sound next, whilst lacking in variety the score is a perfect representation of how quickly things can turn bad for a Helldiver. As you land on the planet and are exploring you will be treated with a quiet mellow tune, this will quickly change when you are greeted with waves of enemies. There is nothing like standing back to back with your squad awaiting extraction as dramatic music reminiscent of final battles in big budget Hollywood movies plays, again it is these moments that set Helldivers apart from other top down action games.
Now the gameplay, this is where Helldivers really shines and this is what will keep you coming back to play it again and again. The premise is simple, you with up to three others drop on an enemy planet and you are given a series of objectives that you can complete or fail. Failing a single objective does not fail mission, you will still get the chance to extract but will be penalised when it comes to receiving XP. Helldivers is simple on paper but I cannot stress enough, this game is addictive as hell! I can’t remember the last time a game completely consumed me and I have not been able to put it down since purchasing it.
You will face three different alien races as a Helldiver. The Illuminate are an advanced bunch, capable of futurist feats and able to kill you in a single blow with a shot from one of their laser cannons. Next are the Cyborgs, these guys are heavily armed and to face them you should be to, unless you want to end up as roadkill underneath one of their hulking tanks. Finally, my personal favourite, the Bugs. These come in all shapes and sizes and can prove quite deadly to an inexperienced squad.
How you tackle these three enemies differs massively, having a single load out will simply not cut it. Take the time in the lower difficulty zones to see how the enemy operates and find their weaknesses. This should adequately prepare you for what is to come but you can never be sure and believe me when I say everything in Helldivers is out to kill you but more on that later.
There is simply so much to this game that completionists will easily be able to squeeze 100 hours of gameplay from Helldivers. You collect research points which allow you to upgrade weapons or stratagems, you get these by either collecting samples found in the map and by levelling up your character. When you have collected enough you are presented with so many options it can be a tough choice. Do you upgrade your machine gun to hold more rounds? Do you upgrade your APC to give more protection to your team? The list goes on but it is important to say that all of the upgrades have meaning and will change the way you play, nothing feels tacked on for the sake it.
It is a good idea to make your character strong as mentioned previously everything in Helldivers is out to kill you. Not only is friendly fire always on but the pods your teammates arrive in, defence turrets, mines or vehicles will instantly kill you if you are not careful. Even trying to play the game defensively can quickly end badly. Death for a single  Helldiver is not the end of the mission however, as long as one teammate is alive (and the stratagem isn’t on cooldown) your dead teammates can be dropped back into the action…just be sure to not stand underneath them when they do.
Helldivers does a very good job of making you feel part of an army with the galactic war set up. The war is fought on three sides representing the three different alien races, as you complete missions and secure planets in a particular zone you will eventually reach the alien home world. This will start a timed event calling all Helldivers to focus their efforts to defeat the enemy. Alternatively if there are not enough Helldivers fighting the alien scum the war can reach Super Earth, much like reaching a home world all Helldivers will be called to defend their home.
Besides the small selection of music and underwhelming graphics the one major downside to this game is not capitalising on its humorous tone and Starship Trooper inspiration. Whilst your character will occasionally shout hilarious comments as they fight the enemy this is all we see, I would have loved to see more cutscenes and perhaps be introduced to interesting characters within the universe.
Helldivers gets a score of 90/100. Besides its lack of story content, uninspired visuals and relatively small selection of music the gameplay easily makes you forget all of that. In fact without those minor issues Helldivers would be a perfect game. Helldivers provides some of the best white knuckle co-op action I have ever played and there is no better feeling than making it off a planet swarming with enemies with your whole squad. This game is definitely worth a full purchase as you will want to keep coming back…and bring friends, it gets dangerous out there!

The Room Two is a worthy successor to The Room as it continues to provide plenty of imaginative puzzles within a confined space. Four intriguing rooms, engulfed in mystery and history, offer intricate, mechanical apparatuses ranging from puzzle boxes to physics and combination puzzles.
Graphically The Room Two does a good job providing just enough visual clues as to whether something's possible to twist, slide or generally fit to be fiddled around with. The themes of the rooms are coherent in style and generate a sense of adventure. Even the overarching key puzzles are somewhat related to the theme of their respective rooms and cleverly hide the fact that most smaller puzzles are less pertinent.
The sounds of unlocking, pulling, unclipping and the devices shifting and clicking into place are naturally gratifying. Even though the haptics of the puzzles is lost due to the mouse control on PC compared to the touch controls on mobile, the sound and camera movement convey a good enough feel for the physicality of the objects.
With some escape room qualities, The Room Two is a tricky, short puzzle game in the spirit of its predecessor. It's a wholly recommendable title for any puzzle enthusiast.

I like what I call "thinking games", which The Room 2 definitely is. The puzzles were pretty good, not too difficult, particularly if you play this genre a lot. It did have a faint "Myst"or "Riven" feel to it, due to the puzzle solving. This may not come as a surprise to anyone, but you get what you pay for with Seduce Me.  Unfortunately, this great idea suffers from haphazard plotting, schmaltzy dialogue and under-developed characters.  What could have been an intriguing story that explored interesting ideas ends up a schlocky mess before it's through.  The potential is there, but it's buried beneath writing that reads more like trashy fan fiction than a well structured visual novel.
Close to graduating high school, Mika Anderson inherits her grandfather's estate after he passes from mysterious circumstances.  Forced into her new home by a harsh and unloving father, she finds herself alone and face to face with five bloodied intruders who prove to be much more than they appear.  Becoming embroiled in the affairs of incubi who feed on human sexual energy to survive, will Mika's life ever be the same?
Just let that premise sink in for a minute.  This is a story about a girl who falls for sexual demons, and yet it completely squanders that potential.   There's nothing here to hook the reader beyond a few steamy scenes, and those quickly lose their luster when you realize they're recycled between the story routes.  Almost every event occurs exactly the same way right down to the punctuation.  I understand this is a free game, but that does not excuse lazy writing, especially when the only change between many scenes are the character names on the screen.   Not only does this lead to boredom on the reader's part but fails to sufficiently distinguish the characters from one another.  By the end, the stereotypical personality traits  given each guy feels superficially tacked on as there is barely any difference in their interactions with the protagonist.
The incubi's back stories do little to salvage the situation and actually make them less sympathetic than the main villain who turns out to be the most well developed character of them all.   It takes reading through side routes to get any depth to the story, but what's there isn't half bad.  If only it wasn't hidden away from the main story as the world created is quite interesting.  Building upon the mythos and better working it into the incubi's routes would have added much-needed development to the characters, keeping the reader interested beyond the few lust-filled scenes with each guy.
What is even more baffling is that the non-incubi characters feel more genuine, and their stories more heartfelt, especially Andrew, the dorky normal kid who's a total sweetheart.  Halfway through the game you send the incubi on their way, lose your memories, then pursue a relationship with either Andrew or one of your girlfriends. And while there's nothing deep or profound in their stories, the character interactions are enjoyable and relationships realistic.  Sure, Mika didn't get any passionate make-out sessions with them, but at least they're written somewhat believably.
Which leads me to how unbelievable the relationships are between Mika and her chosen incubus.  So maybe we don't know how a relationship between a human and demon would realistically play out, but when you've written these characters to be sensitive, caring, loving "human" beings who only want what's best for the main character despite having the power to force women into relations with them, it loses all of its edge.  That's not to say I wanted to read about these guys♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the protagonist, but there are interesting questions of consent and seduction that I was hoping would be explored; ideas totally ripe given the incubi's powers of persuasion, and yet they're barely touched upon.  What we get are two characters falling madly and passionately in love with each other for no other reason than that they shared a couple of desperately hot encounters, both of which were initiated by the protagonist.
In the end it felt like the story was a vehicle for the characters to have sex with each other and little more.  If this was indeed the author's aim, the novel would have been better served by either going darker and making the incubi less altruistic, adding needed weight to the story and the prospect for meaningful character development, or stripping it  of all emotional fluff and embracing the ridiculousness of the premise with a more comedic take on the situation.  Either option would have been preferable to what we got.

I wish I could say that the artwork and presentation make up for the deficiencies in the writing, but they're merely passable.  While some of the CG's are fairly nice, others are laughably bad with characters drawn in awkward positions and from unappealing perspectives.  The character sprites could have been more polished, although I have admittedly seen much worse in visual novels with a hefty price tag attached.  Full English voice acting is often touted as a "selling" point for the game, but it's disappointingly mediocre.  A few of the actors do a decent job (James standing out as one of the best), but others are too over-the-top or amateurish.  To make matters worse, the recording software used is absolutely terrible.  BUT, I can forgive these things considering its free to play nature.  I cannot, however, say the same for the writing.
As much as I wanted to enjoy Seduce Me, as hard as I tried finding redeeming qualities in this visual novel, what I came away with was simply not enough to make it worth the 13 hours I sunk into it.  I understand this is a free to play game, and there's a lower standard of quality that is expected from such games.  I get it.  But when the most important part of a novel fails in almost every way, I simply cannot overlook it no matter how little money was spent on its development.    It's truly disappointing as I felt the mythos created had a lot of potential.  I still encourage those who may be interested to check it out.  You have nothing to lose.  Just be sure to temper your expectations going in, you may actually enjoy the few good things here if you do.

This is a game thats all about ambience and story. The actual gameplay is limited, but this is cleverly hidden by the quality of the gameplay it does have, the atmosphere, graphics and story telling you experience on your way through.
Its not your traditional game that tries to impress you with in game mechanics and systems, permutations and sandboxy gameplay. Its a small game, exquisitely crafted and streamlined to be good at what it needs to be and nothing more. Its not a game trying to be a jack of all, but what it does do, its a master of.
Is it a game with lots of replayability? No.
Is it a game set in a massively detailed world with lots of interactive NPC's? No.

SanctuaryRPG is a mess and I'd had enough after playing for 3+ hours.  They should've called this game “1,2,3,3 simulator”.
Here's the game in a nutshell.  Start game by selecting classic (Permadeath) or Softcore (Non-perma death).  Then you'll pick a character type.  You'll do some tutorial stuff but by 20-30 minutes in you'll have everything available to you.  The game is essentially divided into 2 portions, dungeons (grinding) and town (farming).  In dungeons, you'll fight monsters, bosses, run into events, and occasionally get some random items.  In town, you can go to a bunch of different shops, craft items, run your tavern, and fight in a colosseum.
I don't really have a lot of positive things to say about this game.  Graphics and music are both fine, that's it.  If you're into games where all you do is farm/grind, then this is the game for you.  If you can't stand non-stop farming/grinding because you like games that are actually fun and challenging, you should strongly consider never playing this game.  There's a good game in here somewhere, but it's almost as if every design decision was chosen based on maximizing how obnoxious it could be.  I could go on for a long time on the bad stuff, but I'll try to hit the main things.
1.  There's no actual dungeon crawling/exploring in this game (at least there's none in ACT 1).  Rather than go through dungeons or explore, the game gives you a list of areas you can go to along with the recommended level for that area.  You simply press that button “1”, or “2” or “3” and hit enter.  Then  1 of 3 things will pop up:  A. You'll fight an enemy or a boss.  B. An event will occur.  Events just tell you something happening and then you make one of two (sometimes four) choices.  If you choose to pick an option that has you participate in the event, then something good or bad will happen completely at random.  C.  The last thing that happens is you'll find some random item that you don't give a crap about or you'll unlock a mercenary who acts as a passive damage buff in combat.  So 50% of the game devolves down to you pressing 2, fighting an enemy, pressing 2, fighting an enemy, pressing 2, finding an item, pressing 2, fighting an enemy, pressing 2, EVENT!  You find a box: “A” to open box or “B” to leave..... press A, “The box explodes, you're left with one hp”.  Heal up, press 2, fighting an enemy, press 2, fighting an enemy, game now unlocks boss area.  Press 3 to fight boss, beat boss, new area opens up.  Press 3 to go to new area, fight enemy, press 3, find an item, press 3 fight an enemy......... This is the game.  If you found that obnoxious to read, just wait until you play it.  It never stops until your character dies, you beat the game, you kill yourself, or you decide you'd rather go play something interesting.
2.  The other 50% of the game will be spent in the town farming items/gold.  You'll get a crap ton of craftable material.  You'll go to the blacksmith and give him your material and he'll make you a weapon completely at random.  If it's better, press “E” to equip, if it's not, press “S” to salvage it for parts.  There's no inventory system, you either equip it or get rid of it.  You can go to your own base and dig to randomly find items or dig for iron which will allow you to craft a random piece of equipment once you have 100 iron.  You can also craft armor, charms, and other things in your base.  You'll play a terrible minigame every single time you want to craft an item at your base.  How good the item will be is mostly random, especially since the game always picks the 2 character stats it will increase at random.  You can also run a tavern, which will allow you buy beer to sell to customers and randomly get gifts (equipment or craftable materials usually).  Even selling beer to customers isn't fun.  There's a set number of customers, a set price for buying beer, and a set price for selling beer.  If the price for selling is higher, buy beer and sell it until you run out of customers.  I've never seen the price of buying beer higher than the selling price, so the entire tavern is just another farming items/gold system.  The town can take a while to go through when you have a bunch of craftable material.  Then when 95% of the stuff you craft turns out to be crap, you get more craftable material from salvaging it, so you then craft more crap............  It gets old really quickly.
3.  The last thing I'll touch on is the actual fighting.  It seems like it should be quick and easy, but it isn't.  It's needlessly complex and if you actually take your time while fighting, the game would take a long, long, long time to beat.  There are way too many status/damage inflicting things going on during battles, and they occur all over the screen.  You have to pay attention to enemy distance, enemy prefix abilities, status effects on enemies, status effects on you, then you have to look out for the ensnare status effect which shows up at a different spot from the other status effects.  Bosses have bars that fill up for special attacks, you have bars that fill up for things.  Sometimes quick time events pop up after you/enemy take actions, so you need to be on the lookout for these too.  Then there're your choices for actions, these change as you take certain actions, so you'll have to look at what these do each and every time.  Probably the dumbest thing though is that the game gives you the option to press “?” to see a list of what all the different status effects do, but doing this actually takes up your turn during combat and allows the enemy to attack you.  What idiot decided it was a good idea to penalize the player for looking at what a status effect does?  Most of this is irrelevant though.  You see, during fights against normal enemies, all you need to do is press this combination over and over again until you win, “1,2,3,3”.  So that's all you'll do over and over and over and over and over every single fight.  You do have to watch your hp on occasion.  If you see it go down below 40%, press 4 to heal, then go back to pressing 1,2,3,3 over and over again.  This makes a large portion of the game brainless and pointless, as you'll autopilot through battle after battle after battle.  The only time you really need to pay attention to what's happening is during boss fights.  But even then you can just sort of brainlessly chug along looking solely for key words or keeping an eye on your hp, that's how I beat the final boss for ACT I.
I could go on about how horrible this game is but I'll stop.  It really comes down to this.  If you like braindead games where you spend 95+% of your time mindlessly grinding/farming nonstop, then get this game, because it will make you ♥♥♥♥ in your pants.  If you want to play something that will challenge you, requires skill, and will actually activate some areas of your brain, then never play this.

This is only in reference to the co-op features on Helldivers. Myself and a friend have been looking for a local couch co op game to play for a while and this looked like a very good option. We played for 5 minutes and found out that player 2 is only a reflection of player 1 within the game, without their own ability to upgrade or make their own choices, and it is only player 1 that has this ability.
It must be said that I believe the game itself plays very well, it is a fun co op game and has a nice art style, but the local co op is what we were looking for and it turned out to lack the depth we wanted.

Helldivers is a top-down twin stick shooter from developer Arrowhead, on the surface this description is underwhelming but through a combination of diverse enemies and addictive gameplay it has the potential to be the very best in its genre.
On starting the game you are greeted with a slick recruitment video giving you all the motivation you need to drop into enemy territory. You are a Helldiver and that means making the safety of Super Earth your personal responsibility, using a huge range of weapons you will spread “managed democracy” across the galaxy one bullet (or laser or toxic goo or missile or fire etc…) at a time. It takes a very satirical approach to the messaging reminiscent of 1998 masterpiece Starship Troopers.
First up is the graphics, they are not genre defining and by no means the selling point of the game but Helldivers is pretty to look at. By utilising vivid colors and an almost cartoon quality Helldivers is easy on the eye, throughout my time with Helldivers I experienced no graphical or frame rate issues. Most impressive are the weapon effects, each weapon handles very differently and you can plainly see the time and effort that has gone in to the various animations. Bullets from a LMG spray across the screen with smoking shells flying and laser guns overheat with smoke rising from the weapon, it is this attention to detail that really gives this game an edge. The only weapon that left me slightly disappointed was the flamethrower, the first spews out in a steady stream rather than the sustained wide destruction you would want from such a weapon especially as the effects on all other weapons are done so well.
Sound next, whilst lacking in variety the score is a perfect representation of how quickly things can turn bad for a Helldiver. As you land on the planet and are exploring you will be treated with a quiet mellow tune, this will quickly change when you are greeted with waves of enemies. There is nothing like standing back to back with your squad awaiting extraction as dramatic music reminiscent of final battles in big budget Hollywood movies plays, again it is these moments that set Helldivers apart from other top down action games.
Now the gameplay, this is where Helldivers really shines and this is what will keep you coming back to play it again and again. The premise is simple, you with up to three others drop on an enemy planet and you are given a series of objectives that you can complete or fail. Failing a single objective does not fail mission, you will still get the chance to extract but will be penalised when it comes to receiving XP. Helldivers is simple on paper but I cannot stress enough, this game is addictive as hell! I can’t remember the last time a game completely consumed me and I have not been able to put it down since purchasing it.
You will face three different alien races as a Helldiver. The Illuminate are an advanced bunch, capable of futurist feats and able to kill you in a single blow with a shot from one of their laser cannons. Next are the Cyborgs, these guys are heavily armed and to face them you should be to, unless you want to end up as roadkill underneath one of their hulking tanks. Finally, my personal favourite, the Bugs. These come in all shapes and sizes and can prove quite deadly to an inexperienced squad.
How you tackle these three enemies differs massively, having a single load out will simply not cut it. Take the time in the lower difficulty zones to see how the enemy operates and find their weaknesses. This should adequately prepare you for what is to come but you can never be sure and believe me when I say everything in Helldivers is out to kill you but more on that later.
There is simply so much to this game that completionists will easily be able to squeeze 100 hours of gameplay from Helldivers. You collect research points which allow you to upgrade weapons or stratagems, you get these by either collecting samples found in the map and by levelling up your character. When you have collected enough you are presented with so many options it can be a tough choice. Do you upgrade your machine gun to hold more rounds? Do you upgrade your APC to give more protection to your team? The list goes on but it is important to say that all of the upgrades have meaning and will change the way you play, nothing feels tacked on for the sake it.
It is a good idea to make your character strong as mentioned previously everything in Helldivers is out to kill you. Not only is friendly fire always on but the pods your teammates arrive in, defence turrets, mines or vehicles will instantly kill you if you are not careful. Even trying to play the game defensively can quickly end badly. Death for a single  Helldiver is not the end of the mission however, as long as one teammate is alive (and the stratagem isn’t on cooldown) your dead teammates can be dropped back into the action…just be sure to not stand underneath them when they do.
Helldivers does a very good job of making you feel part of an army with the galactic war set up. The war is fought on three sides representing the three different alien races, as you complete missions and secure planets in a particular zone you will eventually reach the alien home world. This will start a timed event calling all Helldivers to focus their efforts to defeat the enemy. Alternatively if there are not enough Helldivers fighting the alien scum the war can reach Super Earth, much like reaching a home world all Helldivers will be called to defend their home.
Besides the small selection of music and underwhelming graphics the one major downside to this game is not capitalising on its humorous tone and Starship Trooper inspiration. Whilst your character will occasionally shout hilarious comments as they fight the enemy this is all we see, I would have loved to see more cutscenes and perhaps be introduced to interesting characters within the universe.
Helldivers gets a score of 90/100. Besides its lack of story content, uninspired visuals and relatively small selection of music the gameplay easily makes you forget all of that. In fact without those minor issues Helldivers would be a perfect game. Helldivers provides some of the best white knuckle co-op action I have ever played and there is no better feeling than making it off a planet swarming with enemies with your whole squad. This game is definitely worth a full purchase as you will want to keep coming back…and bring friends, it gets dangerous out there!

Rating: 9/10
Overview: First Person Survival Horror.
The Good:
+ The atmosphere is fantastic, taking place mostly underground in subway tunnels with a few levels above ground. The atmosphere presents a bleak, desperate world with humanity desperate for survival.
+ Gameplay also compliments the atmosphere. Going to the surface requires a gas mask and air filters. Take damage and your gas mask begins to crack and break, blood and condensation will also form on the mask making it harder to see. Scavenging dead bodies and the environment plays a critical role, scrounging up as many bullets, grenades, med-packs, air filters you can find will ensure you survive longer.
+ Despite taking place mostly underground the game never feels repetitive. Every chapter introduces new areas, ideas or story elements that keep the pace moving along nicely.
+ Certain levels are designed to take either a stealthy or action approach. These levels encourage exploration.
+ In the world of Metro bullets are a form of currency but they can also be used as high grade ammunition. A cool concept, one that I would like to see explored in other games.
+ Multiple weapons
+ 4 different difficulty options and 2 different game modes to fit your play style. Spartan mode turns the game into a more traditional first person shooter, giving you plenty more resources, guns reload faster and enemies tend to be easier. Survival mode, enemies hit harder and you get less resources.
+ Great music and sound effects.
The Average:
+/- By doing certain “good deeds” you are awarded moral points, while certain “bad deeds” will cause you to lose moral points. A game mechanic that is never explained in the game. Collect enough moral points and you will experience a different ending. Both endings are short and anti-climactic, so you are not missing much either way.
+/- The voice acting and dialogue leave a lot to be desired.
The Bad:
- A severe lack of enemy variety. For the clear majority of the game you will fight one type of monster that rushes you or human enemies.
Conclusion:
A fantastic first person survival/shooter. The redux fixes a lot of problems over the original and should be experienced for anybody who is a fan of the genre.

First, let me take you back to a time in my youth. A Commodore 64 and an Amiga 500. Games genres didn't seem to have boundaries and game developers came up with cool ideas and concepts. You could walk into independent stores and see shelves of games you had never heard of, take a punt with your weekly pocket money and usually find an gem.
Then games companies found a "formula", make an FPS or RTS and it's a money spinner. People "designing" games stopped being gamers and devs and started being business men and bean counters. Things got grim...until...indie devs making their ideas into games in their home offices (and normally trying to hold down a proper job at the same time). We got back to the golden years of spending a pocket money amount and finding a gem of a game that is just different.
This game is a "golden years gem". It's different, it's not following the formula. OK there are a few indie games you could say the same of but this game just feels, well, different!
How? Well to start with it's the detail. I'm a software developer in real life, we follow the Agile development process and before that we just did everything sit of pants style. This game allows you to create your software company following (loosely) the same methods. Start off as a 1 man team doing everything very seat of pants. Hire staff, grow, expand your business and offices. As you get bigger then start creating teams of devs and designers to either work on core software or more ad-hoc titles.
You can choose to be a business software company, games, art packages or do a bit of both. And here is the gotcha, you actually start to "care" about your business and staff, the game draws you in that deeply.
At the point it's still in early access but I've had no issues with crashes or anything major. There are some points that need polish:
-Needs more options on furniture and equipment. 10 years before a computer terminal is upgraded is a long time and we all know tech moves a lot quicker!
-Non-squre rooms are sometimes difficult to recreate with a 2nd floor (walls don't seem to want to snap to endpoint)
-Networks: I'd like to create networks between servers and desktop machines so I can have control over who have access to what
-Accounts Dept: What about adding an accounts team to pay bills, chase detbers etc?
There is a modding ability so I'm sure the furniture issue will get filled quickly by the community though.
On the whole however this is a great game. I can certainly recommend it to anyone who is working in the IT community and even if you're not apart of the IT Crowd you'll still enjoy the game plus get some insight into how these companies work.
Definately worth my pcoket money!

Yuri fan review!  Just finished playing the third yuri route in Seduce Me the Otome so here are my impressions of the game going through those routes.
*Light spoilers ahead*
The overall plot is okay and I'd consider it slightly above average.  One definite plus is that there are plenty of choices in the game which contributes a strong feeling of immersion within the game.  The main character while being a bit of a blank slate to project yourself on, is still allowed to show a bit of personality and some strength of character which I consider a plus.
On the negative side, the art quality is fairly inconsistent when actually playing the game which isn't too apparent from the promo shots.  Surprisingly enough for a Ren'Py Game, it has fairly poor support for the controller, so my usual way of playing a visual novel: laying back with my computer switched to the big TV screen didn't work.
*A tiny bit heavier spoilers ahead about overall romance route impressions*
The three romance routes I played were Suzu, Naomi, and <secret char>.  Suzu and Naomi's routes were a bit on the short side and didn't really have a lot of attention given to the romance aspect of those relationships.  They also didn't really fit in with the main plot in any integral fashion.  These two routes also played pretty similarly so despite the two characters being very different in personality. the second of these two routes played won't really offer much new variety to the game.
As for <secret char>, she actually fits very well within the main plot and there's a fair amount of attention paid to some different stages of the romance.  Also one thing I liked are those few parts where the player character challenges her as part of the romance as sometimes visual novel routes fall into a trap where you're made to be too much like the character you're pursuing and/or too acquiescent to their personality.  Overall, this route is definitely my favourite of the three.
Overall I'd recommend it to fellow yuri fans.  Even if two routes are short and undeveloped, you can't say that they overstay their welcome.  With another very good yuri route, it's likely worth a yuri fan's time and definitely worth the price.

Chester Alan Arthur (October 5, 1829 – November 18, 1886) was an American attorney and politician who served as the 21st President of the United States (1881–85); he succeeded James A. Garfield upon the latter's assassination. At the outset, Arthur struggled to overcome a slightly negative reputation, which stemmed from his early career in politics as part of New York's Republican political machine. He succeeded by embracing the cause of civil service reform. His advocacy for, and subsequent enforcement of, the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act was the centerpiece of his administration.
Arthur was born in Fairfield, Vermont, grew up in upstate New York, and practiced law in New York City. He served as quartermaster general in the New York Militia during the American Civil War. Following the war, he devoted more time to Republican politics and quickly rose in the political machine run by New York Senator Roscoe Conkling. Appointed by President Ulysses S. Grant to the lucrative and politically powerful post of Collector of the Port of New York in 1871, Arthur was an important supporter of Conkling and the Stalwart faction of the Republican Party. In 1878, the new president, Rutherford B. Hayes, fired Arthur as part of a plan to reform the federal patronage system in New York. When Garfield won the Republican nomination for president in 1880, Arthur, an eastern Stalwart, was nominated for vice president to balance the ticket.
After just half a year as vice president, Arthur found himself in the executive mansion due to the assassination of his predecessor. To the surprise of reformers, Arthur took up the cause of reform, though it had once led to his expulsion from office. He signed the Pendleton Act into law and strongly enforced its provisions. He gained praise for his veto of a Rivers and Harbors Act that would have appropriated federal funds in a manner he thought excessive. He presided over the rebirth of the United States Navy, but was criticized for failing to alleviate the federal budget surplus, which had been accumulating since the end of the Civil War.
Suffering from poor health, Arthur made only a limited effort to secure the Republican Party's nomination in 1884; he retired at the close of his term. Journalist Alexander McClure later wrote, "No man ever entered the Presidency so profoundly and widely distrusted as Chester Alan Arthur, and no one ever retired ... more generally respected, alike by political friend and foe."[3] Although his failing health and political temperament combined to make his administration less active than a modern presidency, he earned praise among contemporaries for his solid performance in office.
