This game, in a word, is odd. The story is very disjointed; as the game warns you in the very beginning, it does not hold your hand at all - nor does it explain much to you. I would have welcomed a little hand-holding if it had meant a clearer story, because everything else about the game was pretty great. A lot of the puzzles fell flat, but only because most of them paled in comparison to the very first one you solve, which is fantastic. The game's atmosphere is perfect - absolutely stunning but ominous and, at times, creepy - and the beauty of the landscape and graphics makes all of the long, uneventful walks between destinations interesting. The only thing bad about the fact that your character is physically incapable of walking at a faster speed than a leisurely stroll is that many of the puzzles - and plot mechanisms - take place in random and oftentimes remote places, forcing you to explore the entirety of most areas to find it, which gets old fast. But apart from a lot of vagueness and open ends in the plot and the slow speed Prospero walks at, it's definitely a worthwhile game to play. Even if you don't understand it, it will leave you feeling strange and unnerved for days, weeks, and maybe even months after finishing it.

I'm sad that it's over, but glad to have experienced it.  The world in this experience is beyond gorgeous, and that really helps you become so immersed in it.  I found myself stopping quite frequently just to enjoy the scenery and amazing views that come along with it.  You have to unfold the story yourself, with nothing to guide you along, it's really up to how patient and attentive you can be, and you must be willing to explore the landscape if you want to make any progress.  If you're looking for something with beautiful scenery, a mystery to solve, and a gripping storyline, then hit the "add to cart" button right now, because The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an experience that should not be missed.  Thank you, The Astronauts, you've made a gem of a game.

It's a music-timed twin stick shooter with horrible execution. When the drums beat, your main generic lasers fire. If the bass drops, you get a damage shield around you. Enemies come from all corners against a static 2D muddy background picture. Overall, the game's graphics tend to be confusing and not visually appealing. The weapon fire color from enemies is not different than your own weapons, so it can be very frustrating to try to tell which are your shots and which are the shots that will hurt you. The game has some skill leveling for some odd reason, and it isn't described well enough. The game lets you guess what the icons for the different skills mean. If you are getting stuck on a level, you can try to grind the same level over and over again to increase your skills, but that work seems to go away when you move on to the next level. The experience point system goes back to zero for the new level and your skills are back to the base level again. Meaning that your hard work doesn't transfer to different stages, leaving you feeling like your previous effort has been useless. There isn't anything really rewarding or satisfying for completing a level, other than unlocking the next stage which has similar-but-not music that can be hard to anticipate if you are trying a stage for the first time.
Verdict: Music is not very memorable and gameplay is not rewarding. Give this one a pass.

I received this game for free, and I'm glad I did, because I would have regretted spending money on it. When I first heard about it, I thought "Great! It's another Beat Hazard Ultra!". That was my first mistake. I really like BHU. I like other twin-stick shooters like Geometry Wars and Waves. This game is not like those games. It's true I haven't played a lot of this game, but I've played enough to see how some things work, and there's virtually nothing to motivate me to continue playing. Here are some reasons I don't like this game.
1. No instructions. Not really a big deal, you can figure it out, but it's nice when you're not forced to guess what key to press to enter a level, among other things.
2. No sound effects. This game certainly has music, but, your weapons make no sound, your enemies make no sound, nothing makes sound. There is only music when you're playing. I guess in some ways, that could be nice. Maybe you like the ambience, I don't know. I don't like that. I'm trying to play a game, and having some audio feedback would be nice.
3. Lack of contrast. By this, I mean that enemies don't stand out from the background. Or, at least, if they do, the background is cluttered with plenty of things that 'stand out' just as well as enemies. I suppose you could get used to it after awhile, but until you do, it's easy for your eyes to focus on some moving object in the background and completely miss the missile or laser or whatever that's about to hit your ship.
4. Lack of control. You can do two things in this game: move, and choose which direction to face. You have NO control over what weapon to use or when. I tend to prefer games that give me options and flexibility over how I play. Speaking of weapons, your ship constantly switches between projectiles. You could play a song several times, learn every beat and how your ship responds to every note in that particular song, and try to  build your strategy around that. But I don't want to. I don't like flying around, wanting to shoot an enemy but being unable to and so I just fly around and aim at what I want to kill next, only to have somethign happen in the song that shoots two lazers at a 30 degree angle from your front, so you miss the ship you were aiming for, and then because it's a song and things change all the time, your lazers VERY quickly change to somethign else with some other attack pattern. So you can try to anticipate it, or react to it, and you can fail repeatedly. This is in opposition to the other games I like, where your weapons are pretty standard, and you choose when to use them, and if they change, it's probably very obvious what it's changing to and when it's changing so you can actually do something with it.
5. There are enemies that spawn in the middle of the map, abruptly, with no warning. It's not linked to the song that I can tell. It just happens. Combined with my 3rd point, this makes it disorienting. I'll kill an enemy, think an area is clear, refocus my attention, and suddenly I'm being surrounded and hit by enemies that are on a half of the screen that was literally clear a second ago.
6. Bad scaling. The game description advertises a fluctuation between fast-paced mayhem and calm tension depending on what the music is doing at the time. Beat Hazard Ultra does this same thing, and I think they do it quite well. When the song is fast and loud, enemies zip around the screen, but your weapons are at full power, and so it can turn into an intense, all-out battle. But then when the song slows down, BHU shuts down your weapons. They're still there, but they're very weak. To compensate, the enemies also slow down and also lose their weapons. It gets calm, and you can take a moment to breathe, but you've still gotta be careful with your flying to avoid getting backed into a corner. In Dub Wars, however, enemies move the same speed (as far as I can tell) regardless of what the song is doing. At fast/loud parts, as in every other part, your weapons are constantly switching it up so you never have a consistent way to take out enemies, and at slow/quiet parts, you just have no weapons at all. Which means it's basiclly the same game, except instead of any potential to kill things, you can only dodge.
7. Bad scaling. Generally, if a game allows you to collect stuff that you can then spend on upgrades, the game will also let you keep those upgrades. This makes sense, for reasons I won't explain. Dub Wars, however, has you collect "wub" in a song, and then when you die you can spend it on better health, or shields, or lasers, or side lasers, or whatever. Except that any upgrades you get don't carry over to the next level. So for every song, you basically start fresh and have to grind up for any upgrades you may want. Speaking of upgrades, they present you with several sliders for each thing you can upgrade. Except that the sliders don't work. I thought I'd be able to grab it and drag it up or down to choose how many points I want to allocate to a particular thing. But nope. You have to click a little plus or minus sign at the top or bottom of each slider. Once you allocate points, you can turn the upgrade off again, or just make it less, which is nifty, but it's still an unintuitive way of doing it. This is on top of the game giving you no indication of exactly how the upgrades work. So, ok, upgrading 'health' gives you more hp and upgrading one of your lazers does more damage, right? Sure, ok, fine. That's easy. But how much does it change? I have absolutely no idea. I don't know how much of a difference it makes. Also, for the 5 or so different kinds of weapons upgrades you can choose from, it wasn't readily obvious to me which is which. They have a name that you don't see anywhere else, and there's a preview image (just an image, most of which is just your ship), but it doesn't exactly look the same way it does in the song. There certainly seemed to be more types of projectiles in the game than what I could upgrade, and since they're so dependent on what is happening in the song and may only actually be in use for half a second at a time, upgrading any one of the weapons seemed pretty silly. To add to the confusion for new players, each type of projectile seems to get reskinned for each song, just to keep you on your toes.
There was probably more, but, I don't know what anymore. I guess it would have been nice to have the option of playing my own music if I wanted to.
I will say that it's not ENTIRELY bad. I didn't get very far, so I don't know what all it has to offer, but some of the music is decent. Obviously this depends entirely on your personal tastes, but it's pretty clearly dubstep, and you probably wouldn't be checking it out if you didn't enjoy that genre. Also, the game is sort of pretty. Sort of. I personally don't really like the enemy design and such, but, I like flashing neon and stuff. Light shows are pretty cool. This game doesn't provide the best visuals, but it was one of my favorite parts of the game.
In short, I just feel like this game could use a lot of polishing in a lot of areas. I have no idea what the actual development process was, but it gives me the impression that there were some ideas that were thrown together somewhat quickly, and not much attention was paid to how the parts actually work to provide a user experience. If some areas were adjusted, this game might be quite good. Reading some of the other reviews, it sounds like it's gone through a handful of updates already which changed the user experience rather drastically, so there is some hope. But as it stands, I am unimpressed.

SanctuaryRPG is a unique experience and an overall good game with some flaws.
Note: there aren't any direct spoilers, but characterizations of story elements. So if you don't want to know if the ending was good/bad or if the story was refreshing/terrible, you probably don't want to read further
Pros:
-The game's art 100% ASCII art and it looks pretty cool
-The music direction is on point; music is always thematically appropriate and pleasant
-The battle system is interesting and there is a lot you COULD do with it
-The story up until Act IV is decent
-The loot system can be entertaining
-There is depth to the stats and class system
-There is no inventory space regarding equipment, which makes loot-based decisions more important
Cons:
-Story past Act III is virtually nonexistant ("legion warriors" are repetitive and seem like placeholder bosses)
-Battle system rewards repition until boss fights, making the game feel grindy
*That being said, when you first start out it feels interesting and fun
-The crafting system, while initially interesting, becomes very grindy once you figure it out
-The loot and crafting system drops entirely random drops, which makes trying to find "ideal loot" hard and grindy
-There is no inventory space regarding equipment, which makes equipping your character strategically difficult and wastes a lot of the variability in equipment effects
Meh
-The ending didn't feel decisive to me, but it did feel appropriate for the game
-The music, while very good, felt repetitive due to the grind (noticibly so in Act IV)
-The town NPCs all have the same dialogue througout acts, while there is clearly potential to vary that dialogue with changes in the story
-Having grinding being important to the gameplay means that having an astronomical amount of funny names becomes critical
-The humor is hit or miss; the game has its own references [namely to potatoes] and occasionally makes use of nonsequitor jokes. (I personally enjoyed it but can completely understand why others would not)
Overall, I felt like the pros were good enough to outshine the cons. This is especially true if you're new to the game. I didn't really feel the cons of the game until the last couple of hours.

Fans of dystopian sci-fi and post-apocalyptic depictions of the future, look no further..this is definitely a game for you.
Probably one of the most immersive FPS titles I've played in a while, with atmospheric lighting effects that put big name competitors like Bethesda's Fallout series to shame. This is a rather standard linear romp through the claustrophobic ruins of Moscow that offers no  gameplay innovation or gimmicks.  You'll want to check this title out for the fun of the ride alone, as the dreary story set-up and ambient/industrial soundtrack more than make up for it.
Tout up to three weapons that can be lightly enhanced at shops,  manage battery power for your flashlight and ration out air filters for your gask mask -- that pretty much sums up the activity within the rather meaty campaign, clocking in at nearly 15 hours. The gunplay is a variety of DOOM-style frenetic combat, classic duck & cover shootout, with even a  bit of stealth thrown into the mix as well. This is a game best played on hard difficulty, as the sense of urgency and survival become all the more apparent. Ammo and air filters encountered in the field are more scarce, the enemies stronger and in larger numbers.
The pacing of the game is fantastic--You'll spend some time in the dark, dimly lit caverns and tunnels of Moscow, but you're also treated to some great topside segments in which you'll have to wear the gas mask at all times. These portions felt the most immersive, and convey a true sense of alienation from the world you're depserately trying to fix.
Storywise, you'll be playing as a young Russian who has survived the nuclear fallout of World War III. He embarks on a quest to save his dirtied, cramped colony within the Metro tunnels from being overrun by feral mutants..and that's pretty much it.
A lot of the characters thoughts are reflected through various "Log" entries hidden throughout levels. This is about as much replay value you're going to get from the game. Some of them are a bit hard to find, I definitely missed a fair portion of them. You'll learn a great deal about the backstory and events leading up to the crisis by listening to various NPC's populating the Metro settlements, or by eavesdropping on bantering sentries when on a mission. Being fed a bit more story would have been nice, but having to look and listen for it ups the immersion factor even more.
This is a grab when on sale for 4.99 or so, and an outright steal when bundled with its sequel, Last Light.  Fans of Fallout, Wasteland or RAGE are going to feel right at home, here. Next to nothing to pick over in terms of post-game content, but you may want to revisit the lovely desolation of Moscow for the sake of nostalgia alone.
Definitely going to check out the sequel.

Metro 2033 and 2034 are solid, archetypical AAA FPS titles for those looking to get their cheeki breeki on. The writing is exceptional by modern FPS standards, and I believe that can be owed to it's origins as a series of science fiction novels.... Having said that, there are a couple bits to watch out for:
PROS:
+The redux makeover makes for a gorgeously decrepit world.
+A great, melancholy soundtrack.
+Unique post apocalyptic setting makes for one hell of a underground roadtrip.
+Slavs
CONS:
- There are some fragments of writing that are essential to the story of 1 and 2 that don't make a whole lot of sense once you really think about it. I can't elaborate due to spoilers, but trust me on this.
-A whole third of the cast is voiced by Steve Blum and once I noticed I could not unhear it.
- While the graphics and presentation are for the most part great, there is a weird uncanny valley thing going on with a lot of the character model's faces. I think it's the eyes- just try counting how often they blink.
- On some occasions, the autosave/checkpoint system just straight up wouldn't trigger. So I'd make it through an area, die further on, then have to go WAY back, do it all again, only to have the game save for me at a spot that it didn't previously. Very frustrating.
+/- The game has a morality system of sorts that will determine an ending for you. It's not quite as big as it sounds, but if you go in shooting for the "good" ending, you're gonna want to look it up online as it's...actually a little convoluted with what gives you good karma and what gives you bad, ie In one scenario, watching a guy get executed gives your morality points, but actually saving him by killing his executioners won't give you morality points. You can also get good karma by staring at some corpses. It's really weird, guys.
--------------------------------
And this last bit is not a criticism, but a warning. You'll be offered to pick a gameplay style in both Redux titles: Spartan or Ranger. Ranger is billed as being a more survival horror approach with an emphasis on stealth, scrounging for ammo, and greater damage for you and your foes, plus no UI for immersion.
I went for Ranger mode, but it was a REALLY bad idea for a first, blind playthough of the series. This is most damning in 2033, where the game will not notify you of QTEs...Quite frustrating. In addition, the difficulty and game tweaks of ranger mode really don't mesh with the campaign, which was clearly designed with an action, Spartan mode in mind. It's fine for the first 2/3rds, but by that last chunk you're going to have so many action set pieces and horde defense scenarios that you may have to straight up restart some levels just to conserve enough supplies to have a chance at enduring these segments.
So just avoid Ranger mode during your first playthough. It's not worth the added frustrations for a tad bit more immersion.
CONCLUSION:
I would say the good outweighs the bad, and flawed or not, the Metro games are a unique pairing- it's not very often a book gets adapted into a video game, and as a result there some creative choices you might not have otherwise seen in big FPS gaming titles. Is it the next STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl? Not at all, and you'll be disappointed if you go in expecting that, but it absolutely stands on it's own merits.
It's for sure worth checking out when on sale.

The economy is relatively robust, there's some fun time-keeping challenges in keeping everything balanced, and there's a good bit of variety in vehicles/ crops/ activities/ etc. The graphics aren't great (crops will pop in when you're about 10 meters away, despite being able to render the buildings and mountains in the far distance), but I'll admit, they do the job. Every time I've opened the game the controls have, to some degree, randomized, including at one point, mapping one of the buttons for activating a key tool to the button for turning left. This was the most annoying example, and the first I came across, but there have been plenty of other occurences of two completely separate functions (e.g. changing what crop you sow, and activating the machine that sows fields) to the same button, or with functions completely missing. If this was the first week of the game's release, I'd let it pass, but not in a game that came out in 2010.

First thing I have to say is that the game is VERY satesfying to play, explosions feel really good and firefights can be both short and deadly or drawn out depending on how they unfold. Only problem that might be is that many units, tanks especially, are very durable and you won't take down a medium tank with less than three-four shots most of the time.
Many people complain about microtransactions and DLC and they're somewhat right, you'll at least want to buy the Western Front Armies DLC if you plan to play multiplayer, and you should play multiplayer.
The game isn't as pay to win as some claim, all the commanders are almost equally good although you will be missing out on some fun if you don't own every commander. Also the game is full of Axis players so you're gonna gave more fun playing as the allies, with less time spent waiting and all that.
When it comes to being a single player game the game has a short campaign and quite a few "challenge maps" known as Theaters of War(DLC), these include co-op maps if you have a friend to play with. And having at least one friend to play with is quite important if you want to enjoy the game properly, the multiplayer matches at least as they come in 1v1, 2v2, 3v3 and 4v4. For the Americans there a campaign called Ardennes Assault(DLC), it's quite good and I'd say it offers more than the original campaign in the gameplay department, but less in the story department.
All in all I'll recommend this game to anyone who likes RTS games and have at least one friend who does too. But keep in mind that it might very well get expensive if either of you want to try all the game has to offer.

This is a game that really hits you in the feels.  It's a game about the experience, the emotion and seeing the sights.  There's an excellent story to explore here, but the keyword is "explore".  There's absolutely no handholding and you can miss several sections that, whilst not necessary to the story, help to give a bit of background and depth to the characters and scenario that you wander through.  It's also an extremely difficult one to review without spoilers, so I'm splitting the review into two sections - info regarding graphics, handling and such at the top and the main issues and points people have raised and what to look for lower down.
So, here we go:
GRAPHICS
It is stunning.  The design team apparently created everything from real world textures and it shows, the places you go through are beautiful.  They look like a real woodland or a real mine or a real Churchyard from Northern Scotland or anywhere in the North of Europe.  The water moves so realistically you could almost think it was a video, rather than a model.  It's phenomenal what they have done and I hope more teams adopt this practice, even though it is intense work at high levels for most PCs.  It is worth it.
SOUND
It's a refreshing change to play a First Person exploration game where I'm NOT a silent protagonist.  The voice acting is excellent, though occasionally the dialogue sounds a little hackneyed although that fits in with the story content.  Other characters, who you interact with indirectly are realistically portrayed, with well-written dialogue and good voices.
Environmental sounds are well suited too.  Birds have a selection of calls, bugs can be heard and the sounds from water, fire and the creaking of trees and rustling of grass are all very accurate.
CONTROLS
Keyboard and mouse controls are simple but serviceable, personally I would have liked a bit more control options for the mouse as I have a gaming mouse and the game is lacking in sensitivity settings and programming settings for those.  I didn't play using a controller so cannot give a review of those, sorry!
EXTRAS
There are some nice hidden bits in-game, little touches that help to build the game world and characterisations and there are also some acheivements to get on Steam, though a guide will help with a couple of the more obscure ones.
***POSSIBLE SPOILERS IN SUMMARY***
I loved this game.  It's a  great detective story and the twist ending had me in tears.  Nothing in it is especially difficult, apart from one section in the mines and that can be completed through trial and error.  The mine section is irritating and feels out of place, but it is in keeping with the running theme of the game - a childs' imagination and memories.
The biggest issue most people have is that they don't know what to do to start with.  It doesn't hold your hand, it doesn't tell you where to go, it just sets you loose and lets you explore in the hope that you can find out what happened to Ethan Carter.  Look at everything, run through the woods, explore the houses and realise that, as free-form as the game seems, it has been carefully crafted to push you towards the right direction.
If you want a game where you can take your time, think and enjoy the journey, then I recommend this game.

Wishmere is a hybrid beat-em-up/fighter that tends more toward the fighter half. On the scale of the simple yet effective Fight N Rage to the technical Streets of Fury EX, it stands a few steps beyond Streets of Fury, probably even more technically minded than Guardian Heroes. To construct your combos you need to figure out which of your moves link together through study of the exhaustive move-list of various normal command moves with various chaining properties. The movesets of singular command moves end up feeling like DMC or Smash Bros on some level. Combos do not usually run long, usually three hits, reset, three hits, ult, but those three hits are all different moves. It was only late in development they added just an XXXX combo. That tells you how much they want you exploring the movesets rather than mashing X. I have seen a lot of KoF comparison but I have never played KoF so I cannot speak to them.
And these movesets deserve exploration. A half dozen characters each with wildly different fighting styles: A dash happy flame attack brawler. A mage with counters and options that can attack independent of his current state. A dark lord whose main gimmick is area control... This is a great roster, and every one is designed and balanced differently and smartly. I cannot speak to high level play but all the gimmicks are so different and interesting that I am interested in most of the cast.
There is a versus mode that is, unfortunately, local play only and with no AI.  That is a shame as it looks like an absolute blast if you can get a fighting minded friend at the screen with you. I can not, sadly.
So, for most of us the value is in the beat-em-up portion, and everyone still shines there even if you can't round someone up for versus play. The enemy variety is not much to write home about, but the levels are appropriately quick and the encounters will typically involve you exploring your character's moveset more than the enemies. To support this, there is a scripted story mode that takes you through all of the characters (Sadly without much chance to explore each character so you may have to practice a bit as you change.), as well as a Free Mode that plays the story as any character you like. Most of the content comes from Base of Darkness, which is a sizeable assortment of wave battle levels without context; just pick a level and throw down. In each of these modes you collect upgrades for your characters that you can cash in for various perks on the skill trees. Make certain moves charge faster, add a stock for your Edge move, or even add a new mechanic for some of your ability moves, the skill trees are unique for each character and always interesting and add a bit of replayability as you can try slightly different builds. The flashy character can spec for damage bonuses for stylish combo-heavy play or to boost his fire effects, for instance.
The bosses are a bit of a let down: Big, slow moving hyper-armored jerks who just walk up, stare at you for a second, and then swing a power attack. You pound them a bit, block their attack, and go back to pounding. Repeat until dead. Clearing mooks in a combat system that rewards combos only to then get this big fat anti-combo thing blocking your path is a bit of a paradigm shift but like most awkward things in Wishmere it's still perfectly manageable.
I gotta give a shout out to the story. Wishmere's story is perfectly genre-standard and I love it. A LOT of heart went into this; probably too much. In a 3 hour story mode that you could probably run through in 40 minutes tops, it is unbelieveably dense without running long in terms of cutscenes. You go from high school students to a superhero team, with betrayals, rivalries, inner turmoil, multiple crises of confidence... It just rolls through story beat after story beat with lightning speed. Three seasons of anime or comic book storytelling and thrills are all crammed in here. There's even a Deadpool-esque character cracking wise all game (Thankfully the game ends right when she's getting close to getting annoying.). It's all way, way too much for a short beat-em-up but the energy and heart the authors put into it shines through without feeling indulgent at all. I imagine 90% of you reading will think I'm nuts for liking a "generic" story so much and I can't hope to convince you otherwise. But I liked it a lot, dammit.
In the end, the core of Wishmere is a combat system that really demands some elbow grease to learn it. You will start playing it and see none of your attacks flow except for the XXXX combo, you will have to experiment to try to figure out what you can chain together. It is really tightly engineered, probably over-engineered, but it works if you are willing to learn it. I don't think the combat system is for everyone; trying to piece together a combo to find out Up+Y, Forward+X, Neutral+B (With maybe a time stop extension after that followed by an aerial combo.) is what you're meant to do may not jive with you. I'm still not all that good with it, but I enjoy what they have put together. Wishmere is something different, and that may not be for everyone, but I find it really compelling and worth exploring. And the sheer amount of quick-playing content makes it easy to pick up, play, and explore.

SanctuaryRPG caught me completely by surprise. I love older RPG's such as Nethack, Wizardry and the like and I was expecting something akin to that. What I got was a bit different, and I'm glad I took the plunge. It is more akin in some ways to games like Oregon Trail. Acting as a sort of roguelike adventure, you create a character and are given their generated backstory. Then you hop into the world proper exploring areas, fighting monsters, and trying to improve your character enough to take on the next major challenge. There are fun mini games as part of the game mechanics such as the crafting system where you need to balance the quality, durability, and "heat" of an item as you craft them. The combat itself acts in a similar resource management fashion, having the player link skills together into combos while constantly repositioning themselves in the battle to distance themselves from heavy handed enemy "charge" attacks and make sure they are properly managing their HP and MP for when enemies do big damage.
Another thing I really like is the sense of humor. I have not put a lot of time into the game yet but already there have been lots of fun little jokes that don't take away from the overall experience and really give the game personality. The aesthetics are great (I love that there is a character creation system in a game comprised entirely of ASCII) and the music is bloody fantastic with sounds that span several eras of gaming while remaining modern and appropriate to the source material.
These guys have crafted something really special. For the price I feel like I have already gotten my moneys worth only after about an hour of playing, and it is clear that there is far more depth to be found than that.

I died many times without actually getting why. SanctuaryRPG: Black Edition can be very random at times. And while the gameplay tempts you to rush encounters, since most of them can be resolved by pressing the same two or three keys over and over, doing so can quickly lead to disaster when an opponent suddenly does something unexpected. Like reducing you from full health to.. nothing.
After losing two high level characters in situations in which I had absolutely no idea what I could have done differently, my butthurt reached a point where I simply had to uninstall.
So in conclusion, I have to give a thumbs down for this one. But that's just me. If you are less of a filthy casual than me and can stomach losing hours of gameplay to hard-to-grasp mistakes and/or generally have the patience to pay attention to more or less the same screen, looking for slight differences in statuses and numbers to avoid these mistakes in the first place; go for it! The game is not very expensive. And for the price, you can get quite the amount of entertainment out of it. Just don't expect it to be overly casual.

I personally hated this game. I came into it with only positive expectations and was severely let down. I mourn the loss of the 4 dollars that went into buying this garbage.
Let's start with the comedy, which many people say is one of this game's strongsuits. This game has very "adult" comedy, but it ironically comes off as very childish. It's like some 7th grader talking about how much he loves weed and drugs, and making dumb♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes to his equally dumb friends. The references to other video game series are only references, and don't really hold any comedic weight. The funniest parts in this game are when characters are conversing, without any dumb gimmick. The witty dialouge is so much more enjoyable than "Do a Barrel Roll XD" or &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥XD".
The story isn't much better, however, I don't think anybody actually cares about the story. I wouldn't either, if it didn't hinder the game to the extent that it does. The entire game takes place inside of a simulation, which makes it feel like nothing you do has any weight. Who cares if you die? Who cares about the people you're killing? It's only a simulation. All game I was begging to be taken out the simulation, and put in an actually appealing environment. The story is essentially just you doing a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t withh the excuse of that it's "weakening the simulation".
The gameplay was simply aggravating. I remmber being stunlocked to death many times, especially by the people with bats. This is not challenging gameplay, this is annoying gameplay. The boss fights usually turn into a game of "Find the exploit" Since fighting them is so boring. Shooting feels incredibly dull too, it's as if I'm shooting a paintball gun. The powers are by far the best part of this game, but it gets extremely annoying when I have to switch to one of my boring powers in order to deal with people who are stunlocking me. The powers also lose their excitement as the game wears on though.

Great game, really. It's super fun and has awesome writing. Dialogue is top notch and the voice acting is brilliant, it's funny as well. What this game does right is that the city isn't built around the super powers, instead the super powers are built on top of the city. The missions are very good as well, coupled with moments that are hard to find in games that tries to do the same as Saints Row. Graphics, sound and music are all well done, gameplay is better than it was in other Saints Row games as well. Saints Row is king of silly open world games, but shows that they can make a extremely well done story as well.

For no moment I have thought: "Oh god those mechanics are awful", but instead I was so invested in the story that the game has created that I cared very little for anything else. I just wanted to reach the end and see how this wonderful, well structured, misterious story was about to end. And that was the time when everything fell apart. If it wasn't for that ending I could have given you a positive review and a 9.5/10 but that ending! Why does it enrage me so much? Well, it is because that ending invalidates everything that the player has done during the game. We (the players) have investigated, tried to solve a mistery, sometimes we ran away in fear from monsters(btw that part made me jump on my chair, well done!) you have made us feel invested in this wonderfully crafted story and at the very end.........(spoiler alert)........one could sum it up in: It was just a dream, Prospero doesn't exisists, Ethan Carter is dying and the Chthulhuesque creature "The Sleeper" was just a dream manifestation of Ethan! So what you (the player) did, has never happened in the fictional world of "The vanishing of Ethan Carter" you were just a fragment of the imagination of a dying child and nothing that you have done has affected the world in any way. Well, at that time I felt actually betrayed by the game! So what I did was not real but just a dream all the misteries remains with the answer: "It was a dream"? Really?!?!?! The lowest denominator of twist endings: "It was a dream" was actually used for one of the most interesting story and concept that I have seen for a very long time?!?! So yeah, that was it. That is why I am giving you a bad review, to sum it up: wonderful game, I despised the ending so much that I needed to express it with a bad review. I am sorry, I know that it couls sound very childish and not objective but I can not help myself. I think however that your company has created a very impressive game and I would love to try your future games.
Sincerely,
Jackskelter

Half-Life 2: Episode One continues the storyline, picking up right where Half-Life 2 ended (and if you haven't played that, none of the events here will make any sense), and has the same minimalist approach to exposition. I was quickly back in control of Gordon Freeman, courtesy of my mysterious alien allies, dealing with the fallout from my confrontation with Dr. Breen, and trying to evacuate City 17 with my new best friend, Alyx Vance.
Gameplay effectively builds on what existed in Half-Life 2 and has a good variety of exploration, combat, platforming, puzzles and story; I never had an opportunity to pilot any vehicles, but didn't miss it; There's a greater focus on a single AI companion resulting in a lot less opportunity for frustration; There's still a problem with physics objects and platforming, but those sections seem better designed around those flaws and
less frustrating; And, again the ending is quite the cliffhanger, though it feels a bit less abrupt compared to its predecessor.
Episode One is a fantastic continuation of Half-Life 2's story. The difference here is that Alyx has become your co-op partner. She's a great character and I'm happy you get to see her more here.

Wishmere is an excellent game and I highly recommend this game to those that love "old school" beat em ups, or wanting to get into the genre.
The gameplay is great, it really does have that old-school beat em up feel to it.  The attacks are quite fluid and fast too.  Although there are some differences that separate this game from the rest.  You can perform combos to do high amounts of damage.  There is an active block that you can utilize to negate damage.
As for characters, each one has their own unique set of special moves and secret arts.  Special moves can be used on their own or can be used in a combo, kinda like a finisher.  Secret arts are like your ultimate moves, some can wipe out enemies on the screen, while others may grant you additional attack powers.  There are also team attacks that you can perform with another player that can potentially wipe the screen of enemies.
There are currently two modes that you can play, arcade and story mode.  Arcade mode has 3 difficulties:  easy, medium, and hard.  These 3 difficulties are basically like horde mode except it is not infinite, after you beat 5 rounds the level ends, but you can always replay.  Then you have your endless mode, the rounds are infinite and you play until you run out of health.
As for story mode you get to learn more about the characters and the lore of the game.  There isnt much currently, but will definitely be expand upon as the game gets updated.
There is only local coop as of now.  Online coop is TBD.  From a singleplayer standpoint the game is still very enjoyable, not one moment did I ever get bored from playing by myself.  That is not to say I dont want Online MP, I would love to see it implemented.
As for hours to price ratio, you will definitely get your moneys worth from this game and more.
Overall Wishmere is an excellent game to play and add it to your already awesome collection of games.  I hope this review helps you in deciding whether to purchase the game or not.

First of all, saying that saying this game is genius is a understatement is an understatement in and of itself, this game is the Hawking of game designs, it's that original and unique. It's like they put the best parts of several genres into a blender and this game is the delicious smoothie that came out. There's Rogue-like, Text-Based adventures, and Turn-based RPGs elements, and an outstanding humour as well. Also, it's all in ASCII. Yes, you read me right, and that was one of the best design decisions made by the developers, I'll get into that soon.
Several years ago, someone known as The Matron searched and found a legendary sword capable of destroying armies by itself, and with that sword, she set out to destroy the world as we know it.
But then, a hero appeared, a powerful man, a born leader, the guiding light to command us all. Cyrus, The Magnificent (Y'know, Tim, The Enchanter's little brother). After the great war that occurred after our Hero's arrival, and our victory, The Matron was sealed in an ice crystal, but after some time of peace, she broke out, escaping back into our world, and Cyrus, Disappeared…
Now you, brave hero, must stop The Matron once and for all, and rid this world of darkness.
The game's story is really clever and funny, creating a randomly generated one for each character you make, and trust me, you will have to make several before completing this game, giving you plenty of backstory to read, all of them incredibly hilarious.
The game is like a text adventure game, the screen displays several actions, and you choose one of them, but it requires a lot of strategy, as the combat is turn-based and really difficult to master. the game also has several rogue-like elements to it, perma-death and unlocks for future runs, and everyone knows that's how you get to my good side, I adore rogue-likes. But don't be fooled, this game has very little RNG to it, it is all strategy, without that you won't win the game! There's also a lot of character development and creation, you can choose a class, a race, and a weapon specialization, it's a bit complicated at first, but when you get the hang of it, you see how well done it is.
The graphics are honestly amazing for ASCII, it shows how much time the developers spent on making the enemies and the scenery, and the music and sound effects are just wonderful, it truly feels like those old games, and there's also a cover of the soundtrack in the piano, and it is lovely.
Everything is just so old-school, I love it.
And that brings me to the main selling point of this game, It looks and plays like the old MS-DOS games, but with a modern design, story and humour to it, and it feels great, this game is nothing short of genius, you've really got to commend the developers for making such a great piece of gaming art.
Overall, if you've lived in the era of the birth of gaming, you've got to play this game for the nostalgic value, and if you haven't, you also need to play this game to get an idea of how games used to be, it's just a wonderful piece of game history and art.

SanctuaryRPG is probably one of the best RPG's I've played, and this is in large part due to it's simplicity. It has complex combat mechanics like Dwarf Fortress, quality battle music of any 90's era RPG, the humor of The Hitchhiker's Guide, and the feeling of nostalgia for older games that very few "8-bit RPG roguelike mashups" can accomplish.
If I had two complaints for this game, they'd be as follows: I wish the game was available on Linux. I program enough to know that this game is written in C++, and from what I can tell, uses libraries that are available on Linux. It may not be as easy as "press button to Linux", but it'd be nice for the few fans who don't often use Windows.
My other complaint is that I wish I knew about this game sooner; this game would have made my childhood.
10/10

As a millenial, I was astonished about the detailed pictures you can get out of ASCII symbols. The music is not bad either.
Those positive things said, this game does not feel good to me. As you do not see any moving sprites, it is naturally very much focussed on text and numbers, which means reading all the time (of course without voice acting). The omnipresence of stat numbers makes the combat and world exploration quite abstract and static. As this kind of technology cannot possibly win you over on a visual level, the writing could have been the means to create some kind of atmosphere. Unfortunately, the creators missed this opportunity, making an attempt on a weird surrealistic humour that did not make me laugh once (Pony Island was much cleverer in my opinion). Even worse, it destroys the immersion again and again, and you should not do that in an RPG unless you are really talented in writing self-ironic and fourth-wall-breaking scripts.
It is interesting to try out new and old concepts as alternatives to the modern mainstream, but there is a reason why ASCII-interfaces are not used anymore. Sorry - 3/10 from me.

I'll start by saying this is probably the best $0.79 i've ever spent (and also pardon my sub-par attempt at reviewing, i'm not used to this)
Combat consists of going through combo-attacks, while keeping an eye out and reacting to enemy attacks. There will be various prompts warning you of enemy attacks, so you have a turn or two to react accordingly. During combat there are also various other abilities and prompted-actions you can perform (react to an enemy attack by charging, grappling, etc.).
Leveling is not limited to grinding enemies though, as you can study in the library, play the crafting minigame (provided you have the materials) to gain xp, as well as tending to a Bar.
Progress relies pretty heavily on your current gearing, so mining ore and collecting materials to craft items should be a priority... or you can get lucky and RNGesus will give you awesome gear.
TL:DR: Combat is turn-based, trying to brute force it will quickly lead to death. Craft or find gear to kill stuff faster and not get turned into mush. Burn all the Potatoes. Do not try to approach hobos, they hurt. Enjoy the glorious soundtrack. Do not contract dysentary.

I found this game a couple years back when it first entered early access. As a fan of both dual stick shooters and electronic music, I decided to purchase this for the small price of $4.99.
This game has been through several different iterations, almost every time i launched it it was different. Recently though, it seems to have been completely overhauled, save the music(which is a shame).
In its current form, the game feels too dependent on grinding for currency to use the upgrade system. The levels are significantly harder than any of the iterations i played previously, contributing to the overall grind-y feel.
I was dissapointed to see only a few songs added over the 2 years this game has been in development, however i understand why the developer chose not to add more. The whole mechanic of the game is based on each individual song, so you get a much more responsive feel to each level. This being the fact that different sounds correspond to different weapons firing (the mechanic that made me like the game in the first place).
However, this mechanic is also the games downfall. This makes it much more difficult to add music to the game, as each song has to be built independently from any others. As well as some songs have up to 10 seconds of nothing triggering weapons where you basically just run around the screen trying not to die.
overall, at $9, i dont recommend this game. If you can get it on sale though, id definitely say pick it up.

Got this for free from Loot Crate and I love it. I was confused as to why my ship didn't fire when I clicked and was laughing when I found out the music is my weapon. Replayability is huge with tons of upgrades specific to each level, and I mean, you can honestly replay a level til you're sick of the song.
Can definitely recommend if you're a dubstep fan, you get to know a lot of new music and artists, and definitely also recommended if you enjoy the space ship pew pew games.
Only downside from me is that the backgrounds sometimes move and looks like enemies/missiles, can make it disorienting but not too bad.

PROS:
-rhythmic gameplay in a non-band game (see: Necrodancer, Retro/Grade, Super Hexagon, and...sadly those are my only examples)
-Fast paced arcade shooter stuff, bullet hell on higher difficulties
-Really addicting, amazing music
-Mind-blowing background and bullet graphics (though some animations seem to not play when you kill certain enemies with certain weapons - is it a bug or just the method of killing?)
CONS:
-At times quite disorienting (lots of projectiles may blend with the environment, or enemies might sometimes spawn right on you without telegraphing such as in Choose Your Weapon)
-Some songs' styles are a bit all-over-the-place in terms of consistency (some songs have a really melodic style to it for the first half and then suddenly break out into trap or bend their rhythm, though they do provide really nice opportunities for weapon use). While I can excuse it, I would have liked if the songs focused on the instruments/sounds that the weapons already had before those moments, to keep a flow going like with the first song.
-No custom song system as of December 30th 2016; we neeeeed it~!
OTHER COMMENTS: the difficulty seems slightly biased toward leveling up, but given you're supposed to learn the songs and levels inside and out through replaying, I don't mind it. Keeps the levels fresh and adds optional difficulty without the need for a huge roster of different songs.
OVERALL RATING: 8.5/10, definitely worth the cheap price and even more worth the music. I'd put it somewhere between Necrodancer and Retro/Grade in terms of style, music, and gameplay. If you buy cheap games for novelty, I'd say get this now - the devs just put out a new song/level and the recent surge of activity has piqued my interest in any additions to the game. Here's to hoping that the game continues to have support and updates over the months!
Also, Jerod @the8bitdrummer on Twitch had a stream in which he raised money for charity and passed out five copies of this game with permission from the creators. The dev team are respectful, fun, and lovely people (with awesome music taste ;) )

The slogan of the game is 'Good Night. Good Luck'. Now, first, you might think you're utterly shagged at night time, and while it is true when you start off or play on Nightmare for some reason,
, it's more 'Good Luck' to the zombies finding you, and then catching you or killing you before they die themselves.
Now this is Dead Island, and in fact, a zombie game done right. A kinda desolate, but simple plot, with fun gameplay, a good co-op system, insane weapons (I mean, just the mention of the EXPcalibur is enough), and honestly a well done villain. You learn to sympathize with your fellow survivors and even enemies, which is a merrit in itself.
The amount of gore is just
. Seeing a head get sliced clean off and then do 5 flips before it hits the ground never grows old, and dropkicking zombies in the face and watching them sommersault off the building?
. Human enemies are a bit of a annoyance early on, but when you can start laying the smaams down on them, it's fun as all hell. I think the reason why combat works in this game is cus it focuses on you to be accurate (hitting enemies in the leg stuns them, while head has a high chance of a insta-kill) and to keep moving (a lot of attacks are movement base, such as Grapple, Vault, Vault Drop etc.)
It's expansion, the Following, is just every amount of better that it needs. It's fun, it's new, and it tests your abilities even further.
So, to summarize, if you have no friends, get this game. If you have friends, get this game. If you have money, get this game. I'm not kidding, I doubt you'll go wrong with it.

We are basically told "If you want to play this game, you will follow our vision - any deviation will not be tollerated.  We are right and anything you want to do is wrong."  So, no mods, no cheats, nothing the developers haven't put in themselves (see note below).
If there's one place modding SHOULD be allowed, it's in the single player game - it cannot spoil the experience for anyone else, only yourself.  And who better than you to say what you find enjoyable?
One other thing that bugs me - the cut scenes have a dreadful 'graphic novel gone wrong' look to them and the interface feels blocky and gets in the way, so other than the story (i.e. single player campaign) there's not much to recommend it.
* Note: while I've not found any way to mod the SP campaign, there are several ways to cheat.  But when activated the save option is disabled, so unless you're going to play the whole thing in one sitting, it's a bit pointless.

Recommended for those are into retro-style games, unique RPG experience and catchy tunes.

1. Control and Gameplay : it's easy to get used to the gameplay (mostly use only ONE letter/number to do action), it's does not require high requirement pc (because the design is so simple), so far no lags/ bugs. Some skills / status are hard to remember (there are A LOT of them), but there is a tutorial book so rest assured.
2. Fun Factor : I like the catchy tunes and the game simple design, reminds me of older type of rpgs on older consoles. Because of the simple control of the game, I could do something else by playing (for example: eating my ramen). Also, there is a difficulty slider (if you want the game easier/ harder). There are a lot of choices we need to make and it AFFECTS the actual gameplay. I like it because I could make my own story as well.
3. Graphic : very cute even though it's only using simple ASCII art. Very refreshing concept and contrast to the mega popular 3D objects. No special interface for this game, though. I don't know why can't it open the steam overlays to capture images (?) Too bad there were a lot of moments to be remember.
4. Replayability Value : VERY HIGH because there are several save slots for different characters (with each different jobs), different playstyle (even though some moves are similar, just some minor changes in names/ description), different quest and difficulties (still the main quest is same for all playtrough), and also the main reason is :
5. Sound : catchy tunes also I get some free piano style music dlc. Unless you want some real "music", this one will not amuse you that much.
6. Story : can't say it's good yet. So far, all of the character have same main story and it's kinda linear and "gimmicky". If you want real story (and you are not into the "make your own story" thing), this game offers not much of a complexity of a heroic story. The conversation also doesn't hold any meaning to the story.
7. Value for Full Price : to support the great indie developers out there, why not? But yaay I get it when Steam Winter Sale being hold, so got it for only 10% of full price. It's kinda pricey for full price, but still okay since I realized making this kind of game need some deep thoughts from the devs.

- This game has evasion and block, but late-game bosses kill you via unavoidable, everlasting and incurable % max HP bleed, doom, and mana threasing.
- This game has heals, but ALL of them deteriorate when you use ANY of them in a boss fight. I basically had to drop half of the combo set that has heals in it in order to preserve heal power for the last one third boss gauge.

3) Forget about new game+
- This game has classes, but all classes have the same 1, 2, 3, 3 combo with little to no variations (same damage, same cost, same heal effects), the same mantras, the same specials, the same force barrier, the same time reversal, the same ultimates, etc.

It's a good and enjoyable game but only for its first act where you’re still discovering new mechanics and the game itself.. After that it becomes a mindless grinder with the most uninteresting and cliche story ever. Just go to the blacksmith, exchange scrap for new weapon, salvage or equip it. Get more resources. Get quest (always the same), check if there’s some new weapons for sale. Next, go to market and buy stuff for blacksmith and take quest. Go to library – read books. Get exp. Create more books with hides. Go to your camp, dig some holes. Upgrade your camp. Craft randomly generated swords, shields, armor and charms. Go to tavern, sell beer, get quest to kill some mobs. Finally go kill some mobs with the same pattern: press 1, press 2, press 3, press 3. Repeat. Sometimes you need to avoid incoming attack with repositioning, heal yourself with 4 or use special attack with R. That’s it. Repeat all the steps all the way through to the end of the game. Mindless. User reviews for this game are misleading - for a "overwhelmingly positive" you're expecting an amazing game instead it's at most just OK. I don’t know, maybe it’s just nostalgia thing for some people, but I don’t get it. I’m not recommending it, maybe if you’re getting it for less than euro than it’s worth trying, but other way it’s not worth it. Like I said before, if it ended up in ACT I than I would’ve left a recommendation, but as time passed it became more and more dull experience. This game fails as a rougelike and with its uninteresting story fails as a RPG too.

~Warning: Spelling may fry your brain, I just got done streaming this after being up for 19 hours. I'm tired.
First off, Let me just say that I'm a very nitty griity reviewer. I make it a point to rub it in everyone's face what is wrong and what is right within a game, be it story, delivery, or the gameplay itself. It makes it hard to for me to say yes or no upon writing a review.
Luckily: I didn't have that issue here.
Long story, short:
This game is short, sweet, charming, and... Hell, great to look at.
Playtime expected on first run: 2-5 hours
Overall Rating: 9/10
Cons:
My only issue with this game is the "hitcheck" system on the rocks, which can make you stuck for a short while. This is a minor issue though, as f7 fixes that at the cost of 1-3 minutes of progress at most; often only costing 30 seconds or less in most cases.
Difficulty.
This game is a bit on the easier side with all the checkpoints, but getting from one checkpoint to the other can offer a challenge, which is fun.
The gameplay.
The gameplay takes a little getting used to, being a physics game. But after you adjust to the game, it does everything right. Nothing feels choppy, and this game doesn't try to be anything it's not. On top of it all, it's really relaxing and enjoyable.
The story.
This story is so charming that in the end, I was left speachless. This gam- no, adventure, was thrilling to watch, as the story unravels. Be warned that the voice acting did feel a little monotone, but that did as much harm as it did good, and was enjoyalbe in the end.
The price.
It's slightly overpriced, but only if you plan on playing it once, like myself. If you are a completionist, you could be looking at a 10+ hour game, with unlockables and challenges to test your skills. It's also very nice to look at and explore when you can.
The breakdown:
I base my rating on 5 simple things: Gameplay, Story, Price, Stability, and overall experience within the game. The last one holds the most weight, as a cheap, wellmade, story rich game can feel worthless if it bores the Hell outta me.
Gameplay: 9/10 ~Fun to learn and play
Story: 9/10 ~It's a ride, with very little holes in it.
Price: 8/10 ~Not too pricy, and many things can be done to add to the game's lifespan.
Stability: 9/10 ~Game never crashed or critically failed on me once, and I streamed it on twitch the whole time.
Experience: 10/10 ~I felt like I was in the game myself experiencing all of the marvel along with the character.
Overall: 9/10 ~Worth the buy. Good for a calming night with nothing to do.

I wanted to believe in Moonbase 332. I didn't care about the graphics but I wanted to believe in a little FPS that I could enjoy.
Moonbase 332 having been in many bundles, I got a key for myself thanks to that. I decided to give it a try yesterday because I was wondering if it would be any better than Galatic Hitman. And it is better than the latter. At least, levels are differents, you have a lot of weapons and the enemies are moving.
You're arriving in a secret base used by Austria to develop a virus that would have infected Germany. And guess who will clean it? You!
While the story isn't the plot of the year, I was immediately thrown into my biggest mistake: changing binding keys. Yep, it was still in beta. But I would have never imagined that I would loose my reload button. I couldn't reload ANY weapon. Any! I had to wait until I wasted my bullet to reload.
And the reload action.... My god, why is it so slow for the dual weapons? Even other games take less time for that.
I never understood why Zombie Nazis, walkyries with crossbows and slashers appeared in the game... or flying skulls for the matter. For a game about infected people, the developer added some paranormal stuff.
But the best? I don't know how the zombies with bazookas managed to hit me even when hidden. And I was dodging the rockets, I really was. Apparently it's vain because they're hitting you each time. That's how I managed to loose many of my lives.
Because you have 10 lives before a gameover... and you have to keep counting. Because the HUD only shows the weapons and your ammo. No health bar. You don't know if you need to reload a save or not.
About the weapons, they're nice: the shotgun is powerful through three bullets isn't enough. I couldn't enjoy two weapons because despite showing having still ammo, they refused to reload when it was at 0. I cursed that because they were among the most powerful! Yay!
I don't care about the graphics but when you see the last bonus level, you're asking yourself why it's more "alive" than the main story. And in general, bonus levels are refreshing.
And why did the dev ignore completely puzzles? I mean, the last bonus level showed that you could have mixed shooting and brain. But no, you're just running around to find buttons to open doors.
The big problem is also that I've crashed constantly at the end of a loading level. The only answer you'll get is "reload the autosave - problem solved". Yeah, apart that my computer is in the recommended specs and that having the message "FPSC stopped working" without any cause is hard.
I would have been more positive about the game if it wasn't for the crash, some problems with enemies with bazookas and my ♥♥♥♥ed up rebinding, though I think that the dev will probably patch that one.
Between Galatic Hitman and Moonbase 332, choose Moonbase 332 because the dev did work on the game and didn't take you as fools. But in the end, I can't recommend it if the game is always crashing. I really can't. Would the problem disappear, then, you can go ahead and try it.
Sorry to put a "No" for this game. I really wanted to believe in the game. I was happy to see the keys in the bundle. I put it in my wishlist. In the end, I still want to believe that there will some improvements though....

I was expecting another Dead Island game to an extent..... perhaps Dead Rising: Parkour Edition.  What I got was something else.... I loved the Open-World Rpg/Action FPS mashup that was Dead Island..... warts and all it found a place in my permanent playlist.  Dying Light, while only giving you one character and thus one set of skill-trees (as opposed to the 4 in DI and the 5 in Riptide), is a more polished and in some ways more ambitious experience.  The graphics are AMAZING and on my GTX970 with no GPU bottleneck I get a consistant 60 fps fully maxed as long as I turn off V-sync..... v-sync want to drop it down to 30 anytime it dips even slightly below 60.  While Dead Island gave you several cool maps to explore and lots of side quests- I'm finding Dying Light's maps to be denser with things to do and the parkour element adds a verticality to the world that increases the density of the world exponentially.
In the beginning DL gives you the experience of being a helpless survivor of a zombie apocalypse.... you can take on the weakest zombies 1-on-1 but as you add a second, third.... ninth, tenth.... running becomes a more viable option.  Luckily the parkour aspect of the game is REALLY REALLY fun.  An Agility Skill-Tree slowly enhances your speed, agility, and parkour skill but even at Level 1 Agility it's a blast to jump from roof to roof, weaving between swarms of zombies.  As you continue fighting you level up your Power Skill Tree.... eventually being able to fight on even terms against some of your stronger foes.... swarms will still mess up your day quite badly if you take them lightly however.  A Survivor Skill Tree includes more misc. skills and abilities including better crafting, bartering, and some gamechanging power-ups.  It is also linked to the quality of loot in the world..... level up Survival enough and you'll start finding firearms, bows, and much stronger and varied melee weapons.  You get lots of consumable items ranging from firecrackers to distract zombies to molotov cocktails to freezing grenades that turn zombies into zombicicles.
I'm 60 hours into my current playthrough and apparently have roughly half the game left including about 15 current side-quests and quite a few optional areas to explore.  I have yet to play the DLC so I won't comment on that- but the base game has already been worth what I've paid and I've got quite a lot left to play.  A few last notes- there is a day-night cycle and the game is.... quite different... at night.  The scary zombies come out at night and it makes it quite an adventure just to make it from one safe-house to another.... you eventually get some tools to assist with survival at night.... but I'm always worried when I see the sun start to go down and I'm not close to a safehouse.  Lastly- I've only played on the hardest difficulty and I highly recommend it.  It makes every enemy encounter memorable and stressful, especially early on when you don't have on-fire baseball bats with nails sticking out.....

Up front: This game is very short - exepect to finish it in four hours or less unless you somehow miss one of the puzzles and have to backtrack. It offers no real replay value - while the story is presented in a non-linear manner where the only puzzle you need to complete before the others is all the puzzles before the last one, there is no variation. Only one solution for any given puzzle, and all puzzles must be completed to finish, leading to a sense of guide dangit if you bypass one of the early ones, which could be easy to do if you weren't coming the land. If you can tolerate a short and linear game for a vivid experience, I'd recommend it.
That is the only major complaint I have with the game - the plot is very good with an excellent ending, the narrator is pleasing to listen to ( although not as good as a Bastion ), the environments are fairly detailed with a sprinkling of places you can't enter as part of the plot railroad. The soundtrack is great, and the sound work is just as good. The graphics, while not the best in the world, are very well done and sell the setting.
The main puzzles are fairly simple, but interesting - you will be attempting to solve murders of people and must track down each clue before you enter a timeline where the events must be placed in the correct order ( which can lead to some guesswork as not all are clear until you get it wrong the first time ). The side missions are more varied - you chase an astronaut and go into space, you must navigate a house where all the doorways have portals in them, making them line up correctly to reach the wizard's protected room, and a few others.
If the developers were to release a TellTale-type chapters game following the mentioned but unelaborated previous cases of the player, Paul Prospero, I'd be all over that in a heartbeat, but the experience itself is worth a few bucks - certainly as much as you'd pay for a visual novel or light book - but not quite 10 dollars - once it reaches the 5 dollar mark it becomes worth it.

I bought this game because it had a very similar look to Alan Wake, another game I would recommend if you enjoy this.
The game starts out innocent enough gradually becoming more and more eerie as it reaches the climax. Using interesting game mechanics and problems/puzzles that will more than likely have you reaching for a pad of paper or a wiki I found it was difficult to come to grips with at first, but once I understood the basic mechanics (or actually read the notes left behind) it was quite simple to pick up, and very interesting to unravel.
The gameplay itself is very fluid, no loading screens to ruin the serenity or immersion which is very impressive, visually stunning and very well put together.
I have 2 gripes with this game:
1) It is totally open plan, the game makes it very clear from the start that it isn't going to hold your hand, because of this I walked straight passed 2 puzzles, missed the 3rd and did the the 4th scene first, then went back in case I'd missed something - Also when getting achievements later I found you can get through almost 90% of the game without actually completing any of the puzzles. Obviously you won't have a clue what's going on when you are eventually forced to solve one, but I think a lot of people will get themselves confused by the non-linear gameplay and stop playing.
2) There is a jumpscare - don't get me wrong, they have their place in the gaming world, but this really didn't seem like the game. Fair play to the dev's they did it ONCE, and after it happened I learned not to do it again. In a game where you don't meet another person throughout, and the only interaction you have with "other people" is your inner monologue and flashbacks, when I saw a ghoulish figure I thought he was another flashback or puzzle piece. I was certainly not expecting him to dive on my screen and devour me, it just seemed out of place with the atmosphere of the game.
TL;DR
It took me 3 hours to get all the achievements and finish the game to an extent where I am happy I didn't miss anything, and took enough pretty screenshots to last a lifetime, probably not worth the RRP steam has it for, but if it's in a sale I would definitely grab it.

It's an IT engineering/office manager, which for some messed up reason is actually fun to me.
It best compares to games like MadGames Tycoon, GamersGoMakers and obviously the inception of the entire genre - GameDevTycoon by Greenheart games.
The office part is very close to MadGames Tycoon, which means that you are building the entire building. It's not exactly "The Sims", but it gets the job done, once you've memorized the categorization of items. The building part is solid. It all happens on grids, but then again you are building an office and not a theme park. It doesn't throw standard rooms at you. The game gives you the freedom to build and think about your layout and build a muli storied building to be proud of, because those things aren't cheap to build.
Speaking of money, the economy in this game is maybe not the best presented, but DEFINITELY the most detailed of all current indie games about management. It's all there; A field of competitors putting out their games, a stock market of your competitors, including hostile takeovers, aswell as a software market that is ever shifting from one product to the next. Distribution channels matter. Marketing matters. You create your own office and structure it in groups and rooms that help you engineer the software. The other companies will always keep you on your toes!
If you don't have the leading Operating System at the beginning of the Game, there will be a decision to be made: Go with your hope on your own OS, but a small portion of the market, or bow to the big guy and just develop tools for his OS. If you make more money than him that way, you might actually be able to buy the next bigger company. Sweet monopoly!
You can take your company on many paths in the game. You don't have to be a video game company, as in all the other games. You can be the guys that do tech support for other companies and do contract work in separate teams. You can stay a small company and just serve a high priced niché product, like putting out the best 2D or 3D graphics tool. You can be a company that just creates marketing bubbles, etc.
The path to success isn't an easy one at first. You will have to put some effort into the first hours. The way I learned, was to try over and over again on a limited budget, without endulging the 500k starting option, which is also there. If you do well in the beginning, you can take a 100k loan over 2 years and actually pay it back!
The game is steadily developing, but not exactly at the speed of light. The technology is solid and it's completely playable with lots of features. The detail in some parts of the game, makes you wish for even more options and challenges. I literally wished, the game ran at a slower pace, but gave me more trouble in the day-to-day management. I barely remember any of the workers names after a game. They are totally just numbers, because they are looking like little plastic figures.
If I have to fire Karen from accounting (accounting should also be in the game and isn't btw.), it should feel a bit of a downer, because I should be able to see the sad little face afterwards and I'm not, which ironically gives me a sad face, which you can't see either.
TL;DR
Solid stuff; Walls of Numbers; Detailed Market; Learning Curve
