***
2033: a well crafted mixture of an old-school and modern shooter (leaning more to the modern side) with an incredibly well crafted atmosphere and visuals. The combat is decidedly average, but is saved by great-feeling and great-looking weapons and by the fact that it's well paced and I very rarely felt overwhelmed by it. The story keeps a lot to itself (which I liked) and offers some choice with regards to the ending (which I don't like, since Last Light picks a canon ending and throws everything else away), the supporting cast is reasonably memorable and decently voice acted (with Russian VA at least).
The only two things I can really criticize are the facts that the game at times feels very inconsistent with its combat mechanics (trolley ambush and Librarians were a pain and felt more luck-based than anything else) and that the cutscenes were extremely repetitive and at odds with the gameplay itself.
If you're looking for silly comparisons, it's kind of like the narrative gameplay of Half-Life 2 and the atmosphere of STALKER (and I'd say that the Andrei Tarkovsky film had an even greater influence than the STALKER games) had a mutated baby.
***
Last Light: to me personally, this is a strictly worse version of the original game. While the story is, broadly speaking, more fleshed-out and filled with characters that develop a closer relationship (for better of for worse) with the protagonist, it feels a bit too exposition dump-ey at times. While that in itself isn't a huge problem, more and LONGER and still repetitive cutscenes were added (sure, a few select are really visually impressive and break the mold a bit, but most were still just you getting captured and then rescued, both COMPLETELY out of your control), there are more large combat encounters (which just drives the point that the combat in these games is average at best home ever so painfully) and for some weird reason, now we get a bunch of weird boss-fights that completely break the combat mechanics established by the game up to that point, and are then never reused. Now, this would be fine if this was a throwback-oldschool shooter, but it still tries to be grounded and 'realistic', and those boss battles feel completely out of place (I'm not even going to mention the fact that in some boss fights you have to shoot specific places at ONLY specific times, and are guided by glowing red signs...) and... boring.
Even with all that, I'd still recommend the game to anyone who enjoyed the original, just bear in mind that you might find yourself disappointed with the sequel.

I really hate to give this game a negative review, but it really didn't deliver what I wanted.
There are three main points I want to adress that would improve the game.
1) Feedback from the screen. In this game, the music only controlls the character... Thats it. There is no system put in place that controlls screen effects (such as screen shake or motion blur) enemy patterns, or color changes. In music games, you need the full experience, this only has it partially done.
2) Design. This game in my opinion is lazily put togeather. Each stage is a square in which you fight in. There are no walls exept for on the outside, and it is the same size in every level. Not only that, but the enemy design in all over the place, but very condenced at the same time. In each stage, you will see the same 3-5 enemy types over and over. And it changes every level. None of them are the same stage to stage, but they are really repetitive in the ones they are in.
3) The upgrade system is horrible. If you are someone who wants to get the best ship they can by the end of the game, this game is not for you. The upgrades are level to level, and not permanite. This means that if you want to grind for levels, it's only going to give you points on the level you are on. This is understandable if you think of it in the way that they don't want you to farm for a long time, but not get so over-powered that you can beat every level first try, but it still doesn't make sence after that. Not only this, but upgrades change nothing on the visible ship. You can get as many upgrades as you like, but your ship will stay the exact same all the way. Although this is a minor detail, it still annoys me on a low level.
Alright, now that all the bad things are there, lets list some good ones.
1) There is controller support. I always find this to be a plus because it encourages more casual gaming. It also makes the movement a whole lot easyer.
2) The bullets and music fit togeather very well. There might not be much else with the music, but when the bullets shoot, I can really see it fitting with the music in every way. This also leads me to something else that could be improved - quiet points in music. Whenever you are going throgh a build up, or the start of the song, it has no aspects that help you shoot. Everything stops, and you are left up to your doging skills. This is very annoying, and partially ruins the gameplay.
So, this is a good game. Would I recommend it? No. At least not for this price. If you are wanting to try this game, I would recommend getting it from a place like♥♥♥♥♥or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Or just wait for a sale.
So, final words. This game is a good concept, but it was not made in a way that satasfies.

A Story About My Uncle's irresistable charm is established within the first few seconds of starting the game, and it never lets up. From the voice of the narrator to the scenery of the different locations you visit,

It can be argued that the game's length is a bit on the shorter side, clocking in at around 2 hours to complete the story. Yet, this succinctness lends itself to the fairytale nature of the game, never overstaying its welcome in any one setting, and quickly wrapping up when the story was done and told.
If it is one thing I would like to point out to the developers, it is the scene involving the giant eye worm in the caverns. I loved it! While not particularly difficult, as well as being a very short aspect of the game, the atmosphere it created was simply fantastic and fitting. Just as the eye worm really represented the setting it was found in (dark, strange cavern), I would have liked the other settings to also have their own equivalents. For example,
Overall, A Story About My Uncle is a sweet game that caught me by surprise with its incredibly huge jumps and fantastic story delivery,

Take elements from Portal, Bioshock: Infinite and Dear Esther and mix them in the blender - the result?  A first-person platformer on floaty mountains with the narrative pacing of Dear Esther.
You are a nephew who has discovered a suit from your uncle's laboratory that will take you to a mysterious place where rocks float on air.  The suit acts as a device that tethers platforms much in the same vein as Just Cause but with limited usage.  Like portal, the whole mechanic is soly based on that specialized item.  The passive narrative is driven by the player recalling his experience as you move on allowing the exposition to slowly reveal the elements of this strange new world and universe.  I would go on but that would go into spoiler territory.
Because I don't believe in a scoring system, I will present my review in binary fomat listing the postives and negatives of the game.  I believe it is up to the user to judge the content of the review rather than the overall value of the score:
+ Very polished for an indie title.  The UE3 engine runs optimially with nary a frame-drop at 60fps.
+ Control scheme is simple with utilizing only the directional keys, spacebar and the two mouse buttons.
+ Tethering system gives a sense of vertigo, like Bioshock: Infinite's rail-hook but with the flexibility of a grappling hook.
+ Voice-acting is well done and is presented without being too over-the-top nor does it take itself too seriously
- Even for a short game, the game has quite amount of level-padding.
- Platforms can get very confusing esepcially how much agency you have over gravity.  Getting disoriented can happen on occasion that can throw off the player's sense of direction.
-  Some scripted occasions take control away from the player with micro-story elements.  It woud've sufficed being in the background just like the reset of the narrative.
Overall, it is one experience I highly recommend, especiallly for an indie title.  I hope to see more ambition from their games in the near future.

This game is great. And it's hard. And at sometimes frustrating. Is it ever unfair? No never. I would recommenend everyone who likes games like VVVVVV or Super Meat Boy to play this game.
The game really upholds to the standards of the jumping into a tiny spot and then progress. As you probably see from the graphics and stuff it really pays some what of an homage to VVVVVV. But don't let that full you cause it's actually much more entertaining then that game.
Does this game present anything new? No, not really. It mixes various elements of various games together. It has a bit of VVVVVV, a bit of Super Meat Boy and even a bit of Metroidvania-style towards it. The VVVVVV-part explains itself by lookiing at the trailer/screenshots. The graphics and atmosphere really do the game a lot of good. Super Meat boy-part comes from the tight controls, the sometimes pixelperfect jumping/timing and the fact you always should be watching your surroundings. And then the Metroidvania-part. This game gives you a great open map which can explore, but some parts are not reachable yet, you have to get a skill or a certain 'key' to progress. In this you encounter bosses. So has it fighting? Nope, this game cleverly combines it's puzzles with the bosses, so no fighting.
Does the game have anything bad then? Well, yes, for me personally, the keyboard seemed a bit less smooth then controller. But that is a personal preference. Also the game is addicting like hell, you want to find everything, you want to explore every corner of the map. So yeah, I encourage you to try the game. Apart from the fact that the game is free, it's also a pretty awesome game.

Despite suffering development woes in the early 2000's, VTM: Bloodlines managed to materialize as a stellar game. I played this religiously upon release, though never to completion because of numerous, game-ending bugs. I have endeavored to rectify that situation by giving it another chance concurrently (though I highly recommend downloading the unofficial patch). It doesn't necessarily have to be Halloween to enjoy this game. The World of Darkness, as imagined by Troika (r.i.p., unfortunately), hits the coffin nail on the head, as it were. Bloodlines effortlessly combines the merits of RPG, action, exploration and story; it is this last element that perhaps shines above all. If you were to consolidate all of Bloodlines text into a novel, it would be a wonderful read. The Source Engine was brand spanking new upon Bloodlines release, and I feel the graphics have survived relatively well. "But enough talk, have at you!"

Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines is a wonderful game with a tragic history; a perfect translation of a pen-and-paper game to a visual media that nearly faded into obscurity. And while it is a shame we may never witness a masterpiece like this for quite some time, Bloodlines is a relic that demands your worship. Sure it has all the basics of a great RPG, fun combat, open world, skill tress, ect. That's not what matters here though. In this game The World of Darkness is not a setting, it is a real place, rich in history and populated by characters who are convincing, complex, and flawed. So many RPGs before have simulated being some fantasy warrior, but what  of being a vampire? To be one of the damned and the fallen? To be a beast clinging to every last shred of humanity? Only Bloodlines has dared to offer one such experience, and while sometimes shocking, it is also always entertaining.

I tried to give this game a chance. I've tried since launch. But over 2 years I simply cannot wait anymore. The game is absolutely fine if you just want a casual RTS going around shooting dudes and playing a dumb story. But as a fan of CoH1 and wanting to get better at this game it just falls apart. Entire playstyles are locked behind $4 paywalls or grinding. The AI in this game is horrible, even more so than the 1st. For instance, I have 5 squads that all have a bazooka and I fire on a Panzer 4 at point blank and it does absolutely nothing. Then I get almost all of my dudes killed waiting for their slow asses to reload. The overall pacing is really odd too as if you stop to take a breather and regroup you're pretty much ♥♥♥♥ed. This game is about constant attacking and it gets really tedious. No more can I take a good defensive position and hold the line while my armor supports an ally attack. Almost every infantry unit in the game has some sort of way to kill defensive positions and the aforementioned slow AI will just sit there missing all their shots while grenades are spammed at you while you miss.
Overall I wouldn't recommend this if you're looking for a competetive RTS. And the sad thing is I can't even give you a better alternative since it seems like RTS is pretty much dead besides some niche titles. Maybe just get the older Relic games instead. They probably don't have a playerbase left though.
PS: If you think this is some CoH1 fanboy raving at how the new game isn't good it should be noted I've spent well over $100 on this game. I gave it much more of a chance than I should have.

Take elements from Portal, Bioshock: Infinite and Dear Esther and mix them in the blender - the result?  A first-person platformer on floaty mountains with the narrative pacing of Dear Esther.
You are a nephew who has discovered a suit from your uncle's laboratory that will take you to a mysterious place where rocks float on air.  The suit acts as a device that tethers platforms much in the same vein as Just Cause but with limited usage.  Like portal, the whole mechanic is soly based on that specialized item.  The passive narrative is driven by the player recalling his experience as you move on allowing the exposition to slowly reveal the elements of this strange new world and universe.  I would go on but that would go into spoiler territory.
Because I don't believe in a scoring system, I will present my review in binary fomat listing the postives and negatives of the game.  I believe it is up to the user to judge the content of the review rather than the overall value of the score:
+ Very polished for an indie title.  The UE3 engine runs optimially with nary a frame-drop at 60fps.
+ Control scheme is simple with utilizing only the directional keys, spacebar and the two mouse buttons.
+ Tethering system gives a sense of vertigo, like Bioshock: Infinite's rail-hook but with the flexibility of a grappling hook.
+ Voice-acting is well done and is presented without being too over-the-top nor does it take itself too seriously
- Even for a short game, the game has quite amount of level-padding.
- Platforms can get very confusing esepcially how much agency you have over gravity.  Getting disoriented can happen on occasion that can throw off the player's sense of direction.
-  Some scripted occasions take control away from the player with micro-story elements.  It woud've sufficed being in the background just like the reset of the narrative.
Overall, it is one experience I highly recommend, especiallly for an indie title.  I hope to see more ambition from their games in the near future.

I hate zombies, but really love this game. On the downside, the story for the core game, (not the expansion, The Following, which has a MUCH better story), is pretty bland. You're an agent for the Global Relief Effort tasked with recovering a document for your bosses. To do this, you enter a quarantined zone filled with zombies and zombie variants.
The villain for the core game is every stereotype you can imagine following every corny trope possible. The hero, Kyle Crane, might be the most idiotic survivor in any game I've ever played because of one particularly stupid moment early in the game. Needless to say, he grew on me later, but his bad choices reflect the bad writing.
The saving grace for the core game is the gameplay and immersion. Holy crap, there were so many times I felt like I was *in* the game running for my life, exploring for supplies, and caring about survivors. After playing the Dead Space series, Resident Evil Series, and The Evil Within, I can say that this game nails the immersion factor; houses, apartments, even shacks all feel like people used to live there. Any place you go could be the last place you'll ever visit. If you ever wondered what it'd feel like to live in the world of "The Walking Dead" during an outbreak, this game pretty much nails it. The crafting system can be a little unbelievable at times, but it helps bring some creativity to killing what would otherwise be fairly repetitive enemies.
Also, the town of Harran is AMAZING. The graphics are gorgeous, and except for a few dropped frames every now and again on my rig, the game runs smooth as silk. The Infected are an apporpriate threat, with the regular zombies being slow but dangerous in mass, and the other zombie types adding the need for strategy to survive. And of course, the night game with the Volatiles brings some of the most tense moments of any game I've played to date.
I'd add that if you want to play this game, the learning curve is steep at the start and even weak zombies take forever to die at the beginning. It takes a while of building skills, but as your Survivor level improves, you'll have access to making and buying much better weapons. You'll go from prey to predator by the time you're done, just stick with it. The early parts can be frustrating, so remember... this game is just as much about the flight as it is about the fight. Learn to run and run well, and you'll be rewarded for it.
Overall, definitely recommend. If you pick this up though, try to get it on sale with the expansion, The Following, which improved a lot of the core game.

I have never written a review on here, but considering this is one of the best games and one of the most underated games ive ever played, ive decided to try my hand at it. Starting off, i know it may say i only have a couple hours on record with the game, but id like to stamp that out now. I played this game years back off an old game engine before steam was a thing, buying it again now is more comfort and support for me, like buying an old book that you read years ago. I have well over 200 hours in the game, and about a thousand in the series. So let me dive in, and let you know what this game is about.
Geneforge is more than a game, its a book, an experiance, a choice, and a beautiful combat system all in one. It cries out to the imaginiative, the 3 am readers, the DnD players, the indie game searchers. What it lacks in graphics, it makes up 10 fold in story. The game puts you in the middle of an entire world and has you influence the outcome of it. In the first game, you find yourself in this estranged world, where the game gives you a brief history of it, then immediately tears that away. It isolates you, shows you that you must survive, and asks you what to do to survive. But that is only the first part. once you gather your bearings, you have to forge a path. At first the paths seem clear, good or evil, but the more you progress the more you realize there is no good. there is no evil. This game makes you question everything, with the only clear progression being that of power. You single handedly experiance the start of a world rebellion, and reitre as a god or a soldier by the end. The same picks up in each consquensial title later on, each putting you, a young shaper, smack dab in the middle of the biggest points in history of this new world. The hours, weeks, months of text painstakingly put into this game alone makes it a solid game, but the combat is fantastic too. You play a tactics style turn based micromanaging comabt system, sort of like fallout: tactics or final fantasy: tactics. But instead of pre determined abilities, like everything else you determine your path. Conjure up an army to fight for you, use magic and objects to trick your opponets and take them out one by one, or don a helmet and sword and slash your way through hoards, the choice is yous. My by far favorite part of it however, has to be the fact that nothing is safe in this game from you. It emphasizes that your choices can change the entire reality. No npc cannot be killed, although it may be hard. The world will form to what you want it to, if you are brave enough to undergo the task. Dont take this as you cannot lose, for the wrong desicion will put you in a spot where you cannot escape. But understand that you are free to make that deicion, you are free to make any desicion. This is the closest i have ever come to DnD Freeplay.
Pro's: Excellent story line, worth of a novel of the highest value.
Freerealm as hell, you are free to make any desicion you want, nothing stops you, you shape the future and history alike.

This game was probably the best 0.79 cents I'll spend for a long time.
I'd recommend it to anybody craving a good turn-based RPG. Progression is often heavily gated by the quality of the loot that you're able to find and craft, but that was a plus for me, because I love RNGesus with all my heart.
Though you shouldn't need to do too much of it, grinding is actually pretty pleasant, because you won't have to wait for animations to play. Things will move as quickly as your fingers will allow them to. However, going on auto-pilot all the time is almost guaranteed to kill you: SanctuaryRPG challenges players by forcing them to adapt their strategies (which are generally pretty simple) to an extensive list of modifiers that determine how each enemy should be approached (e.g. some reflect damage, some are immune to your ultimate, some drain your mana, etc...). This is especially true for fights against bosses, which can have multiple modifiers at once.
Combat is really smooth. As always, your goal is losing the race to the end of your health bar, but there are other factors besides HP and MP to consider during fights. Every turn, you'll have to keep track of your distance from the enemy, debuff stacks, ult status, combo count, buff durations, buff costs (they tick over many turns), guarding, action commands (e.g. grapples, hit confirms, charges), and other things. The game's interface is deceptively simple, because even though each element is easy to understand on its own, juggling all of them at once in short turns is a fun challenge.
Gearing up and allocating stat points is really intuitive, but you can still make some pretty creative builds. My best character so far was a level 58 Goern Assassin with bows that focused on DEX and VIT.
I really enjoyed the music. If you're interested, I'm pretty sure you can find the full in-game OST and the piano version of 12 of the in-game tracks on youtube.
I thought the ASCII was cool, but that's obviously just a personal thing. Some of the landscapes are pretty lackluster, but the enemies, weapons, and other larger-scale objects look gorgeous.
I'm going to keep playing, because it does a great job scratching my itch for a simple yet highly engaging RPG. I'd happily pay up to 15 bucks for it if I had to buy it again. If you're even mildly curious about what the game is like, just pony up when it goes on sale again, because reviews and gameplay footage will not do the experience justice.

It's simply awesome. It's like Star Trek with a much smaller crew. But you basically have all the same options like targeting specific systems (or even people), shifting energy to and fro, trying to breach their hull, gunning down their shields and boarding the ship. But at the same time, you have to watch your resources. Every torpedo you fire might be missing in a later battle, every jump costs you fuel and if you run out of fuel, you're dead in the water waiting for mercy of a merciless universe.
Yes, I have to cope with the randomness of the encounters and their results, but then again, the campaigns aren't that long. Don't buy this game if you don't like skilling yourself to win, because you will die a lot and then retry with a different strategy and hopefully more luck. There are so many possible ways to outfit your ship and win.
Blow them to pieces? Sure.
Mind Control? Why not?
Cloak and avoid their attacks? Hell, yeah!
Set their f-ing ship on fire and drain their oxygen? Yepp.
Send a load of insectoid warriors over to rip their gunning stations (and gunners) to shreds? I can see that happening!
Don't expect the enemy to hold back, though.
For everyone who doesn't mind a little SPOILER and wants to die one less time: There's not only a final battle (surprise, surprise), but you'll have to fight the enemy flagship three times. So don't put all you got into this one battle (like I did), is all I'm saying.

At this point I think everyone who's interested in playing FTL already has, but in case you haven't (or haven't tried it with the expansion) I highly recommend it. A game I really wanted to enjoy, but sadly, even after nearly three years of release.. the combat is horribly unusable for what it could and should have been when other games like Dead Island did it so well.
Weapons break insanely quickly with limited repairs. Granted there's tons of weapons to be found in the world; pipes, planks and the like, but you'll go through them so quickly it's unfunny.
Some enemies early in go down to a single slap to the head with a hammer, others I've spent literally five minutes kicking and weapon striking; and they still got up even after repeated blows to the head that should have left them looking like Sloth from the Goonies.
Bladed weapons felt worthless; you'd think stabbing someone who's on the floor, in the head, with a large knife would equal dead. Nope. Just got to flail away at them, kick them while stamina regens, repeat.
Only 'sure' way for a efficient kill I've found is by booting the buggers into the laid out spike traps littering the world. Stabbing them repeatedly in the head? hammering them with a lump of concrete on rebar? naaah... they get stabbed in the arm by a spike on a barrel; instant ragdoll dead.
"Maybe" it gets better later in and you find some godly weapon of worth a damn
"Maybe" combat improves once you learn to make/find projectiles like a bow or a gun; lord knows the second faction has an arsenal of them.
As it stands though after nearly six hours in this; it's boring and frustrating when you spend half the time running, and the other half manotonously punching/kicking/hammering/stabbing the same five or six zombies over and over hoping they die before your weapon breaks for the third time, or you can lure them in for the mighty barrel boot.
Only thing I can honestly recommend? it's made me want to start playing Dead Island again so I can play a decent zombie game with crafting and quests in it.

This is hands down the best software development game I've played, and there are quite a few in the market now (Game Dev Tycoon, GamersGoMakers, Mad Games Tycoon etc.)
What sets it apart for me is the soft simple graphics and the smooth interface. It is very easy to learn the controls and build big impressive looking office complexes. It also allows you to customize the pace, difficulty and starting locations for varied experiences. In the simulation/management genre, this game is right up there with the best of them.
You start with youself as the founder of the company building a simple little office and starting to work on a few small contracts. From there you start developing your own software: Antivirus, games, operating systems, audio and visual design software, and more. As you grow, you can expand your office and workforce. It's entirely up to you how much you'd like to micromanage. You can assign team leaders and send them on HR and project management courses allowing them to hire and manage teams and their own projects completely independently. The game scales incredibly well as you expand your company.
Some might find the spreadsheets a little overwhelming. I actually like it because it makes my little virtual company feel real. This game was really well thought out and you have all the data you might need at your disposal.
Negatives? Not much. It is early access so there are some glitches, and the game could do with more content. Most notably furniture is currently a bit limited, but that said all the necessary stuff is already there for you to have heaps of fun. There's also some minor balancing issues that will be sorted out later but again nothing gamebreaking and nothing that will ruin your fun. So far the developer of Software Inc. has built a great foundation for what will probably become one of the most unique and fun management simulations on the market.

The fundamentals of this game are great, but the stupid issues that won't ever be fixed means you need to wait until this title goes on sale for $5. The devs have abandoned the game and/or don't seem capable in fixing some problems that are well-known, like the invisible cursor, matchmaking, and more.
The post-mission screen takes way too long and you have to spam the E key to get past it. The user-interface in general needs work, but it won't ever get fixed because the game is done and the devs are gone.
I've seen some CRAZY desync moments in this game. Flying space robo dogs. This is usually due to the horrible matchmaking where you often get matched with players on the other side of the planet. Ping times are completely hidden from the player, probably because the playerbase is small and they don't want you to think the game is dead already (it is).
There is no single player. Playing alone is somewhere between not fun and impossible. You must have a party to do most missions and there are no CPU players. It's all online. When this game goes out of style, nobody will be playing it because nobody is playing it.
Don't buy the DLC. Some items are basically Pay2Win, like the all-terrain boots, but most of the important stuff you can earn in the game, and it's more fun to learn to use what you've got before you get new stuff anyway.
The current PC release price of $20 is a too high considering the game has been out on PSN for quite awhile now, and as far as I can tell, there won't be any future content development for the game.
Beyond my complaints above, this is a great party game with some weird/scary jingoistic humor. You, unquestionably, play the part of the good (bad) guys as you desperately fight to expand your liberal (oppressive), freedom-loving (exploitative) democracy (totalitarian empire).
Much laughs will be had as you do a supply drop over your party or run yourself over with your own tank, but it won't last long. Once you start doing the higher-difficulty missions and start running into the matchmaking issues, once you've waited the two minutes after each and every game is over while spaming the E key, and once you realize the game's development stopped before it was even release on PC, the fun will be over and you'll move on to something else.
Get it on sale. Skip at full price.

I have a lot of mixed feelings on this one, it was really hard to thumbs up it but harder to NOT thumbs up it, and I just wanna write it down dang it leave me alone, this game really doesn't deserve 50 paragraphs written about it but screw it I guess I'm doing it anyway.
I'm gonna start with the pros first so we can get it out of the way. Biggest best pro we got here is THE MUSIC. It's really nice. I really dig it. I don't think everyone will love it, but one thing I really respect about it is that there's like 15+ songs for fighting regular enemies. Most rpgs, turn taking ones especially, will make you go into a battle and play the same song over and over and over and over for every normal battle until you hate yourself. This one just puts a buncha songs in for every enemy. SURE sometimes it'll be a stupid weak skeleton and the music will sound like a final boss, but I appreciate it anyway.
SECOND! I like the graphics/ascii style. It's a cute style, has its charm. People who see screenshots can easily decide if they like it or not, you'll pretty much get what you expect. My only issue with it is that the background often times does not mimic the area that's being described. Like you'll supposedly be in hell and you'll see a background of mountains. There's not exactly a large supply of graphics and ascii stuff.
Third, the battle system is all right. It's a turn taking rpg, I mean how much can you do with it, unless its a strategy turn taking rpg? It does what it does all right, it tried to even spice it up to make it feel more actioney when it isn't at all. It almost feels fast paced at times. There's some cons with it which I'll bring up later, but I'll just say it's not the worst thing.
ANYWAY, lets get to the cons. This game has two major cons that just really hold it back. I wanted more from this game, and it's a bit frustrating. It can make it seem like a thumbs down to me and some people because it's the worst kind of thing, where you like what you're playing but you just want MORE of it.
First and biggest con. This game is a rogue-like for some reason. It's advertised as one, for sure, it didn't come as a shock. I expected it to be different, I suppose, done better. For everything I played with this game, I just don't think it was necessary for it to be a rogue-like at all. I think making it a rogue-like held it back on many many many levels.
So you got yourself a rogue-like and you see there's different classes! Cool, I thought they'd actually play differently, and that's where the rogue-like part comes in. Nah, they all play pretty much completely the same, but with different stats. I wouldn't mind this at all if, you know, you didn't lose everything when you die.
Then there's the story. Maybe the story changes every time you play? Nope, it's the same exact thing, some exact quests, same exact grind. I'd be okay with the grind, I really would, but what fun is there grinding for literally 6+ hours, and then dying to a random enemy because you let it get 2 swings on you and you scrolled by the text too fast? That's what ended my last game, and I did not feel the desire to keep going.
Going on with the grindy aspect, there's A LOT of items in the game, and a lot of randomly generated crafting items. You'll have to spend QUITE sometime making stuff if you want to get the best equipment, leveling your skills, and just in general crafting and sorting through the junk. Then, once again, if you die, its all gone. What's the reason for it?
There's just no change. You'll get some different enemies in between, but they're just healthbars, there's no "story" change in anyway whatsoever. There IS an option to play without perma-death, but it's marked as "not-recommended" and you'll lose out on "extra bonuses" whatever those are. I think it's safe to assume most people are gonna do the normal perma-death version because you don't know what's in store for you or how different it will be.
ALL in all, I think it was just a really bad decision to make this a rogue-like. There's just too much grinding and virtually no reason to ever start a new game. It's not like Binding of Isaac where one run will take at most an hour, and you might get random items that completely change how you play the game every time.
Imagine it's like Pokemon, but once you get a white out in Pokemon, you gotta start ALL over. Sure, it's not hard to do that at all, but why would you want to? Some people make specific challenges for that, and that's fair, but the regular game does not punish you with that because it knows that would be foolish and unfun.
Okay, well I got that outta the way. The second big con is partially because of the first con still.
The story. It's very shallow AT TIMES and the first two acts have the tone just ALL over the place. For a text based game, a story is very important, but I feel the writer/game dev/whoever was held back by the fact that it's a rogue-like. The descriptions and story events are written very quickly and there's not a huge burst of information, which can be done really well at times.
But for this game, it feels it leaves more questions than answers, and a lot of the questions aren't very fun questions. There is a lack of a world in this game, it's not explained incredibly well, and doesn't go into great description of what it is even as you go on. The tone can go from being incredibly serious to dopey memes in the same sentence. There was one part where this guy is trying to rebuilt a robot in the likeness of his dead daughter right? Seems a pretty dark and sad thing, and then one of his failed creations is like "404 daughter love not found, hug.exe not responding" and it just really really takes you out of it.
A lot of the humor can feel like "le random" at times too. There are potatoes in the world, and for whatever reason, everyone hates potatoes. A lot. It's never explained. If it was explained, maybe I could give it a pass, but it's usually just "UGH POTATOES, I HATE THEM" like and it just makes you think of "le penguin of doom XD" and you die a little on the inside.
At the same time, the story can be pretty nice. I really liked the descriptions of hell and the hell beings. At that point they mostly did away with dumb meme jokes, and I appreciated it. Wish though that they delved deeper into that, tried to make sense of what it was doing, instead of being really sarcastic and uncaring about your story. I get the feeling like the author was afraid to try on this a lot. I see the potential, but they were worried it would look cliche and dumb. Personally, I feel it's better to try than just not try at all, but I suppose that was their way of trying, so I don't know.
SO I wrote like 60 grillion words on a dumb 80 cent game. There were some bad times, it's very flawed, but overall I really liked the experience and I'm genuinely glad I played it, if not for the fact that it made me want to play more text/ascii adventures. Anyone who read all this disjointed garbage of a review, sorry, because it certainly sounds like I'm making it seem like its a terrible game while recommending it.
TL;DR: 80 cents is fine, anything more than a buck, I don't think so.

It's simply awesome. It's like Star Trek with a much smaller crew. But you basically have all the same options like targeting specific systems (or even people), shifting energy to and fro, trying to breach their hull, gunning down their shields and boarding the ship. But at the same time, you have to watch your resources. Every torpedo you fire might be missing in a later battle, every jump costs you fuel and if you run out of fuel, you're dead in the water waiting for mercy of a merciless universe.
Yes, I have to cope with the randomness of the encounters and their results, but then again, the campaigns aren't that long. Don't buy this game if you don't like skilling yourself to win, because you will die a lot and then retry with a different strategy and hopefully more luck. There are so many possible ways to outfit your ship and win.
Blow them to pieces? Sure.
Mind Control? Why not?
Cloak and avoid their attacks? Hell, yeah!
Set their f-ing ship on fire and drain their oxygen? Yepp.
Send a load of insectoid warriors over to rip their gunning stations (and gunners) to shreds? I can see that happening!
Don't expect the enemy to hold back, though.
For everyone who doesn't mind a little SPOILER and wants to die one less time: There's not only a final battle (surprise, surprise), but you'll have to fight the enemy flagship three times. So don't put all you got into this one battle (like I did), is all I'm saying.

I tried to give this game a chance. I've tried since launch. But over 2 years I simply cannot wait anymore. The game is absolutely fine if you just want a casual RTS going around shooting dudes and playing a dumb story. But as a fan of CoH1 and wanting to get better at this game it just falls apart. Entire playstyles are locked behind $4 paywalls or grinding. The AI in this game is horrible, even more so than the 1st. For instance, I have 5 squads that all have a bazooka and I fire on a Panzer 4 at point blank and it does absolutely nothing. Then I get almost all of my dudes killed waiting for their slow asses to reload. The overall pacing is really odd too as if you stop to take a breather and regroup you're pretty much ♥♥♥♥ed. This game is about constant attacking and it gets really tedious. No more can I take a good defensive position and hold the line while my armor supports an ally attack. Almost every infantry unit in the game has some sort of way to kill defensive positions and the aforementioned slow AI will just sit there missing all their shots while grenades are spammed at you while you miss.
Overall I wouldn't recommend this if you're looking for a competetive RTS. And the sad thing is I can't even give you a better alternative since it seems like RTS is pretty much dead besides some niche titles. Maybe just get the older Relic games instead. They probably don't have a playerbase left though.
PS: If you think this is some CoH1 fanboy raving at how the new game isn't good it should be noted I've spent well over $100 on this game. I gave it much more of a chance than I should have.

Just when you thought a farming simulator would be stupid and boring, you fire up this gem and remember how much fun you had playing with tonka trucks when you were small >_<. This game is more fun than it should be, and allows for some hilarious situations if you decide to drive like a fool, or attempt to use farm equipment in ways not intended.
It does allow for more serious play as a simulation if that is your thing, with many different ways to farm, and a lot of freedom in where you do it.
The one thing I did not like about this game is how the methods of farming are quite alien to the ones I have seen living in farm country (in America, the simulator is euro themed which is fun, but did not make it feel very real for me). Instead of making circles around the fields it seems designed to go across, turn around, go back, ect. Nothing wrong with that, but it is less efficient and realistic (at least for the area I live in, I am not sure if this is how it is done elsewhere). This might be just a symptom of your AI farmhands being hilariously dumb. Nothing stopping you from doing zigzags while driving yourself if you wanted to, but in order to make full use of the hired help, you must very carefully align your derpy farmhands who will just drive back and forth until they reach the edge of the prepared land (mostly...sometimes they might just sit there all lazy like soaking up pay :P)
There are many mods for other maps, AI changes and implements, but I have not used them much myself. I tried a couple for AI improvements and maps but the ones I used made little difference for me, and I preferred the stock map.

Great storyline, old school combat/graphics style. Difficulty in torment is legit and with 5 main factions and a myriad of choices, lots of replay value.
Gameplay is not simply just about slaughtering everything in your path - stealth and non-combat skills will be needed to clear the game.
Monsters don't respawn which means that your experience is limited (in particular, your minions get xp when you get xp); but this is only an important factor (getting minions early means they can level up more by the end game and are thus stronger than 'fresher' ones) in the harder difficulties.
Two minor complaints:
1.) I can't move the screen easily (arrow keys only) since you're usually clicking with your mouse to move the party and its awkward to have the left hand on the arrow keys to move the screen around
2.) A 'solo' style is virtually impossible on the harder difficulties (even with all your points in solo stuff like spells and stats rather than creations)
Awesome game, and great bang for the buck!

Hearing the ragged breathing of one of the nighttime beasts closing in on me through headphones while making a mad dash through dark city alleyways and moonlit rooftops is exhilarating.
Add in lots of bonus content and the co-op experience and this is near the top of my list of favorite games.
Definitely recommended, worth your time for sure.

I like the movie based game with good ideas. I like as the game makes fun from scenes do not want to be a realistic reflect of the saga. As the gamer finished the story line, can start the grinding of the further achievements/red bricks/gold bricks/chars/etc. to be 100% completed which could be boring a little bit as the time is running away.

You know, graphically I would say it is pretty good looking with a number of special effects used, like various depths of field, excellent water materials, and, of course, moments where everything on the screen explodes into a chaos of plastic pieces. The Endor jungle looks great bathed in shadows and the typical LEGO foliage but has some little fun bits added in like third-person moments where you follow a character up close and blast away in.
It uses a really solid depth of field effect at that time. Whether the levels have you taking an X-Wing through an asteroid field or even later battling out on jumbo floors. The game knows what it needs to do and, for the most part, presents it really well. I said for the most because as with most LEGO games it does see some slow down when a high number of particles are on the screen, but for the most part, it's fine and runs well.
There isn't much more to say here; the game doesn't go out of its' way to do anything other than to continue the tradition of past titles showing new locations and it does that well. It always got that good crisp image quality and toy-like effect to it.
This is some of the best sound I think I've heard in a LEGO game now. While the occasional odd mixing with characters suddenly sounding really weird, for the most part, the sound spectrum is actually wide and things like laser blasters have that small sizzle you recognize from a mile away. What does continue to happen though is the odd issue where one explosion might be loud and bassy and have a good top and bottom end while others are missing the bottom end completely. But as a package, I would say that the sound is really good.
As with most of the titles, there is both, resampled and newly recorded voice and once again, the difference is noticeable. Sometimes resampled voices from the movie sound overly hushed because too much natural data had to be removed to get them into the new environment. Worse yet, they sound a bit like someone recorded them over a telephone, while newly recorded voice sounds are as crisp as possible. Also, a couple of voice actors have returned to do some lines. I would say it's a complete package: It's good "voice work" but still held back by the occasional terrible effects.
Once again the game has you tracing from one location to the next engaging in small stories, wandering around in small hub worlds and building, bashing, smashing, electrifying, “lightsabering”, force-throwing and basically just creating absolute chaos everywhere you go.
You start out on Endor and right away lear some of the new skills like multi-building LEGO pieces, which is basically one pile of LEGO used to build a couple of structures to get by particular puzzles instead of the more traditional "go here, go there" gameplay of the past. While the idea that something cool really tightens up the speed of the gameplay, it also sees a direct reflection in the function of the levels, tightening the possibilities for exploration. Now you are just going from one spot building a fish tank, filling it with water moving it three feet and dumping it on a fire instead of the discrete discovery spread out across those locations.
However, there is a bigger problem with LEGO Star Wars: The Force Awakens. All LEGO games are inherently embedded into the movies in which they find themselves exploring. Force Awakens used the climax and ending of Episode VI: Return of the Jedi then leaps into the future where the entire First Order is led by Kylo Ren and tries to spread it onto six hours of gameplay and it shows drastically. While this has been done before it's that unique gameplay plus this that sort of makes it feel a little bit odd.
But there is some cool stuff as well: Exploration of downed Empire ships shows the continued vertical and unique crossplay gameplay loops that LEGO has always been known for. While flying TIE-Fighters and X-Wings may not be the most complex moments of the game, they excel at offering small snippets of chaotic goodness as you fly around the surface of planets or Imperial ships.
Some of the new character interactions like face recognition and unlocking locations are actually really cool but one of my favorite aspects is the new cover battles ("Blaster Battles") where you build up something, jump into it, shoot some enemies or hide behind some covers.
The side missions are really excellent, especially the ones that flesh out later stories of Star Wars and are basically considered official. It's absolutely a missed opportunity that there aren't more of them and that they require unlocks to get to, resulting in only a small amount of players actually getting to experience them.
LEGO Star Wars: The Force Awakens is solid but it absolutely suffers under the fact that so many Star Wars games have come and brought their A-game to the table in terms of quantity of content and here, much of it is either stuck in a small amount of fiction spread across many hours or needlessly locked away. At least, the normal aspects of LEGO are here with a large number of ships and characters you can unlock and even though those often are just a unique combination of other characters, it's fun to see some of the goofy costumes and ship designs. One thing that the game excels in is the spirit of LEGO. In fact, despite any other misgivings, the insight jokes, overall location humor, and poking fun into the source material is some of the best ever.

A great game if you're into leading a small civilisation in the beginning of the human race through the ages, competing against other Civs and working with City-States.
There are five different ways to win - Time victory where you get scored based on your performance up to a specific year, Domination which the civilisation that holds all other civs original capitals will get, Cultural where the civilisation that has the most cultural/tourism influence on other civs (100% on each) will win, Diplomatic which is taken by being voted World Leader in the United Nations, and Science which is taken by the first Civ that completes the moon landings.
The gameplay is very diverse with a tech tree to explore, many things to build including normal buildings such as barracks  or mines, and also wonders which are very useful depending on what kind of victory you're aiming for. War is also quite fun with strategy being the main focus and also how well trained/modern your units are.
The diplomacy is quite simple but enough with trade, alliances and asking other civs to do things for you.
Graphics are quite good for a board game style and aren't very demanding on your graphics card, just your processor but lag wouldn't affect you much, since this is like a board game.
Sounds are also quite nice and help the game feel more lifelike, so all in all I'd definitely recommend it.

NOTE:
Okay, I have edited this review.
I orignially gave this a negative rating because:"The game ran smoothly for the first two hours, but I began encountering NPC bugs where companions wouldn't follow the path they were programmed to walk. I fixed this by restarting the level. After four hours, I can no longer go further in the game because I encountered a bug where I can no longer fire or switch weapons, interact with the world, or reload. I can only walk, jump, and run. I have tried to reload checkpoints, relaunch the game (quitting out and relaunching the game)"
I got this a few more times, plus one hard crash and some stuttering.
However, the game is not broken or unplayable as I originally thought.
NEW REVIEW:
Metro 2033 Redux is the first Metro game I ever played and I fell in love with the game when I first played it on the Xbox One.
Some positives:
*The gun customization and weapon types are still great (and I especially love my Tikhair or however you spell it)
*I love how the story is the maturing of a young man into a cold-hearted Ranger or one with a more sympathetic attitude about him.
*The moral system is woven exceptionally well into the game without feeling hamfisted.
*The stealth is still great and rewarding than going gung-ho into danger, as that will get you killed on the harder difficulties.
Some negatives:
*The voice acting, as some other reviewers have pointed out, can be hit or miss, with the kids especially being pretty hard on the ears.
*All the bugs I encountered, as mentioned at the top.
All in all, if you want to experience a great game then definitely buy this. However, with all the bugs I got, I would recommend getting it on sale to play it safe.

I wasn't sure what to expect when I first played this game. I bought it on a whim while it was on sale, after I had seen a screenshot of the artwork on a website. I know now that The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a beautifully crafted work of art. The visuals in this game are stunning, the soundtrack is incredible, and the way the story is revealed is interesting, and unique. The game specifically states that it does not hold your hand, thus it is up to you to figure out what to do. I'll admit I had some troubles figuring out what to do at first. However, it's not hard or complicated.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter loosely reminds me of Dear Esther. The main difference being that in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, you interact with the world much more than in Dear Esther. But both games utilize a narrator that helps drive along the story, both environments are gorgeous, and both games have great soundtracks.
I only have three small issues with the game. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a little on the short side. It is only a few hours long, depending on how fast you move.  Another issue is with the ending, it's a wee bit of a let down. But I'm just being picky. Finally, I thought the voice acting could have been much better. The actors seemed very inexperienced. But aside from these minor things, the game is still fantastic. I do not regret my purchase at all.

Twin stick shooter with very strong teamwork focus. Gameplay is great, and it's technically very stable. Easy to hop in and out of games. The one flaw is that ingame voice chat is set to "always on" by default instead of "push to talk", but there's no icon on screen to tell you you're transmitting, so everyone is going to be hotmicing until you politely tell them where push to talk is (or mute them).
That's way more text about the negatives than the positives, when they're reaaaally minor. This game is excellent. Near perfect. Very good couch play too.
So what is it? It's a top down shooter, where you're soldiers of the dis *uh* I mean utopean Super Earth, defending Freedom and Democracy and Libertea by shooting alien scumbags in the face. You liberate planets by completing all the missions on them, where each mission has a series of objectives - arm SAM site, capture territory, destory alien base etc. The enemies are without number and just keep spawning - overwhelmingly so at higher difficulty levels - so the point of the game is mostly to fight your way past/through the enemy to complete your objectives and then GTFO to the extraction site.
It's from the makers of Magicka, so accidental teamkilling is a hillarious constant. In particular, players call down supplies or join a game in progress with a drop pod screaming out of the sky, which will obliterate anything it lands on. I've lost count the number of times I've joined a game and my pod has wiped out someone's mech, because they weren't paying attention :D
Unlike Magicka, though, the multiplayer programming is solid as a rock. I was dreading online play, expecting it to be a buggy mess (like Magicka is), but instead it's really smooth.
Get this game, get yourself some controllers for your computer (xbox ones will work), get some friends together, and have yourself a Hell of a good time on the couch. And it's still excellent playing online with randos (better with better teammates, of course).

There are 5 separate factions, each with their own political and moral opinions, quests, storylines, and endings. Hands down the best zombie game out there. I only have 25 hours on the steam version of the game, but I have hundreds of hours clocked in on this game on GOG version. I finally got it on steam so I can play it with some friends and give the Developer tools a go.
This game has it all;
A great storyline, INTERESTING characters that have background stories of their own, the parkour on this game is amazing (a bit quirky at times, but hey, nothings perfect),♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of side missions aside from the campaigns main story line (which takes ages to complete unless you speed run things!), tons of weapons and blue-prints to slay hordes of zombies to your hearts content.
Pretty much, if you like beating zombies up, GET THIS GAME.

I am not a huge zombie fanatic and I haven't played the other games in this genre. As a standalone title not comparing to anything else, I was pleasantly surprised and had a fun time playing. It does a great job with the "open" world though filling the map with objectives becomes a little tedious after awhile. The parkour is among the best I've seen implemented, with quick second planning and timing paramount to hop skip and jump from rooftop to fence to rooftop. Night time is genuinely scary with baddies that are strong and frightening to deal with head on. Graphics are solid and the story is not great but not horrible either, with decent voice acting and some decent side stories. It's no Witcher 3 but it does an admirable job.
A couple of key things that were inexplicable choices. The beginning few hours is an unbearable slog. The melee weapons like pipes and wooden legs are totally ineffectual and it took way too long to get to a point where I could complete objectives and upgrade my character. Now full disclosure I played on Hard to start because I dont' have the time to play games through twice so maybe it was a little artificially more difficult because of that. However once you've upgraded a few levels it becomes much more fun and you have more options with how to deal with enemies - whether you want to avoid or fight directly.
And the grappling hook, which you get a little over half-way through the game.... yeah. It's very cool.... and game-breaking. It would be fine if it had a very short range and just helped you get up a couple of levels when you need a "leg" up. But this thing straight up shoots you half-way across the screen and doesn't obey any law of physics. i.e. if you grapple down from a high perch (one that you'd normally die from) you'll just be pulled straight to your grapple with no ill-effects. This made the second map much less fun because I didn't have to use any of the parkour skills I developed. It felt like a mod that you'd use after you already beat the game and not an included tool during the campaign. You could say "just don't use it dummy!" and you'd be right. But unfortnately there is not fast-travel system and so it can ultimately get super tedious doing missions side-missions that fling you across the map for no good reason and so the hook at least ameliorated some of that frustration. They should have just done a fast travel in my opinion but hey, what do I know?
Also... that ending. Ugh. Pretty anticlimactic. But the journey was impressive with solid gameplay and graphics and a story that propels you forward just enough to want to keep playing. Wish there was a little more variety in mission types but overall a solid experience.
Just get the game to tell EA that they suck. Plus you get a great game.

You have to win the game… no really, you have too. It seems as if thats the only point of this 8 bit adventure by Pirate Hearts but really, there’s so much more. The game is simple enough, but complex beyond anything you could fathom, and may leave you lying dead in your bathtub come morning. With that being said, You Have to Win the Game is great. Reminiscent of the MS DOS genre of video games from the 80′s with the retro feel of playing Atari saturday morning, You Have to Win the Game brings all of that and more to the table.
I first encountered this game in the Steam Greenlight forums and looked a little deeper when I saw the words “Free To Play.” After downloading YHTWTG it sat in my download folder for weeks before I actually tried it, but when I did, it changed my life. Normally simple games like these catch my eye, I play for 10 minutes and the game is dead to me afterwards, but this one was different. This one called to me, randomly, I would find myself clicking on the icon and I would quickly get lost in the games nostalgia.
Plagued by the notion that I had to win the game, I decided I wouldn’t let this game get the best of me, and I vowed to complete it. At first glance it doesn’t seem as if YHTWTG is hard, and might just be your simple everyday platformer… What’s that they say about judging a book by its cover? I was wrong, dead wrong, this game takes a sincere amount of thought and intuitiveness to complete.
With no storyline other than having to win the game, you set out with NO IDEA of what exactly it is that you have to do. Its your standard platformer out of the 8 bit era, with a great retro feel, and reminded me a lot of Kid Icarus for NES. There are no monsters to fight, only a few to avoid while you have to make a series of hard and precise jumps in order to move forward to the next screen. Each screen is also appropriately named for what you may encounter while on your quest to winning the game. It might be a catchphrase, one liner or an obscure saying depending where you are in the level.
You Have To Win The Game is loaded with hours of gameplay, power ups, and special abilities that will all aid you on your adventure. Beating this game with a 100% completion rating is more satisfying than that after sex cigarette, and should be played at least once by any serious indie gamer.

I wasn't sure what to expect when I first played this game. I bought it on a whim while it was on sale, after I had seen a screenshot of the artwork on a website. I know now that The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a beautifully crafted work of art. The visuals in this game are stunning, the soundtrack is incredible, and the way the story is revealed is interesting, and unique. The game specifically states that it does not hold your hand, thus it is up to you to figure out what to do. I'll admit I had some troubles figuring out what to do at first. However, it's not hard or complicated.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter loosely reminds me of Dear Esther. The main difference being that in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, you interact with the world much more than in Dear Esther. But both games utilize a narrator that helps drive along the story, both environments are gorgeous, and both games have great soundtracks.
I only have three small issues with the game. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a little on the short side. It is only a few hours long, depending on how fast you move.  Another issue is with the ending, it's a wee bit of a let down. But I'm just being picky. Finally, I thought the voice acting could have been much better. The actors seemed very inexperienced. But aside from these minor things, the game is still fantastic. I do not regret my purchase at all.

I'm basically echoing what most review-ers are saying, here, but the game is beautiful, strange, and short. I would recommend getting it while it's on sale (as the full price is not worth something which can easily be beaten in one sitting, as I did), though you should definitely get it.
It is worth noting that, for me at least, the game peaked at the beginning and never quite picked back up. The first mystery you solve is in my opinion the best, and those that follow get progressively easier and less engaging as time goes by.

If someone were to ask me for an incredibly non-linear RPG I could name a few.  There's Deus Ex (The original), Mass Effect, and then there's the cult classic that is Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines.  A heavily overlooked title to be sure, Bloodlines is a one-of-a-kind game.  It's rare to find a non-adventure game where pretty much everything you say and the type of person you turn out to be changes how the game is played drastically.  In that sense, this game is what I would consider the true successor to Deus Ex.
Much like Deus Ex, the game revolves around making choices.  For instance, there can be a story chain revolving around some character, and just because you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥him off earlier you've drastically changed the course of the chain.  This might sound shallow by the way I'm explaining it, but some of the consequences behind ones choices aren't immediately noticeable, which adds to the game's unpredictability.  Skills also play into the choices, much like they can in Knights of the Old Republic, and not only offer more choices, but they also offer more ways to play the game.
Also like Deus Ex, the game almost always offers several ways to go about missions, though not with the versatility of Deus Ex (and understandably so).  There's usually a direct approach, a rather intuitive sneaking approach, and a charismatic approach, though each of these approaches can branch off into other approaches as well, which gives the game quite a bit of replay value.  Similarly, because your a vampire, you are also given skills that, depending on which race you are, can give you even more ways of going about the game.
The only real downside to the game is its combat system.  Well, specifically, it's hand-to-hand combat system.  It's kinda...bad.  It's somewhat clunky and inaccurate, but it isn't terrible and can certainly be enjoyable, and if you don't like it you can always employ your skills and/or grab a gun.
If you're looking for an incredibly non-linear title, this game is definitely for you.  Despite its age, the game hits many strides in its storytelling and non-linearity, and it hearkens back to the days of Deus Ex on more than one occasion.  The side-quests can also be shockingly impressionable, such as one mission where you go to an abandoned hotel and...well, it'd better that you just play it.  Pick up this game, it's a very good title.  If you're looking for a deal, it almost always goes on sale during the Halloween Sale.

Absolutely brilliant game in every aspect, this is my favorite horror RPG of all time! There is just so many options to choose from, both in development of your character’s personality and fighting style. You can basically play the game exactly the way you want the game to be played. I’ll recommend this game to everyone who likes a good dark and twisted RPG full of morbid and black humor.
As a newly embraced kindred you are given a lot of choices that could alter your overall storyline. If you believe in good or evil then your world might get turned around, as it all depends on point of view - your point of view. Will you seek allies to strengthen your fate or will you simply end up betraying them due to trust or individual differences?
An important condition for your new and eternal existence is your beast within and the craving for blood that follows. Going without blood when you’re thirsty will make your beast unsatisfied and release from the chains of you, till it once again will be filled and in slumber. This could break your most important rule - keep your identity hidden, keep your race a secret, respect the masquerade. Mortal curiosity could be your final death, if not by them then by your own, revealing the secrecy of your species is tolerated as betrayal as you will condemn the masquerade.
There is a lot of clans to choose from, even the choice of clan can alter the perspective people talk and greet you within the world. Every clan has unique armor and skill sets. All of the clans can choose the same stats depending on which role the player wish to play the game. Your stats affect your social and combat abilities.
Do you want to slice and dice or do you want to take your enemies out from a distance? You can choose your fighting style in combination with your clan’s skill set to create your own unique play style. However blood is limited so remember to feed when you can.
Your social abilities can help you to dominate, convince or seduce others to have your way. That can help you grant access to locations, free goodies or even a free blood snack!
Don’t forget to catch a squishy rattie when passing through the sewer. Why… one might ask…? Well… they’re deliciously tasty and uhm, ratties provide a fine amount of blood! Tasty, tasty ratties.
The game has only been improved by time, thanks to a great and active modding community and the unofficial patches, which I highly recommend to everyone who would like to play the game, as it fixes some of the game’s glitches and bug issues.
The game offers quality gameplay and storyline plus a huge amount of playtime and replay value.

For one reason or another, it seems like video game characters never really have time to smile. Most of them are either heading off to war, saving the world, or righting a grave injustice, and these stressful situations lead to plenty of world-weary bald men fighting for a better life. Thankfully, some characters just seem happy to be here. Simon from Adventure Lamp seems like one of those. Sure, he was stranded by a cave-in, and he does have to traverse through five worlds with only a particularly resilient hat to aid him, but at least he seems excited about going on an adventure. Once you play through the first few stages of Simon’s game, you’ll probably share in that excitement too.

Ever wanted to play a cute platformer? Wished for a platformer to use something new? A game surrounded by the use of a hat? Adventure Lamp, developed and published by Ryan Davis, is for you!
In Adventure Lamp, you play as Simon equipped with a hat to accompany him throughout his journey. The game is built around the idea of losing your hat. But never fear, for the hat will always return to Simon's head. Each time you jump the hat launches in the air higher than you, how high depending on how you make Simon jump. In addition, you can aim the arc the hat will travel, whether it be across a gap to hit a button or to set it down. The hat doesn't just hit buttons though. Each level has a chance of a red enemy being included that can easily take you out in one hit. The one weapon you can defend yourself, even for a few seconds? Your hat. This addition of a hat easily sets apart Adventure Lamp from the other platformers.
Each level contains a new puzzle that builds off of the previous ones. Along with the overall chapters adding in a new mechanic unique to the chapter to mix up how you play. While Simon's hat is constantly used to progress through puzzles, the game does switch it up some levels to make the hat cause havoc. From erasing your puzzle progress to activating a deadly weapon. This allows the difficulty progression to be constant, with a little spikes towards the end. I would be lying if I didn't say I rage quit a couple times towards the end.
Adventure Lamp is not overly demanding and there's a high chance it will easily run consistently. It also adds some options to turn off certain elements, such as menu and background movement, for the game to run more consistently or if the player prefers it.
The only weird thing about this is that a command prompt will open when launching the game through Steam. This is mostly to take care of a bug, but you can start without the command prompt by browsing for the application in local files.
Adventure Lamp uses it's simple backgrounds and foregrounds to invoke what each unique chapter brings. Each level has a simple looking design, harnessing a complex solution. Despite the simple design, this does not take away from the atmosphere.
The soundtrack is upbeat and cheerful throughout Adventure Lamp adding a lighthearted side to the otherwise gloomy overtone. Not going too overboard to where the soundtrack bothers the player, but enough to energize you to continue.
There is surprisingly a lot of replayability in Adventure Lamp. While the main game may seem short depending on how skillful you are, there is a secret NewGame+ that will appear upon completion. NewGame+ adds two new side stories with the same levels. However, you play a different character with different mechanics. This adds more difficulty to otherwise easy puzzles as you need to learn how the new character moves and to use their own way to defeat enemies and press down buttons.
If you are an achievement hunter, Adventure Lamp also provides replayability in the achievements. Speed running the main game in 30 minutes and finishing using only the mouse is included with the achievements.
+Progression of difficulty
+Visually cute and charming
+Nice soundtrack
+Creativity used with the integration of the hat
+ Secret NewGame+
+/- Command prompt when launching
-Spending too much time aiming can cause Simon to move
-Hard to control precise movement with an analog stick
I highly recommend Adventure Lamp, especially if you love platformers.

Adventure Lamp, developed and published by Ryan Davis, is an indelibly cute puzzle platformer about hat physics. Yes, that's right.. hat physics. This is what differentiates the game from the multitude of other indie platformers in the Steam catalog.
The game captures your attention because the cuteness factor is turned all the way up to twelve. However, it manages to keep it because it is designed very simply but presents enough of a challenge. The majority of the 150 levels are short and are intended to be completed relatively quickly. As a result this generally means that you're never stuck on any one level for too long. There's more than a sufficient amount of content within the game to satisfy even the most content hungry gamer.
Seriously, the game is entirely about the hat. Every time you jump or bounce your hat leaves your head. You can also throw, toss and do whatever else you want to do with your hat to help you avoid all of the nasty pitfalls. Your hat is deadly. It will serve as a weapon to rid the screen of slimes. The slimes often generate very quickly meaning that every action that you take after losing your hat has to be taken that little bit quicker.
However, despite the hat being your greatest ally there are a number of levels where that is just not the case. The more you lose your hat the worse the situation is for you. This provides a great little twist in a game that could be perceived as relatively straight forward otherwise.
Perhaps the most surprising thing about the game is the manner in which the atmosphere is presented. My initial thoughts were that I wouldn't want to live in this world and I wondered why the character is such a charming little individual given the darkness that surrounds him. The place is very gloomy and almost deathlike.  This is most noteworthy because it is in stark contrast with the remainder of the game including the sound. The sound is very cute which is in line with what I have come to expect from the game. As a result it seems like there is a real clash of atmosphere here. It doesn't really impact the game negatively but it is curious game design decision.
Partially. The game has Steam achievements, 13 in all, but it presently lacks trading cards. Hopefully cards are released in a future update.
I loved the cuteness of the game. I fell in love with the hat physics. The system was intelligently designed and gives the title a different selling point. I might balk a little at the price but that's because there are so many cheaper alternatives. But in all, Adventure Lamp is a really solid platformer that is worthy of your time if you are a fan of the genre.
