Adventure Lamp is an indie platformer game, developed Ryan Davis. It’s about hats.
No, not in the Team Fortress 2 sense, in a “this hat is your one and only tool, and it can do everything” sense. The game is your classic platformer, you work through various levels and have to get to the end to progress to the next one. There are enemies, jumps requiring apparently godlike precision, puzzles, speed, you name it. The thing that sets this game apart from other platformers, however, is the hat. That oh-so-helpful headpiece. The beautiful bonnet; the heroic headgear; the panama of puzzles; the hat, the myth, the legend.
Built into the game is a simple physics system: your hat does not like to stay on your head. When you jump, your hat is launched. The hat can be thrown, dropped, whatever. This is very useful when you need to hit a button across a jump that is far too long to make. The physics on the hat can be a little hard to predict sometimes, but this added element to the platforming genre makes a lot of difference. The hat is not just a tool however… Small red enemies populate the world of Adventure Lamp, and they all have one weakness. Could you possibly guess? Yes, you got it! That hateful helmet of havoc! Essentially, you play as a small, blue, blobby Odd Job. Do I even need to finish the review?
The game doesn’t rest on its laurels either, some of the puzzles ignore the hat element completely and focus on a more “the hat is gonna ruin everything you love” angle, so instead of using your hat to ensure victory you’re fighting against the physics to keep the hat on your head to avoid defeat. That damn hat. I trusted you.
I myself am not a fan of platformers. Mario? No thanks. Super Meat Boy? I gave up after about ten minutes. Adventure Lamp though, the hat gimmick sold it for me. Gone are the hours despairing at my mistimed jump, and are replaced by cheers of victory as my glorious belamped chapeau strikes down all buttons, ne’er-do-wells and spiky red blobs of death before me.
The atmosphere of Adventure Lamp is quaint, the simple backgrounds are gloomy, evoking the feeling that you really are trying to make your way out of a cave. The foreground is always quite simple, and each chapter brings something new to the table (wind particles, lava, reduced vision) etc and are all pulled off well. Simon the Archeaologist himself is also very cute, and watching his slightly nervous expression as he figures out the puzzles is highly entertaining.
The sound design evokes a cutesy affectation as well, with cheery music and cheerful sound effects that contribute to the lighthearted nature and feel of the game.
The game isn’t at all demanding, and it ran consistently at 60fps with no problems whatsoever. The only problem that I came across was closing the game – after exiting you need to head to task manager and kill the process or it will still run in the background. Weird bug, I know, but not game breaking.
Hats all folks, the review’s done. If you like platformers, this game would be a great addition to your library. It’s cute, it’s funny, and it uses a hat as an all-purpose tool, from harbinger of destruction to a button pusher. Even if you don’t like them, the hat mechanic is interesting enough to give it a shot at least. I do, however, recommend waiting for a sale. While fun, it isn’t £8.99 fun.

This has to be one of the most underrated games on Steam. I missed the release last year and accidentally found the game while searching for games under the management tag, and what a nice surprise it was! This is hands down the best software development game I've played, and there are quite a few in the market now (Game Dev Tycoon, GamersGoMakers, Mad Games Tycoon etc.)
What sets it apart for me is the soft simple graphics and the smooth interface. It is very easy to learn the controls and build big impressive looking office complexes. It also allows you to customize the pace, difficulty and starting locations for varied experiences. In the simulation/management genre, this game is right up there with the best of them.
You start with youself as the founder of the company building a simple little office and starting to work on a few small contracts. From there you start developing your own software: Antivirus, games, operating systems, audio and visual design software, and more. As you grow, you can expand your office and workforce. It's entirely up to you how much you'd like to micromanage. You can assign team leaders and send them on HR and project management courses allowing them to hire and manage teams and their own projects completely independently. The game scales incredibly well as you expand your company.
Some might find the spreadsheets a little overwhelming. I actually like it because it makes my little virtual company feel real. This game was really well thought out and you have all the data you might need at your disposal.
Negatives? Not much. It is early access so there are some glitches, and the game could do with more content. Most notably furniture is currently a bit limited, but that said all the necessary stuff is already there for you to have heaps of fun. There's also some minor balancing issues that will be sorted out later but again nothing gamebreaking and nothing that will ruin your fun. So far the developer of Software Inc. has built a great foundation for what will probably become one of the most unique and fun management simulations on the market.

I like Helldivers, I really do, and that is why I have given it a thumbs up, but I would nonetheless like to talk about the negative aspects of the game.
I could go on and on about how great the tactical elements of the game is, how absoulety engulfing the atmosphere is, and how beautiful the different planets are. I could, but I won't.
There are a few holes in Helldivers, and though they are few, the few are pretty big in my opinion. So let me take them one for one.
First and foremost, if you're planning on playing this game, play it with a friend. If you don't have any friends who want to play the game with you, find someone in the online world. But whatever you do, don't play alone. It can be done on planets with very easy to easy difficulty, but as soon as you get to medium (at least on the cyborg planets), you will be rushed and destroyed by your enemies, especially the damn dogs. You will maybe be able to handle singleplayer if you go full on LMG's and shotguns, and the EXO-suit as your backup, but if you like me prefer to be a sniper, picking off your foes from a distance with a single bullet, then good ♥♥♥♥ing luck surviving when 30 foes are coming at you full speed, using rush, ranged, and aoe attacks. It was maybe done like this so it would "force" the players to play together, which makes sense, but it's still kind of annoying if you, again like me, don't really like playing tactical games like this with complete strangers.
Second complaint, is the armor system. Though I know it's not an RPG, it would be nice with some sort of customization, other than just cosmetics. You can choose from a variety of armor sets (they unlock as you level up or if you buy the 'packs'), but they don't do jack. You can look really cool, and SEEM like you have a lot of armor, or SEEM like you can hide in the terrain, but oh no. There is a perk that gives you more armor, but as there are other perks that are so much more useful, it seems stupid to choose armor as a perk. The weapon system works well, with quite a few weapons, all upgradable (though not very much), and they can fit all sorts of playstyles. But as I mentioned in the previous complaint, if you plan on playing the game alone on anything above easy, then you can say goodbye to all those fun weapons like sniper, ray gun, flamethrower or whatever, and just go with the shotgun or LMG (if you want to live).
I do have friends to play the game with, so I do have fun with it, but when I sometimes feel like playing the game and my friends aren't around, then I just kind of can't, and when you reach a certain level the easy missions just become boring and repetitive with no challenge whatsoever.
TO CONCLUDE:
A very good game, based around good tactical gameplay with friends or strangers, with wonderful landscapes and great atmosphere. There are a lot of different objectives as you move up to the more challenging planets, and covering your friends, going back-to-back as you defend an outpost, mowing down troops of cyborgs, calling down reincofrcements, feels amazing. The guns feel powerful, and have a real kick to them.
The game is however based 90 % on multiplayer or co-op, as playing alone is near impossible. The armor system could use some tweaks, and some actual statts would also not be bad. Otherwise leveling up just feels like you're doing it to get the new stratagem (airdrops of sorts) and nothing else. I want to be beaten to death because I picked a fight with a monster on a very challenging planet, and then come back 10 levels later, and bash its skull right back in, and feel like I've gotten stronger with time, but new, slightly stronger, weapons, and new ways of carpet bombing the enemies really doesn't count as progression in my world.
I will recommed this game if you're looking for a game that requires tactical skill and teamwork, and is pretty simple and straightforward.

Adventure Lamp is a fun little platformer that has some issues that keep it from being perfect.
I had a lot of fun with Adventure Lamp. The game is really charming. The mechanic where you have to throw your hat to defeat enemies and activate buttons/switches is creative. The artwork is good. If you like charming platformers you should really enjoy the game.
There are a couple issues that keep the game from being perfect though. First I found the game to be on the easy side. If you are looking for a challenging platformer, Adventure Lamp is not going to be it. The puzzles are really simple and straightforward. I play a lot of platformers though so that might be a contributing factor in me thinking that the game was on the easy side.
The second issue is that the game is on the short side. I actually beat the main game in about 1.5-2 hours. The game does feature a new game+ though. The new game+ seems to feature the same levels but you play them as different characters  with different abilities so you have to address the levels in different ways. There are at least two different characters that you can play the new game+ as.
The final issue is there are some technical issues. The longer I played the game the more the framerate seemed to suffer. For the most part the framerate is really good but the more I played the game the more I encountered a jumpy framerate that would jump from around 60 frames to about 20 frames per second. This didn't ruin the game but it did lead to some deaths. The other technical issue is that the game for some reason continues to run in the background even after I quit the game. The developer has had several updates to the game already so I am guessing these issues will be resolved soon.
Basically Adventure Lamp is a good platformer that is fun to play but is a little on the short and easy side. If you enjoy platformers I think you should enjoy Adventure Lamp.

Adventure Lamp is a charming  plaformer with simple, physics-based puzzles that range in difficulty. I had the opportunity to play Adventure Lamp before it was released on Steam through Itch.io.
The art style is quaint and effective. Adventure Lamp's story reflects this, with a focus more on progressively challenging puzzles and less on an involved story. The main gameplay concept of throwing one's helmet is simple, but tricky to master with timing and puzzle elements introduced in later levels. The Xbox 360 controls are solid, and options allow a handful of ways to utilize the controller to suit your input style. In addition, the game offers mouse-only controls, which are surprisingly workable. It also offers unique ways to play through the main storyline after beating it, which was a welcome surprise.
My only real gripe with the game was the airborne movement, which I had occasional trouble with. Due to the nature of aiming the helmet with the left stick on an Xbox controller, sometimes I would have trouble moving precisely in the air and aiming at the same time. I spoke with the developer about this briefly, and I believe he has addressed this in the latest update. I had no similar issue with the keyboard controls.
A few of the puzzles seemed a little uncharacteristically difficult for their spot in the story, but the variety of puzzles lent well to the utility of the main mechanic. I played through two stories over two evenings, leading to a shorter but satisfying experience. All in all, I would recommend this game if you've got a soft spot for unique gameplay and adorable platformers.

March 2015 Update:
Game Video is updated, as are the screenshots.  Controllers work better.  You can see an increase in clarity of the graphics; they're better but they're still pixellated on the parallax backgrounds ("Urban" level - perhaps by design) and overall have a flash game/amateur look to them.  Again, perhaps this is by design and I just don't agree with the new direction/design of the graphics.  Most important to me, however, is the incredible disconnect between what this game is and what it should be as far as gameplay goes.
Fired projectiles are too slow, this is especially noticeably on the "Urban" level - but it'll frustrate you at some point on every level.  Weapon and music sychronicity need work.  I believe this should function like a reverse Rock Band.  In that game, easy has very few fret colors to hit and those fret colors increase with more difficulty.  Your game is a music/rhythm game, do it in reverse.  On easy, fire weapons like crazy.  As the difficulty is increased, lower the amount of weapons firing - or better yet leave them as is and either decrease their damage or increase the # or strength of the enemies.
This is a shoot'em up, there should be weapons and ships firing all over the place, but the weapons in this game, except during drops in the song, feel anemic for the most part  There are also far more infrequent than they should be.  There are litterally LULLS on every level, at least one, where no weapons are firing at all and there are usually still enemies around.  So you're just running away from them until a part of the song comes up where you do have weapons.  This isn't fun, its frustrating.
I'm not asking for a bullet hell update - but keep it interesting and the screen activity BUSY.  And please give more attention to the projectile weapons.  Speed them up and make them more frequent.  I'm kiling most enemies with the side-firing immediate area weapons because they're more useful.
I don't know.  You've made some progress, but I'm still left exasperated at this game.  Eclipse and Tough Guy are the best levels out of the bunch, though.
Original Review:
I don't know what happened, but scrapping everything that everyone liked about the game, including some of the music, and starting over with "all new" everything was not a good move.
The original presentation, in fact even the current demo movie and screenshots on this store page, of Dubwars was essentially Geometry Wars played to Dubstep music where the music dictated what weapons fired and when.  It was a neat idea, a gorgeous looking game, and a concept that I enjoyed - sort of a different take on Audiosurf but not with your music.
As of the Fall/Winter 2014 update - they completely redid everything - supposedly all better.  But it's not all better.  The entire look of the game has an amateurish look to it now.  Like the original developer(s) left or Mura Interactive suffered an exodus of talent and that talent took their work with them.  It looks and plays like a Adobe Flash game that someone made in high school before they got good at making anything.
Did the Geometry Wars guys threaten to sue Mura Interactive for copyright infringement?  What happened?  At this point, isn't this false advertising - it's nothing like what is represented above?  I regret backing the Kickstarter for the amount that I did.  I can't imagine I will see ANY of the tier rewards I pledged for; however, I will take my bitter medicine and make the first review I've ever put on Steam to say that, at this point, you should only get this game if it's free or gifted to you.  It's not as bad as some of the "Early Access" trash that is out there, but it has definitely fallen victim to that curse.

I played the original Metro 2033 several years ago and enjoyed every minute of it. Needless to say, I also greatly enjoyed Metro 2033 Redux. That said, a few of the game’s faults seemed more apparent to me this time around—possibly because gaming has come so far since 2010. Fortunately, those flaws aren’t enough to drag down one of the best story-driven first-person shooters on the market.
I’m fairly sure everyone knows what Metro is about, but here’s the quick version just in case: World War III has left the world in a deep nuclear winter. Millions of people died when the bombs fell, but a handful of others have learned to survive in their harsh new environment. In Moscow, these people have set up a crude society of city-states at various stations in the city’s subway system. In addition to killing each other, these people have to contend with horribly mutated creatures that like to kill and eat them, a variety of nasty environmental hazards like poison gas, and the stark realization that they may never again see the light of day. It’s pretty depressing stuff, for sure. But it makes for an excellent game.
You play as a young man named Artyom, who discovers that his station is in grave danger of succumbing to a new threat to the metro system. Artyom sets off from his home station to find help and warn others before his community is overrun. As you might expect, things don’t exactly go as planned. I don’t want to spoil anything, so I’ll say only that the story is surprisingly strong and that the game does an excellent job of weaving likeable, interesting characters into the narrative. Most of them die, but that’s to be expect in the post-apocalypse, I guess.
Even some of the enemies are likeable in Metro 2033, which goes out of its way to remind you that everyone is human. At one point, I drew my silenced revolver on the head of an enemy soldier conversing with a friend. Then the soldier started talking about how much he missed his children and his family. He talked about how he just wanted to go home. And damn it, I couldn’t pull the trigger after I heard that.
There are a few trips to the bombed-out surface in Metro 2033, including an extremely disconcerting, tense mission to the Moscow library. But, as you might have guessed from the name, you’ll be spending most of your time in dark, dank metro tunnels. Fortunately, the new graphics engine makes even endless concrete corridors look eerily beautiful, especially when it comes to the lighting effects.
Those effects aren’t just for show, either. You’ll need to stay in the shadows—especially during encounters with human enemies— if you intend to play the game stealthily (which is, I think, the intended playstyle).  You can also sneak around some monsters, though the game will frequently lock you and your friends in a room with a bunch of terrifyingly fast beasties that want to eat your face. At that point, it’s time to drop the act and go all Call of Duty on the uglies with the variety of satisfyingly customizable weapons you collect and upgrade throughout the game. I enjoyed these last-stand style fights, though they were sprinkled in a little too heavily and eventually became pretty predictable and repetitive.
Metro 2033 Redux is not without its faults. There are at least two chapters where the game’s otherwise excellent level design and pacing fly out the window and frustration creeps in. One mission in particular finds you sneaking your way through a crumbled building and jumbled parking lot on your way to your next objective. The path through is not at all clear, which can lead to a seriously irritating number of game reloads until you get it “right.” There are also stealth sequences that seem to come down more to trial-and-error memorization rather than player skill or intelligence. That’s a shame, because the stealth mechanics in Metro 2033 are very, very good.
I also found fault with some of the game’s “survival” aspects. While these can be toned by selecting a more action-oriented mode when starting a game, that isn’t really the way Metro is meant to be played. For the most part, it keeps things interesting to have to guard the condition of your gas mask, make sure you have enough filters to keep yourself from suffocating on the surface, and manage your ammo.
But because the game doesn’t allow you to save any time, relying instead on an archaic, checkpoint-based auto-save system, mismanagement of your resources can leave you stuck in a progress-breaking corner. About halfway through the game’s lengthy final level on the surface, I discovered that I was out of filters. This led to a number of extremely frustrating deaths until I managed to find a tiny stash of filters that would buy me the 30 seconds needed to advance to the next life-saving cutscene. Earlier in the game, my gas mask was shattered by a monster. With no replacement available, I proceeded to die repeatedly and unavoidably following the last checkpoint I'd hit. The only solution was to load up an earlier checkpoint and try again—a maneuver that cost me about an hour and a half of my life. I know what the devs were going for, but that’s questionable design.
Still, Metro 2033 Redux is a very strong game. It’s got enough to do and discover that it’s worth at least two playthroughs, each of which will take you 8-10 hours. That may not seem like a lot, but Metro 2033 is one of those games you’ll always remember despite its faults. It’s worth checking out for shooter or post-apocalyptic fans.
To sum up:
-Excellent setting and compelling story
-Generally strong level design and pacing
-Great visuals
-Fun, immersive gameplay with plenty of customization options
-Sometimes relies too heavily on scripted encounters
-Some missions are irritatingly murky
-Some questionable design decisions can hamper the experience

It took months for the developers to address the crosshair position reset issue.  Even after they provided a "fix" to allow the crosshair to always be visible, it was such a terrible implementation.  The crosshair is unrealistically "visible" in game, and it is extremely easy to lose track of it due to its small size and high transparency.  At higher resolutions, the size did not scale, and thus punished higher resolution displays.  There is no way to control the transparency/opacity.  There are also no color options for users to choose something that didn't blend easily into the background.
Since the game was ported to the PC, the developers failed to understand the extreme differences between input devices on the new platform.  A desktop computer has two primary input devices: a keyboard and a mouse.  Obviously, the keyboard share extremely similar properties to a controller, such as one key press will indicate one specific action or movement or gunfire for example.  However, the mouse on the other hand, is a much more complicated issue.  The mouse's primary role is to serve as a cursor aim for the player, similar to, but not equal to the function of a joystick on a controller.  After a weapon is readied for fire, the player can aim using this input device to attack a target.  So, what's the problem here?
The problem lies in the fact that a joystick and a mouse are two very different types of input devices.  For months, the game implementation caused the crosshair to appear in front of where the helldiver is facing when readying a gun for fire.  For a controller, that's not a problem! In fact, that situation is ideal because the neutral position of a joystick snaps back to the center, which is also coincidently the neutral camera position of a helldiver.  This creates a synergy where the helldiver, the controller, and the background cursor, are all in complete sync.
What about the mouse?  The mouse has no such neutral position!  For decades, ever since the first home desktop computer was made available, the mouse served as a input device to control various things in an operating system UI.  The physical position of a mouse on the mousepad was mapped to a specific cursor position on the screen.  As long as tracking was correct, the cursor and mouse position was in perfect sync with a 1:1 (x,y) position function.  Under normal and proper use, the user would never need to constantly lift up and drop the mouse to reset positioning.
But what did the developers of helldiver do?  They didn't change the crosshair design of the game for months.  They broke the natural and fundemental design of what a mouse was suppose to be, claiming that it felt "more natural" for this style of position reset input.  They insisted that the mouse cursor/crosshair, which users have relied on for the same cursor consistency for decades, was the wrong philosophy in their game.  However, many users on their discussion forums didn't believe so as you can easily read on their forums.  The act of a cursor randomly appearing in a place where brain did not expect it be, caused a user disorientation from said inconsistency.  The user has to "remap itself" and reset its positional hand-eye coordination each and every time the player readies a weapon for fire.  Yet instead of immediately patching the game, they took months to do so.
So, they fixed it right?  Now there isn't a problem?
Of course not.  Their current implementation, while it does maintain more consistency of a cursor, lacks proper visibility.  The cursor on the screen and human vision tracking are suppose to maintain constant syncronization under normal use.  But if visibility is not consistent, the user will get the same disorientation after losing their cursor.  Just suppose you were to use your cursor in Windows the same well helldivers is now.  What if the cursor was generally very small and  90% transparent and only turned solid upon pressing a mouse button.  Would you consider that intuitive in design?  Many users would get nothing but headaches with this type of implementation.  It is extremely disorientating to the user because there is a lack of cursor consistency for the brain.
Some argue that the existence of a true and visible cursor would create an unfair advantage for PC users compared to the controller on a console.  The fact is, anytime you have a mouse for aiming, it will generally always beat out a joystick.  I don't deny that, especially when playing a first person shooter.
However, Helldivers was not designed as a first person shooter.  All the units in the game: the helldivers, the different guns, the turrets, the tanks/vehicles, all have different turning speeds.  The very existence of a turning speed mehcanic for all units in game prevents the abuse from a player just sniping everything as quickly as they physically can.  If this was a first person shooter, I'd agree that a mouse would give an unfair advantage.  But lets face it, this isn't an FPS.  We are all bounded by the same turning speed mechanic in the game, controller or mouse.
As of date, the developers of Helldivers has not made the cursor fully visible.  When I mean fully visible, I mean a large, opaque, and proper colored one for clarity.  They seem to feel that PC users have no right comfortably play the game without mental disorientation because perhaps they might gain an unfair advantage over other platforms.  This same type of philosophy would also support games with flashing lights that causes seizures, because after all, if the seizures weren't there, perhaps the game would be too easy.
Rather than develop games with proper inputs for various platforms, they have misunderstood that their inherit game mechanics already prevent the abuse they are trying to prevent.  The developers have chosen to value the illusion of more gameplay balance between different platforms over human mental health.  Thats right, you heard me.  The devleopers believe "balance" is more important than human mental health.  And in turn, they only cause unnecessary mental harm to players who only wish to enjoy their game.  Some have raged, some have refunded, some have just simply stopped playing.  This was the result of all of this.
I personally would not recommend this game for the PC.  Perhaps, through a console controller, the design makes perfect sense and I would highly recommend it.  But for the PC, the developers don't seem to have any interest in adjusting their design to accomodate for extremely different input environments as compared to a controller.

Helldivers is a top-down, cooperative action game set in a generic sci-fi setting. Up to four players work together to complete objectives during missions to unlock experience points, gear, and research points to upgrade their gear. Chains of missions can be beaten to conquer planets, which feeds into the Helldivers meta-game, which is quite clever. In the meta-game, humanity is fighting a war on three fronts (corresponding to the three alien races you’ll encounter). Each front is divided into sectors, and as you conquer each sector you get closer to the enemy home planets, which when defeated knock that enemy out of the current “war”. Every planet individual players defeat contributes to the point threshold in each sector, which is conquered when the required threshold is reached. Occasionally the enemy will go on the offensive, forcing you to defend planets (and ultimately Earth). If Earth falls, the current war ends and a new war begins in a presumably alternate reality.
Helldivers requires a sense of humor. It’s designed to be played with four players, and each player is constantly calling in orbital bombardments, resupply drop pods, vehicles, and equipment. Each one of these can kill you when they enter the map. You’ll die if you stand in front of a teammate while he’s firing, if you’re too close to his mech when he walks, if you jump out of your vehicle while it’s still moving and it runs you over, if you jump off the side of a cliff, drop a grenade at your own feet, or die from the actual enemies in the game. It’s all part of the fun, but it presupposes that everyone is taking a similar, light-hearted yet directed approach to the game.
In my experience, the community is fun and welcoming, for the most part happy to work together to collect samples and complete goals. All in all, Helldivers is tremendous fun and provides excellent value. It’s a shame that several DLC are considered essential to enjoy the game to its fullest, but I suppose you can always get those on sale.

I bought this game years ago simply to see the ending to the cliffhanger that Half Life 2 provided. And I utterly hated this game, at the time I thought everything was poorly designed with my main complaint being the lack of ammo and weapons for the amount of enemies you have to kill. I considered it one of the worst game I ever played and it turned me off of Half life so much that I didn't bother buying the 2nd episode. I still haven't played it and I'm planning on buying it tomorrow during the Holiday Sale.
But after completing Half life 2 with some mods I decided to install episode one again and take it for a spin, fully expecting to hate it again. I was pleasantly surprised though Episode one is still the weakest game in the Half Life Franchise. First off my initial complaint of the lack of ammo for your weapons just... isn't a thing anymore. Maybe I just sucked and wasted too much ammo but I never had a problem. Though I wish that the crowbar was given to the player in the beginning of the game, instead of the half-way point where you no longer need it. Having a viable melee weapon early on in the game against the headcrab zombies would have been really nice instead of having to constantly run around the map looking for cement blocks to shoot at them with your Grav Gun.
Also the game is really dark, this in of itself isn't an issue but due to the fact that your flashlight uses energy you basically have to stop and stand still in the dark for a few moments while your flashlight charges, which really kills the game flow for me. I wish they just made the Flashlight not use your suit's battery so it could stay on indefinitely.
I also really liked the Zombine enemy. They become a priority when dealing with hordes of Zombies and they can be actually quite helpful for you when they pull out a grenade and go kamikaze. If you're quick enough to get away they can  usually kill the horde of zombies for you. You can also shoot the grenade out of their hand or snatch it from them with the Grav Gun. It's all these things that makes them a fun dynamic new enemy which makes up for the lack of new weapons or features.
There are also a lot of great gunfights with the Combine and the firefight in the Hospital is definitely the best part of Episode one. Also Alyx is a treat too though I found her animation to be a little stiff and lifeless at times. Beat the game and when you're on the train, just look at Alyx and you'll see what I mean. She looks like a Mannequin at points and for a game whose main selling point is having Alyx fighting with you it seems like a big oversight, especially since the source engine has proven before that its quite good at making life-like animations.
But the biggest problem I have with the game is that it is waaay too short. I have around 6.9 hours clocked in and thats after 2 playthroughs. I believe my first playthrough took me about four hours and my last playthough just shy of three. Even in a market in which single player campaigns are getting increasingly short, there is no excuse for Episode one to be this short and it is simply not worth the asking price of $8, even when you take mods like MINERVA into consideration.
Ultimately I would recommend Episode One but with a big asterisk: Do not pay full price for it and understand that it is the weakest game in the Half Life Series, even a game like Blue Shift I feel is better than Episode one. But it has some cool gunfights and helps to continue the story and transition into Episode two. Pay at most $4 and make sure you play the Minerva mod at some point to get your full money's worth.

Great old game, bought it again a few years ago, this time on Steam, because I just couldn't be bothered to use the orginal discs anymore. Still awesome and even more so with the Unofficial Patches, which fix and and restore a ton of bugs and goodies. Unfortunately the patches adds a few bugs of its own, but far less than what used to be.
Game got lots of dialogue options and quite a few that depends on the Sex of your character with different options and endings depending on your choices and humanity rating. The Unofficial Patch 9.5 also unlocks some character creation options like History, that makes some subtle changes to your character and is partially based on your Sex as well.
The RPG, Dialogue, Voices, Music is all pretty awesome and easily worth the play, but the combat can be extremely aggravating, clunky and ungratifying bordering on totally hazardous to your gaming equipment.. It's a dangerous mix. At times this game is pretty awesome and then suddenly incredible crappy and then both at the same time. It's really a matter of timing to make it rock and the game isn't making it easy on you. The game will generally autosave on area transistions, but quite often it won't.
There are three different kinds of basic Combat: Unarmed, Melee and Ranged, but there are also disciplines that add to that. Each Clan has it's own setup, even though some Clans share some disciplines, there are also some common ones like Blood Buff (that increase your stats to deal with those pesky locks in the beginning) and Blood Heal. There is a huge difference between the different branches of combat. The game can be a hell of a lot more of a Thief game than "Thief" itself and while Ranged can be pretty devastating it's quite differert from a regular shooter, because shooting and handling relies more on in-game skill and attributes, than your own skills.
One piece of general advice: SAVE OFTEN!
Without the Unofficial Patch: A few problems on Windows 7/8: Find the vampire.exe and set compatiblity to Windows XP and start-up Steam with  "Run as administrator" and you are good to go.. Or you were. The Patch adds its own shortcut that can apparently be run without further ado or maybe it's because it utilize the same executable..

With the Saints Row The Third being the weird smash hit that it was, with it’s purple ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and farts on jars and♥♥♥♥♥♥ of course there would be a sequel. I even pre-ordered it when it was announcer and to be fair, I don’t regret it at all. However, as with most games, there’s bad sh#t on it and as usual, I will start with that:
First and foremost, the biggest problem this game has is being called Saints Row IV. It is not a proper sequel, sort to speak. If should have been a spin-off, as most stuff that previous games had in terms of gameplay is pretty much ignored here. While previous games were sort of like a more cheerful and hilarious version of San Andreas with tons of toilet humor and crap all over the place, this game suddenly turns into a parody of Prototype and Crackdown, with you collecting orbs to power up, running and gliding through the air with super-powers, and stuff of the like. It does NOT feel like a Saints Row game at times, and that could’ve been fixed by just NOT GIVING THE PLAYER THOSE SUPER-POWERS IN LESS THAN 30 MINUTES OF GAMEPLAY. Suddenly cars, driving and all that crap feels outdated as you can OUTRUN those cars or leap higher than two story buildings effortlessly.
The second problem it has going for it, is the build-up for stuff that happens. Listen, it’s cool that the game has aliens, but why not letting us play as the President for a mission or two before dropping them? Or why showing in trailers that Gat will be back, instead of letting it be a surprise when you find that in the game? It just feels like lazy writing and them trying to cheaply hype the game, as the story feels rushed in a lot of parts.
It also lacks on the activities. The activities here are mostly based arround super powers, which is actually a good idea that I like, however some of them feel redudant as hell. WHY THE HELL ARE THERE 4 DIFFERENT VARIANTS OF MAYHEM!? I know that it's a really beloved activity from past games but COME ON. Regular Mayhem with weapons, Mayhen with vehicles (ufos, tanks and that sort of stuff), Mayhem with a Mech and lastly Mayhem with powers which I must add, is boring and lame as hell as you can only use ONE of your powers, telekinesis. Why!? There were already two other activities that are much better and are based arround Telekinesis (Mind over Murder and the TK Rifts), so adding those just feels like adding a space they couldn't fill with anything better in time.
Lastly, the DLC’s are… Well, a mixed bag. I’d say the only one truly worth it would be the Xmas one. The rest are rather generic, and the Enter The Dominatrix is actually surprisingly quite God-awful and boring. There's also a heavy load of generic and dumb 1-3€ worth DLC's that only add cosmetics, skins or some variant of power or weapon. Those are bad, but the worst DLC of them all has to be the one that adds voice actors for the game as homies. I'm not joking. That's actually a thing, it makes no sense, it's stupid and they're useless, as they don't have super powers like most other homies.
Does the game has good stuff though? Yeah, it’s fun as hell! Now, The Third was a fun game but had parts that felt lame as sh#t, and it truly shows that the devs noticed what worked and what not, as pretty much the entire game keeps the fun factor quite high, with the only exceptions being the damn cluster collecting and other boring garbage activities like the already mentioned Mayhem overdose.
The story is quite entertaining, though feels rushed during multiple times of the game. However, characters are just great and I was unable to even hate ONE of them, which speaks highly of it.
Gameplay, while not feeling like Saints Row AT ALL, is fun, exciting and fast-paced. Really makes you feel like a complete f#cking Badass (as me, sort to speak). Weapons are also a bit less broken… Except for the Dubstep Gun, which when fully upgraded makes most other guns instantly obsolete. Money is also harder to get and upgrades are more expensive, so you won't hit the game-breaking area as fast as you could with The Third.
Something that must also be said is that the game does go back to it’s roots when it comes to make references to previous games. People from Saints Row 1, 2 and The Third make cameos and some of them are actually quite surprising and hilarious
. The game also has a bigger emphasis on references to other video-games, movies and pop-culture in general, which feels like it fits perfectly here.
Not stopping there, the music selection is quite good. Not as good as SR2 as it has less variety… But the themes are a blast to enjoy. The mission and activities soundtrack fits right in, although there seems to be less radio stations. There's a new dubstep station and Reggae makes a comeback, but Funk is still nowhere to be seen. On the voice department, the game has again 3 male voices, 3 female voices and the extra “joke” voice is Nolan North… As Nolan North. Yeah, your boss becomes Nolan North when using it. Must say I usually pick the british one but Nolan made me go through the game a second time to hear his hilarious sh#t at everything.
About the activities, I've already thrown quite the share of sh#t to the Mayhem overdose... But that doesn't mean that the rest are bad. Most of them are there to help you learn how to use your powers properly, which is a really good idea. Races help you get used to the fast-pased movement, Platforming Rifts help you learn how to properly jump and glide, TK Rifts and Mind Over Murder helps you out with the helpful Telekinesis powers and the Fight Clubs from Saints Row 2 make a come-back as a big arena with enemies from previous games on which you can learn how to use your offensive powers properly, all followed with really good music.
The story missions also have way more variety, which was difficult to top it up after The Third. Seriously, it keeps somehow bringing something even more crazy and forth-wall breaking filled with references for you to clear.
Oh, and it also has Coop. Haven’t played the entire game with it as I did with the previous one, but hey it was still tons of fun.
Overall, is it worth it? F#ck yeah. It’s a really good game, but only fans who have played at least The Third will get a really good kick out of it. As SR1 was an Xbox exclusive and SR2 sucks on PC, I recommend you at least play The Third first before going for this. On a price-drop sale, this game is a must buy, although you can totally ignore the DLC’s.

While this game is on the short side, there is an amazing story to be told and experience like no other game has been able to.  From the outset, you are given complete freedom to explore and investigate as you see fit; no set paths and no linear storytelling allows this game to come together organically.  This comes as a great reward as the world of Ethan Carter is beautifully detailed and amazingly executed on both an artistic and technical scale.  The soundtrack which accents the various regions and moods the game sets is also equally beautiful and haunting and doesn't distract you from the experience.
The puzzles presented in the game are a bit (for me at least) on the simple side but don't let that be a deterrent for what is otherwise a great narrative piece.  I really enjoyed the parts where you have to piece together a scene sequentially from a collective of smaller scenes that gives you more perspective into the very strange world you are investigating.  Part of what made this game truly amazing is that you can't really anticipate what you'll discover next and what you usually discover is bizarre and often fascinating.
When the credits finally rolled, it made me stop and think about all that I had experienced and allowed me to come to my own conclusions on the events that took place.  I should further elaborate that it's not a cop out on the story to leave you having questions and drawing conclusions after the credits; it's simply part of the narrative structure.  The ending is satisfying and gives you a brand new perspective on the world it created.  It gives me great incentive to explore the world again, geared with new knowledge and perspective. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with this title and would highly recommend it for anyone curious about it.

Unfortunately the patches adds a few bugs of its own, but far less than what used to be.
Game got lots of dialogue options and quite a few that depends on the Sex of your character with different options and endings depending on your choices and humanity rating. The Unofficial Patch 9.5 also unlocks some character creation options like History, that makes some subtle changes to your character and is partially based on your Sex as well.
The RPG, Dialogue, Voices, Music is all pretty awesome and easily worth the play, but the combat can be extremely aggravating, clunky and ungratifying bordering on totally hazardous to your gaming equipment.. It's a dangerous mix. At times this game is pretty awesome and then suddenly incredible crappy and then both at the same time. It's really a matter of timing to make it rock and the game isn't making it easy on you. The game will generally autosave on area transistions, but quite often it won't.
There are three different kinds of basic Combat: Unarmed, Melee and Ranged, but there are also disciplines that add to that. Each Clan has it's own setup, even though some Clans share some disciplines, there are also some common ones like Blood Buff (that increase your stats to deal with those pesky locks in the beginning) and Blood Heal. There is a huge difference between the different branches of combat. The game can be a hell of a lot more of a Thief game than "Thief" itself and while Ranged can be pretty devastating it's quite differert from a regular shooter, because shooting and handling relies more on in-game skill and attributes, than your own skills.
One piece of general advice: SAVE OFTEN!

You Have to Win the Game is a retro platformer in which you must avoid enemies and obstacles and collect 'abilities' in order to progress. This game is by far my new favorite platformer.
Things I love about it:
•It's addicting (trust me, it is).
•The retro-theme is just beautiful.
•It doesn't have advanced system requirements (pretty much any PC can run it).
•It's a single-player free to play game, so I don't have to deal with internet trolls and annoying 7 year olds.
•Funny little jokes here and there (mostly in the room names).
•Awesome collectables
•You can continue to play after you close the game, you get infinite lives (in normal mode), and there's a lot of checkpoints.
•Very few controls (up, down, left, right).
•It's just a really good game (well made, smooth, etc.)
Things I don't particularly love:
•It's VERY hard, you will die, a lot (some of you may really like that, though).
•Sometimes you will get killed by a spike when you aren't close to it (this is the biggest flaw in the game, it seriously needs to be fixed).
•I'm pretty sure I have carpal tunnel syndrome now (you've got to mash jump button to scale walls when you get the gloves).
•Sometimes you get stuck on a challenge in a room and it takes ages to get out.
•It's a major time consumer (if you've got work to do, good luck).
Overall, this game is just amazing. If you're wanting to play a good platformer, this is the game for you. Why not pick it up? It's free!

This game is a Historical piece for many reasons, the first of which being thta Bloodlines it's one of the best RPG ever made.
Bloodlines launched in 2004 and was the debut of the famous Source Engine, Valve's technology that would later on support nothing less than Half-Life 2. If that isn't enough, the game was the downfall of Troika, a games studio formed by key people from Black Isle, responsible for the first two Fallout games.
The game is deeply hardcore, and completely written for fans of the Vampire: The Masquerade pen & paper RPG. It's a RPG true to the roots, where you spend most of your time exploring, talking and interacting with a world pretty much alive. It not only explores all that it can from the V:tM setting, but borrows everyhting that fits from the World Of Darkness full setting, meaning one can expect to see nothing short of changelings, werewolfs, Kindred Of The East, Mages and who knows what else. The game is full of memorable characters, with decent voice acting and nice models. The quests are very interesting, and tie well with the setting. Surely, this is one of the most ambituous RPG projects ever done, and it's not a surprise that Troika couldn't quite finish it.
A rushed production meant that most of the game wasn't ready by the time it was unleashed upon the world. This resulted in poor reception by the specialized media and worse by players, who where annoyed by semi done quests, lots of bugs and a number of other problems. And since Troika closed doors a few months later, people thought there was no hope.
Nonetheless, a few people could see the jewel inside the oyster and started working on "unnoficial" patches that not only fixed the glitches but also unlocked lots of unfinished content and enabled players to enjoy the whole detailed scenario. To accompany that, ENB has a cool DX patch that improves the graphics and make the game even more obscure and dark that it already is.
If you ever played Vampire: The Masquerade with friend, you owe it to yourself to play the game. If you enjoy true RPGs, you won't forgive yourself for not trying this game. The good is so good that you'll be able to forgive the bad.

I picked up and played through the The Room in a single sitting. I was so impressed that I turned around and picked up The Room Two the same night. If you liked The Room, much of the sequel is the same. High quality visual environments packed around puzzle boxes in mysterious rooms. My one criticism of The Room was its short run time, 2 hours for me with no guides or hints. The Room Two did address this slightly, running somewhere around 3-4 hours total over a couple of nights to untangle its puzzles, but I'm not sure it hit the mark on that particular point.
Compared to the first game, The Room Two expanded the focus of the puzzle solving. In the first game, you were typically focused on a single box at a single table. This time around, you may be working multiple puzzles across multiple objects within a single room. This gives the game more of an escape room type mentality rather than solving a single puzzle box. The downside was that the puzzles often felt less logically connected and lacked a certain polished focus that they had in the first game. Both times that I broke from the game when stuck on a puzzle, were results of (what I felt were) non-sequitur jumps of logic or "pixel hunting" to find some random point in the room that I didn't even realize was a part of the play space until the camera moved in on it. Looking at the Mobile release versus the PC release, I wonder how much of the difficulties I had were a result of more realistic and moody lighting found in the PC version.
Those gripes aside, the game still benefits from (typically) clever puzzles, high quality visuals and excellent sound design. If the psudo-story of the first game was interesting to you, they expand on the lore of the Null and your voyage through the Rooms following your mentor, but the story is never intrusive or even the focus of the gameplay. There's very little else like this that I've found and if you like these kinds of puzzles it's a great fix. If you can get it during a Steam sale, I'd highly recommend the title to anyone. It's priced like a mobile game and an incredible game for your buck given the high quality visuals and hand crafted unique puzzles and interactions. At full price, I would still recommend the game for anyone looking for a good puzzle game.

Crazy wacky ridiculous zany fun!  There simply aren't any other game franchises of this era that bring this level of comedic entertainment value to the table.  Satirical adventure games may have a long history but seldom is that genre barrier broken let alone smashed in such a truly enjoyable way.
The writing is brilliant.  The voice acting couldn't be better.  And the mocap animations work perfectly with the graphical  style to bring it all to life.  The facial expressions alone are remarkable (and usually quite funny) not to mention everything else.  Use of great classic songs at key moments also really adds an extra something special.  Production value is just terrific.
They take a satirical look at, well... whatever they feel like and throw in so many pop culture references you're bound to notice at least some you love.  If you're old enough to remember 8-bit side scrollers, know some classic karaoke, or have noticed anything at all from the past few decades you'll find really enjoyable references/parts in this game.  It's hard not to walk away from smiling (or chuckling).  Personally I find the character interactions to be the most entertaining/hysterical parts of the game and they're nearly a constant thing.
The gameplay itself does take a backseat to the entertainment but that doesn't mean it's not good as well.  It's like playing a video game and getting to enjoy something akin to a really good TV sitcom in the process.
I would recommend playing at least SR3 previous to this game though... a lot of things may not make much sense if you haven't.  Having played SR3 on the xbox and thoroughly loved it,  I actually wasn't going to play SR4 after seeing all the reviews and media focused on aliens and superpowers that turned me off to the idea of it.  I didn't want to spoil my fond memories of SR3.  But I saw a really good deal on this game and feeling nostalgic for those SR3 classic moments I just couldn't resist.  Now that I've finally gotten around to playing it am I ever glad I didn't skip it... it's so much more than the aliens and superpowers characterizations people had been defining it by.  If you loved the great moments from SR3 there are more awaiting you here.  I'd say overall SR3 was still better in some ways but that didn't make this experience seem any less awesome.
If anything, the only "con" I can think of are that there are actually too many fun toys, customizations, and open-world things crammed in that there ends up being little motivation for using/doing after a certain point (especially with special vehicles you unlock given how little you're likely to use vehicles much at all).
Note that my listed play-time for the game is inflated due to just leaving the game paused when I wasn't playing it quite a bit.  Actual play time for a completionist type is more like 40-60 hours for the game and DLC missions/events.

SanctuaryRPG is a peculiar mix of brilliant and lazy design decisions. In concept, it's a turn-based, menu-driven distillation of all the "number go up" bits that make games in the mold of Diablo so addictive. In some places, the game delivers on that concept in a way just short of genius; in others, it goes "eh, whatever, this will do" and calls it a day.
: The battle system is complex and engaging despite its extreme abstraction. Attack and defense abilities, status effects, monster affixes, range (sort of), weapon properties, character class features, and more besides--the better you learn these things, the more successful you'll be. Various elements require that you stay mindful of what's going on rather than run on autopilot, lest you miss opportunities or suffer dangerous consequences.
: The UI is atrocious. You have to mash Enter after every menu choice, as if you were working with a terminal prompt instead of pushing virtual buttons. The mouse does nothing, but the game doesn't bother to hide the cursor in fullscreen mode.
: There are tons of ways to get experience, gold, and items. If you're feeling behind the curve against the current crop of storyline foes, you don't necessarily have to farm lower-level monsters--you can take on some level-matched foes in the arena, read books in the Library, tend patrons in your tavern, or craft, all of which will move you along at least a bit.
: Some of these activities, though, are deadly boring, and you'll roll your eyes when some new system presents itself and it turns out to be yet another thing that awards experience, gold, and random items. Crafting? Experience and random items (you get only minimal input into what you craft). Tavern? Gold, experience, and "gifts" from patrons that are, yes, random items. Fetch quests? Experience and random items. There's all of one well-hidden quest that gives you anything unique or interesting.
: The aesthetic. Well, maybe not
exactly, but at least gutsy and unusual. The ASCII art is well done and the music catchy.
: The art you see has nothing to do with what you're doing, most of the time. You can be trudging through a hellish underworld, and still see pictures of green forests and blue oceans. The writing is terrible; there's a nonsensical main plot about robots and fallen angels that tries to get you to take it seriously even as the rest of the game cracks jokes about potatoes. (If you can even call them jokes. The author seems to think that simply saying the word "potato" is the height of hilarity.) Don't bother talking to NPCs--their dialogue is bland and doesn't change from start to finish.
: Itemization is very well designed. You can't stash old equipment, and each item has at most a core attack/defense stat, two attribute boosts, and an affix. That means that you're almost always trading something off when you upgrade, prompting reconsideration of what's in your other slots. Just changing out a weapon of one category for another can drastically change your play style.
: Permadeath. I don't take offense to the idea in principle--Nethack, that age-old Roguelike, is one of my favorite games of all time. But it doesn't fit at all here. There's not enough variety from one game to the next, games take too long to proceed to the latter stages, and there isn't enough of a skill learning curve to justify it. I recommend playing a couple short games to get the idea, then once you settle on a build you like, backing up your save files as you go.
In the end, I do give this game the thumbs-up because it's such an unusual specimen, and I found it enjoyable enough to play to conclusion on the standard difficulty. But know what you're getting into: it is, in many ways, half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥

Greetings loyal citizens of the greatest Planet in the Universe. Today, at this very moment, you are contemplating the most difficult decision of your life. You're thinking to yourself: "Do I want to protect my homeland, earn the privilege to have children, and gain the respect of my peers?" Or "Am I content with being a coward and most likely an Alien sympathizer?" There's a war out there and Super Earth needs your help!
Fight for Democracy! Join the HELLDIVERS!
....
You wanna know something? Starting off this review with such a cheeky intro, probably isn't the greatest idea. What I should have said was "anything that can go wrong, will go wrong". HELLDIVERS aka Murphy's Law: the videogame is not to be taken lightly. It can be raucous and exhilirating entertainment, but it can also cause finger-pointing, object-throwing, and enough expletives to block out the Super Sun. Also, while this game is excellent in many ways, it also has a handful of design-decisions that keep it just shy from classic status. Still, if I were to end this review right now, I'd say that this game is very highly recommended.
But the review is far from over, so allow me to continue.
If you've seen Paul Verhoeven's
, then you already know this game's story. Super Earth, the greatest planet in the Universe, has declared war on three factions: the cyborgs, bugs, and illuminate. At one time or another, one of these factions may or may not have unleashed a devastating attack on Super Earth. This tragedy must not go un-punished. Aside from destroying every last alien you confront, you're also expected to exploit their resources, assist colonization efforts, and broadcast the message that Super Earth's democracy is the greatest.
To really enjoy HELLDIVERS, you're expected to play cooperatively. This is a four-player game with both online and couch support. Aside from the introduction, there isn't really any campaign mode or much of a story. You assist the war effort by completing missions on various planets.
The most intriguing aspect of this game is that friendly-fire is always on and can never be disabled. While this game can be considered an isometric twin-stick shooter, you can't simply point and fire. No, you have to point and
fire. If you're not paying attention, your next shot might go through a team-mate's skull instead of into the weak-point of a bug, cyborg, or illuminate. This extends to nearly every action in the game. Your re-supply air-drops aren't going to be welcomed with open arms if they crush your allies. These rules make for a game that's a lot more interesting than most others of its ilk. Over time you'll develop an understanding of what actions your team-mates will take. The best teams will operate as one, while the worst will produce a comedy of errors.
A lot of the entertainment comes from adapting to the myriad of situations that can occur. By using strategems, players can receive unique weapons, call ordnance on stronger foes, or acquire vehicles that makes traversing each planet easier. Some of the heavier equipment (such as the RL-112) benefit more with one player carrying the gun, and the other carrying the ammo. It really drives home just how important good team-work can be, and it's the difference-maker on the hardest difficulties. The enemy is infinite, and as long as their patrols spot the players, they will bring as much force as necessary. At this point, the best response is usually to run away. Almost every enemy can be escaped, and will even despawn if you and your allies get out of the immediate area. In short, stealth is the #1 key to success, but not particularly entertaining.
As you continue to play this game, you'll notice that if you can eliminate patrols, then you won't have to worry about much of anything else. This tends to be the optimal way to play, since dealing with adversity will waste time (and leads to deaths). Aside from missions that require destroying a set number of enemies, or boss-fights, the bulk of the game can feel rather barren. All of the neat strategems and intriguing co-op ideas will fall by the wayside, as long as players are sharp and quick enough to take care of patrols.
This is usually the reason why I play with random players. Jumping into games where I don't have any idea what the other players are doing, and then adapt to their behavior/equipment, helps keep the game fun. I like to see danger, I like to see terrible situations, and hopefully we as a team can turn things around to accomplish our objectives. Videogames tend to "grow" with the player. As the player becomes more skilled, the game becomes more challenging to compensate (through difficulty settings or other means). HELLDIVERS can only grow so much, and that can be attributed to the design-decisions of stealth. If there were more missions where the enemy has fortified positions, or the players had to invade planets where there more than just patrols wandering around, it would definitely keep the game fresh for veterans.
Some encounters in this game could also use a little tuning. For example, there are three bosses. The boss of the bug faction does a lot of burrowing in and out of the ground. I've noticed that all too often, shots that look like they hit don't do any damage. For such a large and mostly immobile target, this creature has a surprising number of invulnerability frames. As the fight progresses, larger and more dangerous bugs join in. It's not enough that there are threats from every direction, but the probability for actually damaging the boss drops to .01%. Basically what I'm saying is that this isn't a fun battle. My suggestion would be to slightly decrease the damage that some of the enemies do, or maybe not give certain bugs so much armor. At least when entering a boss-battle, players have ample time to attempt it, and change strategies if their attempts fail. A person only has so much patient though, and rage-quits are always a possibility.
As you play this game, you're bound to notice other players with unfamiliar weapons, strategems, and perks. A lot of these are acquired by completing missions, but there are also a lot of them that are straight-up DLC. I'm... well... not terribly fond of this practice. For example, there is a perk known as the all-terrain boots. This allows players to not be slowed down by marshes or snow. There are planets that are nothing but snow. While it can be considered a situationally useful perk, these all-terrain boots are practically forced on the player. If I opt out of buying this DLC, and my team-mates do, then I'm going to be the one holding everybody back. I've also become overly reliant on the LAS-16 Sickle (a DLC gun). I'm not sure how well I'd do if I went back to any of the other guns, and I don't want to think about it.
With stealth being overpowered and the unfortunate DLC situation, I can't quite call HELLDIVERS a perfect game. Usually when reviewing a game, I don't even think of the word "perfect", but I came awfully close here. The cooperative aspects are absolutely brilliant, the sound-direction is flawless, the mechanics of gun-play and controls are spot-on, and the respect given to friendly-fire is a revelation. It's going to be exceedingly difficult for me to play any other online game that doesn't punish me for shooting my team-mates. This game really does almost everything right, which makes the aspects where it falls just a little short, stand out that much more. Despite this, I wholeheartedly recommend HELLDIVERS.

I love metro and have been a fan since the moment the first game was released on xbox 360 (good times.) I have played the original on console to every end. And it is amazing in all regards. Granted there's the sluggish AI, the (almost) impossible areas to sneak by without the sneak suit, the trolley ride made infinitely harder by the fact that the machine gun was to a shoot-as-fast-as-you-pull weapon and not a spray and pray, and the ridiculous volt driver that blew through librarians with 2 headshots on ranger hardcore - i loved all that, or at least learnt to.
Having played through the campaign twice I can undoubtedly profess here that I prefer the original. The remaster does not do the original justice in many regards:
Funnily enough, though all the visuals have been spruced up and the game made shinier and better looking; I genuinely prefer the appearance of the metro without it. The grimy, just feeling through the dark approach. I feel, that perhaps with the exception of the level above Black Station, that the original was just... overall more fitting in creating the atmosphere that is the world of Metro 2033.
Now what I say next may sound strange as hell but, I prefer the old combat system to the new one. I really do. The one in metro 2033 where you had to slowly move the weapon wheel about to get to what you wanted, so you couldn't actually throw grenades and knives like its nobody's business - survival in the metro is hard and the sluggishness of that system was something that actually added value to the immersion of the experience. In a gunfight, do I really risk the two seconds of trying to put another shell into my shotgun to blow away the nosalis I just stunned, or do I whip out my revolver and blow his face away? Or even better; have no ammo at all in any weapon and just ♥♥♥♥ing pull out the bowie (yes, that knife you use to stab people was actually a weapon you held in the HUD and swung) and give him the sharp knuckled punch. Those were the real fight for your life experiences I had when playing the original.
On top of that what I did actually enjoy was the standardised weapon system of revolver-assault rifle-other weapon, other weapon including shotguns or pneumatics. So although it did limit one's playstyle to having to choose whether they wanted a shotgun or a tihar, it also sort of encouraged one to try playing the game multiple times with the different combinations as certain weapons (silenced ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and scoped AK) were only available at certain levels in the game, and dropping them would mean letting go of those forever as even in the shops there wasn't the customisation options. Now that I can drop and pick up whatever weapons I like, I end up at the armoury with a 1000 MGR easy (non-ranger, survival). I'm a kid in a candy store but I can't even eat everything I want. It becomes pretty boring at that end, because all I need to do in any bad situation is whip out or pick up someone's assault weapon and blow holes in anything bad that comes my way. The sense of survival and running out of ammo is.. just totally absent.
Don't even get me started on the minor details - Sasha (kid) sounds really dumb. When Ulman and Pavel come to rescue the action scene is just totally bleh, even more so when at Black Station. Won't go into those... and even the way the levels were split up in the original, like how the surface level of outside the library and inside were split - those added to the pace of the storytelling which i think is overall, really something critical that the redux lacks.
I won't lie, I probably won't play this game very much. It is, without a doubt an amazing game, but my heart belongs with the original. I reccomend this game, but I reccomend the original much much more. Buy it and play it. It is fantastic, and while not necessarily visually superior; it may be your cup of tea as it is mine.

This game combines a pretty good story with absolutely incredible gameplay and visuals, becoming one of the most immersive games I've ever played, especially on Hardcore Ranger difficulty.
This game is a pretty linear first-person shooter, with light psychological horror elements, and a heavy reliance on stealth (only if you want to be stealthy though). In that respect it actually reminds me a lot of one of my favourite games, Dishonored, in that the worlds in each level are usually diverse, easy to explore, and player choice to how they want to play the game. Although it suffers the same problem as Dishonored, in that it is a fairly short game, taking me roughly 10 hours to beat on my first playthrough (but I have played it through many times on the Xbox).
Positives:
- incredibly immersive
- great weapon variety and customization
- unique world spaces
- absolutely stunning visuals
- just awesome sound quality
- pretty good story (sort of a neutral, but I like it)
- replayability
- many collectables that enhance the story, in the form of diary pages
- multiple endings, differing from playstyles
- very stable
- weapons felt balanced and realistic
Negatives
- game felt shorter than expected
- characters felt underdeveloped
-
- the main plot was driven by the need to save the station, but we don't get enough of a connection to it (you're there for one level)
Overall, even though a few things could have made it better, this is a pretty solid game that is definitely worth playing and immersing yourself in. If you do buy, pick up the Redux bundle that includes the sequel, Last Light, because it improves on almost all of the issues I had with the first game, and naturally continues the story.

There is something eerily charming about a post-apocalyptic Moscow. The world is constructed in such a way as to suggest that even an RPG game could possibly be set in it. Make no mistake, however, this is
an RPG game, it's an action shooter. Although, it must be mentioned, that you spend much time exploring, following someone, or just walking around without actual shooting.
The levels are well-designed, and will keep you engaged without stressing you out. The story is deep and rich in moral elements as well as interesting characters and themes, which is to be expected, since the game is based on a well-received novel. The graphics are top notch. The firefights are intense.
The game might seem linear, but it has more content that at first meets the eyes: First, you can play the game in two different modes. In
mode you get less resources and are encouraged to play smart, employing stealth and taking enemies down silently, or avoiding them altogether. In
mode there are more resources and you get to go "guns blazing" on your enemies. Another factor that can change the way you play and experiencce the game is what weapons you pick and how you choose to customize them. Finally, you could go around the levels exploring the various aspects of the well-crafted, beautifully-depicted world, and you might get rewarded by finding "journals" which include the main protagonist's thoughts on what's happening around him, and providing the player with a sense of character and a window into the hero's soul.
It's a beautiful game. Play it with headphones on and lights off.

After the massive failure that was Battlefront. Star Wars Battlefront II is still the go to game after all these many years. I still find myself enjoying this game and all it's content, that is sadly lacking from the EA released installment. But enough about that mess. We're here to talk about this gem and all it's glory.
Available to you are  a couple of  game modes like Galactic Conquest (my personal favorite) where you are able to build/control fleets that you can navigate on a galactic map against the AI. There are startegic elements present in this game mode like building a fleet over an occupied space to keep the enemy from taking it over without a fight. Usually resulting in a fun space battle. Building said fleets costs money however, which is  usually earned after each turn if you have control of a planet(s) and I believe by succesfully winning a skirmish. Also available to purchase are bonuses that can help you in your campaign - like extra troops, regenerating health, auto-turrets that protect your command posts and enhanced weapon damage. These bonuses are however one time use and only one active bonus is available per skirmish. So you'll have to purchase a new bonus before each skirmish.
The other mode is the Rise of the Empire Campaign where you play as the 501st Legion (Vaders Fist). Mainly taking place during the start of the Clone Wars, beginning with the battle of Geonosis, all the way to the battle at Echo Base on planet Hoth. This game mode mainly has you completing objectives to progress the storyline, such as recovering an item from the enemy, Defending a post from being overrun by the enemy or destroying a target. I wasn't too much of a fan of this game mode, not to say this mode isn't fun, but I would rather just play Galactic Conquest instead. And then there is Instant Action, where you can instantly jump into matches that you set up before hand.
But all that pales in comparison to the great multiplayer that once was. If you were lucky enough to have been able to play this game back when the online was alive and kicking, then you got to witness one of the funnest online games to ever grace this earth.Sadly, the online is no more and the only way to play this beauty is to download some software like Hamachi to play with other people. Even then, there isn't much to hope for since you're not likely to find enough people to fill up the lobby, which is necessary for that true experience. It's just not the same otherwise, as bots don't make for fun matches. I would still recommend people to pick this game up, even today, as it is still one of the funnest games out there and it's certainly much better than Battlefront by a large margin. Maybe some day, fans will come together and revive the online. That, or we can hope that we'll get a true sequel that isn't some stripped down mess that only has it's looks going for it. Until then, Battlefront II is still a viable option to scratch that itch for epic battles on land and in space.

I once read a comment that said "Whenever someone mentions Vampire Bloodlines you just know that someone, somewhere, is installing it again.", and I must agree wholeheartedly. I read that a few years ago, mind you, and I have since found other RPGs to add to my "best RPGs of all time" list. But Bloodlines, despite its age, its sort of mediocre gameplay that can confuse you for being based on a set of rules that are not always apparent, despite its dated visual and lack of character customization... Despite all that, the world, characters and tone still keep me coming back.
Pretty much every quest is interesting, the dialogs are well writen, the urban fantasy setting is something I wish I could see more often in gaming (especially in RPGs) and it has what simply must be my favourite haunted house level in gaming. Ever.
So yes, after almost ten years I still recommend Vampire, if nothing else because it will show you a world like which you won't find in any other videogame.
